https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: What readers bought in October: so many plastic-free food storage containers
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Lauren Gould
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
Each week the Filter newsletter cuts through the noise to bring you smart, practical recommendations on how to live better – from what is worth buying to the tools, habits and ideas that actually last.
In October, we reviewed dozens of items, from sardines to slip-on shoes.
The most-purchased items among your fellow Filter readers ranged from practical – and whimsical – kitchen staples to an all-purpose layering piece for fall’s fickle weather.
Here are your five favorite products of the month, according to the anonymized data we have access to.
Anyday Anydeli Containers
Last week, these versatile, plastic-free containers recommended by Emily Farris, a food writer and contributor, were on sale. Many of you took advantage of the 20% discount, making these containers one of your October favorites.
Angry Mama microwave cleaner
This month, Megan Reynolds, a Filter editor, helped many of your microwaves look brand new with this quirky and effective gadget.
As she wrote in our guide to the best products for creating whimsy: “The grease and caked-on food steams off and can be easily wiped away when you’re done! When this old broad isn’t cleaning my microwave, she sits on the stove, waiting for her next round.”
Blueland Detergent Tablets
We’re always on the lookout for household essentials. These plastic-free dishwasher detergent tablets were a favorite, beloved by Jennifer Regan, our interim photo editor.
Viva Cloth Paper Towels
These paper towels were another unsexy but necessary staple you restocked this month. Reynolds said they’re even “strong enough to be reused – as long as the mess you’re cleaning isn’t too gross”.
Pretty Garden Cardigan
One article of clothing edged its way into your monthly favorites – this oversized cardigan. Paige Triola, a Filter contributor and self-proclaimed fashion minimalist, equated it to “wearing a hug”, which is enough of an endorsement for me.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Em busca da substância do fascismo e de seus seus antídotos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Tábata Silveira dos Santos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Meu sobrinho, do alto dos seus 9 anos de idade, fez um cartaz para levar a um ato da campanha de Lula de 2026, em Esteio, RS, que dizia: “Vote para que a escola pública não seja vendida! Vote 13 Lula” Ao lado, em dizeres menores, ele listava 5 ou 6 escolas públicas que ele conhecia, ou que já estudou, que poderiam deixar de existir se Lula não fosse eleito. Eu me emocionei, porque o conheço. Sei que aquelas palavras passaram pelo seu coração sincero de menino sensível. Ele é crítico à escola pública em que estuda, mesmo assim consegue entender que é um direito importante, e que pode ser melhor do que é. No turno integral, as crianças passam o dia inteiro, em regra, fechadas em uma sala, com uma única professora. Ele já compreende como essa dinâmica é inviável.
Por outro lado, essa dinâmica oportuniza pesquisas históricas profundas, como a que recentemente levou a uma feira regional de ciências, sobre história, memória e identidade. É um raciocínio complexo, que muitos adultos que conheço não alcançam. E é um raciocínio, antes de tudo, produzido por ele dentro dessa vivência de criança pobre, de estudante, incentivado, é claro, pela sua mãe, mas autoral, e profundamente honesto. É uma de suas pautas. Já minha sobrinha, do alto dos seus 6 anos, escreveu com a sua letra um cartaz que dizia: “Vote para que eu cresça sem medo e com direitos”. Algo nesse cartaz rompeu em mim um imobilismo e me move a escrever agora.
Noutro cantinho do Brasil, uma cena me afetou de forma inversamente proporcional. Trabalho na cidade de Governador Valadares, talvez uma das mais reacionárias de Minas Gerais, também conhecida como Valadólares, ou o maior pólo de emigração de brasileiros para os EUA, do Brasil. Num ato de entrega formal em favor de pessoas atingidas pelo rompimento criminoso da barragem de Mariana, de projetos mediados pela Fundação Banco do Brasil, que aconteceu numa escola privada dessa cidade, houve um pequeno porém memorável surto protofascista. A entrega ocorreu durante a campanha do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, por acaso.
Era um ato módico, com controle de público, não houve mobilização, mas o contrário. O evento era restrito às pessoas contempladas, e havia segurança reforçada, até porque estavam presentes representantes do alto escalão do governo federal. Entre as pessoas atingidas presentes no evento, que aconteceu no auditório da escola que tem acesso direto pela rua, havia muitas pessoas negras, algumas ligadas a movimentos sociais. Reproduzo abaixo falas literais que coletei em espaços “públicos”:
“a escola cedeu o auditório para uma premiação lá, não sei quem lá que tá vinculado a esse povo da esquerda, entendeu?”(…)
eles cederam o auditório pra essa galera do mst, esquerdista e tudo mais, não vou nem falar mais, por causa de uma assinatura da barragem de Mariana, e aí nossos alunos ficam sem segurança dentro da escola, (…) um bando de desocupado, um perigo. Alunos lá agora nesse momento na escola, eles entram (…), não tem detector de metais. Pode entrar a porcaria dum povo desse armado dentro da escola, com faca, fazer algum aluno refém, sei lá gente, eu penso no pior, eles entraram na escola! (…)
“que vergonha uma escola católica aceitar comunistas realizarem evento na semana eleitoral! (…)
“que vergonha para o colégio permitir este tipo de evento ideológico partidário de esquerda. Os valores dos cristãos são antítese ao que essa gente dissemina… é preciso ter discernimento espiritual” (…) “estão recebendo aí no colégio terroristas do MST?” (transcrições literais de comentários de pessoas adultas, publicados no instagram, e de áudios que circularam na minha rede, pelo whats app)
Nada de muito diferente do que se falou em todo o país, em distintas realidades. Mas registro na busca da substância de uma sensação estranha, talvez fermentada num lugar muito específico; no encontro de aspectos da conjuntura com lapsos da vivência de estudante de escola pública, de universidade pública, mas que circunstancialmente passou por colégio particular na bruta condição de bolsista, e que esteve depois numa universidade privada de elite, na controversa condição de prounista, de passagem.
Por ter primos que estudaram em bons colégios particulares, convivi, quando tinha a idade do meu sobrinho, com crianças de uma elite decadente (o mais correto seria dizer de classe média), que experienciaram a drástica desvalorização do real operada em 1999. Meus primos eram “ricos” mas eram decentes. Tinham, porém, colegas e vizinhos que eram escandalosamente vis. Talvez a ausência dos pais já reverberasse em transtornos de conduta nos filhos, impúberes delinquentes mimados que andavam em motonetas pelo condomínio fechado, sem capacete, sem habilitação ou mesmo idade para tanto.
Assombravam crianças pequenas e idosos claudicantes por puro prazer; zombavam de trabalhadoras domésticas negras e dos trabalhadores da segurança, que os protegiam, acima de tudo. Minha mãe fazia faxina, ou trabalhava como fiambreira na Walmart, em outra cidade, por menos de R$100,00 por mês. Meu pai nos havia abandonado, de modo que essas eram nossas oportunidades de férias, praia, piscina, essas coisas. Éramos crianças pardas mal vestidas, dignas de pena, naquele meio branco, rico e bizarro.
Em 2026, o breve e profundo manifesto de meus sobrinhos, em defesa da escola pública, contra a sua privatização, e pelo direito de crescer sem medo e com direitos, ganha profundidade em mim. Desperta memórias fortes, sobre nosso percurso escolar e familiar, até eles chegarem, com suas existências tão imensas quanto recentes.
Associadas a esse momento eleitoral, a essas cenas relatadas, passou de novo pelo meu coração a sensação fria de me sentir vulnerável ou pisoteável diante daqueles playboys sem limite. O medo visceral que a impunidade produz, e que regia esses recintos privados que frequentei como bolsista, como filha da empregada, onde crianças ricas crescem aprendendo que a lei que vale é a lei do papai. E, principalmente, a sensação que nos fica dessa experiência de sermos as crianças vulneráveis, expostas, humilhadas, numa fase da vida onde temos pouquíssimos recursos de defesa.
Casos cotidianos de violência racista, gordofóbica, misógina, homofóbica que presenciei nos poucos anos que estudei nesses espaços, onde sempre estivemos à margem, nas bordas de um constrangimento por sermos quem éramos, à beira de uma humilhação, sem refúgio. Crescendo junto com uma tensão no peito, que refletia na minha corcunda progressiva. Me recordo de ter uma única professora negra na escola particular, onde, além de bolsista, eu era a adolescente mais escura. Ela lecionava geografia. Eu a amava, porque se parecia com pessoas da minha família na sua estética e nos seus olhares. Nos apresentou Milton Santos na oitava série, e me arrebatou. Porém, para ser sincera, ela é lembrada por meus sentidos também noutro lugar.
Ainda me retorna a repulsa de a ver sendo conivente e sistematicamente humilhada por um colega meu, loiro de olhos azuis, que chegava num carro chique, que usava tênis caros, que abusava de meninas, e que era, por sua vez, protegido pela direção. Ninguém podia com ele. Era ovacionado pela maioria. Essa professora não reagia, ou perderia seu bom emprego. Eu e 5 ou 6 colegas formávamos um pequeno e acuado dissenso. Éramos da Pastoral, tínhamos boas referências. Foi, aliás, nesse ambiente das Pastorais, anos depois, que aprendi a ter dignidade, repertório e coluna ereta para nos defender.
Flávio Bolsonaro foi também esse tipo loiro e prepotente de estudante, como registram relatos recentes de colegas de escola e de faculdade que pipocaram nessas eleições na nossa timeline. Lembraram dele protagonizando situações de humilhação, intimidação, bullying, posturas preconceituosas, privilégios pagos, envolvimento com gangues, episódios de arrogância em função do cargo que o pai ocupava, tudo com a proteção irrestrita dos pais, desde a infância.
Registrei essa breve conexão porque venho sentindo, pensando, intuindo, há alguns dias, que a educação virou o cerne da luta política no Brasil, seja pela disputa de narrativas, pela noção de verdade, de ciência, pelas realidades paralelas que coexistem, pela possibilidade de se constituir fios ou mapas que nos conectem aos fatos, aos dados, aos contextos; seja pelo conteúdo de lógica formal ou simbólica que falta aos bolsonaristas, acríticos sujeitos reprodutores de notícias ou versões sem substrato ou lastro em fatos concretos; seja pela perspectiva dos modelos em disputa, grosso modo: o modelo privado, sinônimo disso que relatei acima – um império de playboys racistas, o contrário da ética, o predomínio da meritocracia e dos privilégios excludentes, da violência respaldada, sem limites; versus o modelo público, ainda frágil, que paga mal às professoras e servidoras, mas que constitui uma revolução se considerado o acesso universal ao ensino básico e crescente no caso do ensino superior, em perspectiva histórica.
Aqui poderíamos render mais. Temos o desafio e as condições de revolucionar a educação em nosso país, e confrontar os seus contrários que Flávio representa, e é agora. Meu sobrinho, ao defender que o ensino seja público, defende mais do que gratuidade, e representa uma dimensão essencial da democracia que Lula, que acumula mais de 40 títulos de doutor honoris causa, ensina ao Brasil: a ideia fundamental de que todo mundo tem (o mesmo) valor, que todo mundo merece respeito, todos e todas têm o direito de estudar e de viver num ambiente seguro e diverso. Minha sobrinha vai além, e afirma o nosso direito conquistado de sermos quem somos, de nos tornarmos quem quisermos ser.
Do lado de fora de qualquer raciocínio lógico, enclausurados, usando viseiras, estão esses pais bolsonaristas, a defender mais do que o ensino privado como componente de um projeto de sociedade meritocrática; estão a defender um tipo de escola que não considere a própria realidade, composta por pessoas atingidas, negras, trabalhadoras rurais, sem-terra, indígenas, quilombolas, que possuem legados, histórias profundas, vidas inteiras de dedicação a esse país que hoje, enfim, se ergue. Esses pais defendem um projeto de escola que tenha o racismo e o ódio aos pobres como fundamento; não a ciência, não o enfrentamento às injustiças. Recordo de uma síntese de Hannah Arendt, filósofa alemã de origem judaica, nesse sentido: “o problema não é acreditar numa mentira; o problema é quando a verdade já não importa”.
É esse o tom da banalidade do mal, da crise da razão ou da ausência de pensamento (Thoughtlessness, para Arendt), que presenciamos em cada defesa de um miliciano confesso, envolvido com amplos e profundos esquemas de corrupção conectados a esquemas de tráfico de pessoas, evasão de divisas e de lavagem de dinheiro, ao cargo de presidente da república. Flávio Bolsonaro representa o mais vil dos playboys, seu ethos é uma reprodução desse comportamento de estudante de escola particular, educado pelo binômio humilhação & suborno, sem limites, malcriado por privilégios injustos, descendente de famílias escravocratas sanguinárias, que gozam ao infligir dor ao diferente, amalgamado às tradições nazi-fascistas da europa. Não à toa homenageiam insistentemente torturadores, rejeitam resultados eleitorais, investem milhões em estratégias escusas como táticas de manipulação e cibercrime com bots ou a própria influência direta e interessada da Meta. Não por acaso normalizam o crime hediondo da pedofilia, prática e discurso corriqueiro entre os seus.
Flávio foi exitoso em sublevar uma massa de playboys e patricinhas ressentidas, e assim tornar hegemônico na direita o modelo não apenas aceito, mas impulsionado por escolas privadas de elite submetidas à lógica da ameaça, do “eu pago, eu mando”; a lógica que meus sobrinhos, que vivem uma infância humilde e mais engajada do que a nossa, já estão combatendo ao defender conscientemente, nessa idade, a escola pública e os direitos de mulheres e de meninas.
Flávio sempre se comportou, ao longo de toda a sua trajetória, como o playboy que é; funcionário fantasma impune, quando eleito deputado roubava seus empregados, e os fazia pagar seus boletos com salário alheio, lembremos de Queirós – tal como os escravocratas tomavam na mão grande a produção de subsistência dos e das escravizadas. Agia no Estado, ocupando cargo público, sendo pago pelo povo, como se ainda estivesse dentro de uma escola particular, onde o papai pudesse ser acionado para assegurar seu privilégio, custe o que custar. Foi esse espírito mimado que o levou a concorrer ao cargo de presidente; esse espírito que o fez chegar hoje, em fuga, aos Estados Unidos e pedir ao amigo criminoso mais poderoso que possui, declarar um golpe a uma nação, apenas para o proteger da prisão.
Playboys, nessa perigosa combinação da falta de limites éticos com concentração de dinheiro e poder, capazes de emplacar uma verdadeira guerra, um derramamento de sangue inocente, para defender a própria pele do julgamento por crimes que efetivamente cometeu, e ainda se divertir assistindo num camarote ao extermínio alheio, não são mais apenas playboys, sejamos justas. São facínoras.
E existem outros tipos na história que se parecem mais a Flávio Bolsonaro do que José Martí, Charles de Gaulle ou Rui Barbosa, a quem ele se compara. Leopoldo Galtieri, que ordenou a ocupação das malvinas para ganhar tempo e permanecer no governo, Leopoldo II da Bélgica, um monarca hereditário que transformou o estado do congo em domínio pessoal, com trabalho escravo e violências extremas, ou o sobrinho de Napoleão que deu um golpe de estado e que ficou conhecido por promover intervenções militares e milhares de mortes para projetar a grandeza de sua família. Ou o Guilherme II da Alemanha, herdeiro da monarquia, que, para preservar a posição e a influência de sua família contribuiu com a crise que precedeu a primeira guerra mundial. Mais recentemente, Uday Hussein, filho do Saddam, que vivia em festas de luxo, extravagâncias e excessos violentos. A história tem, na realidade, inúmeros exemplares de tipos medíocres e fanfarrões, desde Nero e Alcibíades. Mas o que nos interessa é que todos ou foram presos, ou entraram para a história pela porta da vergonha.
É grave e é grandioso o que acontece no Brasil e no mundo nesse momento, e pouco me cabe nesse cenário, além de engrossar fileiras, ao lado de meus sobrinhos, e registrar umas coisas que me tomam. Mas gostaria de dirigir umas palavras para que dirigentes de escolas particulares desse Brasil percebam em que medida não estão contribuindo com a formação de criminosos de elite. Não me refiro a professoras/es, mas a quem tem algum poder diretivo-pedagógico nessas escolas. Fiquem atentas. Seu posicionamento, nessa quadra da história, não é sobre estar à esquerda ou à direita. Se trata de escolher se vão formar pessoas suscetíveis à adesão a milícias, ao crime organizado, capazes de assassinar gente para movimentarem bilhões às custas do povo e seguirem impunes. Crianças que hoje tem como exemplo alguém que comete crimes bárbaros e foge de suas responsabilidades legais. Podem decidir por serem coniventes com esse rumo, ou se vão punir o protofascismo que cresce nas suas salas de aula, e lhes dar alguma oportunidade de aprender sobre democracia e história do país, a partir das leis 10.639/2003 e 11.645/2008, além da própria LDB.
Num parágrafo final, dentre essas obviedades que escrevo apenas para me livrar de pensamentos que apertam minha mente e da lembrança de que, felizmente, graças a Lula e à nossa luta, tenho uma tese de doutorado para terminar, preciso dizer que nós, esses mais de 64 milhões de brasileiras/os que votamos em Lula, compomos, pelo menos, 5 gerações (20 anos) de estudantes universitárias/os pobres, pardos, pretas, de periferias imensas, indígenas, sem-terra, nordestinas, nortistas, quilombolas dos rincões do sul e dos cafundós dos norte, que acessaram e modificaram o ensino superior, produzindo algo que eu ousaria chamar de o que de melhor se produz em educação e em ciência nesse continente, quiçá no mundo.
Cada sujeito das mais de 15 milhões de pessoas que inundaram nossas avenidas, abertas pelos nossos pais peões e avós analfabetas, passaram direta ou indiretamente pelo ensino público de qualidade – e mais do que passar por ele, o transformaram. Estamos fazendo ciência aplicada, amalgamando saberes populares profundos com ciência de ponta. Esse é o legado brasileiro para o acúmulo social de saber do mundo, em 2026. E isso significa mais do que a quantidade histórica que conformamos; se trata de uma massa qualitativa, pensante, criativa, crítica, questionadora, que se relaciona com o seu povo no campo dos saberes e dos afetos, imparável.
Quem defendeu Lula nessas eleições tinha mais do que paixão ou ressentimento, tinha informação, consciência crítica, autonomia de pensamento, amor pelos seus, compromisso com um país democrático, no sentido substantivo da palavra. Essa juventude que sustentou a luta pela democracia, ao lado das mulheres, dos negros e negras, da classe trabalhadora, da comunidade LGBTQIAPN+, é uma juventude que abre caminho para que a geração dos meus sobrinhos chegue dizendo a que veio. Meus sobrinhos e seus colegas estão chegando para sustentar essa transformação. O petismo ou o lulismo não será apenas uma brecha na nossa história de autoritarismos. Já temos raízes e alcançamos um ponto de não retorno. A base, depois de 20 anos de investimento em educação pública de qualidade, agora sim, vem forte.
*Tábata Silveira dos Santos é doutoranda em sociologia e em desenvolvimento rural na Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/tr.title: The Trump era is over. The world should take note
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/tr.author: David Hearst
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/tr.text:
The Trump era is over. The world should take note
It took nine months, but regime change has finally been achieved.
Nine months after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad director David Barnea put the idea into US President Donald Trump’s head that regime change was possible, it has been achieved.
The only variation on the plan that all three men worked on is that regime change has happened in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, Georgia, Florida, and in Congress - not in Tehran.
The war on Iran is the defining mistake of Trump’s second term as president, and of Netanyahu’s final term of office - but Iran is by no means their sole nemesis.
For the president who knew nothing about Iran, it was more than a bet that went sour. The fact that it was all Netanyahu’s idea makes failure even worse for the leader of an “America First” movement. Iran is a quintessentially “foreign war” that proved the principle on which Trump himself campaigned.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Failure in Iran was different for the prime minister who had the Islamic Republic in his sights for most of his adult life.
It was a classic example of military and intelligence overreach. Netanyahu and Mossad thought they could do to a whole country what they thought they had done to two movements: Hamas and Hezbollah. They totally underestimated the power of the Islamic Republic to resist.
But war on Iran, and the economic disaster it unleashed on both sides of the Gulf and beyond - including record prices at gas stations - are not the real cause of the earthquake that has shaken US politics.
Common nemesis
The Democrats had to collapse first to let Trump in for a second term.
They did this by allowing former President Joe Biden to run for a second term, and compounded that error by choosing his vice president, Kamala Harris, to run instead after he dropped out.
Had Harris won that contest in 2024, no Democrat of any stripe would now be talking about ending military aid to Israel.
Biden and Harris had overseen, supported and armed the first and bloodiest days of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, a policy from which they will never recover.
Sayed is the future, and Pelosi is history. That is the measure of political change that Gaza has produced
Gaza was the Democratic Party’s nemesis, just as it was the British Labour Party’s under Keir Starmer.
It is Gaza that has turned the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) from a force no aspiring US politician would dare to confront into a toxin. It is Gaza that has now become the nemesis of the Republican Party, and the Trump clan, too.
A genocide that was being documented in real time, with images of war crimes often filmed by the perpetrators of these outrages, became the defining issue of the era.
These images defied any words invented to cover up what was happening. The images were in total contradiction to the US line that Israel was “defending itself”. They electrified the Democratic base, as they did to the millions of progressives worldwide who took to the streets in protest.
Just consider how one of Tuesday night’s spectacular winners, US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, started his political journey.
Sayed began as the classic Christmas tree, upon which anyone could pin anything. He was decried by Trump and by his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, as a supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood.
Trump said “he is a Muslim Brotherhood guy, 100 percent” - and most of the US media reported that false claim faithfully.
Policy referendum
Just last week, House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi appeared on a podcast, whose host Donny Deutsch claimed Sayed had made “concerning” comments about the existence of a Jewish state: “That’s antisemitic as far as I’m concerned,” he said.
Pelosi replied: “No, it’s more than concerning. It’s wrong. It’s wrong, and it isn’t a reflection of the Democrats in the Congress of the United States.
“This new person in Michigan, we’ll see if he gets elected to the Congress,” she added threateningly.
Aipac spent $30m trying to defeat Sayed in the primaries and another $9m supporting the pro-Israel candidate, Rogers, in the midterms. Representative Haley Stevens, defeated by Sayed in the primaries, switched sides spectacularly days before the election, jumping to the Republican camp.
That alone boosted Sayed’s chances in a tight race, because Stevens was condemned by the very people who had been warned off endorsing Sayed at the start of his campaign.
Well, “this new person” has not only become a reflection of the new Congress. His election in Michigan became the biggest referendum on US policy on Israel that has ever been seen.
Sayed is the future, and Pelosi is history. That is the measure of political change that Gaza has produced.
The Jerusalem Post was correct to conclude that the election in Michigan alone had grave implications for US support for Israel as a whole.
“One of the clearest takeaways from the election campaign is the political price the war with Iran has exacted on the Republican Party,” its analysis said, referring to the war Israel pushed the US into on 28 February.
“The expansion of the camp critical of Israel, and its growing access to positions of influence, represents a shift that Israel cannot afford to ignore,” it added.
Democratic limits
Of course, we are far from a post-Zionist Democratic Party, still less a Congress that will vote to cut military aid to Israel.
For now, the limits of policy that can be expected from the new crew in Congress have been sketched out by Ro Khanna, the US congressman whose van was surrounded by armed settlers during his last visit to the occupied West Bank.
Khanna has pushed for official US recognition of a Palestinian state, opposed unconditional military aid, and advocated a permanent ceasefire and non-violent resistance - but for all that, he backs Zionism and Israel’s “right to exist”.
“I believe that Zionism is self-determination of the Jewish people, and the right for Israel to exist. And I support that. What I don’t believe is if it means Greater Israel,” Khanna said last year, adding that he believes there must be a “two-state solution”.
In other words, neither Khanna nor anyone else in the “new” Democratic Party is going to do anything about ending apartheid, let alone the occupation.
In giving credence to the idea that the two-state solution is still possible, Khanna’s position flies in the face of what happened to him during his visit, as well as the unanimous opinion of all Jewish Israeli parties - both pro- and anti-Netanyahu - in last week’s election, all of whom have doomed a Palestinian state.
But here, we should distinguish between the politicians and the movement that propelled them to power. Who would have thought three years ago that US public opinion would have travelled this far? This is a long conflict, and its solution will be long, too.
The ball is still rolling, and it will not stop.
This global movement supporting Palestinian self-determination will not be assuaged if all that happens is a return to the status quo that reigned on 6 October 2023; if, say, more food and supplies get into Gaza, but the siege itself is maintained, or if settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank calm down, but the settlements themselves remain.
Shaky ground
Across its history, Israel has relied as much on the liberal Zionist support of the centre-left as it has on the neoliberal right. Both those terrains are now shaky ground.
For US Republicans, the lessons of this defeat are even starker. The massive Democratic congressional victory on Tuesday was triggered by soaring living costs, tariffs, and huge instability in US-driven wars.
But behind much of this instability was Trump’s relationship with his two closest allies: Russian President Vladimir Putin and Netanyahu.
However much Trump now tries to claim his name was not on the ballot, the record shows he campaigned in 30 rallies for losers. That is not a good look for a populist
The MAGA faithful who have parted company with Trump, like talk show host Tucker Carlson - and even those who have not declared their hand, like Carlson’s friend, Vice President JD Vance - will feel empowered by this result.
Trump will continue to blag that what the US does at home and abroad is what he, the president, and he alone decides to do. The only voice that matters to him is the one in his head.
He will cast his veto. He will encourage another government shutdown.
But history has shown there are forces that Trump fears. He fears the bond market and the opinion of Wall Street. He fears the battle for succession.
The time is long past when he could claim to be a victim of the Democratic establishment. He is now one of Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s patriarchs whose autumn might have already come.
However much Trump now tries to claim his name was not on the ballot, the record shows he campaigned in 30 rallies for losers. That is not a good look for a populist.
Tighter scrutiny
Beyond Washington, the midterms will clearly be seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term as president, whether or not Trump limps on as a lame duck.
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he expected Washington to continue the war, seeking Tehran’s “unconditional surrender”.
Perhaps, but a resumption of air strikes would be politically even more suicidal after such a result than it was before. Vance called the result a direct consequence of the Iran war.
Trump is a falling object. As such, everyone but his closest coterie will be less than eager to pick up the phone next time it rings.
The Trump clan will now come under ever-tighter financial scrutiny from the new Congress. Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to become chair of the House Oversight Committee, was not joking when he warned Trump to “lawyer up”.
Trump clan members have gorged themselves at the trough of every crisis, every impending tariff. In any other environment, it would be called insider trading. In Trump’s White House, it was business as usual.
All the dealings of his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, will come under ferocious scrutiny.
Of particular interest to the House Oversight Committee will be the Trump family’s lucrative business relationships with foreign investors and government-linked figures, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.
In January 2025, four days before Trump’s inauguration, UAE-backed investors paid $500m for a 49 percent stake in World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded by Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump.
The investment was backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE’s national security adviser and brother of the country’s president.
The Wall Street Journal reported that $187m of the initial payment went to companies linked to the Trump family, while $31m went to companies associated with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s Middle East envoy and a co-founder of the venture.
Clear warning
Following the money, investigators could move seamlessly to all of the Gulf states’ bribes to Trump and his family.
That probe should include the Board of Peace, which should now, by rights, be scrapped and replaced by a UN international structure.
If the Netanyahu camp in Israel is trembling at where the US appears to be headed, Gulf leaders should be in no less than a panic.
Iran’s drones and missiles punctured the bubble of security that gave small but intensely wealthy states the illusion that they were protected from the chaos around them.
The midterm results will have a similar effect. They have surely reinforced the message that the Gulf states have been throwing their money away by investing in Trump.
The internationally powered movement for Palestine that propelled these changes in the US is not going to go away. If anything, it will gather in intensity
True, we do not know what Trump would have done, had they refused to invest in him. Would he have pulled the plug on the vulnerable Turkish economy if President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had not invested so much political capital in Trump? We may never know.
But that time is past.
For their own security, Middle Eastern powers must turn to regional alliances and mutual defence guarantees as their template for the future.
UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman both built their country’s strategies around Trump. That surely is the worst investment decision either could have made.
Everyone kowtowed to Trump. Before the main attack on Iran, the Doha Forum in Qatar last year turned itself into a Trump edition. His sons were the stars of the show, and the halls were filled with American delegates. It showed crudely in which direction Qatar was turning.
Europe was no different. Will it now stand up to Trump and turn itself into a real competitor to US policy, especially over Ukraine?
And finally, the midterms contain a very clear warning to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government.
The internationally powered movement for Palestine that propelled these changes in the US is not going to go away. If anything, it will gather in intensity.
If Burnham is perceived to be delivering empty promises to Palestinians in particular and the Arab world in general, as former US president Barack Obama did in his Cairo speech, Burnham will suffer the same fate as Starmer.
Talking the talk on Israel’s occupation will not be enough. Burnham will have to walk the walk, too.

'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?
The Democrats secured a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday, but one critical question remains unresolved: is US President Donald Trump now more or less likely to resume the war on Iran with the election cycle over?
Before the midterms, the US appeared to be on the verge of launching a new, wide-scale attack against Iran.
The families of US diplomats were evacuated from the region, and additional US military assets flooded into the Middle East. Arab leaders issued cryptic warnings about a devastating new conflict.
But the attack many diplomats and analysts expected around election day never materialised. In fact, Republicans are now blaming the Iran war, and even Israel, for their blistering defeat at the hands of the Democrats.
Trump said on Wednesday that "it's largely true" the Iran war and high fuel prices tied to the conflict led to his party’s historic defeat.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Fleur Hargreaves

Israel detains Palestinian activist without charge
Israeli police have detained Abed Abou Shhadeh, a former city council representative of the Palestinian community in Jaffa, a southern suburb of Tel Aviv, Al Jazeera reported on Wednesday.
Palestinian legal group Adalah told Al Jazeera that Israeli police searched Abou Shhadeh’s house and arrested him overnight but have not yet charged him with anything.
The rights group said he is currently being held in a detention centre and is due to appear in an Israeli court later on Wednesday.
“This is not a criminal investigation – it is a campaign to silence Arab journalists and political activists,” Adalah said.
Wafa also reported on Wednesday that a Palestinian man and a foreign solidarity activist were injured on Wednesday evening after being beaten by Israeli settlers in the village of al-Duyuk, west of Jericho.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society told Wafa its crews treated the wounded and transferred them both to hospital.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/freed.title: 'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/freed.author: Sean Mathews
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/freed.text:
'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?
The Democrats secured a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday, but one critical question remains unresolved: is US President Donald Trump now more or less likely to resume the war on Iran with the election cycle over?
Before the midterms, the US appeared to be on the verge of launching a new, wide-scale attack against Iran.
The families of US diplomats were evacuated from the region, and additional US military assets flooded into the Middle East. Arab leaders issued cryptic warnings about a devastating new conflict.
But the attack many diplomats and analysts expected around election day never materialised. In fact, Republicans are now blaming the Iran war, and even Israel, for their blistering defeat at the hands of the Democrats.
Trump said on Wednesday that "it's largely true" the Iran war and high fuel prices tied to the conflict led to his party’s historic defeat.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vice President JD Vance said more bluntly on Wednesday, also blaming the Trump administration’s ties to Israel for his party’s thrashing.
Notably, the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, posted his support for Vance’s analysis on X. People familiar with the White House have described him as an ardent anti-interventionist who has opposed the US war on Iran.
'We are going to end this war'
A nine percent collapse in oil prices on Wednesday reflects a shift in expectations. Merissa Khurma, founder and CEO of Amena Strategies, told Middle East Eye that an election outcome could see Trump’s inner circle and Congress constrain the president from resuming the war.
“This all depends on how elected members in the House and Senate work together to ensure a change of course with Iran and what Trump is told by his advisors,” Khurma, who is also a non-resident fellow at the Baker Institute at Rice University, told MEE.
Several reasons could dismiss this reasoning when it comes to Trump.
The president has boasted about his “veto power” over Congress.
While Trump told Politico on Tuesday during election coverage that he didn't want to just "sit around there for two years vetoing everything", the 80-year-old billionaire who is prohibited from running for a third term may also feel unconstrained by lawmakers.
Under the Constitution, only Congress has the authority to declare war, but the last US president who sought out congressional approval for the use of military force was George W Bush in 2001 and 2002.
Still, experts say the scale of the Democrats' victory could constrain Trump. With 54 seats in the US Senate and 237 in the House, the party has a comfortable cushion that will give it subpoena and investigative power.
“It is hard to predict what Trump will do, but it matters how Democrats work with Republicans willing to cooperate on stopping further escalation,” Khurma said.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer put the Iran war at the heart of the Democratic Party’s agenda on Wednesday.
“We are going to end the war,” Schumer said.
"We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he added.
Despite this rhetoric and downward move in oil prices, the deployment of military assets in the Middle East suggests escalation is likely.
'Trump is freed up'
The US has two aircraft carrier groups and an amphibious assault ship in the Arabian Sea. A third aircraft carrier group is arriving in the region.
Meanwhile, Iran’s leadership appeared to savour Trump’s political collapse.
“The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz - and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington,” Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said in a post on X.
Even as Trump acknowledged the Iran war played a part in his party’s stunning defeat, he expressed no doubts about launching a war on Iran at the start of the year.
"I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” he said.
Some experts say that a bitter US president with no electoral constraints may decide to resume attacking Iran.
“If anything, Trump is now freed up for another round of strikes,” Alan Eyre, a former senior State Department expert on Iran, now at the Middle East Institute, told MEE.
“The new Congress won’t be seated until January, and even then it is questionable how much real ability they will have to constrain the president, so I don’t think it changes much,” he said.

Egyptian doctor who undertook medical missions to Gaza will now go to US Congress
Egyptian-American surgeon Adam Hamawy has won his bid for Congress in New Jersey’s 12th congressional district, joining the blue wave across the US and making history as the first Muslim and Egyptian American to represent the state.
During his victory speech in the midterm elections on Tuesday, he spoke directly to the people in Gaza, saying: “To the men, women and children of Gaza and Palestine. Your smiles give me the courage and the hope to fight for a better world."
Republicans previously held the majority of the House of Representatives with 218 seats, four more than the Democrats at 215, but come January, Hamawy is one of the congressional wins to give his party a majority. with a whopping projected 250 seats, according to MS Now.
Middle East Eye attended Hamawy's watch party in Princeton, New Jersey, where he declared during his speech that he was ready to get to work and vowed to “hold Donald Trump accountable”.
“I'm a surgeon, and I can tell you that we are going to stop the bleeding. We are going to fight for every American that's been left behind by the establishment that has been ruling Washington for so long.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Christian voters in Washington state divided by common religion: ‘I don’t think the US is God’s kingdom on Earth’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lok Darjee
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A few days before the Fourth of July, Ron Peterson, the 38-year-old pastor of Longview United Pentecostal church, stood beneath a large white tent in a parking lot in Longview, Washington.
Surrounded by church members selling fireworks for a fundraiser, Peterson remembered watching area residents rally after an industrial accident at the local paper mill killed 11 people in May. “We can all come together,” he said. “There’s not going to be sections in heaven.”
At least two-thirds of his church members are Latino, Asian, Black or of multiracial backgrounds, according to Peterson. His congregation reflects a racial diversity that complicates the political image of evangelical Christians, who are largely (but not all) white, overwhelmingly backed Donald Trump in 2024 and tend to support his hardline immigration agenda.
But in this corner of southern Washington, even among churchgoers, there’s also a diversity of opinion about the role of religion in politics.
Peterson grew up poor in an Oregon household he describes as more New Age than Christian and works full time in sales while pastoring. He sees church as a place where people in his community – including families dealing with addiction or other crises – can come for support and succor.
He also holds views that place him squarely in the country’s culture wars. He believes that people like him – white Christian heterosexual men – have become targets.
“People need someone to blame,” he continued. “I think the ire is towards white Christian males. Now, they want to call them white Christian nationalists. But being white and Christian is actually, if you’re truly a Christian, a wonderful thing for society.”
He recounted being called into a meeting with human resources after singing a Christian hymn at work.
“I sang His Eye Is on the Sparrow. And because it said, ‘Jesus is my portion,’ I had to have a meeting with HR. Someone got offended,” he said. The Guardian could not independently verify his account.
He contrasted that experience with what he sees as greater tolerance for sexually explicit music. “So you can sing about sleeping with a bunch of women. [But] I can’t say Jesus?’
Peterson gives Trump high marks even as he criticizes the president’s lack of fiscal discipline. Peterson said, “From the standpoint of righteousness, he’s done more to help the country than any president, maybe ever.” But he argued the president was not a true fiscal conservative and that “from the standpoint of fiscal responsibility, I think he’s probably done worse than almost any president.”
For Peterson, Trump’s shortcomings appear to matter less than his willingness to advance causes important to the pastor’s faith. Asked about Trump’s felony conviction in the New York business-records case, the jury that found him liable for sexually abusing the writer E Jean Carroll, and his infidelity, Peterson brought it back to the supreme court – the justices Trump appointed, whose 2022 Dobbs decision overturned Roe v Wade. “Allowing the supreme court to hear Roe versus Wade again, I think that was very important,” he said, before acknowledging that his judgment ultimately “comes back down to my faith”.
‘Politically religious’
Religion has always been a factor in American life, and evangelicals have made the Christian right into a political powerhouse. Here in Longview, faith has featured in the neck-and-neck contest for Washington’s third congressional district. The Democratic incumbent, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, faces Republican John Braun in one of the nation’s most-watched House races. Both candidates have drawn on religion to connect with voters; Braun has defended expressions of religious and conservative speech on college campuses, and Gluesenkamp Perez, whose father served as an evangelical pastor, attends a Capitol Hill Bible study and has discussed sometimes feeling that her Christianity has embarrassed her Democratic party colleagues.
But a common faith does not mean common political stances. As Daniel HoSang, a Yale University professor who studies race and conservative political movements, put it, “For some, the idea of America as a Christian nation means protecting their freedom to practice their faith in a country they believe was founded on Christian values.”
For others, it means something more far-reaching – and potentially dangerous: a country where Christianity occupies a privileged position in government and public life, at the expense of people of other faiths. “If it’s a Christian country founded by Christians for Christians, that then authorizes discriminatory treatment against members of other religions,” he said.
In the nearby city of Battle Ground, I met 41-year-old dietitian Laura Oltmann at a new Italian pastry shop, where she expressed concern about religion’s growing influence in local politics and the treatment of immigrants under Trump’s administration.
The Ridgefield resident and registered independent grew up in a conservative Christian family where religion was often presented in strict terms of right and wrong. She studies the Bible, listens to morning devotionals on her way to work, and attends a small church near Battle Ground. The congregation, which she estimated has between 100 and 150 members, meets in a school, where worshippers unpack equipment each week before putting it away again. Oltmann said she felt called to mentor others and teach the Bible.
But she’s grown uncomfortable with what she views as the increasingly exclusionary bent of the Republican party and the idea that being Christian meant holding a particular set of political beliefs.
“I don’t really like that we’re conflating being Christian with being politically religious. Those are different things,” she said.
She also openly rejects the idea that the United States has a special claim to Christianity; in the Christian nationalism that Peterson referenced, proponents believe that the country was divinely chosen by God and founded to promote Christian values. “I don’t believe that America is, like, God’s kingdom on Earth,” she said.
That tension is particularly evident in her views on abortion. She does not believe it can be reduced to a simple political choice. She supported Gluesenkamp Perez in 2024 despite the congresswoman’s support for abortion rights.
“That’s definitely been a difficult conflict for me personally,” she said. “But I also feel that there’s just something about the power of choice and for a woman to be able to make that decision with her doctor.” Oltmann, who says it’s time for a female president, questioned the consistency of opposing abortion while resisting government programs that support children and families.
“You’re gonna be anti-abortion, but you’re not gonna support children’s programs, children’s nutrition, children’s schooling, the things that they need to function,” she said. “Are we taking a stand on these children’s lives, but not their growth and development? You know, that has to be both. As someone who follows Christ, how can I tell people that I don’t think they should feed kids, you know?”
Oltmann’s ballot-box decisions sometimes revolve around the compassionate politics she wants. “We need a leader who not only can lead and make decisions and communicate well, but can have empathy and see the problems,” she said. “Like, we don’t need a dictator.”
As a healthcare professional, Oltmann has been troubled by Trump’s immigration crackdown. “At one point, there was a concern that there was gonna be ... ICE coming into the hospital,” she said.
For her, the issue went beyond immigration policy. It was about how people should be treated, regardless of their status.
“I want people to be able to feel safe, to have access to healthcare. And to be able to thrive in their communities. And if you’re living in fear, how can you function?”
Oltmann ultimately voted for Gluesenkamp Perez because the congresswoman strikes her as “pretty middle of the road”, the same place she puts herself.
And “to be honest, the person she was running against [before] came across this very Christian nationalist, and that scares me more than probably anything”, she said.
That was Joe Kent, the Republican who lost to Gluesenkamp Perez twice and later served as director of the National Counterterrorism Center. During the 2022 campaign, CNN and other outlets reported that Kent had ties to white nationalists, including an interview with a Nazi sympathizer. Kent has denied the characterization and has distanced himself from extremists. He could not be reached for comment.
However, according to Oregon Public Broadcasting, Kent appeared on The Battle Ground Project, the Christian localism podcast co-hosted by the area pastor CR Wiley and an executive at the local electronic-equipment company, Maddox Industrial Transformer.
According to Frederick Clarkson, a research analyst who studies Christian nationalist movements for Political Research Associates, Christian localism emphasizes building influence within smaller communities, where religious groups may have greater opportunities to shape local institutions, businesses and government.
“It’s easier to get theocratic control, the fewer [the] people in the territory [that proponents] are trying to control,” he said.
An April investigation by Oregon Public Broadcasting found that Camden Spiller, Maddox Industrial’s co-owner and chief executive, was connected to more than a dozen corporations that purchased over 30 properties in Battle Ground in six years.
Spiller has described his Christian faith as one motivation for investing in the community. In an opinion essay, he cited a passage from the biblical book of Jeremiah: “Seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you.”
Some residents welcomed the investments as a revival of the city’s downtown. But others worry about religious influence on politics or the concentration of so many local businesses in the hands of a few. Spiller and his brother also own the city’s newspaper, among other interests.
Battle Ground’s mayor, Eric Overholser, also works at Spiller’s company. On 1 June this year, Overholser read two proclamations supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and another recognizing the federal designation of antifa as a domestic terror organization. Two weeks later, Overholser signed a proclamation celebrating nuclear and traditional families, defining them as a husband, wife and children.
Spiller is also financing a new chapel for First Presbyterian church of Battle Ground, where he also serves on the board. The church’s pastor, Wiley, has longstanding ties to Doug Wilson, a self-described Christian nationalist who has built a network of churches, schools and other institutions around his religious vision based in Moscow, Idaho. Wilson has advocated banning abortion and incorporating Christian religious principles into American law. Wilson’s publishing house, Canon Press, has published several books by Wiley.
The Guardian contacted Spiller and Wiley with detailed questions about their possible involvement in Christian localism but received no response by publication time.
Clarkson warned that efforts to establish religious authority through local institutions could pose a longer-term threat to democratic governance, although he cautioned against overstating the movement’s influence. “It’s important to understand the severity of their ideas without exaggerating their immediate consequence,” he said.
The greater concern, Clarkson argued, was what could happen if one interpretation of Christianity gains the power to govern people who do not share its beliefs.
“To the extent that it grows in influence and becomes synonymous with Christianity, to whatever degree, that’s a threat to democracy in the United States,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Man arrested as girl, 17, found in Oregon after disappearing from Utah last year
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A 17-year-old girl who disappeared last year from Garden City, Utah, has been found in Oregon, and a 39-year-old man has been taken into custody.
The recovery of the teenager took place last Sunday, following a 500-plus day search involving Oregon law enforcement, the FBI’s Salt Lake City field office and the Rich county sheriff’s office in Utah.
According to the FBI, the man was taken into custody without incident.
In a statement following the girl’s recovery, the FBI director, Kash Patel, said: “Tonight, local police in Oregon brought a minor who had been missing for a year and a half to safety, acting on information provided by our FBI Salt Lake City field office.”
“We are grateful she can return home, and we will continue working with our partners to hold those responsible accountable. To anyone using gore groups to target and exploit children: the FBI and our partners are coming for you. We are using every tool at our disposal to combat nihilistic violent extremism, bring offenders to justice and protect America’s children,” Patel added, referring to online communities that target and extort children and teenagers.
According to the FBI, investigators with the agency and the Rich county sheriff’s office had been working on the case for more than a year, following leads from across the United States and internationally.
Authorities have not released additional details about the circumstances surrounding the teenager’s disappearance or recovery, citing the ongoing investigation.
However, local reports have identified the teenager as Kylie Arellano, who was last seen by her family on 29 May 2025.
Speaking to NBC’s Dateline last December, Arellano’s mother Stephanie Coleman said that on the night her daughter disappeared, the two had been texting.
“She goes: ‘I love you mama. Goodnight.’ I said: ‘I love you too, baby girl,’” Coleman told Dateline, adding that their messages were exchanged at 9.44pm. Arellano’s phone reportedly shut off just eight minutes later, at 9.52pm.
Arellano’s family noticed she was missing the next morning, with Coleman saying: “Her jacket was … left in the driveway. Stuff was packed, her Xbox was gone.”
On Monday, Coleman posted a message on the Help Bring Kylie Arellano Home Facebook page, saying: “My babygirl was found SAFE today!! We did it KOAS ARMY.”
The Guardian has approached Coleman for additional comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Xavier Becerra wins California race for governor with vows to resist Trump’s agenda
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lauren Gambino in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic former health and human services secretary, was elected governor of California, marking the historic ascension of a longtime public servant who has vowed to resist Donald Trump’s agenda for the final two years of his presidency.
Becerra, 68, is the son of Mexican immigrants and will become California’s first Latino governor since 1875, a milestone in a state where more than 40% of residents are Latino and nearly one in two children has an immigrant parent. Becerra was the overwhelming favorite to defeat Steve Hilton, the Republican endorsed by Trump.
California’s next governor will inherit the world’s fourth largest economy and America’s largest state, a Democratic stronghold that has served as a bastion of liberal resistance since Trump was first elected in 2016. The majority of its residents are deeply dissatisfied with the Trump administration, amid immigration raids and policy threats that have targeted the state’s environmental policies and university system.
“As Governor, my mission is straightforward, but not simple: deliver a California we can afford and defend a California we can’t afford to lose,” Becerra told supporters at a victory party in Sacramento, the state’s capital.
The incoming administration will face the daunting task of addressing the many issues that bedeviled the last: high cost of living, a housing shortage, homelessness, rising insurance premiums, wildfire risk and widening wealth inequality in a state that relies on – yet increasingly reviles – its billionaires.
The race to succeed Gavin Newsom, who is term-limited and openly weighing a presidential run, began as one of the most unpredictable gubernatorial contests in recent California history, with no clear frontrunner and many twists. By its closing stretch, however, the contest had mostly settled into a sleepy affair.
Becerra centered his campaign around the idea of restoring the “California Dream”, focusing on affordability issues such as making healthcare universally accessible. He also promised to stand up to the president, repeatedly reminding voters that he had sued the Trump administration 122 times as California attorney general during Trump’s first term.
The British-born Hilton blamed the state’s woes on Democratic governance in Sacramento, which he said resulted in excessive regulation, high taxes and an unaffordable state. He promised a platform of tax cuts, cheaper fuel and smaller government.
The path to November was hardly straightforward for Becerra, a former congressman, attorney general and Biden cabinet secretary. For much of the race, Becerra languished in the low-single digits, struggling to break out of a crowded field, which, under California’s open primary system, rewards the top two vote-winners regardless of party.
His prospects were deemed so dim, he was among the contenders party officials encouraged to exit the race so as to not inadvertently split the vote and allow for a “Republican lockout” in the general election. But when former congressman Eric Swalwell’s campaign collapsed amid sexual assault allegations, Becerra’s fortunes began to change. He edged past the billionaire progressive Tom Steyer and secured the top spot, alongside Hilton, on the November general election ballot.
How to regulate artificial intelligence, a major engine of California’s economy, looms large for the next governor. Silicon Valley’s technology companies and investors have increasingly challenged Sacramento’s regulatory ambitions, particularly around AI safety, labor protections and datacenter construction.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and Auzzy Byrdsell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
- 1. First Black female governor in US Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, won victory over Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in the Georgia governor’s race to become the first Black female governor in the country. Bottoms had faced scrutiny over her rocky single-term tenure as mayor between 2018 and 2022, during which time violent crime surged. But on the gubernatorial campaign trail, she emphasized her ability to fight the Trump administration. Bottoms has also made history as the first Black person and woman to occupy Georgia’s top office.
- 2. First Muslim in the US Senate Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s highly contested Senate race, defeating Republican Mike Rogers to become the chamber’s first Muslim member. His identity frequently came under attack throughout the race from both Rogers and Trump.
- 3. California’s first elected Latino governor Xavier Becerra has made history as the state’s first elected Latino governor. Becerra broke through a crowded Democratic primary after an underwhelming start. He was widely favored to defeat Republican challenger and conservative pundit Steve Hilton, given the state’s Democratic stronghold. The son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra is set to govern over a state where more than 40% of its residents identify as Latino.
- 4. Texas’s first Latina governor Democrat Gina Hinojosa pulled off a stunning upset, unseating the three-term governor Greg Abbott. She will be the state’s first Latina governor and the first Democrat to win the office since 1990. Hinojosa’s campaign gained little traction at first, as Abbott trounced her in campaign funding. She soon became a fierce contender, touting her focus on affordability and opposition to new data centers, the latter of which made Abbott vulnerable to criticism.
- 5. First female Native American governor Deb Haaland, the former US interior secretary, comfortably won New Mexico’s gubernatorial race. Haaland thanked voters in a Tuesday night X post. “You chose a future where New Mexico comes first, where working families have a chance to get ahead, and where every New Mexican has a voice,” she wrote. “Whether you voted for me or not, I will always be your governor, too. Because this campaign was about all of us, and the future we deserve.” Haaland is a member of Laguna Pueblo.
- 6. Florida’s first Black governor Republican Byron Donalds will be Florida’s first Black governor, succeeding Ron DeSantis who has reached his term limit. The three-term congressman, whom Donald Trump endorsed, made affordability central to his campaign, while avoiding mention of the unpopular war with Iran and ensuing spike in oil prices.
- 7. First openly gay man elected to US Senate Chris Pappas, a New Hampshire representative, was elected to the US Senate, making him the first out gay man to serve in the chamber. Pappas tore into Trump, Elon Musk and others who backed his opponent, John Sununu, at a victory party with his spouse, Vann Bentley, standing nearby. “They threw money, attack ads, and outright lies at us every day for months,” Pappas said. “But we beat them anyway, didn’t we?”
- 8. First Native American woman elected to Senate Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, is the first Native American woman to be elected to the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe and a member of the White Earth Nation.
- 9. First Black governors of Wisconsin and Nevada David Crowley won Wisconsin’s governor race, becoming the first Black person to hold the office. Crowley’s victory came against many odds: He dropped out of the race over the summer, only to rejoin at the urging of outgoing Democratic governor Tony Evers, and his Republican opponent, Tom Tiffany, greatly outspent him. Aaron Ford, Democratic candidate, defeated Republican governor Joe Lombardo and will serve as the first Black governor in Nevada. He previously was the state’s first Black Senate majority leader and attorney general.
- 10. First female governors of Ohio, Minnesota and Tennessee Amy Acton, a Democrat, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become Ohio’s first female governor. Amy Klobuchar, democrat, beat out Republican state House speaker Lisa Demuth to become the first woman to be elected as governor in Minnesota. And Marsha Blackburn, a Republican, is the first woman to be elected as governor of Tennessee.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: College Activists Push Back as North Carolina Republicans Seek Another House Seat
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Alice Scott
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
As part of a Trump-led gerrymandering effort, North Carolina GOP leaders redrew the state’s congressional district map in 2025 with the hopes of achieving an 11–3 majority.

Even though 2025 gerrymandering only affected two congressional districts, it has become something of a rallying cry for student activists across the state.

As the president of the College Democrats at Eastern Carolina University (ECU), Thomas Remington is used to hearing from people who aren’t politically engaged. After all, he is often talking to college students—a demographic that traditionally votes at one of the lowest rates of any group in the United States—ahead of an election known to generate less voter turnout than the presidential race.

But recently, Remington has heard something surprising from these self-described apolitical students.

“Students are saying, ‘I’m not all that politically engaged, but I remember when they gerrymandered,’” Remington said. “It’s been really interesting to see how many people know what the word ‘gerrymandering’ means now.”

The gerrymandering that these students are referencing is the redrawing of North Carolina’s congressional district map in 2025. In North Carolina, the redistricting aimed to give Republicans an additional seat in the US House of Representatives, which would secure an 11–3 majority over Democrats. The effort followed a Trump-led push for states to redraw congressional maps that would favor Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections.

The redistricting is one of many attempts that college activists across North Carolina say Republicans have taken to try to increase their majority in the House. But with the midterms just days away, those activists believe the attempts might be backfiring.

North Carolina currently has 14 seats in the House—10 Republicans and four Democrats. The state’s new congressional district map focuses on making District 1, currently represented by Democrat Don Davis, Republican.

To do this, leaders of the state’s GOP-controlled General Assembly moved six reliably Republican counties from District 3 to historically Democratic District 1. They also shifted four counties previously in District 1 to safely Republican District 3.

But Remington said this has made the District 3 race more contentious than Republicans anticipated.

ECU is located in District 3, which is currently represented by Republican Greg Murphy. The last time Murphy was up for reelection, in 2024, he didn’t even face a Democratic challenger.

“Now we’re telling people, with the makeup of the district, if we vote enough, we actually can flip this seat,” Remington said.

Indeed, the Center for Politics recently shifted NC-3 from “Safe Republican” to “Likely Republican,” according to a September 29 report. Early voting tracked by Vote Tracker, a project of the Civitas Center for Public Integrity at the John Locke Foundation, shows a strong performance from blue voters in District 3.

As of Tuesday, October 27, about 47,600 Democrats have early voted, while Republicans have cast around 29,500. In addition, 29,760 unaffiliated voters have cast ballots. This is taking place as voter turnout has surged across North Carolina—up by about 50 percent from the last midterm election cycle.

Remington said he has noticed particularly high turnout among students. “In 2024, we were fighting for every vote we could get to go to the polls. This time, a lot of people that we’re approaching are not only saying, ‘Yeah, I’m going to go vote,’ but, ‘I’ve already done it,’ and they flash us their sticker.”

In Pitt County, where ECU is located, Remington said young people are currently making up almost 8 percent of the electorate, almost double what it was in 2022. Though Democrats are historically more likely to vote early, Remington said he remains hopeful about the District 3 race.

“The Republicans have dropped six figures into District 3 to defend their incumbent,” Remington said. “We’re going to have to talk to as many prospective voters as we can. We truly think that we could be the difference makers in a surprise on election night.”

At Elizabeth City State University, students are watching the other congressional race affected by 2025 gerrymandering unfold. ECSU is located in Elizabeth City, in North Carolina’s First Congressional District.

Malachi Bass, the president of ECSU DEMS, said that 2025 redistricting has changed the way the organization has thought about voter mobilization efforts. He said the organization has been working since the beginning of the school year to register voters and encourage turnout. Bass said that ECSU DEMS is planted at busy locations on campus at least once a week, sharing voting information with students.

District 1 historically houses the state’s majority-Black counties. By shifting six reliably Republican counties out of District 3 and into District 1, the maps have a effect of diluting the political power and voting strength of communities of color. At ECSU, Bass said the gerrymandering has led to an outcry from students.

ECSU also lost its on-campus early voting site, which Bass said many students felt was another attempt to suppress their votes. The polling site had been used by Pasquotank County voters in general elections since 2020. But despite the impact of this loss and the gerrymandering of District 1, Bass said he doesn’t think voter turnout will be depleted.

“I feel like voter turnout will be very high,” Bass said. “A lot of us students are about business now. We really want change, and we really want to make a difference.”

Bass said he has seen a strong response from ECSU DEMS’ voter registration efforts. To promote civic engagement, students organized a march to the polls on October 27.

Bass said he remains confident about Democrats’ ability to maintain control of the district. In fact, Davis recently outpaced his Republican challenger, Laurie Buckhout, in third-quarter campaign finance reports, and the race is widely considered to be a toss-up at this point.

Even though 2025 gerrymandering only affected two congressional districts, it has become something of a rallying cry for student activists across the state. Micah Mangot, president of the UNC-Chapel Hill Young Democrats, said she has been talking to students frequently about last year’s redistricting as part of the organization’s voter education efforts ahead of the midterms.

Mangot said she has used the new voter maps as a way to encourage support for North Carolina State Supreme Court Justice Anita Earls, who is currently seeking reelection.

“People are getting more and more informed about the fact that our maps are incredibly rigged, and the only way to undo that is to elect Democratic justices to the state Supreme Court to undo the gerrymandering that has crippled this state,” Mangot said. “I think that people are able to make that connection in a much more salient way than they were previously when the maps weren’t as unbalanced.”

District 1 and 3 aren’t the only contentious Congressional races in North Carolina. The state’s 11th congressional district, which encompasses much of western North Carolina, is seeing an unexpectedly tight race between Democrat Jamie Ager and Republican Jennifer Balkcom.

Though NC-11 is a traditionally safe Republican seat, the race faced a massive political shake-up in August when incumbent Chuck Edwards abruptly withdrew from his reelection campaign. Edwards dropped out of the race after the House Ethics Committee recommended his censure for “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”

This has opened up an opportunity for Democrats to flip the seat. Seth Digh, president of Western Carolina University’s College Democrats chapter, said student voters scored a major win when election officials decided to approve an early voting location on WCU’s campus. However, Digh noted that the site was not granted without a fight.

It was previously announced that WCU would lose its on-campus early voting site. Instead, students who intended to vote early would have been sent to a location 1.53 miles from the center of campus. Digh said getting to that polling site took 40 minutes and required students to walk on the unprotected side of a four-lane highway.

After bipartisan pressure from WCU student organizations election officials reversed course, eventually agreeing to place a polling location at WCU’s Health and Human Services Building—which Digh notes is still removed from the University’s main campus, but is closer than the off-campus site.

With the on-campus polling site reinstated, Digh said he is seeing high voter turnout among students. Vote Tracker currently shows that over 59,300 Democratic voters have cast their ballots in the District 11 race. Democrats are outpacing Republican voters, who have cast about 43,400 ballots so far. However, unaffiliated voters are turning out the highest, with over 71,000 ballots cast.

“It is very clear that the Western site on campus, even at HHS [Health and Human Services], is doing ridiculous numbers,” Digh said. “While Democratic turnout is slightly lower, it’s still very high, and unaffiliated turnout is really high this year, especially for a midterm.”

Given this, Digh said he is hopeful about Ager’s candidacy, which he thinks appeals to many WCU students.

“We are still feeling the effects of Hurricane Helene, and that has become a huge divisive campaign issue in the NC11 congressional race,” Digh said. “Both Chuck Edwards and Jennifer Balkcom have had enough time to release funding that we know that they have more than enough control over to provide critical aid to the 15 westernmost North Carolina counties. You drive around here for long enough, you can feel that. You can feel that things are not affordable.”

Other campuses have not been so lucky in their polling site appeals. Earlier this year, state and local elections officials denied petitions for a primary and general election early voting site at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University’s campus in Greensboro.

The campus had an early voting site for the presidential election in 2024. But the campus didn’t have one in the last midterm election in 2022, so elections officials declined to open one for the 2026 midterm. The off-campus polling site is about a 40=minute walk from NC A&T.

But Xavier Jones, the political affairs director of NC A&T’s College Democrats chapter, said this decision, which he thinks “was meant to keep us down,” has ended up “just firing us up more.”

Last week, NC A&T’s College Democrats organized a march to the early voting site, which was attended by more than 300 students. Jones said the organization is also arranging a shuttle service that will pick A&T students up at a nearby church and drive them to the polls. The shuttle will make a stop to pick up students at the neighboring UNC-Greensboro campus.

Jones said the issues of gerrymandering and polling sites have been a reminder of students’ power in the midterms. He said he and the College Democrats are going to continue to pursue efforts to encourage voter turnout right up until Election Day.

“It’s just ridiculous the effort that these Republicans have put into stifling young voter turnout,” Jones said. “It’s about us as a voting bloc, as a community, as a demographic, the power we hold, and the power that I think we need to realize we’re coming into.”

Alice Scott is a 2026 Puffin student writing fellow for The Nation. She studies journalism at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and has reported for PBS NewsHour and published in Texas Highways magazine and the Austin American-Statesman.
