https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/lorchestre-d.title: L’orchestre du Nouveau Monde livre un concert géant sur la Place de la République à Paris
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/lorchestre-d.text:
Après plus d’un mois de mouvement lycéen et des manifestations qui ont réuni des centaines de milliers de personnes dans les rues notamment les trois derniers samedis, l’heure est plus que jamais à la convergence des luttes ce jeudi 5 novembre. Augmentation des salaires, défense des services publics, justice fiscale, refus du budget d’austérité à 54 milliards soumis au parlement par Sébastien Lecornu…
Autant de mots d’ordre de l’intersyndicale pour cette journée de grève et de manifestations auxquels s’ajoutent les revendications de la jeunesse pour le droit d’étudier dans de bonnes conditions (remplacement des profs, réhabilitation des locaux, suppression de Parcoursup…).
1 512 appels à la grève et plus de 260 manifestations à travers l’Hexagone étaient recensés par la CGT ce jeudi matin. « Cela va être une belle mobilisation », observe Marylise Léon, secrétaire générale de la CFDT, avançant des remontées du même ordre que ce « qu’on avait sur les retraites ».
« Cette journée de grève a une double utilité : obtenir les hausses de salaire et contrer un budget qui fait payer aux travailleurs, aux précaires et aux retraités la facture des politiques en faveur des ultra-riches et des grandes entreprises », résume Thomas Vacheron, secrétaire confédéral CGT.
Le gouvernement, lui, continue de jouer la carte de la répression avec des manifestations entravées par les préfectures comme à Paris où le parcours, finalement au départ de République, n’a été arrêté qu’à la dernière minute. De son côté, le ministre de l’Intérieur Laurent Nuñez a annoncé mobiliser 70 000 policiers et gendarmes, promettant « une réponse d’une extrême fermeté » aux éventuels « débordements ». Face à la réponse autoritaire du gouvernement qui tente ainsi d’esquiver une réponse sur le fond des revendications, de nombreuses organisations ont dénoncé hier les attaques contre l’État de droit.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Manifestação em Brasília cobra fim da violência contra povos indígenas e demarcação de terras
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Ana Gonçalves
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Indígenas e apoiadores ocuparam a região do Museu Nacional da República, em Brasília, nesta quarta-feira (4), para denunciar a violência contra os povos originários e cobrar a garantia de seus direitos. Com o lema “Pelos povos indígenas! Sangue indígena, nenhuma gota a mais!”, a mobilização reuniu diferentes reivindicações, entre elas a demarcação de terras, a regularização dos territórios e o acesso à educação e à saúde.
A manifestação também chamou atenção para a situação enfrentada por comunidades indígenas em Mato Grosso do Sul, especialmente os povos Guarani e Kaiowá, que denunciam ameaças, ataques e assassinatos em seus territórios.
A violência na região tem sido alvo de denúncias e investigações. Em outubro, a Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) acionou a Polícia Federal para apurar relatos de mais de 30 ataques contra indígenas em Mato Grosso do Sul. No mesmo período, denúncias de ameaças de envenenamento da água utilizada por comunidades Guarani e Kaiowá também foram encaminhadas a órgãos federais.
Segundo levantamento do Conselho Indigenista Missionário (Cimi), o Brasil registrou 258 assassinatos de indígenas em 2025, dos quais 37 ocorreram em Mato Grosso do Sul. Os números integram o relatório anual de violência contra os povos indígenas.
Para Gualoy, indígena do povo Guarani Kaiowá, a presença em Brasília foi uma oportunidade de levar ao conhecimento da população a violência enfrentada pelas comunidades no estado. Ele destacou que os ataques atingem diferentes integrantes dos territórios, incluindo mulheres e crianças.
“Estamos aqui trazendo a questão dos povos indígenas Kaiowá, que vêm sofrendo ataques de violência. […] Os ataques atingem as mulheres indígenas, as crianças, os assassinatos dentro do território. A nossa presença hoje é trazer essa indicação aqui nessa manifestação em Brasília, para que as pessoas possam saber sobre a situação”, afirmou.
Demarcação e direito à educação
Além da denúncia de violência, a regularização fundiária e o acesso à educação estiveram entre as principais pautas apresentadas durante o ato. Morador da Aldeia Eco Rural, no Setor Noroeste, em Brasília, Francisco Filho Guajajara participou da mobilização para reivindicar a regularização do território onde vive e a ampliação das políticas públicas destinadas aos povos indígenas.
“Nós estamos aqui reivindicando porque falta regularização fundiária do nosso território. Nós precisamos do nosso território, nós precisamos da nossa educação. Por isso que estamos aqui”, declarou.
Francisco também chamou atenção para a necessidade de ampliar o acesso dos povos indígenas ao ensino superior. Ele defendeu a presença de uma universidade indígena nos territórios e destacou que estudantes de diferentes regiões do país precisam se deslocar até Brasília em busca de formação.
“Estamos aqui lutando pela nossa causa, pelo nosso direito, pela nossa educação, pela nossa saúde, pelo nosso território”, acrescentou.
A reivindicação ocorre em um momento de implementação da Universidade Federal Indígena (Unind), criada pela Lei nº 15.418/2026, sancionada em maio deste ano. A instituição tem sede prevista em Brasília e a proposta é ampliar o acesso dos povos indígenas à formação superior, com atuação em diferentes regiões do país.
A pressão sobre o Congresso Nacional para garantir os processos de demarcação também apareceu nas falas dos participantes. Estudante de Inteligência Artificial Aplicada à Gestão Pública na Universidade Federal de Goiás (UFG), Gabriel Eduardo, defendeu que a mobilização popular é fundamental para cobrar a atuação dos parlamentares.
“É importante que deputados e senadores entendam que o Brasil é terra indígena e essa terra precisa ser valorizada e as vidas indígenas precisam ser preservadas”, afirmou. Para ele, embora o governo federal tenha demonstrado apoio à pauta indígena, é necessário pressionar o Legislativo para que as demarcações avancem.
Desde 2023, a Funai registra avanços em diferentes etapas dos processos de regularização territorial. Até outubro de 2026, o órgão contabilizou 20 territórios homologados, 21 declarados como de posse indígena e 21 estudos de identificação e delimitação aprovados. Os números, no entanto, representam etapas distintas do procedimento de demarcação e não significam que todos os territórios estejam com a regularização concluída.
Mobilização reúne apoiadores
A manifestação também contou com pessoas não indígenas que participaram em solidariedade aos povos originários. Moradora de Brasília e agente socioeducativa Joice Silva afirmou que decidiu comparecer ao ato por considerar necessária a defesa dos direitos indígenas.
“Estou aqui em defesa dos povos indígenas. […] Estou aqui em favor dos povos indígenas”, declarou.
A jornalista Maria Virgínia Pantuso, integrante do Coletivo Kizomba, destacou que a proteção dos povos originários deve ser entendida como uma responsabilidade coletiva. Para ela, a violência contra essas populações tem raízes históricas e exige mobilização permanente.
“O genocídio indígena não acontece de hoje, é de muito tempo, e é dever de cada cidadão e cidadã participar desses atos e lutar pela demarcação das terras”, afirmou.
Estudante de Farmácia da Universidade de Brasília (UnB), Beatriz Nobre também relacionou a mobilização à defesa da democracia e à necessidade de garantir condições de vida para os povos originários. Ela mencionou denúncias de envenenamento da água de rios que abastecem aldeias e assassinatos motivados por questões políticas.
“Não há uma revolução, não há transformação da sociedade sem passar pelo bem viver de todos os povos. Então é muito importante que a gente esteja nessa luta junto com todos os povos, porque a luta é pela liberdade, pelo bem viver no nosso país e no mundo”, disse.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120367.title: Ostafrika | Somalia: »Nichts ist übrig von meinem früheren Leben«
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120367.author: Bettina Rühl, Mogadischu
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120367.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Ostafrika
Somalia: »Nichts ist übrig von meinem früheren Leben«
Die Somalierin Sharifo Aden Nur ist vor der schweren Dürre und vor Konflikten nach Mogadischu geflohen. Hunderttausende teilen ihr Schicksal.
Sharifo Aden Nur sitzt vor der Wellblechhütte, in der sie Anfang des Jahres Zuflucht fand. Die Unterkunft steht in einem Lager für Binnenvertriebene am Rand der somalischen Hauptstadt Mogadischu. Sharifo Aden rettete sich mit ihren sieben Kindern hierher, weil der Regen in ihrer Heimat im Süden des ostafrikanischen Landes über Monate ausgeblieben war. Die Ernte auf ihrem Feld vertrocknete, ihre Tiere gaben keine Milch mehr – sofern sie überhaupt überlebt hatten.
So wie Sharifo und ihrer Familie geht es vielen. Bereits nach der letzten Schätzung des UN-Flüchtlingshilfswerks von Ende 2023 suchten mehr als 600.000 Menschen Zuflucht in den Camps im Bezirk Kahda am Rande Mogadischus, wo auch Sharifo lebt. Sie kamen, weil der Kampf zwischen der islamistischen Shabaab-Miliz und der somalischen Regierung ihre Dörfer erreichte. Und weil Wetterextreme infolge des Klimawandels ihre Ernten vernichtet und das Leben dort unmöglich gemacht hatten. Nach der historischen Dürreperiode 2020 bis 2023 blieben auch in den darauffolgenden Jahren die Regenzeiten wiederholt aus oder fielen zu schwach aus. Auf die extreme Trockenheit folgten oft plötzliche, heftige Regenfälle, die auf den ausgedörrten Boden zu verheerenden Überschwemmungen führten. In diesem Jahr verschärft das Klimaphänomen El Niño die Situation.
Seit Ende 2023 hat die Zahl der Geflüchteten in den Lagern von Kahda deshalb vermutlich eher zu- als abgenommen. Laut UNHCR leben im ganzen Land 3,3 Millionen Binnenvertriebene und fast eine halbe Million Flüchtlinge und Asylsuchende, vertrieben durch Naturkatastrophen und anhaltende bewaffnete Konflikte. Und das bei einer Einwohnerzahl um die 20 Millionen.
Auch Sharifo Aden Nur floh erst vor dem Krieg, dann vor der Dürre. Während sie ihre beiden Jüngsten auf dem Schoß hat, erzählt sie, warum sie nach Mogadischu kam. Bis zu ihrer ersten Flucht vor rund dreieinhalb Jahren lebte sie mit ihrer Familie in Buulo Marer, einer fruchtbaren Gegend in der Region Lower Shebelle im Süden Somalias. »Aber dann flogen Mörsergranaten in unser Dorf«, sagt sie. Die Stabilisierungstruppe der Afrikanischen Union habe gegen islamistische Milizionäre gekämpft. »Meine Tante sagte schließlich, dass wir alle fliehen sollten, wir hätten gegen die Bewaffneten keine Chance.« Weil Sharifos Ehemann ihre Felder nicht unbewacht lassen wollte, machte sie sich mit den Kindern und der Tante alleine auf den Weg, zu Fuß 130 Kilometer bis Mogadischu. »Das war sehr anstrengend, und ich hatte große Angst.«
In der Hauptstadt fand sie immerhin Unterschlupf in einem Lager, und manchmal für einen Tag oder zwei einen Job in der Stadt, der etwas Geld für Lebensmittel einbrachte. Nach einem Jahr wollte sie zurück in ihre Heimat, hoffend, dass die Lage dort wieder sicher genug sei. »Ich wollte meine Felder wieder bestellen.« Doch die guten Zeiten, an die sich die Bäuerin noch erinnerte, waren vorbei: »Der Fluss war ausgetrocknet, auf den Feldern ist kaum noch etwas gewachsen.« Früher hätten sie zwei Hektar bestellt, jetzt habe das Wasser nur noch für einen gereicht. Sharifo baute Sesam an. »Wir wollten wenigstens überleben, aber auch dafür hat es nicht mehr gereicht.« Dann seien die Shabaab-Milizionäre zurückgekommen. »Danach ist alles auseinandergegangen«, erinnert sich Sharifo: Wer irgend konnte, ergriff wieder die Flucht. Vor der Trockenheit und vor den Waffen.
Einmal seien sie fast drei Stunden lang gegangen, um Wasser zu holen. Eine der Frauen in ihrer Gruppe war schwanger. »Unterwegs hat sie ihr Kind bekommen. Es gab keinen Arzt. Wir haben sie unter einen Baum gebracht, ihr geholfen und die Kinder ferngehalten.«
Mit einem Stück Stoff machten sie anschließend das Baby sauber. »Danach hatten wir nichts für die Mutter. Kein Essen, nicht einmal Wasser. Wir haben nur eine wilde Pflanze gefunden.« Damit konnten sie, im rohen Zustand, wenig anfangen, und ohne Wasser konnten sie die Pflanze nicht kochen. Aber sie hatten eine Idee: »Wir haben die Pflanze so lange gekaut, bis sie weich war und die Frau sie schlucken konnte. Den Brei haben wir ihr gegeben.«
Wenn sie im Lager der Binnenflüchtlinge in Mogadischu von ihren Verlusten erzählt, geht es nicht nur um die verlorenen Felder, um eine geplünderte Ernte und um das verendete Vieh. Es geht auch um den Verlust von fast allem, was ihr im Leben Freude macht. »Früher waren die Menschen ehrlich zueinander«, sagt Sharifo. »Sie haben einander geholfen. Mit der Dürre, den Kämpfen und der Gewalt hat sich alles verändert.« Das sei auch im Flüchtlingscamp Kahda so, in dem sie nun lebt: »Hier helfen sie jetzt eher den Menschen aus dem eigenen Clan. Andere werden verachtet.« Zwar habe es bereits früher Konflikte und Konkurrenzkämpfe zwischen den Clans gegeben, nun aber seien sie viel gnadenloser, der Ausschluss von anderen härter.
Sharifo spricht weiter, obwohl ihr die Trauer das Sprechen schwer macht. »Früher war ich glücklich.« Sie sei zu Hochzeiten oder anderen Festen gegangen, auch nach der Ernte wurde gefeiert, und für diese Gelegenheiten zog sich Sharifo besonders schön an. »Wir waren eine Gemeinschaft. Manchmal haben wir die ganze Nacht lang gefeiert, wir haben gesungen und getanzt.« Die Tiere fanden damals noch genug zu fressen und gaben Milch, aus Teilen davon machte Sharifo Butter. »All das ist weg«, sagt sie abschließend. »Es ist nichts mehr übrig von meinem früheren Leben. Übrig geblieben ist nur die Frage nach dem Essen. Wenn ich aufstehe, wenn ich einschlafe – immer frage ich mich, wo ich zu essen herbekomme, für mich und meine Kinder. Essen, Essen, Essen. So hat sich mein Leben verändert. Das tut weh.«
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-trump-adm.title: Opinion: Trump Administration Policies Put Immigrant Survivors of Domestic Violence at Risk
https://citylimits.org/opinion-trump-adm.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-trump-adm.text:
Share This Article
“Immigrant survivors face intertwined vulnerability—either the gender and sexual violence they escaped in their home countries or the intimate partner violence happening at home in the United States.”
From day one of Trump’s second term, the federal government began dismantling key protections that immigrant survivors have counted on to seek domestic violence support, immigration relief, and other services without fear the government would victimize them further with arrest or deportation.
This week with both National Immigrants Day and Domestic Violence Awareness Month, immigrant survivors and their advocates want to put into stark relief that escaping violence or coercion at the hands of intimate partners or family is far from the only hurdle to reaching security. Under Trump 2.0, the U.S. government is now the ultimate abuser.
As two directors from a leading civil legal services provider, we have collectively served thousands of clients who faced both domestic violence and the immigration system. Immigrant survivors face intertwined vulnerability—either the gender and sexual violence they escaped in their home countries or the intimate partner violence happening at home in the United States.
Under previous administrations, the United States afforded certain protections for noncitizens experiencing domestic violence within the U.S. and provided a safe haven for those fleeing domestic and gender-based violence abroad. While the system was far from perfect, the current administration’s combination of rollbacks of critical protections and ramped up immigration enforcement is a crisis for immigrant survivors.
On inauguration day, Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rescinded guidelines preventing immigration enforcement arrests at “sensitive locations,” including domestic violence shelters, hospitals, and courthouses. Survivors questioned if it was safe to seek orders of protection, medical care, or shelter services.
In New York City where we serve clients, masked agents began physically restraining women, roughly handling pregnant women, and warehousing people in inadequate conditions in immigration courthouses. These incidents are horrifying, considering ICE recruited dozens of new agents with histories of domestic violence and other crimes during its recent hiring expansion.
Our attorneys who show up at immigration courts daily witnessed the chilling effect these arrests caused as immigrants must weigh the impossible: continuing their immigration case versus deportation back to an unsafe place. In a survey last year, 70 percent of attorneys and advocates for immigrant survivors reported that their clients were concerned about going to court for matters related to domestic violence protections. The Alliance for Immigrant Survivors found 50 percent of immigrant survivors abandon legal action because they fear ICE detaining them in court.
Within roughly the first week of Trump taking office, DHS stripped key protections granted to immigrant survivors of domestic violence, human trafficking and other crimes under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), which prevented immigration authorities from arresting, detaining, and deporting crime victims for decades.
Among the changes are more stringent requirements for survivors to provide documentation of abuse—evidence many survivors don’t have. Access to special visas granted to crime victims under VAWA, so that prosecutors can more easily pursue domestic violence or trafficking cases, are already restricted, putting thousands of immigrant survivors at risk. And if followed, Project 2025’s blueprint for the Trump agenda calls to eliminate these special visas completely.
ICE partnerships with local law enforcement further endanger immigrant survivors because calling 911 for domestic violence has led to more immigrant victims being detained. With law enforcement now deputized as immigration enforcement and incentivized to aid federal agents in deportations and arrests, ICE handed abusers a potent tool of coercion and control: the threat of deportation.
Many immigrant survivors face obstacles in safely separating from their abuser because they are forced to rely on their partner legally and financially, especially if their partner is their U.S. citizen sponsor supporting their application for a green card or legal permanent residence. Their ability to have work authorization and work lawfully is also tied to these proceedings. Making the problem worse, the Supreme Court effectively ended Temporary Protected Status and DHS proposed a policy change, both drastically limiting immigrants’ access to employment authorization.
Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” also unleashed a torrent of attacks on access to public benefits, including revoking SNAP, Medicaid, and Children’s Health Insurance Program eligibility for survivors of domestic violence and human trafficking. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that 90,000 people will lose SNAP food assistance benefits. Most advocates agree: “most domestic violence victims rely on SNAP to help address their basic needs and to establish safety and stability.” Trump’s proposed 2027 budget promises even more cuts, including $14 million for transitional housing and $15 million for legal assistance programs.
The Trump administration is further threatening immigrant survivors’ independence with an unlawful new “public charge” rule that will deny lawful permanent resident status if they or their children receive public benefits. Confusion surrounding which benefits might qualify—now or in the future—discourages immigrant survivors from seeking benefits they might otherwise use on their path to personal stability.
Even more cruelly, Trump’s Department of Justice ended exceptions for federal assistance previously designated as necessary for the “protection of life or safety,” which included federally-funded community-based organizations providing domestic violence and homeless services. Without these supports for basic necessities and financial independence, safety and security is dwindling under Trump 2.0.
Amid this backdrop of aggressive immigration enforcement and benefits restrictions, the demand for immigration and domestic violence legal and support services are higher than ever. In addition to calling on national elected leaders to rein in immigration enforcement and restore federal funding for public benefits, we must boost funds for the nonprofits stepping up to help fill the gaps.
Because every day, advocates like us will show up, fight against those who wield their power unjustly, and empower people to chart their own path toward safety, stability and independence.
Alet Haywood is director of New York Legal Assistance Group (NYLAG)‘s Domestic Violence Law Unit and co-director of the Domestic Violence Litigation Clinic at St. John’s University School of Law. Melissa Chua is director of NYLAG’s Immigrant Protection Unit, adjunct professor for the Deportation Defense Clinic at Brooklyn Law School, and transition advisor for New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Committee on Immigrant Justice.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/texa.title: Warnings About ICE at the Polls Risk Their Own Kind of Voter Suppression
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/texa.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/texa.text:
Anxiety over ICE at the polls is a double-edged sword for the Trump administration: There’s the fear that federal immigration agents will illegally descend on voters, and there’s the threat that by boosting awareness of that fear, activists and journalists will help the federal government carry out the work of voter intimidation.
“Even just rumors of [ICE at the polls] are going to spread fear. That’s not what we want,” said Daniela Padilla, deputy director at Texas for All, a statewide coalition of organizations working on democracy and justice issues. “Even your reporting around, ‘We’re watching for ICE at the polls’ — it could scare voters.”
In Texas, a 40 percent Latino state where a longtime Republican grip on power now finds itself in question, there are real concerns that Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents could pop up in targeted communities to make people afraid to go out and vote on Tuesday. But while the possibility of election interference has been discussed as one of several “big ticket items” of this year’s midterms, Padilla said, “the biggest threat that we face in Texas this year is voter suppression.”
That suppression can take many forms. In Tarrant County, for example, where local officials closed 92 polling locations, reports from early voting indicated some election officials wrongly turned away eligible voters. More than fearing ICE would actually approach the polls, Padilla and several organizers working on election integrity and voting rights in Texas told The Intercept they were worried that journalists amplifying the Trump administration’s stated plans to “surround the polls” with ICE and federal agents could function as an inadvertent form of voter suppression.
Federal and state law prohibits federal immigration agents from being inside polling sites and bar any form of voter intimidation. Those laws haven’t stopped the Trump administration and its allies from threatening to deploy ICE and military personnel around the country during elections. In August, the Department of Justice announced that it planned to send at least 1,000 federal monitors to oversee midterm voting, prompting multiple states to assert they would not let them inside polling locations. As states like Maine prepared to respond to the federal presence at the polls, the DOJ claimed to Newsweek it “never said” it would send federal law enforcement to the polls.
“The Trump administration has been spreading fear for months, refusing to say that they will not send ICE to the polls,” said Emily French, policy director at Common Cause Texas. “I think that the main function of this discussion around ICE at the polls from the Trump administration is scaring people into staying home on Election Day.”
According to Brianna Brown, executive director of the Texas Organizing Project, disinformation efforts are a common voter-suppression tactic in Texas. “So we’re trying to reassure people it’s safe to vote,” she said.
Texas is home to one of the most dramatic potential Senate upsets in the country, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico leading in the polls over the state’s scandal-plagued Republican attorney general Ken Paxton in a race that could see Texas end up with a Democratic senator for the first time since the ’90s. And the 32 million-person state has enough voter suppression strategies even without ICE in the picture, Brown said, pointing to a 2021 bill that banned drive-through voting, weakened protections for disabled voters, and gave more power to poll watchers appointed on behalf of a candidate or political party.
“Texas is just like a perfect storm,” Brown said.
When ICE showed up at a polling site in San Antonio in May — marking the first known case of ICE at the polls in the country during this year’s primaries — the county sheriff kicked the agents out. Even then, it did not appear that the federal agents were targeting someone in the process of voting; they had arrived at the scene shortly after state police, with whom they work closely, pulled someone over in the polling site’s parking lot.
That day, staff at the Texas Organizing Project and a group of civil and voting rights organizations working as part of the Texas Election Protection coalition helped coordinate outreach to the local sheriff to get ICE removed from the site.
The state coalition is part of a nationwide effort to protect this year’s elections from interference — federal or otherwise. In Texas, the Lawyers’ Committee and several other groups including the Barbara Jordan Leadership Institute, Common Cause Texas, and the Texas Civil Rights Project have been training people to help make sure voters know their rights on Election Day and that they report any instances of voter intimidation — whether an eligible voter is wrongly turned away or someone spots ICE — to a national hotline.
“We want to inform people, but we don’t want to scare them from coming to the polls,” said Khanay Turner-Osborne, executive director of the Barber Jordan Leadership Institute. She said she hasn’t heard much concern about ICE showing up around polling sites in Tarrant County, where she’s based and where people can vote at any polling site in the county. But still, for voters in hotspots of ICE activity and other forms of voter suppression, the group has told them to consider voting at a different eligible site, she said.
The group wants to help people prepare, Turner-Osborne said. “But I don’t want it to be in a way that deters people from voting.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Hybrid events help turn up Art Week Tokyo’s buzz
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: The Art Newspaper
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A sure sign of an event’s arrival in the international art calendar is the number of collateral programmes it attracts. This year is a watershed for Art Week Tokyo in that regard, with multiple partners set to amplify the city’s November buzz.
Leading the way is a new project by the founders of the alternative art fair Basel Social Club. Tokyo Jazz Club, which takes place from 1 to 8 November in a former capsule hotel in the Jimbocho neighbourhood, will combine contemporary art, performance, music and food to create a hybrid space between an immersive exhibition, a social environment and a reimagined marketplace. According to co-founders Robbie Fitzpatrick and Yael Salomonowitz, the event is inspired by the history of jazz culture in Japan. “Jazz offers us a mode of thinking—a language of improvisation, listening and collective presence,” says Salomonowitz.
Also exploring notions of hybrid space is Project O+O: Gabriel Orozco at Higashi-Yama Tokyo. Orozco is collaborating with designer Shinichiro Ogata to turn a restaurant into an extension of his home from 6 to 29 November. Billed as a “living exhibition where artworks, specially designed objects and culinary experiences converge”, the project is co-presented by Mexico City’s Kurimanzutto and Tokyo-based producer Jam Acuzar.
Meanwhile, Serakai Studio, backer of the new Hong Kong cultural space Gold, is hosting a durational performance and installation by Taiwanese artist Liang-Jung Chen (4-5 November) as part of Certainly Tokyo, its pop-up exhibition at Path Omotesando.
These events reflect the global scope of Tokyo’s creative scene. Not to be outdone, homegrown media art and VJ duo MES is curating a lineup of DJs and performers for AWT x Shibuya Parco Art Night on 4 November.

https://gothamist.com/news/child-dies-in.title: Child dies in raging Upstate New York measles outbreak
https://gothamist.com/news/child-dies-in.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/child-dies-in.text:
A child in Lewis County has died from the measles, marking the first death from the disease in New York state in 30 years, state health officials announced.
State and county health officials did not offer additional details about the child who died. In a joint statement, they called for privacy for the child’s family.
The death comes as the highly contagious disease continues to spread through undervaccinated communities upstate in an outbreak that prompted Gov. Kathy Hochul to declare a state disaster emergency last month.
“I am heartbroken to learn that a child in Lewis County has died after contracting measles,” Hochul said in a statement Monday evening. “As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through.”
The measles is a highly contagious disease that typically brings on symptoms such as a runny nose, watery eyes and a fever before a rash emerges several days later, according to the state health department.
In New York, there have been 178 confirmed cases of the measles this year through Oct. 24, with most cases recorded since August, according to the state Department of Health. All but eight of those who got sick were outside of New York City.
Health officials in Otsego and Seneca counties, which have been affected by the outbreak, told Gothamist the true toll is likely much higher than the official count shows, however.
Outbreaks of the disease are also raging across the country, including in neighboring Pennsylvania. Nearly 5,000 cases of the measles have been confirmed nationwide this year as of Oct. 30, the highest number since 1991, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
New York state health officials said they have offered to assist Lewis County with community outreach and vaccination efforts, “both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak.”
Hochul’s disaster emergency order also allowed more types of health care workers to administer vaccines and conduct measles testing.
But some people in areas affected by the outbreak remain resistant to vaccination, according to healthcare workers and county health officials upstate.
People with ties to Amish communities in New York say they are among those most affected by the outbreak, though state and county health officials have declined to say which groups are bearing the biggest burden.
The outbreak comes as some Amish New Yorkers are seeking to add a religious exemption to the state’s school vaccine mandate.
Nationally, cases of the measles are rising as childhood vaccination against the disease declines, according to the CDC.
Hochul called out the Trump administration following the Lewis County measles death, saying the fatality is a “devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
President Donald Trump and his administration have called in recent months for children to be immunized against fewer diseases. Although the CDC continues to recommend vaccination against the measles, Trump has suggested the measles, mumps and rubella shot should be split up into three separate vaccines.

The Art Newspaper reports that the Italian parliament is weighing a new law that would create a formal process for returning art and cultural artifacts that were stolen by Nazis and Italian authorities under Benito Mussolini during World War II. The proposal was introduced by a member of Brothers of Italy, the party headed by prime minister Georgia Meloni and has been called “an act of civilisation” by representatives of heirs of those whose property was stolen.
If the proposal is enacted, the government would have six months to establish the system, which would consist of a five-person committee that examines the provenance of objects that were confiscated and looted as a result of racial persecution between 1933 and 1945. The committee’s findings would be submitted to the original owners or their heirs. If no living heirs can be located, the decision would be announced to the broader Jewish community in Italy.
“We are not merely talking about property claims, but about restoring human dignity, memory and the fundamental principles of our constitution,” Federico Mollicone, a Meloni ally who introduced the bill in March, told The Art Newspaper.
Italy has been slower than other European countries in instituting restitution legislation that affects Jews. France created such a commission in 1999, and the UK established the Spoliation Advisory Panel in 2000 to evaluate claims to works held by British state institutions. According to The Art Newspaper, experts say this delay is due to a national reluctance to confront the country’s fascist history, a lack of transparency about provenance in museums, and other factors.
Gideon Taylor, the president of World Jewish Restitution Organization, said, “Italy is obviously a central country in the world of art … and yet on this issue of the Holocaust restitution it had barely scratched the surface in addressing it.”

https://hyperallergic.com/doris-salcedo-.title: Doris Salcedo on Colombia's Refusal to Forget
https://hyperallergic.com/doris-salcedo-.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/doris-salcedo-.text:
Doris Salcedo on Colombia's Refusal to Forget
“Works of art last much longer than their governments,” she told Hyperallergic in an interview following the far-right president’s removal of works from the National Museum.
Lee esta entrevista en español.
On October 15, dozens of objects were removed from display at the Museo Nacional in Bogotá under the orders of the country’s far-right president, Abelardo De la Espriella. Among them were artworks and materials related to LGBTQ+ and feminist movements; the country's 2016 peace agreement with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC); and the campaigns of left-wing leaders Carlos Pizarro and Bernardo Jaramillo Ossa, both assassinated in the 1990s, whom De la Espriella has called “terrorists.” The objects were reinstated within two weeks by a court order, but the incident roiled the nation: Hundreds took to the streets in protest and faced police repression.
In the days that followed, I called Doris Salcedo. The last time we spoke was in 2021, when her installation-space “Fragmentos” in Bogotá — an “anti-monument” marking the end of Colombia's bloody guerrilla war, with a floor made of melted-down FARC weapons shaped by women who suffered assault during the conflict — had been usurped by conservative populist president Iván Duque. Now, in a different but hauntingly resonant context of state-sanctioned erasure, I turned to Salcedo to help make sense of this moment.
The Colombian artist has made a practice of memory. Her deeply poetic works, comprising both intimate sculpture and expansive, site-specific public interventions, exist at the intersection of historical trauma, mourning, and tribute. They conjure the victims of political violence and disappearance not by simply remembering or looking back, but by delicately articulating the contours of their absence.
Salcedo and I spoke ahead of her trip to New York, where she is presenting new works at White Cube gallery on November 13. She shared characteristically elegant reflections on Colombia’s pain, its echoes in the present, and the country's legacy of political art: “They know they are going to be portrayed,” she said, in a pointed reminder to those in power, “and that works of art last much longer than their governments.”
Our conversation, published in both English and the original Spanish below, has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Hyperallergic: Hi, Doris. It’s a pleasure to hear you. You know, when I emailed you, I thought: I can’t believe it’s been five years since we last spoke. And now, writing to you again, in this context ... Is everything okay with you, all things considered?
Doris Salcedo: Yes, what a complex moment. Well, let’s see, it’s very difficult to live under an authoritarian government that moves very quickly. That is, in two months it has destroyed what Trump took two years to destroy. Colombian society reacts in unusual ways. And of all the scandals, of all the consensuses this president has broken, for some reason that is hard to understand, this act of censorship at the Museo Nacional is the one that has been most publicized and the one that has provoked the most widespread anger. That is, a series of extremely serious events has occurred, but society has not mobilized and has not raised its voice. In this case, it has.
H: I was thinking of what’s happening in the United States with Trump and the Smithsonian. Generally speaking, people here haven’t mobilized significantly in response to Trump’s crackdown on museums. But in Latin America, it seems people feel very attacked when governments touch art and culture.
DS: Yes, because it’s censorship. I don’t know if it’s because of the history of repression we carry with us, because we’ve already lived through it, because we already know what it’s like. And maybe because young people feel very threatened. But the reaction has been beautiful, moving, strong. Young professors from different universities took their classes to the steps in front of the museum and taught there, in the street, in front of the museum. This happened on October 15, and since that day, every single day we’ve had people in front of the museum. It’s a very beautiful and very moving thing.
H: How fantastic! That space is being activated in an incredible way, the complete opposite of what the government intended.
DS: It’s a bit curious, because the Museo Nacional was a museum that for quite a few years, not only under this administration but under previous ones, particularly the last one, was very badly run. It had poor leadership, with poor programming, and it was a somewhat lackluster museum. And now, this act of censorship brings it into the light. Seeing those square rectangles, those ghostly rectangles with a little dust, where the paintings have been removed ... those absences become an extremely powerful presence. People have reproduced the paintings and the objects taken out of the collection, and those reproductions are displayed at the museum’s door. That is, this act of censorship gave enormous fertility to the cultural world, which reacted in an intelligent and creative way.

"I identified far more with the despairing woman than I did with the cherished Virgin"
By Celia Paul, Hilton Als
It’s odd to be an object of desire. Because along with it comes the ferocious desire to be wanted, even if one can’t be had. Reading Celia Paul’s new book, Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice, is like looking at a ghost of wanting. All ghosts want something as they move from room to room in the imagination, and what they want, generally, is to finish what they feel is unfinished business, to find the love that once was theirs, or never was theirs. There are many ghosts in Celia’s book, and they are animated, for the most part, by her ferocious will, her desire not to be ignored by the people she wants most, even if, or especially if, that desire can’t be reciprocated. But Celia is too intelligent a person to settle for the limits of her own imagination; by the end of the book she knows that wanting what you can’t have is just another way of being by yourself. What’s remarkable is that she doesn’t blame anyone for denying her what she can’t have; she’s interested in exploring it. There’s a painting in the book I love especially, one of Celia’s reimaginings of Giorgione’s La tempesta, a great Renaissance work featuring a woman nursing a child and a soldier standing nearby. In Celia’s 2023 version, featuring just the woman and the child, she is both of the characters in this dramatic field; it’s like looking at the figments of a dream, and who was it who said we are all the characters in our dreams?
IN ANNE CARSON’S GREAT POEM “The Glass Essay” she marks the stages of her grief at the loss of a lover by the appearance of a “Nude,” each time different, until her final healing: “Nude #1” to “Nude #13.” In my own life, the loss of my first lover (and the father of my son), had repercussions for all my future romantic liaisons. In other words, I never fully got over him. People have asked me if he was “the love of my life,” and I have to admit that he must have been, purely on the grounds of his lasting impact. I have never reached “Nude #13.” I loved my husband, Steven, and he loved me, but I craved unrequitedness. I identify with Marcel Proust’s narrator in The Fugitive, volume six of his great novel In Search of Lost Time, who, in grief following the death of his lover Albertine, becomes obsessed with one lover after another, his infatuations almost seamlessly flowing from one to the next. In the section entitled “Sojourn in Venice,” Proust wrote: “I had to consent to a further departure from the principle of the individuality of desire.”
My first lover was unfaithful to me throughout our relationship. I learned early on how to endure and be self-sufficient so that I didn’t get hurt. I never fully allowed Steven into my life and I continued to harbor infatuations. I am ashamed now but not healed. I suppose I must be looking for forgiveness.
Steven and I had bickered with each other on our last day trip to Padua from Venice. We had spent a long time walking up and down the main street looking for a shop that would sell him a needle and thread because a button had come off his jacket. He had been snappy with me, and at first I couldn’t understand why.
We had travelled from our usual apartment in the Cannaregio area. Like the apartment I am in now, it was on the top floor of an old building, but the windows of the main room looked directly onto the canal and the Tre Archi bridge. The apartment was spacious and minimally furnished. It had a peaceful, fresh atmosphere, the light from the water rippling across the surfaces of the ceilings and walls, making the air feel cool and aqueous.
At that time, I was unsettled by my feelings about a man who seemed to be a reincarnation of my first lover but who I knew was gay. I sketched the stakes in the flat water of Sacca di San Girolamo. The two wooden beams, tied together by rope, were rocked by the water. They appeared to be in a rhythmic embrace induced by the movement of the current, suggestive of sex between two men. Everything I saw was imbued with a yearning. I made studies of the two Tintoretto paintings on either side of the altar in the Scuola di San Rocco, Mary Magdalene and Mary of Egypt. In both paintings, Mary appears to be in an erotic dialogue with a tree. I was Mary and my unavailable lover was the tree. He was everywhere for me. One evening, after a day of rain, Steven and I wandered in the Giardino della Misericordia, close to our apartment.
It was November and the grass and paths were strewn with autumn leaves. The air was damp and mild and full of the scent of woodsmoke. It was very still. Time seemed to have stopped. I sat on a bench, with Steven beside me, and sketched the scene—the branches of the trees with a few leaves clinging on, the trunks embedded in leaf detritus. The light was grey. It was a melancholy sight. As I drew, I was sad, and, in my mind, I compared the desolate garden to a graveyard. No passion could flower for me.
When now I remember Steven’s comforting presence beside me, I am deeply sorry. He must have been very hurt. I didn’t talk to him about my feelings for the other man, but he knew. Steven and I simply couldn’t discuss it. A gulf would have opened up between us. But this was the cause of his irritability when we trudged the length of Padua’s main street looking for a needle and thread. I made him aware of how pedantic he was being, and he called me selfish. He was right. How self- absorbing obsessive love is. How narcissistic.
The Scrovegni Chapel in Padua is dedicated to St Mary of Charity and was painted by Giotto and his team of helpers in 1303 to 1305. The events of the lives of the Virgin and Child line the walls and the ceiling, presided over by the figure of God at the height of the triumphal arch to the left of the church as we enter. God is dressed in a long white robe (which reminds me of my father’s missionary robe that he wore in my earliest memories of him in India). Giotto’s God has his right hand raised in benediction. His garment is sunlit and he is surrounded by blue sky populated with angels and saints who seem to be in movement, floating on the breezes of the high mountain air. Its celebratory mood is a contrast to the Last Judgement, which is its opposite in mood and color. The human beings are not freely dispersed around the central figure of God, in this panel, but ranked in strict tiers from the lowest unfortunates to the highest saints. Nothing and no one is allowed to break the ranks. The colors are those of the earth – terracotta and sepia and ochre.
Throughout, the design of the chapel mingles the homely with the divine, life with death, virtue with sin—and they all fit together as a whole. Even the worst atrocity has its rightful place and is necessary to the scheme of things, even adding to the beauty.
I wonder if the truthfulness of Giotto’s paintings in the Scrovegni Chapel is bound up with the method by which they were made. They are frescoes and the painted images are integrated into the walls, arches and ceilings of the chapel as if they are part of the architectural formation of the building itself. Fresco painting involves laying dry powdered pigment onto the wet plaster so that the pigment is absorbed into the plaster and becomes one with it. Somehow, this fact seems to echo the rightness of the way things are naturally formed in the world—like the coloring of rock formations or the markings on an animal’s hide. There’s a humility in the process, too. No gilt-framed showing-off.
I love the domestic scene where baby Mary is being bathed by a maidservant sitting on the floor. The maid-servant has just dipped a flannel into the white basin of water at her feet and is now holding the flannel up to wash Mary’s face. Mary is sitting on her lap, clearly loving being the focus of such tender attention.
Mary appears to be equally doted upon as an adult—this time by her husband, Joseph—in the scene of Jesus’s birth. A red cloth has been spread on a rocky shelf within a mountainous landscape. The cloth seems to melt into the cold grey stone of the rocks around the figures. Mary is lying on the cloth and turning to cradle Jesus, who is lying next to her. She is wearing a long blue dress and her elegant limbs are stretched out so that she takes up the whole of the sleeping space. There is no room for Joseph, who is sitting on the floor leaning his back against the bed, watching the sheep and being ironically observed by a donkey. I think of the wonderful tale by Isaac Bashevis Singer entitled “Gimpel the Fool” in which Bashevis Singer tells the story of a cuckolded man who knows he has been duped and is now carelessly treated by his wife, but nevertheless goes on being devoted to her and her child. Gimpel loves “each tiny pore” on the skin of the child who he knows is not his own. His unselfishness prevents him from being made to look a fool, and instead he is dignified by it, sanctified by it.
The figure of “Infidelity” stands in contrast to the tolerance and acceptance shown by Joseph in Giotto’s depiction of the nativity scene. It is a mysterious monochrome ghost, whose gender is unclear, wearing flowing robes and a heavy helmet pulled down low over the brow and standing in a dark doorway; the grey lips are sensual and the eyes, in the shadow of the helmet, are pale and smoky. The figure’s outstretched hand holds up a tiny fairy-like woman at eye level. The two characters are joined by a thin rope tied around the neck of the helmeted one, the end of which is in the clasped hand of the fairy, who is in profile, looking towards her enormous companion. She appears to be its creation, born out of infatuation. The panel is like a scene sculpted in marble commemorating obsessive and illicit love; in such instances, the loss of the object of desire feels like an amputation, because the unobtainable lover is an extension and part of oneself. The figure of one’s dreams and longings has no basis in reality: The loved one does not, and cannot, have a free and separate existence.
The image that had the most powerful effect on me, and which I can’t get out of my mind, is the one entitled “Despair”: A woman has just committed suicide by hanging herself. The rope round her neck is attached to the window frame behind her, and the weight of her body is apparent by the tightness of the rope. Her arms are lowered and her hands clenched. Her head has dropped at an awkward angle onto her chest and reminds me exactly of my husband’s last moment, when his head dropped onto his chest and I knew that everything was over.
The memory of Steven’s lifeless face, and the finality of his passing, finding its echo in Giotto’s hanged woman, reawakened my grief, and my guilt. I identified far more with the despairing woman than I did with the cherished Virgin.
Celia Paul (b. 1959, Trivandrum, India) lives and works in London. Her memoir Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice publishes on November 12 with New York Review Books.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Can Iran’s new supreme leader make peace from behind the scenes?
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Can Iran’s new supreme leader make peace from behind the scenes?
Mojtaba Khamenei’s consultations suggest a new system of decision-making is taking shape, but can it deliver a compromise like the 2015 nuclear deal?
Iran’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, is exercising power without appearing in public or allowing his voice to be heard. Since succeeding his father in March, he has governed through written statements and decrees, while reports of his meetings with senior officials offer a glimpse into how he exercises power.
The meetings announced in May and August appeared intended primarily to reassure Iranians that their new leader was alive and exercising authority. But a series of four meetings announced within 11 days in October, involving the heads of Iran’s parliament, judiciary and national security establishment, as well as senior military commanders, suggests something more: a new system of decision-making taking shape.
The meetings come as Tehran weighs its options between negotiations and renewed confrontation with the United States and Israel. They also invite comparisons with the consultations that preceded the 2015 nuclear agreement. The question is whether Iran’s new leadership is preparing for a similarly consequential decision, and whether this system is capable of making one.
The new Khameneism
For nearly 37 years, Ali Khamenei’s rule rested on his direct personal presence: speeches setting red lines, public meetings with commanders, political elites and ordinary Iranians. His son came to power in different circumstances. Injured in the February 28 strike that killed his father, he was advised, according to sources close to him quoted by Reuters, not to appear or release audio recordings for fear of being tracked.
His rule has taken shape through decrees rebuilding institutions, decisions channelled through a narrow circle of trusted officials, and the testimony of others in place of personal appearances.
The October meetings followed appointments to replace military and security commanders killed in the war. In August, Khamenei appointed his military adviser, Mohsen Rezaei, as his representative on the Supreme National Security Council; Rezaei later became its secretary. Six military appointments followed, including Ali Abdollahi as chief of the Armed Forces General Staff, Ahmad Vahidi as commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Ali Azmaei as IRGC Navy commander. Abdollahi was also instructed to complete the merger of the General Staff with Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters.
The sequence of Khamenei’s reported meetings is revealing. Those announced in May with President Masoud Pezeshkian and Abdollahi, then head of Khatam al-Anbiya, and another with Pezeshkian announced in August, served chiefly to reassure Iranians that the new leader was alive and exercising his duties. October’s meetings appear to have constituted a systematic round of consultations reaching from constitutional institutions to the armed forces.
At his first reported meeting with the military leadership he had reconstituted, announced on October 31, Abdollahi, army commander Amir Hatami and Vahidi reportedly briefed Khamenei on military readiness in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman.
Iran thus appears to be moving from reconstruction to operation: activating a decision-making system rather than merely establishing the leader’s presence.
These consultations unfolded alongside intensive mediation, with each stage of internal consultation following an external diplomatic development.
On October 20, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, carried a Qatari-Pakistani compromise proposal to Tehran. According to Arab media reports, it envisaged unannounced inspections of nuclear facilities in exchange for Iran receiving the interest on its frozen funds in Qatar. Khamenei’s meeting with Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, was announced the following day.
On October 26, Munir returned with Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. Their discussions produced an understanding that regional security was the responsibility of the region’s own states. Rezaei also announced that Tehran had sent Washington a proposal concerning the Strait of Hormuz with a seven-day deadline. Khamenei’s meeting with Rezaei, who had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance, was announced the next day.
On October 30, Qatari mediators held 12 hours of talks in Tehran, coordinated with the White House, after US envoy Tom Barrack suggested an initial understanding was close. Khamenei’s meeting with military commanders was announced the following day.
This timing suggests that internal consultation has become the other side of external mediation.
The statements from these meetings carry two parallel, not contradictory, messages. In the meeting with Rezaei, Khamenei insisted on Iran’s conditions for ending the war, escaping the debilitating state of “neither war nor peace” and managing the Strait of Hormuz. In his instructions to the commanders, he demanded immediate retaliation against any threat without geographical limits, an expanded list of US and Israeli targets, and emphasised that Iran would decide when any renewed confrontation ended.
Repeated appeals for unity suggest an awareness of competing views within the political elite over war and negotiations.
Yet the meetings appear to have defined the upper and lower limits of Iran’s choices, rather than settled on a particular course: at one end, rejecting an intolerable continuation of “neither war nor peace”; at the other, preparing to widen the war if attacks resume. Between these limits lie a settlement on Iranian terms, pursued through Ghalibaf, Rezaei and the mediators, or continued mutual pressure while strengthening the domestic front.
The gap remains wide. Washington wants nuclear concessions before negotiations resume; Tehran first wants the naval blockade lifted, frozen assets released and oil exports restored.
Significantly, Khamenei spoke of conditions “set by the country’s officials”, not by himself. The wording distributes responsibility among institutions and preserves room for him to embrace or disown an eventual outcome.
The comparison with 2015
There are echoes here of the lengthy consultations before the nuclear agreement of July 14, 2015.
A secret channel in Muscat opened with Ali Khamenei’s approval. On September 17, 2013, he spoke to IRGC commanders of “heroic flexibility”, reassuring the military before negotiations. In June 2015, he set out his red lines, and in October he issued a letter of conditional approval. Responsibility for the nuclear file passed from the Supreme National Security Council to the Foreign Ministry under Mohammad Javad Zarif, a sign that the political decision had been made.
The resemblance is clear: a supreme leader establishes red lines, delegates negotiations to trusted figures and brings the military into the process before a major shift.
The differences are deeper. The earlier process lasted around two years under sanctions, not war. Today’s consultations were compressed into 11 days amid armed confrontation, a naval blockade and the approaching November 3 US midterm elections.
Ali Khamenei spoke in his own voice; his son speaks through written statements. Diplomats led the earlier negotiations; now two figures with IRGC backgrounds, Ghalibaf and Rezaei, play central roles. Where the earlier backchannel ran through Oman, today mediation involves Qatar and the countries of the Mecca Agreement, signed on August 7.
Above all, “heroic flexibility” was presented to commanders as preparation for an agreement. Today, conditions for a settlement sit alongside an expanded list of military targets.
The deficit of trust has also deepened. If the legacy of 1979 shaped Washington’s view of Tehran, and the US withdrawal from the nuclear agreement in 2018 shaped Tehran’s view of Washington, the wars of June 2025 and February 2026 have added a layer of mistrust that no technical agreement can easily overcome.
The consultations thus resemble those of 2013 in form but not function. Then, they prepared the ground for negotiations; now, they prepare for a choice between negotiation and escalation.
The seven reported meetings suggest that the new Khameneism may be more than an attempt to fill a leadership vacuum. Its decision-making machinery appears to be in place and functioning, even though the supreme leader’s presence can be established only through others.
Yet every announcement intended to dispel doubts produces more of them, without photographs or details of exactly when and where the meetings took place. The legitimacy of decisions remains partly dependent on the legitimacy of the leader’s presence.
Can this system, with its new commanders and parallel messages of compromise and deterrence, make a decision as consequential as the one taken in 2015, when war has raised the political cost of flexibility beyond what a leader who has yet to appear publicly may be able to bear?
The father saw and was seen; the son makes his presence felt through endorsements and influence from behind protective barriers.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ra.title: Rare Albrecht Altdorfer Renaissance Painting Heads to Sotheby’s, French Police Recover Six Stolen Picasso Engravings, and More: Morning Links for November 5, 2026
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ra.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ra.text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.
Good Morning!
- The Themed Entertainment Association reports that museums in China are the world’s most visited in 2025, while American federal museums have experienced a drop in attendance.
- French police have recovered six stolen engravings by Pablo Picasso and arrested seven suspects involved in the theft.
- Filmmaker Barry Avrich responds regarding his upcoming unauthorized documentary film, “Shadow Man: Inside The Secret World of Larry Gagosian.”
The Headlines
RENAISSANCE RARITY. A Renaissance painting by German artist Albrecht Altdorfer, thought to be one of the earliest Western landscape paintings of its kind, is heading to Sotheby’s for the December 9th London auction after spending about 70 years tucked away in a private Swiss collection, The Guardian reports. The exceptionally rare painting, lengthily titled, A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky, was made around 1520 and is estimated to be worth $3 million to $6.7 million (£3 million to £5 million). The painting by Europe’s first so-called “pure landscape oil artist” was identified earlier this year and is only the third such landscape painting identified by the artist. It is “one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field,” said George Gordon, co-chair of Sotheby’s worldwide old masters department. Plus, New Yorkers will get a chance to see it from November 7 to 19 at Sotheby’s, before it heads to London.
CATCH ME IF YOU CAN. French police recovered six stolen engravings by Pablo Picasso on Tuesday and have arrested seven suspects involved in the theft, reports Belga News Agency. Just before 2 a.m. on October 2, two people broke into a restaurant in Mougins, a hilltop village on the French Riviera, where Picasso had lived, and stole the original engravings hanging in a private room. They escaped by car and were aided by accomplices. The engravings were made in the early 1930s and are reportedly in excellent condition. They belong to the restaurant owner and are estimated to be worth over €100,000 euros ($112,400). Asked if it was still safe for the restaurant to exhibit the works, lieutenant-colonel Guillaume Plaidy told AFP it is “an obligation to continue exhibiting art today.” And if anything is stolen, “we will track them down, and we will find them,” he said.
The Digest
New research from the Themed Entertainment Association shows that museums in China are the world’s most visited in 2025, while American federal museums have experienced a drop in attendance. [Ocula]

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Defensoria e Consulado da Colômbia realizam atendimentos a migrantes em Fortaleza
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Entre os dias 6 e 7 de novembro, a Defensoria Pública do Estado do Ceará (DPCE) em parceria com o Consulado-Geral da Colômbia no Rio de Janeiro realizam uma agenda conjunta de atendimentos voltada à população colombiana que vive no Ceará. A iniciativa busca facilitar o acesso a documentos, serviços consulares e assistência jurídica, com atenção especial às pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade e àquelas privadas de liberdade.
De acordo com o defensor de segundo grau Bheron Rocha, a parceria entre o Consulado da Colômbia e a Defensoria Pública se funda no compromisso de que o acesso à justiça das pessoas migrantes, especialmente aquelas em situação de maior vulnerabilidade, não podem ter fronteiras. “É necessário construir caminhos permanentes de cooperação institucional”, explica. Em setembro deste ano, o defensor esteve no Consulado-Geral da Colômbia, no Rio de Janeiro, para debater estratégias para aprimorar o atendimento a colombianos privados de liberdade, com dificuldades documentais, sem contato com familiares ou em situação de rua.
A programação tem início na manhã desta sexta-feira (6), com visita às unidades prisionais junto aos defensores do Núcleo de Atendimento ao Preso Provisório (Nuapp), onde haverá esforços para identificar e acompanhar demandas de pessoas estrangeiras privadas de liberdade, especialmente sobre o contato com familiares e acesso à assistência jurídica. Durante o turno da tarde, haverá uma visita institucional da cônsul-geral da Colômbia, Diana Paz, à Defensoria Pública. No sábado (7), das 8h às 16h, a sede administrativa da Defensoria, em Fortaleza, receberá o Consulado Móvel, evento promovido pelo Consulado-Geral da Colômbia no Rio de Janeiro, em articulação com o Consulado Honorário da Colômbia em Fortaleza e com apoio da DPCE. Durante a jornada, cidadãos colombianos poderão solicitar serviços como emissão de passaportes, cédulas de cidadania, inscrições consulares, autorizações de saída de menores, reconhecimento de firma, procuração e registros civis.
A programação conta ainda com atendimento jurídico da Defensoria por meio do Núcleo de Direitos Humanos e Ações Coletivas (NDHAC), 2º Grau e Nuapp. Para a supervisora do NDHAC, Mariana Lobo, é preciso abrir frente na garantia de direitos. “São pessoas que, muitas vezes, desconhecem seus direitos, encontram barreiras de idioma, têm vínculos familiares interrompidos ou não sabem a quais instituições recorrer. Nosso trabalho é identificar essas situações, oferecer orientação jurídica e construir, junto às instituições, caminhos para garantia de direitos”, destaca a supervisora.
O atendimento com o Consulado Móvel só pode ser efetuado mediante agendamento prévio, que pode ser realizado por meio do QR Code disponibilizado nos canais oficiais do Consulado-Geral da Colômbia no Rio de Janeiro. Os interessados devem consultar previamente as orientações do Consulado sobre documentação e agendamento dos serviços.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US accuses Mexican judge of $2m bribe to free accused drug trafficker allegedly linked to ex-Olympic snowboarder
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A Mexican judge has been arrested and accused of accepting $2m in bribes in exchange for releasing a suspected Canadian drug trafficker from custody, US officials said on Thursday.
Luis Benítez Alcántara was overseeing extradition proceedings in Mexico in 2024 for Canadian citizen Andrew Clark, who was charged in the US with helping to run a billion-dollar drug-trafficking group allegedly headed by the former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, the justice department said in a statement.
Benítez is accused of releasing Clark from custody after accepting the bribe payments, according to the statement.
Clark was arrested days after his release and removed to the United States, where he faces drug-trafficking and murder charges.
The statement said Benítez, 49, was arrested on Sunday in Colombia. He is charged in a nine count indictment with being an accessory after the fact. It was not immediately known if he has a lawyer.
US officials will request Benítez’s extradition from Colombia, the statement said.
“Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States,” the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said in the statement.
It is the latest arrest in the US investigation into a multinational drug-trafficking network allegedly run by Wedding, who became a top FBI fugitive accused of moving cocaine from Latin America into the United States and orchestrating several killings. Wedding was arrested in Mexico earlier this year and flown to California, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and drug charges.
Dozens of people have been arrested in connection with the alleged drug network, and authorities seized large volumes of drugs, weapons and cash, as well as millions of dollars’ worth of automobiles, motorcycles, artwork and jewelry in its investigation.
Clark’s attorney, Matthew Lombard, did not immediately respond to messages on Thursday.

Aipac spent $55m on losing congressional candidates in midterm elections: Report
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) spent more than $84m in the 2026 US midterms, but nearly two-thirds of those funds were spent on losing candidates, according to a new report from Responsible Statecraft.
Aipac’s Super Pac and other groups spent $55m on failed candidates. The largest portion of those funds, about $32m, was spent trying to defeat Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.
The results marked one of Aipac’s worst performances in years, suggesting that the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has contributed to soaring cost-of-living issues, resonated strongly with voters.
In the 2022 midterms, Aipac’s Super Pac, United Democracy Project, saw 69 percent of its expenditure spent on races backed by the organisation that won. That number was even higher in 2024, after Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with 87 percent of its spending going to successful races.
In his victory speech earlier this week, Sayed pointedly called out Aipac, naming a higher figure spent against him, which may reflect the additional contributions of smaller Super Pacs.

“To Aipac, who spent $42m against us. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice," he said, referring to Aipac’s attempt to defeat him in the Democratic primary.
Aipac also spent heavily trying to defeat Daniel Biss, a critic of Israel’s policies. Biss, the former mayor of Evanston, Illinois, and grandson of Holocaust survivors, won the Democratic primary in Illinois's 9th congressional district earlier this year, even though Aipac spent almost $6m against him.
Biss easily carried the heavily Democratic district on Tuesday night.
Despite losing some high-profile races, Aipac is far from irrelevant.
Aipac claimed victory on Wednesday, saying on X that "more than 234 candidates supported by AIPAC members" had won their races.
Aipac did not provide a list of what races it was referring to, and for context, there are thousands of candidates who ran races in the midterms, but it remains an organisation to reckon with in Washington, DC.
The Democratic leaders of both the House and Senate have received funding from Aipac members.
“We congratulate Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries on the resounding victories for their caucuses,” Aipac said in a statement.
Still, opponents of Aipac heralded Tuesday’s results as a watershed moment in US politics. Aipac Tracker, which tracks the organisation’s influence in Washington, listed 30 members of Congress who won their seats eschewing Aipac ties.
In an election postmortem, Vice President JD Vance wrote on Wednesday that Republicans lost the elections because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which Aipac endorsed, and due to its relationship with Israel.

https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.title: Advocatenkosten voor deontologische raad wegen op journalistiek
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.author: Steven Vanden Bussche
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.text:
Journalisten en media worden geconfronteerd met dure advocatenbureaus die mensen bijstaan tijdens de behandeling van deontologische klachten voor de Raad voor de Journalistiek. Die verregaande juridisering jaagt journalisten en media, klein én groot, op kosten terwijl hun verzekering hiervoor niet tussenkomst.
Eind vorig jaar onthulde Apache hoe twee Belgen verdienen aan een omstreden Congolese belasting op het gebruik van een mobiele telefoon. Journalist Thibault Coigniez achterhaalde hoe de Antwerpse diamantair Philippe Heilmann en de Brusselse zakenman Jérôme Spaey met hun bedrijf 5C Energy een lucratief contract sloten met de Congolese overheid. Het contract zelf blijft tot op heden een Congolees staatsgeheim.
Heilmann was niet opgezet met de publicatie. De Antwerpse diamantair werd nochtans tijdig gecontacteerd voor een weerwoord, zijn reactie werd in het artikel verwerkt en ook nog eens integraal gepubliceerd onderaan het artikel.
De Raad stelde geen inbreuken vast op het principe van waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving, maar jaagde Apache wel op kosten
Begin 2026 eisten advocaten Olivier Sasserath en Herman Croux verregaande aanpassingen aan het stuk. Via een ingebrekestelling dreigden Heilmanns advocaten met een schadeclaim. De diamantair diende ook een klacht in bij de Raad voor de Journalistiek, die zich buigt over het deontologisch handelen van journalisten en media. Het bedrijf 5C Energy stuurde tot slot een Recht van antwoord dat Apache, hoewel er geen juridische verplichting was, integraal publiceerde.
Aangezien Heilmann geld veil had om het gespecialiseerde Brusselse advocatenbureau MVVP op Apache af te sturen, zag de redactie zich genoodzaakt ook een advocaat te raadplegen. Na heen-en-weer geschrijf tussen advocaten en een hoorzitting, besliste de Raad voor de Journalistiek om de klacht van tafel te vegen. De Raad stelde geen inbreuken vast op het principe van waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving, maar jaagde Apache wel op kosten.
Doe een gift op BE55 5230 8045 8444 (met vermelding ‘STOP SLAPP’) of via onze giftenpagina.
Geen alleenstaand geval
Eerder dit jaar diende een gepensioneerde politieman via zijn advocaat klacht in tegen Humo en een journalist. De politieman werd eind jaren 90 van het Dutroux-onderzoek gehaald. In een commentaarstuk wees journalist Douglas De Coninck erop dat de agent destijds een verband zag tussen de bende rond Dutroux en twee Franse gangsters die opdoken in het onderzoek naar de Bende van Nijvel. De journalist handelde onafhankelijk, meende de Raad, en had geen “kwaadaardige bedoelingen” zoals de voormalige politieman opwierp.
Freddy Kempeneer, hoofdredacteur van Persinfo.be, een nieuwssite die regionaal nieuws uit het Pajottenland, de Zennevallei en de Denderstreek brengt, werd dan weer verrast door de aanwezigheid van een advocaat tijdens de hoorzitting. De klager, een schepen die zonder omgevingsvergunning verbouwingswerken liet uitvoeren, bracht Kempeneers niet op de hoogte dat een advocaat zijn belangen zou verdedigen.
“Ik voelde me daardoor benadeeld, te meer er ook geen beroepsmogelijkheid is tegen uitspraken van de Raad”, zegt Kempeneer. “Had ik dat geweten, dan zou ik me ook laten bijstaan door een advocaat. Dat die advocaat daar plots stond, was voor mij ook intimiderend.” De klacht bleek grotendeels ongegrond, op een feitelijk element en te weinig responstijd voor wederhoor na.
Er zijn het afgelopen anderhalf jaar nog meer voorbeelden gepasseerd waarbij advocaten de klagers bijstonden, maar finaal bot vingen bij de Raad: bij een klacht van een opgepakte verdachte crypto-oplichter over berichtgeving bij HLN en een gesanctioneerde deurwaarder bij opiniesite Doorbraak.be.
Niet gedekt door verzekering
Charlotte Michils, algemeen secretaris van de Vlaamse Vereniging van Journalisten (VVJ) merkt op dat een procedure voor de Raad voor de Journalistiek laagdrempelig en gratis is. De zaak komt pas voor de Raad wanneer er geen minnelijke schikking getroffen kan worden.
Karl van den Broeck: “Voor die éne zaak moest Apache ruim 5.000 euro ophoesten, terwijl het dossier feitelijk onderbouwd was en op een deontologisch correcte manier afgewerkt”
“Als de ene partij een advocaat in de arm neemt, is het niet onlogisch dat ook de andere partij dat overweegt”, zegt Michils. “De aanwezigheid van een juridisch professional brengt immers de nodige techniciteit in het dossier waardoor het meer tijd en middelen vergt om je te verdedigen. Voor minder kapitaalkrachtige partijen kan dat een probleem zijn.”
Omdat de Raad van de Journalistiek geen schadevergoedingen toekent, dekt een verzekering burgerlijke aansprakelijkheid ‘beroep en uitbating’ juridisch advies en bijstand bij de Raad voor de Journalistiek niet.
“Dat zorgde ervoor dat Apache voor die éne zaak ruim 5.000 euro moest ophoesten, terwijl het dossier feitelijk onderbouwd was en op een deontologisch correcte manier afgewerkt”, zegt Karl van den Broeck, hoofdredacteur van Apache. “We betreuren die manier van werken en maken ons daarover ook zorgen.”
