https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/c.title: Can Bus Riders Form A Voting Bloc? We’re About To Find Out
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/c.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/c.text:
The riders on the bus say, “Fast and free.”
Transit activists want to turn bus riders into their own constituency and voting bloc that can support Mayor Mamdani and other elected officials who install bus lanes and fund free service — and punish politicians who favor their car-driving counterparts.
Earlier this year, Mamdani embedded his 2025 campaign vision for fast and free bus service in an official city plan that promised to dramatically change the layout of streets across the city. 
To steer that vision, advocates with the Riders Alliance hope to organize bus passengers as a powerful political force.
“We’re really thinking about how to grow our organizational membership and build organizing hubs across the city that can really push bus rider organizing forward and create a more militant base of bus riders,” said Divya Sundaram, the campaign manager with the newly announced Fix the Bus campaign.
The Fix the Bus campaign represent a slight course correction for the Riders Alliance, Sundaram told reporters on Thursday.
Rather than encouraging bus riders and residents to support specific bus lane projects, the organization will instead focus on activitating riders in three key locales where the city wants to execute its ambitious bus rapid transit plans: Tremont Avenue and Fordham Road in the West Bronx; Northern Boulevard in Queens; and on Flatbush, and Church and Utica avenues in Brooklyn.
Beyond building new constituencies of bus riders to support faster buses in those neighborhoods, the campaign will also promote the mayor’s related goal of fare-free buses. That will require finding a durable funding stream that enables fare-free, frequent and reliable bus service. 
The promise of better buses drove Mamdani’s electoral success, and Gov. Hochul endorsed a joint city-MTA plan to speed up city buses. Both developments signal a rare opportunity for bus riders to secure dramatically improved service.
After two previous mayors touted bus priority plans that failed to liberate buses from traffic or reverse ridership declines, organizers said they’re not assuming this one will work without a good push from the public.
“Buses are of particular importance in outer borough communities, Black and brown communities, low-income and working class communities, so there needs to be more organizing, more energy of activation than to fix something high-profile, like for example Penn Station,” said Riders Alliance Director of Policy and Communications Danny Pearlstein. 
“We have a mayor who ran for office on fixing the bus, we have a governor who’s working closely with him, and they’re poised to take bus riders more seriously,” Pearlstein added. “But they still need that extra push to keep buses and bus riders at the top of the agenda. We need to make sure that we achieve the plan to the utmost because we’ve seen plans before.”
The campaign will offer operational support to bus riders who want to organize for better services, and Riders Alliance plans to hold events for riders to share their commuting frustrations and meet each other, assigning a lead organizer to each of the three geographic focus area. 
The ultimate idea, Sundaram said, is to help riders find, speak with and organize each other, and begin to think of themselves as people who ride the bus and deserve world-class bus service — not as people who have no other choice. She likened the vision to that of labor unions or the tenant rights’ movement, whose members explicitly “identify as tenants.”
“We’re trying to change how bus riders themselves actually feel and think about taking the bus,” she said. “I think a lot of bus riders see the bus as, frankly, an inconvenience, something that they have to ride, not that they want to ride. It’s a real marker of class in New York City, and what we really want to do is replicate and build on some of the lessons that we’ve seen from tenant organizing or union organizing.” 
Riders Alliance is not the first member-based organization to show interest in supporting the mayor’s transit goals. 
Before he took office, leaders from some of Mamdani’s most prominent left-wing backers — including the Working Families Party and the New York City Democratic Socialists of America — said that supporting the mayor’s bus plans went hand-in-hand with supporting the rest of his agenda. And the NYC-DSA’s Transit Working Group recently began its own bus rider outreach efforts to marshal support for both fast and free buses.
The task of persuading the city’s bus-dependent areas to support faster buses — and streets that prioritize buses over cars — is somewhat new territory for transit organizing. 
Subway-rich neighborhoods have typically presented the strongest opportunities for previous efforts to pass congestion pricing and secure dedicated MTA funding. Indeed, a neighborhood’s proximity to subway stations mechanically predicted the geography of Mamdani’s electoral success in 2025.
“The subway map maps very closely onto the places where the mayor did incredibly well in the primary last year,” said Pearlstein. “The bus map is a little bit different. Bus-dependent neighborhoods looked a little bit different, and that’s where we want to go. … It’s also places where there are a lot of people who drive, and bus riders’ invisibility is compounded by that fact.”
Skeptics in these neighborhoods have argued that bus upgrades only cater to transplants, a line of argument that has fueled reactionary backlash. 
Even though bus riders largely hail from non-white, working class populations, everyone from Holocaust-minimizing media outlets and neighborhood cranks to City Council members and the previous mayor have tried to stymie faster buses by saying bus lanes are for newcomers instead of the established community.
Sundaram said the Riders Alliance won’t avoid those conversations about change, but plans to focus its messaging on the ways that the bus specifically serves working class communities.
“I think there are a lot of valid concerns around how are our communities changing and who is New York really for,” she said. “And I think we have a lot of shared commitments and focus on [keeping] New York affordable for the people who actually built and keep the city running. Bus riders are nurses and home care workers and teachers and students, and the bus is getting those people the places they need to go.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/b.title: Bronxites: Don’t Sacrifice Our Waterfront Access For Yet Another Amazon Warehouse
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/b.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/b.text:
Bronx residents are calling on Gov. Hochul to block an Amazon contractor from converting a former New York Post printing plant into a last-mile warehouse they say would inundate the area with trucks and sacrifice a huge chunk of the borough’s waterfront.
Environmental activists with South Bronx Unite say that logistics giant Prologis, which builds warehouses across the city, wants to convert the dormant printing building — located in Port Morris across from Randalls Island — into a last-mile fulfillment warehouse.
Jeremiah Kane, a vice president at Prologis, met with representatives from South Bronx Unite on Oct. 6 and told them that the company planned to tear down the existing printing plant building and replace it with a last-mile warehouse. 
Prologis’s top tenant nationally is Amazon, according to its most recent Securities and Exchange Commission filing.
The South Bronx waterfront, meanwhile, already hosts a large Fresh Direct warehouse in the Harlem River Rail Yard, which abuts the lot right next to the former newspaper plant. Researchers from Columbia University blamed the Fresh Direct warehouse for increasing motor vehicle traffic after it opened in 2018. With 1,000 Fresh Direct diesel trucks driving through the neighborhood each day, residents are understandably hostile to the possibility of another truck-heavy logistics operation opening in the lot directly next door.
“There’s this feedback loop of ‘Oh well, there’s warehouses here, so it’s a great place to put another warehouse’ instead of ‘Oh there’s warehouses here maybe and 60,000 people live here, maybe we should like think about other other things we can do,'” said South Bronx Unite spokesman David Rosales.
Port Morris and Mott Haven are stuffed with warehouses, and the city government so far has failed to regulate their associated emissions and traffic impacts. One option for doing so is an indirect source rule, under which the city would use a points-based system to force  warehouse owners to electrify their fleets and shift some deliveries to cargo bikes.
Researchers with South Bronx Unite believe that New York state has an opportunity to stop the warehouse development because the state Department of Transportation owns part of the land beneath the Post building.
Originally constructed by the defunct New Haven Railroad, the Harlem River Yards stretch from Lincoln Avenue to slightly east of Willow Avenue. The Penn Central Railroad, which acquired the site from NHR in 1969, sold it to New York State DOT in 1982. Nine years later, the state leased the land to a real estate developer, The Galesi Group, which operates the property under a subsidiary known as Harlem River Yard Ventures. The Post building sits on a lot which includes the easternmost piece of the Harlem River Yards, plus a former MTA bus depot, which the state sold to Harlem River Yard Ventures in 1999.
Before anyone builds anything, South Bronx Unite wants the state to investigate whether it has any direct control over how the land can be used, and if it does, to block a new warehouse from materializing.
“There are restrictive covenants that are tied to the lease that give both the city and the state certain enforcement rights over the land, so an ask that we have for the state is to essentially confirm whether or not these covenants are still still active,” said South Bronx Unite’s energy and economic justice advisor, Zoe Voss Lee.
Lee encouraged the state make use of its cumulative impacts law, which legislators intended to dissuade developments if they add more pollution to historically polluted areas.
“Since the plan for this is to become a warehouse, we can anticipate that there will be significant numbers of trucks that will be brought to the area,” she said.
Rather than another warehouse, South Bronx Unite wants the city and state to open the Bronx Kill waterfront to the public. Rosales pointed to the fact that the state Department of Environmental Conservation has highlighted SBU’s own Mott Haven-Port Morris Waterfront Plan in its official Open Space Conservation Plan.
For the former Post facility, South Bronx Unite envisions a hub for community solar power and a green manufacturing and job-training space. Formerly industrial waterfront spaces — such as Brooklyn Bridge Park, the East River waterfront parks in Manhattan and Brooklyn, Hunter’s Point South and Brooklyn Marine Terminal — have experienced, or will soon experience, second lives as mixed-use neighborhoods. 
As the city has shifted so much of the waterfront away from warehouses and heavy industry, Bronxites while they haven’t received the same treatment.
“Brooklyn and Queens and Manhattan have started to move away from that a lot more, and it feels like in the Bronx it’s moving a lot slower,” Rosales said. “At the end of the day, this stuff comes down to the willingness to do it, the willingness to prioritize it, the willingness to fund it.”
The old Post building is a short walk away from the abandoned and crumbling E. 132nd Street Pier. That proximity has led South Bronx Unite to speculate whether Prologis will pitch the warehouse as part of the city’s “Blue Highways” program to move more freight around the city by boat. That could make the project more palatable to decision-makers, but EDC has already identified locations for that program, and none of them include the pier or anywhere else in the Harlem River Yards.
Lee noted that Kane, the Prologis executive, told the trade publication BisNOW that he was interested in using the Blue Highways program to roll trucks onto and off of boats, in contrast to using small vehicles or even cargo bikes or quad bikes. His comments raised the group’s hackles because they suggested Prologis’s plan would invite even more truck traffic.
“We had a call with Prologis, they were positioning this development as part of the Blue Highways program, but we know that this is not formally a part of EDC’s Blue Highways initiative,” she said. “With the roll-on, roll-off model of Blue Highways, it’s likely that there will be increased truck traffic around the places where the hubs or the last-mile warehouses are actually located.”
The activists oppose the E. 132nd Street Pier’s potential conversion to industry because it conflicts with their vision for opening the waterfront. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who subscribes to the same vision, allocated $1 million just this year to the city’s Department of Small Business Services, who can use the grant to put in oyster reefs, clean up the shoreline and eventually rebuild the pier to restore public access to the pier.
“A concern that South Bronx Unite has regarding the potential of this site being a blue highway, has nothing to do with the premise of blue highways, which of course make a lot of sense when it comes to moving trucks off the road,” said Lee. “It has to do with specifically the positioning of this warehouse and the fact that the site for barging would be the 132nd Street Pier, which has been a project that has been prioritized for public access to the waterfront.”
For now, New York State DOT does not consider itself a participant in the fight over the warehouse. An agency spokesperson said the potential project is entirely privately owned. “The State Department of Transportation can confirm that it owns a portion of Harlem River Yards and has a ground lease with Harlem River Yards Ventures (an affiliate of the Galesi Group) on that portion of property,” said New York State DOT spokesperson Rolando Infante.
A spokesperson for Prologis said the company has only looked at a site that includes completely private land. The company spokesperson also denied that it bought the former Post printing plant, and that it is planning on building a warehouse for Amazon on the site.
“Prologis is not currently under contract to buy the former New York Post printing plant,” said spokesperson Mattie Sorrentino. “We are evaluating the site, as we do other potential projects in the region. Prologis has studied maritime freight options at the site, but the site has not been selected for the Blue Highways program. We have been part of the regional business community for years, investing in the local economy. We have and will continue to grow relationships here and be a long-term partner.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/04/w.title: Wednesday’s Headlines: Election Earthquakes Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/04/w.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/04/w.text:
If you want to know why Darline Graham lost her brother’s Senate seat in South Carolina — admittedly, it’s a great story — click somewhere else. You’re reading Streetsblog — and we’re focused on local elections and getting us more damn bike lanes, baby.
Second, there was a major Blue Wave in Southern Brooklyn, as Hunter Rabinowitz pointed out below. We’re not partisans at Streetsblog, but our readers know what candidates are fighting for our issues and which — looking at you, Assembly Member Michael Novakhov who famously defended super speeders — don’t.
“Tonight, New Yorkers voted for a government that moves as fast as they do,” Mayor Mamdani said in a statement issued late on Tuesday night. “From opening outdoor dining faster to speeding up street safety projects to accelerating housing production, we are cutting red tape that will directly address the affordability crisis and help New Yorkers stay in the city they love. Now comes the work of turning these votes into results.”
Oh, and speaking of elections, they have consequences — meaning we’re going to name names if a majority of the current City Council doesn’t get its act together and sign onto the Stop Super Speeder bill (which currently only has 17 co-sponsors). Albany has given the city the power to rein in the most reckless drivers — sociopaths with 16 or more speed-camera tickets in 12 months — but the Council still has to pass a bill to make it happen.
Do it, please.
In other news:
Garbage judge: Check out this Brooklyn jurist who thought she could get away with trash violations because she’s a busy lady! (Law Journal followed by NY Post)
A woman was badly injured by a hit-and-run driver in Manhattan. (Patch)
A Lower Manhattan community board wants a bus lane on West Street. (The Broadsheet)
And, finally, what are you doing Friday night? I hope you’ll join me at the “War on Cars” live show at Hunter College hosted by the folks (and Friends of Streetsblog) behind the popular podcast (tickets and info here). The show will feature the city’s former DOT visionary Janette Sadik-Khan, plus a screening of Clarence Eckerson Jr.’s feature-length documentary about the creation of Paseo Park, the city’s gold standard open street. Eckerson discussed his legendary career as the auteur of Streetfilms on the current episode of “War on Cars” with Sarah Goodyear and Doug Gordon.
And speaking of those two, they made a fun video to promote the live show:
Tabloid legend Gersh Kuntzman has been with New York newspapers since 1989, including stints at the New York Daily News, the Post, the Brooklyn Paper and even a cup of coffee with the Times. He's also the writer and producer of "Murder at the Food Coop," which was a hit at the NYC Fringe Festival in 2016, and “SUV: The Musical” in 2007. He also writes the Cycle of Rage column, which is archived here.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/04/t.title: The Disconnect: New York City’s Bike Lanes Remain Far Short Of A Network
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/04/t.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/04/t.text:
New York City’s bike lanes routinely failed to link up with one another, and often dump cyclists onto unprotected paths, according to a new visualization of “connectivity” that reveals how far Mayor Mamdani still has to go to realize his promise to make the Big Apple’s streets the “envy of the world.”
Under city law, the Department of Transportation must log the number of “turn choices” available to cyclists when they are on bike routes and want to head in a different direction without leaving the cycling network. The agency does not have to publish connectivity stats until 2028, so one advocate took it upon himself to map out the interconnectivity using the city’s own data.
The number of “turn choices” is a slightly abstract concept, but not a new one; the Bloomberg administration believed “connectivity” was a key metric, beyond mere mileage, for showing how well its network was spreading.
The connectivity index basically shows how many options cyclists have to stay within a safe network, said Jehiah Czebotar, the street safety activist who mapped it.
“It’s the difference between having the bike lane for the majority of it, or whether, as soon as you make a turn, you’re on your own,” said Jehiah Czebotar, a street safety activist behind the map. “It gets to whether or not you can get to where you need to go.”
For example, Ocean Parkway in Brooklyn has a nearly five-mile protected cycle path, but it scores low on connectivity, because for much of its length no protected bike lanes intersect it. Adding more connections would also encourage more ridership because cyclists don’t have to ride on treacherous streets without safe infrastructure to get to routes like Ocean Parkway.
On a citywide scale, Czebotar’s map visualizes how there’s a relatively dense network of protected bike lanes and safe greenways in Manhattan — mostly south of 110th Street — while across the city, the protected lanes or greenways just terminate or don’t connect to much else. The more bike lanes that intersect with other bike lanes, the more “connectivity.”
The city has steadily been increasing its turning options over the last nine years, Czebotar found, but mostly on unprotected paths. When it comes to protected paths, Manhattan has a plurality of connections at 37 percent of turning choices. In the other boroughs the protected network becomes far more anemic, with corridors that connect to few other safe cycling routes for much of their length.
Czebotar tallied a total 8,365 turn choices for cyclists across 2,758 intersections, out of the city’s roughly 40,000 total junctions. At the ground level, say, if two bike paths meet, that offers a cyclist four turn choices — eight if both lanes go in both directions.
DOT continues to build bike lanes without good connections to the existing network, and has not touched long-existing spines of protected paths, like Queens Boulevard and many of the greenways at the further reaches of the city.
“Even in 2026, DOT has a habit of building stub bike lanes,” said safe streets advocate Jon Orcutt, who directed policy at the Department of Transportation during the Bloomberg and part of the de Blasio administrations. “It sort of leaves cyclists hung out to dry in many parts of the city.”
And since police have pulled back on traffic enforcement, unprotected bike lanes are largely useless because they are filled with illegally parked drivers, Orcutt added.
“In a city that does zero traffic enforcement on bike lanes the Class II [unprotected paths] just don’t really count,” he said.
The former city transportation official said that DOT has made strides in recent years in politically friendly territory, like Astoria, Queens.
Orcutt lobbied former Council Speaker Corey Johnson to include mandates for connectivity in the 2019 Streets Master Plan, so as to add a metric beyond just annual mileage requirements for new paths.
But for unknown reasons, the Council wrote the law so that DOT won’t have to report those until 2028, almost a decade after the law passed. Other mandates, such as a mileage guideline for protected bus and bike lanes, kicked in in 2022, but the agency has repeatedly failed to meet those legal benchmarks.
The city actually used to publish a bike connectivity index in the annual Mayor’s Management Report as a “critical indicator” with annual targets during the later years of the Bloomberg administration, between 2008–2013. But the city stopped releasing the stat upon the ascension of Mayor Bill de Blasio in 2014.
Experts across the globe have long beat the drum that building a bikeable city relies on a network — as opposed to paths that don’t connect to anything else.
Transportation planners in other cities have successfully used that approach to maximize the number of people switching to cycling, including in the Netherlands in the 1970s, or Paris over the last decade.
“You really need to expand the network, because, of course, you need a good network to attract as many clients as possible,” Charlotte Guth, former head of cycling programs for Paris, said at a recent panel discussion in New York City about building a “bike city.”
A spokesperson for DOT said officials plan to emphasize safe connections in the upcoming annual update to the Streets Plan, due on Dec. 1. However, the rep also said focusing on connections alone would put more bike lanes close to existing paths, rather than prioritizing expanding the lanes further geographically.
“We want more New Yorkers to bike because it’s a safe and efficient way to get around — and we know the best way to encourage people to do so is to provide access to nearby street infrastructure that makes them feel safe,” DOT spokesperson Vin Barone said in a statement. “This will be a key goal detailed in our upcoming Streets Plan and we look forward to sharing more very soon.”
Kevin Duggan joined Streetsblog in October, 2022, after covering transportation for amNY. Duggan has been reporting on New York since 2018, starting at Vince DiMiceli’s Brooklyn Paper, where he covered southern Brooklyn neighborhoods and, later, Brownstone Brooklyn. He is on Bluesky at @kevinduggan.bsky.social and his email address is kevin@streetsblog.org.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Democrats eye historic upset in Mississippi Senate race as Republican blame game begins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
Mississippi count continues with Democratic candidate ahead by a razor-thin margin
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the 2026 midterms where almost 24 hours after Democrats secured their historic sweep of the US Congress, two Senate seats remain in play.
Counting in Alaska is expected to continue into Thursday, while in deep red Mississippi, Democrats could be close to pulling off another almighty upset. Currently, Democrat Scott Colom is leading his Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,138 votes with almost 96% of the vote counted.
In the last few hours, votes for Colom have been outpacing those for his Republican opponent, although new batches of votes have not been reported for several hours now.
Although a race this close would automatically trigger a recount in some states, Mississippi has no law on the books for initiating a recount.
Democrats haven’t won a US Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982, and Donald Trump carried the state by 22 points in 2024. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state elected a Black person to that office.
Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friends with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician. In 2015, he unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions.
Meanwhile, after Democrats secured their historic wins in last night’s midterm elections, Republicans are beginning the blame game:
- Donald Trump claimed Republicans fared poorly because he was not on the ballot – after repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot.
- JD Vance pointed to Trump’s ongoing war in Iran as the “obvious” culprit for the loss.
- Pete Hegseth’s role leading the unpopular war could lead to him taking the fall – despite Trump publicly backing him. Republicans including Trump foe Thomas Massie have criticized the defense secretary.
- Ron DeSantis, Florida’s governor, said the “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” was caused in part by his party failing to target their ad spending on issues that would motivate voters.
According to exit polls from the Associated Press, voters said the cost of living and government corruption were their two top issues. But how will Trump cope with this new political reality?

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.title: Lab-grown meat was supposed to save the world. What happened?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.author: Erin Somers
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text:
On 5 August 2013, a man and a woman ate a burger. Not just any burger: a world-historic burger, made from cattle cells grown in a laboratory by Mark Post, a professor of vascular physiology at Maastricht University in the Netherlands. The burger had taken two years to produce and cost €250,000 (about £210,000 at the time), money furnished by the Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Now it was being tasted in public for the first time at Riverside Studios in London, at an event attended by 200 members of the press and livestreamed to thousands.
To make this particular burger, Post had extracted stem cells from the shoulder muscle of a living cow, then cultivated them in plastic containers filled with a nutrient-rich supplement called foetal bovine serum, which is derived from cow foetuses. The cells eventually became 20,000 strands of tissue, which in turn became a single 140g patty. Post believed that beef produced this way had the potential to dramatically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and slow the climate crisis. Raising cattle for consumption requires massive amounts of land and water – and massive amounts of feed grown at a high environmental cost. He projected that global demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it the old-fashioned way, at which point our food systems would become unsustainable. But that didn’t have to mean a mass recalibration of our consumption habits or a global shift away from red meat. Post and his team had found another way.
Standing at a blond-wood island on an otherwise empty soundstage, Post lifted the kind of stainless-steel cloche usually found on a room service cart to reveal his creation. The raw patty sat in a petri dish on a bare plate, where it shone wetly under the studio lights. With the ITV London anchor Nina Hossain presiding, a Cornish chef named Richard McGeown pan-fried the burger in sunflower oil and butter for two volunteer tasters: Josh Schonwald, the Chicago-based author of The Taste of Tomorrow: Dispatches from the Future of Food, and Hanni Rützler, an Austrian nutrition scientist. So precious was this meat that they were given just the one burger to share between them. It was served deconstructed, alongside a sesame-seed bun, lettuce and tomato – showmanship to sell the burger a bit, give it context. The patty itself was reddish brown, flat and perfectly circular. When Schonwald and Rützler cut it, the burger did not bleed.
The two of them ate with forks and knives, passing the plate, sawing off thoughtful bites. Chewing slowly. Afterwards, they rendered their verdicts. “I would say it is somewhere on the spectrum between a Boca Burger and McDonald’s,” Schonwald told a reporter from NBC. “The absence of fat makes a big difference. It has the texture, which I was not expecting. It was like an animal-protein cake.” Rützler noted the burger’s blandness to a reporter from Science. “There is room for improvement here,” she said. At the end of the event, about €113,000 worth of burger remained uneaten. But none of this stopped Post from predicting that meat cultivated in a lab would become a consumer product within the decade.
The event – the theatrical reveal, the PR spectacle – triggered a kind of gold rush. One hundred and forty companies sprang up in six continents, trying to replicate what Post had done with beef across a range of other species: chicken, pork, fish, even quail. Investment to the tune of $3bn (£2.2bn) flooded into the sector. True believers claimed that cellular agriculture would not only fight the climate crisis and global food insecurity but also slow the spread of zoonotic disease and antibiotic resistance. A company called Upside Foods touted its plans to “set the new standard for meat” and to “make meat a force of good in the world”. A company called Vow created an enormous woolly mammoth meatball, though no one was allowed to eat it, since the DNA came from a fossil and the company didn’t know whether it was actually fit for human consumption. The thinktank RethinkX predicted that cultivated meat would decimate the US beef industry by 2030, reducing demand for the conventional variety by a whopping 70%. As the organisation wrote, “We are already on the cusp of the deepest, fastest, most consequential disruption in food and agricultural production since the first domestication of plants and animals 10,000 years ago.”
And yet, despite the frenzy, the meat itself never arrived. The challenges were numerous. There was the exorbitant upfront cost of building manufacturing facilities and the daunting amounts of energy required to run them. There was the difficulty of producing sufficient quantities of the stuff, at a price point low enough for people to buy. There was the lack of a highly skilled workforce trained to operate the new technology. There were rounds and rounds of inspections by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). There was even, occasionally, the unwanted appearance of rodent DNA in research samples, which happened to the companies Upside and Eat Just. After peaking in 2021, investment began to fall off. In 2023, the industry raised a measly $177m globally.
But it wasn’t only venture capitalists who had started to grow sceptical of cultivated meat. The technology soon became a target of conservatives. The state governments of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Indiana, Montana, Nebraska and Texas moved in quick succession to legislate against cultivated meat, passing laws that banned its sale, production, or both. The Florida governor Ron DeSantis made a media event out of signing that state’s law, posing for pictures in front of a blood-stained cutting board piled high with steaks. “Take your fake lab-grown meat elsewhere,” he said. “We’re not doing that in the state of Florida.” In 2024, the industrial biotech consultant Joel Stone told the New York Times that, if he had to put odds on it, the likelihood of the industry producing even 10% of the meat supply in the foreseeable future “would be zero”. Today, cultivated meat is available for purchase at just one store in the world: Huber’s Butchery in Singapore, where customers can buy packages of lab-grown chicken shreds from a manufacturer called GOOD Meat.
These developments were inconvenient for me, a person who became obsessed with the prospect of tasting cell-grown meat just as the possibility of ever doing so seemed to recede before my eyes. I was enthralled by the story of the meat, which seemed to contain so much of what defined this era of American life: dubious techno-optimism, bombastic culture-war posturing, carnival oddities like the mammoth meatball. It presented a snarl of competing motives, a mix of altruism and cold-blooded striving for capital (nothing can ever exist just for the common good; it has to make someone a billionaire). There was also the fact that I had been a vegetarian for almost 20 years.
The last meat I ever ate was a hotdog at Shea Stadium in New York in 2007. I don’t remember how it tasted – probably like every other hotdog I had eaten before. I washed it down with an exorbitantly priced but very cold Budweiser in one of those metal bottles. I quit eating meat after that, not because the hotdog had been disgusting but because I didn’t like the sensation of the inevitable bad bite, the periodic tangle with gristle or tendon or bone. Then my abstention grew into habit, and the habit was reinforced by other concerns: the catastrophic environmental consequences of industrial meat production; the creeping doubt, as I grow older, that I’m necessarily higher in the cosmic order than a chicken or a cow. But cultivated meat raised a compelling question. If you could subtract some of the downsides – make meat less destructive, engineer away its aesthetic flaws – what reason would there be not to eat it?
This question had begun to feel moot as the potential of cultivated meat grew less and less promising. But just when it seemed as though Post’s vision would never be realised, encouraging news emerged from a surprising place: North Carolina. In May 2024, when many of his peers were fleeing the sector, Jeff Bezos granted $30m through his Earth Fund to establish the Bezos Center for Sustainable Protein at North Carolina State University, an initiative dedicated to developing “dietary proteins that are environmentally friendly, healthy, tasty and affordable”. The donation cemented the state’s status as a new global centre of the cultivated-meat industry. The Bezos Center would join the North Carolina Biotechnology Center, an economic development organisation for the life sciences in Research Triangle Park.
On the commercial side of things, Believer Meats, an Israeli company producing cultivated chicken, had recently broken ground on a 200,000 sq ft manufacturing plant in Wilson, North Carolina. The plant would be the largest cultivated-meat facility in the world – capable, the company claimed, of producing 9.5m kilos of engineered chicken per year.
In September 2025, Believer received a “no questions” letter from the FDA, indicating that the agency did not encounter safety concerns in its inspection of the company’s products. “We are proud to be commercialising in this state, creating high-quality manufacturing jobs and enabling us to realise our vision to lead food innovations that care for the planet,” said Believer’s then CEO, a man named (for real) Gustavo Burger, in a press release celebrating the milestone. I got in touch with the company shortly after. In a Zoom meeting with Heather Hudson, Believer’s chief product and growth officer, and Rodrigo Lavall, from sales and marketing, the two dangled the possibility of a ribbon-cutting ceremony. They could tentatively plan something and invite me down to visit.
The whole thing felt a bit Wonka-ish. No one from the press had been allowed inside the factory yet. Only a few professionals in the field had even toured it. Why should I get the golden ticket? But I tried not to question my good fortune. Excited by the prospect of exclusive access, I started planning a trip to the Triangle. If lab-grown meat had a future, I might find it there. Maybe, I thought, I’d even get to taste it.
On a mild day in early December, I arrived at NC State’s sprawling campus, home to about 40,000 students. I expected it to be lively, teeming with kids, but it was eerily dead. Rohan Shirwaiker, the friendly, bespectacled director of the Bezos Center, met me in a pristine building where I didn’t see a single student. Everyone, he explained, had gone home for the holidays.
The Bezos Center aims to address, as its website puts it, the “critical barriers and gaps” still dogging cultivated meat. The process has changed as the industry scales up. It’s no longer Post labouring over a single burger in his lab for years at a time. Cultivation now takes place in sterile factories that look more like breweries, with cells grown not in culture dishes but in giant, stainless-steel bioreactors. Producers have also moved away from feeding the cells with foetal bovine serum, which is expensive and requires harvesting cow blood from slaughterhouses (not exactly a good look for a cruelty-free alternative meat product). The industry now relies on what is referred to as “serum-free media”, or SFM, proprietary compounds that vary from company to company. Still, the basic science remains the same: in one typical version of the process, stem cells are harvested from a living animal via needle biopsy, then nourished in solutions containing glucose, vitamins, fats, minerals, proteins and amino acids, which are swished around inside a reactor to ensure an even diffusion of nutrients. In these conditions, the cells divide, multiply and differentiate just as they would inside an animal. They are ready for harvesting when they reach the desired density: roughly within two to eight weeks, depending on the species being cultivated.
But what also remains is one of the industry’s fundamental challenges. You cannot simply grow a steak – yank it out of the reactor and slap it on the table at a restaurant – because a steak contains multiple kinds of tissue. At the moment, muscle and fat can only be cultivated separately, and typically they do not form solid matter but a semisolid slurry that must be taken from the reactors, washed, combined with other ingredients for flavour and texture, and extruded or 3D-printed into something you would recognise as meat: a burger or a nugget or a meatball or a fillet. Some companies are trying to circumnavigate the slurry stage by building scaffolding inside reactors for cells to cling to, producing a firmer product. (Certain types of cells don’t like floating in a tank all free like that. Tissue, I’m told, wants to adhere to bone.)
The cost of all this has come way down since Schonwald called Post’s burger an “animal-protein cake”, but right now, cultivated meat is far more expensive than the real thing. At Huber’s, in Singapore, the ominously named GOOD Meat 3, which contains only 3% chicken cells, sells for $5.62 (£4.20) per 110g serving. Meanwhile, chicken at my local supermarket, containing 100% animal cells, starts at $3.49 per 450g.
Shirwaiker took me on a tour of the Bezos Center’s brand new protein lab, which was still being set up. It was spacious and filled with light, lined with 3D printers and a humming but empty stainless-steel fridge. The printers, in particular, were huge and impressive. But the lab was still in the early phases of assembly; cables dangled from the ceiling, waiting for equipment that had yet to be delivered.
As Shirwaiker and I walked back to his office, we discussed the day’s shocking headline: while I was travelling to North Carolina from my home in upstate New York, news broke that Believer Meats was being sued for $34m by Gray Construction, the firm that built its hulking factory in Wilson. Believer had recently defaulted on an agreement to pay Gray an instalment of $22m. Maybe I should have seen it coming: after her initial enthusiasm, Hudson, my contact at Believer, had ghosted me in the days leading up to my trip.
I asked Shirwaiker what all this meant. He was as surprised as I was. He thought that the plant was so close to opening that the staff just needed to turn on the lights and boot up the chicken vats. No one knows yet what happened at Believer, he told me. It was unclear whether the company would survive.
Before I left the Bezos Center, Shirwaiker introduced me to the concept of the Gartner Hype Cycle. To me, it had the ring of an old concept, a framework invented in the mid-20th century by an economist or a professor. But no: it was formulated in 1995 by a woman named Jackie Fenn, who worked at the consultancy firm Gartner. Its purpose, according to a YouTube video made by the company, is to help you – a savvy investor, the video assumes – “understand the real risks and opportunities of an innovation so you can avoid adopting something too early, giving up too soon, adopting too late, or hanging on too long”.
Shirwaiker showed me a chart to illustrate. The x-axis was time, and the y-axis was visibility. The cycle begins with an “innovation trigger”, when a new technology is introduced to great fanfare, then arcs upward toward the “peak of inflated expectations” as excitement mounts. But this rise is inevitably followed by a dramatic fall, when investors realise how difficult it’s going to be to actually commercialise the innovation. Later comes a gentler climb up the “slope of enlightenment”, when second- and third-generation products emerge, until, finally, we reach the “plateau of productivity”, the slow, unflashy development of the technology. If Post’s burger was the innovation trigger, I asked Shirwaiker, where were we now? He circled the deep valley in the middle of the chart: the “trough of disillusionment”.
Before leaving campus, I tried Hudson again. I let her know that I was in the area and asked if I should “stop by”, as though the Believer facility were a conveniently located coffee shop rather than a meat factory in a rural area. I immediately received an auto-response that her email account was no longer active. Then I thought, what the hell, and decided to drive out to Wilson, about 45 minutes from Raleigh. I’ll go to see what’s up, I figured. I’ll talk to someone face-to-face, have some sort of confrontation with a person overseeing the plant – maybe even Hudson herself.
Rural North Carolina felt enormous, flat and empty. The landscape was almost featureless; huge swaths of nothing streamed by, and then I hit factories. Believer was located among a loose cluster of manufacturing facilities. To get there, I had to turn off a main strip containing a Chick-fil-A, a Bojangles, a McDonald’s and a Best-N-Burgers. At one point, I yielded to the flashing lights of what I thought was an emergency vehicle, only to find, as it passed, that it was a pickup truck towing a meat smoker. I was surrounded by the stuff. I thought of Post’s prediction that demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it. Sometimes it seems that this will happen tomorrow.
What I found when I got to Believer was grimmer than I expected. Not a chipper-then-confused-then-annoyed desk clerk wondering who this was showing up at a meat factory without an appointment, but no one at all. The facility was deserted, gated: a royal-blue cube under a pale late-autumn sky, millions of dollars of groundbreaking technology locked inside.
There is a widespread feeling in the US that everything is a hoax or a Ponzi scheme, and this feeling is only reinforced by the news. The news that self-driving taxis, when they become confused, are actually operated remotely from the Philippines. The news that the mysterious invention that could scan your blood for any number of disorders was an era-defining scam. The news that the crypto entrepreneur who pledged to secure the longtime survival of the human race was actually stealing $8bn of his customers’ money to fund his polycule in the Bahamas. I became paranoid, standing in front of the abandoned car park, that cultivated meat was just another lie, or a semi-lie, or a bluff. That the reason the meat was so difficult to get my hands on was that it did not exist. The possible implosion of Believer was disappointing not just because it represented a setback in the quest to reduce our carbon emissions and fortify our food systems against climate collapse, but because it seemed to confirm that we live in a cheap, mendacious world, where what passes for progress almost always turns out to be a confidence game.
The morning after my reconnaissance mission, more news broke: Believer was declaring bankruptcy and would shutter the factory in Wilson before it printed a single chicken strip.
I had timed my trip to North Carolina to coincide with the first annual Global Forum for Plant-Based and Alternative Proteins, held at the North Carolina Biotechnology Center. This was how I found myself cloistered among the faithful as their meat dreams unravelled in real time. All the local industry players were in attendance, and more had flown in from around the world. We were sitting together in NCBiotech’s blandly carpeted lecture hall for the opening session, listening to optimistic remarks about international collaboration, an opaque joke about an extruder, a shout-out to “Ian in the back from the insect side”, all the while knowing that the industry’s biggest gambit yet had just failed. With Believer gone bust, I hoped to salvage a glimmer of optimism for the industry from the day’s proceedings – or, at the very least, an honest assessment of what had gone wrong.
During a break in the programme, everyone filed out and congregated in the atrium. We were in the trough of disillusionment, but we were also in the divot of gossip. We were in the furrow of hanging around outside the auditorium talking excitedly. We were in the ravine of wanting to know what the hell had happened. I was surrounded by guys in crisp button-ups and thermal gilets and navy-blue blazers. There were not a ton of women present. All around me, speculation began to fly.
“There was a time about three or four years ago, post-pandemic, the money was so easy to come by. All you had to do was put a pitch deck together, and VCs would throw money at you.”
“They have a pretty star list of investors.”
“Yeah. That doesn’t guarantee a success.”
“They got the building up. The building is ready to, like, turn on.”
“It’s probably gonna be a liquidation. Again, we’re all assuming. We don’t know what the heck’s going on.”
“There’s got to be some news out of Israel.”
Later, we heard from venture capitalists who had no choice but to address the news head on. “I mean, elephant in the room: Believer Meats just down the road basically went out of business,” said Steve Simitzis, from Replicator VC, a firm that invests in early-stage food-tech companies. “I don’t have any information about it, but I would speculate that building factories around technology that isn’t ready at scale is probably a cause.” Well, duh, I thought. The VCs on the panel saw Believer as a cautionary tale. Don’t scale too quickly. Lower costs. Make something consumers actually want to eat. All these observations were sensible, even obvious, and yet wasn’t it also the case that the VCs themselves had put pressure on companies like Believer to expand rapidly in order to provide the returns they sought?
In the afternoon, we all tried to rally for a tasting of products by food startups. At last, I was sampling things. I drank some kind of fizzy peach tea. It was not immediately obvious to me what the innovation was, so I asked the young guy handing out the cans about it. It’s supposed to be refreshing, he said. Like after a run you can drink one and it won’t make you puke. Curiously, though, there was no cultivated meat on offer. The Research Triangle may be an industry hub, but the product did not seem to be available here. The product was still a prototype, or the product was too expensive to give out as samples. The closest thing on hand was plant-based vegan meat. I tried wheat-based turkey and wheat-based pepperoni from a company called The BE Hive. I tried “some kind of pulled meat”, as the person wheeling it out from the kitchen described it, from a company called Delight Soy. It had a stringy texture and was an orangish brown. I tried a fungi-and-soy-based salmon substitute from a company called Juicy Marbles. This one was very close to tasting like salmon. They had got something right, everyone around me agreed. To our wonder and dismay, Juicy Marbles had nailed the fishiness. Probably algae in there, someone remarked. We nodded. Yes, probably algae.
The experience was nauseating, though the cube of salmon tasted good. Or rather, it would have tasted good if you could isolate taste from the other senses. Like, if you didn’t see the morsel of fake fish, or feel it in your mouth, or smell its oily smell. And if you didn’t also know that it was synthetic. The knowing added a layer of queasiness. The idea that they would infuse soy with an unappealing smell for verisimilitude – a cloying, marine smell, like the hold of a fishing boat.
So all it would take for this thing to be palatable would be to experience it in a sensory vacuum and preferably context-free, or immediately after a blow to the head that wipes out everything you know about it. Then it would be pretty nice.
In January, a few weeks after my trip to the Research Triangle, a man ate a chicken sandwich. He ate two, actually: one made with conventional chicken and one made with a cultivated fillet. In a video of his visit to the Upside Foods factory in California, he stands next to a vat of swirling chicken cells. The cells are foamy, the cheerful yellow of Campbell’s broth. The man’s name is Jimmy Donaldson, though he’s known more widely as the YouTube sensation MrBeast, and he thinks that cell-grown meat has a lot of advantages. “These chickens don’t get diseases,” says MrBeast. “So then you don’t have to worry about a disease spreading on the farm and then you eating a sick chicken.” When it’s time to try to guess which sandwich is which, he can’t do it. “I honestly can’t tell,” he says, before guessing wrong.
Watching the video on my phone, it irked me that MrBeast had tasted the meat. That should have been me standing next to the churning chicken water. For months I’d been trying to find cultivated meat on the east coast; I had even considered buying it from Singapore on the grey market. Nothing panned out. Finally, Rohan Shirwaiker sent me details for a public tasting in the Bay Area held by Mission Barns, another partner of the Bezos Center. It would take place at the supermarket Berkeley Bowl West, which had previously sold a limited run of the company’s meatballs.
On a Friday in February, I flew out to San Francisco and got a cab over to the Mission Barns office, which was located in SoMa, on a desolate and unlovely block of warehouses. Not many Waymos swooping by out there, but at least it felt appropriately industrial, with the office upstairs and bioreactors below. Not that I got to see them: when I asked, I was gently rebuffed with the excuse that the company was in the process of moving to a larger facility in Alameda. I felt the ambient paranoia I’d experienced in North Carolina start to kick in again. After the collapse of Believer, Mission Barns seemed like one of the American companies closest to having its products on grocery-store shelves. At the end of last year, it received USDA approval for its cultivated pork fat. At the time of my visit, its products included bacon, pepperoni, meatballs and a couple varieties of sausage.
Bianca Lê, a smiley, put-together Australian and the then head of external affairs at Mission Barns, took me up to the company’s third-floor office, which contained a large kitchen on one side. As we sat at the wooden island, she told me about the origin of the cells for all of the company’s cultivated fat: a single Yorkshire pig named Dawn who was still, according to the company’s marketing materials, “happily roaming free” in an animal sanctuary in upstate New York, not far from where I live. Dawn reminded me of Dolly the sheep – a mascot for something much larger than herself. One wants to picture her soulful.
“Can I ask how Dawn was selected?” I said, hoping to hear something about Dawn as a superior specimen, the fattest, happiest, healthiest, smartest pig in the US.
“Yeah, honestly, it’s not that interesting of a story,” said Lê. “It’s just that she was available.”
The Mission Barns cultivation process takes about two weeks. At the end, they drain the bioreactors until they are left with just the fat slurry. “It’s white, it’s semisolid, it’s really pasty,” Lê said. That slurry is then combined with plant protein to create the final product, which typically contains less than 10% of animal cells per serving. I tried to understand how they got the fat out of one container and into the next, miming a large scoop or shovel, but this part was a secret. The company’s ultimate goal, Lê told me, wasn’t even to sell products but to license the system itself.
Mission Barns’s then CEO, Cecilia Chang, appeared: another smiley, put-together Australian. As she joined us at the counter, I asked her about the biggest challenges the company faces. “The timeline on being able to get costs down fast enough to get to a point of profitability,” she said. “The technology is there, but investors have really aggressive timelines.” Chang also mentioned a newer hurdle: the distrust of food science stoked by Donald Trump’s secretary of health and human services, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Still, the industry was trying to look at Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement as an opportunity rather than as a disaster. After all, MAHA is focused on protein; Kennedy’s new, inverted food pyramid features steak at the very top. And, although the movement broadly disdains processed foods, Chang told me, it may appreciate that cell-cultivated meat is usually organic and antibiotic-free. I recalled the lay wisdom of MrBeast: “These chickens don’t get diseases.”
As we chatted, Zachary Tyndall, Mission Barns’s product-development and culinary manager, prepared some meat for me in a frying pan. Tyndall is a former chef who once worked at the three-Michelin-star restaurant Noma, an apprenticeship that seemed unnecessary for the level of cooking involved here. He used a spatula to roll a single meatball around in a pan. The meat was a pale, pinkish beige, like real pork. It’s not that different from cooking conventional meat, he told me, though maybe a little bit quicker, since the company’s meatballs are precooked and only need reheating. It smelled savoury, like food, and indeed, it was food. I’ll give it that.
I received my meatball on a tastefully speckled earthenware plate. Though nearly delirious with excitement, I tried to zoom out for a second and glimpse the situation with objectivity. I was looking at a single small meatball in the middle of a plate in a chilly, industrial office thousands of miles away from home. This was what I had elected to pursue over the course of months with single-minded determination. With all eyes on me, I used the fork to cut it in half and took a bite.
The taste. The taste was not terrible. It was seasoned, oregano-heavy. It even had a kick. Everyone was watching as I chewed, so I feigned deep consideration, the way you do when the waiter brings you a sample of wine at a restaurant. “Hmm,” I mused. I am contemplating the tasting notes, my face said. I am weighing the mouthfeel. I tasted the salami too, which looked exactly like regular salami. It tasted like salty paper. Salty paper with a kick – they’re good about putting in the kick. I could not find much to say to Chang and Lê about the meat, though I tried. The phrase “blandly inoffensive” came to mind. The word “anticlimax” came to mind. This was what I had come all this way for? To eat something that felt like mushy cardboard in my mouth?
“It’s good,” I managed to tell them. Then, suddenly, the nausea hit, a taste of vomit in the back of my throat. It was the Juicy Marbles effect again. The problem was not the flavour, not the texture, but the knowing. The Knowing. Knowing about the fat tank, about the sticky white substance. The envisioning of the scoop. The knowing about Dawn, an ordinary pig who was available, and the extraction process that took her cells. Earlier, I’d thought this feeling was triggered entirely by Juicy Marbles’s ersatz fish odour, by its inherent artificiality. I hoped it would be different with the cultivated meat, which was, in the end, an actual animal product, at least in part. But no. If anything, it was worse.
The next day at Berkeley Bowl West, a large grocery store across the Bay, I watched a couple of dozen customers line up to taste the meatballs. Lê explained that Mission Barns has a fanbase, people who follow the company’s progress and register for events in advance. Here, a new contingent of the public revealed itself to me: my fellow cultivated-meat-curious. They were young and slightly goth. They were gen-Z vegans with lip rings and huge black trousers that flapped in the wind. Aside from these devotees, the crowd was made up mostly of people who happened to be at the grocery store for other reasons: Saturday shoppers, parents with kids in tow, people in athleisure. It was a warm and sunny February morning, a good day for a free sample. Passersby queued up, mildly interested.
Previous tastings had drawn protesters. In 2024, the week before the Florida cultivated-meat ban went into effect, Upside Foods hosted the Freedom of Food pop-up, a tasting on a Miami rooftop that was pitched as a protest of the new law. A chef from Caja Caliente, a restaurant in Coral Gables, made chicken tostadas with chipotle crema while a group of conventional-meat zealots parked a van in front of the venue’s entrance. The van was affixed with a huge LED screen displaying criticism of lab-grown meat. No long-term health studies, it read. Secret chemical formulas.
But nothing like that happened in Berkeley. Tyndall stood at a hot plate, gamely rolling the meatballs around a pan and placing them into small bamboo trays. As the samples were distributed, I made myself eat another one to see if my reaction would be the same as the day before. Instantly, I was clobbered by the Knowing, but around me, muffled sounds of approval rose from the crowd. A few people told me, shrugging, that the texture seemed right. A child, maybe two years old, accepted a meatball from her dad. She ate it happily, bobbing around like little kids do, with no objection.
A woman in a fleece jacket walked around asking tasters to fill out a survey on an iPad. She was an independent researcher conducting a study on consumer acceptance of cultivated meat for Tufts University. After the science, this is one of the biggest challenges to the product’s long-term success. Do people actually want to try it? Do they want to incorporate it into their diets? According to a report published last year by the Good Food Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting alternative proteins, only 18% of Americans find cell-cultivated meat extremely or very appealing, and almost 60% say they are somewhat or very unlikely to buy it. Interest typically decreases with age and increases with educational attainment, which tracked with my own observations. The goth college students were the most excited by the meatballs, but even they were muted in their praise. No one said “I love it” or “Hell yeah” or declared it a triumph. I did not hear the word “yum”.
The days of cultivated meat as a possible panacea for the climate crisis are long gone. Many of the industry’s biggest players – the ones still in business, anyway – are now embracing a more modest role in our food system. Since I tried its meatballs earlier this year, Mission Barns has announced a new strategy: it is pivoting from retail to wholesale and developing new products that will combine plant protein with conventional pork fat – to be replaced by their own, cultivated fat only once they’ve achieved a certain scale. Elsewhere, cellular agriculture is being used to create exclusive novelty items that could be fairly described as Frankenmeat, whereby their freakiness and limited availability are not liabilities but rather the selling points. Vow, the Australian company behind the mammoth meatball, has also developed a variety of Japanese quail foie gras as part of its objective to craft meats “unconstrained” by “the limits of nature”. Why, one might wonder? No real reason, except that they can. This, at least, feels like a more fitting use for cultivation technology and a more honest reflection of the ecosystem that has financed it.
This isn’t to say that engineered food needs to be virtuous to justify its existence. Before I left Berkeley Bowl West, Dixon gave me a tour of the store’s produce section, which was filled with the inordinate splendour of California. There must have been 20 varieties of crazy-looking mushrooms. She insisted I take two sumo citrus oranges – the ones with the bump on top – back home with me. Sumos aren’t naturally occurring; they were created in the 1970s by Japanese scientists who crossbred two citrus hybrids in a bid to produce a more flavourful, seedless fruit that might sell better than existing varieties.
I peeled a sumo and ate it as I walked through Berkeley. The afternoon was hot and windy, but the orange was sweet, hydrating, refreshing. Enormous and delicious. It was one shade paler than a traffic cone, with a palm-filling heft. It was perfect: a perfect example of an orange. A miracle, really, how it had just been handed to me.
A longer version of this piece appeared in the September edition of Harper’s

du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://taz.de/US-Aussenpolitik-nach-den.title: US-Außenpolitik nach den Midterms: „Trump will Ergebnisse für die Geschichtsbücher produzieren“
https://taz.de/US-Aussenpolitik-nach-den.author: Tanja Tricarico
https://taz.de/US-Aussenpolitik-nach-den.text:
US-Außenpolitik nach den Midterms: „Trump will Ergebnisse für die Geschichtsbücher produzieren“
Eine Mehrheit der Demokraten im Kongress kann der US-Regierung das Leben schwer machen, sagt Sicherheitsexpertin Claudia Major. Außenpolitisch rechnet sie mit Chaos.
taz: Frau Major, nach dem Sieg der Demokraten bei den Zwischenwahlen ist US-Präsident Trump sehr angeschlagen. Kann die Welt erstmal aufatmen?
Claudia Major: Es gab eine große Begeisterung in Europa. Verständlicherweise. Aber in der Außen- und Sicherheitspolitik könnten die Ergebnisse mehr Chaos bedeuten.
taz: Warum?
Major: In der Außenpolitik und im Handel gibt es weniger Kontrolle durch den Kongress. Deswegen können wir uns darauf einstellen, dass wir eine neue Runde Streitereien haben werden. Also mehr institutionelle Konfrontation, aber kein Kurswechsel in der US-Außenpolitik.
taz: Also Sie glauben, dass Trump jetzt noch stärker die außenpolitische Bühne nutzen wird?
ist Politikwissenschaftlerin und Expertin für Sicherheitspolitik. Seit März 2025 ist sie Senior Vice President für Transatlantische Sicherheitsinitiativen des German Marshall Fund.
Major: Ja, davon gehe ich aus, weil die US-Exekutive da weniger vom Kongress kontrolliert wird. Und er wird versucht sein, „legacy shopping“ zu machen, also Ergebnisse für die Geschichtsbücher zu produzieren. Das erhöht wiederum das Risiko neuer Konflikte und härterer Forderungen an Europa. Und: Es ist noch nicht Januar. Denn erst dann nimmt der neue Kongress seine Arbeit auf. Das lässt Trump und seinen republikanischen Verbündeten einen Zeitraum, in dem sie noch mit weniger Kongressbeschränkungen handeln können. Jetzt hat Trump noch die ganze Machtfülle mit Blick auf Russland, auf die Ukraine, mit Blick auf Iran, Entscheidungen zu treffen, die dann, wenn die Demokraten wieder da sind, nicht mehr so einfach rückabgewickelt werden können.
taz: Was heißt das konkret für die Ukraine?
Major: Ich habe keine Glaskugel. Aber hier ein Beispiel: Der Kongress hat die Kontrolle über Zuwendungen, und das ist eine Chance für die Demokraten, die Unterstützung für die Ukraine auszuweiten. Sie können auch eine der vielen Untersuchungen anstoßen, ob die bereitgestellten Gelder richtig eingesetzt worden sind und ob die Regierung alle ihre Verpflichtungen umgesetzt hat. Aber das Problem ist, selbst wenn der Kongress sagt, das wollen wir, heißt das nicht, dass die Waffen wirklich geliefert werden oder dass bestimmte Sicherheitsarrangements wirklich umgesetzt werden, weil so viel Macht bei der Exekutive liegt. Ähnliches gilt für Europas Verteidigung und die Nato, zum Beispiel die Stationierung oder den Abzug von Truppen. Selbst wenn der Kongress versucht, die transatlantischen Beziehungen zu stabilisieren, wie schon im letzten Jahr mit dem National Defense Authorization Act, der Leitlinien für das Pentagon festlegt, kann der Präsident rhetorisch politisch alles wieder infrage stellen. Auch das schwächt die Abschreckungsbotschaft. Es geht nicht nur um Fähigkeiten, also Soldaten, Drohnen, Panzer, sondern auch darum, ob man den USA glaubt, dass sie zu ihren europäischen Verbündeten stehen, und das hat der Präsident immer wieder politisch infrage gestellt.
taz: Also gibt es überhaupt keinen Grund zur Freude?
Major: In Europa gab es eine instinktive Freude. Natürlich!Demokratischer Wandel funktioniert! Aber Trump hat ja sogar seine eigene republikanische Mehrheit mit Blick auf die Ukraine ignoriert. Warum soll er sich jetzt von der demokratischen, also aus seiner Sicht, dem Gegner, irgendwie einengen lassen?
taz: Wie sollten die Europäer jetzt reagieren?
Major: Auf jeden Fall sich nicht zurücklehnen. Die Europäer müssen mit dem Kongress noch viel mehr zusammenarbeiten, aber gleichzeitig auch mit der Administration den Kontakt bewahren. Sie müssen Netzwerke und ein Vertrauensverhältnis zu beiden Parteien und den unterschiedlichen Strömungen darin aufbauen und pflegen. Die Demokratische Partei ist immer noch tief gespalten und es nicht klar, wie sie sich aufstellen wird.
taz: Keine Hoffnung für die transatlantischen Beziehungen?
Major: Also der Ansatz: „Der Populist ist abgewählt, und das wird schon wieder“ – das ist leider nicht so. Was hat die Wahl entschieden? Die hohen Lebenshaltungskosten, der Krieg in Iran und die schlechte Performance dieser Regierung. Europa, die Außenpolitik außer Iran, hat kaum eine Rolle gespielt. Wenn Post-Trump Rubio heißt oder wenn Post-Trump Vance heißt, dann können wir uns nicht in die Hängematte legen. Selbst die Demokraten haben in den letzten Jahren klargemacht, dass die strategischen Prioritäten der USA nicht mehr in Europa sind. Was die Europäer sich wünschen, ist Vorhersehbarkeit und Verlässlichkeit. Das wäre schon ein Fortschritt.
taz: Was folgt daraus?
Major: Das gleiche, was eigentlich seit anderthalb Jahren für die Europäer gelten sollte. Nicht nach Amerika gucken und über jedes Stöckchen springen, was uns Trump hinhält, sondern überlegen: Was wollen wir? Wie kommen wir dahin? Also agieren und nicht reagieren. Wir machen uns immer noch viel zu sehr abhängig von Washington. Zugespitzt heißt das: Wenn jetzt alles wieder gut wird in Washington, investieren wir dann nicht mehr in Verteidigung? Das kann ja nicht die Antwort sein.
taz: Trump sieht sich gerne als Friedensbringer und möchte in die Geschichtsbücher eingehen. Könnte dieser Geist zu einem möglichen Waffenstillstand in der Ukraine führen?
Major: Ich würde mich freuen, wenn es so wäre. Aber er hat das seit anderthalb Jahren versucht und bislang ist das am fehlenden Interesse Russlands gescheitert und der fehlenden Bereitschaft der USA, Russland massiv unter Druck zu setzen. Ein Krieg endet in der Regel entweder, wenn einer gewinnt, wenn es eine Intervention von außen gibt oder wenn es eine Pattsituation gibt und für beide Seiten aufhören attraktiver ist als weitermachen. Aus russischer Sicht hat Trump nicht das umgesetzt, was sich Moskau erhofft hatte, also ein Ende des Krieges zu russischen Bedingungen. Aber aus russischer Sicht ist es immer noch attraktiver, weiterzukämpfen als aufzuhören und ernsthaft zu verhandeln. Für die Ukraine läuft es gut an der Front, aber im Hinterland ist die Situation katastrophal, weil Flug- und Raketenabwehr fehlt. Russland verfolgt seine Entvölkerungsstrategie noch umfassender als in den letzten Jahren, da es mehr und neue Systeme hat und mit Luftkrieg das zerstört, was es militärisch nicht erobern kann: die Lebensgrundlagen, vom Bahnnetz zu Supermärkten, Strom und Datenzentren. Mit dem Ziel, die Ukraine mürbe zu machen, noch bevor der Winter richtig losgeht. Warum sollte Russland jetzt einen Kompromiss eingehen?
taz: Immerhin hat die First Lady, Melania Trump, einen temporären humanitären Waffenstillstand in Oleschky erwirkt. Ist das kein Zeichen?
Major: Dass die humanitäre Katastrophe in Oleschky so gelöst wurde, dass sich Russland zum ersten Mal darauf eingelassen hat, das ist eine wunderbare Nachricht. Es wäre hervorragend, wenn jetzt der nächste Schritt käme und ein sektoraler Waffenstillstand folgen würde, etwa für Getreidelieferungen über das Schwarze Meer. Aber das setzt Bereitschaft voraus. Trump hat immer wieder Druck auf den ausgeübt, auf den er Druck ausüben kann. Das ist die Ukraine. Und bei Russland war er weniger gewillt, so viel Druck zu machen, dass sich das russische Kalkül verändert hätte. Es scheint mir eher wahrscheinlich, dass wir wieder in taktische Verhandlungszyklen einsteigen, die wir die letzten Jahre schon gesehen haben, wie in Istanbul. Dann gibt es wieder mehrere Verhandlungssitzungen und dann hört es wieder auf. Bis sich das Kalkül der Beteiligten verändert.
taz: Sie meinen die nächste Verhandlungsrunde zwischen Russland und der Ukraine in der kommenden Woche in Abu Dhabi?
Major: Ein sektoraler Waffenstillstand wäre doch ein schöner Start. Wenn wir von einem sektoralen zu einem umfassenden Waffenstillstand und dann zu Verhandlungen kommen – das wäre hervorragend. Aber ich sehe momentan leider keinerlei Anzeichen, dass Russland seine Position verändert hätte.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar.
