https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘It’s kind of a melting pot’: how one US city transformed a highway into a leafy oasis
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Carl Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Passing through the Mojave desert on State Route 14, going by landscapes Hollywood uses to represent alien planets, a driver might not expect to find a walkable, tree-lined boulevard.
 
But there are nine beautiful, leafy blocks on West Lancaster Boulevard, a piece of what used to be Highway 14. They were redeveloped as part of a mixed-use urban streetscape in the city of Lancaster, California in 2010.
 
The BLVD, as it’s been rebranded, is home to 250 public and private enterprises, from banks, tattoo shops and restaurants to museums, a performing arts centre and a public library. City Hall is just a block south.
 
The city invested $11.5m (£8.5m) to transform a busy thoroughfare into an inviting public space. The three lanes in the centre of the former five-lane road were replaced by a series of tree-lined ramblas – Spanish for “avenue” and “watercourse,” because dry stream beds served as streets in early cities.
The redesign was planned and funded by the city of redevelopment agency. Within four years of completion, it had generated more than $270m in economic output, attracted $130m in investment, created hundreds of jobs and prompted the building or renovation of hundreds of housing units, according to the city.
 
The revitalisation has also created more intangible benefits, residents say.. The city centre the feels like a gathering space, they said — somewhere where they can feel like part of a community.
John Elford, the manager of Lancaster public library, was a reference librarian when construction began. Customers were angry about the disruption, and many complained about a major city centre thoroughfare being torn apart.
 
“Suddenly it was all done, and they had the grand opening,” Elford says. “Everybody loved it and the complaints stopped.”
The more beautiful and walkable space encouraged people to get out of their cars, he says. People who hadn’t visited the library began to wander in. Their questions began to change. Instead of asking for a specific title, visitors wanted to know where the fiction or non-fiction sections could be found. They started spending time in the library, perusing books or reading quietly.
 
The change has made the library feel more like a community space that all residents can share, Elford says. In the past, encounters with homeless patrons sometimes drove other visitors away from the library. But Elford says people have come to know their unhoused neighbours, and sometimes witness their transformations through contact with the library’s social workers.
 
“They start to get to know that person without actually introducing themselves to them,” he says.
Property and business owners went into partnership with the city in 2013 to create the BLVD Association, a property-based improvement district — a defined area where businesses work together as caretakers and promoters with funding from city taxes.
 
In 2016, the association launched an ambassador programme, hiring representatives to walk the BLVD and assist visitors and businesses. Brian Morris Jr has seen occasional problems with begging or break-ins during his six months on the job, but not enough to keep the area from feeling safe and livable, he says.
Nicole Stevens runs Pretty Little Poppy Marketplace, a business focused on selling wares from local vendors. She has lived in Lancaster since 1993, and has a long perspective on how its “main street” has changed. The reimagining has brought small businesses and families together, she says. “I’ve enjoyed being able to bring my boy down here.”
 
Alex Arreola, a cashier and marketer at the Sassy Bird restaurant, says he’s become friends with residents and business owners because it’s easy and pleasant to just walk around. “A lot of cities don’t have this walkable spot,” he says. “It’s a big benefit, the best place in Lancaster right now.”
Lancaster opened a museum on the BLVD in 2012 to house exhibits and education highlighting the history, art and culture of California’s Antelope Valley. Kim Calderwood, the museum’s art programme manager, grew up in California City, about 40 miles from Lancaster.
 
The Burns Pharmacy, which is still open, was the only place on Lancaster Boulevard that she recalls visiting with her family as a child. She was excited by the area’s transformation, from more foliage to all the businesses and restaurants targeting a younger clientele.
 
It’s a common occurrence for people to discover the museum in the course of rambling on the BLVD, including Lancaster residents. “They’ll say: ‘I was wondering what this place was,’” Calderwood says. “‘I didn’t realise we had a museum here.’”
 
Nanette Rushing, the owner of Nantiquez Vintage Flair, also works in a museum of sorts. Exhibits are for sale: an Oscar de la Renta dress, rhinestone jewelery, a fringed buckskin mountain suit. She staged estate sales and sold items she collected in stores that belonged to other people before she came to the BLVD 10 years ago.
“This street dictates a lot of things, from food to music to art,” she says. “It’s kind of a melting pot, and we can always have more of that up here. I’m glad to be a part of it.”
As sunset approached, Lancaster resident Frazier Farrell walked past a farmer’s market on one of the ramblas. A booth for cemetery plots sat between one with dried fruit and nuts and a large display of fresh produce.
 
The BLVD is a popular place with younger residents, he says. They can drift between bars, the theatre, restaurants or standup comedy. The museum where Calderwood works has an open mic night and figure drawing classes. Farrell has been a student and model. He often encounters friends when he visits the district and has made new ones among the business owners.
 
Calderwood says the main complaint she hears is about the slow speed limits in the district. “I’m definitely biased towards this sort of city planning,” she says. “It’s just not something that we get out here, or pretty much any other place I’ve lived.”
A version of this article was originally published in Governing.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: My childhood was one of survival and resilience. How can I model a joyful life for my kids? | Leading questions
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
I’m a child of first-generation immigrants and have always carried a story of survival and resilience. My parents were part of a “lost generation” who sacrificed a lot to put us all through university. There was a very defined path for success, some of which I followed and some not. I married outside of race; I made work choices for financial stability. I don’t know how to enjoy things that other people seem to. Hobbies, travelling, home renovations … I look at those like “what is the point?”
I want to say it’s because my upbringing was not full of leisure activities; my parents only allowed us to focus on academic topics. Now that I’m a mother though, I wonder how I can role model some of this “living well for its own sake” for my children. It’s hard to find simple joys actually joyful. Growing up, everything needed to be “applied” towards something, and it feels that mentality is informing everything I do. Any advice on how to break free and live in the moment?
Eleanor says: Sometimes the means take over the end. Like a strangler fig. We start out doing something as a way of achieving something else we value – as a means to an end. But over time, it takes up so much of our schedule and mental prioritisation that it starts to twist and wrap around the things we actually value. It crowds them out, competes for vital nutrients, until it wins. It becomes the thing we value for its own sake; the means become the end.
It happens with money. We start trying to get money for the good life it’ll bring, but over time we’ll throw parts of a good life on a pyre for the sake of getting more money.
And it happens with hard work.
Your parents decided to sacrifice, work hard, give things up. The original reason to do that was as a means to a better life. That’s why it’s worth making the mammoth sacrifices immigrant families make: leaving the place and people they knew, working hard in a new country, sometimes in multiple jobs or new languages. Nobody thinks it is worth doing these things because they are a temple to worship for their own sake. It is worth doing these so that life will be better for the generation after you. It is a means to an end – that things will be better for your kids.
Over time, though, the means can become the end. The organising mythos can become that we work hard to work hard; that it is the thing worth valuing for its own sake.
To think that way is to let the real value get strangled. Exactly like you said, everything growing up needed to be towards something. Couldn’t your quality of life, and your child’s, be what you were all working towards? Wasn’t a better life the point?
You asked how to break free.
Start with the feeling, not the activities. Don’t approach leisure as if it also needs a defined path. Other people might find joy in travel and home renovations, but you don’t have to. The first (only?) question is: what ignites a feeling of joy in you?
It can take time to get back in touch with your own reactions to things. Like finding the mind-muscle connection to a disused part of your body, if you’re long out of touch with asking “Do I enjoy this?” you may have to ask many times before you can detect the answer.
So don’t start with the hope that things will deliver joy and in-the-moment immersion right away. It might not feel like that at first. You can start in an exploratory way instead. Fieldwork. How does this make me feel? What can I detect in myself?
The joys that come to you might be totally specific to you. Some people feed crows. Some people dance disco. Some people preserve weeds. Making more room for enjoyment in your life is also the task of making more room for your actual self – how you actually feel, what you actually like. When you’re slow and still enough to ask what you truthfully feel about something, you’re already living more in the moment.
Your parents sacrificed a lot for you, and you’ve worked hard to honour that. You can cash in some of the hard-earned chips – be the person for whom life could be better – without feeling like it’s wrong. The point wasn’t to accumulate chips for the chips’ sake. Don’t let the means become the end.
The reader’s letter has been edited.

https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Autor-Joseph-.title: Nachruf auf Autor Joseph von Westphalen: Der Sterbesalat
https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Autor-Joseph-.author: Klaus Bittermann
https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Autor-Joseph-.text:
Nachruf auf Autor Joseph von Westphalen: Der Sterbesalat
Joseph von Westphalen konnte mit dem Montblanc-Füller umgehen wie Errol Flynn mit dem Degen. Nun ist der Romanautor und begnadete Polemiker gestorben.
Es war schon lange still um ihn geworden. Dabei hatten wir in den Neunzigern und Nullerjahren häufig und manchmal stundenlang telefoniert. Er erzählte von seinen neuen Entdeckungen alter Jazz- und Bluesstücke, von neuen Romanen, an denen er gerade arbeitete und die meistens mit einer neuen Amour fou zu tun hatten, der Joseph von Westphalen immer wieder verfiel. Vor allem in seinem letzten großen Roman „Der Liebessalat“, den er nur schrieb in der Hoffnung, dass das Buch in die Hände einer unbekannten Schönen fiele, die er auf einer seiner Lesungen gesehen hatte.
Westphalen schrieb also nicht aus Gründen des Ruhms und des Ehrgeizes, sondern aus dem einzigen Motiv, das die Mühe lohnt, ein Buch zu schreiben. Ohne die von ihm begehrte Frau, die schon eine fast mystische Aura verbreitet, wäre er „im Handumdrehen verhungert, verblödet, verrottet“, schrieb er.
Ihm war das Lächerliche durchaus bewusst, das hinter der schmachtenden Liebe zum Vorschein kommt und sich nicht selten als klebriges Selbstmitleid entpuppt. Das heißt, er stellte sich auch selbst infrage, wozu ein Breton in seinem Frauenanbetungsroman „Nadja“ nicht fähig gewesen wäre. Insofern hatte Westphalen mehr mit Balzac zu tun, der ebenfalls auf verschwenderische Weise der Liebe seinen Tribut zollte.
Ein besessener Vielschreiber
1945 in der Oberpfalz geboren, studierte er in München Literaturwissenschaften, war kurze Zeit von den Maoisten fasziniert und veröffentlichte schon bald im Haffmans Verlag, in dem fast die gesamte Riege der Neuen Frankfurter Schule erschien. Mit seinen Duckwitz-Romanen „Im diplomatischen Dienst“ landete er bei Hoffmann & Campe einen großen Erfolg. Westphalen war ein besessener Vielschreiber, der in mehreren Verlagen gleichzeitig veröffentlichte.
Dabei sorgte er im Kulturbetrieb immer wieder für Aufregung, weil er auch ein begnadeter Polemiker war, der kein Blatt vor dem Mund nahm, wenn er Neigungen zum Mainstream und zur allgemeinen Verblödung feststellte. Dies war vor allem während der Wiedervereinigungseuphorie der Fall. 1990, nicht lange nach dem Fall der Mauer, erschien ein Pamphlet mit dem Titel „Von deutscher Bulimie. Diagnose einer Freßgier“, wobei ihm die Vergeblichkeit seiner Kritik an der deutschen Einheit natürlich bewusst war.
Jahre, nachdem die Zeit Monika Maron und ihn zu einem wöchentlichen Ost-West-Dialog eingeladen hatte, bedauerte er seine „Beißhemmung“ gegenüber der „maulig-mopsigen Zonnentussi-Art meiner Briefpartnerin“, der er viel zu geduldig den Westen zu erklären versuchte, „als gälte es, eine misstrauische Behörde zu besänftigen“. Er schreckte vor Beleidigungen nicht zurück, die er allerdings immer mit hinreißender Verve begründete.
Als 1998 die Anthologie mit Bestsellerverrissen „Sorge dich nicht, lese!“ in der Edition Tiamat erschien und das Scherz-Verlagsimperium sich in seiner den Titel betreffenden Urheberrechtsehre verletzt fühlte, weil man glaubte, der jahrelang Platz 1 der Spiegel-Bestsellerliste belegende Ratgeber „Sorge dich nicht, lebe!“ von Dale Carnegie müsse vor unzulässiger Kritik mit einer einstweiligen Verfügung geschützt werden, ließ es sich Joseph von Westphalen nicht nehmen, unter dem Titel „Sorge dich nicht, zahle!“ eine furiose Anklage in der Süddeutschen Zeitung zu verfassen.
Beinahe ein Verlagsruin
Er forderte den Scherz-Verlag auf, die angedrohte Strafe bei Zuwiderhandlung von 10.000 Mark fallenzulassen, Scherz solle sich vielmehr entschuldigen und als Wiedergutmachung die Restauflage aufkaufen. Tatsächlich brachte der Artikel Westphalens Scherz dazu, die Klage aus Imagegründen zurückzuziehen. Der Verlagsruin war abgewendet. Mit seiner Montblanc-Feder wusste er so elegant umzugehen wie Errol Flynn mit dem Degen.
Anfang dieses Jahres verfasste Westphalen einen Nachruf auf seinen Freund Ulrich Enzensberger („es ist wirklich fürchterlich mit dieser Sterberei“) in der Süddeutschen. Ein Anlass, wieder mit ihm in Kontakt zu treten. Postwendend kam eine lange Mail, dass er wie eigentlich immer dabei sei, einen Roman zu schreiben, aber da er mit ihm „keine Frauen mehr beeindrucken“ wolle, fehle der Druck, aber der Impuls, einer bewunderten Frau bis ans Ende der Welt zu folgen, sei noch da.
Der Roman bleibt unvollendet, denn der literarische Freigeist und Husar Joseph von Westphalen ist mit 81 Jahren in München gestorben.
Klaus Bittermann ist der Verleger der Edition Tiamat.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.text:
Saudi coalition intercepts missile fired towards Medina
Interception comes after Saudi civil defence agency warned of potential danger near the strategic port of Yanbu.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.
The announcement on Thursday came just minutes after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency warned of potential danger in the area near the strategic port of Yanbu.
“Air defence intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Medina region,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a post on X.
The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have rejected any suggestion they were targeting the city, saying such accusations were a “blatant and grave falsehood”.
Houthi Military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X that “our operations target only oil facilities and military bases” and called the allegation a lie.
Among their attacks on airports, energy infrastructure and military sites, the Houthis have targeted the port of Yanbu on several occasions in recent months.
“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Yanbu Governorate to alert of a potential danger,” read a statement published by the agency online.
The agency later announced that the threat had passed.
Yanbu is a major oil export hub and a key outlet for oil shipments transported through the kingdom’s East-West pipeline.
The port and pipeline have played a key role since the outbreak of the United States-Israeli war on Iran in February, helping Riyadh ship crude and fuel to global markets.
Separately, Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces made gains in the Sanamat area in Taiz governorate, where fighting continues to rage.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Thursday that government forces carried out 1,298 “targeting operations” against the Houthis in the past 24 hours and “managed to gain control” of Sanamat.
The latest operations killed about 400 Houthi fighters and destroyed 132 vehicles, cars or heavy weapons placements, he said. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.
Yemeni government forces previously reclaimed Taiz’s Dhubab district and key positions near the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Meanwhile, on the al-Jawf front, military engineering units continue to clear recaptured sites of mines and booby traps, al-Nazili added.
Late last month, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.
The Houthis have not confirmed a death toll and have in the meantime been firing missiles regularly towards Saudi Arabia, hitting multiple airports and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.
Yazeed al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the course of the conflict increasingly appears to be moving towards a prolonged war of attrition as the government offensive has not shifted the balance of power over the past 30 days.
“The conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics inside Yemen; it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the war involving Iran,” he added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.title: The blame game: How the US midterm shock is shaping Israel’s race for PM
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.text:
The blame game: How the US midterm shock is shaping Israel’s race for PM
The Republican midterm rout is helping shape who leads Israel next, as Netanyahu’s US ties turn toxic.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long sold himself as the leader who will ensure that ties with the United States, the country’s most important ally, remain strong. The endorsement he received in the run-up to Israel’s parliamentary elections last month from US President Donald Trump added to that perception, in the same year as Washington and Tel Aviv jointly went to war against Iran.
Then came the US midterm elections, and the disastrous performance of Trump’s Republican Party. Early analysis of why the Republicans lost so badly has in part focused on that war with Iran, and the United States’s relationship with Israel. Both were highlighted by US Vice President JD Vance.
Suddenly, Netanyahu’s argument that he is the US-Israel relationship’s secret sauce looks much weaker. If anything, it can be argued that Netanyahu, and his policies – resulting in a genocidal war in Gaza, the Iran war, and numerous attacks in the wider region – have made Israel politically toxic in the US.
Many Israelis are now worried that the country can no longer rely on unquestioned support from the US. And as Israel’s political leaders jockey to try and form a government following the parliamentary elections, the opposition has laid the blame squarely at Netanyahu’s feet, and argued that it is another reason he should not be allowed to form the next government.
Yair Lapid, a former Israeli prime minister whose party is a member of the bloc seeking to unseat Netanyahu, stressed his own ties to members of the US Congress in a social media post. He added that he believed US voters were not so much against Israel as “against extremist ministers who say crazy things. They’re against settler violence; they’re against a government they don’t understand; they’re mainly against Netanyahu — for them, anything connected to him is toxic”.
Avigdor Lieberman, another opposition leader, echoed what many in Israel are said to suspect: that Trump’s election-day announcement that US military aid to Israel would end had been traded for his endorsement of the prime minister. “The price of Trump’s support for Netanyahu – $3.8bn dollars a year,” Lieberman wrote on social media.
“With America stopping the money it has channelled to Israel for so many years, the defence budget, already 7 percent of GDP, will have to rise. Israelis will feel it in their pocket. But then, you can’t be a rogue state and expect things to continue as before,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said. “In Israel, Netanyahu continues to do what he has always done so well, turning one segment of the population against the other. He’s now trying to delegitimise the Arabs by saying they stole the elections, in order to stop the opposition having the Arabs as partners.”
No substantial change
Israel’s general election on October 27 left Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc with 53 seats in parliament, eight short of the 61 needed to form a government.
The opposition bloc led by former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot got 48 seats, while the Arab-led parties – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List – have 19 seats. The Arab-led parties have both said that they will support Eisenkot for prime minister.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have rejected suggestions of a unity government with Netanyahu, leaving him without a clear path to a majority.
It is now up to Israeli President Isaac Herzog to nominate a politician to form a government, but he has yet to do so.
As things stand, Eisenkot’s self-styled Zionist bloc, which has previously ruled out serving alongside the Arab-led parties, stands to benefit from their backing from outside the government, despite Netanyahu’s attacks.
Eisenkot’s prospects were boosted further on Thursday when United Torah Judaism (UTJ), Netanyahu’s longtime ultra-Orthodox ally, declined for the first time since 2009 to recommend him or anyone else to form a government, an apparent defection that weakens the prime minister’s position while giving a boost to his opponents.
But Eisenkot replacing Netanyahu as Israel’s prime minister does not necessarily mean that he will be able to reverse Israel’s declining popularity in the US. An April Pew Research Center poll suggested that public attitudes in the US are as negative towards Israel as they are towards Netanyahu, noted pollster Shibley Telhami, the director of the University of Maryland Critical Issues Poll.
“Our own poll found that most Americans would not change their view of Israel, even if there is a new government without Netanyahu,” said Telhami. “Any government of Israel would be swimming against the rising public tide … I don’t think any government of Israel could return relations back to where they were five years ago.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.title: Top US civil rights official resigns
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.text:
Top US civil rights official resigns
New Democratic Congress expected to probe Trump Justice Department civil rights office’s handling of Epstein files and ICE killings.
As President Donald Trump’s administration prepares for a flurry of congressional investigations into shootings by immigration agents and the Jeffrey Epstein files, the top official in charge of the United States Department of Justice’s civil rights division has resigned.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday confirmed Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s departure in a post on social media.
“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon,” Blanche wrote on X. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”
A top Trump ally, Dhillon was confirmed to her role in April 2025 and has overseen a dramatic overhaul of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, which is tasked with enforcing anti-discrimination laws. Hundreds of former Justice Department officials penned a letter last December decrying the “destruction” of the agency division under Trump.
Dhillon is the first high-ranking official to resign from the Trump administration since US Democrats swept both chambers of the US Congress in the country’s pivotal midterm elections on Tuesday.
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely become the new chair of the powerful House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Accountability, pledged on Wednesday to take on four major investigations, including abuses of power by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and the Epstein files.
Dhillon reportedly told her staff earlier this year that her office, which has typically been charged with investigating law enforcement killings by police officers, would not be looking into the fatal shootings of two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – who were gunned down by ICE agents in Minneapolis.
In May, Garcia accused the administration of continuing to shield Trump from scrutiny related to unreleased documents tied to the Epstein investigation
During a closed-door hearing in which Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, was asked by lawmakers about the case, the California Democrat Garcia alleged Dhillon repeatedly intervened to block questions about the president’s connection to the release of the files.
The Justice Department referred Al Jazeera to Blanche’s social media post when asked when Dhillon submitted her resignation. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Trump met Russian envoy after he appeared with Melania Trump and Ukrainians
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Trump met Russian envoy after he appeared with Melania Trump and Ukrainians
Trump again said a major Russia-Ukraine deal is ‘very close’, but gave no specifics.
US President Donald Trump has said that a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.
“I think we’re going to be very close to settling Russia-Ukraine,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, while declining to disclose details of his conversation with Dmitriev.
“There’s going to be an agreement. It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that the effort could include “all of Europe”.
Trump has frequently predicted that an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close. Negotiations have, however, picked up in recent weeks.
Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.
The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came after a diplomatic gathering hosted by First Lady Melania Trump, which brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together to mark and build on the localised six-day truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October. The US president did not attend the event.
The temporary ceasefire ran from October 27 to November 1 and allowed for the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians from the besieged, Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as the delivery of critical food and medical supplies.
Senior officials from both countries attended on Thursday, including Dmitriev; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.
Melania Trump also spoke at the event, which the White House described as “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.
“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.
The first lady presented Putin’s and Zelenskyy’s representatives with large white envelopes and asked them to deliver her personal letters to each leader. Dmitriev presented her with a painting by an 11-year-old girl, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sent her the Order of Princess Olga, a Ukrainian award recognising her role in the ceasefire.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Nothing better encapsulates the dysfunction that was Everton under Farhad Moshiri than the idea that an unknown vandal with a can of spray paint could influence the club’s managerial direction. “Pereira out, Lampard in” they daubed on a wall at Goodison Park when it appeared Vítor Pereira was in line to replace Rafael Benítez in 2022. Alarmed by fan protests, the Everton board opted instead for Frank Lampard and, while his tenure ended 12 months later with the club immersed in another relegation battle, there will be appreciation for the Coventry manager when he makes a first visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday. The connection between Lampard and Evertonians was genuine and a factor in keeping the club up in 2022. Both parties will be glad to see the other emerging stronger from those troubled times. Jack Grealish, meanwhile, will again be absent for Everton after his recent disciplinary breach, although the manager, David Moyes, said: “We will be working again with Jack soon.” Andy Hunter
Back in September, when Leeds thrashed Newcastle 4-1 at Elland Road, talk of European qualification filled the West Yorkshire airwaves. Since then Daniel Farke’s side have drawn three and lost two of their ensuing Premier League games, scoring just two goals along the way. Given that their final pass has persistently let them down, optimism is turning to pessimism. Farke would call it realism. The German – who could probably do without facing Roberto De Zerbi’s improving Tottenham on Saturday – is confident his side are improving but knows they cannot expect to run before properly mastering the art of walking. “We don’t have the individual quality [of the Premier League’s leading teams],” conceded Farke on Thursday. “We have to compensate by being tactically spot on and good at winning second balls. It’s not a criticism of my players, it’s reality. The dream of Europe is allowed but we know our main aim is to reach 40 points as quickly as possible.” Louise Taylor
Martín Zubimendi has yet to start a Premier League game this season after falling down the pecking order at Arsenal and the Spain midfielder is likely to be the subject of speculation that he could seek to depart in January. The emergence of Myles Lewis-Skelly as an alternative in the No 6 position at the end of last season has had an impact on Zubimendi after he had been a regular starter for most of his debut campaign in the Premier League. The 27-year-old signed from Real Sociedad for around £55m 15 months ago and Mikel Arteta has insisted he remains an integral part of his plans. But with the Arsenal manager trying to find the right balance in his midfield after the arrival of Bruno Guimarães, Zubimendi will be hoping he gets another chance to stake his claim against Hull on Saturday after starting in the narrow win over Slavia Prague in midweek. Ed Aarons
Álvaro Arbeloa is proof that a struggling young manager working in England for the first time can bounce back after a difficult start. Arbeloa was sliding towards the sack a month ago but he has responded at Fulham, who have taken seven points from their last three games, and will hope to extend the unbeaten run when Matthias Jaissle’s inconsistent Newcastle visit Craven Cottage. It is an inviting fixture for Fulham and a big one for Newcastle, who were poor when they lost to Everton on Monday. Jaissle, hired as Eddie Howe’s replacement in the summer, is already under pressure. But the 38-year-old could take inspiration from how Arbeloa has given himself breathing space at Fulham. Jacob Steinberg
Oliver Glasner has previous. He led Wolfsburg from mid-table to the Champions League but fell out with the club hierarchy and left in 2021. Glasner next guided Eintracht Frankfurt to Europa League glory but was openly critical of the squad’s imbalance and quality in four separate outbursts and departed in 2023. His time at Crystal Palace was a great success but after accusing the Eagles’ board in January of “abandoning” his team with the sale of Marc Guéhi to Manchester City, the Austrian left this summer for Nottingham Forest, where he became the fifth head coach in less than a year. You can probably guess where this is going. After Saturday’s defeat by Brentford left Forest 19th, Glasner was typically abrasive: “If the players buy in [to my methods], I think we can have a turnaround. And if not, the sixth manager will come in.” We’ll soon find out if Glasner has won the players around with City visiting Nottingham this weekend. If Forest’s woeful form continues, Glasner may either walk or get his marching orders from trigger-happy owner Evangelos Marinakis. Michael Butler
Pierre Sage pulled no punches in his assessment of Eddie Nketiah’s career after his excellent winning goal against Fulham last week in the EFL Cup. “I think his potential is higher than his performance for the moment,” said the Crystal Palace manager. “And we have to reduce this gap – because he needs it, the team needs it.” Nketiah is now 27 and won his solitary senior cap for England in 2023 after becoming the record scorer for the under-21s while he was still at Arsenal. His chances of adding to that look unlikely these days having been relegated to third-choice striker at Selhurst Park behind Jean-Philippe Mateta and Jørgen Strand Larsen. But with Mateta suspended for three matches after Palace’s appeal over his red card against Tottenham was rejected, Sunday’s meeting with Liverpool could be another chance for Nketiah to show his ability after scoring a late winner against them in Palace’s thrilling win over Arne Slot’s side last year. EA
It has been three weeks since Brighton’s fans were savouring a famous 5-0 thrashing of arch-rivals Crystal Palace at the Amex. But the quirks of the fixture list meant that Fabian Hürzeler’s side played five successive games on the road since then, including two trips to face Manchester City. While they lost some of the momentum from the Palace victory in the defeat by Liverpool at Anfield, last week’s Premier League win over City showed they are serious contenders for the top four and perhaps even more. But Brentford’s visit to the south coast should provide a real test of those credentials as the owner, Tony Bloom, renews his rivalry with his west London counterpart Matthew Benham, who traditionally eschews his seat in the directors’ box for one in the away section. EA
Eli Junior Kroupi did not take the headlines in Bournemouth’s win over Leeds but his cheeky nutmeg and sumptuous no-look pass to set up Amine Adli for the Cherries’ second goal was a reminder of why the youngster continues to be linked with a move to Arsenal, Bayern and PSG, despite being sidelined recently. Kroupi scored 13 Premier League goals last season – only Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney, Michael Owen and Romelu Lukaku have reached that total as teenagers – and only Erling Haaland and Will Osula enjoyed a better goal-per-game ratio in 2025-26. Kroupi’s foot injury, sustained in pre-season, has been carefully managed but after three substitute appearances in the wins over Manchester United, Aston Villa and Leeds, will Marco Rose be tempted to start Kroupi at Ipswich? Evanilson is in red hot form as the central striker but Kroupi is just as comfortable as a No 10 and surely has to play if he is fit as Bournemouth chase a seventh consecutive win in all competitions. MB
It is not quite six months since Sunderland beat Chelsea 2-1 at the Stadium of Light and qualified for Europe for the first time in 53 years. A day when Régis Le Bris’s side eclipsed the Club World Cup holders and Enzo Le Fée upstaged Enzo Fernández concluded with Sunderland finishing seventh. During the prolonged post-match celebrations, the captain, Granit Xhaka, grabbed a microphone and declared: “This is just the beginning – we want more.” Fast forward to gloomy November and it is not quite working out like that with even the excitement of next month’s trip to Milan overshadowed by anxiety. Sunderland are bottom of the Premier League, Le Bris concedes his side are in a relegation fight and Xhaka has looked a shadow of his former self ever since Chelsea tried and failed to sign him in the summer. Is Xhaka capable of turning back time? Sunderland securing just a second league win of the season depends on it. Louise Taylor
Can Manchester United win two games of football on the bounce for the first time this season? Being able to pose this question sums up the state Michael Carrick and his side are in as they seek to build on Tuesday’s chaotic comeback victory over Roma. Aston Villa arrive five points better off than their hosts and are everything United are not: stable, upwardly mobile and boasting a manager in Unai Emery who consistently improves players and yields results. As the international break beckons after this last Premier League fixture of the weekend, will Carrick survive what could be an eighth loss in 15 matches? Possibly, if it is not another humiliation, but the truth may be that even United’s erratic executives do not currently know the answer. Jamie Jackson

The poll commissioned by J Street, a US-based pro-Israel think tank, shows a deep gap between how Jewish American voters view organisations like Aipac and Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, compared to how the state of Israel and its allies in the US portray antisemitism.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: ‘In moments of pain, football comes together’: Spain says goodbye to Jesús de Miguel
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Sid Lowe
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The narrow streets of Navahermosa in La Mancha were fuller than they have ever been on Thursday afternoon and quieter too. Silence accompanied the funeral cortege as its made way from the funeral home to the parish church of San Miguel Arcángel carrying Jesús de Miguel Alameda, “Demi”, the Tenerife striker who died after an on-field collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono three days earlier. Only 3,587 people live in his family’s village but now they were joined by the game he loved. “We wanted to be close to his parents, his wife and daughter. In moments of pain, football comes together more than ever,” said Luis de la Fuente.
The Spain manager did not say much else; there was not much else he could say, not much anyone could. These have been dark, desperate days, days when it was impossible to assimilate what has happened, and there will be more. “We will get through this together but we will need help, professional help,” the Tenerife president, Felipe Miñambres, said.
The club’s majority shareholder, Rayco García, had cried as they left the building where De Miguel’s body had laid in Santa Cruz de Tenerife and he asked the striker’s teammates to be close to his widow Maria, when he had vowed they would for ever take care of his daughter, Clara.
Maria was in the stands with 16-month-old Clara in her arms when, in the 96th minute of Monday’s second division game, she saw her partner chase a ball up the pitch to the centre circle where Owono crashed into him. De Miguel’s father was watching it from the hotel Alameda in Navahermosa, where he goes for most games. His son’s football career had mostly been played not far from there and from the Leganés home where he had grown up – at Fuenlabrada, Inter Madrid, Unión Adarve and Navalcarnero, then Salamanca and Castellón – but now he was 1,000 miles away.
Medical staff rushed on to the pitch. Players stood, terrified, while for six minutes De Miguel was treated there. He was then taken on a stretcher to the ambulance waiting in the corner where, the club reported, they were able to re-establish a pulse. He was transferred to the Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz, where medics succeeded in getting him to breathe again. He remained in a critical condition but, with his body temperature lowered, he was stable, they said.
With De Miguel’s parents hurrying to find a flight to Santa Cruz, where García collected them, doctors told Tenerife there would be no news until the morning. But at 3am, there was another call to say his condition had deteriorated neurologically. At 8am, he passed away; Tenerife announced his passing at 8.31am. He was 30. The preliminary autopsy pointed to a trauma of the thorax: commotio cordis which can only occur upon impact within a 40-millisecond window in the cardiac cycle. A routine investigation was opened, the focus not just on Owono but the medical protocol applied.
Football is supposed to be a safe space, a refuge, an escape. All those lines about giving your life to the game are not supposed to be literal. This didn’t make sense. The images and the outcome shocked; the contradictory combination of the improbability and the plausibility of it all made it harder still to come to terms with: this couldn’t happen yet it could have happened to anyone. “I am the same age,” Raphinha, Barcelona’s captain, said. There is an everyman quality about De Miguel. He was also a partner, a father. “How we loved him,” García told Cadena Ser. “He was so humble, his feet on the ground.”
His teammate Javi Alonso said: “He was a worker, a footballing labourer. He was in the AFE, the players’ union, and helped me a lot. He was a great teammate and a good person, wonderful. He was always willing to help.”
He had begun in the academy at Leganés, a modest start to a career at modest clubs; real football. It hadn’t been easy and he had endured injuries too. He met Maria when he was playing for Navalcarnero in the third tier: she lived in one of the houses in front of the small, municipal ground with its astroturf pitch. It was not until he was 27 that he played “professionally”, always understood in Spain as referring to the first two divisions. He took his teams there too, twice winning promotion.
He never played in the top flight and played 40 games in the second division: he was not a star and was not rich. García vowed that his daughter would not want for anything. Fran Sol, a former Tenerife player, started a crowdfunding page for his family.
Almería said that their gate receipts when they play Tenerife would go to the family. During the funeral one of the eulogies noted that playing in segunda for Tenerife was his dream, finally fulfilled at 30: this wasn’t the end of his career; it was the start. When they won promotion, he told reporters: “When I started playing as a little kid, I never thought I would live all this.”
An interview he did with Ser Tenerife resurfaced this week in which he said: “Nothing in life is easy. There will be good moments and bad ones too; it is a path you have to walk. Making fans happy is what makes you proud; seeing people celebrate goals is the loveliest thing in football.”
Now they mourned him, desperately sad. Outside gate No 9 at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López, fans brought flowers and left candles. So too did the squad, standing in silence. The Spanish Federation cancelled all Copa del Rey games. The Champions League went ahead; Como’s Nico Paz, whose father played for Tenerife, held up a T-shirt in his honour. Messages came in from across the game; minutes’ silences were held. Las Palmas announced that they will wear their third kit this weekend, because it is blue and white, the same colour as their rivals’ shirt.
They would prefer not to play at all. The players’ union De Miguel was part of said it wanted to stop, that it had canvassed footballers and they agreed: they were not ready, their heads not right. But La Liga decided all games will go ahead except those involving Tenerife, Andorra and De Miguel’s former club Castellón – a decision they did not finally confirm until Thursday afternoon.
By then, De Miguel’s funeral had finished. His body was flown to the mainland on Wednesday, the decision made to hold the funeral in his parents’ village, although there will be an event at Tenerife’s stadium on Saturday, open to everyone. Tenerife’s players and staff boarded a charter at 7am on Thursday and then went to Navahermosa by bus, all of them. The presidents of the AFE, the federation and the league came; the presidents of Real Madrid and Atlético Madrid, too. Representatives from clubs across Spain. Andorra’s owner, Gerard Piqué; president, Ferran Vilaseca, and general manager, Jaume Nogués.
The minister of sport, Milagros Tolón Jaime. Pablo Blanco, ambassador of Sevilla, the club that lost Antonio Puerta and José Antonio Reyes. Their midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili, a former teammate, who had asked for leave; the head coach, Luis García, said: “We’re people above all else.”
Before the cortege set off, Manuel Hernandez, De Miguel’s agent, said: “In those difficult moments, we want to thank everyone from the bottom of our hearts for the words and gestures, all the support we have received. We’re very grateful; to feel so much affection towards Jesús and see the impact he made on people is something we will always take with us. Jesus leaves a void that is impossible to fill but also leaves everyone who was fortunate enough to share their life with him great memories.”
Wreaths of flowers from all the clubs he had graced in his career covered the hearse as it edged towards the church, following the cross-bearer there, slowly and in silence. There was not enough room in the church for all those who were there. When they eventually came out on to the plaza again, Tenerife’s players lifted the coffin on to their shoulders and carried their teammate back through the crowd to his final resting place in Navahermosa.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.title: Nithya Raman wins LA mayoral race, becoming city’s first South Asian mayor
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.text:
Nithya Raman wins LA mayoral race, becoming city’s first South Asian mayor
DSA-backed Raman will lead America’s second largest city, promising action on homelessness and affordable housing.
Nithya Raman, a progressive Los Angeles City Council member, has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, putting her on track to become the first South Asian to lead the second-largest city in the United States.
The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with Raman holding 52 percent of the vote.
Raman, 45, overtook Bass despite the incumbent’s support from prominent Democrats such as California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.
Her campaign was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), with her victory coming as part of a surge in visibility and electoral wins for the left-wing political movement.
A record number of candidates backed or affiliated with the DSA won federal offices in Tuesday’s midterm elections. On its website, the DSA has claimed credit for contributing to at least 300 candidacies or ballot referendums during the midterms, and it said it is on track to count 105 of those as victories.
Some of those wins came in congressional races, with figures such as Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros and Chris Rabb winning their first terms as US representatives.
Raman’s victory in Los Angeles follows another high-profile democratic socialist winning a mayor’s race in New York City last year: Zohran Mamdani.
Raman was born in India and worked as an urban planner before running for office. Once an ally of Bass, she had initially endorsed her re-election campaign but reversed course, entering the mayoral race in February, just hours before the filing deadline.
In her victory speech, Raman promised to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.
“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she told the crowd.
Raman also pledged to expand affordable housing, improve neglected city services and take a different approach to homelessness by deploying more medical teams to assist people who are unhoused.
In addition, she called for replacing the city’s police chief over concerns about cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
Raman now faces the task of delivering on those promises in a city of more than 3.8 million people.
Los Angeles also faces the challenge of hosting the 2028 Olympic Games, which open in July of that year.
With the result, Bass has become the first Los Angeles mayor in more than two decades to lose a re-election bid.
Her defeat follows a difficult four years in office. Her administration faced mounting criticism over the city’s homelessness crisis and its response to the deadly Palisades Fire, which broke out while she was overseas and devastated communities across the Los Angeles area.
In a statement on Thursday, Bass congratulated Raman and said she was committed to ensuring a smooth transition.
“Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles. You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me,” Bass wrote.
“Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.text:
Generation Z and young voters help redefine US politics after midterms
Melat Kiros becomes the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress, embodying a new era of political representation.
The outcome of the 2026 US midterm elections has marked a historic shift in American politics, with diverse candidates winning office and the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress.
Of the 117 Generation Z candidates who ran for Congress this year, 24 won their primaries and made it to Tuesday’s ballot, according to the organisation Future Caucus.
Among them was Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old Ethiopian-born democratic socialist from Colorado, who became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.
Kiros, a lawyer turned doctoral student, won a stunning primary victory earlier this year, with the first-time candidate beating 30-year incumbent Representative Diana DeGette in the Denver-area seat.
After winning the primary, she told supporters that she was taking the fight to “Donald Trump and the oligarchy”, abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), passing Medicare for All and ending the “genocide in Palestine”.
She joins Representative Maxwell Frost of Florida, who became the first Gen Z member of the House in 2022.
Young people voted overwhelmingly for Democrats, according to an Associated Press news agency voter poll.
After relatively high support for Trump in the 2024 election, young voters snapped back towards the Democratic Party in this year’s midterms.
The AP Voter Poll showed about seven in 10 voters under 30 nationally said they supported the Democratic candidate in their local US House race, while about three in 10 said they voted for the Republican. That was a dramatic shift from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Kamala Harris.
Most first-time midterm voters, who skew younger, also supported the Democratic candidate.
Both young voters and first-time voters made up a fairly small share of the electorate. Only about one in 10 voters in the 2026 national electorate are under 30, for instance, which limited the impact of the shift.
But young voters’ displeasure with the country and its leadership was clear. About half of young voters said they were “angry” about the way things were going in the country, compared with only about one-third of voters aged 65 and older. And about six in 10 voters under 30 said one reason for their vote for the US House was to express opposition to Trump, compared with about half of voters aged 30-44 and about four in 10 voters aged 45 and older.
Young voters shifted towards the Democrats in each of the Senate races where the Democratic Party picked up a seat, including in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.title: South Africa’s ANC on track for new lows in local polls
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.text:
South Africa’s ANC on track for new lows in local polls
The ANC was on about 32 percent of the vote after almost half of the votes were counted in municipal elections.
South Africa’s early municipal election results have shown the African National Congress (ANC) with a sharply reduced vote share, weakening the long-dominant party’s control of key cities such as Johannesburg.
The ANC was on about 32 percent of the vote, with the Democratic Alliance (DA) in second place at 25 percent, after more than 60 percent of the votes had been counted in this week’s municipal elections, data from the election commission showed late on Thursday.
Meanwhile, former President Jacob Zuma’s breakaway opposition uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party was in third place with 8.5 percent, below levels suggested by opinion polls.
About 15.9 million of 29.2 million registered voters cast ballots, the electoral commission said, putting turnout at an estimated 54.5 percent, up from 46 percent in the pandemic-hit 2021 local elections.
The ANC, which has been South Africa’s largest party since it led the country out of apartheid in 1994, has tended to do worse in municipal elections than nationally and has acknowledged its failures in local governance.
From nearly 70 percent of the national vote in 2004, the ANC fell below 50 percent for the first time in the 2021 municipal elections, winning 46 percent.
At the 2024 national elections, it managed just more than 40 percent and was forced to accept a unity government with nine other parties, including the DA.
The party, now led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, has borne the brunt of criticism about years of municipal mismanagement that have left South Africans grappling with failing water supplies, persistent power cuts and crumbling public services.
It has also faced corruption allegations, while splinter parties have eaten away at its support base.
The results of this week’s local ballot will offer a key measure of voters’ sentiment ahead of the 2029 general election.
Control of the country’s eight major metropolitan municipalities is up for grabs, alongside dozens of district and local councils.
The MK party had been tipped as one of the few parties capable of securing an outright majority in the eastern port city of Durban.
But projections by the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a state-funded research body, put its support there at 32 percent.
The DA, meanwhile, was forecast to retain control of tourist magnet Cape Town with 56 percent of the vote, with its leader, Geordin Hill-Lewis, already declaring victory.
The party was also leading with 34 percent in Johannesburg, the country’s financial capital, after running a spirited campaign spearheaded by its former leader, Helen Zille, 75, according to CSIR projections.
With outright majorities far from assured in several major cities, the results could usher in another round of complex coalition negotiations, with parties bargaining to assemble the alliances needed to govern.
Final results are expected on Sunday.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120367.title: Landesparteitag in Hameln | 41 Grüne wollen den Genozid in Gaza anerkennen und ernten Sturm
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120367.author: Matthias Monroy
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120367.text:
- Politik
- Landesparteitag in Hameln
41 Grüne wollen den Genozid in Gaza anerkennen und ernten Sturm
In einem israelkritischen Antrag berufen sich die Parteimitglieder auf die Vereinten Nationen. Nicht nur die Lokalpresse gibt sich alarmiert.
Ein Grünen-Mitglied, das bis vor Kurzem dem Kreisverbands Stade angehörte, hat einen brisanten Antrag für die kommende Landesdelegiertenkonferenz in Hameln gestellt. Darin fordert es, dass die Partei den israelischen Militäreinsatz in Gaza als Genozid anerkennt. Niedersachsens Landesverband soll die Bundes-Grünen auffordern, sich dem anzuschließen. 41 Mitglieder aus Kreisverbänden wie Hannover, Stade, Lüneburg, Göttingen und Oldenburg-Stadt unterstützen das Ansinnen. Dazu soll am Wochenende abgestimmt werden.
Der vor einer Woche vorgelegte Antrag stützt sich auf den Bericht der Untersuchungskommission der Vereinten Nationen vom 16. September 2025, der Israel Völkermordhandlungen in Gaza zuschreibt. Die grüne Bundespartei soll darauf hinwirken, dass Deutschland die Empfehlungen des Berichts umsetzt. Dazu zählen ein Stopp von Waffenlieferungen bei begründetem Verdacht auf Verwendung im Genozid, die Verfolgung deutscher Beteiligter, die Unterstützung von Untersuchungen und Sanktionen sowie die Zusammenarbeit mit dem Internationalen Strafgerichtshof, der in der Sache gegen Israel ermittelt.
In der Begründung verweisen die Antragsteller*innen auf renommierte Wissenschaftler wie Omer Bartov und Amos Goldberg sowie auf Organisationen wie Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch und die israelische Menschenrechtsgruppe B’Tselem. Die Zuständigkeit der Grünen sei gegeben, da der damalige Vizekanzler Robert Habeck und die damalige Außenministerin Annalena Baerbock die zustimmende Haltung Deutschlands zum Gaza-Krieg entscheidend geprägt hätten. Daraus folge eine besondere Verantwortung der Partei.
Kritik von jüdischen Verbänden
Nicht nur die Lokalpresse ist wegen des Antrags aus dem Häuschen. Die »Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung« (HAZ) fragt, ob die Grünen nun ein »Gaza-Problem« bekommen, und lässt dazu Michael Fürst, Präsident des Landesverbandes der Jüdischen Gemeinden in Niedersachsen, kommentieren: »Der Antrag fördert den Antisemitismus in Deutschland«, sagte Fürst ohne Erläuterung. Eine Annahme beschädige das Verhältnis der jüdischen Gemeinden zu den Grünen »dauerhaft«. Mit der grünen Kultusministerin Julia Willie Hamburg, die in Hameln zur Spitzenkandidatin für die Landtagswahl 2027 ernannt werden soll, könne er daher nicht zusammenarbeiten. Ähnlich äußert sich gegenüber der »HAZ« Rebecca Seidler, Vorsitzende des Landesverbandes der Israelitischen Kultusgemeinden von Niedersachsen.
In dem »HAZ«-Artikel kommen nur Kritiker*innen des Antrags zu Wort. Daran stört sich Espen Rechtsteiner vom Kreisverband Lüneburg, der die Abstimmung zur Anerkennung des Genozids am Wochenende unterstützt. Jüdinnen und Juden würden häufig allgemein für Handlungen Israels in Haftung genommen, sagt Rechtsteiner dem »nd«. Auch in der »HAZ« erfolge diese Gleichsetzung.
Gegenantrag soll Thema »differenzierter betrachten«
Die Grüne Hamburg hatte der »HAZ« im Interview erklärt, mit dem Beschluss der Kreis-Linken hätten sich diese »eigentlich disqualifiziert«. Die designierte Spitzenkandidatin sagte auch: »In einer Zeit, in der jüdische Menschen überlegen, Deutschland zu verlassen, weil sie hier Angst haben, tragen politische Parteien eine besondere Verantwortung, welche Signale sie aussenden.«
Die Grünen-Landesvorsitzende Greta Garlichs ist von dem Antrag ebenfalls nicht angetan. Die Partei teile »die Sorge über das unermessliche Leid der Menschen in der Region«, erklärte sie, ohne jedoch die Betroffenen zu nennen. Und: »Ein Landesparteitag ist jedoch kein Internationaler Gerichtshof.«
Dem widerspricht Rechtsteiner, der auch Mitglied der Grünen Jugend ist: »Wir haben eine klare Haltung zu Völkerrechtsverbrechen Russlands, aber wenn es um den Genozid in Gaza geht, ist es doch sehr still.«
Deutschland zweitgrößter Waffenlieferant Israels
Im Antrag begründen die Mitglieder der Kreisverbände ausführlich, warum in Hameln auch internationale Politik behandelt werden sollte. Die Grünen trügen wegen ihrer Rolle in der Bundesregierung nach dem 7. Oktober 2023 besondere Verantwortung, heißt es in dem Antrag.
Deutschland sei nach den USA der zweitgrößte Waffenlieferant Israels: Von 2020 bis 2024 stammten laut dem Internationalen Friedensforschungsinstitut in Stockholm 33 Prozent der konventionellen Waffenimporte Israels aus Deutschland. Fregatten und Torpedos für die Marine sowie aus Deutschland motorisierte Panzer seien auch in Gaza zum Einsatz gekommen.
Ähnliche Anträge fanden auf früheren Grünen-Parteitagen, auch auf Bundesebene, keine Mehrheit oder wurden derart umgebaut, sodass sie Israel am Ende nur noch zur Einhaltung des Völkerrechts ermahnen.
Gegenantrag des Landesvorstands
Auch zum Stader Antrag gibt es seit Dienstag einen Gegenentwurf des Landesvorstands der Grünen mit dem Titel »Für die Stärke des Rechts statt des Rechts des Stärkeren«. Er betont das Existenzrecht Israels sowie die historische Verantwortung Deutschlands für den Schutz jüdischen Lebens. Zugleich beschreibt er das Leid der palästinensischen Bevölkerung in Gaza und die Verschärfung der Lage im Westjordanland. Für eine abschließende rechtliche Bewertung des Genozidvorwurfs möge die Entscheidung des Internationalen Gerichtshofs abgewartet werden, heißt es weiter.
Den Antrag kritisieren die Landes-Grünen auch, da dieser »nichts zum Existenzrecht Israels und zum Terror der Hamas« sage. Bewusst, kontert der Initiator Claas Goldenstein auf nd-Anfrage: »Der Antrag bezieht sich ausschließlich auf die Anerkennung des Genozids in Gaza und Verpflichtungen, die sich für uns direkt daraus ergeben. Die Hamas kommt nicht vor, weil sie für diese Beurteilung nicht relevant ist.«
Auch die Grüne Jugend spricht regelmäßig von einem Genozid in Gaza. Gleichzeitig werden die Taten der Hamas vom 7. Oktober immer wieder als terroristisch benannt.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

Supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and Aipac drive antisemitism
A supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s (Aipac) actions are increasing antisemitism in the US, according to a new poll.
The poll commissioned by J Street, a US-based pro-Israel think tank, shows a deep gap between how Jewish American voters view organisations like Aipac and Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, compared to how the state of Israel and its allies in the US portray antisemitism.
The poll says 66 percent of Jewish voters in the US believe that Aipac’s campaign spending against candidates who criticise Israel actually increases antisemitism in the country.
In addition, 60 percent believe that Jewish organisations that label harsh criticism of Israel as antisemitic are exploiting concerns about antisemitism to defend unpopular Israeli government policies.
Notably, 80 percent of Jewish voters believe that Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank and Gaza are increasing antisemitism in the US.

“Conventional wisdom about the impact of Jewish concerns over antisemitism and what it means to support Israel often misses the mark on how Jews process these issues in America’s political context,” Jim Gerstein, founding partner at GBAO Strategies, which conducted the poll between 28 October and 3 November, said.
“The reality is that Jews express nuanced thinking on these issues that is frequently missing in the extensive media coverage of the Jewish community,” he added.
The US midterm elections marked a sweeping Democratic victory where the US war on Iran and US support for Israel played a central role in races such as Michigan.
Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed won the race there in a historic landslide against Aipac supported Republican candidate Mike Rogers.
Sayed, who campaigned on cutting US aid to Israel along with other Middle Eastern countries and condemned Israel’s genocide on Gaza, won 60 percent of early Jewish voters, according to a poll by Mercury Public Affairs.
The poll also showed that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has been smeared as being an antisemite, had a higher favorability rating among Jewish Americans, 49 percent, compared to outgoing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, at 20 percent.
Overall, the poll from GBAO Strategies found that 72 percent of Jewish voters supported Democratic candidates and that 76 percent supported sanctions against “violent West Bank settlers”.
The president of J Street said the poll underscored the falsehood of stereotypes about Jewish voters in the US.
“Jewish Americans have been treated as a political football throughout this election cycle, with politicians and commentators insisting that our community demands unconditional support for the Israeli government. These results tell a very different story,” Jeremy Ben-Ami said.
“Jewish voters overwhelmingly backed Democrats, strongly oppose President Trump and support holding the Israeli government accountable for its actions. They want American leadership that advances peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians, and they are rejecting the idea that supporting Israel means writing its government a blank check,” he added.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: DP World Tour ready to embrace rebels including DeChambeau after LIV Golf collapses
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Matt Hughes
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The DP World Tour is expecting an influx of players from LIV Golf next year and is ready to extend an olive branch to all the former rebels, including the face of its doomed revival, Bryson DeChambeau.
The two-time US Open winner had been due to sign for LIV 2.0 next season, saying recently their “business plan made a lot of sense” and that the reborn rebel tour would “last forever,” but instead they began bankruptcy proceedings in a New Jersey court on Thursday following the withdrawal of their primary financiers, BC Partners.
In a 13-minute hearing LIV’s lawyers announced formal plans to liquidate rather than set up a new tour following the decision of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund to withdraw their funding from next season.
PIF spent more than $7bn in five years setting up the rebel tour that split golf in two before protracted talks over merging with the PGA and DP World Tours involving US president Donald Trump that ultimately collapsed.
“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in court. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximising wind-down in their business.”
LIV subsequently released a statement confirming their withdrawal from the sport. It read: “Since April 2026, the league’s leadership team, with the support of its independent directors and advisors, has run a disciplined and thorough process to identify the best path forward for the company and its stakeholders.
“Despite extensive discussions, the relevant parties were ultimately unable to reach a consensual resolution of certain outstanding terms of the transaction contemplated by the Restructuring Support Agreement (RSA).
“As a result, the RSA has been terminated, and the transaction is not expected to move forward at this time.”
LIV’s withdrawal just a month after announcing BC Partners’ funding has left their players facing uncertain futures, although many of them will have the option to join the DP World Tour through a variety of means, if not the PGA Tour.
DeChambeau is ineligible to join the PGA Tour, where he has not played for more than four years, due to a blanket ban on LIV players that runs for 12 months from the date of their last tournament appearance on the Saudi Arabia-funded circuit.
The 33-year-old has never been a member of the DP World Tour, but as a former major winner has an option to join that expires next year, with 16 November the deadline for applications.
Under DP World Tour regulations major champions are given a five-year window for joining, but 12 months is taken off for every year the option is not activated, leaving 2027 as the last season open to DeChambeau.
The major champion window has already expired for LIV players Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson, although the DP World Tour will permit them to play at certain events under their new Invite Policy, which represents an attempt to add value to lesser tournaments.
Such invitations will not be offered to premier events such as the PGA Championship at Wentworth or the Scottish Open, but a tournament victory elsewhere would permit the winner to apply for category three membership of the DP World Tour facilitating a full return.
Other LIV players eligible for invitations include Joaquin Niemann, Thomas Pieters, Charles Howell III and Lucas Herbert.
In addition around 15 LIV players, including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton, still hold DP World Tour membership so are eligible for every event. Although Sergio García resigned his membership in 2022 to join LIV the Spaniard’s career earnings mean he retains a category ranking and is able to reapply, which he has said he will do.
With no indication from the PGA Tour that they are willing to relax their one-year ban following LIV’s implosion many of the rebels appear likely to play at DP World Tour events, following the example set by Patrick Reed. On leaving LIV Golf in August 2025 the American joined the DP World Tour and is currently No 2 in the rankings, earning a PGA Tour card for next season.
While they have not commented publicly, DP World Tour officials are understood to feel that LIV’s imminent liquidation has vindicated their new hardline approach to the tour. Any player who signed up for LIV 2.0 would have been banned from the DP World Tour next year and been ineligible for the 2027 Ryder Cup, with chief executive officer Guy Kinnings saying the players must “make a choice,” a new policy that led to Rahm and Hatton leaving LIV. While LIV 2.0 did have $300m of funding in place from BC Partners they were unable to secure enough players to service the planned 17-tournament global season.
With the two main tours both making clear that the era of conditional releases and “double dipping” was over only 15 players led by DeChambeau agreed to stay on, with the Financial Times reporting that only four of them signed contracts.
BC Partners claimed last month that they had 30 players committed to sign up, with another 10 still deliberating, but proved unable to agree financial terms with enough of them, as they confirmed in a statement following the court hearing.
“BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf,” it read.
“While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders.”

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/emmanue.title: 5 novembre : la force a changé de camp
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/emmanue.author: Sébastien Crépel
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/emmanue.text:
5 novembre : la force a changé de camp
Avez-vous remarqué ? C’est devenu un mantra presque comique des chaînes d’information et des stations de radio. Aucun intervenant, même le plus hostile à la grève, ne peut plus omettre de reconnaître que les revendications de la jeunesse et du mouvement social sont « légitimes ». C’est un passage obligé. Ce n’était pas gagné il y a à peine un mois.
La vie chère, les salaires, les fins de mois difficiles, le nombre de professeurs, les salles de classe… Tout le monde égrène les sujets en convenant doctement qu’ils sont importants. Et pour cause : 88 % des Français approuvent ces exigences, selon un sondage Elabe. Avec 1,6 million de personnes dans les rues ce jeudi 5 novembre, elles sont en effet devenues matériellement incontournables. C’est bien ce qui gêne dorénavant la droite et l’extrême droite, dont même les électorats se retrouvent massivement dans les slogans lus dans les cortèges.
Cette soudaine marque de considération sonne faux, après des années de criminalisation et de répression de syndicalistes et de manifestants éborgnés, amputés, arrêtés, traités comme moins que des chiens. Comme s’il suffisait aujourd’hui de dire aux exploités et à leurs enfants : nous admettons que vos vies comptent. Mais le mouvement social ne rentrera pas à la maison muni de cette simple assurance.
Quand le mouvement est la masse
Il n’a que faire d’une validation par Emmanuel Macron et sa bande ; il attend les réponses qu’on lui refuse en termes de moyens pour les services publics, pour le niveau de vie. Ce jeu de Tartuffe dure depuis des semaines. Il était déjà à l’œuvre dans la détestable culpabilisation du mouvement social avec l’affirmation, fausse, que les regrettables violences et destructions du 17 octobre seraient la cause de l’effacement médiatique et politique des demandes des manifestants, alors que c’est exactement l’inverse.
Qu’on arrête de se payer notre tête. Même quand les défilés sont calmes, la Macronie réagit toujours par le mépris et la matraque. Si la répression faiblit et que les revendications s’imposent aujourd’hui, c’est parce que le mouvement gagne en puissance, et qu’il est la masse. Il est plus difficile de disperser un million de personnes qu’un millier. La force a changé de camp.
Le journal des intelligences libres
« C’est par des informations étendues et exactes que nous voudrions donner à toutes les intelligences libres le moyen de comprendre et de juger elles-mêmes les événements du monde. »
Tel était « Notre but », comme l’écrivait Jean Jaurès dans le premier éditorial de l’Humanité, le 18 avril 1904. 122 ans plus tard, il n’a pas changé.

Je veux en savoir plus !
