https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Architect Kae Ito creates a modular ‘secret garden’ for Art Week Tokyo's bar
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Azby Brown
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Since its inception in 2022, the pop-up AWT Bar has become one of the most appreciated hubs of Art Week Tokyo. This year, the architect Kae Ito has been commissioned for the spatial design. Ito opened her independent firm Office Itokae in 2025 after ten years at the Pritzker Prize-winning firm Sanaa / Kazuyo Sejima & Associates in Tokyo, where she worked on notable projects like the Better Co-Being pavilion for Expo 2025 Osaka, the Inujima Landscape Project and myriad exhibition designs in Japan and abroad.
Her AWT Bar, titled Kuru Kuru, she says, is intended to evoke a “secret garden”. Ingenious openwork structures of stainless steel and acrylic are distributed throughout the space, their placement guided by a geometric design on the floor. Multimedia elements by the artist Nile Koetting further enliven the space.
Ito recently spent time in Mongolia investigating ger, the traditional nomadic homes of the region, which are designed to be easily folded up and moved. Like those, Kuru Kuru is made of modular, collapsible elements, composed of rings and semi-circles, with a simple locking mechanism to render them stable. Colour-coded acrylic hemispheres have flat upper surfaces that form seats, tables or counters. These exquisitely fabricated units call to mind orreries or models of atoms. An aluminium-covered wall with circular service openings reinforces the science-lab vibe. Ito says, “I’m hoping [the bar] encourages people to have a happy time, eating and drinking with other visitors.”
Chef Ryuichi Yokomizo’s orchestration of the culinary experience at the AWT Bar is a sophisticated inversion of expectations. Following nine years at the Michelin-starred Joël Robuchon restaurant in Tokyo’s Ebisu district, the 30-year-old chef was asked to helm La & Le in Aoyama, which opened in March this year. For Art Week Tokyo, he is presenting two canapés: a gâteau of duck rillettes and pain d’épices, and a tarte tatin-inspired sablé.
These pleasantly deceiving creations display a beautiful autumnal colour palette, and reward the diner’s attention. The beautifully constructed savoury option layers duck rillettes over dark pain d’épices, finished with foie
gras mousse, a paper-thin slice of apple, caramelised walnuts and delicate sprigs of micro amaranth. The tarte reimagines the classic tarte tatin, layering deeply caramelised apple over a sablé Breton base, topped with a quenelle of calvados-infused buttercream and artfully placed micro celery. Each masquerades as its opposite: the savoury rillettes appear at first glance to be a dessert, while the sweet tarte appears savoury.
“I’m deeply interested in the element of surprise in cuisine,” Yokomizo says. “My theme for Art Week Tokyo, Entre, centres on the Japanese ideas of tsunagu—to connect—and aida—the space between,” he says. “Like art, cuisine changes with one’s point of view. I hope to show how simply changing the angle of approach can transform eating into an entirely different experience. I believe that sharing good food and drink in this way can foster deeper communication.”
The artist-devised cocktails on offer are similarly inventive. Mariko Mori’s All That Shinesuses luminous kuzumochi spheres, tapioca balls and rose caviar to evoke “the invisible ripples that are sent out into the world as our souls interact”. For Part-Time Job, Yoshihiro Suda reached back into his past as an illustrator for cider and whisky brands to make a cocktail as bittersweet as his memories. Natsumi Aoyagi’s sudsy Caipirinha de Cinco Sabões (Caipirinha of Five Soaps) is accompanied by a fable that alludes to the drink’s historical rural Brazilian roots. Combining uniquely ambitious design, cuisine and cocktails, the AWT Bar promises an unforgettable multisensory experience.
• AWT Bar, Art Week Tokyo, 4-8 November

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘Travel guides are far from neutral forms’: Art Week Tokyo video programme goes off the map
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Lisa Movius
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Generations of tourists have criss-crossed the world clutching dog-eared guide books. With lists of must-see landmarks, advice on local customs and listings of places to eat, drink and sleep, guide books promise to contain all that you could ever need to know about foreign places.
This year’s Art Week Tokyo (AWT) Video programme challenges that assumption, with a selection of single-channel moving image works that ask what is mapped, and what is left out of view.
“My interest in travel guides is less in them as a genre or style of literature,” says sector curator X Zhu-Nowell, “and more as a form that choreographs bodies within inhabited spaces, idealised landscapes, and any other kind of locale that has been deemed necessary to map out.” The showcase considers geography as shaped by migration, memory, labour and ideas.
Of the ten artists showcased in Your Travel Guide To…, five are from Japan and one is from the Japanese diaspora. Zhu-Nowell, who is the executive director and chief curator of Shanghai’s Rockbund Art Museum, has worked with four of the artists previously, including Berlin-based Kandis Williams, who has never shown in Japan before. “It’s important and meaningful to bring their work in this context alongside new companions,” Zhu-Nowell says.
Connecting countries
Williams’s video A Travel Guide: Black Gothic in South Korean Horror (2025) draws upon Victor Hugo Green’s famous The Green Book guide for Black Americans during the Jim Crow era. “It identified restaurants, hotels, gas stations, soda shops and other businesses where Black travellers could expect to be served and were at less risk of harassment or price gouging,” says Zhu-Nowell. Williams reflects upon this history and frames the work around “the political reality that mobility equals power”. Showing the Black American artist moving through Korea connects the two countries’ shared “musical aesthetics, histories of suppressed mourning, and experiences of militarisation and state violence.”
Zhu-Nowell also highlights New York-based artist Ken Okiishi’s “addictive” video Brian at Home (2020-25), which consists of Zoom calls with the artist’s personal trainer, who lives in a “smart-home hellscape” in New York City called “Denizen” with “a seemingly endless array of app-based appliances and perks”. Okiishi walks the viewer through this “highly designed public/private space [to] watch its promise of frictionless inclusivity start to come apart”.
The exhibition also includes the Berlin- and Beijing-based He Xiangyu, while Linda Iha, Fuyuhiko Takata and Atsushi Yamamoto are based in Japan, as were the late Keiichi Tanaami (1936-2024) and Hiroyuki Oki (1964-2025), both masters of handcrafted moving images. This range of perspectives combines for a nuanced exploration of how “travel guides are far from neutral forms, and often do a poor job of concealing that lack of neutrality”, Zhu-Nowell says. “Each form they take reflects the long and complex history these objects have as difference-mediating technologies and storytelling devices.”
The curator cites as an example the “the infamous 18th-century ars apodemica guides that instructed wealthy European young men on a ‘world tour’ how to observe, behave, and even listen to ‘others’ in foreign cultures”, an entitled inverse of The Green Book. “Those pocket travel guides that proliferated at the end of the 20th century are also fairly famous,” Zhu-Nowell says. “Today, new forms, digitised and even more pocketable, have emerged from a self-described ‘nomadic’ class of travel-influencer globalists. But in every case, the framing power of travel guides underlines [philosopher] Katherine McKittrick’s point about how geography is never a neutral space.”
• AWT Video, SMBC East Tower, 1F Earth Garden, 1-3-2 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, 4-8 November, 10am–6pm

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Five exhibitions to see during Art Week Tokyo
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Paul Laster
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Utanhole, KaiKai Kiki Gallery, ongoing
Rising Japanese artist Utanhole creates dreamlike, pastel-hued paintings that blend cinematic suspense with manga-style precision. Born in 2001, she graduated from the Tokyo University of the Arts in 2025. She characterises her signature style as “soft violence”, a thematic concept defined by intense emotional and visual contrasts. Utanhole’s paintings depict calm young figures with soft colours, delicate forms and innocent faces set against chaotic scenes of collapsing cities, weapon-laden spaces and deadly explosions, highlighting the stark contrast between innocence and chaos. Her work draws on chūnibyō, a Japanese term for intense, dark adolescent fantasies. Rather than shocking, the Tokyo-based artist’s solo gallery debut features new large-scale paintings and a selection of drawings that explore the inner coping strategies and desires characteristic of contemporary youth culture.
Seeds and Roots: How to Cultivate a City, Tokyo Opera City Art Gallery, until 20 December
Exploring how city residents can re-engage with nature in an increasingly artificial environment, this group exhibition uses art to investigate the new ecosystems thriving in the literal cracks of asphalt, including non-native species, self-sustaining plants and organisms that coexist with concrete and plastic. Core themes include reshaping urban nature, revitalising bodily sensations and integrating cross-disciplinary views. As human activities disrupt ecosystems, the boundary between natural and artificial blurs. The exhibition promotes coexistence with these changes rather than resisting or reverting to the past. Artworks are metaphorical seeds inspiring visitors to imagine roots reconnecting with the earth and senses. The show includes artists such as Tomoko Azumi, Yasutake Iwana, Akari Kaneko, Akiko Ikegami, Yoko Daihara, Yoji Ohno and Akane Saijo, who use everyday activities—living, wearing, eating and excreting—to reimagine our environment.
Miho Dohi, Hagiwara Projects, until 12 December
A celebrated Japanese artist, Miho Dohi is internationally known for her small, intricately layered, tactile abstract sculptures, which she calls buttai, a Japanese term combining the characters for thing and body. She produces enigmatic assemblages that creatively combine common natural materials with industrial parts, relying on intuition, experimentation and physical activity rather than pre-planning fixed forms. During creation, she repeatedly flips her pieces to break away from a single viewpoint. The process is complete when an original, unexpected structure naturally emerges from the chaos. Returning to the gallery for her fourth solo show, the Kanagawa-based sculptor presents new works in materials that seem heavy yet hang lightly on walls or from the ceiling, as if floating in space.
Alicja Kwade: La Pêche miraculeuse, Pace Gallery, until 25 December
Alicja Kwade is a conceptual artist acclaimed for her interdisciplinary work across various media, all aimed at questioning human perception. The Polish-born, Berlin-based artist is recognised for her methodical, almost scientific approach to abstract existential questions. She uses natural materials and everyday objects to explore deep philosophical and scientific ideas, including space, time, gravity and social constructs. Kwade’s first solo show at Pace Tokyo explores empty space—the space within and between objects—and the unseen, unexperienced, unknowable in-between. Through sculptures and works on paper featuring peaches, clocks, tunnels, stones and clock hands, the exhibition addresses what constitutes the world, the transitional space between objects, and the viewer’s reflections on existence.
Nam June Paik: The 20th anniversary of his passing, Watari-um, the Watari Museum of Contemporary Art, until 23 November
Known as the “father of video art”, Nam June Paik trained as a classical pianist and musicologist before turning to visual art. A key figure in the 1960s Fluxus avant-garde movement, the late South Korean artist reshaped Modern art by using television sets, broadcasting networks and video recording devices as materials for sculpture, performance and installation. Drawing on the museum’s extensive collection, the retrospective examines how his innovative ideas—combining technology, Eastern philosophy and nature—remain relevant in today’s world of smartphones and AI. Rather than viewing him solely as a tech-focused artist, the show highlights Paik as both a performer and a deep thinker. The exhibition’s Japanese title Jugemu comes from a traditional rakugo story about endless life, symbolising the idea that Paik’s art and impact will endure forever.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ruinart invites Tadashi Kawamata to create work for Art Week Tokyo
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: The Art Newspaper
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A little bit of France has come to Tokyo. Maison Ruinart—the world’s oldest champagne maker—has invited Japan-born, Paris-based artist Tadashi Kawamata to create a work for Art Week Tokyo.
Conversations with Nature 2026 will take place in Ruinart’s pop-up champagne and art bar in Daikanyama. Kawamata is known for site-specific installations made of wood and furniture parts. For this work he visited Ruinart’s vineyard near Reims, making works in response to what he felt there—the morning mist, the wind, the birds and insects.
The three installations he created “ask us to reconsider the relationship between nature and humanity”, according to a statement.
• Ruinart Champagne & Art Bar, Daikanyama T-Site Garden Gallery, 16-15 Sarugaku-cho, Shibuya-ku, 28 October-8 November

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/03france.title: Pretending to listen
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/03france.author: Magali Della Sudda & Grégory Rzepski
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/03france.text:
‘What matters to me,’ French education minister Édouard Geffray told France Info on 6 October, ‘is that secondary school students are heard within a democratic framework. Last night I launched a platform where every student can contribute and explain their problems and expectations.’ But when journalists asked whether this was simply a repeat of the offer made to the Gilets Jaunes in early 2019, the minister seemed lost for words.
Back then, in an attempt to resolve that crisis, the government – supported by a consortium of consultancy firms and startups  – had launched a huge consultation exercise, also based on a digital platform. Right at the outset they warned they would only consider contributions submitted online. But, in fact, the authorities never responded to the exercise at all. They also spirited away the books of grievances compiled by rural mayors and the protesters who gathered at roundabouts. Since then, successive governments seem in fact to have gone ever further in the opposite direction in response to protesters’ demands for equality and democratic freedom.
The consultation on pension reform (2018-19) and the Citizens’ Convention on Climate (2019) illustrate how public participation in decision-making is generally confined to collecting views on decisions already taken by the authorities. These contributions are promptly disregarded when they prove too ‘subversive’.   Although the 2015 consultation on the proposed Law for a Digital Republic attracted 8,500 responses, it ultimately proved ‘pointless in substantive terms’, according to the Observatory on Digital Rights and Freedoms, because ‘the government adopted virtually none’ of the proposals ‘that had received the most support from Internet users’, notably the ones about free software. This was somewhat ironic, given that the law, by enshrining open public data and digital access for all, was supposed to get the country used to ‘civic tech’.
A world of ‘civic tech’

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/02france.title: Seen and heard – French youth on the barricades
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/02france.author: Laurent Bonelli
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/02france.text:
Every school pupil, university student, trade union representative or politician interviewed about the current protests in the media is under pressure to ‘condemn the violence’. The government won’t be outdone. Right at the outset, education minister Édouard Geffray drew attention to a ‘shift’ from barricades outside schools to ‘urban violence’ (Le Monde, 2 October 2026). Interior minister Laurent Nuñez announced that he had given ‘no instructions to exercise restraint’ (TF1, 2 October 2026).
Protesters were subjected to an unprecedented police crackdown. Thousands of people, the majority of them minors, were arrested and taken into custody. Several demonstrators have been maimed by tear gas grenades, stun grenades or rubber bullets. Police unions are trying to justify the violence by pointing out that hundreds of their officers and gendarmes have been injured since the beginning of the protests. The presidents of France’s regional councils have condemned the cost of the destruction. In response, the government is fast-tracking a bill known as ‘breaker pays’, which aims to make people protesting in groups liable in civil court ‘once they are aware that crowd dispersal has been ordered due to ongoing violence or property damage’.
Not everyone agrees that violence defines this social movement. Nathalie Arthaud, a spokesperson for the Trotskyist organisation Lutte Ouvrière (Workers’ Struggle), joked on the set of BFM TV, ‘I know the flames make a nice backdrop. And they must look very pretty because you’ve kept this background for most of the day, making it look like we’re in the midst of a civil war. But that’s not what’s actually happening’ (3 October 2026). The placards held aloft during marches also push back against the dominant media narrative: ‘Burning a bin only bothers the trash’ and ‘When young people point to their future, imbeciles look at the burning bins.’

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/01edito.title: France's widening revolt
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/01edito.author: Benoît Bréville
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/01edito.text:
Lucie and Robin have little to complain about at their secondary school in southern France - it has recently been refurbished and class sizes aren’t especially large. But on 17 October they joined a demonstration in solidarity with less fortunate students. ‘Even if things are OK for us in Rodez, it’s not like that everywhere, especially in the suburbs,’ they told a local news reporter.
This solidarity between school students from places with apparently little in common has mainly developed through social media, where there is much sharing of experiences, video clips and messages of support. It’s one of the distinctive features of the movement that has swept France since the start of this academic year. Another is that this mobilisation, unlike many previous ones, did not grow out of opposition to an education reform, but erupted suddenly, during an election year, in protest at the general deterioration of state education.
The same concerns crop up everywhere, in towns and suburbs large and small, from Créteil to Lamballe, Vaulx-en-Velin to Villefranche-sur-Rouergue, as well as in Paris, Marseilles, Mayotte (off the east coast of Africa) and French Guiana (South America): dilapidated, badly insulated school buildings, teaching posts unfilled, timetables full of gaps and ever-longer school days, the higher education web portal Parcoursup and its incomprehensible algorithm… Not to mention an increasingly bleak future, with artificial intelligence threatening jobs, climate change threatening the planet and the spectre of war threatening Europe.
It may seem surprising that secondary school students from the banlieues and rural areas should join forces after 15 years of relentless talk about France’s ‘territorial divide’, which has entrenched the idea of a gulf between the France of the big cities and ‘the periphery’, and between urban and rural youth.
According to this view, which is widespread in the media but contested by researchers. (…)

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malm-rooney-.title: Let Andreas Malm Speak
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malm-rooney-.author: Chris Saltmarsh
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malm-rooney-.text:
Let Andreas Malm Speak
Britain has banned climate scholar and left-wing activist Andreas Malm from visiting the country. Following the ban on Hasan Piker, it points to an alarming repression of pro-Palestine speech in Britain.
Andreas Malm’s work has been among the most important of any scholar in any academic field over the past decade. His theoretical and strategic contributions have led developments in our understanding of the climate crisis’s basis in capitalism and fed debates about how to respond.
Yet last week, Britain’s Home Office banned Malm from entering the country, on the grounds that his “presence in the UK is not considered to be conducive to the public good.”
Malm had been due to visit London to speak alongside Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori at a Tribune magazine event, attend the academic conference Historical Materialism, and be interviewed by BBC Radio 4.
No specific reason was given for the ban. But it seems that the government’s decision is due to Malm’s principled opposition to the proscription of the direct-action network Palestine Action, officially labeled a “terrorist organization.” The move came a fortnight after publisher Faber & Faber announced that it would withdraw Sally Rooney’s novels from the UK market due to her support for Palestine Action, which means she is unable to collect revenue in the country. She too had fallen victim to the government’s silencing of free speech on Palestine, and to measures widely condemned by leading authors, artists, and public figures.
In June, American left-wingers Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur had already been banned from entering the UK.
The decision by Andy Burnham’s government to ban Malm represents a further attack on the Marxist left. It denies ordinary citizens the opportunity to hear from someone who speaks and writes so clearly about the imminence of climate catastrophe, the horrors of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and their entanglement.
It is surely no coincidence that these are the two areas in which Burnham’s government is failing resoundingly.
The ban on Malm comes in the same month that Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea despite the Labour Party’s 2024 manifesto commitment to issue no new licenses for oil and gas.
It also comes just a few weeks after Burnham insisted that Labour could not work with Green councilors who failed to renounce their party’s policy holding that “Zionism is racism.” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s recent emotive denunciation of Israel’s ethnic cleansing and settler violence does not do enough to stop the material support that the British state continues to provide to the genocide.
Malm is not an extremist from whom the British public needs protecting. His work is resolutely in the Marxist tradition but is cited widely by scholars across disciplines and spanning the political spectrum.
The Destruction of the Earth
Malm’s contributions are many. His seminal 2016 work, Fossil Capital, is perhaps the most important theoretical account of the historical entanglement of fossil fuel production in capitalism. The Progress of This Storm stakes out a clear position in ecological Marxist debates, asserting the need for human agency in confronting the crises we face. In the early 2020s, Corona, Climate, Chronic Emergency and How to Blow Up a Pipeline elaborated on this with essential contributions to debates on climate strategy following the insurgency of Extinction Rebellion and school climate strikes. Coauthored with Wim Carton, Overshoot and The Long Heat then offered masterful accounts of the ideological and technological bases of the march toward climate catastrophe.
More recently, Malm’s impassioned 2025 work, The Destruction of Palestine Is the Destruction of the Earth, places Israel’s genocide in Palestine in its proper historical setting, locating it in the context of British empire and enduring expansion of the fossil economy.
Malm, like Rooney, is no terrorist. In fact, it is the power of his ideas and the clarity of his expression that make him particularly dangerous for the British government. It clearly fears that Malm — like Rooney, Palestine Action, and Just Stop Oil (JSO) — will expose their inexcusable negligence on the most consequential questions of our time.
This episode raises a sobering question not just for the Marxist left, but for anyone in Britain committed to freedom of speech and political expression, and anyone who might expect to publicly criticize any government failing to act on genocide and climate collapse in the coming years: If Burnham’s government is prepared to ban Malm from entering the country, how many of its own citizens would it gladly deprive of their political freedoms if it had the opportunity?
This is an instructive moment. The only real difference between Burnham’s Labour and his predecessor Keir Starmer’s rule lies in the world of vibes and affect. Burnham says he identifies with ordinary people’s problems, names neoliberalism as an enemy, and shares your cultural tastes, perhaps evoking some combination of hope, nostalgia, and northern English pride.
But his government shares with Starmer’s an inability to confront the precipitous decline in living standards, an enthusiasm for growing the destructive defense and AI industries, and ongoing material support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
It leaves untouched the massive intensification of state repression of peaceful protest introduced under the last Tory government (in response to Extinction Rebellion and JSO), which was extended to Palestine Action by Starmer’s government.
Even worse than Starmer’s, Burnham’s government has abandoned Labour’s hard-won commitment to stop new fossil fuel production in the North Sea.
Each of these positions undermines the medium- to long-term viability of human civilization as we know it. The banning of Malm is an insight into how ostensibly center-left governments will deal with political dissent as they fail to address the crises in the years to come.
The Marxist left, within and outside the UK, is not only a legitimate political tradition that must be protected from repression on principle. It is the political tradition offering the strongest insights and most vibrant debate on the nature of the crises we face and how to overcome them. Its repression is an assault on everyone.
We should express our solidarity with Andreas Malm and Sally Rooney. But this situation also raises wider demands: for the de-proscription of Palestine Action and the repealing of anti-protest legislation. And, more materially, for an end to the UK’s practical support for Israel’s genocide in Palestine and to fossil fuel production in the North Sea.
Each of these claims are basic expressions of humanity and should be uncontroversial to state out loud in Britain today. It is the moral responsibility of anybody in the public sphere to express them. Burnham’s government rejects them all, and for this deserves our unrelenting opposition.

https://gothamist.com/news/trump-adminis.title: Trump administration sends election monitors to NYC, NJ
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-adminis.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-adminis.text:
The United States Department of Justice said Tuesday it’s sending election monitors to polling sites in Manhattan and Brooklyn in New York, and three counties in New Jersey.
It’s the first time the DOJ is sending election monitors to all 50 states, according to the federal agency. The Trump administration has previously said it planned to deploy about 1,000 monitors nationwide, but hadn’t announced specific locations.
The DOJ said election monitors would be in Manhattan and Brooklyn as well as Westchester, Albany and Erie counties in New York. In New Jersey, they’ll be monitoring polls at Middlesex, Bergen and Union counties. Portions of Union County are in the 7th Congressional District, where Republican Tom Kean Jr. is hoping to fend off a challenge from Rebecca Bennett. The race is considered among the most competitive in the country as Democrats try to take control of the House.
Local Democratic leaders, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, have issued statements in recent weeks, urging voters not to be intimidated by federal authorities near the polls and warning that election interference and voter intimidation are illegal.
James said in a statement last week that while it is normal for the DOJ to send election monitors to polling sites, they can't demand identification from voters, interfere with poll workers or engage in political activity near the polls. She said if poll workers encounter people identifying as DOJ monitors without advance notice, they should contact county election officials.
The DOJ said the monitors would include workers from its Civil Rights Division, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and Office of Personnel Management observers.
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said during last week’s installment of WNYC’s “Ask Governor Sherrill” call-in show that state officials have been working to ensure those running elections throughout the state know how to protect voters’ rights.
“We have been briefing all of the poll workers, all the municipalities and the counties to make sure that they understand all their rights and that they are alerting us,” she said. “If there are any concerns at their polling place, we will be in court very, very quickly to shut down any attempt to interfere with our elections.”

https://gothamist.com/news/floyd-bennet-.title: Floyd Bennett Field gets $10M for project to reopen historic hangars
https://gothamist.com/news/floyd-bennet-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/floyd-bennet-.text:
The historic hangars at Floyd Bennett Field are getting closer to reopening to the public for the first time in nearly a century.
Gov. Kathy Hochul committed $10 million in funding on Monday for the first phase of a two-part plan to transform the shuttered hangars at New York City’s first commercial airport into a public space that can host educational programming as well as cultural events.
The redevelopment will reopen hangars 3 and 4 to the public for the first time in nearly a century.
“These haven't been open to the public in nearly a century,” said Anastasia Yankopoulos, director of development and capital projects at Jamaica Bay Rockaway Parks Conservancy.
“People being able to step on the same ground where famous aviators of the golden era were, like, fixing their planes, that’s the biggest excitement.”
The first phase of construction on hangars 3 and 4 includes building renewable energy sources onsite, the conservancy said. The plan includes solar power on the roof and geothermal energy in the lawn in front of the buildings. The structures will also get bathrooms and other upgrades for use as a large events space such as concerts.
The conservancy plans to break ground in early 2028, after the National Park Service finishes improvements to the building exteriors. The total time of construction is estimated to span one year for the first phase. The conservancy is fundraising for the project.
“This money from the governor was such a huge boost to get this project to where it needs to be,” said Elizabeth Stoehr, deputy director of the Jamaica Bay Rockaway Parks Conservancy.
The second phase, which could begin shortly after, would further build out the space with an observation terrace and an area for purchasing food and beverages. Hangar 3 is slated to support park activities such as kayaking and biking.
Hangar 4 will host research projects with the Science and Resilience Center of Jamaica Bay, which is restoring West Pond. The structure will house labs, classrooms, meeting rooms and a workshop. In total, the redevelopment will add approximately 50,000 square feet for public use.
“The very fabric of the building, the very bricks, the very concrete were sentinels of this incredible aviation history and this idea that real innovation happened there,” Stoehr said. “It is thrilling that we get to work in this space that has such historical significance.”
In their present condition, hangars 3 and 4 are not accessible to the public or acceptable for use. Since the airfield was decommissioned, the hangars have not had much usage.
“The hangars have never been appropriately programmed and used to their full potential,” Yankopoulos said.
Floyd Bennett Field is a defunct airport in the Marine Park section of southeast Brooklyn, located on Jamaica Bay. The airstrip was opened in 1931 after roughly three years of construction and a cost of approximately $4.5 million. In 1933, Floyd Bennett Field had more than double the flights of Newark Airport, and was the second-busiest airport in America.
During World War II, the airfield became a naval base until 1970. The Coast Guard continued to use the facility for its helicopters until 1998.
In 1974, the airstrip reopened as part of Gateway National Recreation Area and managed by the National Park Service. While the flights no longer take off from the airfield, the New York City Police Department uses the runways as a helicopter base and another runway is reserved for radio-controlled craft enthusiasts. The current facility also has a campground and hosts astronomy events.
The surviving original structures are listed in the National Register of Historic Places. According to the National Park Service, many famous aviators and historic flights took-off from Floyd Bennett Field, including Amelia Earhart, John Glenn and Howard Hughes.
The airport is named after Floyd Bennett, a navy pilot who was the first to fly over the North Pole. Bennett died at the age of 37 from pneumonia shortly after a mission to rescue a stranded crew during World War I.
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Floyd Bennett.

https://gothamist.com/news/remote-learni.title: Remote learning day for NYC schools means remote chance of learning, parents say
https://gothamist.com/news/remote-learni.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/remote-learni.text:
New York City schools were closed for Election Day — and many parents said they’d cast a vote for no more remote learning days if it were on the ballot.
For many families, the remote day kicked off with a familiar ritual that began in the pandemic: kids struggling to log on. Marie Onaga, a Brooklyn resident and mom to three kids ages 6 7, and 11, said she had pandemic flashbacks.
“I had this visceral response …. trying to get to Zoom class in time, trying to find the materials,” Onaga said.
Making sure all three kids signed on and attended classes was a herculean task.
“The Wi-Fi signal doesn't extend to all of the convenient parts of our house. So it's just been kind of a mad dash,” she said.
She praised teachers for doing their best, but she said the school calendar “just feels crazy to me.”
The remote day is tied to the city’s public school calendar, which is packed with cultural holidays. In recent years, the city has added Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year and Juneteenth to its holiday schedule. State law requires 180 instructional days.
Officials thought they had found a solution to the calendar conundrum by pivoting to remote learning during snow storms and Election Day. But when schools are closed and classes move online, parents are left scrambling to manage tech glitches and Zoom school with their own jobs.
Multiple parents told Gothamist they had difficulty logging Tuesday morning. At P.S. 130 in Windsor Terrace, parents received an email about technical delays due to the “overwhelming number of students” trying to log on to platforms.
Education department spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said the delays were brief and did not prevent kids from accessing remote classes.
"All systems remained accessible and performing well throughout the morning, and remote learning has been proceeding as planned,” she said. “This morning, the TeachHub dashboard, which directs families to remote learning platforms, experienced slower than usual response times.”
David Bloomfield, education professor emeritus at Brooklyn College and The CUNY Graduate Center, has advocated moving the public schools’ start date before Labor Day to create room in the crowded calendar and boost learning.
“Quality is sacrificed when Zoom is used to accommodate the calendar’s limited number of instructional days,” he said.
Brooklyn parent Aimee Kraft called November a “jack-o'-lantern month” with Election Day and Veterans Day off plus a half day for parent-teachers conferences in between. “I feel like there’s so many days off, there’s so much inconsistency, it just becomes really really complicated as a parent and as a professional,” said Kraft, a dentist with two kids aged 6 and 12. She suggested putting some of the holidays back on as school-days but with excused absences allowed for families’ religious and cultural observances.
Education department officials steered reporters with questions about the calendar issues to the teachers’ union, the United Federation of Teachers. The union’s contract with the city requires the school year begin after Labor Day.
Onaga said it’s clear teachers also struggle to manage remote days, especially teachers who are also parents. She said she watched as her first grader’s gym teacher kept shifting his video as he switched from crunches to jumping jacks, showing his own child doing remote learning in the background.
“He's a parent too,” she said. “So, it's been kind of crazy for all of us. … I just wish that we'd have an extra day of in-person instruction at some point in the year.”

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-posts-rec.title: MTA posts record riders over Halloween, marathon week
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-posts-rec.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-posts-rec.text:
It was a banner week for the New York City subway.
Last Thursday, 4.72 million people rode the subway, the most in a single day since the COVID pandemic shut the city down in 2020. The next day, the system saw its highest Friday ridership day since 2020 at 4.5 million.
On Halloween Saturday, 3.27 million riders got on the subway, the most on a Saturday since 2016. And during the New York City Marathon, the subway saw its highest Sunday ridership on record.
The numbers highlight the MTA’s continuing post-pandemic recovery as it has campaigned to get people back on the trains after lockdowns. The subway’s seven-day rolling average — which calculates the average daily ridership for each week — reached 4.19 million riders last week, its best week since the pandemic, MTA data shows.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a statement that the MTA’s investments in the system had paid off.
“From the streets to the subways, New Yorkers were on the move this weekend in record numbers,” Hochul said. “The subway is the lifeblood of our city and from Halloween to the marathon, the major events that make New York special simply would not be possible without mass transit.”
New York City Transit said it deployed additional subway service throughout the weekend in anticipation of the spike in straphangers. And it was needed: Videos posted to social media over Halloween showed massive crowds entering and exiting the West 4th Street subway station ahead of the popular Greenwich Village parade.
Mass transit serving the tri-state area has also shown promising signs of recovering from pandemic-era lows in ridership. When New York celebrated the New York Knicks’ championship title with a ticker-tape parade through lower Manhattan on June 18, the Long Island Rail Road and Metro-North Railroad service posted a post-pandemic ridership record of 369,482 and 302,486 riders, respectively.
The night the Knicks actually won the championship — just the week before on June 13, a Saturday — subway ridership was above 3 million riders and more New Yorkers got on the system after midnight than on the New Year’s Eve coming into 2026.
Danny Pearlstein, policy and communications director for transit advocacy group Riders Alliance, said the MTA’s strong numbers show the subway system remains the “bedrock that connects New Yorkers” and that continued investments are needed to sustain its heavy use.
The MTA is making billions in dollars of investments to improve the existing infrastructure of subways, buses and railroads through its five-year capital plan that will purchase hundreds of new subway cars, rehabilitate train repair yards and add modern signal systems.
The transit agency is also constructing the Second Avenue Subway, which will extend the Q line by three stations into East Harlem, and is in the design phase of the Interborough Express, a light rail line that will connect more than a dozen subway stations between Brooklyn and Queens.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Yes, Stevie Wonder is playing MSG. No, you can't afford tickets. See these shows instead.
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hank Shteamer
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
The concert of the month, and maybe the year, will go down at Madison Square Garden on Nov. 19, when Stevie Wonder plays a 50th-anniversary gig for a little album called Songs in the Key Life. We regret to inform you, however, that the show is sold out and that resale prices are frankly unbelievable.
If you’re not one of the lucky ones already holding a ticket, don’t despair: While you may miss Stevie, November brings a ton of other enticing show options to NYC. An international folk fest, top-notch indie acts young and old, the final local appearance from a beloved jazz outfit — read on for the full rundown.
Brooklyn Folk Festival
“Everywhere you go there's this incredible grassroots music that's been around for hundreds or thousands of years and is played by regular people,” Eli Smith said in 2014, describing the sounds he spotlights at the annual Brooklyn Folk Festival, which he founded back in 2009. What’s special about the weekend-long event is that it defines “folk” as a sensibility rather than a genre. Alongside bluegrass pros like Tony Trischka and eminent singer-songwriters such as Bonnie “Prince” Billy, this year’s edition also presents Balinese music from Gamelan Yowana Sari; Lonnie Holley, the Alabama multimedia artist and improv-driven musical force; Dolunay, which performs Turkish and Rumeli songs; the Cherokee singer-songwriter Agalisiga “Chuj” Mackey; and much more across three nights, with late-night after-parties at Red Hook’s Jalopy Theatre.
This Is Lorelei
It’s funny that Nate Amos’s weirder musical project was the one that broke first. The guitarist and producer first rose to indie-rock prominence with Water From Your Eyes, his quirky duo with vocalist Rachel Brown. It’s only more recently that serious buzz has built for This Is Lorelei, the solo act he’s been working on for a decade-plus. His latest album under that moniker, The Singer in My Band, is one of the most critically acclaimed albums of the year, and deservedly so: Amos is an expert songwriter (he once said of the Beatles obsession he inherited from his father, “That’s kind of the closest thing to a religion that I’ve ever had”) who churns out timeless tunes informed by power pop, classic rock and country.
Durations
Public Records, Pioneer Works, Roulette, Whitney Museum, Nov. 9-15
Like the Brooklyn Folk Fest, Durations, which sprawls across various Brooklyn venues as well as the Whitney Museum during its weeklong run, is another conceptually driven happening that welcomes in many different aesthetics under a broad umbrella. As the organizers put it, the idea is to explore “how music connects body, mind, and imagination across time.” They’ve picked the right performers to help ensure a transcendent trip: Among the dozens of acts performing throughout the week are the master soundscapist William Basinski; revered electronic-music veteran Suzanne Ciani; accomplished composer Eiko Ishibashi, performing along with a silent film by Drive My Car director and close collaborator Ryusuke Hamaguchi; and incisive poet and theorist Fred Moten, appearing in his riveting duo with bassist Brandon López.
Chat Pile + Soul Glo
The past few years have seen a renaissance in wild, punk-descended sounds, and these two bands have both been major catalysts of that new wave. Chat Pile are one of the most unlikely breakout successes in recent memory: an Oklahoma City quartet (named after the toxic mining waste that still mars their home state) that marries controlled noise-rock bludgeon to howling catharsis and glints of melancholic beauty. They’re out behind their excellent latest, Who Loves the Sun, with support from Soul Glo, a Philly outfit that layers frontman Pierce Jordan’s unhinged inner monologues over a precision hardcore-punk attack.
The Bad Plus
The Bad Plus started out the 2000s as one of the buzziest groups in jazz and gradually evolved into an institution. Earlier this year, they announced a farewell tour, which makes its final local stop this month. If you mainly remember them as the piano trio that covered Nirvana and Aphex Twin, it’s worth checking back in while you still can. Now focused almost exclusively on original material, they’ve done some of the best work of their career with their current quartet lineup.
mary in the junkyard
David Addison, drummer for the rising London trio mary in the junkyard said recently that their name, dreamt up spontaneously by vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Clari Freeman-Taylor, handily describes “the sound of having like pretty, sort of angelic things and then junkyard, grime and noise and stuff.” Role Model Hermit, their debut album from earlier this year, nicely balances intimacy and abandon, framing lovingly constructed songs with ear-catching textures like swelling strings and postpunk-y percussion. Already a local favorite, the band returns for a two-night stand at Baby’s All Right.
Mary Lattimore
Each month, the Guggenheim extends its hours on the third Thursday of each month for its Late Shift performance series. The pre-Thanksgiving installment is a great one: a solo performance by Mary Lattimore, a harpist who has expanded the sonic possibilities of her instrument during the past decade-plus. Employing loops and effects the way a guitarist might, she weaves a magic carpet of sound that’s easy to get carried away on. Especially when combined with the museum’s stunning spatial design, this one ought to be a real sensory voyage.
LCD Soundsystem
Knockdown Center, Nov. 19-22; Dec. 10-13
In 2011, James Murphy famously went out on top with LCD Soundsystem, the dance-punk band that helped to soundtrack the first decade of 21st-century NYC life. He once said that watching the band get bigger and bigger “just kind of sickened me,” so he threw a triumphant farewell bash at Madison Square Garden and called it a day. That is, until five years later, when he re-formed the band at the behest of David Bowie himself. LCD aren’t as aligned with the zeitgeist as they once were, but they’re still a massive draw, as evidenced by this 12-night residency spanning two big Brooklyn and Queens rooms. Come “Dance Yrself Clean” with Murphy & Co.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-election-r.title: NY election results: Polls close soon for governor, congressional races
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-election-r.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-election-r.text:
New York voters have until 9 p.m. to cast their ballots in the governor’s race and hotly contested congressional contests that could help decide which party controls the U.S. House of Representatives.
Voters will decide three statewide races, headlined by Gov. Kathy Hochul’s battle against Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive.
Democratic Attorney General Letitia James also faces a challenge from Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor, while incumbent Democrat Tom DiNapoli faces Republican investor Joseph Hernandez.
But only a handful of key congressional races could have national implications.
That includes Republican Rep. Mike Lawler’s battle versus Democrat Cait Conley, a former Army officer, in the 17th District in the Hudson Valley. Further north, Democrat Blake Gendebien, a dairy farmer, is squaring off against Republican entrepreneur Anthony Constantino in the 21st District, a seat now held by retiring Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik.
In the New York City area, Democratic Rep. Tom Suozzi faces Republican Mike LiPetri in the 3rd District, which includes part of Nassau County and a small portion of northeastern Queens.
Voter turnout appears to be trending upward in much of New York state compared to 2022, the last time Hochul and the congressional midterms were on the ballot.
In New York City, about 1.8 million people voted in person or by mail as of 6 p.m., according to the city Board of Elections. With hundreds of thousands of additional votes expected by 9 p.m., the total will easily exceed the 1.8 million people who voted in the five boroughs four years ago.
Statewide, nearly 2 million people voted during the nine-day early voting period this year — a 66% jump from four years ago, according to the state Board of Elections’ unofficial tally.
Each of New York’s 62 counties saw a considerable increase, including an 83% jump in Queens and a 73% jump in the Bronx — two Democratic strongholds Hochul is counting on to juice her re-election effort. But New York City’s total increase (60%) trailed the rest of the state (71%). It was also 6% less than the city’s record early voter turnout in last year’s mayoral race.
Polls close at 9 p.m. across the state, with local election boards reporting results as they come in throughout the night.
Delays are expected, however, in Westchester County, where a programming issue with ballot scanners prevented voting machines across much of the county from counting ballots.
The state Board of Elections issued a statement saying the ballots are secure and will eventually be scanned. But it could complicate efforts to determine the winner of the Lawler-Conley race in a timely fashion.
The 17th District spans both sides of the Hudson River, including northern Westchester County.

https://gothamist.com/news/voting-machin.title: Voting machine snafu may delay results in NY House race between Lawler, Conley
https://gothamist.com/news/voting-machin.author: Karen Yi, Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/voting-machin.text:
Malfunctioning voting machines in Westchester County could delay results in one of the country's most closely watched congressional races, which could decide whether Democrats take back the House of Representatives.
The battleground 17th Congressional District race between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and his Democratic challenger Cait Conley includes parts of Westchester, just north of New York City, where a software glitch prevented scanning machines from tabulating thousands of paper ballots as voters went to the polls on Election Day.
Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins said late Tuesday that it’s unclear whether those ballots would be counted before the end of the day as both parties seek a joint court order to determine a protocol.
“ Right now they have not determined whether or not they are going to count them tonight,” Jenkins said on WNYC’s All Things Considered around 5:30 p.m. “That is a little up in the air.”
Jenkins said both campaigns want to make sure they can properly oversee the counting.
Conley, a former Army officer and counterterrorism official, hoped for strong turnout in the parts of the district in northern Westchester County, which backed Vice President Kamala Harris by more than 25 points in the 2024 presidential election.
The New York Board of Elections said the voting snafu stemmed from some scanning machines not getting a needed programming update, preventing them from reading and recognizing the paper ballots. Ballot reading software was updated in machines in a single Westchester municipality but was not made elsewhere in the county
The BOE said ballots were collected and secured in bags until they could be properly scanned and counted
“Accuracy will never be sacrificed for speed,” the BOE said in a statement.
In a phone interview with Gothamist, Conley said her campaign was working to ensure the process's security and integrity.
“ As a candidate, of course you want to get the results sooner than later, right?” Conley said. “But at the end of the day, what matters is voters having their voices heard. And so right now, what we need to focus on is how do we ensure in a bipartisan way that we get to an outcome where every single vote is counted.”
Lawler’s campaign did not return a request for comment. But in a press conference earlier in the day, Lawler said he expected the counting to be done tonight.
“ I would suspect, you know, we're gonna be in the early morning hours when we get an answer. But the bottom line is we need to have an answer tonight,” he said.
The race between Lawler and Conley was one of the most expensive in the country in both candidate and outside spending. Lawler’s political base is in Rockland County, where strong turnout in past elections helped propel him to victory.
The national Democratic Party has tried to oust Lawler since he was first elected in 2022 in a district with more enrolled Democrats than Republicans. He was one of only a handful of Republicans who won their seat last cycle despite voters in their congressional district supporting Harris for president.
Lawler tried to stress his independent streak, highlighting times he’s opposed President Donald Trump. At the same time, he campaigned alongside Trump and voted for his signature “One Big Beautiful Bill” tax cut.
Conley sought to tie the two together at every opportunity, calling Lawler a “puppet” of the president. She won a crowded primary in June to challenge the Republican incumbent.
Jenkins said Westchester County would conduct a thorough review of what caused the problem with ballot scanning machines so it does not happen again.

https://hyperallergic.com/mamdanis-five-.title: Mamdani's Five Ballot Questions Pass, But Arts Groups Remain Skeptical
https://hyperallergic.com/mamdanis-five-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/mamdanis-five-.text:
Mamdani's Five Ballot Questions Pass, But Arts Groups Remain Skeptical
Concerns over landmark sites and lack of public input have dampened trust in Proposal 3, in particular.
Two arts organizations remain concerned that one of New York City's approved ballot measures could weaken review processes over public land usage, leaving areas such as landmark sites vulnerable to hasty sales and without sufficient community input.
All five ballot measures passed with strong support in yesterday's midterms, though the Municipal Art Society (MAS) of New York and the New York Landmarks Conservancy objected to parts of Proposal 3, which expedites the review of eligible projects in three areas: street safety construction, the sale or leasing of city-owned property, and the acquisition of office space for city employees.
Both groups, along with organizations such as the League of Women's Voters, have expressed varying levels of agreement with its three bundled target areas and called for them to be considered separately for independent review.
The measure is one of five put forth by the Commission on Government Efficiency, a 15-member panel assembled by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. All items aim to streamline city operations through revising the City Charter, such as reducing city contractor paperwork and setting aside a rainy-day fund in case of emergency.
"New York has had a strong tradition of public participation and robust debate, and over time, that's been chipped away," Andrea Goldwyn, the director of public policy at New York Landmarks Conservancy, told Hyperallergic.
Goldwyn's primary concern is with the second prong of Proposal 3, which reduces public review when the city sells or transfers unused development rights at landmark sites. Originally, most sales or leases of city-owned property underwent a seven-month review process called the Uniform Land Use Review Process (ULURP) and required City Council's final approval.
Proposal 3 allows projects not believed to have a sizeable impact on the surrounding environment to bypass final City Council approval and go through a 90-day fast lane called the Expedited Land Use Review Procedure (ELURP). Projects approved for ELURP can be concurrently reviewed by community boards and borough presidents, and city-owned landmarked property can be sold without City Council approval. Undevelopable land can additionally be sold to owners of adjacent properties without a public auction.
The proposal also excuses the Department of Transportation (DOT) from notifying elected officials and community boards before starting major projects deemed necessary for safety, and can instead notify those stakeholders when construction commences. Consultations with the Police Department, Fire Department, the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities, and the Department of Small Business Services remain mandatory.
"We've gotten calls from people who see new projects going up in their neighborhoods that they didn't know about," Goldwyn continued. "I think we're going to be seeing more of that because people aren't going to have the kind of notification they're used to having."
The final part of the proposal removes hearing requirements and approvals from the City Council and the City Planning Commission about acquiring or leasing office space for city employees, instead leaving it solely to Yume Kitasei, the commissioner for the Department of Citywide Administrative Services. Local community boards and all five borough presidents must still be notified of each proposal.
In an earlier statement, MAS stated that trimming down these review processes "could make it easier to sell or transfer valuable public land and development rights without sufficient safeguards to ensure lasting public benefits."
MAS called for a stronger framework that determines how public lands can be used. Such recommendations include prioritizing land for parks, affordable housing, and other projects that serve the public, rather than selling or leasing land to parties with unclear interests.
"Streamlining government processes should not come at the expense of public accountability or lasting community benefits," the statement adds.

https://hyperallergic.com/miquel-navarro.title: Miquel Navarro, Sculptor of Cities Real and Imagined, Dies at 81
https://hyperallergic.com/miquel-navarro.author: Lisa Yin Zhang
https://hyperallergic.com/miquel-navarro.text:
Miquel Navarro, Sculptor of Cities Real and Imagined, Dies at 81
In this column honoring those we lost in the art community, we remember a leading Spanish sculptor, a Dutch museum leader, and an Indian modernist.
In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.
Miquel Navarro (1945–2026)
Spanish sculptor of imaginary cities
The Spanish artist's hometown, Mislata in Valencia, served as a lifelong inspiration for his City sculptures, large-scale installations that invite visitors to walk through hundreds of abstract geometric shapes as skyscrapers. Fittingly enough, his imaginary cities became part of real urban landscapes, in the form of public works in Spain and abroad.
He was one of the artists to represent Spain at the 1986 Venice Biennale, and received the Spanish Ministry of Culture's Premio Nacional de Artes Plásticas (National Award for Plastic Arts) that same year. His work is in the collections of the Guggenheim museums in New York and Bilbao, Museo Reina Sofía, Centre Pompidou, and more.
"Today Mislata loses one of its most beloved residents, a friend and a genius," Mislata Mayor and President of Fundació Miquel Navarro Carlos Fernández Bielsa said in a statement translated from Spanish, "a generous person and a world-renowned figure in sculpture, an irreplaceable creator."
Ursula von Rydingsvard (1942–2026)
Sculptor of monumental objects
Partially inspired by her childhood incarceration in post-World War II refugee camps, her enormous sculptures were whittled from massive cedar beams, including “Cedrus” (2016), an almost 20-foot-tall (~6 m) tornado made from 15,000 pounds (~6.8 t) of wood. Her work is in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and more.
“She was like the sun," Courtney Childress, her studio manager, said in this statement. "She was this force that pulled people in and kept them orbiting around her.”

https://hyperallergic.com/claire-valdez-.title: Claire Valdez Will Be Your Artist in Congress
https://hyperallergic.com/claire-valdez-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/claire-valdez-.text:
Claire Valdez Will Be Your Artist in Congress
The artist, former cultural worker, and union organizer won a seat in the US House of Representatives by nearly 70 percentage points.
Among the historic wave of triumphs for Democrats in yesterday's midterms, New York State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez, an artist, former cultural worker, and union organizer, was elected to represent New York's 7th Congressional District in the United States House of Representatives.
After a resounding win in the June primary, the 37-year-old Democratic Socialist will represent the so-called "Commie Corridor," a district encompassing north Brooklyn and western Queens that also overwhelmingly voted for Valdez's endorser, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, last November. She defeated her opponent, Republican Melvin Rivera, by 68 percentage points, and will succeed retiring Democratic Representative Nydia Velázquez, who has held the seat since 2013.
Central to Valdez's campaign were measures aimed at protecting unions and workers' rights, and addressing the affordability crisis.
"As somebody who once aspired to be an artist and came to New York to pursue that dream, the purpose of our movement is to make sure that anyone can be an artist, that everyone has the time off, and the living wages, and the healthcare, and the space to pursue passions, to spend time with family, to live a good life," Valdez told Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara in an interview in June this year.

https://taz.de/Nadeln-und-Naegel-in-Hall.title: Nadeln und Nägel in Halloween-Bonbons: Die wirkliche Gefahr
https://taz.de/Nadeln-und-Naegel-in-Hall.author: Ambros Waibel und Valérie Catil
https://taz.de/Nadeln-und-Naegel-in-Hall.text:
Nadeln und Nägel in Halloween-Bonbons: Die wirkliche Gefahr
Fälle von manipulierten Süßigkeiten an Halloween ängstigen. Wie ist der Stand der Ermittlungen? Und ist vom Süßen oder Sauren in Zukunft abzuraten?
Wie bei anderen religiösen Festen spielen Lebensmittel eine große Rolle bei Halloween. Während Nikolaus und Weihnachten eher im privaten Kreis gefeiert werden, ist das gemeinschaftliche Ostereiersuchen, etwa in Zoos und Freizeitparks, inzwischen weit verbreitet. Halloween unterscheidet sich durch eine besondere Geste und Sozialität, wenn überhaupt dann noch mit den Sternsingern zu vergleichen.
Die Geschenke kommen von Privatleuten und sind damit keiner Kontrolle unterworfen. Wenn Halloween ist, sind es die Schwachen, die Kinder, die Fordernden sind und nicht die ewig gegängelten Bittsteller. Es erinnert an Fasching und Karneval, an die temporär verkehrte Welt.
Kinder fordern, Kinder treten allein in eine (fremde) Erwachsenensphäre, Kinder nehmen Geschenke von Fremden an und sind im Dunklen allein unterwegs. Die englischsprachige Maxime „Never Take Candy from a Stranger“, also „Nimm niemals Süßigkeiten eines Unbekannten an“, ist für einen Tag ausgesetzt.
Es ist naheliegend, dass Halloween damit genug Projektionsfläche bietet für reale Ängste und popkulturelle, sogenannte „Poisoned Candy“-Mythen. Diese „Poisoned Candy“-Mythen sind ein hartnäckiges Phänomen, das jährlich an Halloween wieder aufflackert, unabhängig davon, ob die Fälle echt sind oder nicht: Demnach sollen an Halloween verteilte Süßigkeiten mit gefährlichen Gegenständen wie Nadeln oder Rasierklingen versehen oder gar vergiftet worden sein, um gezielt Kinder zu verletzen. Und ein Blick in die aktuellen Nachrichten lehrt, dass das sehr wirklich werden kann.
Ermittlergruppe in Österreich
Ein Großteil dieser Fälle konnte in der Vergangenheit widerlegt werden. Manchmal enttarnte man sie als Form der Massenhysterie. In anderen Fällen entstand dieses Gerücht, wenn ein Kind unerwartet starb, nachdem es zufällig eine Süßigkeit gegessen hatte, und ein Schuldiger gesucht wurde.
Bekannt ist auch der Fall eines Vaters aus den USA, der 1974 Zyankali in Brausepäckchen mischte, um die Lebensversicherung seines achtjährigen Sohnes zu kassieren – und sich dabei vom „Poisoned Candy“-Mythos inspirieren ließ.
Oder aber es handelte sich lediglich um eine versehentliche Kontamination, wie es in Rheinland-Pfalz dieses Jahr geschehen ist, oder um einen Produktionsfehler, bei dem etwa ein Metallgegenstand in eine Verpackung geraten war. Urteile des Bundesgerichtshofes unterscheiden hier übrigens zwischen „arteigenen“ und „artfremden“ Fremdkörpern. Der Verbraucher könne eine völlige Gefahrlosigkeit nicht erwarten.
Meldungen zu am Halloween-Wochenende in die Hände von Kindern gekommenen manipulierten Süßigkeiten kommen aus deutschen und österreichischen Bundesländern. In Wien wurde die Ermittlergruppe „Treat“ des österreichischen Bundeskriminalamts gebildet. Für Deutschland teilte das BKA auf taz-Anfrage mit, dass ihnen das Phänomen „grundsätzlich bekannt“ sei, die Verantwortlichkeit jedoch bei den Landeskriminalämtern liege.
Der Holzspieß im Schokoriegel
Das LKA NRW sprach auf Anfrage von 24 gemeldeten Fällen. Verletzte habe es keine gegeben. Erkenntnisse darüber, wer dahinterstecken könnte, gebe es nicht. „Über Tätergruppen oder Motive zu spekulieren“, heißt es weiter, sei deshalb „unseriös“.
Das LKA Bayern spricht von 25 gemeldeten Fällen – ebenfalls ohne Verletzungen. 2 Fälle wurden in Hamburg, 3 in Brandenburg gemeldet, 9 in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, wobei sich ein Kind leicht verletzt haben soll. Auch die anderen Bundesländer verzeichneten Fälle.
In einem Fall im thüringischen Landkreis Hildburghausen hat sich inzwischen herausgestellt, dass ein neun Jahre altes Mädchen den Gegenstand, einen Holzspieß, selbst in einen Schokoriegel gesteckt hat. Wieso das Kind dies gemacht habe, sei bisher nicht bekannt, sagte eine Sprecherin der Polizei der dpa. Der Vater des Mädchens hatte eine vorherige Anzeige bei der Polizei zurückgenommen. Auch in Bayern gibt es mittlerweile 2 Fälle, in denen Kinder eingeräumt haben, Süßigkeiten selbst mit Gegenständen präpariert zu haben.
Auch aus Ungarn und Kanada werden Fälle gemeldet. Es kam bisher zu leichten Verletzungen im Mund bei Kindern, die Polizei rät zur Vorsicht, warnt aber auch vor Panik.
Sadismus und Halloween
Was aber könnten, unseriös gefragt, mögliche Motive sein für das Verteilen von manipulierten Süßigkeiten, dieses „feige und hinterhältige Verbrechen“, wie es der österreichische Innenminister Gerhard Karner (ÖVP) nannte?
Lisa Natter von der kriminologischen Forschungsgruppe beim Bayerischen Landeskriminalamt (BLKA) sagte auf dpa-Anfrage, den Begriff „Halloween Sadism“, habe der US-Soziologe Joel Best bereits in den 1980er Jahren geprägt.
„Er hat das als moderne urbane Legende untersucht, die als wahr erzählt wird und auch gesellschaftliche Ängste ausdrückt, deren tatsächliches Ausmaß aber häufig durch empirische Belege nicht gedeckt ist“, erklärte Natter. Wichtig sei dabei: Einzelne Fälle – wie jetzt in Deutschland, aber auch zum Beispiel in Österreich, Irland, Dänemark und Norwegen – würden damit nicht bestritten. „Es zeigt sich vielmehr, dass die Erzählungen als Resonanzraum für allgemeinere gesellschaftliche Ängste dienen.“
Die Polizei Essen sagte der Süddeutsche Zeitung, man gehe von mehreren Tätern aus, die Anregungen im Internet gefunden haben könnten. Auch über soziale Medien koordinierte Aktionen seien möglich. Über Ermittlungserfolge sei aber nichts bekannt, viele Verfahren seien wieder eingestellt worden.
Das Auto ist die Gefahr
Und trotzdem ist Halloween kein völlig harmloses Fest. Auch in diesem Jahr wurden Kinder und Jugendliche mit Reizgas verletzt, mit Messern und Schreckschusswaffen bedroht und beleidigt. Auch hier ist die Motivlage diffus.
Eine konkrete Gefahr gibt es am Ende aber doch: Das Risiko für Fußgänger durch ein Auto getötet zu werden, ist an Halloween ohnehin schon erhöht. Für Kinder bis 17 Jahren, das zeigte eine 2018 veröffentlichte Studie, ist es in den USA an diesem Tag dreimal höher als an anderen Tagen.
Noch gefährdeter sind Kinder von 4 bis 8 Jahren. Für sie ist das Risiko sogar 10-mal so hoch. In Niedersachsen etwa wurde ein siebenjähriges Mädchen beim Halloween-Spaziergang von einem Auto erfasst und schwer verletzt.
Achtsam sein auf den Straßen ist das Motto. Und wie bei anderen frohen Festen bleibt am Ende die Erkenntnis, dass man sich den Spaß an Halloween nicht nehmen lassen soll. Wer daran denkt, dass ein Weihnachtsbaum Feuer fangen kann und es sogar bei der Ostereiersuche zu tödlichen Unfällen kommt, wird das Risiko für Kinder an Halloween nicht kleinreden und schon gar nicht ausschließen – aber zu einer abgewogenen Einschätzung kommen können.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

Trump im Magageddon
Nach dem Verlust der Mehrheiten in beiden Kammern des Kongresses wetzen Trumps einstige Vertraute bereits die Messer.
Der Staub lichtet sich, und der Blick auf die Wahlen in den USA offenbart ein politisches Jahrhundertbeben. Die Demokraten gewinnen beide Parlamentskammern und konnten sogar in republikanischen Hochburgen Erfolge erzielen. Die Strategie der Republikaner, auf Trump-Loyalisten zu setzen, ist gescheitert. Und so werden sich in den kommenden Monaten weite Teile der US-Rechten von Trump distanzieren.
Den Startschuss gab sein Vizepräsident J.D. Vance. Mit beinahe übermenschlicher Geschwindigkeit fiel er noch am Wahlabend Trump in den Rücken. Auf X postete er eine verblüffend realistische Analyse über die Gründe für die Niederlage: der Iran-Krieg, hohe Lebenshaltungskosten und die Beziehung zu Israel. Da brachte es auch nichts, den Rassismus-Regler im Wahlkampf auf »volle Pulle« aufzudrehen – die Preise an der Tankställe und in den Supermärkten blieben dieselben, und die Menschen haben das bemerkt, und jeder macht Trump dafür verantwortlich. Es wird interessant sein, was dies auch für die zukünftigen Beziehungen zu Israel bedeutet.
Und so beginnt das Maga-Schiff zu sinken, während die ersten Ratten von Bord springen. Damit für Vance der mediale Vorteil einer Vizepräsidentschaft für eine eigene Präsidentschaftskandidatur nicht zum Nachteil wird, beginnt dieser jetzt, vermehrt Trump zu kritisieren.
Der Präsident könnte dabei Opfer seines eigenen Prinzips werden, das er 2015 im Vorwahlkampf in einem Kommentar zum vorherigen republikanischen Präsidentschaftskandidaten John McCain auf den Punkt gebracht hat: »Er hat verloren, danach habe ich ihn nie mehr so sehr gemocht. Denn ich mag keine Verlierer.« Der ambitioniertere Teil seiner Weggefährten wird sich daran ein Beispiel nehmen.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://taz.de/DFB-Kader-von-Juergen-Klo.title: DFB-Kader von Jürgen Klopp: Manchmal ist die Form entscheidend
https://taz.de/DFB-Kader-von-Juergen-Klo.author: Frank Hellmann
https://taz.de/DFB-Kader-von-Juergen-Klo.text:
DFB-Kader von Jürgen Klopp: Manchmal ist die Form entscheidend
Der Nationalmannschafts-Kader von Bundestrainer Klopp ist für die nächsten Aufgaben etwas konventioneller aufgestellt. So gehört nun auch Niclas Füllkrug dazu.
Vergleichsweise locker hat Jürgen Klopp auf seinem Barhocker gewirkt, als er sich am Donnerstag auf dem DFB-Campus zum Interview in die Umkleidekabine setzte. Fragen stellte statt einer Journalistenschar nur Pressesprecherin Franziska Wülle für den verbandseigenen TV-Sender. Trotz aller Lässigkeit versicherte der Bundestrainer, es sei ihm schwergefallen, für die letzten Nations-League-Gruppenspiele gegen Serbien in Belgrad (13. November) und gegen die Niederlande in Berlin (16. November) seinen 24-köpfigen Kader zu nominieren, „weil – und das ist eigentlich die gute Nachricht – es wieder mehr Spieler verdient hätten, dabei zu sein. Aber so soll es sein.“
Gleichzeitig bewies der 59-Jährige, dass er nicht dogmatisch vorgeht. Es wimmelt in der Bundesliga nicht an klassischen Mittelstürmern mit verlässlichen Quoten. Wenn einer wie Niclas Füllkrug in Bundesliga und DFB-Pokal in zehn Spielen zwölfmal trifft, muss er wieder in den Kreis der Besten zurückkehren. „Er hat unterschiedlichste Tore geschossen. Er hat einen unglaublichen Einfluss bei Werder Bremen“, lobte Klopp.
Obwohl der 33-Jährige an der Weser seinen dritten Frühling erlebt, hatte der Bundestrainer zwischenzeitlich den Eindruck erweckt, eine Rückkehr mache aus Altersgründen keinen Sinn. Ein Missverständnis. „Ich bin jetzt nicht mit all meinen Aussagen, die ich in Halbzeit-Interviews getroffen habe, so glücklich“, räumte der 59-Jährige ein.
Klopp erzählte, er habe Füllkrug nach seinem Auftritt im ZDF-Sportstudio kontaktiert. „Es war eine Freude, die Entscheidung zu treffen, und es war auch eine Freude, sie ihm mitzuteilen.“ Wäre morgen die Europameisterschaft, würde er „Fülle“ sofort mitnehmen, denn: „Manchmal schlägt Form alles andere …“
„Bunter Mix“
Klopps Aufgebot vereint Perspektive mit Pragmatismus. „Wir haben in der Mannschaft einen bunten Mix aus sehr jung und durchaus erfahren dabei.“ Zwar fehlen logischerweise viele der Überraschungsgäste aus dem Frühherbst – etwa Mika Baur oder Bambasé Conté –, aber immer noch sind 13 Akteure dabei, die keine Verantwortung für die WM-Blamage in Nordamerika trugen. Mit zwei Siegen soll noch das Nations-League-Viertelfinale im März 2027 erreicht werden. Das wäre auch wichtig, um in der Qualifikation für die EM 2028 nicht gegen einen Großen wie Spanien oder Frankreich spielen zu müssen.
Das geht im Tor los, wo „Marc-Andre ter Stegen als Nummer eins in die Spiele geht“. Es gehe auf dieser Schlüsselposition um „große Stabilität“, und der Schlussmann von Ajax Amsterdam habe „die meiste Erfahrung“. Vertreter sind Alexander Nübel und Jonas Urbig. In der Innenverteidigung sind Jonathan Tah und Nico Schlotterbeck als eingespieltes Gespann gesetzt, als Back-up gelten Waldemar Anton, Malick Thiaw und überraschend Finn Jeltsch, von dem Klopp „langfristig“ so viel hält, dass er den 20-Jährigen vom VfB Stuttgart gerne mal rechts probieren würde. „Er ist ein sehr dynamischer, schlauer Kerl.“
In der Zentrale setzt Klopp mit Kapitän Joshua Kimmich, Aleksandar Pavlović und Tom Bischof auf einen „kleinen Bayern-Block“. In diesem Mannschaftsteil brauche es „Physis mit technischen Fähigkeiten – und ein bisschen Torgefahr wäre auch nicht schlecht“.
Dafür steht Überraschungsgast Wael Moyha. „Es gibt nicht viele 17-Jährige, die in der Bundesliga spielen, das allein ist schon ein herausragendes Merkmal“, sagte der Bundestrainer, der mit Moyha „drei Gespräche“ führte, die alle „top“ gewesen seien. Klopp sagte, man habe sich mit der Familie darauf geeinigt, „dass wir ihn einfach mal mitnehmen zum Sehen“.
Im Sturm habe er sich für die Freiburger Entdeckung Derry Scherhant und Said El Mala entschieden, weil dieser auf einer neuen Position in Köln „das Spielfeld auf einer neuen Position kennenlerne“. Der Frankfurter Younes Ebnoutalib habe ihn als „positive Überraschung im ersten Camp überzeugt“. Ungeachtet der Unruhe um seine Person ist auch Lennart Karl dabei, den Klopp als „Toptalent“ pries.
