https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120368.title: »Gen Z«-Proteste | Gen Z
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120368.author: Leni Karrer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120368.text:
- Kultur
- »Gen Z«-Proteste
Gen Z
Generationen unter einem Sammelbegriff zu fassen, ist sinnlose Gleichmacherei. Was die Gen Z allerdings vereint, ist der Wille mitzubestimmen.
Die Gen Z steht diese Woche so sehr im Fokus, dass man meinen könnte, es erscheint bald eine neue Serie: »Inside Gen Z« – und alle reden darüber. Mit meinem Jahrgang 1997 liege ich genau an der Grenze der Einteilung: Je nach Definition beginnt die Gen Z 1995 oder 1997 und reicht bis zu den Geburtsjahrgängen 2010 oder 2012. Und so »dazwischen« fühle ich mich auch: Ich trage zwar weite, tief sitzende Hosen und »Layering Shirts« (also zwei Oberteile übereinander, ganz im Y2K-Stil der 2000er), aber keinen Sleek-Bun oder Crop Tops. Ich habe Instagram und Snapchat installiert, aber kein Tiktok. Ich weiß, was »Type shit«, »Rizz« oder einen »Ick« haben bedeutet, aber verwende die Begriffe nicht in meiner Alltagssprache. Memes und kurze lustige Videos liebe ich hingegen über alles.
Wahrscheinlich kann sich niemand mit allen Attributen seiner Generation identifizieren, dennoch wird vor allem die Gen Z gerne als homogene Gruppe betrachtet.
Dabei sind wir so heterogen wie jede andere Generation auch, vielleicht sogar heterogener als alle vor uns. Denn als erste Generation, deren Aufwachsen vollständig vom Internet geprägt wurde (»digital natives«), lassen sich unsere Interessen und Lebensrealitäten nicht mehr so einfach zuordnen und gehen enorm auseinander. In den sozialen Medien landen wir etwa in algorithmischen Bubbles, die kaum verschiedener sein könnten.
Trotzdem sprechen wir über bestimmte Altersgruppen, als hätten sie einen gemeinsamen Lebenslauf und eine gemeinsame Meinung. So gehöre ich auch zu der Generation, von der behauptet wird, sie studier zu lange, sei meistens am Handy, wenig belastbar und vor allem unpolitisch.
Unpolitisch waren wir aber nie. Wir sind inmitten multipler Krisen aufgewachsen: Corona-Pandemie, Klimakrise, Kriege in der Ukraine und Nahost gehören allesamt zu unserem Alltag. Wir sprechen offener über psychische Gesundheit, Bedürfnisse und Grenzen, wünschen uns ein Leben, in dem neben dem Job auch noch Freizeit bleibt – was alles enorm politisch ist.
Warum sollen wir uns auch aufopfern für eine Arbeit, deren Lohn nicht reicht, die Miete zu bezahlen, von der wir nicht mal wissen, ob wir ihretwegen eine Rente erhalten werden? Warum sollen wir für ein Land im Zweifel den Kopf hinhalten, das es nicht schafft, gleiche Bildungschancen für alle zu schaffen?
An dieser Stelle widmet sich Leni Karrer der bezahlten Care-Arbeit und schreibt alle zwei Wochen über Phänomenales aus Popkultur, digitaler Welt und Feminismus.
Für ebenjene Themen demonstrierten junge Menschen am 31. Oktober unter dem Motto »Gen Z regelt«.
Die Berichterstattung vorab glich, wie Ricarda Lang es formulierte, einem »voyeuristisches Warten auf Grenzüberschreitung«. Man hatte den Eindruck, einige Seiten wünschten sich fast, dass es zu Ausschreitungen kommen würde, um die Proteste im Nachhinein zu diskreditieren. Dabei gab es vor Beginn der Demonstrationen keine weitergehenden Erkenntnisse zu Gewaltaufrufen.
Zu Gewaltausbrüchen und Plünderungen kam es dann in vereinzelten Städten leider doch – allerdings überwiegend nach Ende der Demonstrationen und durch Menschen, die nicht an den Protesten teilgenommen hatten. Die Organisatoren distanzierten sich von den Ausschreitungen. Trotzdem sollte man die Proteste nun im Nachgang – genauso wie die Generation als solche – differenziert betrachten.
Was feststeht: Junge Menschen gehen aus Sorge um ihre Zukunft auf die Straße. Sie glauben noch daran, dass Veränderung möglich ist. Diese Hoffnung sollten wir nicht enttäuschen.
Dafür braucht es Verständnis statt Überheblichkeit – bei Medien und Politik gleichermaßen. Wer, wie Dorothea Schupelius (»Welt«), alle Demonstrierenden pauschal als »narzisstische Kinder« bezeichnet, trägt kaum dazu bei, deren Anliegen ernst zu nehmen. Dass die SPD immerhin einen nationalen Bildungsgipfel fordert, ist ein Anfang. Entscheidend wird sein, dass dort nicht nur über junge Menschen, sondern auch mit ihnen gesprochen wird.
Ich habe große Hoffnung in meine Generation. Nicht, weil wir alle gleich ticken – das tun wir ganz offensichtlich nicht. Sondern weil wir trotz aller Unterschiede noch daran glauben, dass sich etwas verändern lässt. Vielleicht braucht es also gar keine neue Serie namens »Inside Gen Z«. Wir sind längst nicht mehr nur Gegenstand der Erzählung. Wir wollen selbst mitreden.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump is soothing the midterms loss with what he loves best: interior design | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
As you’d expect, the right is in a shambles right now. Elon Musk is making jokes about his “election-interfering space lasers” and pretending that he really, really doesn’t care that he threw away nearly half a billion dollars trying to influence the midterms. JD Vance is writing long essays on social media about how he agrees the Iran war was a bit of an oopsie.
Donald Trump, meanwhile, seems to be going through his own idiosyncratic grieving process about the Republicans’ historic midterm beating. The president has skipped all the way past shock, denial and anger and landed at the “admiring my beautiful renovations” stage of grief.
In his very first public appearance after the midterms, Trump did not offer a path forward for the Republicans or unpack what went wrong. Instead, he stood at the construction site where the new White House ballroom will be built and waxed lyrical about how incredible the building will be.
“This has been a structure the likes of which has never been seen anywhere,” Trump told the press corps as a building crew prepared to install the final beam in the ballroom. He then spent more than 20 minutes talking about “magnificent columns”, marble floors, cocktail rooms and Corinthian design.
Finally, in great detail, he explained what the public was so desperate to know: why were the ballroom’s kitchens going to be underground? “If I put the kitchen on top, you would lose three walls, because a kitchen takes about 30% of the space,” Trump noted.
“I love construction,” the president added, before signing a beam with a black Sharpie.
The midterms did eventually come up, but only because reporters insisted on asking about all that nasty business. “If I were on the ballot, I would have won,” Trump shrugged. I guess he forgot the part where he told voters: “Just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot.” According to a Washington Post analysis, he repeated variations of this statement 63 times.
Trump’s reaction to the midterm loss this week was noticeably different from what it was in 2018. While Republicans may not have been rebuked quite as badly then as they were this year, they still lost the House of Representatives. In the aftermath of that defeat, Trump reacted with his characteristic conspiracy and anger. He called the results a “tremendous success” and insulted his enemies. “Mia Love gave me no love, but then she lost,” Trump said in the 2018 press conference, referring to a Utah Republican who lost her House re-election bid. “Too bad.”
Then again, Trump 2.0, as we have all come to painfully realize, is a very different beast from the first incarnation. While the president’s reaction to Tuesday’s defeat may seem bizarre, it is in keeping with the priorities of his second term. Despite all his threats about running for president again, Trump seems to have accepted that this will be his last stint in the White House and is focused on leaving a legacy. He wants to slap his name on as many things as possible, renovate whatever he can get his little hands on, and build a bunch of self-aggrandizing monuments.
“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere,” Barack Obama joked at a recent Ohio rally, in reference to Trump’s aesthetics obsession. “He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV.”
Trump did not find this particularly amusing. “I paid for it myself. I fixed it, and now it’s more beautiful and in better shape,” the president said in defence of his White House upgrades. Obama, he added, just didn’t get it because he is a man who “doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing”.
Trump’s construction projects may soon end up being undermined by more than just jokes. Democrats are already scrutinizing the funding of the ballroom. Now that they control the House and Senate, they could even move to block some of Trump’s building plans, arguing that they haven’t been authorized by Congress and are therefore illegal. And they could clamp down on some of the renovation excesses: despite all his guff about bringing jobs back to America, Trump has outsourced the carving of his ballroom’s Corinthian columns to Italy.
But even if the Democrats manage to rein Trump in, he’s still made an indelible mark on Washington. Work on his 250ft “triumphal arch” could get started this week if a judge gives approval. And the president has just wrapped up a $14m project to clean up the “filthy” Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rid of the algae blooms turning it green.
It’s been a long and difficult battle against the algae but, in a press conference on Monday, the eve of election day, Trump declared “mission accomplished”. In the last press conference before polls opened, Trump did not make a final plea to voters – instead he patted himself on the back about how wonderful the pool was looking. Standing in front of a sign that said: “Back, and more beautiful than ever!” Trump declared that the pool project should unite all Americans. As voters, angry about the price of groceries and gas, prepared to register their anger at the voting booth, Trump held up pictures of rusted pipes and explained the virtues of painting the pool “American flag blue”.
And look, I’ve got to give the president his due. The water does look a bit clearer now. And it’s certainly doing more reflecting than the president is.
- Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

https://taz.de/UN-Klimakonferenz-in-Anta.title: UN-Klimakonferenz in Antalya: Kein Zukunftskanzler
https://taz.de/UN-Klimakonferenz-in-Anta.author: Nick Reimer
https://taz.de/UN-Klimakonferenz-in-Anta.text:
UN-Klimakonferenz in Antalya : Kein Zukunftskanzler
Friedrich Merz fährt nicht zur UN-Klimakonferenz. Mit solch gestriger Klimapolitik wird die CDU weiter an Bedeutung verlieren.
F riedrich Merz fährt nicht zur diesjährigen Weltklimakonferenz. Darauf hat sich der Bundeskanzler bereits vor Beginn der COP 31 im türkischen Antalya festgelegt. Und das ist auch konsequent: Merz schert sich keinen Deut um das drängendste Menschheitsproblem. Der Kanzler ist ein Politiker aus dem 20. Jahrhundert, der immer noch Politik wie im vergangenen Jahrhundert betreibt. Statt eine treibhausarme Zukunft einzuläuten, verlängert er und sein Kabinett die fossile Wirtschaftsweise, die uns die Klimaerhitzung erst eingebrockt hat.
Vor Jahresfrist hatte Kanzler Merz auf der Klimakonferenz COP 30 im brasilianischen Belém noch einen „bedeutenden Beitrag“ versprochen, den die Bundesrepublik bei der Schuldenbegleichung der Industriestaaten an die Länder des Globalen Südens zahlen wird. Tatsächlich hat die Regierung Merz dann aber die Klimagelder zusammengestrichen. Es ist also sogar klug, dass Merz nicht nach Antalya reist: Ihm bleibt so die Peinlichkeit auf der Weltbühne erspart.
Der eigentliche Skandal an der Absage von Friedrich Merz an den UN-Klimagipfel aber ist, dass er glaubt, damit durchzukommen. Tatsächlich nämlich hat der Hitzesommer mit 16.000 Todesopfern nicht dazu geführt, dass ein Sturm der Entrüstung das Wahlvolk auf die Straße treibt. Während jedes feige Attentat mit Toten oder Verletzten wochenlang analysiert und ausgewertet wird, verursachen die Hitzetoten bei der Mehrheit nur ein müdes Schulterzucken. Dabei müssen wir nicht in den Himalaja gucken, wo abreißende Gletscher ganze Täler auslöschen. Dieser Hitzesommer, die Niedrigstpegel, die sterbenden Wälder zeigen doch: Da gerät jetzt etwas aus dem Takt.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Und während sich der Klimawandel verselbstständigt, diskutieren wir noch über ein Verbrenner-Aus. Schluss damit! Wir kennen die Lösung längst und praktizieren sie in Teilen auch schon. Wenn die Union weiter nur mit gestrigen Konzepten Zukunft gestalten will, wird sie noch mehr Bedeutung in diesem Land einbüßen. Ein Kanzler, der nicht zur Weltklimakonferenz reist, kann kein Zukunftskanzler sein.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.title: US-Avantgarde-Literatur | Lyn Hejinian und die unheimliche Klebrigkeit der Sprache
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.author: Stefan Ripplinger
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.text:
- Gesund leben
- US-Avantgarde-Literatur
Lyn Hejinian und die unheimliche Klebrigkeit der Sprache
»Mein Leben« von Lyn Hejinian, eines der intelligentesten, strengsten und komischsten Bücher der US-Avantgarde, erscheint endlich auf Deutsch.
Während unser Leben zusehends auseinanderfällt, gibt es doch etwas, das es zusammenzuhalten scheint: Sprache. Was gestern, vorgestern und vorvorgestern passiert ist, was uns Hinz ins Gesicht gebrüllt und Kunz uns zugeraunt hat, der doofe Kalauer aus der Werbung und vielleicht auch eine Zeile aus einem Schlager, all das kann der Kneipenplauderer oder die empörte Chatterin zu einem Lebensabschnitt zusammenkleistern.
Die US-amerikanische Dichterin Lyn Hejinian hat mithilfe des Klebstoffs Sprache eines der komischsten und intelligentesten Bücher der jüngeren Avantgarde collagiert und es einigermaßen kühn »Mein Leben« genannt. Auch ihr Leben setzt sich aus vielen bunten Mosaiksteinen zusammen, aber man bemerkt deutlich die Fugen: »Der Kolibri, nach allem, was wir wissen, könnte von früh bis spät singen. Wir waren in Frankreich, wo jedes Wort wirklich ein Vogel war, ein singendes Ding. Ich lache, als wären meine Töpfe sauber.« Es ist eine Autobiografie und doch wieder nicht, am ehesten ist es ein polytonaler Abgesang auf alles Autobiografische, Autofiktionen eingeschlossen. Nun ist dieses Meisterinnenwerk endlich auf Deutsch erschienen.
Zunächst einige Hinweise zur Orientierung: Die 1941 geborene Kalifornierin Hejinian lebte, ganz im rousseauistischen Stil, mit anderen, unter anderem dem Saxofonisten Larry Ochs und ihren Kindern aus erster Ehe, in einem selbst gebauten Haus im Mendocino County. Sie gründete 1976 den Verlag Tuumba Press. Nachdem sie sich 1983 in Leningrad mit dem Dichter Arkadij Dragomoschtschenko angefreundet hatte, lernte sie Russisch.
1980 schrieb sie die erste Fassung ihres verblüffenden Buches. Das Chaos der Erinnerungen hält sie darin durch ein formales Exoskelett zusammen: Der Text hat 37 Abschnitte mit je 37 Sätzen, weil sie gerade 37 geworden war. 1987 entstand die endgültige Fassung. Nun war die Frau acht Jahre älter, also gibt es 45 Abschnitte mit je 45 Sätzen. Die Abschnitte beziehen sich nur lose auf das jeweilige Alter. Im dritten Abschnitt findet sich tatsächlich ein Satz zum dritten Lebensjahr und im neunten und zehnten je etwas zum neunten, im Allgemeinen wird bunt gewürfelt. Gespenstisch ist allerdings, dass Hejinian im 42. Abschnitt auf den Anfang von Dantes »Commedia« anspielt, »in unseres Lebensweges Mitte«, und tatsächlich hatte sie mit 42 die Mitte ihres Lebens gerade überschritten; sie wurde 83.
Um was geht es also in ihren Sätzen? Es geht um Familienmitglieder: den Onkel mit der Warze, den Opa, der als General paradiert, oder um ihren Sohn Paull; es geht um Gewächse: erschöpfte Fuchsien oder Steckrüben, die sich danach sehnen, »ein Mensch zu sein«; um Stranderlebnisse; um Pferde und Ponys; um Vögel als Vögel und als Wörter; um ominöse Ratschläge (»Gib einem Blinden nie Geld, ohne einen seiner Stifte anzunehmen«) oder Spruchweisheiten (»Keine Verlockung ist größer als das Zurückblicken«); um impressionistische Malerei oder die Kirchenfenster von Chartres. Einmal erlaubt sie sich einen Scherz auf Kosten des Dichters William Carlos Williams, dessen pseudomaterialistische Devise »No ideas but in things« war. Bei ihr lautet sie: »Keine Ideen außer in Kartoffeln.«
Wieder andere Themen kommen gerade nicht vor: Hejinian gesteht in einem Aufsatz (»Schreibheft«, 104/2025), sie habe die Kommunistenverfolgung und ähnliche Zeitereignisse ausgeblendet. Immerhin finden sich soziologische Glanzpunkte wie dieser: »Willkürlich interviewte Frauen mit Walkman widersprachen dem Eindruck, sie stellten Entfremdung zur Schau: ›Wir haben die 80er‹, sagte eine, ›wir tun nichts weiter, als den Raum einer nicht-historischen Perspektive unterzuordnen‹.« Schwangerschaft und Geburt werden zwar beiläufig erwähnt, doch fehlt Intim-Körperliches, obwohl die Dichterin bemerkt, sie habe sich in der Schultoilette übergeben müssen, weil sie sich so nach ihrer Mutter gesehnt habe. Hejinian webt ihr Netz aus vagen Feststellungen und unbeweisbaren Protokollsätzen.
Als postmoderne Penelope trennt sie zwar das, was sie bereits gewebt hat, nicht wieder auf. Aber sie zieht die Fäden mal hierhin, mal dorthin. Einzelne Bilder, Wörter und Wendungen kehren, manchmal minimal abgeändert, an verschiedenen Orten wieder. Das erhöht die Irritation beim Lesen und macht die Übersetzung zu einer herkulischen Aufgabe, die nur zwei ausgewiesene Dichter bewältigen konnten: Sonja vom Brocke und Norbert Lange.
Schon die ersten drei Wörter des Buches beweisen, wie schwer es die beiden hatten: »A moment yellow«. Das ist mit »Ein Augenblick gelb« korrekt wiedergegeben, zumal da Hejinian an anderer Stelle schreibt, ihre früheste Erinnerung sei das Gelb von Butterblumen. Doch kann »yellow« auch eifersüchtig und feige bedeuten. Da im selben Satz Purpur vorkommt, also auf das Verwundetenabzeichen »Purple Heart« und damit auf die Tapferkeit des Vaters angespielt wird, der im Weltkrieg kämpfte, wirkt das Gelb schon nicht mehr ganz so gelb. Eindeutigkeit zu zertrümmern – mit dem feinsten Uhrmacherhämmerchen, das zur Hand war –, ist die unverhohlene Absicht Hejinians. Vom Brocke und Lange führen sicher und kenntnisreich durch diesen irisierenden Text. Nirgendwo lassen sie sich zu den Kunststückchen hinreißen, mit denen andere Übersetzer sich selbst in den Vordergrund spielen. Das verleiht dem Text wohltuende Nüchternheit.
Oswald Wiener schrieb, die Leben der Spießer seien Romane aus dem 19. Jahrhundert. Angesichts der seit Jahren über uns hinwegrollenden autobiografischen Welle mögen sich manche fragen, ob sie die Widersprüche des Lebens in ihr untergehen sehen wollen. »Erinnerung ist die Währung meiner Klasse«, spottet Lyn Hejinian und zeigt uns mit »Mein Leben«, wie im Erinnern gegen die Erinnerung gedacht werden kann.
Lyn Hejinian: My Life. Mein Leben. A. d. amerik. Engl. v. Sonja vom Brocke und Norbert Lange. Wunderhorn, Heidelberg 2026, 300 S., br., 26 €.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.title: Global stocks tumble as AI panic grips markets after Democrats’ midterm success – business live
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.author: Graeme Wearden
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.text:
Introduction: Global stocks tumble as AI panic grips markets
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Fears that the Democratic Party’s blue wave in this week’s midterm elections will sink the AI investment boom are roiling markets, following heavy losses on Wall Street last night.
Asia-Pacific markets are a sea of red (unlike the US election map on Tuesday night!), as investors ditch tech stocks after more than $3.2tn was wiped off the US stock market yesterday.
Today, Japan’s Nikkei stock index has slumped by almost 6% – its worst drop since April 7 2025 during the ‘liberation day’ tariff panic.
South Korea’s KOSPI is down 6.7%, and Taiwan’s TAIEX has dropped by 4.5% in a broad rout.
Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets, called the market action “a bit of a disaster”, explaining (via Reuters):
 “(Clients) were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out.
“All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints, ... because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money.
“And it’s not just a slap in terms of valuation. It’s basically a whole policy and six-year structural shift that says we’re now going to pause, we’re now going to cool AI, we’re now going to cool data centres, approvals and equity capital markets.”
After months of warnings that AI valuations were too high, and that the bubble might burst, US investors dashed to the exits en masse yesterday. The Nasdaq tech index slumped by 5.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 lost 4.36%.
Memory chip makers, who had been profiting from the AI boom, led the fallers – SanDisk slumped 22% and both Micron and AMD lost 17% of their value.
Chip giant Nvidia led the fallers on the DJIA, down over 9%.
Analysts pointed to policy uncertainty as Democrats are more critical of data centres, which could slow the rollout of AI investment – especially given public opposition to the sector.
Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, says it was a “brutal sell-off” as fears about the future of the AI buildout gripped the markets.
 The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom.
The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations. Earnings season has been an overall disappointment for the markets, with Magnificent Seven results so far undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down.
So, it could be a ‘tin hats on’ day in the markets. Investors will also be watching the latest US jobs report, for clues into the health of America’s labour market.
The agenda
- 7am GMT: Lloyds house price index
- 9am GMT: UN’s FAO food price index
- 1.30pm GMT: US non-farm payrolls jobs report
- 3pm GMT: University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence report

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/hauts-de.title: « Je suis sans-papiers simplement parce que l’administration n’a rien fait pendant dix mois » : ces couples binationaux malmenés par l’État et privés de titres de séjour
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/hauts-de.author: Simon Guichard
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/hauts-de.text:
Ils sont mariés depuis de nombreuses années, mais leur conjoint étranger n’arrive plus à faire renouveler son titre de séjour à cause des dysfonctionnements de l’administration. Ces situations ubuesques génèrent du stress, de lourds frais d’avocats et conduisent parfois même à séparer des parents de leurs enfants français, alors que leur statut devrait les empêcher de rencontrer ces montagnes de difficultés.
Des vies suspendues à un mail de la préfecture. Jane*, une ressortissante britannique, est mariée à un Français depuis près de dix ans. Le couple vit dans les Hauts-de-Seine, où elle travaille en CDI dans une grande entreprise. Jusqu’en 2025, elle était titulaire d’un titre de séjour de cinq ans. « Dans mon dossier, il n’y a rien à instruire, rien à contrôler, se désole la jeune femme. Il s’agit juste de renouveler un titre existant obtenu sans difficulté. »
Comme des milliers d’étrangers en attente du renouvellement de leur titre de séjour en France, la Britannique se heurte au silence de l’administration. Pourtant, Jane a suivi toute la procédure à la lettre. Un an avant l’expiration de son titre de séjour, elle tente comme prévu de déposer son dossier sur la plateforme en ligne de l’Administration numérique pour les étrangers en France (Anef). Seul problème, le service en ligne obligatoire du ministère de l’Intérieur dysfonctionne : elle ne peut pas déposer sa demande.
Kafka à la préfecture
Pour contourner l’obstacle technique, elle envoie son dossier par mail à la préfecture. Le début d’une série d’interactions kafkaïennes avec l’administration. Sans réponse, elle passe ensuite aux courriers recommandés. Les accusés de réception reviennent signés, mais toujours pas de signe de vie de la préfecture. Pour faire bouger les choses, elle décide de saisir le support national du ministère de l’Intérieur. L’administration lui répond que son dossier est incomplet : il manque l’attestation de dépôt que la plateforme Anef, en panne, n’a jamais générée.
Le lendemain, miracle : l’administration lui...

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to win
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to win
His historic victory in Michigan shows that Muslim Americans need not abandon their identity or Palestine to succeed in politics.
Messages popped up on my WhatsApp account from New York, Gaza, Pakistan and Australia. Friends and colleagues were following Michigan’s Senate race, talking excitedly about Abdul El-Sayed. As the results from Wayne County sealed his victory on Tuesday, I felt something I had rarely felt before in American politics: not a muted relief that someone had lost but genuine joy and hope that someone had won.
El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health director, defeated Republican Mike Rogers. He will be the first Muslim ever elected to the United States Senate. As a Muslim American from Michigan, this hit home.
Like many in Michigan’s Muslim community, I knew of Abdul long before he became a fixture in national headlines, from his 2018 gubernatorial campaign to his Friday sermons in local mosques. As Ramadan began this year, I attended one of his town halls for Muslim constituents. Before a few dozen community members and leaders, Abdul pledged to fight for all Michiganders. His sincerity and commitment to that pledge remained evident even as the pressures of the campaign intensified. I have seen him attend funerals for community members near my home and watched him go from person to person, greeting people with kindness. Even in the final days of an exhausting campaign, he responded personally to messages from the community, including mine.
We attended the same university, the University of Michigan, where he once helped lead the Muslim Students’ Association. I later served as a college student body president there. Just days before the election, Muslim alumni (including me) invited him to a football tailgate party with students, parents and graduates. His former teachers and students have spoken to me with pride about the person they knew.
Muslim Americans are often asked to celebrate any politician who occasionally says “salaam” or appears in a mosque before Election Day. Abdul was not an outsider to our community coming to court us. He belonged to it.
During the campaign, I welcomed hundreds of local Muslim community members, out-of-state political candidates canvassing for him and members of his staff into my home. People heard from those closest to him what this race could mean for Muslim Americans. The enthusiasm felt different from the familiar, dispiriting bargain of voting mainly to stop someone worse.
Two years ago, I wrote about why I would vote against genocide in the 2024 presidential election. That decision was shaped by my work with Palestinian healthcare workers, by witnessing the realities in Palestine firsthand and by outrage at the Biden-Harris administration’s complicity in the genocide in Gaza. Neither I nor many of Michigan’s Muslims have forgotten. But this time, the ballot offered something other than just a protest vote: a candidate who had opposed Israel’s genocide against Palestinians from the outset while also caring about the range of issues affecting Michiganders.
His willingness to speak truth to power attracted immense hostility from Washington’s elites. President Donald Trump repeatedly mocked Abdul’s name, treating “Muhammad” – his middle name, meaning “the praised one” – as an insult. Political opponents and even some voters insinuated that his faith alone made him suspect, recycling unsubstantiated allegations tying him to groups and movements he did not belong to.
Abdul responded with dignity and directness. When critics made his name the issue, he spoke about groceries, housing, healthcare and affordability. When challenged over his opposition to genocide, he questioned the premise that wanting children to live free of bombs was somehow hateful. He did not accept the proposition that a Muslim must disown his community or Palestine to qualify for public office.
And most importantly, he fought back. Many Muslim voters I spoke to felt they had found someone willing to fight for them, to challenge the presumptions and racism of journalists, pundits and media outlets rather than accept their unjust framing.
His victory speech began with the words his opponents had tried to weaponise: “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.” He recalled having said “inshallah” – “God willing” – whenever he was asked about winning. Now, he said, it was time for “alhamdulillah”, or “Praise be to God.”
That moment was electric, not because Arabic phrases alone are a sign of solidarity – even former President Joe Biden said “inshallah” in a debate before proceeding to commit genocide against Palestinians and aid the bombing of mosques and burning of Qurans – but because his Muslim identity had survived a countrywide effort by special interest groups and racists to make it disqualifying. His faith, Islam, is a value system he actively chooses every day, a commitment he strives to live out in public life. His being Muslim mattered to me more than his Arab ethnicity or ancestral origins, a simple happenstance of birth.
There was money behind the attempt to stop him too. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s (AIPAC’s) affiliated super PAC spent roughly $30m in Michigan’s Democratic primary, an extraordinary investment to defeat someone who openly opposed US support for Israel’s genocide and apartheid. In his victory speech, Abdul thanked AIPAC for the chance to beat it twice. One loss will not dissolve the lobbying group’s power. But Michigan demonstrated that AIPAC spending need not amount to a veto over who can win.
After Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York, sceptics suggested that a Muslim candidate outspoken about Palestine could only win in a liberal metropolis, not a state that Trump carried in 2024. El-Sayed travelled from small towns and villages to industrial cities and suburbs, visiting churches and mosques, and he won statewide.
Michigan has long been a centre of Muslim American life, from Dearborn’s famous Arab restaurants and coffee houses to Hamtramck, the first Muslim-majority city in the US. Generations have built mosques, schools, businesses and institutions while enduring suspicion and discrimination. There is irony in Michigan electing a Muslim alumnus of the University of Michigan, which has faced legal challenges over its treatment of antigenocide protesters. Some of the voices that were treated as dangerous on campus found a home at the ballot box for the first time.
Other Muslims across the country made history too. My mentor, friend and colleague Adam Hamawy, with whom I served on a medical mission in Palestine documenting harm to people’s health, won his congressional race in New Jersey and travelled to Michigan to support Abdul. Darializa Avila Chevalier, Aber Kawas, Nabeela Syed and so many others won seats in Congress and state legislatures across the country, refusing to accept that their silence on human rights abuses is the price of participation.
Yet our celebration does not mean we have suspended all judgement. Some Muslims I spoke with vehemently opposed Abdul’s decision to campaign alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Barack Obama. Their administrations’ policies, from facilitating the genocide in Gaza to conducting drone strikes against civilians in multiple Muslim-majority countries, remain at the forefront of people’s minds. I understood their anger and shared their apprehensions about normalising the killers of children. Yet many of us still voted for Abdul because we believed in his sincerity and because he had repeatedly made clear that he did not agree with every policy of those backing his campaign. I am under no illusion that one senator alone will end the systems and structures of exploitation that fund war machines abroad and fail their own communities at home. Muslim representation risks becoming hollow if mistaken for the only tool for liberation.
And that is precisely why the substance of his campaign matters. Abdul connected the fight against endless war to the fight for healthcare, clean water and a liveable wage. He spoke of a mother trying to keep her children on lifesaving medication and a worker fighting for a union. He insisted that the money spent destroying someone else’s children has a cost for children in the US too. His politics asked whether Americans could both recognise their own self-interest and show humanity towards others.
His election does not make US government policies any more just overnight. It does not bring back a single Palestinian child. It does not absolve the Democrats, Washington or any of us of complicity. And it certainly does not entitle Abdul to six years in the Senate without scrutiny.
But it destroys one convenient lie: that Muslim Americans must choose between being unapologetically Muslim and belonging fully to American public life.
For years, we were told to lower our voices, soften our names and reconsider what we advocate for if we wanted to succeed. On Tuesday, Michigan delivered its verdict. The man they tried to make unelectable will now sit in the US Senate. Alhamdulillah, he does not need to become less Muslim to serve his state – and the rest of us do not need to police who we are to demand a better future for ourselves and the generations to come.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘Too many stories exist only to make you think you’re on the right side’: Cristian Mungiu on Fjord, the Cannes winner which divided Europe
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Philip Oltermann
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
‘Pffff!” Cristian Mungiu lets out an exasperated sigh. We are sitting in the basement of a London hotel, at the end of a long morning of back-to-back interviews for the Romanian film-maker, and his press handler has just snuck into the room to remind him of his next appointment across town. But Mungiu blanks him and leans on to his table, because he wants to tell one more story.
In 2013, Mungiu was part of a delegation of European auteurs who travelled to Brussels to meet the then president of the European Commission, José Manuel Barroso. At the time, the EU and US were in talks to slash barriers to trade between the two economic blocs, and the film-makers were lobbying the Commission to spare their industry from the deal.
If countries weren’t allowed to subsidise their own productions, one argument went, European cinema would become a stolid mush of homogenised co-productions – “Europudding”, as people called it at the time. To those ends, they would no longer be able to create national dramas like Mungiu’s own 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days, a riveting abortion thriller set in cold war-era Bucharest that had won the Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2007.
Barroso, an economic liberal, was not impressed, and the meeting became heated. “He was very angered that in spite of all his attempts to create a united Europe, people in, say, Estonia were still reluctant to watch a film from Portugal,” says Mungiu, his own frustration with that attitude bubbling to the surface once more. “One Europe? It’s the right direction, sure. But it has still only been tens of years since all these people were fighting each other and everything was based on national states and national cultures. Historically speaking, that wasn’t a long time ago. Let’s go in that new direction, fine – but you can’t pretend we’ve already got there.”
I suspect Mungiu is keen to tell this story for two reasons. His latest film, Fjord, is about people from different European cultures coming together – but also about how different national identities continue to keep them apart. Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu, a Romanian-Norwegian couple with five young children, move from Bucharest to her native country in the icy north. The Gheorghius are devout evangelical Christians, yet the liberally minded locals welcome the newcomers with open arms in spite of their anti-modern way of life. Mihai, an engineer, and nurse Lisbet both find employment, the children settle at school; they make friends with their neighbours, headteacher Mats, lawyer Mia and their teen-rebel daughter, Noora.
But when a PE teacher notices bruises on the body of the Gheorghius’ eldest daughter, Elia, tolerance turns to distrust. Child protection services become involved, and Mihai does his family no favours when he denies that he has abused his children, but insists that a slap on the bottom can sometimes be necessary, to teach that “you can’t escape punishment when you’re wrong”. Soon, the state separates the parents from their children, including their newborn baby, and the Gheorghius’ family values become a diplomatic incident.
Since his 2007 Cannes triumph, Mungiu has made several films that deal with the social consequences of globalisation and migration – a particularly prescient subject for a Romanian, given that 25% of his compatriots live abroad. Beyond the Hills (2012) and Graduation (2016) revolved around characters who have returned from working abroad or are desperate to leave Romania to do so; 2022’s RMN dealt with protests over Sri Lankan migrant workers in a rural village in Transylvania.
But Fjord – and this is the other reason Mungiu’s encounter with Barroso is relevant – is not just a film about globalisation, but also one shaped by a globalised economy. It is an international co-production of the kind that Mungiu’s delegation had warned the European Commission about, shot in Norway and edited in Romania, its sound designed in Finland and mixed in Denmark. It’s also his first English-language film, and the first to star two Oscar-nominated A-listers, Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. Mungiu almost sounds embarrassed about it: “It has a lot to do with the financing system,” he says. “I’m not a big fan of this system, to be honest,” he adds, sheepishly.
Yet Fjord is no Europudding, but something altogether classier and more refined – more of a Euro-flan, with a bitter layer permeating the sweetness. It still has all the stylistic hallmarks that have made Mungiu the standout film-maker of the Romanian new wave: a pacing that makes viewers feel they are living the Gheorghius’ ordeal in something like real time, but also a renunciation of manipulative edits or closeups that could coerce us into fully taking their point of view.
Fjord is cinema as Rorschach test. How the bruise on Elia’s back came about is never fully explained. Whether you are more outraged by the Norwegian state’s dogmatic liberalism or by the Romanians’ disciplinarian ways is designed to tell you more about yourself than the characters on screen. “We watch too many stories that are there just to confirm to you that you are on the right side of things,” Mungiu says. “In the last 10, 20 years we started making a lot of films in which everything is clear and the author takes you by the hand and tells you what you need to believe: they are the good guys, they are the bad guys.”
Fjord won the Palme d’Or at Cannes this year, putting Mungiu in the distinguished league of directors who have won the most prestigious prize in arthouse cinema twice, which includes such luminaries as Michael Haneke, Francis Ford Coppola and Ken Loach. Ironically, some of the film’s most positive reviews since were from Norway, he says, where “nobody considered the film a criticism of Norwegian society, not even [Norway’s child welfare authority] Barnevernet”.
But not everyone at Cannes thought Fjord was a deserving winner. The two films that scored highest with the critics, interestingly, were also Euro-flans: Polish director Paweł Pawlikowski’s German-language Fatherland and Russian film-maker Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, a coproduction between France, Latvia and Germany. In Mungiu’s native Romania, some critics felt the film was unduly forgiving of corporal punishment. In France, one critic complained about Fjord’s “proto-Nazi” portrayal of the child-protection officers. “Beneath its veneer of a fair film, beneath its stated desire to depict two opposing value systems, Cristian Mungiu constantly chooses sides,” wrote David Fonseca in Le Rayon Vert. The trial the film puts on, it declared, was “a sham”.
Such withering invective seems over the top, and at the very least ignores the film’s subplot – a nascent homoerotic relationship between the Gheorghiu’s eldest daughter and her neighbour-classmate that shows up Mihai’s autocratic rule within his family. But it’s probably fair to say that Fjord is a conservative film with a small “c”: not in the brash and hectoring way that modern conservative parties are, but doubtful and self-questioning, yet conservative nonetheless in its instinctive distrust of the state.
“I come from this very authoritarian society and I’ve seen that it’s not good to give people too much power because there are natural tendencies to abuse it,” Mungiu says. “I want to make sure that we don’t get back to this situation in which somebody knows better than us what’s good for us – I’ve been there.” He chuckles sardonically. “I have so many fans in France who are communists. Well, I’m so sorry that they didn’t come to spend the 70s with us in Romania. Not to mention the 50s!”
Mungiu does not want to be labelled a conservative. “The fact that I’m presenting these arguments without commenting doesn’t mean for a second that I’m in any way a supporter of conservative values and of all the intolerance that they carry.” His criticism of liberal societies such as Norway, he insists, is above all due to the fact that he has higher expectations of them. “They are more educated, so they should be the ones initiating a dialogue with the other side. The conversation starts when you have this patience to listen.”
In one scene in the film, one of the Gheorghius’ daughters is told that her sexuality is an entry ticket to hell. I ask Mungiu how much patience that young girl should have, listening to these bigots. “I’m aware that it’s more complicated in reality,” he concedes. “But you should ask yourself, why are we in this situation? After years and years of trying to make the world a more liberal place, we ended up by having a more illiberal kind of world. Haven’t we maybe exaggerated in some areas with the way we were trying to force things? It’s like trying to ripen a banana with a hairdryer. It doesn’t work like that. People need time.”
Later, I check the box office figures for Fjord and realise that the film beat Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey to reach No 1 in Norway on its opening day, which would surely have pleased José Manuel Barroso. In 2026, the idea that Estonians may flock to cinemas to watch a film from Portugal no longer seems quite so absurd. Meanwhile, in Hungary and Serbia, Romania’s neighbouring countries, young voters have toppled Christian nationalist strongmen. People need more time, until they don’t.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Can America ever return to pre-Trump politics?
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Can America ever return to pre-Trump politics?
The US midterms were a rejection of Donald Trump’s politics of division, but his legacy may be impossible to undo.
“I think it’s safe to say that we are tired of being pitted against each other. We are tired of being told to hate each other. It has been 10 years of this kind of politics. Politics as blood sport. Politics as trolling and owning. Politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all the time.”
So said Senator-elect James Talarico in his victory speech on election night after he won the first United States Senate seat in Texas for the Democratic Party in almost 40 years.
I don’t like Talarico or his policies, but I agree with him on one thing: The American people are tired of being pitted against one another. We need more uniters and fewer dividers in the Republican Party and US politics in general.
This is the conclusion many American voters seem to have reached after 10 years of Donald Trump dominating the right.
A decade ago, he forcefully entered the political scene with a radically different approach and provocative rhetoric. He won his first US presidential election by attacking his opponents with clever and cutting nicknames. Crooked Hillary. Low-energy Jeb. Pocahontas. Little Marco. Crazy Bernie. Lying Ted.
All were aimed at diminishing his rivals in ways that only a rapturous crowd of adoring MAGA fans could really appreciate. His attacks played well on social media and reflected an American culture that was far less deferential to the political establishment, far coarser in its language and far more interested in being entertained than being informed.
Trump’s attacks, performed live at his raucous rallies, had all the earmarks of a professional wrestling bout. It was blood sport at its most basic level. And Trump’s supporters ate it up, loving how he stood up to an elite that obviously despised them.
His opponent in the 2016 presidential election, Hillary Clinton, called half of his supporters a “basket of deplorables”.
Seven years before Trump formally entered the race for the White House, Barack Obama in a speech in San Francisco had said that people like them “get bitter, they cling to guns or religion or antipathy to people who aren’t like them or anti-immigrant sentiment or anti-trade sentiment as a way to explain their frustrations”.
Trump gathered up these angry voters, many of whom had protested during the Tea Party movement, and created “Make America Great Again” (MAGA). They loved the visceral way Trump communicated. They loved that he promised to end illegal immigration and free-trade policies that destroyed manufacturing jobs.
Trump’s rhetoric, coarse as it was, seemed honest, authentic, unscripted, and totally real, not poll-tested, not AI-generated, not written by expensive speechwriters. Trump was talking to them, not at them. He had listened to their fears and promised to fight back with a vengeance.
When Trump claimed the political establishment had stolen his re-election, he didn’t sit idly by, accepting the results. He consulted his lawyers, came up with a dubious legal strategy and then unleashed his supporters on Capitol Hill, hoping upon hope that their pressure would bend the hallowed traditions of presidential succession to his will. It didn’t work, but it also didn’t disqualify him.
Over the four years of President Joe Biden’s administration, Trump survived legal attacks, threats of imprisonment and assassination attempts to become an invincible force who seized power again in 2024. His ascent seemed like destiny.
But as it often does, the fickle winds of the electorate changed direction. They used to love his unconventional approach to politics, but now they wanted him to deliver on his promises to lower inflation and gas prices. He had once promised to keep us out of foreign wars, but that promise was broken, too. Perhaps he had a good reason to attack Iran, but he failed to make a convincing case to the American public, and voters quickly grew disenchanted with another broken promise. The vice president himself said that the war is what cost the Republicans the election. But it was more than just the war. Voters were tired of the whole act.
When Trump told his voters to imagine that he was on the ballot, it wasn’t just his supporters who made this election a referendum on Trump. So too did angry Democrats, disgusted independents and more than a few former MAGA minions.
They said this election was about affordability, but it really was about an undisciplined president who refused to colour inside the lines, who blundered into a costly war, who didn’t stop his administration from detaining and deporting high school baseball coaches and Uber drivers and domestic employees, and harboured too many white supremacists within his ranks.
He alienated women, Hispanics, Asians, Arabs, African Americans and offended well-educated Midwesterners who couldn’t stomach his language or his antics any longer. The great MAGA coalition that he assembled for his historic 2024 victory dissipated in one election night, tired of the nonsense and wanting a change in direction.
Things are so bad for Republicans that they lost all kinds of members, from House leaders like Richard Hudson, to tremendously flawed MAGA warriors like Ken Paxton to seasoned and effective Appropriators like Susan Collins. Conservative Republicans lost. Traditional Republicans lost. Moderate Republicans lost. All kinds of Republicans lost. It is a total and complete rejection of the GOP, top to bottom. An unmitigated disaster.
There are two questions that remain. What will happen to the MAGA movement now? And can we ever return to the good old days before Trump made politics a blood sport more akin to Ultimate Fighting than to the World Wrestling Federation?
The answer is this: Unless Republicans fundamentally change how they communicate to voters and what they promise to do for them, they will not win another election. MAGA will be lost forever. Governing is about building coalitions, not about belittling potential allies with sophomoric attacks and needlessly partisan rhetoric.
Like Andrew Jackson, President Trump has forever changed American politics, and it is highly unlikely that we will ever completely return to the good old days of disagreeing without being disagreeable. But voters showed that they had grown tired of Mr. Trump’s brand of disagreeableness by delivering to the Democrats a huge political victory.
This election was not an endorsement of Democratic policies. It was a referendum on Trumpism and his caustic brand of politics. We will see if he got the message.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: ‘Every day, someone loses a hand or a leg’: the brutal reality of India’s textile recycling industry
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Anjul Behal in Panipat. Photographs by Elke Scholiers
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: IRGC says two oil tankers ablaze after collision with mines in Hormuz Strait
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Mera Aladam
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
IRGC says two oil tankers ablaze after collision with mines in Hormuz Strait
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy announced that two oil tankers caught fire after being struck by mines while attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
The statement said that the two "offending" vessels - "one in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz and the other in the Strait of Hormuz itself" - were attempting to pass through an "unauthorised route".
They subsequently collided with mines, caught fire and were stopped in the water.
"These two tankers turned off all their navigation and identification systems and were trying to leave the unauthorized route of the Strait of Hormuz with the support of the aggressive and terrorist American army, but after hitting a mine, they caught fire and stopped," the IRGC said.
"The Strait of Hormuz is closed by God's grace and the efforts of the IRGC Navy, and there will be no change until the seven conditions are met, and the efforts of the aggressive CENTCOM forces to force tankers to pass through the unauthorized and mine-contaminated area will result in nothing but successive and shameful defeats"

Nous sommes dans un moment où la campagne électorale pour élire un nouveau président de la République en mai 2027 se déroule dans une grande confusion. L’année 2026 a été marquée par de longues sécheresses, des incendies ravageurs, des tempêtes et des inondations dévastatrices. Elles font reculer notre souveraineté alimentaire tandis que les réparations coûtent de plus en plus cher et font croître le bilan carbone de l’économie du pays malgré une croissance atone. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: US judge halts construction of Trump’s triumphal arch in Washington, DC
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
US judge halts construction of Trump’s triumphal arch in Washington, DC
Judge Tanya Chutkan orders a 14-day pause on the so-called ‘Arc de Trump’ project in Washington, DC.
A United States federal judge has ordered a temporary block on the construction of President Donald Trump’s 250ft (76-metre) “triumphal arch” in Washington DC.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Friday, ordered a 14-day pause on any construction on the arch, despite the Trump administration last week saying it could begin as soon as Thursday.
The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) held a nine-hour hearing on Thursday, which resulted in a final vote of 8-4 in approval of the arch, despite the protest of dozens of witnesses who were against the construction.
Judge Chutkan’s decision follows a series of lawsuits that have been filed challenging the construction of the arch, including a group of Vietnam war veterans, who filed a suit in February.
Trump has proposed building the arch by the Arlington National Cemetery, where war veterans are buried, which caused concerns that it could block the view between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.
The veterans said in a court filing that the line of sight between the two was “carefully designed to symbolise the unification of the country after the Civil War and the strength of a united nation”.
Trump first proposed the arch last year to mark 250 years of US independence, claiming it would be like other famous arches, such as the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris in 1836.
The so-called “Arc de Trump” is only one of many projects Trump has proposed in Washington. On Friday, he signed a proclamation designating his Oval Office and Cabinet room as a national monument.
Many of his plans have been blocked in the past by several judges, and after the Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections this week, those plans could face increased scrutiny.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: True North by Paul Theroux review – an American’s view of Canada
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Blake Morrison
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
Paul Theroux’s arrival in Canada doesn’t go well. An immigration officer called Sweeney finds a small pocketknife in his car and fines him $500 for failing to declare a weapon. “I’m going to make you famous,” he angrily tells her, stumping up. Maybe he will, with this book. Canadians are reputed to be polite and easygoing, “slaves to their courtesy”, but the country has changed enormously in recent years. Will Theroux find it stuffed with Sweeney-ites? Luckily the answer is no.
He issues a warning that, after 11 previous travel books, this may be his last; global overtourism appals him and so does much travel writing. But he shares Jack Kerouac’s delight in being on the road, and from his home in Massachusetts it’s just a four-hour drive to the border. His purpose is less to check out “the strangers next door” than to visit the village of Yamaska, in Quebec. It was there that a Frenchman called Antoine Theroux settled in the 17th century; a dozen or more Theroux families still live there; one local street is called Rue Theroux. The author isn’t only made welcome but presented with a certificate of honour by the local mayor. He repays the honour with a long chapter of family history.
A joshing relative calls him ratoureux, a mischief-maker, and the next time he visits he heads on to see the mischief in Ottawa, where truck drivers are staging a protest against the Trudeau government. It’s a scene of mayhem in freezing weather, “a mob of truckers and their huge vehicles occupying and violating a handsome city”. He’s intrigued by the unleashed anger. By the time the protest ends, with the ringleaders arrested, he’s heading west on the Trans-Canada Highway.
He describes his process as “idly motoring, looking and listening”. Budget motels are preferable to swanky hotels because it’s easier to strike up conversations; ditto in cheap eateries. It’s a hit-and-miss method (not everyone is forthcoming or insightful) but he gathers stories wherever he goes – from foresters, pig farmers, lobster fishers, plumbers, moose hunters, historians and social justice campaigners. As an American whose president has threatened to take over Canada as the 51st state, he’s tainted. But people are friendly, not hostile. And Trump’s insults bring defiance, with a flurry of Maple Leaf flags and “Canada – Not for Sale” T-shirts. Come the 2025 election, the fancied populist loses and Mark Carney triumphs.
Despite the surge in patriotism, Theroux is struck by how few people consider Canada to be their home. Many are “unmelted migrants” living in “ethno-bubbles” or “ethno-burbs”, he writes; they have come from elsewhere and – whether Filipinos, Sikhs or Somalis – often see themselves as short-term expats. Some white Canadians Theroux talks to say they feel displaced, too. In 2022, the population expanded by over one million and even among the mild-mannered, younger citizens, there are those who struggle to accept the change.
The groups with the greatest grievance are First Nations, not least the Cree. British and French colonialism robbed them of their heritage, then demeaned them as idle, drunk and dishonest. Reparation and apology have been slow. Though far more visible than Indigenous people in the US, they’re “aliens in their own land”. With his colonialist ancestor guiltily in mind, Theroux describes how much they have endured, from old-world scalping to more recent “starlight tours” where Indigenous men in trouble with the police were taken to remote spots in freezing weather at night and left there, often to die.
This is the dark side of Canada, with so-called Indian residential schools a particular horror. Indigenous children were forced into them to be “educated”, that is made Christian. Theroux is told that many died in unmarked graves, including 250 at a school in British Columbia. Paedophilia was widespread, too. One school had an electric chair wired up to punish children with shocks; at another, when any pupil wet the bed, the soiled sheet would be draped over their head. The last such school shut down as recently as 1997.
Theroux accumulates stories by listening to CBC on his car radio and even when he’s back home, at his desk. Many novelists are quoted, for their perspectives on Canadian cities or regions, some of them past stalwarts of Canlit (Mordecai Richler, Margaret Laurence, Sinclair Ross), others at work today (Margaret Atwood, Miriam Toews). In Edmonton he meets Jan Morris’s son, the victim of “the fantasies and the deceptions of a chilly woman who’d been his fond father”. Whereas Morris stuck with cities in her book O Canada! (“never resorted to the road, never camped, never roughed it”), Rue Theroux is rural, meandering through the wilds, the Prairies, the great outdoors.
At 85, and despite the thousands of miles he drives from east to west, the author’s energy seems undimmed. Downbeat at the start, he’s rejuvenated by the end, ready for another road trip, eager to see the Yukon, Hudson Bay, Labrador. If nothing else, he’ll get back to Yamaska, the village of his ancestors.
