https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Lebanese pack bags and stock up amid fears of new Israeli escalation
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Lebanese pack bags and stock up amid fears of new Israeli escalation
Lebanon faces renewed fears of another Israeli escalation, with residents preparing for potential conflict in the south.
Beirut, Lebanon – During Israel’s intensification of its war on Lebanon in March, Aya stayed at her home in Abbasiyeh, in southern Lebanon, despite the risks. At one point, she says, her neighbour’s house was targeted by an Israeli attack.
The attacks have subsided after an ostensible ceasefire was initially announced in April. But the sounds of war have not ceased.
“There’s always drones around and sounds of detonations, but we’ve grown thick skin,” she told Al Jazeera.
In recent weeks, however, fears have intensified around a potential third Israeli intensification since 2024. Many Lebanese are now living in limbo, especially those in areas that previously witnessed intense Israeli attacks.
Aya said her family has prepared extra medication for her grandparents, in case a new round of conflict makes it difficult to obtain. Others are preparing bags and extra food, and keeping their electronic devices charged should the attacks start again.
She also said she would leave her home if Israeli attacks intensified again, rather than stay as she had before.
“I don’t have the energy for this anymore,” she said. Instead, she has been thinking about leaving Lebanon.
“I just can’t handle going through another displacement, especially while watching people around me carry on with their lives as if nothing is happening,” she said. “I know it’s normal, but for me it’s mentally exhausting.”
Fears of an Israeli intensification
The Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah and Israel have been at war since October 2023. Since then, Israel has killed around 9,000 people in Lebanon, according to the Lebanese health ministry, mostly during escalations in the autumn of 2024 and in March and April 2026. Israel invaded Lebanon during each offensive and has since occupied up to 10 kilometres of territory, where it has established a so-called “Yellow Line”. Below that line, Israel continues to destroy towns and villages, while it has already made border areas uninhabitable, possibly for years to come.
A ceasefire was announced in April, just over a week after Israel launched more than 100 attacks on Lebanon in less than 10 minutes, killing more than 350 people. Then in June, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-brokered framework agreement to set up “pilot zones”, as part of which the Israeli military would withdraw from those areas and the Lebanese army would move in to disarm Hezbollah.
Following the ceasefire and framework agreement, active fighting between Hezbollah and Israel has eased, despite Israel’s ongoing attacks and destruction of homes and infrastructure in the far south of Lebanon. Those who live above the Yellow Line are mostly out of the line of fire but hear constant explosions and drones, and at times have struggled to access their land.
In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump has reportedly considered launching another round of attacks on Iran, in coordination with Israel. Iran has warned that if such an attack happens, it would retaliate against targets in the region. This has led to questions over whether Hezbollah, which is backed by Iran, would return to conducting its own attacks against Israel.
Israeli officials have also accused the Lebanese army of failing to meet its part of the framework deal – something the Lebanese army denies – in what analysts say might be an effort to build justification for another bombing campaign in Lebanon.
“When it comes to Lebanon, Israel doesn’t need that instigation,” Mohamad Bazzi, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera. “It destroyed more of the south under the ceasefire of April 17 than before it. Again and again, Israel has shown its willingness to carry out its policies, to destroy as much of south Lebanon as possible, to make it uninhabitable, and to punish the Shia community and there is no reason it won’t do more of the same if the US and Israel restart the Iran war on a large scale.”
Bags packed, batteries charged
In July 2024, Ramez, who did not want to use his real name for security reasons, was sitting in his bedroom in Beirut’s southern suburb of Haret Hreik when he heard loud explosions. Soon after, the neighbouring building collapsed on his apartment.
Since then, he has stayed in his family’s second home, about a half-hour drive southeast of Beirut.
“The war for me never really stopped,” he told Al Jazeera. “Going to sleep is a gamble between insomnia, nightmares or panic attacks. Even if every country in the world disposed of every single bomb and every single bullet and every single gun, the trauma will stay there.”
He said his family has postponed returning to his home in Beirut’s southern suburbs, known as Dahiyeh, over concerns the attacks could restart. “Personally, I can’t possibly even consider sleeping there without hallucinating the building collapsing in on me again.”
Ramez said he is keeping his batteries and power banks charged, his water supply steady for months and his car’s petrol tank full.
Other people interviewed by Al Jazeera who are from Dahiyeh or the south said they keep go-bags packed.
“People have been planning for a few months,” Karim Safieddine, a non-resident fellow with the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told Al Jazeera. “Dahiyeh hasn’t been filled with people in the past few months. At night, it always empties a bit and everyone has a very, very delicate escape route that’s very quick.”
Economic pain
While general anxiety has gripped many in Lebanon over another round of intense fighting, people are also feeling the economic crunch.
The World Bank said in August that it expects inflation in Lebanon to rise to 17.5 percent this year.
And analysts fear that could have severe security consequences.
“As this cycle repeats itself, people get worn down, exhaust their savings and their goodwill, and I think that adds to the possibility of social explosion,” Bazzi said. “Lebanese society will blame Hezbollah for instigating against Israel and by extension [some will blame] the entire Shia community.”
Jad Dilati, a Lebanese analyst from Nabatieh, in southern Lebanon, said that some families have continued to pay rent for apartments in other parts of Lebanon in order “to secure alternative accommodation in case another war breaks out”.
But after three years of war, he said, “that’s a privilege that not everyone can afford”.
Analysts also warned that another round of fighting could increase sectarian tensions in the country. They say Israel has tried to foment internal strife in Lebanon, often by warning non-Shia communities in the south against hosting displaced people. And with people already barely getting by economically, another round of fighting could cause a sectarian spark.
“It is a combustible mix that could explode through something unexpected,” Bazzi said.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 will expose the conflicts and contradictions of the world’s fossil fuel reliance
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Holding a climate conference under the presidency of one coal-obsessed country might be regarded as a misfortune for the planet – sharing it between two starts to look provocative. But at this year’s Cop31 UN climate summit in Antalya, coal exporter Australia and coal consumer Turkey will be trying to shift the focus away from dirty fossil fuels and towards clean electricity, with a target on the table to meet 35% of final energy demand from electricity by 2035.
Will they succeed? The geopolitical outlook for Cop31 is worse than for almost any recent “conference of the parties” under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza are destabilising global alliances, an unpredictable White House is sowing economic uncertainty and AI is threatening to unleash digitised chaos.
But with an El Niño weather system supercharged by fossil fuels already wreaking havoc and yet to peak, the climate is showing where the real potential for earthbound catastrophe lies. For the next fortnight, Down to Earth will bring you twice-weekly updates from the Cop31 negotiations plus, when the gavel finally comes down, a final assessment of what progress has been made – and where negotiations have fallen short in Antalya.
But first, this week’s most important reads.
Essential reads
- ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
- The Amazon’s canary in the coalmine: what a tropical fish can tell us about climate upheaval
- The next global pandemic could be brewing on a mink farm in Utah – and little is being done to stop it
In focus
That Cop31 is happening in Antalya, but presided over by Australia, is the product of a last-minute compromise struck last year at Cop30 in Belém. Australia had wanted to hold a Cop since 2021, when Anthony Albanese made it one of his key promises ahead of the climate-inflected general election he won the next year. Turkey has also wanted to hold a Cop for some time, and claimed to have agreed with the UK, hosts of the Glasgow Cop26 conference in 2021, that 2026 would be its year.
For complicated reasons dating back to 1992, when the UNFCCC was signed, Australia and Turkey fall in the same group as western Europe when it comes to being allowed to bid for the presidency, which rotates annually between five regional groups. There is no mechanism within the treaty for resolving situations where two countries cannot agree on their bid, and no provision for a majority vote to decide among competing options.
Despite this inauspicious start, the two countries seem to have worked well together in the run-up. Australia will chair the negotiations, taking charge of issues such as the “just transition” to help workers in fossil fuels adjust to a low-carbon economy, the loss and damage fund (which has come into renewed focus after the catastrophic glacier collapse in Nepal), other forms of climate finance and progress on emissions cuts.
Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, which is a programme of voluntary commitments that runs alongside the formal negotiations. This year, the quest to electrify the global economy will be the central plank, with initiatives on cutting waste and methane – two topics beloved of Turkey’s first lady, Emine Erdoğan – also on the list.
Cop31 is also the first major international meeting after several momentous elections: the US midterms, which delivered a pummelling to Donald Trump and the Republicans, and Brazil’s presidential poll, won by the president, Lula da Silva. The latter was regarded as a relief for the Amazon, which Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, was likely to have opened up to further rampant exploitation.
And it is the last such outing for another familiar figure – António Guterres, who has used his two terms as secretary-general of the UN to speak out on the climate as none other. Expect a fiery farewell.
With some items of good news to celebrate, the outlook for Cop31 is not all bleak. But delegates would do well to read the latest UN reports on what it will take to minimise the now inevitable overshoot of the 1.5C threshold. Preventing temperatures rising beyond 1.8C will require massive and urgent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, while global carbon emissions have yet to peak. Phasing out fossil fuels has never been so urgent.
Inevitably, the fossil fuel predilections of both hosts will come under scrutiny. Australia could start to shift its reliance on fossil fuel exports in favour of clean electricity, Australia’s Cop31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, told the Guardian when we caught up with him at the mid-year climate talks in Bonn in June. But he refused to put any kind of end date on coal.
Coal remains Turkey’s biggest source of power, despite a push for renewable energy, and the country’s national climate plan allows for an increase in its greenhouse gas emissions, rather than a cut. A group of 50 frontline organisations from Turkey, Australia and other coal regions around the world wrote to the Cop presidents this week to call for an end to coal mining and use.
Mehmet Dalkanat from the Afşin-Elbistan Platform for the Protection of Life and Nature in Turkey said: “People in Afşin-Elbistan have lived with coal for 40 years and have already paid a heavy price in pollution and the impacts of coal.” He points towards the cancellation of plans to expand the country’s largest coal-fired power plant in July. “[This was] a major victory for local communities who have been fighting for years, and a powerful source of hope for a coal-free future,” he said. “The Cop31 presidencies must build on this local victory to accelerate the phaseout of coal and deliver a just transition.”
Though freedom of expression is curtailed in Turkey – as it has been in three of the previous four Cop host countries – expect more such protests in Antalya. We’ll be following developments throughout the summit, with our daily liveblog bringing you news, analysis – and a look behind the scenes of one of the most vital meetings on the planet.
Read more:
 Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence
 
Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels
 
Overseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coal

Turkey halts Turkmen gas imports via Iran under US pressure
Turkey had to stop gas imports from Turkmenistan through Iran due to US pressure, Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar revealed on Thursday during a briefing with journalists.
Ankara began receiving gas from Turkmenistan in March 2025 under a deal to supply 1.3 billion cubic metres annually using Iranian infrastructure. Turkish gas importer Botas had an import licence for the arrangement valid until 2033.
However, Ashgabat cut the flow of gas in October 2025, saying the two countries had a short-term contract and that, without an agreement on volumes or prices, it could not sell gas to Ankara.
Bayraktar said earlier this year that Ankara had planned to resume gas imports from Turkmenistan via Iran, but those plans did not materialise.
He has now revealed that the real problem was the US-Iran war, which started in February.

“Then we stopped because OFAC, (US Office of Foreign Assets Control), somehow involved in this,” he said. “And although we were not paying anything to Iran, the situation escalated between Iran and the US, that is flowing south now.”
Bayraktar said Turkey has spare capacity in the Trans-Anatolian Gas Pipeline and could easily double the volume of gas exported to Europe.
He added that Azerbaijan’s gas reserves were slowly being depleted and that Turkmenistan’s “abundant” gas could offer a viable alternative to meet the needs of both European partners and the Turkish market.
Yet infrastructure challenges, including the dispute over exclusive economic zones in the Caspian Sea, make it harder to build a gas pipeline connecting Turkmenistan to Azerbaijan.
Turkey’s own gas contracts with Iran are also expiring in November, and it remains unclear whether Ankara is ready to renew them. US sanctions targeting Iran intensified earlier this year, forcing countries in the region to take action against Iranian businesses and the financial sector.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: How Israel is tightening its grip on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
How Israel is tightening its grip on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem
Israeli restrictions on teachers and pressure to adopt Israeli curriculum threaten Palestinian education in the city.
Jamal Shalabi is a 66-year-old chemistry teacher living in el-Bireh, in the occupied West Bank, but since 1998 he has taught in occupied East Jerusalem, making the commute through Israeli checkpoints every day.
The process was tiring, but it allowed him to work. But he now fears that soon won’t be the case, after he was informed by his school’s administration that he was one of 180 Palestinian teachers whose travel permits allowing them entry into East Jerusalem would be revoked upon their expiry at the end of the 2026-27 academic year.
The denial of entry permits to teachers is one of the most prominent restrictions imposed by Israel on schools in East Jerusalem, which, like the West Bank, is illegally occupied Palestinian territory, but which Israel considers part of a unified Jerusalem under its control.
Permits were already a problem for teachers like Shalabi this year, when the issuance of documents was delayed until September 15, two weeks after the academic year began. Permits were also delayed last January. The delays in both January and September led to school strikes in East Jerusalem, a move intended to exert pressure and demonstrate a unified stance against these Israeli measures.
Shalabi explained that even when the permits are approved, they are severely restrictive. The documents can only be used during specific hours, which teachers are not permitted to exceed. The teachers are also prohibited from being anywhere other than the schools.
“These permit restrictions have been in place since the war on Gaza in 2023; we can no longer reach the Al-Aqsa Mosque to pray, nor can we accompany students on school field trips, as the permits are strictly limited to the workplace,” he explained.
“Moreover, for the first time, we were barred from entering Jerusalem for an entire week during the recent Jewish holiday of Sukkot,” he added.
Imposition of the Israeli curriculum
The permit restrictions come alongside wider measures affecting Palestinian education in East Jerusalem, including policies introduced under a plan approved by the Israeli government supposedly aimed at “reducing socioeconomic gaps” in East Jerusalem, whose population is majority Palestinian, despite Israeli efforts to increase the number of Jewish settlers.
The government plan also aims to increase the number of Palestinian students studying the Israeli curriculum. It does so by conditioning funding for new schools on the adoption of the Israeli curriculum, alongside programmes to train teachers within the Israeli education system.
A report by the Israeli human rights organisation Ir Amim warned that the policies exploit educational needs to undermine the autonomy of Palestinian education, as well as its national and cultural identity.
The report further warns of the repercussions of a law that prohibits the employment of teachers who hold university degrees from Palestinian educational institutions, a measure likely to exacerbate the existing shortage of teachers in East Jerusalem’s schools.
According to Ir Amim, approximately half of the education budget allocated under the Israeli government’s plan for East Jerusalem is directed towards expanding the teaching of the Israeli curriculum.
Furthermore, Israeli authorities make the adoption of this curriculum a prerequisite for the opening of new state-funded schools, which the organisation views as a form of pressure on both schools and parents to abandon the Palestinian curriculum.
The number of Palestinian students in East Jerusalem studying the Israeli curriculum was only in the hundreds 15 years ago. But by 2020, the figure had risen to more than 10,000.
The numbers have risen sharply since then. By 2024, it had risen to almost 20,000, according to Palestinian officials, and then to more than 27,000 the following year, according to figures cited by Ir Amim. Palestinian officials estimate that more than 45,000 students – approximately 38 percent of the total student population in the city – are now studying the Israeli curriculum in the 2026-27 academic year.
A principal of a school in East Jerusalem, who requested anonymity for fear of repercussions from Israeli authorities, told Al Jazeera that the expansion of the Israeli curriculum to tens of thousands of Palestinian students is the culmination of years of policies aimed at controlling education in East Jerusalem.
He argued that the situation represents an unprecedented threat to Palestinian education; the imposition of the Israeli curriculum is not merely an academic choice, but a policy designed to forcibly impose a new reality.
“This policy is not limited to official schools affiliated with the Israeli municipality; it also extends to private and community-based schools,” he added. “It involves [an attempt to replace the Palestinian curriculum] with a distorted version printed under the supervision of the municipality that erases and falsifies Palestinian history, geography, and national identity.”
The principal further explained that schools face direct threats, including the loss of funding, financial support, and operating licences if they refuse to introduce classes teaching the Israeli curriculum. This, he explained, was part of an Israeli five-year plan aimed at promoting the “Israelisation” of Palestinian education.
This included strict, rigorous oversight mechanisms, including on-site inspections and monitoring within classrooms, as well as the searching of students’ schoolbags to confiscate original Palestinian textbooks and prevent them from being taught.
“Israeli authorities intervene directly in the appointment of school principals and teachers, revoking the licences of those who don’t comply with their directives. Furthermore, this oversight extends to academic and personal persecution through targeting students, even for their personal social media posts or opinions, and employing disciplinary committees and police summonses to intimidate both staff and students,” the principal explained.
Al Jazeera has reached out to Israeli authorities, but has yet to receive a response.
Classroom shortage
Schools in East Jerusalem face a deficit of 2,283 classrooms, according to calculations by Ir Amim.
The organisation’s report warns that even if the Jerusalem Municipality’s plans to construct new classrooms are fully implemented, the crisis will not be resolved; a shortfall of approximately 1,100 classrooms is projected to persist by 2032.
For its part, the municipality estimates the current shortage at about 1,500 classrooms, a figure Ir Amim disputes because it says the calculation relies on outdated data.
Ramadan Awad, spokesperson for the Union of Parents’ Committees for Jerusalem Schools, told Al Jazeera that some classrooms contain as many as 42 students.
He explained that the shortage of classrooms is not merely a matter of insufficient space to enrol students; it also creates challenges within the schools themselves. Some institutions are forced to accommodate large numbers of students in cramped rooms, making it difficult for teachers to engage with individual students or monitor their academic progress.
Awad added that some schools have begun seeking out any available building to rent and convert into a school, even if it was originally a residential apartment or a commercial property.
“Such spaces often lack the essential features of a proper school, such as open courtyards, laboratories and rooms dedicated to extracurricular activities,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: ‘Instead of scuba diving on shrinking reefs, we helped regrow them’: readers’ best conservation tourism experiences
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
Coral reef restoration in Tanzania
The Ropes of Hope works for coral reef restoration in the Mafia Island marine park, off Tanzania. Instead of scuba diving to see shrinking reefs, we got involved with a project regrowing them. It’s the brainchild of Jean de Villiers, a South African molecular biologist who talked my teenagers through the underwater coral gene bank research and community involvement. Our ocean-view tree house accommodation didn’t hurt, with hot chocolate and cake hoisted up fresh each morning. In an educational U-turn, our eldest now studies sustainable development – Jean is doing something right.
 
Claire
Rewilding in the Scottish Highlands
Trees for Life, founded 40 years ago, is a rewilding project aiming to restore the glorious Caledonian forest across the Scottish Highlands. Typical volunteer weeks involve groups of up to 10 adults staying in bothies where you live and cook together and spend days on tasks such as planting, monitoring wildlife, surveying vegetation and maintenance work. They take place in some of the most beautiful and remote locations in the Highlands such as Glen Affric, one of the largest wild native forests in the UK where my partner and I spent a week we’ve never forgotten. There’s no wifi or fancy frills but a life-changing opportunity to work and live in a truly wild and beautiful part of Scotland, make new friends and feel your body and mind respond to hard but vital work.
 
Cal
Closer to nature in the Netherlands
The Holenberg forest in a remote corner of the Netherlands is the gateway to the Maashorst nature reserve, where I stayed in a Cabin Anna – an eco-aware experience that is as much an ethos as it is accommodation. Tucked away among a canvas of trees, heather and wetlands, the focus of these self-sufficient woodland cabins is on reducing man’s negative impact on the landscape, from the bed linen to the recycled waste-product cups, knives and forks. The simple wooden cabins are candlelit and sleep two – outside nights on the terrace gazing at stars are encouraged. You can hire bikes or hike through the forest to explore, including seeing and sensitively interacting with cows, goats, sheep and bison to enhance awareness of the natural world.
 
April
A buzzy experience in Italy’s South Tirol
Thanks to a stay at the Rinner Hotel in the South Tirol, my young teenagers and I discovered the generous contribution that bees make to our planet in terms of life, sustainability and conservation. Everything at this family-run Alpine hotel is centred on apiculture and the bee. There is an api wellness experience, including the inhalation of healthy beehive air while listening to the meditative buzzing of bees, hands-on sessions, beekeeping courses and a delicious dining menu of organic honeys – including a gala honey feast, with each course connected to sweet nectar produced on site. All electricity is generated from waste wood products that would have been thrown away, and the food, including organic wheat and barley, all comes from the green fields of the South Tyrol. My wife said I came back as a more relaxed, cooperative, sweeter person – a fine compliment to the bees.
 
Nigel
Walking with rhinos in Uganda
At Uganda’s Ziwa Rhino and Wildlife Ranch, conservation comes with mud, nerves and a very wet ending. Our guide, SP, treated rhino trekking like a game: he was captain, and victory meant spotting three rhinos. Walking silently along the winding “rhino highway”, we encountered mothers and calves just 25ft away, watching them graze in the wild. Ziwa is Uganda’s only place to see wild rhinos, part of a project to restore these endangered giants. SP called their favourite muddy wallow and salt lick the “rhino supermarket”. We even found the alpha male. Then the heavens opened. Game won; dryness lost!
 
Roy
Swap plastic for cat food in Montenegro
Last summer, while exploring Kotor, Montenegro, a local person’s recommendation led me to a cat park just inside the Old Town’s North Gate. In this quiet corner, sun-drowsy cats sprawled across the warm ground, while mischievous kittens tumbled over one another. Beside them, a curious recycling machine offered an irresistible exchange: feed it empty plastic bottles in exchange for cat food for the town’s feline residents. After collecting my plastic waste for a week, I brought it here, a simple way to give something back to Kotor.
 
Lucy
Wild spaces teeming with life in Kent
We love Elmley Nature Reserve on the Isle of Sheppey in Kent for its remote, windswept landscapes and the long, seemingly barren stretches of land that are in fact teeming with life. One of my favourite memories is getting out and about at dusk, listening to the little owls hoot to one another as the gloom closes in. There’s something special about being somewhere so exposed and yet quiet, surrounded by owls (and other wildlife) going about their own lives. Elmley makes you slow down, pay attention and realise that even the emptiest-looking landscape is full of life.
 
Matt
Winning tip: a sea turtle hospital in Calabria, Italy
We spent September bicycle touring in Sicily and Calabria and one of the highlights was a few days in Brancaleone, a typical Italian working town. We visited the Sea Turtle Recovery Centre in the old railway station. The centre is manned entirely by volunteers and since 2006 they have rescued and rehabilitated more than 700 turtles. The staff are enthusiastic, friendly and informative. They charge a small entry fee and it’s by appointment only, but it is a joy to visit.
 
Anne

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/canada/ars.title: Arsenic, plomb, cadmium… Empoisonnés par une fonderie, les habitants de Rouyn-Noranda au Canada en lutte contre le mastodonte industriel Glencore
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/canada/ars.author: Tom Demars-Granja
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/canada/ars.text:
Fondée il y a cent ans, la ville de Rouyn-Noranda (nord-ouest du Québec) est au centre d’un régime d’exception permettant à la fonderie Horne de polluer au-delà des seuils tolérés. Face à ce passe-droit mortel, les habitants tentent de lutter contre ce mastodonte industriel soutenu par le gouvernement québécois.
Rouyn-Noranda (Canada), envoyé spécial.
Il suffit de se promener dans les longues allées vides du centre-ville pour s’en rendre compte : toutes les rues mènent à la fonderie de cuivre de Horne, un colosse d’acier et de poussière dont les deux cheminées dominent Rouyn-Noranda depuis cent ans.
Seuls signes de vie dans le quartier résidentiel autour de l’usine : des camions de déménagement et quelques pick-up. Quatre-vingts maisons, dont un quart est abandonné, y sont éparpillées sur une zone de 700 mètres de largeur et 100 mètres de longueur.
« La fonderie payait les réparations des voitures »
Le quartier a toujours vécu dans un entre-deux. À peine adolescent, George (le prénom a été modifié) en a déjà conscience. Réfugié derrière l’entrebâillement de sa porte d’entrée, le jeune garçon rapporte une anecdote qu’il tient de sa famille : « Pendant longtemps, la fonderie payait les réparations des voitures rouillées par la pollution. »
La pratique a eu cours dans les années 1980, lorsque l’acide attaquait la peinture des véhicules. Des feuilles A4 blanches avec quelques lignes de texte imprimées ont été scotchées sur plusieurs portes d’entrée : « Défense de pénétrer. RAS (pour Richmond Advisory Services, Inc., une société spécialisée dans le courtage hypothécaire) a pris possession de cette propriété. »
Le point de bascule date de mars 2023. Les habitants du quartier apprennent alors par voie de presse que le gouvernement du Québec a autorisé la fonderie Horne à racheter 60 bâtiments afin de créer une zone tampon. Malgré les protestations des...

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Indonesia names fourth wiretapping suspect as political intrigue deepens
Scandal is driving divisions between President Prabowo Subianto and predecessor Joko Widodo, sparking security concerns.
Indonesian police have named a fourth suspect in a scandal focused on the alleged wiretapping of President Prabowo Subianto.
At a news conference late on Thursday, police named a senior law enforcement official with the initials SU as the latest suspect. Three officials were arrested earlier in the week, in a scandal that has exposed a deepening rift between the president and his predecessor – and former ally – Joko Widodo, and sparked security concerns.
Police said that the new suspect served as monitoring chief at Indonesia’s Criminal Investigation Agency between 2010 and 2019. Local media later identified him as Slamet Uliandi.
Investigators alleged that SU, who was the head of the investigation agency’s information and technology unit from 2021 to 2026, gave the go-ahead for the wiretapping.
Cybercrime unit director Suhermanto told a media conference, “When the other two suspects were about to wiretap, they got approval from SU. They also asked his approval before deleting interception records.” Suhermanto added that SU had not yet been detained due to a health condition.
Three senior police officers were arrested on Tuesday, including the former national police chief and Prabowo’s chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is widely known as a Widodo loyalist.
The case has piled more pressure on Prabowo, with public discontent growing over his costly populist policies and weakening investor confidence in Indonesia’s $1.5 trillion economy.
Police are still investigating the motives behind the attempts to intercept Prabowo’s communications, and have so far questioned 13 police officers and five criminal and IT experts.
The national police chief has also formed a special team to investigate the case, spokesperson Trunoyudo Wisnu Andiko said.
Jakarta remained calm on Thursday and Friday despite the deployment of thousands of troops in the wake of the wiretapping revelations. Military tents and buses were seen in the capital, as well as a small number of soldiers.
Prabowo took office in 2024 after winning the election in a landslide as the continuity candidate for Widodo. Joko Widodo’s son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, was also elected as Prabowo’s vice president.
Lawmakers are now also considering a probe into the eligibility of Raka in what could be the first step towards removing him from office.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: Dear Andy Burnham: the full story of enslavement has to move beyond comforting stories
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Matthew Stallard
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
In May 1767, a notice was placed in the Manchester Mercury for “Any Gentleman, or Lady, wanting to purchase a Black Boy, 12 years of age” to inquire on Market Street, at the site of today’s Uniqlo clothes shop.
After 15 years of painstaking work through the scattered fragments that recorded and pointed to Manchester’s enslaving history, I still don’t think I have come to terms with my moment of discovery, a few months ago, of those few words captured in black and white. The sale of a human being, a child, on our busiest shopping street.
The reality of Manchester’s relationship with enslavement is something that we as a city are yet to fully appreciate and are only slowly beginning to unravel.
Andy Burnham’s article published in the Guardian on Friday is the most positive response yet by a UK prime minister to calls for full recognition and reparation for Britain’s role in transatlantic enslavement. It offers hope and new space for dialogue and development.
From the point of view of Britain’s collective memory and understanding, however, the statement leaves space for greater depth of engagement and reflection to inform a national and local understanding of the true scale and reality of this history.
While clearly acknowledging that “Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people”, the region’s former mayor chose to lead and close his piece by referring to Thomas Clarkson’s 1787 anti-slavery speech at Manchester Cathedral and the letter of solidarity from a group of Mancunians, collectively described as “workingmen”, during the Lancashire Cotton Famine.
On the surface, these seem natural touch points that a leader might use to draw inspiration from progressive moments in our history. However, understanding our local or national relationship with enslavement by focusing on a few short windows of solidarity and success in more than three centuries of brutalisation, dehumanisation and systemic profiting and reliance is like trying to tell the entire story of the Norman conquest through looking at a single panel on the Bayeux tapestry. In the dark. With just the light off your mobile phone.
Many readers, perhaps, will think this is splitting hairs. But consider for a moment the difference between these statements: “We were the first country to end the slave trade” v “It took us 250 years to end the slave trade.”
Or, from a Mancunian context: “Starving cotton workers stood in solidarity with enslaved people during the civil war” v “The whole economy and development of industrial Manchester relied on enslavement and public solidarity with the enslaved came about once the cotton had already been already embargoed for years.”
The 1863 Lincoln letter that Burnham refers to came 56 years after Britain had ended its own transatlantic slave trade and 25 years after slavery was ended in Britain’s colonies – a period during which Manchester’s economic reliance on enslavement actually grew.
In 2007 UK government and lottery funding was deployed in a nationwide programme to commemorate the bicentenary of the abolition of the British slave trade. This was the most widespread collective effort to date to conduct local projects around these themes and resulted in hundreds of exhibits and events.
One of the biggest reflections from communities and historians after that programme was the concern that in many areas it resembled a national “Wilberfest” – with a disproportionate focus and celebration of white abolitionists’ successes. We naturally want to tell ourselves a positive story about our national history, and by far the most comfortable aspect of it is abolition and the eventual success of those campaigns.
And as for Mancunians, we are rightly proud of our progressive history and working-class identity. The Cotton Famine story – that thousands of out-of-work operatives met on New Year’s Eve 1862 and voted to support the union blockade of vital cotton supplies to Lancashire on humanitarian, anti-slavery grounds – in particular, appeals to our best version of ourselves with its “workingmen” aspect. This is echoed in our memorial landscape, where the only public marker of the fundamental reliance of the emergence of the world’s first industrial city on enslavement is the statue of a white man: Abraham Lincoln.
That meeting and letter from Lincoln thanking these working men is a fact. But less than four years earlier, on the eve of civil war, the activist Sarah Parker Remond bravely declared from the stage of the city’s Athenaeum that she was “convinced that, as a rule, the heart of Old England beat truly to the anti-slavery cause, but in Manchester and Liverpool she had found something that approximated more to the pro-slavery spirit of America”.
In the Guardian’s Cotton Capital series, published after it acknowledged its founders’ links to transatlantic enslavement, we showed how Manchester as a city, its institutions, and its textile production grew in symbiosis with the expansion of the Cotton Kingdom of the US South from 1790 to 1860 – at which point 80% of its raw cotton came from enslaved labour in America.
These facts were not lost on Frederick Douglass, who five weeks before his 1846 arrival in town succinctly and perfectly analysed the colonial-capitalist system, which the Manchester Men stood at the head of shaping and financing: “I will give you an invariable rule by which to ascertain the price of human flesh in the United States. When cotton gets up in the market in England, the price of human flesh gets up in the United States”. Seventeen more years of unprecedented slavery-based economic growth ensued before the Lincoln letter was drafted.
All of this, of course, came after the abolition of British slavery in the 1830s. New research into local anti-slavery debates for the forthcoming landmark exhibition at the city’s Science and Industry Museum exhibition (in partnership with the Guardian and the Scott Trust Legacies of Enslavement programme) has shown that calls for the abolition of British slavery surged into Manchester’s political debate directly in response to the uprising of up to 15,000 enslaved people in Demerara in 1823, only to drop off again until becoming a key election issue in 1832 after the Christmas Uprising of about 60,000 enslaved people in Jamaica, which finally forced the British establishment into decisive action.
Burnham fails to mention in his piece that the British people were very much “made to pay for the wrongs of slavery” at that point. The eventual 1838 emancipation from British slavery was bought through a government loan of £20m in reparations to the enslavers, who re-invested much of it into British and imperial economic development. The formerly enslaved people received neither financial compensation nor land.
As the exhibition’s consultant historian, I would like to invite the prime minister to join us in Manchester next year, where we will be attempting to give a much broader and holistic context to re-ground our collective memory of our shared history. He would be welcome to invite the culture secretary and the heads of the Heritage Fund and Arts Council. He can even bring all the G20 leaders and the king, too, if he’d like.
As the UK builds towards the bicentenaries of abolition in 2033 and emancipation and compensation in 2038, we need to see commitments of serious investment into descendant-led programmes and multi-year community engagement and research to tell the fullest story possible.
By no means should we knock down or decry those aspirational moments that challenge us to live up to the highest ideals of solidarity and shared humanity. But Burnham’s call to “confront our complicated history” does not involve telling yourself the best, most comforting version of that story.
That erases the true scale of our reliance on the slavery system, the injustice of state compensation paid to enslavers, and the vital agency of Black abolitionists in forcing debates through mass uprisings, radical intellectual analysis, and public provocations and testimony. It also means we cannot fully understand or come to terms with the reality of our local and national history and achieve true repair and restitution.
- Matthew Stallard is a writer and historian of industrialisation, colonisation and enslavement

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Justiça barra plano do Governo do DF para capitalizar BRB com imóveis públicos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Ana Gonçalves
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Justiça do Distrito Federal declarou inconstitucionais dispositivos da lei que autorizava o uso de imóveis públicos e ativos de empresas estatais para reforçar o patrimônio do Banco de Brasília (BRB). A decisão foi proferida pela 2ª Vara da Fazenda Pública do DF, que julgou parcialmente procedentes duas ações populares contra a Lei Distrital nº 7.845/2026 e determinou a nulidade dos atos administrativos e societários realizados com base nas previsões consideradas inconstitucionais.
As ações questionavam a possibilidade de utilizar bens pertencentes ao Distrito Federal e a empresas públicas como a Companhia Imobiliária de Brasília (Terracap), a Companhia Urbanizadora da Nova Capital (Novacap), a Companhia Energética de Brasília (CEB) e a Companhia de Saneamento Ambiental (Caesb) em operações de capitalização do banco.
Na avaliação do magistrado, a legislação não demonstrou adequadamente o interesse público necessário para a utilização dos imóveis e deixou de observar exigências previstas na Lei Orgânica do Distrito Federal para a desafetação de bens públicos. A sentença também destacou que as empresas estatais possuem autonomia patrimonial e que seus bens não podem ser tratados como extensão do patrimônio do governo.
A decisão determina a nulidade de atos que dependam diretamente dos dispositivos invalidados, incluindo operações de alienação, transferência, utilização ou constituição de garantias com os imóveis previstos na legislação. O entendimento, porém, não impede que o governo busque outras formas de fortalecer financeiramente o BRB, desde que respeite os requisitos legais e constitucionais.
Os pedidos de ressarcimento de danos ao erário foram rejeitados por falta de comprovação de prejuízo patrimonial concreto. A Justiça também reconheceu a perda parcial do objeto das ações em relação à Gleba A da Serrinha do Paranoá e a um imóvel do Setor de Indústria e Abastecimento (SIA), retirados anteriormente da relação de bens prevista na lei.
Lei foi aprovada em meio à crise do Banco Master
A Lei nº 7.845 foi sancionada em 10 de março pelo então governador Ibaneis Rocha (MDB), após aprovação do Projeto de Lei nº 2.175/2026 pela Câmara Legislativa do Distrito Federal (CLDF), por 14 votos favoráveis e 10 contrários. A proposta autorizou o governo a mobilizar imóveis públicos e ativos avaliados em até R$ 6,6 bilhões para reforçar o capital do BRB.
Entre as alternativas previstas estavam a transferência de imóveis ao banco, a venda de terrenos e a utilização dos bens como garantias em operações financeiras. O texto também autorizava operações de crédito com o Fundo Garantidor de Créditos (FGC) e outras instituições financeiras, além da criação de fundos imobiliários.
A medida foi apresentada pelo governo como uma estratégia para recuperar a capacidade financeira do banco, que enfrentava dificuldades após operações com o Banco Master. Entre os imóveis inicialmente incluídos no projeto estavam sedes de empresas públicas no SIA e uma área de aproximadamente 716 hectares na Serrinha do Paranoá, região ambientalmente importante para a recarga hídrica do Distrito Federal.
A proposta provocou reação de movimentos sociais, ambientalistas e parlamentares da oposição, que questionaram a falta de transparência sobre a situação financeira do banco e os riscos de transferência de patrimônio público para operações financeiras.
Em abril, o Ministério Público do Distrito Federal e Territórios (MPDFT) também ajuizou uma ação direta de inconstitucionalidade contra a legislação. O órgão apontou problemas na tramitação da proposta, ausência de avaliação prévia dos imóveis e falta de comprovação do interesse público. O Ministério Público também alertou para os riscos ambientais relacionados à inclusão da Serrinha do Paranoá no projeto.
Antes disso, a lei chegou a ter seus efeitos suspensos por uma decisão liminar em ação popular. O GDF recorreu e conseguiu reverter a suspensão em março, restabelecendo temporariamente a validade da norma. Posteriormente, diante de questionamentos e mobilizações, o governo encaminhou alterações para retirar a Gleba A da Serrinha do Paranoá e um imóvel do SIA da relação de bens.
Operações com o Master estão sob investigação
A necessidade de reforçar o patrimônio do BRB está relacionada à crise desencadeada pelas operações financeiras realizadas com o Banco Master, controlado pelo empresário Daniel Vorcaro.
Em março de 2025, o BRB anunciou a intenção de adquirir parte do banco privado. A operação, que previa a compra de 49% das ações ordinárias e 100% das ações preferenciais, foi rejeitada pelo Banco Central em setembro daquele ano.
Paralelamente à tentativa de aquisição, o banco público realizou operações bilionárias com o Master, que passaram a ser investigadas pela Polícia Federal. Em setembro de 2026, a investigação apontava prejuízo de aproximadamente R$ 17 bilhões nas operações entre as duas instituições, realizadas desde 2024.
Segundo informações reunidas pela PF, houve um fluxo atípico de R$ 12,2 bilhões do BRB para o Master nos primeiros meses de 2025. A investigação também questiona a origem e a qualidade dos créditos adquiridos pelo banco público, incluindo carteiras que teriam sido revendidas por meio de empresas com indícios de irregularidades.
Vítimas de irregularidades
Em outra frente para tentar recuperar os recursos, o Governo do Distrito Federal solicitou ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), nesta quinta-feira (5), que o BRB e o próprio DF sejam reconhecidos como vítimas das irregularidades investigadas no caso Master. A Procuradoria-Geral do DF também solicitou a transferência ao banco de R$ 2,24 bilhões bloqueados em uma conta de Henrique Vorcaro, pai do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.
Os valores foram localizados pela Polícia Federal em uma conta na antiga Reag, durante as investigações da Operação Compliance Zero. O governo argumenta que os recursos têm origem em atividades criminosas e devem ser destinados prioritariamente à reparação dos danos causados ao banco. O pedido foi encaminhado ao presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin, e ainda aguarda análise.
Em outubro, a PF apontou participação do então governador Ibaneis Rocha nas articulações para a tentativa de compra do Master. De acordo com o relatório encaminhado ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), decisões estratégicas do BRB eram submetidas previamente ao chefe do Executivo distrital.
A decisão judicial sobre o patrimônio público representa mais um capítulo dos questionamentos sobre as medidas adotadas pelo governo para enfrentar a crise financeira do banco. Embora a sentença invalide os mecanismos previstos na lei para utilização dos imóveis e ativos das estatais, o fortalecimento financeiro do BRB ainda poderá ser buscado por outros caminhos legais.
Procurado pelo Brasil de Fato DF, o Governo do Distrito Federal não apresentou posicionamento até o fechamento desta reportagem. O espaço segue aberto para manifestações.

From a former Kentish oast house to an award-winning 1950s home an architect built for himself

Anna White

Horsmonden, Kent
This detached oast house makes for a characterful home. The circular kitchen and breakfast room sit on top, opening into a rectangular living room. Underneath is the circular bedroom along with two other bedrooms. In the grounds is a detached workshop/home office, a summerhouse and a wood-fired hot tub. The village is centred around a green and there’s a pub, a school, a church and a store. It sits within the High Weald national landscape, an area of outstanding natural beauty, and is close to the village of Goudhurst.
£750,000.
John D Wood
, 020 8819 3604

View image in fullscreen
Little Kingshill, Buckinghamshire
In a quiet village in the Chilterns is Klee House, an award-winning home built by an architect for himself in the 1950s. It was remodelled in 2004. The five-bedroom house has a two-bedroom annexe, a gym, a studio and a heated swimming pool. The plan was inverted to make the most of the views. Four of the bedrooms are on the ground floor. On the first floor is the open-plan sitting room, dining space and kitchen – which has an exposed-brick fireplace and wood panelling – plus a fifth bedroom.
£2m.

, 020 3795 5920
Photograph: French+Tye/The Modern House

Cardinham, Cornwall
On the south-east edge of Bodmin Moor is this stone-built property. The sitting and dining room – which is about 10 metres (32ft) long, with a vaulted ceiling – is on the first floor and has views towards the Glynn valley. It has a central fireplace and doors that open on to a seven-metre wide west-facing terrace. Steps connect the terrace to the garden. The kitchen is next to the living room. Downstairs are four bedrooms (one is used as a study). A conservatory provides another link to the garden. Cardinham Woods are only minutes away, and offer walking and cycling trails.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Israel’s President Herzog to name candidate to form government on Sunday
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Israel’s President Herzog to name candidate to form government on Sunday
Announcement comes after majority of Israeli lawmakers endorse Eisenkot over Netanyahu.
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has said he will name a candidate to form the country’s next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers backed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Herzog made the announcement on Thursday after holding marathon talks with parties elected to the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.
Some 67 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu.
In televised remarks at the end of the talks, Herzog said that although the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best chance of assembling a governing coalition.
He said he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday, and make a pick on Sunday.
Israel’s October 27 election left neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, handing Herzog the difficult task of choosing a candidate in a deeply divided country.
Netanyahu’s Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but his wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total.
Eisenkot’s alliance of four Jewish-led parties, which spans the political spectrum from centre-left to right, won 48 seats despite polls that had predicted a close race.
Two parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.
Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the support of a comfortable majority of lawmakers.
“We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List, which represents an alliance of Arab parties, told The Associated Press news agency.
Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, said his 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015, and urged Herzog to give him the mandate “as soon as possible” so he could form a national emergency government.
Separately, Netanyahu suffered a setback on Thursday when United Torah Judaism, one of the two main ultra-Orthodox parties and a longtime ally, declined to recommend any candidate.
The party broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Yariv Oppenheimer, a member of the Democrats, a party in Eisenkot’s alliance, told Al Jazeera that he saw “no reason” Herzog would not choose Eisenkot on Sunday.
He said United Torah Judaism had signalled that its support was available for the right price, meaning that a good enough offer from Eisenkot could give him the numbers he needed.
“It’s very clear that Netanyahu doesn’t have a chance to establish a government at all,” he added.
Once nominated by Herzog, the candidate will have 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu will remain prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed, or through another election that must be held if no candidate succeeds.
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote.
Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.
Israel’s Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on Israel’s elected officials to protect public trust rather than shake it.
“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. High voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing, he said.
Netanyahu’s allies on the far-right, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Pressão popular leva prefeito do Recife a voltar atrás e cancelar show de Jorge e Mateus no Ano Novo
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O show público da dupla Jorge e Mateus no Recife, marcado para o dia 27 de dezembro, dentro da programação oficial de Ano Novo, foi cancelado nesta última terça-feira (3). A decisão foi anunciada pelo prefeito da capital, Victor Marques (PCdoB), após uma série de críticas levantadas com a circulação de um vídeo recente, no qual o cantor Jorge aparece em um encontro de artistas sertanejos em apoio o derrotado candidato à presidência Flávio Bolsonaro.
Na ocasião, Jorge chegou a declarar: “pode chorar, mas eu não voto no PT”, parafraseando uma canção de seu repertório, no encontro realizado em Goiás durante as eleições. Com a circulação do vídeo, surgiram uma série de críticas em relação à escalação do sertanejo na programação de ano novo de capitais como Recife e Fortaleza, onde Lula teve 61,27% e 60,07% dos votos, respectivamente.
Internautas também passaram a comentar sobre supostas falas xenofóbicas de Jorge em relação ao Nordeste. Em nota divulgada à imprensa, o cantor nega essas declarações. “Nunca fiz essas declarações e jamais me referiria dessa forma a uma região pela qual tenho tanto carinho, admiração e respeito”, diz Jorge (confira íntegra abaixo).
O show da dupla gerou repercussão política na capital pernambucana. No início da semana, o prefeito Victor Marques chegou a gravar um vídeo sobre os pedidos de cancelamento do show, defendendo que era preciso “respeitar e conviver com todos que pensam diferente de nós”, fazendo necessário “superar divisões”.
Surgiram então críticas ao posicionamento do prefeito. Pedro Alcântara, vice-presidente do Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), divulgou um vídeo em suas redes reforçando a necessidade de cancelamento do show enquanto uma demanda orgânica da população recifense.
“O nosso presidente disse que era preciso desarmar os palanques na política, mas, na vivência cultural do povo com nossa terra, é preciso, sim, afirmar a preferência popular”, afirmou Pedro. Na mesma semana, Jô Cavalcanti (Psol), vereadora do Recife, apresentou um projeto de lei na Câmara proibindo a contratação de artistas que cometam xenofobia contra o povo nordestino.
Na noite da última terça-feira (3), Victor Marques anunciou, por meio de suas redes, que a dupla não mais se apresentaria no Réveillon recifense. Ele afirmou que “não há mais clima para a apresentação da dupla”, diante do espírito de confraternização da festividade. No mesmo dia, o prefeito de Fortaleza, Evandro Leitão (PT) também anunciou o cancelamento do show na capital cearense. Em ambas as cidades, ainda não foram divulgadas atrações substitutas.
A decisão foi celebrada por figuras políticas progressistas e criticada por conservadoras. O vereador do Recife Eduardo Moura (Novo), publicou um vídeo criticando a decisão por um suposto caráter de perseguição ideológica. “Não é boicote, é preconceito e retaliação contra quem não vota no PT”, afirmou Eduardo. Já o também vereador Thiago Medina (PL) criticou a mudança de rumos do prefeito do Recife na decisão, acusando-o de boicote por opinião política.
CONFIRA A NOTA DE JORGE
“Diante de algumas informações que circularam nas redes sociais nos ultimos dias, considero importante esclarecer que as falas que estão sendo atribuidas a mim, especialmente em relação ao nordeste e ao povo nordestino, não são verdadeiras.
Nunca fiz essas declarações e jamais me referiria dessa forma a uma região pela qual tenho tanto carinho, admiração e respeito.
Faço esse esclarecimento em meu nome, por se tratar de uma situação relacionada a mim, e não ao mateus ou à nossa trajetória como dupla.
Ao longo da minha carreira, tive o privilegio de conhecer todos os estados do nordeste, cantar para milhares de pessoas e receber um carinho que sempre levarei comigo.
Tenho uma gratidão imensa pelo povo nordestino, por sua cultura, sua história e por tudo que essa regiao representa para a música brasileira e para a minha própria caminhada.
Respeito as diferentes opiniões e acredito que, acima qualquer divergencia, devem prevalecer o diálogo, a empatia e o respeito.
A música sempre foi a minha forma de me conectar com as pessoas, levar alegria e retribuir todo o carinho que recebo.
Independentemente de qualquer diferença, meu desejo é que o nosso país esteja bem, que as pessoas estejam bem e que nunca percamos o respeito uns pelos outros”.
Jorge

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook review – the heir to a legendary eatery … who sets soup on fire
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Lucy Mangan
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
It starts both very well and very badly does Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook. On the one hand, our host’s absolute ignorance of how food works – or pans, or knives, or plates – has a refreshing authenticity about it. Too often in these shows, in which a celebrity goes on A Journey to acquire basic knowledge in what is generally considered to be a normal field of human endeavour, their lack of exposure to it or inability therein is pretended or hammed up. But actor, rapper and comedian Awkwafina – real name Nora Lum, which is what she uses for this series beyond the title, for reasons that will become clear – is the real, wholly baffled deal.
Non-game recognises non-game, and as a kitchenphobe myself, I see the truth in her crouched stance by the oven or hob, fearful yet hostile to anything they may ask of her. We see her pour milk over a couple of eggs she has just lobbed doubtfully into a pan, the tentativeness with which she approaches spatulas and ladles, the hatred in her eyes when presented with raw ingredients – it all speaks to someone who has remained truly untouched by the culinary arts and was, at least until a commissioning editor approached with an idea, happy to remain so.
On the other hand, the scripted voiceovers are bad. “I’ve been known to set soup on fire,” she says. “Which is impressive. As it’s a dish that’s mainly water.”
Fortunately, someone in charge evidently realises these things are letting the side down and reduces their number as the increasingly fun and more than occasionally moving series continues. Nora is, in a frankly unexpected twist, a descendant of “Chinese restaurant royalty”. Her great-grandfather Jimmy founded the famous Lum’s restaurant in Flushing in Queens, New York, in the 1950s. Her family – including her father and the grandmother who raised her after her mother died when she was four – worked there until it closed in 1982. Her grandmother, Powah Lum, is 91 in the show, and although she doesn’t leave the house much, is still a force to be reckoned with. When Nora asks why Grandma didn’t teach her how to cook, Grandma has a simple answer. “You too lazy.”
Whatever the truth of this, Nora is not a lazy presence on screen. She is a ball of energy and charisma, mesmerising in her intensity whether she is focused on mastering wok skills at the Culinary Institute of America (“This should be both harrowing and entertaining to watch,” she says, approaching the work station like a man walking up the line at Verdun) or exchanging gags with her Crazy Rich Asians co-star Jimmy O Yang, as they drive to Texas to sample the Asian-American fusion cuisines that are being invented beyond Manhattan’s Chinatown.
The aim is that she will open a restaurant. This soon changes to a more plausible pop-up restaurant, in nine months’ time. It will pay homage to Lum’s, and to the experience and heritage of the Cantonese, Korean (like Nora’s distaff side), and other immigrants who came to the US and made their way by setting up eateries and adapting their cuisines to local palates, while also introducing their adopted country to something new.
As she travels to various states and learns how to make bulgogi sausages in Fredericksburg, a Peking duck I would sell my soul to taste in San Francisco at Mister Jiu’s, or joint a chicken in 19 seconds with 80s celebrity chef Martin Yan, Nora and her companions piece together the wider immigrant story, of how the next generation were encouraged to become lawyers, doctors, professionals who could escape the relentless hard work of both kitchens and running your own business. Which they succeeded in doing, but at a cost: with no one to inherit them, most family restaurants, like Lum’s, disappeared. But what has been happening in the last few years is that the grandchildren are coming back – crucially, choosing to come back – to start new businesses, often in the old places and being proud to do so.
Grandma Powah sadly died just after filming, but she makes it to the opening night of Nora’s pop-up homage to Lum’s restaurant (“She’s a paid actor,” Nora tells customers, “but it means a lot”), with its walls lined with family photographs and menu full of the old favourites with modern twists. Grandma is a hard taskmaster, so the entire place waits with bated breath when Nora asks if she liked the food. “I ate a lot,” says Powah. “I am proud of you,” she says as she leaves. “All the time.”
This was a fine thing. I don’t need a second helping – unexpected pleasures should not be milked – but it was a fine thing.
Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook is on Apple TV now.

Iran’s Basij chief praises 'resistance cinema', saying that 'change has begun' in US, Israel
Iran’s Basij commander Hossein Taeb has said that the US and Israel are seeing change amid their ongoing attempts at transforming the Middle East's landscape.
"Today, we say that change has begun in America and Israel, and we will soon see it across different areas," he said during the closing ceremony of the 19th International Resistance Film Festival in Tehran.
His highlighted the use of media and film as a way of "disrupting America’s media monopoly", describing it as "resistance cinema".
"The staging of this festival under such circumstances signifies that - much like a combatant who never abandons their launchers during military defence - an artist engaged in the 'perceptual battlefield' does not desert their post, even under the shadow of war, economic siege, or any other threat," he said.
"Through their portrayal of the Resistance, they inflict a new defeat upon the enemy."
Referencing US-Israeli attacks on Gaza, Lebanon, Iraq and Syria, Taeb said: "All these crimes took place; children were killed, and the oppressed peoples of the region suffered. Yet, the true losers in this conflict were the United States and Israel."

https://www.humanite.fr/medias/arcom/apr.title: Après l’attentat raciste de Trappes, comment empêcher (vraiment) CNews de nuire ?
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/arcom/apr.author: Alexandre Fache,Elora Mazzini
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/arcom/apr.text:
Depuis l’attentat raciste commis par Kevin T, ce trentenaire abreuvé aux discours xénophobes de la chaîne de Vincent Bolloré, des initiatives fleurissent pour réclamer des sanctions enfin dissuasives contre le média réactionnaire. Revue de détail.
Une pétition citoyenne réclamant la « suppression » de CNews, des plaintes devant la justice, une nouvelle saisine de l’Arcom, le régulateur de l’audiovisuel… Depuis l’attentat raciste de Trappes et La Verrière (Yvelines), les initiatives se multiplient pour tenter d’empêcher la chaîne d’information du groupe Bolloré de nuire.
L’objectif ne date pas d’hier, mais il a pris une urgence particulière après la révélation des premiers éléments de l’enquête menée autour de Kevin T., l’auteur de l’attentat qui a coûté la vie à Pengo Bossio Wangi, 26 ans, et blessé cinq autres personnes, dont une fillette de 12 ans, tous visés en raison de leur couleur de peau, le 23 octobre dernier.
« Il faut cesser de considérer CNews comme un média », réclame Ali Rabeh
« Kevin regardait souvent les chaînes d’info en continu, particulièrement CNews, a confirmé à l’Humanité Benjamin1, qui a fréquenté l’auteur de l’attentat quand il habitait à Guyancourt. Il avait globalement un discours anti-immigration, négrophobe, islamophobe, à l’instar de ceux d’Éric Zemmour ou Marine Le Pen. Il liait ses problèmes personnels et les problèmes socio-économiques de la France à l’immigration, disait que c’était « la faute des Noirs et des Arabes ». Ces idées, il les exprimait calmement, comme si elles étaient devenues légitimes ou normales. »
Outre la responsabilité politique de ceux qui, au Rassemblement national (RN) en particulier, ont fait leur fonds de commerce de ces discours de haine, se pose avec de plus en plus d’acuité...

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Australia appoint Mike Hussey as consultant for Ashes and Cricket World Cup
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Australia appoint Mike Hussey as consultant for Ashes and Cricket World Cup
Hussey, known as ‘Mr Cricket’ for his technical expertise, will also work with Australia during the LA 2028 Olympics.
Mike Hussey was appointed on Friday as a consultant coach to the Australian team for next year’s blockbuster Ashes series against England and the 2027 Cricket World Cup.
The former Australian batsman revealed in August that England’s new red-ball coach, Stephen Fleming, had informally approached him to be their Test batting mentor.
But the 51-year-old turned down the audacious offer and has instead committed to helping his home nation arrest a batting crisis, highlighted by their recent 2-1 Test series defeat in South Africa.
Hussey, known as “Mr Cricket” for his technical expertise, will also provide coaching assistance during this month’s home T20 series against England and the subsequent four-Test series against New Zealand.
He will additionally work with Australia during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where cricket is on the agenda, and the T20 World Cup in 2028.
“I am extremely excited about being a part of the team in a more formal and meaningful role in the coming years,” said Hussey, who played more than 300 matches for Australia across all formats.
“This team has achieved so much in recent times, to which I hope I can add value to the coaching and playing groups ahead of what will be an exciting and challenging period.”
Hussey has extensive experience as a coach, including with both Australia and England.
He was part of England’s coaching setup when they won the T20 World Cup in 2022 and was the Chennai Super Kings’ longtime batting coach under Fleming in the Indian Premier League. He also led Welsh Fire in this year’s Hundred.
“Mike has been a highly valued part of our staff in the past and brings a considerable skill set which is complementary to the coaches and players,” said Australian head coach Andrew McDonald.
“Not only is his expertise as a player and coach across multiple formats, competitions, countries invaluable, so are his qualities as a person.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: Eduardo e Flávio Bolsonaro fora do páreo: quem herdará sucessão da extrema direita? Filósofo analisa
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: BdF Entrevista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
O ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro está preso. Os filhos Flávio e Eduardo fugiram para os Estados Unidos. Apesar de Carlos, Renan e a primeira-dama Michelle seguirem no Brasil e estarem eleitos, há um espaço simbólico vago pela extrema direita nos rearranjos de poder. Quem deverá ocupar esse lugar?
Ao BdF Entrevista, o filósofo e professor da PUC-Rio Rodrigo Nunes, autor do livro “Do transe à vertigem: Ensaios sobre a extrema direita e um mundo em transição”, avalia que, mesmo sem feitos relevantes, a família Bolsonaro tem um poder nuclear e de indiscutível influência na política brasileira, impulsionado sobretudo pela conjuntura de 2018 e pela canalização do sentimento antipetista.
“A gente pode pensar que a família Vargas já era uma família influente em alguma medida no Rio Grande do Sul, depois uma família que se torna influente nacionalmente depois do governo Vargas, que é um governo muito transformador na história do país. A família Bolsonaro se torna uma família importante sem ter tido nenhuma grande realização”, pondera.
Para Nunes, Bolsonaro teve sucesso durante um tempo na política ao focar em um nicho muito específico da sociedade: os militares. “É com esse público que ele dialoga, seja os corporativos desse setor, seja defendendo uma certa nostalgia da ditadura militar. Ele consegue construir um capital político inicial a partir disso e aí vai conseguindo encaixar os seus outros filhos na política”, avalia.
Nos anos que antecederam a chegada do Bolsonarismo à presidência, houve as jornadas de junho de 2013 (nas quais a população manifestou nas ruas uma insatisfação geral) e posteriormente o golpe contra Dilma Rousseff. “Nessa fase, o Jair Bolsonaro vai aumentando a visibilidade dele e o seu raio de influência, aquele momento em que ele vai conquistando notoriedade como uma espécie de clown de programas de entretenimento, em que ele aparece como essa figura meio ultrapassada, meio deslocada do mundo contemporâneo”, pontua o professor.
Até que, em 2018, com Lula preso, ele desponta como candidato mais viável para tirar o PT do caminho. O filósofo lembra que havia um sentimento de revolta por conta da corrupção na política, alavancada pelas revelações da operação Lava Jato: “Bolsonaro desponta como outsider e, ao mesmo tempo, acaba despontando o candidato mais vivo anti-lulismo. E nesse ponto é que a família acaba adquirindo o capital político que ela tem hoje”, resume.
Na avaliação dos nomes da família com capital eleitoral para a sucessão, a senadora Michelle Bolsonaro aparece com elevado potencial, especialmente na visão do presidente do PL, Valdemar Costa Neto, embora enfrente divergências familiares. “Michelle é uma personagem que todo mundo entende como mais forte, mais competitiva, talvez mais perigosa até que o próprio Jair Bolsonaro. Mas existe uma resistência por parte dos filhos e até um medo muito grande por parte do Jair Bolsonaro de que ela, uma vez liberta das suas amarras, solta para alçar um voo solo, saia nesse voo solo e não volte mais”, avalia.
Fora do núcleo familiar mais restrito, Rodrigo Nunes comenta a possibilidade de o governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), ser esse nome alternativo e moderado. Para ele, essa aposta ganha força à medida que aumenta a rejeição a perfis considerados mais radicais. “Tarcísio é uma figura mais anódina, mais neutra, e por isso consegue transitar melhor por diferentes espaços”, analisa.
Em paralelo, figuras jovens como o deputado Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) correm por fora e contam com o fator tempo a seu favor, enquanto Flávio e Eduardo Bolsonaro veem suas chances eleitorais reduzidas devido às investigações e à ausência do país. “O Eduardo está queimado, sobretudo por ele ter abandonado o posto dele na Câmara e ter ido fazer lobby nos Estados Unidos contra o Brasil e agora não poder voltar por estar sendo investigado por conta da sua atividade de lobby contra o país. Ao passo que o Flávio, eu acho que sempre se soube, muita gente dentro da direita achava que o Flávio era um balão de ensaio, que era uma coisa que não ia, não era para ser, não era para vingar de fato”, aponta. “Eu acho que esses são, certamente, nomes fora do páreo, hoje em dia”, aposta.
O filósofo e escritor também aborda a capacidade de reorganização da extrema direita, que, na avaliação dele, pode ser explicada pela velocidade na formação de novas lideranças por meio da economia da atenção e das redes digitais. “Os influenciadores digitais tomaram conta, colonizaram a política. Eles demonstraram, de 2018 para cá, uma capacidade de produção e renovação de quadros que é absolutamente espantosa”, destaca. Nunes classifica essas figuras de “empreendedores políticos”, estratégia que, de forma tímida, a esquerda conseguiu imprimir um pouco mais esse ano. “A esquerda apresentou uma renovação maior nessas eleições. E um pouco por esse caminho também, do empreendedorismo político.”
