Why one Republican won a redrawn Texas district despite blue tsunami
Republican redistricting largely backfired in Texas and beyond, but at least one redrawn map proved effective in Texas.
Dallas, Texas – Tuesday’s midterms were bruising for Republicans in Texas, a longtime right-wing stronghold.
The state elected its first Democrats to statewide office in 32 years, and the left-wing party held onto four congressional districts that were recently redesigned to favour Republicans.
But Republicans had one redistricting bright spot in a sea of unexpected defeats in Texas this midterm election cycle.
Amid the so-called blue wave, Republican Jace Yarbrough defeated Dan Barrios in Texas’s 32nd congressional district near Dallas, taking control of a heavily redrawn seat previously held by a Democrat.
Yarbrough became the only Republican this year to flip a Texas congressional seat, despite a push under United States President Donald Trump to shake up the state’s map for the right-wing party’s benefit.
So how did Yarbrough buck the trend? He was successful for two reasons, according to Matthew Wilson, a professor at Southern Methodist University who lives in the 32nd district.
“I think he did effectively pivot from a primary strategy to a general election strategy,” Wilson told Al Jazeera.
A constitutional lawyer, Yarbrough had defined his career by litigating progressive policies. But Wilson explained that the cost of living and other economic concerns took an increasingly prominent role in the final months of Yarbrough’s bid.
“In the primaries, the social issues, cultural issues were really important,” Wilson said.
“But then he pivoted very quickly and realised that those were probably not going to have the same resonance in the fall campaign. And so he did talk a lot about lowering prices. He did talk a lot about things that were of concern more to voters in the centre of the electorate.”
Wilson added there was another important factor in Yarbrough’s victory. “It was just the fact that his district was drawn to be so heavily Republican.”
The 32nd district had previously been composed of left-leaning Dallas and its immediate suburbs, but in August 2025, the Texas state legislature voted to reconfigure the congressional boundaries, with the aim of helping Republicans win five extra seats in this year’s midterms.
That push came at the behest of Trump, who called on Republican-led states across the country to follow suit.
Yarbrough’s district was redrawn to include only a portion of Dallas. It now stretches east instead, to encompass several Republican-dominated counties.
The demographics of the district also shifted dramatically.
In 2024, the district encompassed sizeable Latino, Black and Asian communities, accounting for about 60 percent of the population. The new map lowered the share of those demographics, while including several predominantly white areas.
Still, Wilson pointed out that Yarbrough’s victory was far more muted than initially expected. He won 51.5 percent of the vote to Barrios’s 48.5 percent.
“Even in his case, the race was a lot closer than he would have expected,” Wilson said. “So there was a pretty uniform Democratic swing across congressional districts.”
Latino backlash
With the dust settling on the election, Republicans will start the next congressional term in January with 24 representatives from Texas, losing one seat to Democrats this midterm cycle.
Democrats, who will have commanding control of both chambers of Congress, will have 14 House seats filled by Texans.
The four other Democrat-held districts Texas Republicans hoped to gain via redistricting were swept up in the groundswell of opposition to Trump.
In those districts, the party’s redrawn maps largely miscalculated Latino voters, a demographic that makes up 40 percent of the state’s population and swung towards Trump in 2024, according to political experts.
This year, the demographic tilted back towards Democrats with force, fuelled both by affordability concerns and dismay over Trump’s hardline immigration policies, which disproportionately affect Latino communities.
“In political science, there’s a body of literature we call ‘group threat theory’,” Michael Adams, a professor at Texas Southern University, told Al Jazeera. “When a particular group feels that they are threatened, that mobilises them, and we normally see a higher increase in terms of voter turnout.”
One of the most resounding defeats came in the ninth congressional district in Houston, which for years encompassed an area with large Black and Latino populations. Texas’s newly redrawn map cut out some Black communities but left a large population of low-propensity Latino voters.
Democratic candidate Leticia Gutierrez ended up taking nearly 58 percent of the vote against Republican Alex Mealer.
Speaking to Al Jazeera before the election, Gutierrez said her strategy focused on reaching Latino voters through aggressive Spanish-language outreach focused on pocketbook issues.
“I always say that I have a big chunk of family that are citizens registered to vote, but if they don’t hear it in Spanish, they’re probably not going to show up,” said Gutierrez.
“I’m fortunate enough to be able to speak both languages fairly well, and so just again, doing a lot of that targeted getting out the vote, getting in front of voters, door-knocking.”
Latinos make up about 60 percent of the ninth congressional district. The demographic is even more pronounced in South Texas, where Republicans hoped to pick up the 28th, 34th and 35th districts in their redistricting push.
But in a district representing the suburbs of San Antonio, Democrat Johnny Garcia handily defeated Republican Carlos De La Cruz by more than 10 percentage points.
Along the US-Mexico border, incumbent Democrat Henry Cuellar carried his district with nearly 66 percent of the vote over Republican challenger Tano Tijerina, while in the 34th district, Representative Vicente Gonzalez skated to victory by more than 15 percentage points over Republican challenger Eric Flores.
In another border district, Tejano musician Bobby Pulido, a Democrat, unseated Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz, whose 2022 victory presaged a wider conservative shift among Latinos in the state.
Two years later, Trump carried nearly every Latino-dominated border district in Texas, seizing on unrest over immigration policies under former President Joe Biden. He also leveraged the prevalence of conservative social views among the largely Catholic population.
The area had long been considered a Democratic stronghold.
“Democrats are very conservative here. So I’m not surprised that it went for Trump in 2024,” 37-year-old voter Donato Medina told Al Jazeera from the border city of McAllen before the vote.
“But now it’s like people are kind of waking up, because his policies are affecting them directly.”

In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent asks why the media is obsessing over Obama’s Cheesecake Factory joke while largely ignoring allegations of Trump’s sexual assaults. Plus: Republicans prepare to cry election fraud.

Donald Trump and future wife Melania pose with Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

The president of the United States of America has been accused of rape. Again. The president of the United States has been accused of rape in a report issued by the Democrats of the House Judiciary Committee, as part of their ongoing investigation of Donald Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The president has been accused of raping two women, one when she was as young as 13, and sexually assaulting three more. They are among 11 women who provided evidence or testimony that Trump “abused, assaulted, and even raped numerous women alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.”

I have been made to understand that many people do not know about the Judiciary Comittee report—and the fact that five women have accused Trump of sexual assault while in or near the presence of noted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein. I have been made to understand that this is because the mainstream media finds former president Barack Obama’s comments about the [checks notes] Cheesecake Factory more worthy of their attention than the current president’s abuse of multiple women.

If asked, mainstream media types would no doubt argue that the lack of coverage of these latest rape allegations stems from the fact that previous rape allegations failed to “move the needle.” Trump’s sexual misconduct (both alleged and litigated) is “baked in” to people’s understanding of the man. People either won’t believe the charges or won’t care—or else they do believe the women and do care and vote accordingly—but everybody knows what he’s been accused of, generally speaking at least.

I find this line of argument unadulterated bollocks that reveals the deep failure of our mainstream media. It is news when the president is credibly accused of rape. It is important news. While I, too, don’t think these latest sexual assault accusations will materially change the national conversation about Trump or his presidency, that is not an excuse for ignoring, downplaying, or skipping over brutal allegations that he repeatedly assaulted women, including minors.

Journalists cannot decide what other people think is important. Their job is to illuminate what they think is in the public interest. I think reporting on rape allegations levied against the president of the United States is in the public interest. And since I think that, it really doesn’t matter if the public agrees with me.

With that in mind, I, unlike people who work for Bari Weiss, read the Judiciary report. Here are some of the allegations:

Next week, the Republicans are going to lose. I don’t know precisely which ones or by how much: I suspect that Democrats will retake the House; there’s certainly a chance they will retake the Senate. But no matter how things shake out, it’s very likely that the Republicans will emerge from the election with less political power than they went in with.

That’s not surprising. This is a midterm election, and the party in power in the White House usually loses seats in the midterms, just as a matter of course. And we can expect those losses to be exacerbated when the president in power is deeply unpopular, the economy is in the tank, and the country is engaged in a pointless war that it’s not even winning. The laws of political physics say the GOP is supposed to lose next week, and quite badly.

But the Republicans, at least the ones most devoted to the Trump cult, likely have no idea they are about to lose. That’s because Trump and the white-wing media have been feeding them a steady diet of lies, priming them to believe that the only way Democrats could win is if there is election fraud. Their reasons for doing this are clear: If Trump’s base thinks their loss is due to fraud, they will likely support the most antidemocratic measures Trump takes to hold on to power over the will of the people. If they really believe Trump, at least some of them will turn to violence to support his antidemocratic efforts.

A new study from The Washington Post illustrates the complete saturation of the white-wing media by this false electoral narrative.

Nearly 600 high-profile, right-wing social media accounts, podcasts and other online media have published more than 7,000 statements questioning the election’s integrity so far this year, a Washington Post analysis found. That messaging has, in particular, pushed overstated claims that noncitizens are on voter rolls and that mail-in ballots enable widespread fraud—themes that are twice as prevalent as they were during the 2024 election cycle, The Post’s analysis found.

Look, losing can be a shock in the best of times, but when you are priming your audience to think that a loss could happen only through massive cheating and fraud, and that audience has already shown an appetite for violence when it doesn’t get the electoral outcomes it would like, you are playing with fire.

Trump, of course, wants there to be a fire if his party loses. He needs it. He can’t challenge the election if most people agree that his party lost fair and square. He is trying to sow distrust in the system, because distrust is a crucial precondition to violent overthrow of the system.

One wouldn’t expect any particular candidate to tell their supporters, “Hey guys, we’ll probably get our ass kicked tomorrow, but let’s show up and rock the vote anyway.” Candidates need to engender a sense of hope, even if it’s false, until the end.

But one would expect the media to do the work of preparing people to confront reality. What’s the point of all this inane horse-race coverage if it’s not even going to prepare people for the reality of losing?

Unfortunately, the door swings both ways. There isn’t a nefarious conspiracy about how Trump rigged this election that I’d dismiss out of hand at this point. If the GOP pulls off a series of “close” victories in majority-minority precincts because votes didn’t materialize or vanished into thin air, I’m going to be ready to take to the streets myself.

There is no trust left in the electoral system, on either side. Republicans have been actively trying to undermine it, but I’m not sure what Democrats can do to restore it.

The Department of Justice preemptively sued Alaska to delay certification of the results in the Senate race there because there are two candidates running with the same name. The New York Times then Columbus’d the story, reporting that one of the candidates was likely a plant from the Democrats meant to cause confusion among Republican voters.

The thing is, the Times had trouble remembering the most important legal fact of the story: that all of this was litigated, in Alaska, in June, all the way up to the state Supreme Court. That’s what I wrote about. I explained that Republicans had already objected to the other guy with the same name as their incumbent and lost. I explained that the only reason the DOJ is bringing this up again, in October, is to cause confusion and sow distrust in the election, as well as ask for a remedy so antidemocratic that it cannot be allowed.

As I mentioned, the mainstream media is more concerned with President Obama’s comments about the Cheesecake Factory than with the credible rape allegations against Donald Trump. For those who somehow missed it, Obama said, “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Cheesecakegate has inspired a raft of terrible takes, but none worse than the one from the whole-ass editorial board of The Wall Street Journal, which blared: “Obama Goes Socialist, Scorns Cheesecake.” The editorial criticized Obama for, among other things, being condescending toward Middle America with his slam on the Cheesecake Factory.

That last point requires some explanation. The Cheesecake Factory was founded in Beverly Hills, California, which is about as far from “Middle America” as you can get without getting wet. While it now has franchises across the US, it’s mainly an overpriced mall hub that is most popular on the coasts. It’s essentially a diner for people who don’t have access to good diners and don’t mind paying an outrageous premium for diner food. Only a WSJ editor could think that this kind of high-end schlock represents “Middle America.”

I lived in Indiana for 13 months. The chain-store diner-food option was Steak ’N Shake. Applebee’s was another contender. In places I don’t feel safe driving through, the equivalent is Cracker Barrel. There is no place I know of where the Cheesecake Factory’s (shitty) cheesecake represents a thin slice of Americana.

In any event, Trump allegedly sexually assaulted five people while in or near the company of Jeffrey Epstein. Obama made a joke about interior design. If you cannot correctly order the relative political importance of each of those stories, you deserve to dine at the restaurant of your choice with Saddam Hussein in Hell.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Thomas Birmingham
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Corporate landlord American Landmark admitted that its business model priced tenants out. Now, former tenants have filed a class-action lawsuit against the company.

In January of 2025, recalling the eviction that had made him homeless, Diron Kelly told me his corporate landlord had left him living through “a nightmare.”

He said American Landmark, owner of his Charlotte, North Carolina, apartment and some 30,000 others, had a “bully” business model—from raising his rent by some $400 while forcing him to pay fees for frivolous amenities to jumping at the chance to take him to court once his pockets ran dry. “They really messed everything up,” he said.

But starting last week, it’s now Kelly taking the real estate giant to court. On October 20, he filed a class-action lawsuit against the company in an attempt to prove that not only does its model—first revealed by The Nation and Type Investigations in a piece last year—violate North Carolina law but it has left thousands of similar “nightmares” in its wake.

At stake are the likely millions of dollars that the suit alleges American Landmark illegally coerced out of current and former tenants like Kelly.

The lawsuit, filed by Halperin Petersen & Mikkilineni LLP, the North Carolina Justice Center, and Kelly Guzzo, PLC in the US District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, focuses on a state that has been an epicenter in American Landmark’s network of mega-complexes throughout the South. When I traveled to Charlotte last year, I learned that American Landmark had filed evictions against at least 450 residents over a six-month period, and my interviews with dozens of American Landmark tenants revealed how the company had engineered a system to price Kelly and his neighbors out.

Even American Landmark CEO Joseph Lubeck admitted when I spoke to him that the company’s “modeling” assumes that 45 percent of existing tenants will “move out” after American Landmark takes over: “a number of people are not going to be able to afford what we do.”

Kelly’s case, which is seeking additional plaintiffs, asks for restitution for any tenant who has lived in one of American Landmark’s roughly 3,000 apartments in the state since October 20, 2022. “During their tenancies,” the complaint reads, “Defendants have charged Plaintiffs thousands of dollars in unlawful, deceptive, and unfair fees.”

When reached by e-mail, Lubeck wrote, “American Landmark strongly denies all of the specious claims in the suit, which is clearly an attempt to extort money and rooted in antisemitism, like your previous coverage.”

According to the complaint, American Landmark weaponized mandatory “junk” fees to arbitrarily raise its tenants’ monthly costs by upwards of $100 per month. Kelly’s attorneys claim that American Landmark universally implements these fees—described as a “profit center”—in its North Carolina homes.

In 2025, 18 American Landmark tenants told me their first bill from the company surpassed what they believed they should have owed—thanks to the mandatory fees. Though Lubeck acknowledged at the time that he was “sure there are cases where people don’t know what they sign,” he told me that the fees were “disclosed up front and in writing.” In his e-mailed comment on the lawsuit, he again emphasized that “we provide full and fair value for all our residents and for all services, all of which are clearly spelled out and explained in their contracts and welcome packages.”

These underhanded fee structures are an epidemic for modern renters. As private-equity firms and large conglomerates take over more and more US real estate, tenants are losing out on hundreds of millions of dollars through junk fees every year, according to the National Consumer Law Center (NCLC). These fees, especially in cities like Charlotte, disproportionately burden Black and brown tenants. But a 2025 NCLC report found that states have begun pushing back, with at least 20 adopting laws restricting junk fees in some form. In Minnesota, for example, landlords must include mandatory fees in the publicly advertised cost of their apartments.

In December 2025, the country’s largest property manager, Greystar, agreed to refund tenants $23 million after the Federal Trade Commission sued the company for advertising rentals at “deceptive prices” that “excluded several fixed, mandatory monthly fees.” Kelly’s class-action hopes to build on that national precedent.

“In Mecklenburg County alone, more than 50,000 families faced eviction last year,” Peter Gilbert, director of litigation at North Carolina Justice Center, said in a press release. “These deceptive and unlawful fees are one of the primary drivers of evictions as landlords squeeze tenants past their breaking point.”

Specifically, the complaint alleges that the fees violate North Carolina’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act. After American Landmark took over, Kelly and his neighbors soon received an approximately $100 monthly fee for cable and Internet. Though Kelly’s lease, the complaint alleges, describes this package as “additional rent,” the details are buried in one of many lease addendums, and the nonnegotiable cost far exceeds what tenants could find on the open market.

What’s more, American Landmark disconnects the service when tenants fall behind on payments and “continue to charge the Technology Fee even though the tenant is not receiving the service,” the complaint reads. Then, American Landmark “impose[s] a $75 or more fee to “reconnect” the services that they have disconnected.”

“In at least one month, Mr. Kelly was charged over $160 in Technology Fees and Reconnect Fees when his service was not connected,” the complaint reads.

The Nation and Type Investigation’s 2025 investigation found that the technology package was anathema among American Landmark tenants. For that piece, I spoke to Stephen Tuju, one of Kelly’s former neighbors, who e-mailed complaints about the surprise $75 reconnection fee to his property managers. The company inexplicably responded that it would “adjust” the fee to $25.

In my conversation with Lubeck last year, he confirmed that the company disconnects the technology package when tenants pay late. In Tuju’s case, “it’s possible someone made a mistake,” Lubeck said, but “everything is established and fair across the board.” But the new lawsuit alleges that not only does Kelly’s lease authorize only a $25 reconnection fee but that the company nonetheless habitually demands tenants pay $75 or more for it, as it did to Tuju.

Once Kelly fell behind on payments, he allegedly encountered a “cascade” of additional fees American Landmark contrives from the eviction filing process. Under North Carolina law, landlords can charge tenants for court filing and processing fees, as well as up to 15 percent of a tenant’s overdue balance to help cover the cost of eviction attorneys. But Kelly was allegedly once charged “approximately $1,000 in Attorney or Legal Fees on a balance of less than $2,000,” according to the complaint.

Twice in 2023, per the complaint, American Landmark pressured Kelly to pay legal fees associated with evictions the company had never even filed in court. Less than a year later, Kelly became homeless.

Kelly’s attorneys analyzed thousands of North Carolina court records and found that over 40 percent of the tenants American Landmark files evictions against will incur another eviction attempt in the future. Each new case brings new fees. “In 2025 alone,” the complaint alleges, “over fifty tenants went through this cycle four or more times.”

“That’s why I’m still trying to play catch-up,” said Christopher Dawkins, a tenant I met in Charlotte in 2025, of these legal fees. He told me American Landmark charged him around $300 for each of his four eviction cases. “I got kids, too. When you got a lot going on, every dollar counts.”

Not content to have just kicked Kelly out, American Landmark, the complaint alleges, is also violating the state’s Debt Collection Act: Kelly “continues to receive collections notices from a third-party debt collector acting on behalf of [American] Landmark attempting to collect all illegally charged fees.”

Most of Kelly’s supposed debt, the complaint reads, comes from an “early termination” fee. After the company evicted him, American Landmark charged Kelly nearly $3,000 as a penalty for leaving the company unable to collect rent from him through the rest of his now-voided lease agreement.

The complaint alleges that American Landmark tenants “are given no notice” of this “immoral, unethical, oppressive, and unscrupulous” fee “prior to their eviction.”

“I feel like they’re predatory,” Jeff Schuman, a tenant who was evicted in March 2025 from an American Landmark property in Jacksonville and was similarly hounded by a collections agency, told me last year. “They can put a person out on the street with no recourse. I was like, ‘I don’t have anywhere to go and have a small child.’ It was one of the worst experiences I’ve had in my life.”

The scale of the American Landmark eviction machine that chews up tenants like Kelly and Schuman far outpaces state and national norms. As The Nation and Type Investigations reported last year, in one six-month period, the company filed 82 evictions for every 100 units at one Charlotte complex, and after American Landmark bought Kelly’s building in 2022, the company began filing evictions four times more often than the previous owner.

Kelly’s attorneys found a similar pattern: Though landlords statewide filed 12 evictions per 100 units during the 2025–26 fiscal year, American Landmark on average filed 50.

“Red states are very landlordist,” Gil Rushinek, board chair of American Landmark’s parent company, said in a 2024 podcast. In addition to North Carolina, the company owns buildings in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia, all of which have Republican-controlled legislatures. “In free-market capitalism, there are few protections for the tenant. If you want to evict a tenant in New York, you will have a lot more of a challenge than evicting a tenant in Florida,” Rushinek continued. But North Carolina is the only American Landmark locale with a Democratic governor and attorney general, and the chief justice of the lawsuit’s district court was appointed by President Barack Obama.

The case now enters an uncertain period of months, if not years, of litigation. In addition to millions in damages, Kelly’s attorneys are asking for certification of each of their proposed classes of exploited tenants and a jury trial.

Were the lawsuit to yield a substantial payout, the impact could also reverberate internationally, because, as the Nation/Type Investigations 2025 investigation revealed, American Landmark is wholly owned by the Electra Group, an Israeli conglomerate with extensive ties to both illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

Since these ties were first reported, the Electra Group has remained on the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights database of over 200 companies that do business in the illegal settlements. Electra’s business is centered on making it easier for Israelis to commute to and from the settlements by constructing tunnels and roads and operating bus lines on stolen Palestinian land.

Meanwhile, “the IDF is a major client,” the CEO of another Electra subsidiary said on a 2024 earnings call, after the IDF had already killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. “We stand shoulder to shoulder with them in facing challenges and fulfilling missions. We are likely the only supplier that can say we’ve expanded our areas of deployment.… This is a great source of pride for us.” In a podcast appearance the same year, Rushinek described American Landmark as a “big winning card” for the conglomerate.

The class-action lawsuit, should it eventually force American Landmark into a settlement, could therefore result in a payout to tenants like Kelly of revenue that may otherwise have been funneled into the Electra operation that is playing an active role in the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.

But in the meantime, as of the filing of the complaint, Kelly still does not have a place of his own. American Landmark continues to haunt his life—through a belligerent collection agency and the eviction staining his record—despite their throwing him out of his apartment some 29 months ago.

It’s a vision of what may someday befall Paula Hindman, the case’s other named plaintiff.

She retired from decades of program directing at Piedmont Community College in 2022, just three months before American Landmark bought her building in Hillsborough. Eventually, “the fees at my apartment became so expensive that I went back to work part-time,” she said in a press release. She joined the ranks of the tenants I met over and over again when I traveled to Charlotte last year who were on the brink of being priced out for good. Most of them have since been evicted.

So it’s with Hindman and all of American Landmark’s current and future tenants in mind that the complaint is also seeking “injunctive relief,” a court order that would require American Landmark to permanently change its practices in the state. That means no more mysterious charges. No more collection agency calls.

No more North Carolina tenants wrung out to their last dollar.

Thomas Birmingham is the research fellow at In These Times and an investigative reporter based in New Haven, Connecticut.

Wreckers like Haley Stevens are probably the GOP’s last hope of avoiding a wipeout on Tuesday.

Making political predictions is always a fool’s errand—particularly these days, when polls are becoming increasingly unreliable and sometimes even fraudulent. But there are still plenty of signs pointing to a strong Democratic Party victory in Tuesday’s midterms. Democrats appear to be in pole position to recapture the House of Representatives, and have a real chance to gain control of the Senate—something that seemed all but impossible until relatively recently.

We can tell which way the wind is blowing by the fact that Republican super PACs are bailing out of states like North Carolina—which was expected to be a marquee battleground this year but now seems all but lost to the GOP—and moving funds to bolster candidates in even redder states such as Texas and Iowa.

The Trump administration has also noticed how bad things are going, and is flailing accordingly. On Thursday, the White House announced that President Trump was canceling planned rallies in Kansas and Iowa, replacing them with tele-rallies. This news was telling on a number of levels. The very fact that Trump was headed to deep-red states like Kansas and Iowa was a sign of trouble. In more successful years such as 2016 and 2024, he ended his campaigns by going to genuine swing states such as Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania, even making daring jaunts into New York.

Then, on Friday morning, the White House suddenly reversed course and said Trump would be holding the rallies after all. Perhaps Trump was stung by the implication of his previous decision to cancel—it sent the message that Republicans didn’t want to be seen with an unpopular president, and that Trump himself wanted to avoid the stink of being part of a losing campaign—or perhaps this was simply yet another sign of the chaotic, strategy-free nature of Trump’s approach. Not surprisingly, pundits such as Nate Silver and David Wallace-Wells are predicting that we may be watching the beginning of the end of the Trump era.

The president is clearly off his game. When he was at the peak of his political power, Trump would focus on issues that had genuine salience: immigration, the economy, and foreign policy. To be sure, he’d often muddle this message with his personal grievances and gloating, but he still had a coherent agenda. But in 2026, as Jonathan Lemire notes in The Atlantic, Trump’s message has become unusually muddled:

This time around, Trump’s primary rationale for why voters should support the GOP, as best I can tell, is that the affordability crisis is a “hoax,” Bill Maher is a “loser,” and Senator Jon Husted of Ohio has a nice physique. That easy-to-mock message has been accompanied by a staggering number of missteps. Just for starters, he’s belittled the impact of his stalled war with Iran, sided with Russia as it continues to pummel Ukrainian cities, defended an attack ad from the GOP candidate for Ohio governor that repulsed other top Republicans, downplayed high energy prices while boasting that U.S. oil and gas companies are “making a freaking fortune,” embraced AI as the nation turns against it, obsessed over White House construction projects, and spent a lot of time talking about handsome men, Husted being just one.

Trump seems to be engaged not in a campaign of persuasion, but a massive public crack-up And he’s not the only one. Prominent GOP candidates like Ohio gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy and Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton are also melting down. Ramaswamy is still dealing with the fallout from his disgraceful ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton. The truly sordid nature of the ad became clear when it was revealed that Acton’s mother was homeless and deeply troubled, having lost custody of her children after she sided with a husband accused of abusing them. Ramaswamy first doubled down on the ad—but, on Thursday, he yielded to massive backlash and pulled it from the air. As for Ken Paxton, he’s being plagued by so many personal and ethics scandals that even stalwart Republicans such as political strategist Karl Rove won’t endorse him.

The one glimmer of hope Republicans have is that elite Democrats seem equally addicted to self-sabotage. Indeed, this election has often felt like a competition to see which party can inflict the most damage on itself.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has been dogged by the sore-loser behavior of centrist Democrats who can’t abide the fact he won the primary. In particular, his defeated rival Haley Stevens keeps trying to extract political concessions from El-Sayed rather than letting him unite the party against Republican Mike Rogers.

Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan, who lost to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in a bitter Democratic primary for Senate in August, has grown increasingly critical of him as the election draws near, injecting unusual intraparty tensions into the final days of a pivotal midterm contest.

While Ms. Stevens reiterated Wednesday night that she plans to vote for Dr. El-Sayed, she did so through seemingly gritted teeth in a televised interview just hours after her fiancé said that he would be voting for former Representative Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed’s Republican rival. She also called on Dr. El-Sayed to denounce an ad from an outside group that she has argued amounts to “fear-mongering about Israel,” and to take down an ad from his campaign featuring Tucker Carlson.

On Thursday, Stevens seemed to partially relent in her undermining of the Democratic nominee by agreeing to campaign with El-Sayed.

Stevens’s actions are rooted in the internal Democratic Party rift over Israel/Gaza. Stevens is strongly pro-Israel, notoriously saying that “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” And she has company when it comes to undermining El-Sayed. On Thursday, former House speaker Nancy Pelosi went on a podcast and said El-Sayed’s comments on Israel were “concerning.” She added, “This new person in Michigan, we’ll see if he gets elected to the Congress.”

What makes Stevens’s antics particularly despicable is the fact that El-Sayed, like other Muslim candidates, has been subjected to vicious Islamophobia by the Republicans. At a rally in Michigan on Sunday, Trump said, “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator. If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”

Writing in The New Republic, Perry Bacon rightly notes that Stevens’s behavior follows the pattern of centrist Democrats’ “attacking and undermining a compelling Muslim candidate who is also a target of the right.” In 2025, centrist Democrats similarly tried to kneecap Zohran Mamdani, both when he was running for mayor of New York and even after he won the party’s nomination. As Bacon points out, “A Democratic Party that won’t fully accept Muslim candidates isn’t a party that actually practices the principles of democracy, diversity, inclusion, pluralism, and multiculturalism that it preaches.”

Not all Democratic Party self-sabotage is ideological. Some of it is merely motivated by standard dirty tricks, as in the scandal engulfing Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s team worked to recruit a third-party candidate named Dan J. Sullivan so as to create confusion on the ballot with the current Republican governor, Dan S. Sullivan. John F. Kennedy’s campaign made the exact same maneuver in 1946 when he ran against a rival named Joseph Russo. The campaign found a ringer with the same name, and Kennedy sailed to victory.

Still, even if a dirty trick has a storied pedigree, it’s a dirty trick. Peltola might still win the election, but she’s surely alienated some voters.

The good news for the Democrats is that it’s hard to beat Donald Trump in a self-destruction competition. Trump ran in 2024 on a platform of avoiding more wars and focusing on fixing the economy. As president, he launched a disastrous war against Iran, which is creating a new affordability crisis. When it comes to shooting yourself in the foot, Trump remains undefeated.

https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.title: Meet ProPublica’s 2026 Class of Emerging Reporters
https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.author: Talia Buford
https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.text:
ProPublica’s Emerging Reporters Program provides support and mentorships to college students who are pursuing careers in investigative journalism and need additional training and financial support to help advance their goals.
Participants receive a $9,000 stipend, a trip to the annual NICAR investigative journalism conference, occasional training and presentations by speakers. They’ll also be paired one-on-one with ProPublica journalists who can help counsel them on stories, build their connections in the industry and expose them to the varied paths that careers in investigative journalism can take. Past Emerging Reporters have gone on to work at The New York Times, The Associated Press, Fresnoland, Capital B, The Tributary and other outlets.
Our goal is to encourage the next generation of journalists who seek to shine a light on abuses of power and produce stories with moral force that provoke change. In choosing the class, we look for students who demonstrate an early dedication to journalism as a career, through internships, work at local news outlets or work at campus publications. And where those opportunities — which are often unpaid — aren’t accessible, we look for other ways the student has shown an eagerness and a drive to learn the craft.
This year’s class of exceptional student journalists are from schools in Illinois, Texas, Nebraska, Iowa and New York.
Meet our 2026 class:
Annisyn Krebs-Carr (she/her)
Annisyn Krebs-Carr is a senior at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign studying journalism and animal sciences. She is a reporter for Illinois Public Media Student Newsroom, where she reports on the ongoing housing crisis in Champaign-Urbana. Previously, she served as the arts and entertainment editor at The Daily Illini, the independent newspaper at the university. She is now the managing editor and oversees content produced by the entire newsroom. In 2026, she interned for St. Louis Public Radio and formed relationships with the investigative reporters at NPR’s Midwest Newsroom. This is where she developed a deeper appreciation for investigative journalism. As she continues her journalism career, she wants to focus on how the criminal justice system has failed, and continues to fail, Black people. She also wants to explore how environmental racism has impacted lower-income communities. After graduation, she hopes to work in a public media newsroom and report on local stories while honing her investigative journalism skills. Long term, Annisyn hopes to build a dedicated career as an investigative journalist in public media.
Jessica Meza (she/her)
Jessica Meza is a senior at the University of Nebraska, Lincoln studying journalism, advertising and public relations. Jessica works across mediums, including in data visualizations, video, print and social media, with an emphasis on audio reporting. Jessica hopes to begin her career in investigative, in-depth reporting, focusing on marginalized communities. She hopes to use her reporting to amplify the voice of people facing hidden injustices in her community. Other interests include housing, immigration and food reporting. Jessica currently works at Nebraska Public Media as a reporting intern. She previously interned at NPR’s Midwest Newsroom and, as the Hortencia Zavala Foundation intern, wrote for The Fulcrum and the Latino News Network. In 2025, she was part of the team at Nebraska News Service that was awarded a regional Society of Professional Journalists Mark of Excellence Award for its investigative project on missing and murdered marginalized women.
Lajward Zahra (she/her)
Lajward Zahra is a senior English major at Rice University in Houston, originally from El Paso, Texas. Her reporting focuses on politics, immigration and the environment, particularly in Texas. She is a 2026 writing fellow at The Nation and has written for the magazine since 2023. She previously interned with the Houston Chronicle editorial board in summer 2025, reporting and writing on local and state politics, including the Texas Republican Party convention, among other issues. Lajward’s freelance work has also appeared in publications including The American Prospect, Teen Vogue, Business Insider, Rewire News Group and Scalawag. She was a 2024 Asian American Journalists Association Voices fellow.
Thai Theodoro (she/her)
Originally from Brazil, Thai Theodoro studies political science with a concentration in Latin American studies at Grinnell College in Iowa. Now in her senior year, she is the managing editor of The Scarlet & Black, Grinnell’s independent student newspaper. Thai has interned at The Boston Globe, the Des Moines Register and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, and her reporting has been published in dozens of newspapers across the country. She is a member of the New York Times Corps and a former participant in the National Association of Hispanic Journalists’ Student Project. Thai is passionate about telling untold stories, pursuing investigative reporting with the power to challenge the status quo, using the three languages she speaks to reach underrepresented communities, and, of course, writing the occasional quirky story.
Tsehai Alfred (she/her)
Tsehai Alfred is a senior at Columbia University studying English. She is the 150th editor-in-chief and president of the Columbia Daily Spectator, the campus newspaper, and is also an intern on CNN’s criminal justice team. Over the summer, she was a Dow Jones News Fund intern at VTDigger, an accountability-focused newsroom in Vermont, investigating the troubled integration of AI into healthcare, a struggling dairy farming industry, and soaring police use-of-force payouts. Previously, she has interned at City & State New York, covering the 2025 mayoral race and city council; at PBS News as a Gwen Ifill Journalism Fellow; and at her local news outlet, the Virgin Islands Consortium. Her reporting interests include local government, economic inequality, and political and corporate accountability.

https://hellgatenyc.com/bruce-blakeman-m.title: What Bruce Blakeman's Private Militia Clusterfuck Says About How He'd Run New York
https://hellgatenyc.com/bruce-blakeman-m.author: Katie Way
https://hellgatenyc.com/bruce-blakeman-m.text:
Who the fuck is Bruce Blakeman? We're so glad you asked. The Republican Nassau County executive who is challenging Governor Kathy Hochul has been in politics since the '90s. He has unsuccessfully run for state comptroller, U.S. Senate, Congress, and even briefly for mayor of New York City. In fact, a consultant who worked with Blakeman on his Senate campaign told City & State in 2025 that "there are candidates who only will run a race that they know they can win or think there’s a good chance they can win…Bruce has never been like that."
There are more curiosities in Blakeman's backstory. His ex-wife is currently married to Paul McCartney. When he was a college student, he worked as a driver and aide to Nancy Reagan. His brother is named Brad, which I guess isn't too nuts, until you consider that his mother is named Betty and his father is named Robert (Bob!?), which opens up an alliterative Kardashian-style can of worms.
Blakeman, whose most significant political victory so far was unseating a Democratic incumbent in the 2021 Nassau County executive race, was once a Trump-wary Republican. In a 2022 interview with the New York Times, for example, he insisted that despite their shared support for lifting state mask mandates, he and Donald Trump's "personalities and delivery style are very different." But Blakeman has since embraced Trump and Trump-style politics. And for good reason: His star has risen alongside his Trump loyalty, culminating with this (likely doomed) candidacy, which Trump made possible. (Blakeman's campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment for this story.)
Blakeman came into office as county executive promising to lower property taxes, but his efforts have taken a more clout-chase-y turn. Beyond banning mask mandate enforcement almost as soon as he assumed office (he would eventually issue a ban on mask-wearing in public, except for law enforcement agents, in 2024), Blakeman made headlines in March 2022 when he launched a gun collection drive on behalf of Ukraine, reportedly taking the opportunity to purchase and donate an AK-47 himself as part of the effort. When critics asked Blakeman how he was planning to get a bunch of random guns to a foreign country, the county executive lacked specifics. "It's a long process to get that done so that's why we're asking for help from the federal government," he told NBC New York, adding, "Time is of the essence. It’s life and death. That's why we need help."
As Blakeman's time in office wore on and Trump mounted his 2024 presidential election campaign, Blakeman began to adopt more and more of the president's pet causes: In February 2024, Blakeman issued an executive order banning trans women and girls from playing in women's sports leagues in Nassau County, a first in New York state. An NYCLU staff attorney representing a women's roller derby team that sued Blakeman over the executive order described the ban to Hell Gate as "nothing more than a cynical attempt to shut trans people out of public life."
A couple of months later, Blakeman was spotted holding an umbrella for Trump at the funeral of a slain NYPD cop, and since then, they've been buds. Trump has appeared at multiple rallies to stump for Blakeman. The president played a major role in clearing the GOP primary field for Blakeman, telling Representative Mike Lawler not to run for governor. Despite her groveling, he was unhelpful to Representative Elise Stefanik, and she eventually ended her campaign.
Now—although his campaign website notably does not feature an official policy platform—Blakeman is running on using fossil fuels and nuclear energy to bring down utility bills, eliminating income taxes for people making less than $50,000 (though he hasn't explained how the state would cover that), being broadly tough on crime, and promising to put an end to New York's sanctuary state status.

https://citylimits.org/guia-sobre-las-ci.title: Guía sobre las cinco propuestas al reverso de las papeletas electorales de Nueva York
https://citylimits.org/guia-sobre-las-ci.author: Daniel Parra
https://citylimits.org/guia-sobre-las-ci.text:
Share This Article
Las propuestas sometidas a votación introducirían varios cambios en la Constitución de la ciudad, que van desde qué hacer con las pequeñas propiedades de la alcaldía hasta cómo planear el futuro fondo de reserva de la ciudad.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 30 de octubre. Traducido por Daniel Parra. Read the English version here.
Este reportaje se produjo en colaboración con Factchequeado.
La votación anticipada ya está en marcha en la ciudad de Nueva York, donde continuará hasta el domingo 1 de noviembre de 2026, y los residentes tendrán su última oportunidad de votar el martes 3, día de las elecciones.
Además de las elecciones para gobernador, el Senado estatal y la Asamblea estatal, en el reverso de las papeletas de los neoyorquinos se les dará la oportunidad de aprobar o rechazar varias propuestas para modificar la Constitución de la ciudad de Nueva York.
Las cinco preguntas de este año abarcan desde qué hacer con las pequeñas propiedades de la alcaldía hasta cómo la ciudad debe planificar su futuro financiero mediante un fondo de reserva.
Varias preguntas agrupan múltiples cambios en una sola propuesta. La administración de Mamdani —que a principios de este año convocó una Comisión de Eficiencia Gubernamental (COGE por sus siglas en inglés) para redactar las medidas sometidas a votación— las impulsa como una forma de lograr un “gobierno más ágil” y eliminar la burocracia. Sin embargo, los críticos han expresado preocupación por algunas de las propuestas.
City Limits ha elaborado esta guía en la que detalla cada pregunta sobre la que ya se han pronunciado cientos de miles de votantes.
Propuesta 1: Consentimiento revocable y uso de espacios públicos
Cuando una empresa desea construir, explotar o mantener “una estructura sobre, debajo o a lo largo de las calles y aceras públicas de la ciudad de Nueva York”, debe contar con un consentimiento revocable, aprobado por el Departamento de Transporte (DOT por sus siglas en inglés) de la ciudad.
Un consentimiento revocable es un permiso para utilizar espacios públicos, como aceras o calzadas, y para una amplia variedad de estructuras, tales como rampas y elevadores de accesibilidad, bancos, postes de servicios públicos, jardineras, aparcamientos para bicicletas o quioscos, según explicó la Comisión de Eficiencia Gubernamental (COGE por sus siglas en inglés) de la ciudad.
La propuesta 1 pregunta a los votantes si desean incluir las solicitudes de cobertizos para restaurantes al aire libre y cafeterías con terraza en el proceso estándar de consentimiento revocable. Actualmente, estas solicitudes requieren un proceso de aprobación independiente y más largo, con pasos adicionales.
“Los restaurantes pueden tener que esperar muchos meses, llegando en ocasiones a perder toda una temporada de servicios al aire libre, con los ingresos y puestos de trabajo que ello conlleva”, afirmó Andrew Rigie, director ejecutivo de NYC Hospitality Alliance, una asociación sectorial sin ánimo de lucro que representa a bares y restaurantes, que apoya la iniciativa legislativa.
Según COGE, la propuesta sustituiría la audiencia pública y los anuncios en la prensa, obligatorios para las solicitudes de consentimiento revocable, por un portal en línea, donde el público podría revisar y comentar las solicitudes pendientes.
El Center for Independence of the Disabled in New York (CIDNY) y Common Cause New York, una organización de vigilancia sin ánimo de lucro, criticaron este aspecto del plan, alegando que se produce a expensas de “la participación pública y la supervisión legislativa”.
Sin embargo, Rigie contraargumenta que el proceso simplificado sigue preservando “las oportunidades para que la comunidad y los funcionarios electos aporten su opinión” y lo califica como “una reforma de sentido común”.
“La ciudad de Nueva York puede proteger el interés público al tiempo que facilita a los restaurantes de barrio la apertura de terrazas al aire libre y el servicio a sus clientes”, afirmó.
Según la propuesta, la alcaldía podría seguir revocando un permiso si necesitara recuperar el espacio público. Las juntas comunitarias podrían seguir manteniendo audiencias, y el Departamento de Transporte (DOT por sus siglas en inglés) podría decidir que es necesaria una audiencia cuando los comentarios del público así lo exijan.
“Si se aprueba, reduciría el proceso de solicitud de terrazas al aire libre en aproximadamente un 75 por ciento pasando de ocho meses a dos, lo que ahorraría tiempo y dinero a pequeños negocios”, señaló Ann Cheng, directora ejecutiva de COGE.
“También acortaría el proceso de construcción de rampas accesibles, como las que cumplen con la ADA, alrededor de dos meses, y de igual modo ahorraría tiempo y dinero en ese proceso”, añadió Cheng.
Propuesta 2: Cambios en el papeleo de los contratistas de la ciudad
La propuesta 2 combina varios elementos. Autorizaría a la Junta de Política de Adquisiciones (Procurement Policy Board, o PPB por sus siglas en inglés) , encargada de establecer las normas para la contratación y las adquisiciones de la ciudad, a elaborar un nuevo formulario previo a la contratación para determinadas empresas y organizaciones sin ánimo de lucro que suministran bienes y servicios a los organismos municipales.
Aborda uno de los dilemas de la ciudad: a los organismos municipales a menudo les resulta muy difícil realizar compras y los contratistas se enfrentan a un sistema complicado que puede provocar retrasos.
La propuesta sometida a votación autorizaría a PPB a modificar el cuestionario previo a la contratación —que deben completar tanto pequeñas como grandes empresas que aspiren a contratos municipales, independientemente del importe de la operación— con el fin de mejorar la eficiencia. Obligaría a la junta a reunirse periódicamente (al menos una vez cada tres meses) para elaborar un nuevo formulario.
Si se aprueba esta medida, PPB podría adaptar el cuestionario para reflejar mejor el tipo o la envergadura de los contratos en cuestión, según explicó COGE, y, como ocurre con cualquier norma nueva, la ciudadanía podría presentar sus comentarios sobre los cambios propuestos.
La alcaldía estima que la simplificación de los requisitos del cuestionario supondría un ahorro de hasta 30 días en el proceso de contratación, frente a la media actual de aproximadamente 13 meses.
La medida también reduciría la carga de trabajo de los organismos municipales en lo que respecta a los requisitos de información anual sobre los contratos previstos de servicios al cliente.
En lugar de tener que redactar un informe preliminar, convocar una audiencia y redactar un informe final, tal y como exige el proceso actual, las agencias se limitarían a publicar sus informes cada año, informando con antelación a la comunidad de proveedores sobre los contratos que tienen previsto adjudicar, según explicó la Oficina de Servicios de Contratación del Alcalde (MOCS por sus siglas en inglés).
Un subsegmento adicional de esta propuesta convertiría en permanente una disposición estatal (cuya vigencia está prevista hasta 2030) que permite a la alcaldía publicar anuncios públicos en línea y recabar comentarios del público sobre los contratos.
Otras disposiciones permitirían al alcalde delegar en los organismos determinadas aprobaciones de contratos no competitivos por un importe superior a $5 millones de dólares, con la aprobación del líder del organismo correspondiente.
Propuesta 3: Proyectos de seguridad vial, disposición de propiedades municipales y arrendamiento de oficinas
La propuesta 3 combina tres medidas diferentes: seguridad vial, bienes inmuebles de propiedad municipal y alquiler de oficinas.
Esta propuesta pretende agilizar el proceso municipal para la construcción de nuevas infraestructuras de seguridad vial, al tiempo que se mantienen los requisitos de participación y consulta a la comunidad.
Actualmente, cuando el Departamento de Transporte (DOT) planea “grandes proyectos de transporte” —como carriles para bicicletas y autobuses que afecten a cuatro manzanas consecutivas o a 1.000 pies, lo que sea menor—, está obligado a consultar con otras cuatro agencias: la Policía de Nueva York (NYPD por sus siglas en inglés), el Cuerpo de Bomberos, el Departamento de Servicios para la Pequeña Empresas de NYC y la Oficina del Alcalde para Personas con Discapacidad (MOPD por sus siglas en inglés). Ciertas subunidades dentro de esos organismos deben dar su visto bueno a los planes, siguiendo unos procedimientos muy específicos.
Si se aprueba la propuesta 3, el Departamento de Transporte seguiría teniendo que consultar con esas cuatro agencias, pero sin la obligación de que las subagencias den su opinión. En su lugar, correspondería a los responsables de cada agencia decidir con cuáles de sus propias unidades o subunidades consultar, según explicó COGE.
El Center for Independence of the Disabled de Nueva York (CIDNY por sus siglas en inglés) ha manifestado su apoyo a esta propuesta electoral, calificándola de “reformas de eficiencia basadas en el sentido común”.
La medida también permitiría al Departamento de Transporte (DOT) seguir adelante con los proyectos al mismo tiempo que informa a las juntas comunitarias locales y a los funcionarios electos, en lugar de hacerlo después, cuando existe una situación de necesidad inmediata, como los cambios en las calles realizados en respuesta a los datos sobre accidentes y seguridad vial. Los defensores de la medida afirman que protegería los nuevos planes de carriles para bicicletas y autobuses para que no se retrasen o se bloqueen por demandas judiciales, alegando que los opositores suelen aprovecharse de los errores y las irregularidades técnicas en el proceso de consulta interinstitucional para interponer recursos legales.
Según el Departamento de Servicios Administrativos Municipales (DCAS), la ciudad cuenta con un excedente de 1.500 lotes, y la alcaldía afirma que alrededor del 6 por ciento de ellos entraría en la categoría de los 10.000 pies cuadrados que podrían venderse.
Según la propuesta 3, los planes para estos lotes ya no se someterían al Procedimiento Uniforme de Revisión del Uso del Suelo (ULURP), el proceso de aprobación pública de la ciudad para determinados proyectos urbanísticos, sino que pasarían por el nuevo Procedimiento Acelerado de Revisión del Uso del Suelo (ELURP), que reduce el plazo de revisión de siete meses a 90 días.
La Municipal Art Society (MAS por sus siglas en inglés) de Nueva York criticó la medida, no solo por agrupar “tres propuestas vagamente relacionadas” en una única pregunta de la papeleta electoral, sino porque, según afirman, no aborda “dos de las necesidades esenciales de la ciudad: los espacios abiertos y la vivienda asequible”
“Los terrenos públicos de la ciudad de Nueva York son uno de sus recursos más valiosos —y limitados”, dijo Viviane Eng, responsable de comunicación de MAS, en un correo electrónico enviado a City Limits. “Una vez vendidos o cedidos, puede resultar difícil o imposible recuperarlos. Las decisiones sobre su futuro deben guiarse por una visión integral y a largo plazo en pro del bien público, y no simplemente por oportunidades de ingresos a corto plazo”.
Un portavoz de COGE, Jimmy Wyderko, afirmó que la propuesta seguiría manteniendo dos pasos clave del proceso de venta de terrenos de propiedad municipal. “La propuesta no modifica el requisito de subasta pública ni los requisitos de uso del suelo que se exigen al nuevo comprador (es decir, si el nuevo comprador desea construir algo que vaya más allá de lo permitido de oficio, tendría que pasar por un proceso ULURP)”, explicó Wyderko en un correo electrónico.
Marcel Negret, director de ordenación del territorio de Regional Plan Association, afirmó que la normativa actual hace que estos pequeños lotes resulten menos atractivos para los potenciales constructores, en un momento en el que la ciudad está tratando de facilitar la construcción del mayor número posible de nuevos apartamentos para hacer frente a la escasez de viviendas.
“Una forma de verlo es como si se les [a estos lotes] colocara en una situación más ventajosa en el mercado”, señaló Negret.
Los funcionarios de COGE afirmaron que la medida reduciría la carga administrativa que supone la venta de pequeños lotes.
Otra parte de esta propuesta sometida a votación eliminaría la necesidad de obtener las aprobaciones del Concejo Municipal y de la Comisión de Planificación Urbana (City Planning Commission)  cuando la alcaldía alquile espacios de oficinas para empleados públicos. Actualmente, la alcaldía notifica a la junta comunitaria local y al presidente del distrito sobre dichos alquileres, tras lo cual se celebra una audiencia pública y una votación en la Comisión de Planificación Urbana y, posteriormente, en el Concejo Municipal.
En su lugar, el comisario del Departamento de Servicios Administrativos Municipales (Department of Citywide Administrative Services, DCAS) comunicaría con antelación a la junta comunitaria, al concejal local y al presidente del distrito su intención de adquirir el nuevo espacio de oficinas. A continuación, la alcaldía tendría que notificarlo al Concejo y al interventor.
Propuesta 4: Simplificación del proceso de permisos de construcción y transferencia de los permisos de la zona costera al Departamento de Edificios (Department of Buildings)
La propuesta 4 crearía un centro único y centralizado en línea para la tramitación de permisos de construcción, supervisado por el Departamento de Edificios (DOB), destinado a los solicitantes que deseen realizar obras en un piso o un local comercial, o construir viviendas asequibles. Según el COGE, esto facilitaría a los solicitantes la obtención de permisos de construcción en comparación con el proceso actual, que requiere la participación de docenas de organismos municipales diferentes.
DOB tendría hasta 2030 para poner en marcha este centro. Si los votantes la aprueban, también permitiría que más personal del DOB se encargara de aprobar los certificados de ocupación.
Otro aspecto de esta propuesta consistiría en transferir la responsabilidad de los permisos de construcción en la zona costera del Departamento de Servicios a las Pequeñas Empresas al Departamento de Edificios, donde se encuentra la experiencia necesaria, según explicaron funcionarios y defensores de la propuesta.
“En este momento, el proceso puede resultar confuso”, afirmó Tyler Taba, director de política y asuntos gubernamentales de Waterfront Alliance. “Trasladar esa responsabilidad al DOB es un paso práctico para reducir la confusión, los retrasos y los costes innecesarios en los proyectos de la zona costera”.
Propuesta 5: Establecimiento de objetivos de aportación para el Fondo de Reserva (Rainy Day Fund)
Mediante una propuesta sometida a votación en 2019, los neoyorquinos dieron los primeros pasos para crear un fondo de reserva para cubrir los déficits presupuestarios durante crisis económicas.
El fondo actual de la ciudad, conocido oficialmente como “Fondo de Estabilización de Ingresos”, cuenta con casi $1.700 millones de dólares. Sin embargo, no existen objetivos concretos sobre cuánto debería ahorrar la ciudad con él.
Si se aprueba la propuesta 5, la alcaldía fijaría un objetivo de ahorro para el fondo del 12 por ciento de los ingresos fiscales del año anterior. Pero eso no significa que la alcaldía vaya a aportar ese 12 por ciento de una sola vez: la Oficina de Gestión y Presupuesto (OMB), tras consultar con el interventor y la ciudadanía, tendría que elaborar un plan antes de mayo de 2027 en el que se detalle cuándo debe realizar la alcaldía las aportaciones y, en su caso, de qué importe en un año determinado.
La alcaldía aportaría cada año, siempre que se cumpla ese criterio, hasta alcanzar la meta del 12 por ciento. Una vez alcanzado, ya no tendría que aportar al fondo, aunque podría hacerlo si así lo decidieran las autoridades. “Es como la cuenta de ahorros de la ciudad, por lo que se establecería un objetivo del 12 por ciento de los ingresos fiscales del año anterior, con el fin de avanzar hacia la estabilidad fiscal a largo plazo”, explicó Cheng.
Organizaciones que abogan por buenas políticas públicas, como Reinvent Albany y la Citizens Budget Commission (CBC por sus siglas en inglés), instan a la ciudadanía a votar “no” a la propuesta 5, alegando que no es suficiente para obligar a la alcaldía a reforzar sus reservas financieras.
“Votar no a la propuesta 5 no significa oponerse al refuerzo del Fondo. Es un voto que declara que el statu quo no es suficiente y que la ciudad debería hacerlo mejor”, escribió el presidente del CBC, Andrew Rein, en un artículo de opinión publicado en octubre.
La oficina del contralor Mark Levine publicó un informe en abril en el que se sugiere que un objetivo de reservas del 16 por ciento sería suficiente para ayudar a la ciudad a sobrellevar un “período completo por debajo de la tendencia”, como una recesión.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Historian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Harriet Gibsone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Born in Reading in 1973, Lucy Worsley is a historian and TV presenter. She graduated with a first in history from Oxford, before completing a PhD in art history at the University of Sussex. Worsley spent 21 years as chief curator of Historic Royal Palaces, overseeing the Tower of London, Hampton Court and Kensington Palace, among others. She has presented numerous documentary series, including Six Wives, Royal History’s Biggest Fibs and most recently Victorian Murder Club. She lives in London with her husband. Her latest book, Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History, is out now.
This is me at the age of four. It was my career ambition to become a witch. My back-up options were spy and nun.
We were living in Canada at the time. Dad was an expert in cold places – glaciers and permanently frozen ground – and he was embarking on a year’s swap with an academic at the University of Ottawa. My mother made the costume for me to go trick or treating with the family across the road. In my basket are sweets and I look very pleased and very proud.
Because of my father’s job, we moved around a lot. I wasn’t naturally good at making friends, because I’m quite shy. New schools could be intimidating, but I always had a safe space when reading books. Whenever I ask my parents what I was like as a child, they say, “We don’t know, because you were always reading a book and not talking to us.” Deep down, I was a secret showoff. I was flamboyant when adopting somebody else’s clothes or character or persona.
Outside school I had Guides, played musical instruments and acted in plays. Nobody there knew I was an A-grade student, so I was able to pass for normal. But at my state school in Nottingham, I couldn’t hide. I was a weird little nerd, and my studiousness marked me out in a way that I didn’t have the social skills to conceal. Even though I was lonely, I soldiered on because of my political views. For example, the pupils were going to have a “wear what you like” day to protest about the teachers who were always going on strike. I disagreed, and thought the teachers should strike, so I went in my school uniform – a horrendously stupid choice as everybody laughed at me.
I always loved history, but my father, being a scientist, wanted me to take a different path. To please him, I chose science subjects for my A-levels. Halfway through, my mum said, “You’re not enjoying this. You need to do what you want to do, which is history.”
At university, I studied ancient and modern history. It was a period in which I went mildly off the rails: staying up late talking to people who were just like me, organising the rag parade, playing in orchestras, rowing and doing all the extracurricular activities. I didn’t work hard until the very end of my three years, as I was too busy having a lovely time.
As soon as I saw the advert for the role of chief curator at Historic Royal Palaces, I thought, “That’s my job!” It was a lengthy recruitment process, with interviews in different palaces, and at one point I got in a tizzy looking for the right entrance at the palace of St James. A sentry was standing in a box, so I said, “Please tell me where the right way is. I’m desperate.” He wasn’t allowed to talk to me, but in the end he took pity and rolled his eyes in the direction I should go.
The role was high-profile and there was an expectation of what someone doing that job would be like. Historically, it had been done by men, always of a certain seniority – people very much in command of themselves. By comparison, I was 29 years old, small and pale. I had bought a long, dark coat, which I thought made me look grown up. But my youth and inexperience eventually became my superpowers, because everybody could see there was something different about the way I was going to do things. I came to realise that my authority is in building a relationship of trust with the person I’m talking to, not making them think that I know more.
My TV career began when BBC Look North came to make a film about Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire, where I was working. We ended up spending the day together, with me showing them how they could tell the story. That night I was struck by how much I enjoyed the experience. I began appearing as an expert “talking head” on various shows, and in 2008 I did a show about Henry VIII. More followed. The world was changing – I wasn’t Simon Schama or David Starkey – and we were ready for more women to talk about history.
The struggle to look “authoritative” that I’d experienced earlier came up again in my TV career. I would get notes such as, “She needs to wear tailoring. She needs a dark coat.” It felt wrong. I am known for wearing costumes – using whatever it takes to tell a story. Like a primary school teacher, I have no dignity. But that is also the skill that is available to me. The dressing up might be considered frivolous by critics, but clothes tell us about hierarchy and social structures. They are also fun to look at, which is important when making TV.
Each day is different on set, but some are stranger than others. In one of my early shows, I was dressed as a medieval peasant foraging in the woods. My costume was a brown blanket. It was November and really cold, but I didn’t have the confidence to say, “This isn’t working for me.” In the end, I just burst into tears. Crying does work, but it’s better to speak up: I did a programme about the American Revolution once, and said to the producer, “I’d really like to be in the Independence Day procession that goes through Philadelphia on 4 July.” I imagined I’d be in a modest costume with buttons and a hat, maybe playing the cymbals. It turned out I was part of a twirling team and my costume was a skin-tight leotard. The rest of the team were 22-year-old girls. I got changed, but agreed with the cameraman that he would only shoot me from the neck up.
Being recognised is wonderful and terrible, as I’m a showoff but also shy. I’m capable of slipping through the streets of London in my baseball cap and glasses, but one in a thousand people have weirdly impressive facial recognition skills and clock me. Once a lady recognised me from my teeth alone. I also have a distinctive voice. Someone overheard me speaking in a swimming pool and said, “I know that voice!” I thought, “I’m naked, I’m dripping. I don’t want to engage with you just now, but thank you.”
The story of my life has been “the bookworm shall go to the ball”. I’ve had a wonderful career. But since turning 50, I’ve realised I work too hard. I’m endlessly asking myself, “Do you really love your work? Or is it just the capitalist patriarchy that’s making you think you love your work because that’s good for the economy?”
I don’t have the answers. But that’s the job of the historian. To ask the questions – and, for me, to put on the costumes. So has the girl in the photo grown up at all? Perhaps not.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Race Has Been Defined Islamophobia. Will It Be Determined By It?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.text:
As Abdul El-Sayed’s one-time primary opponent attempts to redirect closing arguments in the Michigan Senate contest to the topics of Israel and antisemitism, the Democratic nominee has entered the final stretch of the midterms against a barrage of bigoted attacks over his own race and religion.
President Donald Trump called him a “jihadist.” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. went on a racist rant against Arabs. According to Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, a mailer went out showing El-Sayed’s face next to the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers.
“They are running the most bigoted, hateful, Islamophobic campaign I’ve ever seen,” McMorrow told a local TV outlet. McMorrow, who ran for the Democratic Senate nomination but dropped out before the August primary, is taking a far different tack than Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democratic primary runner-up who has spent the race’s final days painting El-Sayed as an angry antisemite and crossed party lines Sunday to endorse Republican contender Mike Rogers.
Rogers has sought to portray El-Sayed as anti-American and repeatedly tried to tie his opponent to the Muslim Brotherhood. He insists the attacks have nothing to do with faith. But that is exactly how many observers see them, including Muslim Republicans who have been disgusted by the rhetoric.
As the election draws to a close, the Islamophobic attacks have taken a backseat to Stevens’s claims of antisemitism — most prominently concerning a PAC ad that connected high grocery prices to U.S. spending on Israeli military aid — and a personal feud between the former primary opponents. And some of El-Sayed’s allies worry that the Muslim and Arab-baiting attacks will work. One recent poll found that 38 percent of Michigan voters said they would be less likely to vote for a Muslim candidate.
Michigan’s Muslim and Arab organizers have not been taking the attacks lying down, however. In interviews last month, two prominent leaders in Dearborn’s Arab American community described widespread excitement over the opportunity to vote for the man who would be the first Muslim in the U.S. Senate.
“It very much feels like when President Obama was running and his whole campaign was around like hope. That’s what it feels like,” Layla Elabed, the organizing director at Arab Americans for Progress, told the Intercept on October 8.
Elabed, the sister of Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., was one of the key movers in the Uncommitted movement, which urged Michigan voters to withhold their votes from Joe Biden during the 2024 primary in protest of his support for Israel’s war on Gaza. The movement succeeded in making a statement, but also drew criticism from centrist Democrats for allegedly fracturing party unity.
Elabed’s current group is an evolution of the Uncommitted movement. Its canvassers have been knocking on doors to turn out support for El-Sayed and other candidates.
“I don’t think many people in Dearborn are surprised by Haley Stevens,” Elabed told The Intercept on Monday. “Arab American Democrats in Michigan have been sounding the alarm about her for years, warning our fellow Democrats about a pattern of putting political interests ahead of the people she was elected to represent.”
She believes the same coalition that came together for Uncommitted could help push El-Sayed over the top this election.
“Abdul has been able to really take a stand on all the issues that were really important to anti-war voters and anti-genocide voters,” she said. “It’s not a coincidence that that same coalition, that same base of Democratic voters are now all coming out to support us.”
Hers is not the only group seeking to mobilize Muslim and Arab voters, who make up a sizable slice of the Michigan electorate. The Arab American Political Action Committee has also endorsed El-Sayed. Its president, Osama Siblani, said there is widespread enthusiasm for El-Sayed in areas with dense Arab populations such as Dearborn.
Siblani compared El-Sayed’s potential victory to John F. Kennedy’s pathbreaking election as the first Catholic president.
“First of all, he’s qualified. Second of all, he’s saying the right things, he has a good agenda,” Siblani. “His opponent is an asshole. In addition to all of this, he is breaking the ceiling for our community and for other communities. That is a plus.”
The goal of the Arab and Muslim-baiting attacks from El-Sayed’s enemies is clear, according to Nazita Lajevardi, an associate professor of political science at the University of Michigan.
“Islamophobia is a tried and true strategy for garnering a candidate support and swaying the vote,” she said.
Yet it is also possible that the attacks on El-Sayed’s identity will lead to greater turnout in places like Dearborn, she said.
“I think scholarship would tell us that when political elites discriminate, that it does mobilize people into action. Past scholarship would say yes, it would, but it’s an open question,” she said.
Elabed agreed that the attacks are nothing new. “We’ve watched it play out time and time again,” she told The Intercept. Stevens’s about-face isn’t a major development, she said, “It’s that the rest of the Democratic Party is finally seeing what our communities have been saying all along. We weren’t wrong. We just weren’t being listened to.”
Siblani expressed a similar sentiment on Monday. “I’m not surprised, I’m disgusted,” he wrote of Stevens in a text message, attaching an emoji of a person vomiting.
Stevens’s choice to jump ship for the Rogers campaign appears to have galvanized El-Sayed’s base. His campaign announced a one-day fundraising record after his fellow Democrat pulled her endorsement on Sunday.
