https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Documenta 16 hires four new curators
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The curatorial team for Documenta 16 is expanding with the announcement of four new appointments. The new team members are the composer and installation artist Raven Chacon, who was named curator-at-large, alongside the curators and art historians Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus and Noam Segal, who were appointed curatorial advisers.
The next edition of the influential quinquennial contemporary art exhibition, which will take place next year (12 June-19 September) in Kassel, is led by Naomi Beckwith, the deputy director and chief curator of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.
Her team of four women curators—Carla Acevedo-Yates, Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, and Xiaoyu Weng—will develop the exhibition, publications and programming for the upcoming edition.
Chacon unveiled the two-mile-long land art installation Repellent Fence at the US/Mexico border in 2015; in 2022, he became the first Indigenous artist to be awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Bonsu is senior curator of international art, Africa, and diaspora at Tate Modern, where he co-curated Nigerian Modernism in 2025.
Junghaus was the founding director of Gallery8 – Roma Contemporary Art Space in Budapest (2013–2017) and launched the European Roma Institute for Arts and Culture in Berlin in 2017. Segal serves as the LG Electronics associate curator at the Guggenheim Museum in New York and was previously the director of curatorial research in the Master’s programme for curatorial practice at the School of Visual Arts, New York.
According to an online statement, “the [Documenta 16] exhibition and programmes will honour artists as they navigate a world in turmoil, developing strategies and new possibilities for living together amid planetary indeterminacy. Improvisation, experimentation, and collective learning will open new paths.”
The last edition of Documenta in 2022 sparked controversy after two antisemitic images were found in the work People’s Justice (2000), by the Indonesian artist collective, Taring Padi. The work was removed from show and, in the following days, Documenta posted a statement that was attributed to the Jakarta-based collective ruangrupa, who curated the exhibition. It read in part: “We acknowledge that this was our error.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/the-weird-wild-r.title: The Weird, Wild Races We're Watching Tomorrow
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-weird-wild-r.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-weird-wild-r.text:
Did you know there's an election Tuesday? The Hell Gate podcast will be LIVE on our YouTube channel starting at 9 p.m., and we'll be bringing you the type of pipe-cleaner, construction-paper-based analysis you will NOT find anywhere else.
As you await our livestream, please peruse our election-adjacent content: Hell Gate Interviews Governor Kathy Hochul, Our Crash Course on New York City's Ballot Proposals, Hell Gate chats with Clairializa, Who the Fuck is Bruce Blakeman? and A Visit to Battleground Southern Brooklyn. Last week, we had elections-knower Michael Lange on the pod to talk about many things, including what these midterms mean for Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
New York is hardly a swing state, but it's still taken center stage in this year's midterms. A Hudson Valley congressional seat is one of Democrats' best chances for a pick-up, and a North Country seat has become surprisingly competitive. In a year so grim for Republicans that they could lose a Senate seat in Texas, Vice President J.D. Vance is weirdly coming to New York to rally with an absolute car wreck of a Republican congressional candidate. If Democrats take back the House and Senate, leadership of both chambers could fall to two New Yorkers. And while he's not on the ballot, Mayor Zohran Mamdani is looming just as large in this election as President Donald Trump is.
New Yorkers are clearly following this year's elections. Early voting turnout is way up. Kathy Hochul received a kind-of warm welcome in Dimes Square on Friday. Voter registration data released by the state Board of Elections showed that tens of thousands of people have registered to vote since February, most of them unaffiliated with a political party, as City & State reported.
All statewide offices are on the ballot. In New York City, Democrats are working to flip four Brooklyn state legislative seats, and there's a rare swingy vacant Assembly seat in the Rockaways. The election is nigh. The popcorn is out. Here are some of the things we're watching for on Tuesday:
How does Governor Kathy Hochul fare against Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman?
Many underestimated Kathy Hochul, but she has been a surprisingly durable governor. Since the was thrust into power in 2021, she's found her footing, bringing the Legislature to heel, forming a partnership with New York City's juggernaut mayor, and holding her own against President Donald Trump. She's led the way on a national stage with social media regulations, banning cell phones from schools, and pausing data center development.
Still, Hochul is having to answer for an affordability crisis that is pushing people out of the state as the economy seems to be on the brink of transformation. She's facing Bruce Blakeman, the Republican Nassau county executive who claims he can dramatically reduce taxes and energy bills. Blakeman, now 71, has had a patchy career in politics. He bounced around local office in Nassau in the '90s, then lost reelection to the county legislature following deeply unpopular tax hikes in 1999. Blakeman has made several attempts at higher office, running unsuccessfully for state comptroller, New York City mayor, U.S. Senate and for Congress. He did a stint at the Port Authority and then was appointed to the Hempstead Town Council in 2015. So far, his career has culminated with his capture of Nassau's previously Democratic county executive post in 2021.
Then came the theatrical MAGA turn: Sometime around 2024, as Donald Trump was running to take back the presidency, Blakeman got really on board, embracing an anti-trans, anti-immigrant, crime-fighting ideology. In March of that year, he memorably held Trump's umbrella for him while Trump addressed reporters outside the funeral of an NYPD officer. Blakeman ran for county executive on lowering taxes in Nassau, but he found more success charging into the culture wars when he banned trans women from playing sports with cis women in county facilities in July of that year. (A legal challenge to that law is ongoing.) A couple months later, he tried to gather a group of 75 dudes with gun permits to form an armed civilian group that he insisted was NOT a militia. He has raised eyebrows by hosting campaign-style events with Trump in county facilities or using county resources. He directed local police to cooperate with ICE and then called it the "one of the saddest days of my life as county executive" when a new state law forced him to end that partnership.
Blakeman has touted achievements in getting Nassau County on solid fiscal footing, but his decisions to use pandemic federal funds and opioid settlement funds to balance the budget were controversial. He has not managed to lower property taxes so far as county executive, and he's opted to freeze property tax rolls multiple years in a row. That approach has drawn a state audit and accusations that it puts the burden on individuals to contest their now extremely outdated property tax assessments.
This is Hochul's second reelection fight, and she's already saying she'll seek another term in 2030. Polling this year has been all over the place, but most surveys now show Hochul with a lead that at least hits the low double digits.
What's up with fundraising? Hochul has a huge, huge fundraising advantage, which is all the more notable because she opted out of the state's brand-new public matching funds program. She's also gotten a boost from outside spenders, including former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg. Blakeman has opted into the state's matching funds program, messily, and he's benefited from the largesse of Madison Square Garden billionaire James Dolan.
Hochul Yankee Candle Recipe: Aroma of toasted plain English muffin, the beery sweat of a Buffalo Bills bar, baby powder
Blakeman Yankee Candle Recipe: Notes of gunsmoke, Debra Messing's conditioner, the chemical smell of newly printed T-shirts for these "Gen-Z" dancers

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Life mirrors art: the story of Yayoi Kusama
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alex Wang
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
When Yayoi Kusama died in Tokyo on 14 August, aged 97, she left behind a legacy almost unparalleled in contemporary art. The Japanese artist, who arrived in New York in 1958 as an outsider—female, Asian and largely unknown—eventually became one of the most recognisable artists on the planet. Her dots and pumpkins migrated from canvases and sculptures onto handbags and shopfronts; her Infinity Mirror Rooms generated queues around museums and millions of selfies.
Yet Kusama’s visibility has, when it comes to the structures that once excluded her, remained extraordinary.
“Kusama’s global success has had enormous symbolic force,” says Izumi Nakajima, an art historian specialising in feminism and post-war Japanese art. “Yet the exceptional success of an individual woman artist and a structural transformation in the gendered and geographical asymmetries of the art world operate on different registers.” A canon, Nakajima adds, can accommodate “a small number of monumental women artists while continuing to marginalise a far larger number of women”.
That distinction complicates the familiar story of Kusama as a trailblazer for women and Asian artists. Japan in the 1950s and early 60s, Nakajima says, had a substantial cohort of women pursuing experimental practices, including Atsuko Tanaka and Hideko Fukushima. To project Kusama’s present fame backwards risks producing a history in which she appears uniquely radical from the outset. Kusama’s departure from Japan in 1957 was crucial: while Japan’s high-growth era increasingly reorganised women’s lives around domesticity, she pursued her career abroad, relentlessly making both her art and herself visible through exhibitions, photographs, fashion, happenings and the media.
Is fame the same as success?
For the Tokyo- and Vienna-based feminist and queer publishing and research collective Multiple Spirits, the transformation since Kusama’s early career is nevertheless real. Compared with a global art world then dominated overwhelmingly by white men, opportunities to encounter artists from different backgrounds have unquestionably expanded, the collective says. But it questions whether Kusama’s trajectory should still function as a model of “success” when the criteria by which success is measured remain largely inherited from that same art world. “Values and measures different from those shaped by a white male-centred art world are still insufficient,” the collective says.
Nor does Nakajima see Kusama fitting comfortably into another role frequently assigned to her: that of the feminist icon. Rather than treating feminism as “an attribute or categorical designation”, Nakajima argues, it is more productive to use it as a critical method through which to read her work. Kusama’s repetition, sexuality, self-representation and negotiation of the body all invite feminist interpretation. But unlike strands of feminist art that rejected Modernism’s claims to autonomy and universality, Kusama repeatedly resisted being circumscribed as either a “woman” or a “Japanese” artist. “She sought to occupy the position of the universal artistic subject that Modernism had imagined,” Nakajima says.
The Multiple Spirits collective similarly notes a gap between Kusama’s international reception and her popular image at home. In Japan, it says, she is less commonly understood as a feminist icon than as the creator of colourful polka-dotted paintings and installations. The politics of her 1960s happenings—their anti-war messages and calls for sexual liberation—have received comparatively less attention. Rather than reducing Kusama to an individual “feminist” or “queer” identity, the collective argues that these radical practices need to be reconsidered within the social and cultural conditions that produced them.
Journey to global cultural brand
Another paradox lies in Kusama’s transformation from avant-garde provocateur to global cultural brand. In 1966, she appeared uninvited at the Venice Biennale with Narcissus Garden, offering mirrored spheres for sale beneath a sign declaring “Your Narcissism for Sale”. Decades later, the mirrors themselves became among contemporary art’s most coveted attractions. Visitors queue for hours to spend seconds inside an Infinity Mirror Room, phone in hand, while collaborations with Louis Vuitton turned her dots into a globally recognisable luxury motif. Critics have consequently cast Kusama as both a precursor of the immersive “artainment” economy and one of its most successful brands.
For Hidenori Ota, the founder of the gallery Ota Fine Arts and Kusama’s longtime representative in Japan, the artist’s embrace of visibility cannot be separated from the struggle to make herself heard. “I imagine that, in order to deliver a voice that otherwise could not reach people, she first needed to make her own presence larger,” he says. Having directly experienced war, Ota suggests, Kusama sought a language capable of reaching a mass audience, repeatedly returning to the word “love” as a vehicle for criticism.
Kusama’s popularity also made mental illness unusually visible within mainstream contemporary art. She voluntarily lived at a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo from 1977 onward, working for decades at a nearby studio. While frequently connecting her compulsive repetition and artistic production to hallucinations and psychological distress, she generally eschewed disability advocacy. Narratives around Kusama have drawn criticism for reproducing the familiar trope of the “mad genius” who triumphs over adversity, while doing relatively little to address disability, psychiatric experience or accessibility. Nakajima similarly warns against narratives that link women’s creativity to illness, trauma and psychological compulsion: such frameworks, she says, have historically helped women artists gain recognition while simultaneously restricting how their practices are understood.
Perhaps the most troubling asterisk in Kusama’s legacy relates to her descriptions of Black people in her 2002 autobiography, Infinity Net. In the original Japanese edition, she blamed Black residents and unhoused people for the decline of her New York neighbourhood. That, along with other denigrating lines, was omitted from the 2011 English translation. When the comments received renewed attention ahead of her 2023 exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Kusama said she “deeply regret[ted] using hurtful and offensive language” and apologised for the pain she had caused.
A symbol of inclusion
The episode sits uneasily beside the universalist language of love that characterised Kusama’s later public persona. Asked how it should shape her legacy, Ota says: “Rather than simply viewing her through that label of ‘racist’, [her words] should be examined in relation to the social conditions and historical context of the time.” He adds that it requires further debate and study. The controversy nevertheless underscores the limits of transforming a complex historical figure into an uncomplicated symbol of inclusion.
Ota is likewise sceptical of attributing subsequent changes in Asia’s art world to a single artist. “Rather than Kusama changing things herself, I think the larger shifts of the era—particularly the social and economic rise of Asia—were more significant,” he says. “She moved in step with those larger changes.”
The Multiple Spirits collective flags how, in Japan and beyond, as shrinking cultural budgets require museums to pursue larger audiences and alternative funding sources, Kusama shows became reliable for producing economic results. But her visibility has not particularly helped other marginalised artists. “We cannot entrust structural change in the art world to the success story of a minority artist,” the collective says. What matters instead are less spectacular changes: improving working conditions and accessibility, using inclusive language, protecting freedom of expression and connecting such efforts across institutions.
Kusama entered a Western, male-dominated art world and ultimately became bigger than almost any artist within it. But “exceptional success and structural inequality can coexist”, Nakajima observes. Kusama changed who could occupy the centre of contemporary art, but not the nature of that centre.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘Mariko Mori anticipated the zeitgeist’: curator Alexandra Monroe on her new show and how Japan's art scene has changed
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Andrew Maerkle
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The US curator Alexandra Munroe has three decades of experience working closely with Japanese institutions, going back to her landmark survey Japanese Art after 1945: Scream Against the Sky at the Yokohama Museum of Art in 1994. Now she is back in the country as the co-curator of the current Mariko Mori retrospective at the Mori Art Museum in Tokyo. The show is a collaboration with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, where she is a senior curator at large, and has been co-curated with the Mori Art Museum’s director Mami Kataoka.
The Art Newspaper: How has Japan’s museum ecology changed over the years?
Alexandra Munroe: It’s changed enormously. The Yokohama Museum of Art opened in 1989, anticipating the museum boom of the 1990s when municipalities and prefectures across Japan were opening new institutions with extraordinary buildings designed by architects like Fumihiko Maki, Arata Isozaki and others.
Although there were important precursors like the Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura, established in 1951, and the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, established in 1952, there was remarkably little concerted historical understanding of Modern and contemporary Japanese art and its role in global art history. Around the early 1990s, curators and scholars were piecing together how such art had evolved under the umbrella of post-war society—defeat in the Second World War, reconstruction, Americanisation—as well as through the contributions of Japanese artists abroad like Yoko Ono, Yayoi Kusama and On Kawara. The new museums contributed to the tremendous growth of the field, both within Japan and internationally.
Successive institutions have built on that legacy. It’s been gratifying to see the Mori Art Museum develop into a global museum under the trailblazing leadership of Mami Kataoka. The recent Sou Fujimoto exhibition was one of the greatest architectural shows I’ve ever seen, while the solo shows of Louise Bourgeois, Ai Weiwei and Lee Bul, going back 20 years now, are among the most influential for those artists staged anywhere in the world.
All of this has been aided by the simultaneous transformation of the gallery scene, with a proliferation of experimental galleries since 1994, not to mention international galleries representing Japanese artists or movements like Gutai, Mono-ha and Neo-Pop. I also appreciate the role that Benesse Art Site Naoshima has played, through the vision of patron Soichiro Fukutake, in the emergence of Japan as a contemporary art superpower. Only a few hundred people attended the opening of Benesse House Museum in 1992. Now events like the Setouchi Triennale draw millions to the islands when the home population is a few thousand. And Benesse’s commissioning programme has given artists like Yukinori Yanagi, Rei Naito and Shinro Ohtake a platform for staging their most ambitious works.
Recent decades have seen a remarkable expansion of museums in China and Korea, Southeast Asia and the Gulf. At the same time, institutions around the world are facing new challenges with austerity measures and a withdrawal of public support for art. What lessons can Japan offer other art scenes?
I have great admiration—and some envy—for the public funding of Japanese art museums. The Japanese model of collecting regionally yet within an international context is something to emulate. There’s also something to be said for collections focusing on artists whose histories were shaped by the places where they grew up and, in some cases, ran away from. The Nagoya City Art Museum has extraordinary holdings of On Kawara’s works, including rare early reportage pieces, even though he left the region in his teens. The Ashiya City Museum of Art and History’s collection of Gutai is unparalleled in the world. And the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, under the guidance of curators like Kuroda Raiji, has sought to map and reimagine artistic exchanges in Asia.
I commend all the brilliant scholarship that has emerged out of these enterprises.
That said, in recent years Japan has retreated from its post-war identification as an international country. One motivation for doing the Mori show is to stimulate a revival in collaborations that can help bring the work done in Japan into international circulation.
Collaborations between Japanese and international institutions typically take the form of touring shows, whereas intensive co-productions are rare. How did the collaboration between the Guggenheim and the Mori Art Museum come about?
It’s called synergy! In the summer of 2024 both Mami Kataoka and I had begun talking to Mariko Mori about staging a retrospective and we combined forces. Mariko rose to meteoric stardom in the 1990s for Cyborg (1994-95), the first of her series of photomurals inserting herself as a cyborg, and later a Buddhist-inflected deity, into digitally rendered settings. That interest in technology subsequently found form in complex multisensory environments like Wave UFO (1999-2002), the first artwork to incorporate brainwave biofeedback.
I was interested in reappraising Mariko’s work in the current context of technology-based art, specifically digital technologies. Technology is not an obstacle to humanism for her, but a means of envisioning a new kind of humanism that allows for higher states of consciousness. At the same time, Mariko’s engagement with [pre-historic Japanese] Jōmon culture, alternative belief systems and the afterlife resonates with Indigenous and First Nations artists incorporating Indigenous knowledge into critiques of Western epistemes of modernity and linear time.
For her part, Mami has a longstanding interest in art that addresses spirituality in the modern era, which opens up a critique of the dominant trends of contemporary art as established by market forces and Western institutions, so I think Mariko’s work felt urgent to that curatorial research and practice.
It’s a creative partnership.
Yes. Collaboration is integral to Guggenheim programmes like the Asian Art Initiative and the UBS MAP Global Art Initiative. We have consistently partnered with museums, curators and artists across Asia to help us collectively think through the larger argument of global art history and how to present exhibitions that map histories and ideas beyond the Eurocentric canon. The collaboration with the Mori is a direct outcome of that, and I’d say it’s a direct outcome of the Mori’s profoundly international outlook as well.
A compelling retrospective does not just look back but also shows how the artist was ahead of their time. In what ways have we finally caught up with Mariko Mori?
Mariko’s work resonates with the writings of the contemporary philosopher Yuk Hui, who argues for a holistic understanding of technology grounded in Eastern thought and cosmologies, or “cosmotechnics”, as opposed to its bifurcation in modern Western traditions. Mariko anticipated that zeitgeist as a Japanese woman artist who conducted deep research into schools of thought like Pure Land Buddhism and Jōmon cosmology alongside contemporary sciences of the mind.
These are areas of enormous interest to artists now. Look at LuYang, a young Chinese artist who is a serious practitioner of Tantric Buddhism and uses game engines to illustrate themes of transmigration of the soul, multiple selves and the world as an illusion. The Korean new media artist Ayoung Kim also looks up to Mariko for unabashedly drawing parallels between art and technology as ways to “recalibrate our reality”, as Ayoung told me.
I think there will be an enthusiastic response to Mariko’s work from younger artists who are interested in storytelling and altered states of mind, artists who are seeking to break free of the lingering hang-ups of Western art, and anyone looking to just get away to another world.
• Mariko Mori: All That Shines, Mori Art Museum, 31 October-28 March 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘Another way of engaging the city’: centrepiece of Art Week Tokyo sends visitors to venues across the capital
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alex Wang
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
AWT Focus launched in 2023 as Art Week Tokyo’s centrepiece exhibition platform. Last year it took place at the Okura Museum of Art, where Adam Szymczyk brought together more than 50 artists for What Is Real? For 2026, the format is being radically reconfigured. In collaboration with Curated by, the Vienna gallery festival, Art Week Tokyo has invited curators to organise ten exhibitions across ten participating galleries and art spaces around the city.
The shift brings AWT Focus closer to the structure of Art Week Tokyo itself. Unlike an art fair, the annual event has no central venue: its network of museums and galleries is dispersed across the metropolis, with free shuttle buses connecting participating venues during the week. Running from 4 to 8 November, this year’s fifth full edition will bring together a record 56 museums and galleries.
“From the start Art Week Tokyo was conceived of as an event that would evolve in dynamic response to the city,” says Atsuko Ninagawa, the event’s co-founder and director. The multi-venue AWT Focus, she says, offers “another way of engaging the city and its diverse audiences”. Rather than organising the programme around a single curatorial proposition, “the idea is to bring multiple worldviews to Japan”.
Those worldviews take varied forms. Among the ten projects are Polish curator Maria Brewińska’s presentation of Japan-born, Poland-based artist Koji Kamoji at Take Ninagawa gallery; Ekow Eshun’s presentation of British-Sierra Leonean artist Julianknxx at the Space Un arts and culture venue; and New York-based curator Augusto Arbizo’s intergenerational exploration of painting at Yutaka Kikutake Gallery. Elsewhere, curators Greg Dvorak and Kenji Ono draw on the contrasting post-war histories of eastern and western Tokyo for the latest edition of the recurring exhibition series The Constitution of Japan, at Mujin-to Production, with a second site at Aoyama | Meguro.
The city becomes part of the show
For Multiple Spirits, the feminist collective founded by Mai Endo and Mika Maruyama, the dispersed format allows the character of the city itself to enter the programme. “Even within the same city of Tokyo, each place and space has a completely different face,” the collective says. “The location, surrounding environment and flow of people differ from venue to venue”, allowing each exhibition to take shape in relation to its surroundings. The collective also sees potential in moving away from a single curatorial voice towards a more open structure in which “different perspectives by many practitioners” can co-exist.
Multiple Spirits’s exhibition at Waitingroom, Patchwork of Ruffled Wings, draws together zines, textiles and other works through what the collective calls a “vine-like archive”, connecting “girls’ culture, queer culture, artistic movements, underground culture and social movements”. Rather than arranging these histories into a linear genealogy, Multiple Spirits is interested in how cultures are interrupted, inherited or grafted onto others, and how they are shaped by changing social conditions, taboos and forms of resistance. Art Week Tokyo, it suggests, can itself become a site where people with different backgrounds and practices meet, allowing different perspectives to connect while retaining their complexity.
The collective’s own history also complicates any simple division between the “local” and the “international”. Multiple Spirits was founded in Austria and continues to work between Vienna and Tokyo, collaborating with people across national, racial, ethnic and gender backgrounds. Through AWT Focus, the collective hopes to show that the Tokyo art scene encompasses “alternative and diverse activities” that extend beyond any single urban context and are connected through multiple networks.
Looking at Tokyo from elsewhere
For the Seoul-based curator Jaemin Shin, meanwhile, working with Tokyo-based artist and poet Natsumi Aoyagi offers another way of reading the city. Shin first worked with Aoyagi for the 2025 exhibition Patchwork! at the WilloW in Seoul. Her AWT Focus exhibition, Possible Words, Possible World, at Misa Shin Gallery, brings together two multimedia installations concerned with systems of recording and ownership.
One takes Tokyo Bay’s artificial islands—territories whose histories begin with administrative records such as land registries—as its point of departure; the other reimagines relationships beyond ownership and Japan’s family-registration system.
Shin sees parallels between the systems of registration and record-keeping, and patriarchal structures in Japan and Korea. But Aoyagi’s work has also altered her perception of the Japanese capital. “Looking at Tokyo through her work, I stopped seeing just a rigid megacity,” Shin says. Instead, she came to see it as “not a singular structure, but one with fluid and fragile boundaries”.
For Shin, the new AWT Focus format creates further opportunities for such readings. An outside curator can translate culturally specific ideas into different contexts, she says, creating new connections, while the dispersed format enables a more intimate engagement with particular parts of the city. Rather than simply presenting artworks, she says, an exhibition can connect to specific urban and social sectors in Tokyo, shifting the curatorial gesture towards “actively inhabiting the city” through artworks and ideas.
For Eshun, who returns to Art Week Tokyo after participating last year, the new structure also creates opportunities for exchange among curators. “Part of the goal for me, in travelling internationally to events like Art Week Tokyo, is to discover how different curators are working and thinking and making exhibitions,” he says. “It’s a great opportunity to meet and talk and build new relationships.”
His exhibition How Much Light Must I Consume? will be Julianknxx’s first in Japan. The artist’s practice spans geographies and diasporic histories, while the central work draws on oral traditions from Comoros, the small island nation near Mozambique. Eshun resists predicting what connections those histories might generate in Tokyo. “All successful art is predicated on discovery, on unknowing, on the revelation of unanticipated connection,” he says. “The hope is that it sparks new ways of seeing and imagining.”
Building networks beyond the week
Art Week Tokyo’s organisers are also looking beyond the encounters generated during a single week in November. Previous editions have recorded rising audiences: overall attendance increased by 33% between 2022 and 2023 and by another 15% in 2024, while international VIP participation has also grown sharply.
Ninagawa argues that the event has helped build networks and visibility that participating institutions and galleries can continue to develop independently. Internationally, she believes Art Week Tokyo has helped “rebrand” a Japanese art scene that had been overlooked in global discourse. Overseas visitors who once came to Tokyo primarily interested in the city as a tourist destination, she says, are increasingly arriving specifically to learn about Japanese artists and art history—and going on to develop projects from those encounters.
Eshun offers a more personal account of that process. Tokyo’s art world may appear smaller than those of some other global centres, he says, “but it runs deep”. He describes himself as still mapping its “paths and roads and streams and tributaries”, with Art Week Tokyo helping him “find my way and keep exploring”.
That metaphor feels particularly apt this year. Until now, travelling across Tokyo was primarily how visitors moved between Art Week Tokyo’s participating institutions. With the new AWT Focus, movement through the city is no longer simply a means of reaching its exhibitions; it has become part of the curatorial proposition itself.
The ten projects in this year’s AWT Focus
The Quiet
Curator: AugUsto Arbizo
Venue: Yutaka Kikutake Gallery
Augusto Arbizo assembles works by six Japanese and international artists into an intergenerational conversation on painting practices that offer a space for quiet concentration amid the frenetic visual culture of the city.
Erika Verzutti: Portrait of Sculpture
Curator: Julie Boukobza
Venue: Misako & Rosen
Artist Erika Verzutti and curator Julie Boukobza extend their collaboration for this exhibition of monoprints, which builds on a show of sculptures the two produced for a room at the Hôtel Balzac, Paris, in 2025.
The Constitution of Japan 2026
Curators: Greg Dvorak & Kenji Ono
Venue: Mujin-to Production
Curators Greg Dvorak and Kenji Ono take charge of the fourth edition of this recurring exhibition using art to reread the Constitution of Japan. This year’s edition includes works by video artist Fuyuhiko Takata, multimedia duo MES and more.
Nobuko Tsuchiya: Ace of Hearts
Curator: Martin Clark
Venue: SCAI The Bathhouse
Martin Clark, the director of London’s Camden Art Centre, oversees a new site-specific project by Nobuko Tsuchiya, a UK-based Japanese artist known for her sculptural assemblages of found objects that play on the enigmatic and the familiar.
Mary Weatherford: Komorebi
Curator: Jeremy Strick
Venue: Shibunkaku
Veteran US museum director Jeremy Strick presents the first exhibition in Japan of leading Los Angeles-based painter Mary Weatherford, with a focus on recent works on paper accompanied by one of her signature neon paintings.
Natsumi Aoyagi: Possible Words, Possible World
Curator: Jaemin Shin
Venue: Misa Shin Gallery
Korean independent curator Jaemin Shin guides this solo project by emerging artist Natsumi Aoyagi, whose multimedia installations juxtapose poems, moving images, AI-generated imagery, recorded sound and fiction. The resulting works generate multilayered meanings shaped by a speculative imagination.
Julianknxx: How Much Light Must I Consume?
Curator: Ekow Eshun
Venue: Space Un
London-based artist Julianknxx addresses the history of Africa and its diasporas through poetry, performance, film, music and sculpture. The artist’s first exhibition in Japan, curated by Ekow Eshun, will feature multimedia works inspired by salt as well as a series of special choral performances.
Koji Kamoji: Everyday Life
Curator: Maria Brewińska
Venue: Take Ninagawa
Koji Kamoji left his native Japan for Poland in 1959 and went on to become a key figure in the Polish avant-garde art scene. Warsaw-based curator Maria Brewińska has worked closely with the 91-year-old artist to develop an exhibition reflecting on the connection between art and survival.
Patchwork of Ruffled Wings
Curators: Multiple Spirits
Venue: Waitingroom
The queer feminist collective Multiple Spirits uses its eponymous zine as a base for producing artworks, exhibitions and other activities. Patchwork of Ruffled Wings explores the concept of the “vine-like archive” through the presentation of printed matter, textiles and other works by Japanese and international artists.
Taro Masushio and Sophie Nys
Curator: Olivier Mignon
Venue: XYZ collective
Olivier Mignon, the founding director of Keijiban in Kanazawa, juxtaposes works by two artists at XYZ collective. New York-based photographer Taro Masushio addresses themes of queer embodiment and the politics of the gaze, while Brussels-based sculptor Sophie Nys investigates the relationship between language and objects.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/pakistan-cli.title: Life Beneath the Melting Glaciers
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/pakistan-cli.author: Jaclynn Ashly
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/pakistan-cli.text:
Life Beneath the Melting Glaciers
Remote mountain communities in northern Pakistan have contributed almost nothing to global warming, yet glacial floods are sweeping away their homes. Jacobin traveled to talk to the families who are rebuilding with little help from the state.
Bulbul Kaie remembers when summer in Hassanabad revolved around a stream.
The village lies in the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan, a disputed territory in northern Pakistan bordering China, Afghanistan, and Indian-administered Kashmir. Kaie’s family would carry chairs down to the stream fed by meltwater from the glaciers above, where a cold breeze rose from the water. They would spend afternoons on its bank among orchards heavy with apricots and cherries.
“We would sit together, drink tea, and enjoy the sound of the stream until it got dark,” recounts the mother of four. “We used to look forward to summer. The sound of the water made us feel calm.”
Now summer brings dread. “We fear what will happen each year,” the fifty-year-old says.
Pakistan has more than thirteen thousand glaciers, one of the largest concentrations outside the polar regions, many of them in Gilgit-Baltistan. As climate change drives temperatures higher in these mountains, where warming is outpacing the global average, the ice melts faster and rain falls harder and less predictably. Cloudbursts — intense, localized downpours that experts say were virtually unknown here until recently — can now destroy a village in an afternoon.
Last year, Hassanabad was among dozens of villages across Gilgit-Baltistan hit by one of the region’s deadliest flood seasons in years. At least seventy-two people died, and more than a thousand homes were destroyed or damaged.
The floods destroyed half of Kaie’s home. She has yet to rebuild. “I’m only staying here because I have no resources to go elsewhere,” she says, her voice breaking. “I fear for my children’s lives and mental health.”
Kaie is one of thousands still trying to recover. Some live in tents or cracked houses they fear could collapse. Others have been moved onto bare government plots with no land to farm and no way to earn. Few can afford to start again, and the next disaster is rarely more than a season away.
The people living among these glaciers bear almost no responsibility for the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming; Pakistan itself accounts for about 1 percent of global emissions. Yet it is among the countries most affected by extreme weather, and in its remote mountain communities, homes are being washed away, farmland is disappearing, and livelihoods are collapsing.
At the Glaciers’ Mercy
Behram Shah gathers cherries from a tree outside his Hassanabad home and carries them to the table in a woven basket. “We rely on the glaciers for everything,” says the seventy-six-year-old, who has lost about nine acres to floods in the past decade. “Our livelihoods, and even our drinking water, depend on them. We are completely at the mercy of these glaciers.”
Every spring, before the summer melt, villagers would gather at the watercourses to pray over the year’s flow, asking God for protection and enough water for the months ahead, Shah recounts. These days, few still make the journey.
“We used to see the glaciers as the source of our lives,” Shah says. “Now, because of the floods, we associate them with destruction.”
“The cycles that kept us in balance for centuries are being disrupted,” he adds. “All we can do now is pray and leave everything to God.”
Hassanabad sits in the Hunza Valley, in the Karakoram — one of four mountain ranges that meet in Gilgit-Baltistan and contain some of the world’s highest peaks. Its roughly 175 households are scattered across the mountainous terrain, clustered on either side of the stream and up the slopes. Most residents are Ismaili Muslims who farm fields and orchards passed down through generations.
Three miles above the village, the Shisper and Muchuhar glaciers, once branches of a single glacier, eventually drain into the same stream, which runs about four miles down the valley to join the Hunza River. Their meltwater feeds the irrigation channels that keep Hassanabad alive.
In 2018, the Shisper began to surge, exhibiting behavior of a type of glacier that can sit almost motionless for decades or centuries before suddenly lurching forward. It advanced nearly a mile, at one point moving nearly sixty feet a day, before pushing across the ravine and damming the stream draining the Muchuhar.
The lake that formed behind the ice burst four times in four years, sending floodwater down the valley that scoured the ground along the stream’s banks. The last, in 2022, swept away the Karakoram Highway Bridge, cutting Hunza off from the rest of the country for two weeks.
By last summer, the danger was supposed to have passed. The ice still lay across the ravine, says Sher Muhammad, a cryosphere scientist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, but a wide tunnel had opened through it and water was flowing freely.
Then the heat came. One town in southern Gilgit-Baltistan hit 119 degrees Fahrenheit (48.3 degrees Celsius), its highest temperature in nearly three decades. Across the region, streams were already running high as unusually warm conditions accelerated snow and glacier melt.
Chunks of ice broke off and fell into the stream, blocking the flow, Muhammad says. Water accumulated behind the ice blockages until they failed, releasing the impound water downstream. It happened twice, in July and August, damaging houses and farmland, ripping out a section of the Karakoram Highway, and cutting the water supply to Aliabad, Hunza’s main commercial town, and nearby villages.
Over the years, dozens of homes in Hassanabad have been destroyed or dismantled before the floods could reach them.
The Floodwater Threat
What came before the floods, Kaie says, was not a roar. It was a silence.
“It’s very ominous,” she says, sitting on the floor of her home, cracks running down the walls. “The entire flow of water suddenly feels like it stops. And there’s silence for about half an hour.”
In those minutes, the family would run to the bank to see what was coming. If the water looked dangerous, Kaie would send the children uphill to a relative’s house and go back for whatever she could carry.
“When the floodwater comes, it is so strong,” she says. “It carries boulders the size of houses. If it reaches your home, it will pull it from its foundations.”
They have lived this way for years, fleeing when the water rises, returning when it drops. When I visited in August, the family had already fled several times that summer. Their fridge and other belongings were still at a relative’s house up the hill.
Last year’s floods were the worst this part of Hassanabad had seen, residents say. They tore through the orchards between Kaie’s house and the stream and destroyed half the home she and her husband had spent seven years building. The couple had sold most of their farmland to afford it.
She scrolls through her phone to a photograph from before: rows of fruit trees running down to the water. “It was a very beautiful home,” she says, holding up the screen. Outside, the same ground is dry and stripped bare.
Later, the highway was rebuilt. It had always run a couple of hundred feet below the houses until last summer’s flood swept away part of it. The rebuilt section was laid higher up the slope, directly in front of Kaie’s house.
Now cargo trucks hauling goods between Pakistan and China pass a few feet from her door. They shake the walls, rattle the windows, and widen the cracks. Dust hangs in the air.
Her twelve-year-old son sometimes wakes at night, hears the trucks, and thinks the flood has come back, she says. He runs outside, and the family has to find him in the dark.
“This constant uncertainty is causing a lot of psychological issues for my children,” Kaie tells me, her son sitting quietly beside her. “I try to calm them down and assure them they are safe, but they are still terrified of every sound.”
She wants to leave, but her husband drives someone else’s car for a living and does not earn enough to move elsewhere. And no one will buy a house in a village beset by recurrent floods.
“If someone came and gave us money, we would leave immediately,” Kaie says, sniffling back tears. “It feels like torture knowing any day the waters will return and destroy our home we worked so hard to build. And it’s not a question of whether it will happen again; it’s guaranteed.”
Other families have stopped waiting for the water. Each summer, they take their houses apart, carrying off beams, windows, and doors before the floods can claim them.
Around the stream, the floods have carved a deep canyon into the land, with another Hassanabad neighborhood sitting beside it. On a flattened patch scattered with debris, the remains of the area’s jamatkhana, the Ismaili house of worship and community gathering, lie among the stripped shells of dismantled homes.
Living on the Edge
Sultan Ali, seventy-five, an elder and community leader, walks me along the cliff, shouting whenever I get too close to the edge. “The ground is not strong here,” he warns. “It can collapse at any moment.”
He gestures at the canyon below. “You see all of this? This was the most beautiful part of our village,” he says, shaking his head.
Nearby, Dilshad Bano, fifty-three, has come to pick cherries on a plot she abandoned about seven years ago. Floods destroyed half her house in 2019. The family dismantled the rest. “It took many years and a lot of hard work to build that house; we used up all our savings,” she says, standing in the ruins. “Then all of it was gone in a single day.”
They have moved higher up the valley, to a house twenty-five minutes’ walk through the mountains from the nearest road. “When we have health problems, it becomes extremely difficult,” she tells me.
Bano and her brother-in-law, Muhammad Abbas, fifty-five, each received about $900 in government compensation a few years ago, they say. Abbas’s four-room house is now a strip of orange-painted wall at the edge of the drop.
“That money was a joke,” he says. “You can’t rebuild your life with that.” He took out a bank loan and built three rooms at the far end of the village on the only plot he could afford. It floods and erodes like everywhere else.
Beyond some compensation for affected families, officials have done little for Hassanabad, residents say. The state has evacuated families and sent food and medicine after each flood, and rebuilt the road and the bridge. But no one has been relocated, and residents say most of the assistance they received afterward — temporary shelters, food, and bathrooms — came from the Aga Khan Development Network.
“The government is not helping us,” Ali says. “They need to relocate these families because this is a very dangerous place to live. We’re mostly farmers and shepherds and don’t have the resources to rebuild after losing everything.”
There was supposed to be a warning, too. Hassanabad is one of two dozen valleys covered by GLOF-II, a UN Development Programme project with Pakistan’s climate ministry that installed weather stations, river gauges, and sirens across the north. During last summer’s floods, residents say, no sirens sounded.
Muhammad, who was in Hunza at the time conducting a training session attended by officials from the meteorological department who manage the monitoring station, says the sirens are triggered when the water level reaches a predefined threshold. The stream in Hassanabad did not reach the threshold required to trigger the siren, he says. Residents say the siren on the bridge was later swept away by the flood.
Villagers must rely on one another instead. On the hottest days, when the melt runs high, volunteers from the community post themselves along the stream. When they see dust rising from the ravine, a sign that water has broken loose upstream, they quickly warn residents.
“Despite all these disasters and uncertainties, we are more united,” Ali says. “We all realize we are in the same situation, and we only have each other.”
“My Enemy”
Nargisa Khatoon was married in a mud and stone house, with carved wooden beams, that had stood for two centuries. “It was beautifully decorated,” says the eighty-three-year-old.
Her family has lived for generations in Tokorkot, a village in the Nagar Valley across the Hunza River from Hassanabad. They were landowners under the mirs, the princes who ruled Nagar until Pakistan abolished the monarchy in the 1970s.
In 2022, a summer of debris flows struck part of the house and swept away most of the family’s land and trees. For two years, they slept outdoors in a garden beneath a tarpaulin rigged against the rain and sun, or with relatives when there was room, before building the small house Khatoon lives in now.
“I don’t like to remember that day,” she tells me, shuddering. “To see my home swallowed by the water, right in front of me. . . . I was shocked.”
For months after, fear kept the village awake. People walked the riverbank at night, watching the water, wondering whose house would go next. “I still have dreams about those days,” she says.
Khatoon grew up seeing the water as a blessing. It irrigated the fields and grew the walnut trees. “But after the floods destroyed everything around us, I became afraid of the water,” she explains, leaning against the side of her house.
“Now, I see it as my enemy.”
Unlike Hassanabad’s Ismailis, people here are Twelver Shia, the largest religious community in Gilgit-Baltistan. The village of a few dozen families sits where two waterways meet: the Hispar River and the Hopar Stream, which comes down from the glaciers of the Hopar Valley above. The village is hemmed in by flood-prone streams on either side and the river in front. Residents say there is nowhere to go.
The Hopar Stream had flooded now and then for as long as anyone could remember. But in the summer of 2022, extreme heat followed by heavy rain likely destabilized the Daranchi Glacier, according to a study published last year, sending more than twenty debris flows — torrents of water, rock, and mud — down the stream in a single month, a frequency the researchers called unprecedented.
Across Tokorkot and four other villages along the stream, at least twelve houses, schools, forty irrigation and water channels, bridges, and about seventy-five acres of farmland were swept away. The district administration sent some tents, according to residents, and families spent the rest of the summer in them.
When the floods returned last year, destroying a bridge and cutting the road to Tokorkot, families took shelter in the same tents. On the hottest days, families still leave for higher ground, carrying food and sleeping together in tents.
In Tokorkot, the fear is too much water. In the valley above, among farmers whose fields the glaciers feed, it is too little.
Qurban Ali has watched the ice vanish over his lifetime.
When the seventy-two-year-old farmer was young, his family worked fields low in the Hopar Valley, fed by meltwater from the Barpu Glacier. As the glacier thinned, its surface sank and the meltwater level fell with it, until the water dropped below the mouths of the irrigation channels that carried it to their fields. The family abandoned those fields and moved higher, onto land watered by the Daranchi — the glacier behind Tokorkot’s 2022 debris flows.
“The glaciers are going deeper underground day by day,” he says. “So we cannot reach and bring up the water.” Farmers say the Daranchi is thinning too. Satellite measurements show the glaciers here losing mass every year since 2000, with the heaviest losses at their lower ends, where farmers draw their water.
“Our entire life here revolves around the glacier water,” Ali tells me. “If there are no more glaciers, then there’s no more life.”
Hopar sits on a terrace of fields about 330 feet above the Bualtar glacier, known locally as Hopar. From a lookout at the head of the valley, its ice lies directly below, blackened with rock and dust.
When a geographer surveyed Hopar in the mid-1980s, its five villages and roughly four thousand people were irrigating some seven hundred acres of terraces through more than 180 miles of hand-dug channels, with more meltwater than the fields needed for most of the growing season.
Satellite records since 1993 show the snow and ice here shrinking by more than two-thirds, and researchers have also documented fields in the valley being cut off from their water.
But as the melting increases, the same valley is being hit by the floods that have torn through the rest of the region. Lower down, where families live and farm along the Hopar Stream, the water arrives all at once.
Left With Nothing
Rashida sits outside her tent and washes the family’s clothes by hand in water carried up from the Ghizer River, one of the region’s main rivers. It quickly turns brown with silt. She stops, takes a deep breath and wipes sweat from her forehead.
“At our home in the village, we had a washing machine and clean running water,” the thirty-seven-year-old says. “I’m not used to living like this.”
Rashida’s family has lived in this tent settlement since last year, when they were displaced from their village, Hakis Thingi, in the Gupis Valley of Ghizer district, in western Gilgit-Baltistan.
At about 3 a.m. on August 22, a glacial lake in the mountains above Talidas village, in the Raushan area, burst. Officials blamed high temperatures. Water poured down a side stream, triggering landslides on both sides of the valley and sending a powerful debris flow through Talidas, flattening it. The debris then blocked the Ghizer River.
For about six hours, the river stopped flowing as water backed up behind the blockage. By daylight, the ensuing lake was several miles long. Across six villages, the flood destroyed or damaged hundreds of houses and large tracts of land. It also submerged part of the only road connecting the area to the rest of the region.
No one, however, was killed. Shepherds high in the mountains spotted the flood coming and phoned down to the villages below, where trained volunteers moved families out before the water arrived.
About 80 percent of Talidas was destroyed. Upstream, the rising water swallowed houses in Hakis Thingi village and nearby settlements. More than three thousand people from 330 households were displaced — the second-largest displacement in Gilgit-Baltistan since the Attabad disaster in 2010, when a landslide dammed the Hunza River and submerged a string of villages.
A year later, the floodwater in the Raushan area still stretches across parts of the valley, rooftops jutting above its surface.
A resettlement site was built high in the mountains for some of those displaced from Talidas, isolated from the villages and services below. Residents say the government provided the land. The University of Lahore, a private university, funded the houses at about $720 each.
Around sixty-five homes were washed away in Talidas, but only some families were provided plots, residents say. The rest are staying with relatives or in tents.
About twenty-three families from Hakis Thingi, meanwhile, still live in a sprawling tent settlement across the river from their drowned village. Residents say the government has allocated each family about a twelfth of an acre, and aid organizations are providing materials for a one-room shelter with a kitchen and bathroom. But the families, who lost their land and livelihoods, must provide the labor themselves.
The barren plots are only big enough for the shelters, residents say, and they cannot farm because the surrounding land is government-owned. They have relied on private aid, which dried up at the start of this year, and on whatever daily work they can find in construction, farming, or local shops.
When I visited in August, not a single shelter was finished, and the entire community was still living in tents.
“My whole life is different now,” Rashida says, settling onto the ground inside the tent beside her husband.
Nowhere to Turn
In Hakis Thingi, each family had scattered plots planted with almonds, apricots, apples, cherries, and mulberries. They grew their own vegetables, kept cows for milk and sold dried fruit at local markets for the cash they needed for clothes, household goods, and school fees.
For Rashida, her children’s education mattered most. She says all of them did well at school. “Before, we could easily afford to send them to very good English-medium schools,” she tells me. “Now we have to ask [nongovernmental organizations] for help with the costs of government schools.”
“I used to have very big plans for them,” she adds, as her children pull back the front of the tent and peek shyly inside. “I believed they would all go to university.”
“Now I’m just worried about how to feed them each day.”
Residents here say living so close to the Ghizer River — the river that took their homes — also leaves them constantly frightened.
A couple of miles upstream, others never left. Their houses still stand on the edge of the lake. About twenty-four of their neighbors’ homes remain submerged, occasionally reappearing as the lake recedes. Water drains through a natural spillway in the debris and officials have declared the lake no longer a threat.
Zarnisa, sixty, and her husband, Abdul Qayum, eighty, have moved between their home and the tents for more than a year. Their house stayed flooded for about six months, only its roof visible. When the water fell in January, they returned; three months later, it rose again. A few days before I met them, the spillway had widened, the lake dropped and they went home again.
“We are always afraid,” Zarnisa says, guiding me to the edge of her small yard and pointing to the water just a few feet away. “Maybe in a few days the water will rise again, and we will have to flee.”
Zarnisa’s husband has fallen into depression after being repeatedly displaced from their only home. “He’s constantly having panic attacks,” she tells me. From their yard, the roofs of sunken homes rise above the water, a perpetual reminder of what will eventually happen again to their own.
“It gives me a lot of anxiety,” she says. More than her own house, however, she worries about the neighbors whose homes are already gone. “My neighbors were all like family to me. I’m always thinking about them and feeling sad.”
Those neighbors now live in tents on higher ground or in the homes of relatives. They have not been given plots or shelters. One of them is theity-five-year-old Zaibunisa. Her family owned three houses with shops attached, and she ran a small early education school for local children. All of it is now under the lake, along with their land.
“When the flood came, we didn’t have time to grab anything, not even our phones,” Zaibunisa says. “We were left with nothing but our lives.”
With no other land, she pitched a tent outside a relative’s house. “We feel stuck,” she tells me, standing outside the tent she shares with her husband and their three young children. “We need help.”
“No Safe Area”
About a week before the glacial flood, a different kind of disaster struck elsewhere in the Gupis valley.
In Khalti village, the ground is a field of boulders and rocks. “Nobody here had ever feared floods; this side of the valley has no glacier above it,” says Karim Beig, seventy-three, a village elder. “The danger, in living memory, was always avalanches.”
On August 14, cloudbursts hit thirty-seven locations across Ghizer. At least thirteen people died. These downpours can dump four inches of rain or more in an hour over an area just a few miles across, sending walls of water and mud down the slopes within minutes.
One hit Khalti. Residents say eight houses were destroyed in about ten minutes and about four more were damaged. Six members of one seven-person family died. Villagers who reached the wreckage say they heard a small boy crying beneath it and dug him out. Beig and his younger brother, also in his seventies, lost half their house and most of their orchards and land.
Beig leads me through the rubble, then crouches and motions for me to follow him down a crevice. A small backpack and other belongings lie beneath the debris, left behind by families whose homes were crushed by the rocks and floodwater.
Cloudbursts are a “very new phenomenon” here, explains Syed Najam Hassan, an assistant professor at Karakoram International University in Gilgit who uses satellite data to map the region’s glacial lakes. They are associated with the monsoon, which until recently rarely reached these altitudes.
Ghulam Rasul, former director general of the Pakistan Meteorological Department, says the mountains are warming faster than the plains below, strengthening the forces pushing the monsoon north. The Himalaya runs east to west, blocking its path. But toward the west, the wall of mountains ends, and the monsoon is now pushing through into the high Karakoram.
“Now we all feel exposed,” Beig says, balancing on one of the rocks scattered across the village. “Every night when it rains, no one can sleep. Some of us come outside and watch the clouds for any sign of what might happen.”
Communities here have read the signs of approaching glacial floods for centuries, but nothing passed down by their elders tells them what a cloudburst looks like before it comes. Even researchers struggle to predict them, Najam says. A village can be sitting under clear skies while a storm builds over the ravine above, with the water arriving half an hour later.
“Everything has changed since that day,” Beig says. “It’s like we’ve been invaded by something unfamiliar, something we don’t understand and that could attack us at any moment.”
Theses dangers extend throughout the region. “Across Gilgit-Baltistan, everywhere is at high risk,” Najam tells me. “With the climate changing, there is no safe area.”
While the water can eventually recede, the trauma cannot. Nargis Asad, who chairs the psychiatry department at Aga Khan University in Karachi and has studied the mental health of displaced people in Pakistan since the 2005 earthquake, says these communities are not recovering from a single disaster but living in a state of chronic exposure.
“When you are continuously exposed to a threatening situation, there is an ongoing state of worry and apprehension about an impending disaster that can come at any time,” Asad explains. “It becomes a very fearful existence, affecting your psychological, cognitive, and physical well-being.”
“Losing your livelihood and your source of income is also a real trauma,” she adds. “It is a major hit to your identity and creates a sense of helplessness, especially when it is land your family has lived on for generations.”
The toll is physical, too, she says: cardiac problems, disrupted sleep, and illnesses that emerge long after the flood has receded. And the effects can extend to the next generation. “When children live under constant fear, their learning capacity, sense of safety, and sense of trust are all affected,” she says.
At the camp for displaced families from Hakis Thingi, Sher Wali, ninety, sits in his worn tent with his wife, Jamali, sixty, grieving decades of lost work. “All my life, I worked to build on what my ancestors gave me, to give my children more than I had,” he says, his voice rough with exhaustion.
“I lived off the land and cows and had a happy life,” he continues. “But now our children don’t even have milk for their tea or any fruit to eat.” He points through the tent opening to the treeless land outside, the sun beating down.
At night, he takes stock of everything he lost in the floods. “I remember every section of my land, every fruit tree and every piece of property I no longer have,” he tells me. “It pains my heart, and I can’t sleep well.”
“I’m an old man. . . . my life is almost over,” he adds. “But I fear for future generations. Without land or jobs, I’m afraid many of our young people and children will just be left to die.”
