How Workers Can Govern in Zohran Mamdani’s New York
Pro-worker policy isn’t just about the government improving labor standards. Zohran Mamdani’s administration could empower workers to shape and enforce standards by training and organizing each other.
In Amazon’s vast logistics empire, warehouse workers and delivery drivers incur frequent injuries amid stringent performance monitoring and evaluation. The best data we have indicates that many workers are interested in organizing to improve their conditions, yet the same infrastructure used to relentlessly boost productivity is deployed to suppress collective action. Refusing to come to the table even when workers unionize, Amazon is looking to have traditional legal pathways for expressing worker voice abolished altogether — and its algorithmic systems given free rein.
Still, closer inspection reveals stirrings of dissent. Across Amazon’s global network, workers aware of their strategic position in the distribution process are contesting speedup and discipline. Through their mastery of government regulations and the company’s own operating procedures, they are challenging productivity write-ups, refusing unsafe work, and teaching their peers how to navigate Amazon’s increasingly automated managerial systems. They are developing a knowledge base that prefigures more democratic forms of shop floor governance.
Not only are these emergent practices of peer education crucial for strategies of labor renewal, but they can inform a parallel question that has gained traction in the last year — the question of mass governance. Amid a deepening global crisis of liberal democracy, the election of a socialist mayor in New York City has generated interest in not only representing the interests of working-class people but, moreover, expanding opportunities for them to govern the city their labor makes run. Thus far, mass governance initiatives have focused on cultivating engagement at the neighborhood and borough levels, such as through “Rental Ripoff Hearings” and participatory budgeting assemblies. Meanwhile, the workplace remains an underexplored site. Though the Mamdani administration has begun expanding state capacities to enforce labor standards, less attention has been placed on the role that workers can play in this process.
This essay builds a framework of mass governance out of workers’ daily struggles on the shop floor, focusing on peer education as a dual organizing and policy tool. Versed in legal rights, work processes, and relational dynamics, peer educators are uniquely positioned to cultivate shared insights about the harms stemming from employers’ exploitative practices and facilitate tactical experimentation aimed at eradicating these harms together with strategic reflection around transforming the power relations that give rise to them. We term this mode of engagement mass worker education: democratizing the production of knowledge in service of democratizing the production of goods and services. Recognizing the importance of intellectual exchange and political deliberation for worker empowerment, this framework envisions workers as not only enforcing labor standards but shaping them as well.
Following on the Mamdani administration’s expansion of resources for the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) as well as its establishment of the Mayor’s Office of Worker Power (MOWP) and Office of Mass Engagement (OME), the essay considers leveraging this enhanced capacity to institutionalize a role for peer educators in implementing worker protections and building workplace organization. As an exemplary case, we explore the idea of NYC establishing a mass worker education program in parcel shipping operations across the metropolitan area. Administered in partnership with unions and community groups, the program would build training capacity among a corps of warehouse workers and parcel delivery drivers, strengthening their role in enforcing new laws that address harmful industry practices and cultivating broader cultures of workplace safety. We also consider forms of partnership between NYC and New York State that could expand the scope and extend reach of this worker training and legal coenforcement with increasingly nonunion workforces. Last, we discuss how such a program could empower workers to participate in mass assemblies shaping policy development around data collection, deployment of new technologies, and other pressing concerns, helping pave the way toward mass sectoral governance.
Labor Standards Enforcement and the Role of Peer Education
Government agencies around the country are building partnerships with worker organizations to enforce labor standards. Drawing on the knowledge that workers have about their industries and specific worksites, these efforts in coenforcement have achieved important gains in addressing legal violations.
At Amazon’s San Bernardino International Airport (KSBD) air hub in Southern California, for instance, workers organizing with Inland Empire Amazon Workers United have collected and shared information about the facility’s weak safety protections during extreme summer temperatures, leading to several government citations. This work comes on the heels of over a decade of worker education and organizing that has raised consciousness around heat safety in the Inland Empire’s booming warehousing sector and contributed to the passage of statewide heat illness prevention standards.
In response to another acute threat faced by workers — the rapid deployment of artificial intelligence technologies — California, New York, and other states have also begun enforcing new quota transparency laws in the warehousing sector. In 2024, the California Labor Commission fined Amazon almost $6 million for violating Assembly Bill 701, which requires warehousing employers to provide written notice of quotas on which they are evaluated. Here, too, worker knowledge and organization proved crucial to enforcement, with workers at ONT8 (Optical Network Terminal) and ONT9 fulfillment centers sharing information with the Labor Commissioner’s Office under the auspices of the California Strategic Enforcement Partnership.
Increasingly, Amazon is challenging these efforts at enforcing quota standards. In California, the company has appealed the Labor Commission’s citations by arguing that it does not use predetermined quotas to evaluate workers, while in New York, workers report that management has been able to sidestep new quota provisions by evaluating workers on the basis of their relative productivity — a tactic that makes injured and pregnant workers especially vulnerable to heightened work intensity.
In maintaining its de facto quota system, Amazon insists that the data it collects on workflows and then uses to train computational systems constitutes proprietary information. Even in jurisdictions with strong data protections like Germany, the company refuses to give works councils (elected workplace bodies that represent employees’ interests to management) access to datasets and algorithms managed by engineers often hundreds or thousands of miles away from the worksite — the very measures that would enable frontline workers to intervene more directly in the technical processes that shape their working conditions.
Government agencies around the country are building partnerships with worker organizations to enforce labor standards.
In challenging the separation that capitalist production engenders between the conception and execution of labor, peer education offers a potential antidote. At a recent workshop, workers from different Amazon divisions came together to analyze the impacts of AI and explore strategies for expanding worker voice in its design and deployment. As a collective exercise in knowledge production, the gathering showed what may be possible if workers are empowered to disrupt hierarchical information flows in the workplace and policymaking arenas.
Highlighting worker knowledge for policymaking purposes suggests wider implications concerning the intersection of labor renewal and mass governance. For the most part, legislation aimed at supporting efforts to revitalize the labor movement (e.g., the Protecting the Right to Organize [PRO] Act) has been focused on making it easier for workers to organize. As necessary as these measures are for expanding the associational capacities of the working class, they are insufficient for expanding its governing capacities. Unions serve as a potentially politicizing force within the workplace, but they largely operate within legal frameworks that regularize collective bargaining while muting shop floor contestation. These frameworks not only enshrine capitalist control over production but also shift the task of governing away from workers’ daily struggles. Workers can try to influence the policy process either through union representatives appointed to tripartite structures or by lobbying elected officials.
Mass worker education challenges this distinction, emphasizing the agency of workers in more directly shaping and enforcing their rights on the shop floor. We draw inspiration from the factory councils of interwar Europe, experiments with autogestion (self-management) in decolonized Africa and Asia, and the cordones industriales (industrial belts) and comunas (communes) at the heart of socialist projects in Latin America. More immediately, we look to occupational health movements that used peer education to expand popular sovereignty under a range of authoritarian politics of early neoliberalism. During the Brazilian military dictatorship, for instance, metalworkers used their firsthand knowledge of the sector’s acute injury crisis to expose the state’s cosmetic fixes, laying the groundwork for a disability rights movement that made key legislative advances after the fall of the junta. In the Indian state of Chhattisgarh, mine workers in the 1980s partnered with health professionals to train “barefoot doctors” and establish a people’s hospital that broke down hierarchies of expertise in the health sector. Meanwhile, during the Reaganite offensive in the United States, worker movements within the United Auto Workers (UAW) and Oil, Chemical, and Atomic Workers International Union (OCAW) used peer education to link health and safety organizing to broader questions of environmental justice.
Presently, we see this legacy extended by Amazon workers building power across the company’s global network. Through meetings organized by Amazon Workers International and other networks, worker representatives exchange information about hazardous work and bring this knowledge home to share with coworkers on the shop floor. Moreover, in refusing unsafe work during the pandemic and other emergencies, Amazon workers have been articulating a common vision of making company operations safer for themselves and their communities.
These examples illustrate the openings that exist for workers to build shop floor power and influence policy even in challenging conditions. Through spaces of collective experimentation and reflection, workers can confront the root of the harms they face — power relations embodied in the production process itself.
Instituting Mass Worker Education in NYC
In NYC, the Office of Labor Policy & Standards (OLPS), a division of the DCWP, has undertaken important legal enforcement measures in recent years. For example, following the 2010 passage of the New York Domestic Workers’ Bill of Rights, OLPS convened focus groups with nannies, cleaners, and home health aides across the city to discuss violations and other issues. A parallel set of efforts led to the 2017 formation of the We Rise Nanny Training program, through which a coalition of domestic worker organizations have partnered with the Worker Institute at Cornell University in developing a peer education program centering around rights awareness, workforce development, and organizing skills. The coalition has since expanded the program to cover other sectors, training hundreds of nannies, cleaners, and home health aides, as well as day laborers and farmworkers. New research shows that NYC, with its strong enforcement of the Domestic Workers’ Bill of Rights, has seen major improvements in job quality indicators such as overtime relative to the rest of the state.
These experiences highlight the importance of not only responding to legal violations after they have occurred but also promoting organizing strategies that shift larger workplace cultures. A mass worker education program could support legal coenforcement while also equipping workers with resources to exercise greater control over their conditions, addressing shop floor challenges before they become acute.
To illustrate what such a program could look like, we return to the example of warehousing and parcel delivery. With its rapid expansion amid the e-commerce boom, the industry has attracted growing public concern over its impacts on workers, residents, and the environment. Amazon’s invasive deployments of AI and other digital technologies have received particular scrutiny, spurring wider discussion among consumers and workers across a variety of industries. Building on existing legislation and organizing in New York, a program of mass worker education could strengthen governance of warehousing and parcel delivery and serve as a model for other industries.
Legislation passed at the state level over the past five years regulates production quotas and mandates that employers implement injury reduction plans. In 2025, worker and advocacy groups in New Yorkers for a Fair Economy (NYFE) — a coalition convened by the Alliance for a Greater New York (ALIGN) — turned attention to the question of how to implement this legislation effectively. Amazon Labor Union–International Brotherhood of Teamsters Local 1 (ALU-IBT Local 1), representing five thousand workers at the JFK8 fulfillment center in Staten Island, focused on raising awareness of these laws as part of its safety campaign. Following several worker summits and stakeholder meetings, ALU-IBT Local 1 partnered with the Athena Coalition and National Employment Law Project (NELP) to pilot a training around laws relevant to advancing health and safety in the workplace, body and hazard mapping, and formation of workplace safety committees. With support from the Consortium for Worker Education (CWE), ALU-IBT Local 1 has carried out additional training with shop floor leaders and is building a training center near JFK8.
At the city level, the NYFE coalition is currently mobilizing in support of the Delivery Protection Act (DPA), introduced by NYC Council Member Tiffany Cabán in September 2025. The legislation would require operators of last-mile delivery facilities to obtain business licenses from DCWP and directly hire delivery drivers (including those who have unionized with Teamsters Local 804 at Amazon delivery facilities DBK4 and DBK1 in Queens) rather than misclassifying them as independent contractors. Importantly, the legislation would require employers to grant access to an independent certified organization to conduct safety and rights training with workers and managers. Drawing on a recent study commissioned by the NYC Comptroller’s office that shows an increase in traffic crashes and injuries in areas near last-mile delivery facilities like the ones in Maspeth, Queens, advocates argue that promoting the safety of workers would also help to safeguard residents. “The impact goes far beyond us,” according to Luc Rene, an Amazon Teamster based at DBK4. “The endless churn of underpaid drivers creates congestion, pollution, and wear on city streets.” If the bill passes, DCWP could partner with members of the NYFE coalition to develop a coenforcement strategy that builds on work around recent state laws.
Focusing on the training provision, we draw on an insight common among many evaluations of union education programs, which shows that workers more readily incorporate lessons received through peer education as opposed to other forms of pedagogy. A particularly instructive example comes from a peer education program developed to address sexual harassment and violence in California’s janitorial industry, where a coalition of labor and anti-violence organizations created a framework for anti-sexual-harassment training by peer educators, known as promotoras, for janitorial workers across the state. The coalition, which included worker leaders, saw that managers and supervisors often enable or enact harmful behaviors themselves, and determined that trained janitors — particularly survivors of sexual violence — were best positioned to educate their peers about relevant rights and strategies. Coalition members went on to support the creation of the Ya Basta Center in Los Angeles, which has trained hundreds of janitor promotoras to provide peer training in workplaces across California. Drawing on trauma-informed methods originally developed by the East Los Angeles Women’s Center, janitor promotoras facilitate spaces where workers can establish the trust needed to share their stories. These healing spaces have given janitors the confidence to stand with each other in the workplace and speak up against harassment, often joining fights around other issues like wage theft as well.
In New York, working together with an enforcement agency like DCWP as well as key anchoring institutions like MOWP, OME, and CWE, members of the NYFE coalition could set up a training program akin to the promotora program in California. Focusing initially on enforcement of the DPA, the program could prepare a core of last-mile delivery drivers and warehouse workers — including those engaging with local unions — to deliver training around issues of misclassification and safety addressed by the legislation. Like the promotora model, employers across this industry would be required to grant access to peer educators, enabling the program to cover nonunion workforces as well. Through program evaluation, the city could develop an evidence base showing whether and how peer training impacts worker awareness of legal rights and the sense of efficacy workers have in exercising these rights. Drawing on the city’s increasing agency capacities as well as its growing movement of labor and community groups targeting Amazon’s abuses, such work could evolve into the development of a training center like the Ya Basta Center.
Over time, building on emergent city-state partnerships around childcare and other issues, a peer education program could train a corps of warehouse workers and parcel delivery drivers in promoting awareness and enforcement of the right to organize as well as health and safety laws that Amazon and other employers have been known to violate. Given employers’ use of tech-enabled worker surveillance strategies to enforce unsustainable work rates and impede worker responses, peer educators could draw connections between these individual and collective forms of disempowerment. By bringing together workers from different parts of the logistics sector, a mass worker education program could generate broader knowledge about the infrastructures undergirding harmful practices and foster dialogue about strategies for building worker voice across the supply chain. Moreover, linking worker and community safety, the program could also generate support for other legislative efforts.
A partnership between the city and state could assist with the development of this program in multiple respects. First, Albany could generate revenue for the peer education training center by imposing a “robot tax” on Amazon and other corporations investing in high levels of automation. Second, implementing and refining a peer education program at the city level would serve as a test case before expanding its reach across New York state. In California, labor and anti-violence groups leveraged a rich movement ecosystem in Los Angeles, the historic birthplace of the Justice for Janitors campaign, toward establishing the Ya Basta Center as a base for strengthening statewide rights enforcement. A peer education training center based in NYC could serve a similar function. Last and most ambitiously, the state and city could follow the example of work-sharing agreements between government agencies, establishing coenforcement powers between NYS Department of Labor (DOL) and NYC DCWP that promote accountability for serial law breakers and discourage harmful employer behaviors. For instance, current state law mandates annual worksite evaluations by state-appointed industrial hygienists (government officials who identify and control workplace hazards to protect public health). Employers are then required to take concrete steps to address whatever ergonomic risk factors are identified in the evaluations, but it has not been specified what steps employers would need to take to comply. Establishing coenforcement powers between NYS DOL and NYC DCWP would enable the city government to work with unions and other partners in establishing participatory structures.
From the Shop Floor to the Assembly
Recent years have seen numerous proposals calling for sectoral governance as a labor renewal strategy in New York and other parts of the country, including wage boards and tripartite bargaining structures. In their implementation, however, such developments often have been relatively detached from and at times contradictory to grassroots efforts to grow worker power. This disconnect weakens legal enforcement, hampers ongoing policy development that could be responsive to evolving worker needs and concerns, and limits possibilities for the kind of consciousness-raising work that can engender positive feedback loops between policy and organizing. This separation also constrains the capacity of workers to build direct associational power vis-à-vis employers, clients, and other holders of economic power.
In institutionalizing channels for workers to promote labor standards enforcement and shift broader workplace cultures, an infrastructure of mass worker education could amplify the capacity of frontline workers to meaningfully shape policy. Specifically, peer education could build on workers’ existing job-related knowledge to deepen understandings of industry dynamics and relevant policy debates; seed the formation of what ALU-IBT Local 1 leaders have called “tech governance councils,” which would combine strategic reflection on shop floor organizing with proposals for enhancing worker voice in technology deployment; and facilitate recruitment of workers into mass sectoral assemblies. These assemblies could provide a forum for workers from different worksites, occupations, and job titles to convene around developing citywide organizing and policy strategies. Such assemblies could deepen member engagement in areas where unions already have a foothold and provide a space for unions to continue deepening their coalitional relationships with other communities. Critically, amid continued employer attacks on legal rights to free association, mass assemblies could build networks of support for collective action in areas with little or no union density as well.
We end by returning to our opening vignette of Amazon workers resisting acute forms of digital surveillance. Amid growing interest in the regulation of data collection and computational systems, the framework we have proposed would anchor shop-floor governance practices, like the efforts of Amazon workers to teach each other how to navigate the company’s surveillance systems, in the insights of workers who encounter these systems daily. Moreover, in establishing a consistent feedback loop from the point of production to sectoral assemblies and the halls of state power, the policy process would be infused with ongoing experimentation, reflection, and refinement. As Big Tech and other corporate actors seek greater control over nearly every aspect of economic, social, and political life, the Mamdani administration has a historic opportunity to create agile policy mechanisms that can respond to this rapidly shifting terrain — moving from the shop floor up.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mckinney-det.title: Another Detroit Socialist Is Heading to Congress
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mckinney-det.author: Donavan McKinney, Sara Wexler
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mckinney-det.text:
Another Detroit Socialist Is Heading to Congress
Donavan McKinney, a Democratic Socialists of America–endorsed candidate for the US House in Detroit, is set to win his general election today. Jacobin spoke to him before Election Day about why he’s running and what he hopes to accomplish in office.
- Interview by
- Sara Wexler
In 2018, the election of two democratic socialists to the House of Representatives marked the beginning of a new political era. The socialist freshmen, both endorsed by the recently reinvigorated Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), were Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from New York City and Rashida Tlaib, representing Michigan’s Twelfth Congressional District in Detroit.
Eight years later, DSA boasts more than 120,000 members and politicians in elected offices across the country. And after a wave of Democratic primary victories earlier this year, democratic socialists are set to significantly grow their foothold in Congress in today’s general election.
Among the likely socialist victors is Donavan McKinney, who is expected to win easily in Michigan’s deep-blue Thirteenth District in Detroit and join Tlaib in representing the Motor City in the House. Jacobin spoke to him about why he’s running and how growing up working class in Detroit shaped his politics.
- Sara Wexler Why are you running for Congress?
- Donavan McKinney I’m running to bring the urgency that this moment demands. Right now, I represent the poorest state house district in Michigan: $14,000 is the median income. If you divide that up by twelve months, that’s a little over $1,200 a month. And the average rents in our neighborhoods, if you’re lucky, start at $1,300. So that’s all your money down the drain, and you’ve got to worry about the increase in the price of gas and groceries, and insurance costs, whether it’s health insurance or auto insurance. We have some of the highest auto insurance rates in the country. Then childcare costs as well and so many day-to-day expenses. I’m running to represent one of the five poorest congressional districts in the country. What I’m going through on the state level is the same thing. [Being in Congress will mean representing] bigger communities, a lot more people. However, it’s the same narrative — the same story: “I just don’t have enough resources to make ends meet.” So for me, this is about meeting the moment, getting people in these positions who are going to put working families first and put our district first.
- Sara Wexler Can you tell me about your campaign platform? What priorities are you running on?
- Donavan McKinney Universal childcare, Medicare for All, and getting big corporate money out of politics. First, I talk about universal childcare a lot as a state legislator. I coled the movement for Pre-K for all. We have pretty much universal pre-K in Michigan now because of our advocacy and the advocacy of many others. We want to expand that to childcare across the board; we’ll take the fight to Washington, DC, for universal childcare. For my wife and I, that’s the biggest expense in our day-to-day lives, because we have three beautiful children — two boys, four and two, and a baby girl who just turned one. We pay more for childcare for one of our children than we do for our whole mortgage. And you’ve got to think about how impoverished my district is. If we’re living paycheck to paycheck off of childcare alone, I don’t know how everybody else is getting through it. Second, Medicare for All: I’m a big believer because of my mom and what she had to go through. When I was an undergrad at the University of Michigan, I got a call from my mom panicking because she was rushed to the hospital emergency room and they had to do emergency brain surgery. She comes to find out that she had brain tumors growing. And at the time, the only way she could get health care was through her employer; she was working at the time, but her employer didn’t offer it. So she was uninsured. And they did the emergency surgery, but guess what? She got that big six-figure bill for that procedure, and she didn’t have any way to pay it. They put her on a payment plan, but I had to go work three jobs at the time while I was a full-time student to make sure that she got the care she needed. By the grace of God, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) kicked in not too long after that, and she was able to afford health care. But I’m a big believer in Medicare for All, because she had preexisting conditions. Whether you have a preexisting condition or not, you deserve health care. That’s why I’m a big proponent of Medicare for All. There [are so many problems] when it comes to ACA premiums, as well as my seniors on fixed incomes, rubbing pennies together to try to figure out if they should have food on their table for the day or pay more out of pocket for their doctor’s visits and skyrocketing costs when it comes to lifesaving prescription drugs. The third thing I talked about is getting money out of politics. I’ve led that initiative here at the state level. I’ve introduced that legislation two times since I’ve been in office, in back-to-back terms. Each term, we got more and more people. I think the first term we had fewer than ten people sign on. This time around, when we introduced it last year in the state legislature, I think we had thirty or forty people sign on. Now, if you look at every Democrat who’s running for state legislative office here in Michigan, they signed on to the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics initiative. We couldn’t get a hearing in the state house. So organizations and people on the ground decided to take back our power over legislation and create a ballot initiative. They collected six hundred thousand signatures across the state, and that initiative will be on the November 3 ballot. I’m excited about it, because it targets monopoly utility companies, our public utilities, as well as our insurance companies — health insurance companies and auto insurance — which give a lot of money to state legislators to really bend the needle toward them instead of working people. I’m looking to do the same thing federally, to sign onto the legislation of Congresswoman Summer Lee and Senator Bernie Sanders, which gets rid of all that dark super PAC money, as well as to overturn Citizens United. Those are my big three pillars.
- Sara Wexler You grew up working class in Detroit. Can you tell me a bit about your background and how that shaped your politics?
- Donavan McKinney I was born and grew up in Detroit, raised with my mom, my grandmother, and my younger brother. We moved thirteen times across the city; I spent the vast majority of my life in northeast Detroit, which I now represent in the state legislature. And if the general election goes well, I’ll be representing it in the halls of Congress. Like I said, we moved thirteen times. We stayed in cars, shelters, sometimes out in the street. We didn’t know where our next meal was going to come from, but there was no shortage of love and prayers that got us through those tough times. I remember what my grandmother told me growing up. She told me two things that I still live by today. Number one is count your blessings, because you woke up this morning when a lot of people didn’t. You have a roof over your head, clothes on your back, food on your table, and — we live in Detroit, the Motor City — a car to drive. Because our transit system isn’t that good yet, but we’re working on it; that’s something we’re going to take to DC to work on. But you’re able-bodied, you’ve got your mental health, you’ve got your faculties, things we take for granted day in and day out. Number two, she always used to say, “In life, there will always be people better off than you. There will always be people worse off than you, but never fight the urge to give.” And I put that quote on my first piece of literature when I first ran for state representative ten years ago, back in 2016 when I was just a bushy-tailed kid coming out of college, just trying to figure out life. I still live by those two principles today — they’re my North Star. That’s why I’m so passionate about working people and about the service, because that’s what’s forgotten in politics. [I like to say], politics is about the service of the people and bringing humanity and love and leading with your heart back into the politics, which [currently] is so divisive. There’s a lot of hatred, a lot of negativity, and we try to lead with love.
- Sara Wexler It seems like when you were growing up, people’s needs weren’t being met, and the affordability crisis was worsening, regardless of whether Democrats or Republicans were in power. What do you make of this?
- Donavan McKinney A lot of people I’ve talked to view the Democrats and the Republicans very similarly when it comes to economics. I do believe that the Democratic Party is the party of the people. I have seen the Democrats do a lot more than the Republicans in terms of [helping the] working class. But I’m a big believer in the Scripture. Scripture talks about how you can’t serve two masters. What is happening, especially now, is that the Dems are serving the corporate oligarchs, same as the Republicans. You’re either going to have to do what’s best and serve the interests of working people, or you’re going to serve the interests of just a few and increase the wealth of those who are taking advantage of regular working people. For me, we follow what we preach. That’s what people want to see. They want to see receipts. So look at our campaign: we ran a campaign that was people powered. We didn’t take a cent of corporate PAC money or AIPAC [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] money. A lot of our money came from individual people across our district, across our state, across our country, who believe in a different style of politics. Leading up to the primary, our average donation on ActBlue was around $30 or $32, something like that — tens of thousands of people just donating to a vision. I’m forever grateful for it, because we were outspent. My opponent [in the primary], the current congressman, had his own wealth. He made his money off of pharmaceuticals, and so he had his own money to put in. But he also took money from ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] contractors and AIPAC as well as other corporate PACs, crypto, all of that — DTE, our monopoly utility — and just lying on our name, putting a lot of ads out. I’m very grateful, by the grace of God, that people were really waking up and realizing, “You know what? Donovan is better for the job.” We’re bringing a message that resonates with people and brings folks together.
- Sara Wexler Before running for office, you worked for Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Healthcare Michigan, which is the state’s largest health care union. How has your experience with labor organizing informed your politics?
- Donavan McKinney I tell this story a lot about my grandfather. My grandfather passed away late last year during the campaign cycle. I’m trying to not be emotional, because the man taught me a lot. When I was a kid, he used to bring me to the union meetings a lot. He worked at Ford Motor Company in the Detroit metro region and was part of the United Auto Workers (UAW) for forty-two years. One of the most interesting things about my grandfather is that during those forty-two years, he never missed a day of work. I asked him at his retirement party some years ago, “Granddad, how did you do it?” He told me one thing that stood out, which was that he took pride in what he was doing. He knew that, with his bare hands, he was helping change a life or a family’s life. But more important, he knew that not only the union had his back, but that Ford Motor Company had his back. But fast-forward to the year 2026, that work that he had and that salary that he made — that dollar isn’t stretching as far. And these corporations have gotten greedier. Take, for instance, what happened at the Poletown plant in my district, which is on the border of Detroit and Hamtramck. It’s a General Motors factory plant. It’s nicknamed “Factory Zero.” It was the first factory in America, and the first factory in America to be net zero. It was really green, really environmentally friendly and forward-thinking around that. Earlier this year, they cut over a thousand jobs, all union jobs. They cut everybody’s jobs, and then, just a few months later, replaced them with robots. I talk about it in the union halls a lot; I talk about how much it’s bullsh–t and how, at the end of the day, nobody has our back but working people ourselves. We need to start electing folks with the right type of mindset and, more importantly, with the lived experience that [leads them to prioritize working people] over these greedy corporations.
- Sara Wexler That leads nicely into my next question. You’re running as a democratic socialist. What does that mean to you?
- Donavan McKinney I define politics as the redistribution of resources. That’s it; it’s black and white. If you’re in these positions of power and influence, if you’re not trying to figure out ways to bring home as many resources as possible back to your communities and the people you represent, then I need you to get up out of here. That’s what led me to run for Congress in the first place, because I felt like our current congressman wasn’t meeting the moment. We’re going to be able to pick up the phone and do constituent service work, because I understand what it’s like being on the phone trying to get somebody to answer to help when you’re in dire need. My current congressman is known for not picking up the phone, not doing the real constituent work of the job. Half the battle is showing up. The other half is trying to figure out resources to improve the quality of life of the people you represent. So in terms of democratic socialism, I’m a big believer in Dr Martin Luther King’s teachings. And Tupac [Shakur] said it best: “They got money for wars but can’t feed the poor.” You’re telling me we’re spending money for a war that nobody wants — a billion dollars a day in Iran. And you’re also telling me that, with H.R. 1 [the One Big Beautiful Bill Act], the Republican trifecta cut health care and food assistance for the most vulnerable populations across our country. And I thought Republicans didn’t believe in red tape: I thought they believed in slim government and lean government and achieving efficiency in government. But they want to hurt people in order to give a tax break to the wealthiest top 1-percent earners of our country. They’re telling people, “We want you to get recertified every six months for your health care. But we DOGEd government, and we know that you’re not going to get recertified in time because we don’t have the caseworkers to certify you in the right amount of time. Because of the savings we’re going to have on the back end from folks not being able to recertify, we’re going to give a tax break to the ultrawealthy.” That’s not the America I want to live in; that’s not the America people in my community want to live in, or anyone who I know wants to live in. It’s up to us Democrats to level the playing field and right the ship, so to speak. I’m going to push hard as hell and advocate for the poor folks in my communities. A lot of my community is struggling and they’re looking for somebody that’s going to fight for them, and that’s my job.
- Sara Wexler As you mentioned, you were able to oust the incumbent Democrat in your primary. I’m wondering what role different organizations, DSA for instance, have played in your campaign.
- Donavan McKinney I was quoted earlier in the campaign, and I said, “We’re building the biggest and baddest coalition in the country,” which is true. I’ve even had members of Congress call me because they’re like, “Yo, how did you do this?” We have some of the most established folks and even the most conservative Democrats endorsing our campaign, as well as all-the-way-to-the-left DSA types endorsing our campaign. I don’t know if it was just because of me or also because of how bad the incumbent was, but it’s because we’re speaking values. We’re leading with our heart, and we’re following what we’re preaching. We brought together faith leaders, elected officials from the federal, state, county, and local levels, community block club leaders, and unions. I was told I was the only nonincumbent the AFL-CIO endorsed on the federal level when it came to the Democratic primary. So we had the unions; we had groups like Justice Democrats and DSA and so many other great folks coming together and realizing that we deserve better. That was our campaign message: We deserve better. I’m so grateful because I couldn’t have done it without this coalition. I couldn’t have done it without people coming together and realizing that their voices matter and that they have the power to make a difference in our politics and change the trajectory of our country. We’re going to continue that movement as we get sworn in in January. It’s the inside-outside strategy that Dr King talked about. You need people on the outside agitating, advocating, but you also need people on the inside who are willing to listen, willing to really put those words to paper and move legislation very swiftly in this moment, with the urgency that it demands.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Administration Plans To Close 2 Small Harlem Schools, Move UWS School
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
Education officials are proposing to shutter two of New York City’s smallest schools, the first formal closure plans this academic year as Mayor Zohran Mamdani grapples with a growing number of underenrolled schools.
Two Harlem schools are on the chopping block: The Urban Assembly School for Global Commerce, a high school that serves 112 students, and School of Earth Exploration and Discovery Harlem, which serves just 40 children, making it the city’s smallest middle school. Both schools would close at the end of this school year.
Officials also plan to move The Center School, an Upper West Side school serving grades 5-8, to address overcrowding on a campus it shares with a popular elementary school. A plan to relocate the school to a different site last school year fell apart amid intense backlash.
All three Manhattan proposals are expected to come before the Panel for Educational Policy for a vote on Dec. 16.
The city is also gearing up to close a Bronx middle school, I.S. 224, Chalkbeat has learned, though the Education Department has not yet formally proposed it.
The Mamdani administration is facing growing pressure to close or consolidate schools as K-12 enrollment in the nation’s largest school district has plunged in the last 12 years by about 19%, or roughly 187,000 students. Declining headcounts have led to a glut of underenrolled schools that struggle to offer a full range of programs.
It remains to be seen whether these initial proposals represent the beginning of a larger push to merge or close underenrolled schools. Chancellor Kamar Samuels has indicated that addressing small campuses is top of mind and doing so could help reduce costs and expand academic offerings for students on campuses that are increasingly struggling to provide the basics.
“If a school is more underenrolled, it’s more likely not to offer the advanced classes that you need,” Samuels said earlier this year. “It may not offer the level of enrichment that you want to see.”
But Samuels has not shared a detailed roadmap for addressing the problem and has instead pointed to working groups in five of the city’s 32 local districts that are charged with coming up with community-driven plans on enrollment among a host of other issues.
Here’s what to know about the Education Department’s three proposals.
Closure Proposal: School of Earth Exploration and Discovery Harlem
City officials say SEED Harlem has gotten too small to be sustainable. Enrollment has plunged 68% since the 2022-23 school year, and it enrolled just six sixth graders this year.
It is also underperforming, with just 21% of students proficient in reading and in math, according to state tests, roughly half the average in District 5.
The school illustrates one of the central problems with tiny campuses: They are simultaneously expensive to operate and struggle to offer a full range of programs. SEED Harlem spent $93,000 per student last year, nearly four times the city average even as it has been forced to cancel partnerships with outside community organizations and scale back enrichment programs, officials said.
The school serves a vulnerable student population. Nearly all of the school’s students come from low-income families, and half have a disability. Just over half the school’s students are Black, and 44% are Latino.
Closure Proposal: The Urban Assembly School for Global Commerce
The proposed closure of Global Commerce, which Chalkbeat first reported last month, comes as the school has shed nearly a third of its students since the 2021-22 school year. It now enrolls 112 students.
Launched 13 years ago as part of former Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s push to open small themed high schools, the campus has been forced to end its career and technical education programs in supply chain management and marketing. With few staff on hand, its principal and assistant principal have stepped in to teach special education and some of its remaining career and technical programming, city documents show.
Like SEED, the school serves a high-need population: Nearly all of the school’s students come from low-income families. More than 90% of the school’s students are Black or Latino.
The Education Department also cited performance concerns. Just 20% of students met a city benchmark for advanced or career-oriented coursework, compared with 63% across Manhattan.
Despite the school’s challenges, the closure proposal has been gut-wrenching for students and staff, physical education teacher Gilbert Schuerch said.
“The amount of students I’ve held in my arms today,” he wrote on Substack after the closure was announced to the community, “and the number of tears shed — from me and the kids — has only reaffirmed how special this place has become to me and the kids.”
Relocation Proposal: The Center School
Facing overcrowding in its current building on West 84th Street, city officials are proposing to move the school 1.5 miles north to a campus at West 109th Street that houses P.S. 165. Officials say the move will help The Center School and P.S. 9, the coveted elementary school that currently shares its building, shrink class sizes under a state mandate.
The school faced a different relocation proposal last school year to a building on West 61st Street that houses P.S. 191. Families pushed back against the move for a variety of reasons, including insufficient community engagement and because they said the new location would not be able to adequately accommodate the school’s theater program.
The school, which served 247 students last year, is relatively affluent: About 23% come from low-income families, 55% are white, and about 27% are Black or Latino.
Officials plan to upgrade the theater space at the new campus, though they acknowledged the stage is smaller and shallower.
Last year’s proposal to move The Center School also involved eliminating the middle school grades at P.S. 191. Separately, the city proposed to eliminate the middle school grades at Manhattan School for Children and close the Community Action School. Those proposals were withdrawn last school year. An Education Department spokesperson did not say if they are still under consideration.
“NYCPS remains committed to meaningful engagement with communities before issuing any proposals,” Education Department spokesperson Dominique Ellison said in a statement.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-allie.title: Mamdani allies Valdez, Avila Chevalier win House seats for New York
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-allie.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-allie.text:
Three of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s allies are headed to Washington after winning their elections Tuesday.
The elections of Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier were a foregone conclusion given the overwhelming number of Democratic voters in their districts covering parts of Brooklyn, Queens, Manhattan and the Bronx. Nevertheless, their victories signaled the popularity of Mamdani’s brand of politics focused on affordability, taxing the rich and the Palestinian cause.
Democratic incumbent Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Greg Meeks, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Ritchie Torres all cruised to easy victories, as well.
Micah Lasher won the high-profile Manhattan seat vacated by his mentor, retiring Democratic Rep. Jerry Nadler.
Outside the city, two closely watched contests offered Democrats critical opportunities to win House seats.
In the Hudson Valley, the race between incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and former Army officer Cait Conley appeared to be delayed for hours because a technical problem affected voting machines in heavily Democratic Westchester County.
In New York’s North Country, Anthony Constantino, a flamboyant entrepreneur and former amateur boxer, was taking on Democratic dairy farmer Blake Gendebien. They are vying for a seat being vacated by Rep. Elise Stefanik, who is retiring.
Tuesday’s results contrast with the 2022 midterms, when New York played a key role in Republicans winning a slim majority in the House.
That year, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul won her top-of-the-ticket race by six points — a relatively narrow margin in deep-blue New York. Rep. Nancy Pelosi was among those who blamed Hochul’s lackluster performance that year for a handful of key congressional losses down the ballot.
Since then, Hochul, who also won reelection Tuesday, has raised tens of millions of dollars for the state Democratic Party to boost its down-ballot candidates. The effort paid dividends two years ago, when Democrats won back most of the tight House races in New York — except the 17th District held by Rep. Michael Lawler.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-voters-ap.title: NYC voters appear poised to approve outdoor dining, bike lane ballot measures
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-voters-ap.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-voters-ap.text:
New York City residents appear poised to approve a ballot measure Tuesday that would make it easier for restaurants to offer outdoor dining, while another proposal aimed at speeding up construction of bike and bus lanes is also leading by a wide margin.
All five measures were leading by wide margins as of 9:45 p.m., with nearly 86% of voting scanners reporting, according to unofficial results from the city Board of Elections. The outdoor dining measure had 63% support, while the bike and bus lane proposal had 65%.
The proposals were among five amendments to the city charter, which were developed after public meetings held by a commission selected by Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration. The measures sought to cut red tape on everything from curbside restaurant sheds to city contracting.
Here's where each ballot measure stands.
Question 1: Outdoor dining permits
Voters were overwhelmingly backing a measure to cut permitting time and fees that can block businesses that want to offer outdoor dining.
City officials say the application process currently takes up to eight months. The measure would cut that time to two months and save businesses up to $1,800 in fees, according to commission officials.
It would also remove the City Council's power to reject sidewalk cafe applications. The number of businesses offering outdoor dining has fallen about 90% from pandemic-era highs, according to city data.
Question 2: City contracting
Voters were also favoring a measure that would simplify questionnaires and replace certain required public hearings with written comment periods.
The changes are intended to make it easier and quicker for the city to award contracts.
Question 3: Bike and bus lanes
Voters were overwhelmingly backing a measure that would streamline the process for building new bike and bus lanes.
The proposal would also speed up the disposition of unused city property and the leasing of office space for city workers.
Question 4: Building permits
Voters were also backing a measure that would bring construction permit applications into a single digital hub.
It would also put the Department of Buildings in charge of all waterfront construction permits.
Question 5: Rainy day fund
New Yorkers were favoring a measure that would set a target of 12% of tax revenues for the city's rainy day fund, which currently has no target or deposit requirements.
It would also establish a flexible deposit formula, updated at least every four years, and require mayoral approval for withdrawals exceeding 50% of the fund.

https://gothamist.com/news/first-time-nj.title: Rebecca Bennett flips NJ Republican House seat for Democrats
https://gothamist.com/news/first-time-nj.author: Mike Hayes, Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/first-time-nj.text:
Newcomer Democrat Rebecca Bennett has defeated two-term incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Kean, Jr. in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District.
The Associated Press called the race for Bennett at 9:48 p.m.
Hundreds of jubilant supporters embraced and cheered the result in the main ballroom at the Bridgewater Manor where she held her election party. Her victory over Kean, the scion of one of the Garden State’s most well-known political families, notches a win for Democrats in a key swing district as they try to win a House majority for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term.
Bennett, 39, entered New Jersey politics as a healthcare industry executive and former Navy helicopter pilot with 15years of military experience. She overcame a 19,000-voter advantage for Republicans in a district that stretches from New Jersey’s border with Staten Island to the Pennsylvania line. In early voting, Democrats built a sizable 29,000-vote advantage heading into Election Day, which proved insurmountable for Kean and the GOP.
Kean barred members of the press from his election-night campaign event in Basking Ridge. Attendees struck a somber tone as they entered the Olde Mill Inn, where Kean has previously held victory parties.
His loss comes after a difficult year for the Republican, who had an extended, initially unexplained absence from Congress. He ultimately revealed that he was being treated for depression.
Bennett ran as a centrist, much like her fellow Democrat Gov. Mikie Sherrill, also a former Navy helicopter pilot, focusing less on social issues and more on affordability concerns like the rising costs of gas, groceries, healthcare, and childcare.
Like Sherrill, Bennett proved a formidable fundraiser, raising north of $8 million during her primary and general election campaigns. Still, it paled in comparison to an $18 million war chest that Kean and the GOP deployed in the closing weeks of the campaign, outspending Democrats by a roughly 3-to-1 margin on broadcast and digital advertising.
However, several prominent GOP groups pulled funding for Kean as polling showed he was less likely to be re-elected, according to the New York Times.
When Bennett takes the oath of office in January, she’ll become just the second Democrat and second woman since 1980 to represent the district.
Bennett’s rise
Bennett officially launched her campaign in early February 2025. She entered a crowded primary with 10 other contenders. Seven candidates dropped out prior to the primary election. Bennett ultimately faced off against critical care physician Dr. Tina Shah, childcare entrepreneur Brian Varela and former Biden administration official Michael Roth.
Bennett tacked towards the center compared to her fellow Democrats.
She favored a public option for healthcare over Bernie Sanders' ‘Medicare For All’ approach, which many progressive Democrats support. And she did not support progressives’ calls to abolish the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in response to masked agents seizing people on the streets of New Jersey, advocating instead for reform.
She also took a more moderate approach on Israel’s war in Gaza, refusing to call the conflict a genocide like many left-wing Democrats in the state and around the country have done.
At the same time, Bennett shared positions on some issues that are nearly uniformly supported by progressive and moderate Democrats alike. She campaigned aggressively on overturning the Supreme Court’s Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission decision that allows corporations and other outside groups to spend unlimited funds to support political candidates. She also repeatedly called for reversing tax cuts in Trump's 2025 tax and spending bill for the wealthy and corporations.
Bennett notched a convincing win in the four-way primary contest that gave her momentum going into the general election against Kean. She received more than 45% of the primary vote. Shah, the next closest competitor, got just 20%.
Bennett stuck to her moderate positions in her race against Kean to pull independent and moderate Republican voters to her side.
Kean’s campaign troubles
Kean won easily in his last contest for the seat. In 2024, he dispatched Democrat Sue Altman by more than five points, a sizable improvement on his 2022 win over Tom Malinowski.
His 2024 showing also more than doubled Trump’s own margin of victory in the district that year, with the president carrying it by about 2 points.
Kean entered the 2026 race with more than $3 million in his campaign coffers, plus enviable name recognition. Kean is the son of Tom Kean, Sr., a popular, two-term New Jersey governor in the 1990s. Before his election to Congress, Kean, Jr. served for more than two decades in the state legislature. He can trace his American and New Jersey lineage back to 1776 through many politically involved ancestors.
Well before Bennett won the primary, Democrats had begun raising the possibility of flipping the seat in 2026. Sherrill had a strong turnout in the district as a gubernatorial candidate in 2025, carrying it by about two points on her way to an easy 15-point statewide win over Republican Jack Ciattarelli. In early 2026, the national party organization, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, identified the 7th District as one of the party’s top-10 targets going into the midterms.
But Kean’s personal challenges may have been his most insurmountable hurdle in this year’s contest. He went missing from Congress in March with little word from him or his staff beyond a vague explanation that he was dealing with health issues. He finally returned after a 116-day absence, during which he missed over 100 votes. In a short speech from the Capitol in Washington, Kean said he had been hospitalized for depression.
When he returned to the campaign trail in July, Kean continued to face questions over his absence. But the embattled representative and his campaign staff repeatedly declined interviews, rebuffed calls to host public town hall meetings and blocked media from attending campaign events.
Bennett avoided attacking Kean over his absence. Instead, she attacked him on his numerous and lucrative stock trading while in office, sizable corporate donations to his campaign, his lack of engagement over a controversial White House effort to open an ICE detention center in the district, and Kean’s support for Trump’s overall agenda.
During his time in office, Kean fashioned himself as a moderate Republican. He took a moderate stance on issues like raising the limit on state and local tax deductions, protecting New Jersey’s environmentally sensitive spaces like rivers and wetlands and promoting an “all of the above” energy generation approach that includes wind and solar power. But his record also shows he’s voted with Trump 100% of the time.
Some of Kean’s fellow New Jersey Republicans encouraged him to break with Trump as both politicians slumped in the polls. Trump’s favorability rating in New Jersey amongst likely voters hit a record low of 29% in the lead-up to the midterm elections. Kean slumped by five points against Bennett in September and the Cook Political Report shifted its forecast of the race to favor the Democrat.
But he was reluctant to criticize Trump’s far-right agenda and instead defended the president on issues like the Iran war, tariffs and Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which delivered big cuts to housing, healthcare and food programs in New Jersey.
Altman, Kean’s former Democratic challenger in 2024, said Tuesday’s election was “a referendum on Trump.”
“People are reacting rationally,” she said,” I hope tonight this district, but all around the country, there’ll be a resounding referendum against Trump, all that he stands for.”
Other New Jersey races
Democratic Rep. Analilia Mejia defeated Republican challenger Joe Hathaway in New Jersey’s 11th Congressional District. The victory earns Mejia her first full term in Congress. The far-left progressive defeated Hathaway in April in a special election to serve out Gov. Sherrill’s term after she vacated the seat.
Another progressive Democrat, Dr. Adam Hamawy, easily defeated Republican Gregg Mele and Independent candidate Winston Jordan in a contest to replace longtime Democratic Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman in the 12th District.
Both Mejia and Hamawy ran on platforms featuring a host of progressive positions, including abolishing ICE, proclaiming Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide, and supporting Sanders’ ‘Medicare for All’ healthcare plan.
Sen. Cory Booker cruised to victory on Election Night. He’s been re-elected for a fourth consecutive term, including a partial term when he first won a special election to replace Frank Lautenberg, who died in office in 2013.
David Brand and Michael Sol Warren contributed reporting. This is a developing story and may be updated.

A 17th-century Dutch painting looted from France during the Second World War has been recovered by the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans. The painting, Willem Cornelisz Duyster’s Un Buveur (The Drinker), was stolen from Orleans’s Musée Paul Fourché following a Nazi attack on the city in 1940.
The Musée des Beaux-Arts was able to locate the painting thanks to an inventive poster campaign that placed “Wanted” in Wild West-style capital letters over images of artworks stolen from the museum. These were widely shared on social media, the museum’s website, and in various news outlets. Un Buveur was found by a community member in Orléans who took it upon himself to search for the missing works by sifting through online auctions—he found the painting in the catalog for an October 17 sale at the Gloggner auction house in Lucerne. The auction’s listing was initially thought to be a study for Duyster’s work, but after the museum contacted the auction house, researchers confirmed it as the original.
Un Buveur‘s owner purchased the painting at a London auction house in the 1990s, and “immediately proposed to restitute the painting” upon learning of its shaky provenance. “It was pretty natural for him to return it,” said Olivia Voisin, director of the Musée des Beaux-Arts, “Because he felt that he had been able to enjoy it for 35 years, and it was time for it to go home.”
424 paintings are still missing from the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans. They include works by Édouard Manet, Hans Holbein the Younger, Anthony van Dyck, Lorenzo Costa, and one painting attributed to Raphael’s workshop. In the years since the “Wanted” campaign started, three other paintings have also been recovered.

Fil d’Or, a 1953 painting by the British Surrealist Leonora Carrington, has been out of public view for seven decades, part of a family’s private collection in California. Now, it will lead a Heritage sale of modern and contemporary art on November 10, when it is estimated to fetch $250,000–$350,000.
ArtNet reports that the same year it was made, the painting was acquired from the Galería de Arte Mexicano in Mexico City by a family of art patrons. It has remained in their collection since then.
Carrington painted the composition canvas using grattage, a technique developed by Max Ernst that involves scraping through layers of wet paint with a spatula or blade to create underlying patterns. The work’s title is French for “gold thread,” a reference to these delicate marks, and that textured surface reveals an enigmatic bird that stares out at the viewer. Few examples of Carrington’s work employing this Surrealist technique have appeared at auction.
“That elusive quality feels very characteristic of Carrington,” Aviva Lehmann, deputy chairman of fine art at Heritage, told ArtNet. “Her creatures seem to inhabit a world with its own beliefs and logic, and we’re being given a glimpse inside.”
Carrington made the painting in Mexico, where she had emigrated after the outbreak of World War II and where she met other Surrealist refugees, including the painter Remedios Varo. Carrington died in Mexico City in 2011.
Earlier this year, another Carrington painting, Villa Pilar, 1940, went on public view for the first time after it had been missing for decades. Fil d’Or comes to auction amid a surge of interest in Surrealist art. Although Carrington’s own market peaked in 2024, her work continues to sell above historical records.

https://hyperallergic.com/daniel-sikkema.title: Daniel Sikkema Sentenced to Life for Murder of Art Dealer Brent Sikkema
https://hyperallergic.com/daniel-sikkema.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/daniel-sikkema.text:
Daniel Sikkema Sentenced to Life for Murder of Art Dealer Brent Sikkema
The 56-year-old man is accountable for a "cold, calculated murder-for-hire plot," said US Attorney Jamie McDonald.
Daniel Sikkema, 56, has been sentenced to life in prison for his role in the murder-for-hire of his estranged husband, New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) announced today, November 4.
Brent Sikkema, the 75-year-old co-owner of the Manhattan gallery Sikkema Jenkins & Company, was found dead in his Rio de Janeiro residence in January 2024. He was stabbed 18 times. Two months after the incident, Daniel Sikkema was arrested in Manhattan on charges of passport fraud and later received additional counts of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder for hire, and conspiracy to murder a person in a foreign country. A federal jury found him guilty on those charges following a two-week trial in May.
"Today’s life sentence holds Daniel Sikkema accountable for a cold, calculated murder-for-hire plot that resulted in the murder of his husband, Brent Sikkema,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a press release. Daniel Sikkema was also sentenced to five years of supervised release.
“For months, the defendant manipulated friends, family, and employees to execute a killing driven by greed. His actions demonstrated a profound disregard for human life and the rule of law," McDonald continued.
Daniel Sikkema had paid the couple's former security guard, Alejandro Prevez, to kill his husband as their divorce proceedings dragged on. Shortly after the fatal stabbing, Daniel Sikkema sent $5,000 to Prevez and promised future payments. The former security guard was arrested by Brazilian law enforcement four days after the murder and still awaits charges in Brazilian courts, according to the press release.
Brent Sikkema co-founded Sikkema Malloy Jenkins (then called Sikkema Jenkins Gallery) with his business partner, Michael Jenkins, in the early 1990s, where he showed artists including Kara Walker, Sheila Hicks, and Vik Muniz. The gallery currently represents more than 30 artists.

Guillaume Cerutti, the former president of the Pinault Foundation and a onetime chief of auction house Christie’s, has been named as the next president of the Château de Versailles, effective November 9. He succeeds Christophe Leribault, who left in February to lead the beleaguered Louvre in Paris. Cerutti was nominated for the role by Emmanuel Macron, the president of France.
Described by French daily Le Monde as a “stunning vindication,” his appointment is something of a surprise, arriving as it does in the wake of his much-scrutinized departure this past spring from the Pinault Foundation. Cerutti left the private, Paris-based organization after just thirteen months, leading many to speculate about a falling-out with French billionaire François Pinault, the founder of the collection and the owner of Christie’s. Days after stepping down, Cerutti departed all roles connected with Pinault, including those of Christie’s board chair and board chair of the Stade Rennais Football Club, which Pinault also owns through his holding company Artémis. Le Monde recently reported that friction between Cerutti, an avid cost-cutter who sought to slow acquisitions, and Pinault, an avid collector eager to add more works to his private trove, was to blame for the split.
Cerutti is a highly experienced arts and business leader. He joined Christie’s in 2016 as president for Europe, the Middle East, Russia, and India, rising to become CEO of the entire operation in 2017. He was previously deputy chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, having been promoted to the role in 2011 after five years as CEO of Sotheby’s French operation, during which time he elevated the business to become the country’s top auction house. Earlier roles include those of chief of staff to French culture minister Jean-Jacques Aillagon and, before that, managing director at the Centre Pompidou in Paris.
Cerutti is expected to bring his propensity for slashing costs and his talent as a fundraiser to bear at Versailles, which saw the French government slash €3 million ($3.4 million) in operational funding from its budget next year, even as the four-hundred-year-old palace is in the midst of a €200 million ($225 million) restoration slated for completion in 2031.

https://hyperallergic.com/so-youve-been-.title: So You’ve Been Invited to Documenta 16. Here’s Our Advice.
https://hyperallergic.com/so-youve-been-.author: Anonymous Documenta 15 Artists
https://hyperallergic.com/so-youve-been-.text:
So You’ve Been Invited to Documenta 16. Here’s Our Advice.
As two documenta 15 artists who were mercilessly vilified due to our support of Palestine, here’s what you need to consider when you make your choice.
Over the past few months, several artist friends who have been invited to participate in the upcoming documenta 16 have contacted us for advice, asking whether they should accept, refuse early on, or accept for now and withdraw at a later stage. As two artists who participated in documenta 15, we understand the dilemma. An invitation to documenta is not something one receives thoughtlessly. It is hard to turn down, and these days, it is also becoming hard to accept.
A few years ago, exhibiting at documenta was considered a lifetime achievement. But after the multi-faceted attacks on Palestinian artists and works of pro-Palestinian art at documenta 15 — and the collapse of the German state’s moral standing through its support for the genocide in Palestine and considering Israel its Staatsräson (“reason of state”) — this assumption has been shattered. There is no meaningful distance between the German state and its art institutions: Almost every museum, Kunsthalle, and festival, documenta included, is funded by the federal, regional, or municipal government, and thus steered by the conditions those funders set. As such, artists have to seriously ask themselves whether participating in documenta 16 will negatively affect one's career and well-being.
Our friends ask us for advice because of what the two of us, among many others, went through during documenta 15. We were subjected to severe and vicious attacks by the German media, political activists, politicians, and the establishment, built on unfounded, fabricated, and destructive accusations of antisemitism, which eventually led to attacks and vandalism of our exhibition venues, alongside those of other artists. This experience left scars on our lives and careers, making it hard to apply for jobs, funding, or exhibition opportunities. The stress and burnout we had to endure as a result of these attacks were enormous, and the energy it took came from our work and our lives — that toll can’t be overstated. This is why we decided to stay anonymous in this piece: to avoid any return to the stress and fear we had to deal with, which still haunts us even after nearly five years.
To those friends who are asking, and others who are wondering, we will not tell you whether to participate in documenta 16 or not. This is your own decision about what you wish to lend your voice to — personally, politically, creatively. But we can tell you what we wish we had known, and what you need to consider when you make your choice.
Since the beginning of the current genocide in Palestine, the German cultural scene has been in crisis. It has lost its credibility and shown how much it functions as the soft hand of state power. It has no independence from state politics and is unable to stand up against the position of the state due to the way arts and culture are funded in Germany. In 2019, the Bundestag passed a non-binding resolution calling for federal funding to be withheld from any organization or project that supports Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS). Non-binding as it was, it became a political tool to suppress any institutional support for the Palestinian cause. Another resolution in November 2024 tied public funding to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s controversial definition of antisemitism — which documenta officially adopted in early 2025. The rest of Germany’s major cultural institutions, except for a few independent ones, bent with little resistance. Like the others, documenta depends on state and federal funding; and like the others, it has no spine. German institutions are struggling to emerge from this crisis and regain their credibility without revising their positions or standing up to political pressure. At this point and under these conditions, documenta as an institution will likely benefit more from your participation than you will.

Repairs and renovations to the deteriorating building of the New York Studio School (NYSS) have uncovered long-lost murals by Robert E. Locher and Cecily Brown hidden behind plasterboard, The Art Newspaper reports. The school, comprising eight buildings at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, was originally founded in 1907 by artist and collector Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney and became the first site of the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1931.
Two murals by Locher—one in green, the other a trompe l’oeil of doric columns—were commissioned by Whitney for the school’s original carriage house, in what was Whitney’s dining room, and were intended to be viewed by candlelight. Workers discovered them where a bathroom and hallway were to be constructed.
Matthew Ritchie, who was named NYSS’s director last year, has no intention of moving the new bathroom. “Now it will be the most historic bathroom in New York,” he told The Art Newspaper.
Brown’s mural, which features an array of cavorting penises, was painted in the 1990s, when she was a student there. It will become part of the newly expanded gallery space on the main floor.
“Who doesn’t want a Cecily Brown mural?” Ritchie joked. “And then, who doesn’t want pornography in your brand-new public gallery? It’s the perfect combination.”
The school originally served as a drawing club, studio, and gallery from 1907 to 1929 and was populated by Ashcan artists, including Mabel Dwight, Robert Henri, and Edward Hopper, and early abstract artists, such as Stuart Davis, Beauford Delaney, Arshile Gorky, and Georgia O’Keeffe.
In 1964, artist and educator Mercedes Matter founded NYSS with the intent to “restore the conditions for working which make the study of art possible.” Since then, it has hosted a variety of faculty and students, including Rita Ackermann, Jackie Brookner, John Cage, Elaine De Kooning, Morton Feldman, Philip Guston, Jilaine Jones, and Lee Krasner.
