https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: In Alaska’s capital, food comes by water, air or, most often, community sharing
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Stephanie Gravalese
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Forty miles north-west of Alaska’s capital, the highway just ends.
At Glacier Highway’s most northern point, the pavement turns to gravel, the gravel widens into a turnaround and the tire tracks curve back the way they came. At the far end, the woods begin, a narrow hiking trail slipping toward the southern end of Berners Bay.
Locals call this stretch “out the road”. It is the only road that reaches Juneau, population 35,000, and that means virtually everything arriving in Alaska’s capital comes by water or air.
Meghan Stangeland meets vehicles coming off the Alaska Marine Highway ferry to offload boxes of cabbage. As south-east food systems manager at Ecotrust, a non-profit based in Portland, Oregon, working from California to Alaska, she runs its Salt and Soil program, part online farmers’ market, part food hub. In a state capital that has no weekly farmers’ market, the farmers and processors in its network get each order to Juneau however it works for them: often by barge, sometimes by seaplane and even by air.
One figure follows Alaska food coverage everywhere. The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) cites it. So do journalists, policy researchers and anyone making the case that Alaska is vulnerable to supply chain disruption. When the state created an office of food security in 2022, the governor’s announcement led with it, even though, as KTOO reported, no one has ever traced the number to a verifiable source. “Alaska imports 95% of the product that it purchases,” Stangeland says, repeating the often-used number.
“I always caveat that with: that is the product that we purchase. We share so much food, there’s so much subsistence. So it’s not 95% of the food that Alaskans are consuming. There’s so much food economy in the state of Alaska that is not economically transacted.”
That figure cannot measure how Juneau feeds itself, sharing and harvesting from the land. Alaskans took in roughly 46m pounds of wild food in 2014, the state’s most recent comprehensive estimate; in rural areas, that works out to about 275lbs per person per year.
Ricardo Worl recalls about the villages of south-east Alaska: if one person is going hungry, so are their relatives, because everyone shares. Worl, who is Tlingit and from Juneau, is the senior communications officer at Sealaska Heritage Institute, and he describes a regional economy that the import figure only partly captures. About 14 communities dot the region, reachable only by boat or plane. A village of a few hundred people supports only a handful of formal jobs, Worl said, and in the mixed economy that results, cash serves the subsistence harvest, not the other way around.
“Subsistence harvesting in the rural areas is not just culture,” he said. “It’s survival. When we harvest, even if it’s only a couple of fish, we’ll share the best parts, like the heads and the bellies, with grandparents or elders. It’s never just for ourselves.”
Inside Juneau, however, not everyone holds what Stangeland calls the privilege of a boat and a freezer, the space and equipment that processing that volume demands. Worl said that if there is an informal processing center in a community, “it’s going to be in some auntie’s kitchen”.
A family processing food here isn’t just stocking their own pantry for the winter. The food that moves through these networks is hunted, fished, gathered and shared. Growing it commercially in Juneau is a different problem.
Limited farming, abundant sharing
The drive to Joe Orsi’s property heads “out the road”, past the Auke Bay neighborhood north-west of downtown. His steep driveway curves up a hillside through a thick wall of evergreens, revealing how scarce flat agricultural space is in Juneau.
Orsi, a 67-year-old retired research fishery biologist for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, is one of the few farmers supplying Juneau residents and restaurants with locally grown produce. He cultivates a third of an acre with terraced garden beds, endless rows of rhubarb and a large hoop house up the slope behind his home.
It’s a challenging environment for farming. Finding flat, non-marshy land is rare here, and the naturally acidic soil requires improvement. At the height of summer, south-east Alaska gets up to 18 hours of daylight, but the growing season runs only from May through September. Orsi has spent years working out what garlic can actually do in this specific environment. Over time, he tried roughly 45 varieties, paying close attention to what could withstand these soil conditions and that short window.
On paper, the farm provides a modest living, but that is not the point for him. “I may make $20,000 a year. That’s it, not much for all the work I do,” he said. “But I just feel blessed to be able to work the land.”
Some of Orsi’s harvest ends up at Juneau Greens, a hydroponic operation and retail storefront run by John Krapek. Krapek started the business in 2017 with 18 grow beds. Today, he operates 100 in his own retail space. Competing with cheap California produce proved impossible, and wholesale demand from restaurants swung week to week. “When you’re at our scale, we really have to sell every piece of lettuce to make it work,” Krapek said.
His workaround was a weekly subscription model, now 425 residents strong, which stabilized demand enough to open a storefront in 2024. He stocks produce from Orsi and other local vendors alongside his own greens. Krapek said scaling up was never the goal. “It’s really nice to actually know your customer, know the chefs who we deal with,” he said. When subscribers picked up orders at a separate location, the communication was mostly over email. The storefront changed that, he said: “That’s what has been so cool is, like, actually getting to work for this.”
Operations like Krapek’s and Orsi’s can’t feed a community on their own. Stangeland has spent years watching what works in this unique space: a deeply embedded culture of mutual provisioning.
Asked whether that sharing had shifted with rising grocery prices, Stangeland said that’s just always been the way of life: “It’s always been the water that south-east Alaskans have swam in.” She pointed to practices that predate any marketplace, like the first harvest going to elders. “There’s still so much of that that happens in our communities,” she said. “It’s the way it’s always been and continues to be.”
For Worl, the harvest is never individual. “We’re members of a clan, we’re members of a specific community, extended families,” he said. “It’s not going to be: ‘OK, I’m going to process all of this jam, but I’m going to put it on the shelf. Maybe I’ll give some away at Christmas.’ We’re always thinking: ‘Oh boy, there’s a ku.éex [ceremony],’ there’s a payoff party coming, and we better set a case aside, or two aside, to share with them, so there’s that community, the sharing, the responsibility beyond yourself.”
Back at Salt and Soil, Stangeland runs into a different structural gap: federal nutrition programs are designed for farmers selling their own product or stores that buy and resell. A consignment marketplace like Salt and Soil fits neither definition. In 2019, the non-profit created its own program, Healthy Foods = Healthy Families. “We don’t have to jump through the bureaucratic hoops,” Stangeland said. “It’s a much more streamlined initiative to get local food to those who wouldn’t otherwise be able to access or afford it.”
In Sealaska Heritage Institute’s traditional foods and medicine kitchen, students and employees had spent the past few days vacuum-sealing halibut. The Indigenous Science Building, which houses the kitchen, has been open for less than two years, said Anya Nelson, the institute’s Indigenous science and higher education director. Stainless steel counters line one side of the room; a commercial kitchen built for volume processing lines the other. Along the far wall is a hydroponic grow setup.
For Nelson, the space recognizes the deep methodology of traditional survival. The classes also teach the western science behind those methods, the work of generations who “observed and [were] able to create systems and methods that beautifully held salmon and preserved it for months without things like refrigeration”, she said. “There’s so much science in that.”
Joel Bos runs a school garden program through Discovery Southeast that produces 1,300lbs of food a year across two elementary schools. Students follow the harvest through the whole season, from rolling out carrot seed tape in March to cooking soup in October. “A shareable harvest is what creates the buy-in,” Bos said. “They take pride and ownership.”
Ecotrust also operates Moby, a mobile greenhouse that travels between communities on the Alaska Marine Highway. It returned to Juneau this fall at the Dzantik’i Héeni campus for school programming. Almost every community Moby has visited, Stangeland said, now has a permanent greenhouse or high tunnel of its own.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Musk says Tesla to wind down polarising Cybertruck production as sales lag
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Musk says Tesla to wind down polarising Cybertruck production as sales lag
Released in 2023, the truck has become a symbol to some of opposition to Musk amid foray into US politics.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said the company will wind down production of Cybertrucks at its Texas facility amid poor sales.
Trillionaire Musk made the announcement in a post on X on Friday, saying the wind-down would enable the company to increase its production of the new Cybercab model, launched as part of a foray into the so-called robo-taxi industry.
“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk wrote.
Announced in 2019, the Cybertruck’s stark design, featuring an angular stainless steel exterior, proved immediately polarising.
At an unveiling ceremony that year, Musk sought to prove its windows were shatterproof. But the exhibition backfired, with metal balls launched at the car cracking two of the windows.
The vehicle quickly became a symbol of opposition to Musk as he became increasingly involved in United States politics, including briefly leading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) panel tasked by the administration of US President Donald Trump with cleaving federal government agencies.
Musk most recently spent nearly half a billion dollars in the US midterm election campaign in support of Republican candidates, including more than $200 million in support of the failed Senate candidacy of Republican Ken Paxton in Texas. Beyond Tesla, Musk’s SpaceX company is also based in Texas.
But the spending did little to prevent a blue wave in US politics, which saw Democrats take commanding control of the US House of Representatives and Senate. The shift could spell investigations into Musk’s work with the federal government.
Musk had initially predicted the Cybertrucks, which became available to consumers at the end of 2023, would sell at a rate of about 250,000 a year.
The model fell far below that target. In 2024, about 38,965 units were sold. That figure declined by nearly half in 2025, with 20,237 sold.
In his announcement on Friday, Musk did not say whether Cybertruck manufacturing would shift to another factory. The plant in Texas is the only known production site.
In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made”, hailing the “end of an era”.

https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.title: Tate Britain’s ’90s Show Is All Scene, No Substance
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.author: Emily Watlington
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.text:
There is a source of tension raging across the art world lately: the conflict between accessibility and anti-intellectualism, as museums face the challenge of making art feel less elitist, less cold, and less boring without dumbing down to the point of meaninglessness. Tate Britain’s latest exhibition, “The 90s: Art and Fashion,” falls hard on the side of meaningless anti-intellectualism.
The exhibition is curated by Edward Enninful, who was most recently editor-in-chief of British Vogue but, more importantly for this exhibition, became the fashion director of the magazine i-D at the age of 18 in 1990 and led it through the turbulent, dynamic decade that is the subject of his show. Tate has never worked with a celebrity curator in this way before, and Enninful’s presence is strangely felt throughout the exhibition. A wedding gift he received from Steve McQueen—a photograph of McQueen’s hands—hangs on a wall. Many, many i-D spreads are in cases throughout the galleries, some including photographs of Enninful. There is a striking focus on Black masculinity, which is the prism through which Enninful experienced the ’90s. Yet his subjectivity is not clearly articulated, leaving one to wonder: Is it his voice we are sensing through the wall texts and object labels, or is it a more neutral “museum” voice? Is Enninful the subject of the exhibition, via his presence in the lives of the artists and models represented here, or is he the curator?
Being a museum curator is a job that does, actually, require expertise. (I speak with the bias of being one myself). It is a powerful, often invisible role that shapes perceptions of truth and cultural meaning. The trend toward treating it as a celebrity hobby or a passion project is symptomatic of the current wider social phobia of experts and intellectuals. Throughout this exhibition, Enninful contradicts himself: The decade of the ’90s in Britain was about “critiquing commercialism,” but it was also about groundbreaking ad campaigns. It was about “challenging beauty standards,” but also “democratizing beauty.” No point of distinction between fine art and visual culture is identified in Enninful’s show, so fashion, commercial and personal photography, and fine art share space. That could be interesting—it could be a critical choice—but instead it feels like an oversight.
The art and visual culture in this show generally does something. It either embraces or rejects commercialism. It tells a new, sometimes important, story of race, class, or gender in Britain. It highlights what one wall text ambiguously describes as “importance of intimacy in turbulent times.” But is it good? Not especially. Enninful seems to have gone out of his way to choose bad works. Helen Chadwick, a largely good artist, is represented by two works that rank among her weakest. A cast of a hot water bottle that represents a torso by Rachel Whiteread, a really good artist, somehow manages to be the best thing in the show (along with Chris Ofili’s 1998 painting No Woman, No Cry). Small, quotidian, and tactile, it evokes absence and presence at once, the bitter fleetingness of modern life.
But most of the stuff in these galleries? The endless snapshots of parties, wallpaper covered in butts, the many photographs of Kate Moss, videos of fashion shows, enlarged ad campaign stills—very little of it is good. It conveys a certain nostalgia for a heady era, and it makes a strong case for Enninful’s relevance to it. He knew everyone who is anyone, it seems. But that doesn’t make what he chose to show good art, or even art at all. It’s odd, because the ’90s were famously good years for British art: the time of the YBAs and a shifting and condensing sense of British identity, of optimism and progress. The decade fueled the founding of Tate Modern and Frieze London in the early 2000s, and has led to London’s current position as a nexus of international artists and remarkable historic and contemporary art spaces. You would not know that from this exhibition.
Art museums have to fight for relevance in our new attention economy, just like everything else. We are constantly asked to defend them, to make a case for their purpose. With this exhibition, Tate situates the museum alongside the celebrity economy of influence. Supposedly celebrating the last “analog” decade, it instead feels like an act of surrender to the perceived glibness of the digital age. Old-fashioned as it may seem, I don’t think we should equate art with “content.” There is always an appetite for great art, and there is also always an appetite to consider whether, and why, art is great or not. To join the tide of anti-intellectualism that refuses to take this seriously or rise to the challenge of doing so, as Tate has done with this exhibition, is a grave shame.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Sonhar: a luta continua
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Selvino Heck
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
Os próximos anos não serão fáceis, ninguém se iluda, mesmo com a vitória brilhante de Lula. Há uma crise civilizatória, que não se resolve facilmente, nem rapidamente. Cada dia há acontecimentos novos não previstos. No Brasil, em toda sua história, a democracia nunca esteve consolidada, haja vista o período de escravidão, as diversas ditaduras, inclusive militares, e o recente impeachment, com golpe, da presidenta Dilma Rousseff, com todas as suas trágicas consequências.
É preciso, portanto, pensar ações, propostas e futuro de curto prazo. Mas tudo será possível ser feito e consolidado no médio e longo prazos, nos próximos cinco, dez, quinze anos ou mais.
O primeiro e principal desafio no curto prazo: como incorporar/organizar as multidões que se envolveram no processo eleitoral, no segundo turno, em especial as juventudes, as mulheres e o povo das periferias.
Em outros tempos, em idos tempos, nos anos 1970, em tempos de ditadura militar, o trabalho de base estava no centro de tudo. Nos anos 1980, com o surgimento e organização de movimentos populares nacionais, como o Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST) a partir de grandes ocupações, das grandes greves puxadas pelo movimento sindical e, na sequência, a fundação da Central Única dos Trabalhadores (CUT), a fundação do Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), um partido de esquerda com projeto estratégico de país e nação, a fundação de ONGs como o CAMP. O trabalho de base esteve sempre presente e no centro de tudo, acompanhado da criação dos Núcleos de Base do PT, como o Núcleo do PT da Lomba do Pinheiro, que ajudava a articular as diferentes lutas, fazia formação política nas vilas populares e os Núcleos de diferentes categorias profissionais, como metalúrgicos, bancários, professores, funcionários públicos, entre outros.
Assim, aconteceram, nos anos 1980, as Diretas Já, com milhões nas ruas, a preparação da Constituinte, a oitava Conferência Nacional de Saúde, em 1986, pela primeira vez com a participação da sociedade civil, quando se pensou, foi proposto e se construiu o Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS), hoje referência no mundo inteiro.
Garantir e fortalecer a democracia é, pois, fundamental nos próximos anos. Ainda mais depois do resultado das eleições americanas, onde, de alguma forma, à luz inclusive do resultado eleitoral brasileiro, o povo estadunidense resolveu dar um recado para o mundo.
São, entre outros, os enormes desafios durante o quarto governo Lula. E tudo isso em tempos de Inteligência Artificial (IA), cada dia mais presente, e que torna tudo mais fácil, ou não.
Sonhar nestes tempos é plenamente possível, além de urgente e necessário. A utopia está viva, freireanamente.
Vale lembrar, e reler, um poema que escrevi em 1976, em plena ditadura militar, publicado no livro de poesias Em Mãos do Grupo Veredas (EM MÃOS, Lume Editora, 1976):
Abraço universal
Abraço o homem,
suas dores, armas,
cansaços e feridas.
Abraço o mundo
e todas as coisas,
sua esperança e abandono,
sua essência e conteúdo.
Abraço o povo caminhante e peregrino,
suas chagas e alegrias,
seus mapas e inimigos.
Abraço a vida,
suas feras e medidas.
Abraço tudo,
cada coisa e sua bagagem,
cada mulher, cada homem
e sua liberdade.
*Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: New bomb threats target European broadcasters, air traffic
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
New bomb threats target European broadcasters, air traffic
A string of hoax alerts causing flight diversions across Europe this week have broadened to include newsrooms.
A new series of bomb threats caused more flight diversions across Europe on Friday, while also expanding to target a number of media organisations.
British broadcaster Sky said it was one of a number of newsrooms that received a bomb threat. “We have carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities,” a spokesperson said.
Bulgaria’s Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE received emailed bomb threats from a purported “Mikhail Andropov”, headlined “Message to the West”, portraying the threats as a prelude to more disruptions across Europe.
RTE briefly evacuated staff, including radio and television presenters, in Dublin after an email was received on Friday morning. RTE Radio One presenter David McCullagh later told listeners that the threat warned that a bomb would explode within 45 minutes.
The Irish government said hoax bomb claims were also sent to Virgin Media, Newstalk radio and The Irish Independent newspaper and that it was unclear who was behind them.
“However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption,” it said in a statement.
The incidents come a day after hoax bomb threats disrupted more than two dozen flights across Europe on Thursday, and days after other aircraft and a cruise ship received bomb alerts.
‘Hoax threats’ increasing
On Friday, jets escorted airliners flying from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Bucharest and Cyprus through Hungarian airspace due to bomb threats, Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said.
He also said NATO had ordered an air patrol near the Hungarian-Romanian border, the first report that the Western defence alliance had become involved.
Danish police said threats were directed at traffic at Copenhagen airport but that there appeared to be no danger to passengers. The airport said it was “operating normally”.
Czech police registered bomb threats to nine flights departing from or arriving in Prague. An airport spokesperson said no flights had been cancelled as a result.
France said four new bomb threats were made to aircraft flying over French territory, and that all landed safely.
A Ryanair flight from Rome landed as scheduled in Lisbon, CNN Portugal reported.
About half a dozen flights were disrupted on Tuesday and more than two dozen on Thursday, some of them making unplanned landings or being escorted to their destinations by fighter jets.
Al Jazeera’s Frances Read, reporting from London on Friday, said that while the threats have not been credible so far, disruptions appear to be widening.
“The number of hoax threats this week is making governments sit up and take notice about where this might be coming from and also think of solutions for how to deal with it,” she said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: A coragem de Flávio Bolsonaro cabe na bagagem de mão
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Carlos Castelo
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
Casteladas, a coluna de aforismos e pensamentos, traz o gênero literário conhecido por ser o oposto do calhamaço. A frase curta – ou o fragmento – de alegria instantânea, a serviço do humor.
“Penso, logo existo”, disse Descartes. Trump preferiu: “Penso, logo não estou existindo.”
A História se repete porque a primeira vez já deu votos.
Não há poesia depois de Trump.
Eu acreditava conhecer meus amigos. Conhecia apenas os assuntos que evitávamos à mesa.
Não gosto da ideia de vida após a morte. Já tenho dificuldades suficientes com a vida antes dela.
Para o padre Kelmon, todos são iguais perante Deus. Depois, Deus pergunta em quem votaram.
Eu aceito a política. Mas não sei se ela aceita minha honestidade.
Ditadura é a democracia depois de passar pelo jurídico.
Muitos acreditam que Trump é um enviado de Deus. Faz sentido: da última vez que Ele mandou alguma coisa, foi o dilúvio.
Liderar do exterior é fácil: difícil é o líder voltar ao seu país para ver se alguém seguiu.
A direita procurava um mito e encontrou um passageiro.
A coragem de Flávio Bolsonaro cabe na bagagem de mão.
Por trás de todo autoritário, há sempre um fedelho que não sabe amarrar os sapatos.
Quando a polarização perde o nexo, o absurdo vira cômico e não se julga mais a proposta: consome-se o delírio.
A estupidez nunca anda sozinha. Sempre leva uma certeza junto.
*Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Claims of a Ukrainian ‘torture chamber’ went viral. What really happened?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Claims of a Ukrainian ‘torture chamber’ went viral. What really happened?
A woman who claimed that men were being violently assaulted in a house for evading the draft has been arrested.
Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka, Ukraine – A woman wearing a crisp new paramedic’s uniform and impeccable makeup kneels on the ground in front of several police officers guarding the rusty gates of a two-storey house.
She begs, yells and curses, claiming that forcibly conscripted men are being held in the building in the tranquil suburb of Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka, outside the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv.
One of the men has already died, claims the woman, who was later identified as Valentyna Moloda, a 49-year-old nurse who once worked at a plastic surgery clinic and has never been authorised to practise as a paramedic.
The ambulance she arrived in carries the logos of a private medical company that reportedly stopped operating in 2023. A woman from Moloda’s “ambulance team” livestreams the scene as a crowd swells, joining in her chants demanding access to what she calls a “torture chamber.”
“I’m on my knees, let me get to them,” Moloda screams, claiming that “armed people” allegedly “torture” 40 people inside who had evaded the draft.
Her claims resonate with people at the impromptu rally, in a country where conscription officers have become reviled public servants due to their sometimes brutal tactics.
Protesters lob eggs at police and throw tomatoes at the house. The crowd grows to 500 people, with many clashing with officers until midnight.
Clashes and counterclaims
Officials say that Moloda’s “rescue mission” on Monday afternoon – one of the most polarising scandals in Ukraine – was fake and required preparation.
But it had already gone viral online, with tens of thousands of people around the world lamenting Ukraine’s handling of conscription.
Glenn Diesen, a pro-Kremlin political analyst from Norway, shared a video and a photo on X of a teenager who fell while trying to film the house from the fence, claiming the boy was a victim of “great outrage and riots in Ukraine against the henchmen of [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy and NATO.” His post has been widely shared.
Three days before Monday’s incident, Moloda and her driver “conducted a reconnaissance” of the house, Ukraine’s Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov said on Tuesday.
A former top military intelligence officer and one of Ukraine’s most popular and trusted public figures, Budanov interacted with Moloda at the time of the standoff.
Several young men clashed with police and tried to kick the doors of the house open until officers let Moloda and her team inside.
She came back minutes later to proclaim that she had just seen a man on the brink of death, another with a broken spine and one who was so badly beaten he was unable to talk.
“There’s blood on the mattresses,” she yelled, showing someone photos of the alleged victims on her phone, while the scene was livestreamed. “They [urinate] in a bottle.”
But careful observers would have noticed the videos were tagged as having been shot on Saturday. The crowd, however, kept growing, damaging police cars and clashing with officers.
Budanov arrived about six hours after Moloda started her livestream, and said that the besieged house on Solnichna Street had been used by the Azov Brigade, a former volunteer militia group of far-right nationalists and football fans that helped repel pro-Russian separatists in southeastern Ukraine in 2014.
Azov said apprehended deserters were kept in the house, while Azov’s commander Denys Prokopenko called the scandal a “sabotage behind the lines that discredits Ukrainian servicemen and creates a narrative that benefits Russia”.
The group has been accused of neo-Nazi sympathies and torturing war prisoners. The United States Department of State banned it from using US-supplied weaponry between 2014 and 2024, but it grew into a military force and became part of Ukraine’s National Guard. Its founder, Andriy Biletsky, led this year’s “Operation Vivaldi” to push Russian forces out of several strategic areas in eastern Ukraine.
After Budanov’s arrival, four men were allowed to walk out of the house into a bus, including the one Moloda claimed could not move because of a broken spine. The angry crowd did not allow the bus to leave.
‘Unfortunately, people believed that woman’
Al Jazeera visited Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka and talked to more than a dozen residents, who insisted on full or partial anonymity because Monday’s scandal has become so politicised.
“Both sides are wrong,” an elderly man who only gave his first name, Serhiy, told Al Jazeera, standing next to his wife outside a supermarket.
“Azov shouldn’t have kept their people there, and the fake doctor shouldn’t have started all this noise,” he said.
His wife signalled him to stop talking and ushered him away.
Locals laughed off comparisons some have made between Monday’s incident and the massive 2013-2014 protests on Maidan Square in central Kyiv that toppled pro-Russian Ukrainian President Viktor Yanykovych.
“This definitely wasn’t a mini-Maidan,” 17-year-old Mykola told Al Jazeera, a short distance from the house. “Unfortunately, people believed that woman and flocked here.”
Most of the locals called the incident a “provocation”.
Only one man in his 30s said that Moloda “tried to help” and should not have been apprehended on Tuesday.
Moloda was arrested and is being held in custody for 60 days without bail.
Prosecutors said they found evidence proving that she had at least once carried out “rescue services” as a fake paramedic for 107,000 hryvnia ($2,355).
The relatives of a deserter, Andriy Kuleshov, allegedly hired Moloda for about $7,000 to get him out of the Azov house, Pavlo Kurchenko, a senior Azov officer, told the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda.
Kuleshov is listed in Myrotvorets – Ukrainian for “peacemaker” – a controversial online database of alleged anti-Ukrainian figures, for crossing into separatist-controlled areas in southeastern Ukraine multiple times in 2015-2021, where his brother lives.
“[Moloda] wanted to create a political scandal,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “She is also suspected of ties to Russian intelligence. So far, there’s no confirmation of that, but Russia has used this scandal in its interests.”
It did – with the help of pro-Russia Ukrainians.
“People are being kidnapped and tortured. Some are sold to military units, others – to their relatives. The weaker ones simply die of torture and confinement conditions,” Artyom Dmitruk, a former Ukrainian lawmaker with a pro-Russian party who fled for Italy in 2024, said in televised remarks.
The scandal “answers the question about why Russia needs the special military operation, to uproot the resurgent neo-Nazism in Ukraine,” said Mikhail Sheremev, a “lawmaker” in Russia-annexed Crimea.
Violence and corruption
Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion prompted a wave of volunteers to join Ukraine’s military, with tens of thousands enlisting across the country, often travelling to other regions because conscription offices near their homes were overwhelmed.
But after heavy losses and reports of poor planning, corruption and the cruelty of some officers, the number of volunteers fell dramatically.
Since 2023, conscription officers have been combing public places in search of people trying to avoid the draft. They have frequently forced them into their vans, often resorting to intimidation, beatings and torture, as Al Jazeera has reported, along with witnesses and human rights groups.
The officers claim there is no other way to mobilise the tens of thousands of men needed on the frontline to repel Russian forces.
The violence has led to corrupt practices.
As of August this year, 76 conscription officers had been arrested for accepting bribes of up to tens of thousands of dollars, stashing huge sums, and buying expensive properties in Ukraine and abroad.
Some draft-dodgers have secured fake exemptions from medical doctors, while others fled to neighbouring countries, either through bribes or by crossing the border without documentation.
Some forcibly drafted men secured the services of “fake ambulances”, according to prosecutors and police.
In 2025, border guards in the southwestern region of Zakarpattia detained a fake ambulance crew of three men who tried to take a person evading the draft to Romania for $10,000.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: MPT-PR pede indenização de R$ 1 milhão de deputada da extrema direita por assédio eleitoral
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Murilo Bernardon
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Nesta sexta-feira (6), o Ministério Público do Trabalho no Paraná (MPT-PR) protocolou na Justiça uma ação para que a deputada estadual eleita Jessicão (PL) tire do ar uma publicação que incitava demissões de “petistas”. A Ação Civil Pública (ACP) também pede o pagamento de indenização de R$ 1 milhão por danos morais coletivos.
Em 25 de outubro, após a vitória do presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) no segundo turno, Jessicão fez uma publicação na rede social X pedindo que patrões demitam trabalhadores que votaram à esquerda. O MPT-PR havia aberto investigação contra a deputada. O órgão declarou, nesta sexta-feira, que recebeu mais de 100 denúncias relacionadas à postagem.
Nessa quarta-feira (4), o MPT-PR contabilizou o recebimento de 465 denúncias de assédio eleitoral no Paraná. Houve um aumento de 227% de denúncias após o segundo turno das eleições.
A parlamentar escreveu mensagens como “demita o mal”. Na publicação, defendeu que os empregadores rompessem contratos com trabalhadores “petistas” e incentivassem o boicote a prestadores de serviço e estabelecimentos que declararam apoio a Lula. A mensagem tem 1 milhão de visualizações e faz coro com uma série de ameaças a trabalhadores feitas por figuras da extrema direita, como o também deputado eleito no Paraná, Guilherme Kilter (Novo).
Na ação, o Ministério Público alegou que a prática violou “direitos fundamentais assegurados a todo trabalhador” e “a dignidade da pessoa humana”, protegidos pela Constituição Federal. O MPT-PR também exigiu que a indenização seja direcionada a fundos ou programas voltados à defesa dos direitos trabalhistas.
Uma Ação Civil Pública é um instrumento jurídico usado para proteger direitos coletivos, e não apenas o interesse de uma única pessoa. Não há um prazo fixo para a Justiça aceitar ou analisar a petição inicial de uma ACP.
Em nota, Jessicão havia negado o incentivo à discriminação política e disse defender a liberdade de expressão. Como vereadora de Londrina (PR), ganhou visibilidade e engajamento nas redes ao propor e aprovar o projeto de lei que proibia o uso de linguagem neutra em escolas e concursos públicos do município — medida que posteriormente foi declarada inconstitucional pela Justiça. Também foi uma das autoras do projeto de lei municipal que proibiu a exigência do comprovante de vacinação contra a covid-19, em 2022.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: In jailing Joshua Wong, China is telling the world they'd crush every hope for democracy on its soil | Nathan Law
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nathan Law
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Two years ago, I wrote in this newspaper about the lengthy imprisonment of my friend Joshua Wong, who I spent years campaigning alongside for the advancement of Hong Kong’s democracy. He was given an unjust sentence meant to keep him behind bars until January 2027. He was supposed to be released in a few months, when I hoped he would finally be able to reunite with his friends and family and embark on a new chapter.
But this hope was misplaced. The end of the tunnel isn’t next year; it’s late 2036. By then, he will be 40. On Thursday, Joshua was sentenced to another 10 years under Hong Kong’s national security law for colluding with foreign forces. He is the only political prisoner who’s been convicted twice under the national security law. The judge described Joshua and me as “two ringleaders or masterminds” urging foreign powers to impose sanctions and other hostile actions against the Chinese and Hong Kong governments. The judgment cited previous international advocacy work, media interviews, social media posts and the political activities of Demosistō, the youth-led democratic party we founded.
Much of the cited evidence predates the implementation of the national security law, even though the court insisted it was not being applied retrospectively. Before 2020, meeting with foreign parliamentarians, engaging with and speaking to international institutions, and advocating for measures against human rights abuses were ordinary campaign strategies. These were peaceful means through which we tried to hold those in power accountable. The campaigns raised the profile of Hong Kong’s protests and garnered substantial support; they were so effective that Beijing had to impose the national security law to curb them and impose extensive legal punishments.
There is a stark lack of evidence about Joshua’s actions. Prosecutors said that he conspired with campaigners including myself to ask foreign bodies to impose sanctions on China – relying on his sharing of Facebook posts written by me. But these posts did not directly call for sanctions – they made other appeals, including for digital forensic companies to terminate their cooperation with the Hong Kong police. There’s no evidence that Wong himself advocated for imposing any form of sanctions, or that he had any direct link to advocacy work outside Hong Kong. The court also accepted that no organisation or funding supported his activities after the law came into force.
Still, as flimsy as the evidence is, it’s enough to secure him a decade in jail. The crux of the trial is not legal; it’s political. It is clear that Beijing exercises sweeping control over Hong Kong’s legal and political systems. This can be seen in the tightening of the electoral system by introducing an Iranian-style vetting mechanism, in the jailing of peaceful political dissidents and the emphasis placed on the necessity of “patriots ruling Hong Kong”.
When Chinese leaders categorise Jimmy Lai, Benny Tai and Joshua Wong as the “masterminds” behind the 2019 pro-democracy protests, the legal system must deliver sentences that reflect the trio’s “importance”. That’s why Lai and Tai have been sentenced to 20 years and 10 years respectively, and rank among the most persecuted pro-democracy figures in the region. There are now close to 2,000 political prisoners in Hong Kong.
It’s devastating that Joshua has been behind bars for such a large portion of his adult life. I couldn’t even imagine skipping 16 years before I reached my 40s – during which time many people meet their partner, get married, raise a family and settle into a career. Joshua has been deprived of living fully because of his advocacy for important democratic values. The sentence signals to the world that China is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.
As geopolitical competition intensifies and populism rises, human rights are increasingly treated as an inconvenience to diplomatic and economic interests. Governments speak of stability and pragmatic engagement, while political prisoners slowly disappear from international public attention. The Chinese regime has little reason to change its approach if the repression of Hong Kong carries no meaningful consequences, either to trade or its global standing.
Given that Hong Kong was a British colony until as recently as 1997, the UK, in particular, should not regard the territory as merely another foreign policy issue. The Sino-British joint declaration was intended to safeguard the city’s rights and freedoms. The British government should therefore make the release of Joshua, Jimmy Lai and other political prisoners a priority when dealing with Beijing, rather than responding to each new sentence with another ineffective statement of concern.
For months, I had imagined the day Joshua would finally be free. Now that hope has been pushed away for another decade. We must not forget him, and must take urgent action to demand his immediate release.
- Nathan Law is a pro-democracy activist and former legislator from Hong Kong. He is a political refugee in the UK

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Veto or deals: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Veto or deals: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats?
Trump has three options to affect legislation, say analysts: veto legislation, enforce executive orders or make deals.
As the United States midterm election results landed late on Tuesday night, United States President Donald Trump took a phone call from the news outlet Politico.
A wave for the Democratic Party had sunk Trump’s Republican Party. For the first time in his two stints as president, Trump’s Republican Party no longer controlled either chamber of Congress.
But in the phone interview, Trump put on a brave face — and offered an olive branch: He said that he would be willing to work with Democrats.
“They’ve already called, and they want to work with me. I have the right to veto everything, but I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years just vetoing everything,” he said.
While a handful of seats remain to be counted, the Democrats have won comfortable majorities in both the House of Representatives, where they have secured at least 253 seats out of 435, and in the Senate, where they have won at least 54 out of 100.
Trump has since posted a picture on his Truth Social account using the Make America Great Again red baseball hat to read “VETO”. Despite the Democrats’ success, as president, Trump holds broad executive authority, with Article 1, Section 7 of the US Constitution stipulating that the president has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress through a veto.
Congress can override the veto, but would need to have a two-thirds majority, something that the Democrats do not have in either chamber.
But Trump’s comments to Politico underscore an alternate possibility — the president may pick and choose when to veto, and when to work with Democrats.
Bipartisan negotiations
As it stands, Trump has three options: veto legislation, enforce executive orders or make deals.
Since Trump was inaugurated in January 2025, he has passed 292 executive orders: 67 this year and 225 last year, according to the Federal Register.
But now, according to Andrew Proctor, a lecturer in US politics at University College London, Trump has even less leverage than before with Congress.
“I think the biggest thing is we’re probably going to see a decent amount of gridlock. The Democrats are going to try to pass policies, but he’s got the power to veto them, and Democrats don’t have enough seats in either chamber to overcome any vetoes that he has,” Proctor said.
“So that raises questions about, will he try to work with the Democrats at all on passing legislation? I think recent history says that’s unlikely.”
Still, some Democrats have said that they would work with the president to advance programmes central to their campaign promises.
Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, has already said he could work with Trump — even though the US president had used racist and Islamophobic rhetoric to target El-Sayed during the campaign.
El-Sayed told MSNOW on Thursday that if Trump was interested in “getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets and passing Medicare for All, that’s what I ran to do, and I’m looking forward to working with anyone who is willing to do that”.
“He is the president of the United States,” he said. “I’m going to be one United States senator, and if he’s interested in working on issues that I want to work on – getting more people healthcare, ending the Medicare cuts, ending the stupid war, stopping these stupid tariffs with Canada – then let’s talk about doing that and go and deliver for the public.”
Progressive Senator Bernie Sanders has also said, in recent interviews, that he would not rule out Trump signing onto a Medicare for All bill if Democrats pass it in both chambers of Congress. He described Trump as a “politician” who was not “too ideological”.
Proctor argued that Trump could indeed make a deal with the Democrats based on how good it could make him look, but that getting Medicare for All passed in the next two years appeared unlikely.
“I do think that a place where common ground could emerge on healthcare is rolling back, specifically the sort of subsidies that were cut” under Trump’s earlier legislation, he said. “So that would make healthcare more affordable for millions of Americans.”
Proctor pointed out that some Republicans in 2025 had said they were willing to negotiate with Democrats on healthcare reforms.
“That didn’t end up happening, but I could imagine that might be a place for healthcare-specific policy where we could see something emerge,” he said. “I don’t think that a broader healthcare debate on passing Medicare for All, though, is really in the cards.”
Veto or filibuster
Though Trump has said he would be willing to use veto, he has historically not been among the most avid proponents of the practice.
He has so far used the veto twice in this term, and used it 10 times during his first term. Joe Biden used it 12 times in his single term, while Barack Obama used the veto a dozen times over two terms.
Overall, the presidential use of the veto has declined with time: Bill Clinton vetoed legislation 37 times between 1993 and 2001. His predecessor, George HW Bush, used it 44 times in his single term — almost once a month. Ronald Reagan used it 78 times over his two terms.
But Proctor said that Republicans also have a different tool to try and block legislation. That is the filibuster, a tactic that delays a vote on a specific piece of legislation by using an extended debate, which would impact the Democrats’ ability to get something passed.
“This is what they did to [former President Barack] Obama,” Proctor told Al Jazeera. “Senate Republicans will probably try to do the same thing, and it also means that we don’t even get to the point of Trump having the power to veto because the legislation never reaches him in the first place.”
Impeachment
Since the Democrats swept the midterms on Tuesday, calls for investigations against the administration have already emerged.
In his first term, Trump was impeached twice — first for the abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, and the second time for “inciting” the US Capitol riots.
On Tuesday night, US Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee, wrote on X: “LAWYER UP.” Senator Ron Wyden, who is expected to lead the Senate Finance Committee, wrote in a post on X: “Subpoenas.”
However, the Trump administration has already denied any wrongdoing.
“If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Wednesday.
Reports also suggest that impeachment proceedings against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth might be imminent, over the Iran war that Trump and other Republicans have blamed for the party’s losses.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Flim 2026: moeda social de Maricá (RJ) movimenta Festa Literária com soluções digitais
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Banco Mumbuca participa da Festa Literária Internacional de Maricá (Flim 2026) com um estande dedicado à apresentação de serviços e soluções digitais. Os visitantes podem utilizar a moeda social do município, Mumbuca, para realizar compras na feira por meio do Flim Card ou do aplicativo Mumbuca Eventos.
Entre as funcionalidades está o aplicativo que permite transformar o celular em maquininha para receber pagamentos (Mumbuca Pay) e uma nova plataforma de delivery (Mumbuca Food), lançada oficialmente em 27 de outubro.
A programação da 11ª Flim acontece na Orla do Parque Nanci até domingo (8). Estudantes e profissionais da educação de Maricá têm um crédito de R$ 300 para compra de livros durante o evento.
Quem já possui o Flim Card pode utilizar o saldo disponível e fazer novas recargas sempre que necessário. Para quem ainda não tem o cartão, há duas opções: baixar gratuitamente o aplicativo Mumbuca Eventos, disponível para Android e iOS, realizar o cadastro e adicionar créditos via Pix; ou adquirir o cartão físico diretamente na feira, pelo valor de R$ 15.
:: Quer receber notícias do Brasil de Fato RJ no seu WhatsApp? ::
“Participar da FLIM é uma oportunidade de aproximar o Banco Mumbuca da população, apresentar nossos serviços e fortalecer iniciativas que valorizam a cultura e movimentam a economia de Maricá”, destaca Manuela Mello, presidente do Banco Mumbuca.
Com apoio da Companhia de Cultura e Turismo de Maricá (Maré), o Banco Mumbuca também patrocina as premiações dos concursos de dança K-pop e do desfile de Cosplay, integrantes da programação cultural da Flim.
Lançamentos
Durante o evento, a equipe do Banco Mumbuca esclarece dúvidas sobre as funcionalidades da moeda social e o lançamento da plataforma de delivery Mumbuca Food. O estande funciona durante todo o horário da Flim e conta ainda com um espaço interativo, com brincadeiras, atividades e distribuição de brindes.
Um destaque da participação é a divulgação do Mumbuca Food. A plataforma conecta consumidores a restaurantes, lanchonetes, mercados, padarias e outros estabelecimentos de Maricá, permitindo pagamentos com a moeda social Mumbuca ou via Pix.
A ferramenta busca ampliar as oportunidades de venda para o comércio local e fortalecer a economia do município, incluindo a valorização dos profissionais de entrega. Durante a Flim, os visitantes podem conhecer o funcionamento do aplicativo e receber orientações sobre sua utilização. Comerciantes e empreendedores interessados em cadastrar seus estabelecimentos também podem obter informações sobre a plataforma e o processo de adesão.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: What a Trump-Xi-Putin summit could mean – and what it wouldn’t
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
What a Trump-Xi-Putin summit could mean – and what it wouldn’t
A Trump-Xi-Putin meeting at APEC would be a coup for Moscow, analysts say, but Beijing appears lukewarm.
On the sidelines of this month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, an unprecedented three-way meeting between United States President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin could take place.
“China is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing on Wednesday.
“Work is under way to coordinate such a meeting,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday, adding: “We hope that it will be finalised in the coming days.”
Trump has said he is open to three-way talks focused on nuclear weapons. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it,” he told reporters last month.
The three leaders have met separately but have never held formal talks together.
So could the meeting, pencilled in for November 18-19, actually happen, and what would it mean for the rest of the world? Here’s what we know:
What would Russia get out of a three-way meeting with the US and China?
At the very least, a photo opportunity.
“It is a big event,” Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, who he said has described the meeting as a path towards a new Yalta – the 1945 conference where the leaders of the Soviet Union, the US and the United Kingdom shaped the post-war order in Europe.
That allows Moscow to “talk big”, Bratersky said, while putting Ukraine on the sidelines.
Simply being at the table would make Putin “first among equals”, he added, giving him a photo opportunity to show the world that he will be among those deciding the future of Europe’s security architecture after the war in Ukraine.
If the meeting produced results, he said, it would reflect China’s influence on Russia.
“We should take into account that we are dealing with a much weaker US leader after elections,” Bratersky said.
Trump remains in charge of foreign policy, he explained, but will have less leverage if Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress in this week’s midterm elections, start sending money to Kyiv.
“A meeting by itself will be a success,” he said. “Putin will be able to sell it at home”.
Whether anything comes of it should become clear within a month or so, Bratersky said, and the meeting could lead to another during the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December.
If nothing is produced before Christmas, he added, “it will be just a photo op.”
What does Trump want?
Optics and leverage.
Trump wants “a personal, high-drama encounter” that lets him claim he is “dealing with” the other two great powers on his own terms, Inderjeet Parmar, a professor of international politics at City St George’s, University of London, told Al Jazeera.
A three-way meeting would allow Trump to present himself as “the indispensable deal-maker”, Parmar said, talking up potential deals on Ukraine, trade, energy or arms control.
“After the midterms the domestic political need for a foreign policy ‘win’ is real,” he said.
Any image of Trump sitting with Xi and Putin could be spun as evidence that American power still commands the table, he said, “even if the substance is limited or largely symbolic”.
“The domestic audience, and his eroding MAGA base, matters at least as much as the diplomatic one,” Parmar said.
What does China want?
Not a summit on Ukraine.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said he raised the idea of discussing Ukraine with Xi when they met in Beijing on October 30, and could see the “surprise” on his face, Germany’s DPA news agency reported.
Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD that Xi said the three presidents would probably meet in Shenzhen, but not to discuss Ukraine.
He said Xi explicitly pointed out that the Russia-Ukraine war is a European conflict in which the “Europeans must sit at the table”.
Beijing is also likely to swat away Trump’s push for nuclear talks.
Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.
What would a meeting mean for the rest of the world?
Allies could be sidelined.
Parmar said a three-way meeting would mark “a clear break from the post-1945 pattern”, in which Washington coordinated closely with its European and Asian allies before engaging with Moscow or Beijing.
“A free-standing trilateral [meeting] risks treating those allies as secondary players whose interests can be managed after the fact,” he said, adding that those interests could even be traded.
That would be a shift towards “personalised great-power diplomacy”, he said. But the Trump administration still has hopes to drive a wedge between Russia and China, Parmar added.
Fears of a “G3” are “understandable but overstated in institutional terms”, he said, because the three capitals’ interests diverge sharply on Ukraine, Taiwan, technology and the rules of the international economy.
“The real risk is not a formal G3 secretariat, but the normalisation of great-power deals struck with little consultation of those most affected,” he said.
“History offers many examples of such moments. They rarely produce stable order and often leave the excluded feeling the costs,” Parmar said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Gavin Newsom commutes more than 500 death sentences in California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levin in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, has commuted the death sentences of more than 500 people on the state’s death row on Thursday, a move that ensures they can never be executed under future administrations.
The Democrat’s mass commutation at the end of his term has converted all of the state’s death sentences to life without the possibility of parole, the largest clearing of any US death row in modern history.
The move comes after the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee sparked global outrage and renewed calls for a nationwide pause on capital punishment.
His decision impacts 529 men and 19 women who were sentenced to death in the state, making up the largest death row in the western hemisphere, the governor said in a letter announcing his decision.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” he wrote. “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”
Newsom, considered a probable candidate for president in 2028, has long opposed the death penalty and issued a moratorium on executions in 2019. He also dismantled the state’s physical death row chamber in the infamous San Quentin prison, transferring people with death sentences to other facilities where they had more freedom of movement and access to programs – for some, a dramatic change after decades isolated in solitary cells.
The last execution in California was in 2006, but hundreds of people incarcerated in the state’s prisons have continued to live under death sentences, making California home to the largest death row population in the nation.
Newsom’s office noted on Thursday that of the 548 people sentenced to death, 220 of them have waited 15 years or more to be appointed habeas counsel, the legal representation they are entitled to access to fight their cases. And 139 people have waited 20 years or more for representation. If there were no moratorium in place, there are 45 people in the state who are considered to have exhausted their appeals and would be immediately subject to execution.
“This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families,” Newsom said. “I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action.”
The California supreme court will have to review and approve the clemency grants for cases where the individual was convicted of multiple felonies, Newsom said.
The announcement was praised by the American Civil Liberties Union and prominent advocates who oppose the death penalty, including Martin Luther King III, the eldest son of the civil rights icon, and Bryan Stevenson, an internationally renowned death penalty lawyer.
Jeanne Woodford, a former California prisons director who oversaw four executions, applauded Newsom in a statement, noting that more than 200 people nationwide have been exonerated after being sentenced to death: “As someone who has carried out executions in California, I am haunted by the fear that we will execute an innocent person.”
A relative of a victim killed by one man on California’s death row also spoke out in favor of the commutations. Jess Nichol is the sister of Polly Klaas, a 12-year-old killed in 1993 in a notorious case that paved the way for tough-on-crime laws. She said in a statement Thursday that she used to support the execution of the man who killed her sister. “But over time I’ve realized that whether he’s executed has absolutely nothing to do with my recovery or with real public safety. The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need,” she said.
Governors of both parties have taken bold measures to oppose capital punishment over the years, including an Illinois Republican who commuted all 167 death sentences in 2003 before leaving office. In 2024, North Carolina’s Democratic governor, Roy Cooper, commuted 15 death sentences in the state in his final day in office.
Support for the death penalty has been declining across the US, but Democrats at times have been reluctant to do mass commutations out of fear that Republicans will paint them as “soft on crime” politicians who sided with people convicted of brutal murders.
Newsom has supported criminal justice reform efforts, including changes to prioritize rehabilitative programs in prisons. But some advocates over the years have accused him of caving to political pressures on the issue, including when he has vetoed the release of high-profile prisoners even after they have been granted parole.
California is one of 27 states that still have the death penalty on the books.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Google, Meta and TikTok sue California to block law protecting children from addiction risk
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Johana Bhuiyan and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Google, Meta and TikTok have sued California to block enforcement of a new state law intended to limit the risk of addicting children under 16 to social media platforms.
The law, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits such platforms from offering underage children “psychologically exploitative features” that could lead to compulsive use, such as providing personal recommendations and sending videos through autoplay features. It also requires the deletion of children’s accounts with those features.
In separate lawsuits on Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok said the law wrongly compels them to honor California’s preferred means of presenting content to children and substitutes the state’s judgment for that of parents.
They said the law violates the US constitution’s first amendment free speech protections, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which broadly shields online platforms from liability over user content.
The office of Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, who enforces the state’s laws and is the only defendant, said on Thursday it was reviewing the lawsuits. “Our office is committed to defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online,” it added.
Google owns YouTube and is a unit of Alphabet, while Meta owns Facebook and Instagram. TikTok is a unit of China’s ByteDance.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on 10 September, saying children’s safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and California “will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk”.
The law takes effect on 1 January 2027, unless a judge voids it or puts it on hold.
“Parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families,” Jose Castaneda, a Google spokesperson, said on Thursday. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”
In its lawsuit, Meta said California cannot override its editorial judgments about how to curate and display billions of posts, while leaving children free to spend unlimited time on other online platforms that offer similar services.
TikTok, meanwhile, said protected speech “cannot be suppressed solely to protect the young from ideas or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable”.
Other critics also accused California of overreaching. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a non-profit digital rights advocacy group, called the law “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare”.
Many US states regulate children’s access to social media. Countries around the world have similar restrictions, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18bn and limit teenagers’ use of Facebook and Instagram under agreements with nearly all US states, which accused it of violating privacy and consumer protection laws.
In the aftermath of whistleblower revelations that showed Meta was aware of the way its platforms harmed teens, Meta launched a suite of teen safety tools aimed at giving parents more oversight. The company has previously tapped influencers to promote these features around the world as an alternative to social media bans or limitations similar to Australia’s.
Google has come under fire more recently over the use of its AI tools on school devices. On Thursday, parents in California filed a lawsuit against the company alleging their teen daughter made plans to end her life after multiple interactions with AI mode on Google Search. She had access to the AI mode through her school-issued Google Chromebook. The company was also recently forced to backtrack on its decision to cut off a school or classroom’s access to Google Search if teachers or administrators decided not to enable Google’s other AI features for schools.
Google filed its lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California. Meta sued in San Francisco, and TikTok sued in Los Angeles.
The companies and Snapchat parent Snap still face thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis that resulted in such harms as anxiety, depression and suicide.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Who is Nithya Raman, the democratic socialist who will be Los Angeles’s next mayor?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lois Beckett in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Nithya Raman on Thursday unseated Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass after a neck-and-neck race for the leadership for the US’s second largest city.
The young progressive’s victory means that the two largest cities in the US, as well the nation’s capital, Washington DC, have now all elected democratic socialist mayors.
Though Raman’s political ascendance in Los Angeles has sparked many comparisons to New York City’s mayor Zohran Mamdani, her political profile in her home town is very different from Mamdani’s, as is her often tense relationship with the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America.
Here’s some key facts about LA’s new mayor:
Raman broke into politics in 2020 by unseating an establishment Democrat on LA’s powerful city council.
When Raman, an urban planner and political outsider, won a seat on LA’s city council in 2020, it was the first time that a sitting city council member had been ousted in 17 years. One LA political analyst called her win “a political earthquake”. Raman, whose campaign was endorsed by Bernie Sanders, was also the first DSA-endorsed candidate elected to office in Los Angeles. Raman credited her 2020 win to on-the-ground grassroots organizing, telling the Guardian at the time: “We knocked on 80,000 doors, which as far as we know, is a record. By the general election, we had 2,000 volunteers over all. We had 1,000 people just in our Slack.”
She has close ties to Hollywood progressives, including an endorsement from the Hollywood writers’ guild.
At the height of the #MeToo era, Raman served as the entertainment director for the Time’s Up, the organization founded by powerful women in Hollywood that created a legal defense fund for women in all professions to fight back against pervasive sexual assault and sexual harassment.
While older Hollywood celebrities such as Jane Fonda and Samuel L Jackson endorsed Bass, Raman secured endorsements from younger celebrities and comedians such as Mindy Kaling, Adam Scott, and Jaboukie Young-White. Raman’s husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, is a longtime TV writer.
She has also received attention from one very prominent celebrity Republican, former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, with whom she had “a widely publicized private meeting”.
Raman’s key issues are housing policy, homelessness and tenants’ rights.
Raman, an urban planner, has said she joined DSA-LA, which she did in 2019, not because of an “ideological drive”, but “because it was one of the only organizations that was meaningfully talking about housing affordability in the city”. Her mayoral platform calls for building more housing “at all income levels, everything from deed-restricted affordable housing to market-rate housing to social housing to homeless shelters”.
Her goal is to triple annual housing construction in the city, an approach that earned her an endorsement from advocacy group Yimby Action, which believes the best answer to housing affordability is simply building as much housing as possible.
Before she ran for office, Raman co-founded a still-active volunteer organization to help unhoused people in north-east LA.
In 2017, Raman was one of five co-founders of the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, a group that organizes local volunteers in north-east LA to do outreach and advocacy with their unhoused neighbors. The group, which is still active and now claims 800 volunteers, is focused on recognizing “unhoused individuals as fellow members of our community worthy of the same dignity, respect and representation afforded to any housed person”.
Raman won the mayoral race despite a conspicuous lack of support from her city council colleagues – even the fellow democratic socialists on the council.
In a mayoral debate with Raman, Bass, her opponent, brought up Raman’s lack of support from other city council members and city leaders, saying: “Your colleagues have a very difficult time working with you.” The three other democratic socialists who were elected to the LA city council after Raman all endorsed Bass for mayor.
“So the establishment doesn’t like Raman: so what?” Los Angeles Times columnist Gustavo Arellano wrote, arguing that Raman’s outsider status was precisely what voters frustrated with LA’s Democratic political establishment wanted.
Raman, who was among the politicians revealed to have been targeted by establishment Democrats in the 2022 LA city hall audio tape leak scandal, won reelection to the city council in 2024 by a large margin.
At Raman’s election night party, “the political class of Los Angeles was absent,” Kurt Peterson, one of the leaders of hospitality union Unite Here local 11, which endorsed Raman, told Politico. But, he added: “Even though every city councilperson said they were standing with Karen Bass, not very many of the people they represent followed them to the polls.”
While DSA-LA ultimately did endorse Raman for mayor, the endorsement was … complicated.
The local chapter of the DSA did not endorse Raman during the primary, when she entered the race at the last minute after previously endorsing Bass.
After she beat out reality star Spencer Pratt for second place and advanced into the runoff against Bass, DSA-LA did “enthusiastically” endorse her, but noted that “Councilmember Raman’s relationship with DSA-LA, and the broader Angeleno grassroots left, has had some ups and downs”. Among Raman’s downs was “an inconsistent position on Palestine, which eventually resulted in conflict with the chapter over a 2024 endorsement from a pro-Israel Dem club”, the group wrote in its voter guide, noting that they believed she had since “worked with us to improve on this issue”.
But Raman’s DSA-LA endorsement was almost rescinded in a vote of national DSA organizers over her stance on Israel, the Los Angeles Times reported, with a national political committee voting 14-13 against rescinding the local endorsement in early November.
Despite the endorsement drama, DSA-LA was quick to celebrate Raman’s victory, posting a photo captioned, “YUP, that’s our mayor!!!” even before the Associated Press had called the election in her favor.
Raman is proud of her willingness to break with allies and take ‘unpopular’ positions.
Raman touts her political independence – including her willingness to vote against her allies on key policy issues – as the heart of her political identity.
She broke with the DSA on her belief that LA’s mansion tax, which brought in less revenue than supporters had hoped, needed to be reformed, which she called an “extremely unpopular sentiment”.
One Hollywood comedian who supports Raman contrasted her with Mamdani by saying, “She’s not ideological. She’s a wonk,” Vanity Fair reported.
Raman said she was “grateful” for comparisons to Mamdani, but “I am myself”.
In recent interviews, Raman has emphasized her political distance from the DSA.
“The mayoral candidate said she favors the Scandinavian model of social democracy, signaling a belief in a regulated free-market economy rather than the more explicitly anti-capitalist vision embraced by many in the DSA,” Vanity Fair wrote in an October profile.
Asked about comparisons to New York’s democratic socialist mayor, Raman said: “Mamdani is one of the most popular politicians in America right now, and I’m very grateful to be compared to someone who is that skilled as a communicator and a leader. But I am different. I am myself.”

https://hyperallergic.com/doris-salcedo-.author: Hyperallergic
https://hyperallergic.com/doris-salcedo-.text:
Doris Salcedo Traces the Shape of Memory
The Colombian artist reflects on the state’s attempts to erase history, and the people’s continued refusal. Also: How should artists decide whether to participate in documenta 16?
In the face of decades of violence and erasure in Colombia, artist Doris Salcedo has made memory her medium. Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia writes that her poignant sculptures evoke the victims of the devastating guerrilla conflicts “not by simply remembering or looking back, but by delicately articulating the contours of their absence.” Recently, the Colombian government drew ire for removing LGBTQ+, leftist, and feminist objects from the Museo Nacional in Bogotá, later reinstalled after public protests. Di Liscia spoke with Salcedo about the significance of that resistance, the generational wounds of political violence, and how Colombian artists are building paths forward, as they always have.
Meanwhile, artists around the world are grappling with the upcoming edition of the embattled documenta. Two anonymous artists who participated in the last iteration write candidly about the vicious attacks they endured from German media and politicians for opposing the genocide in Palestine. Their practical advice is for artists who are on the fence about showing their work at documenta 16, but it’s also an essential guide to navigating institutional networks that seek to quash meaningful political dissent, the very kernel of artmaking and creativity.
Today, we also report on an investigation into an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon that killed artist Ali Cherri’s parents in 2024, an overdue step toward justice, and the sentencing of Daniel Sikkema, who was found guilty of ordering the murder of his husband, gallerist Brent Sikkema.
More below, including glimmers of hope from the midterms — Claire Valdez will be your artist in Congress, after all.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
Doris Salcedo on Colombia’s Refusal to Forget
On October 15, dozens of objects were removed from display at the Museo Nacional in Bogotá under the orders of the country’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella. Among them were artworks and materials related to LGBTQ+ and feminist movements; the country’s 2016 peace agreement with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC); and the campaigns of left-wing leaders Carlos Pizarro and Bernardo Jaramillo Ossa, both assassinated in the 1990s, whom de la Espriella has called “terrorists.” The objects were reinstated within two weeks by a court order, but the incident roiled the nation: Hundreds took to the streets in protest and faced police repression.

The first major restoration in more than thirty years of Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel altarpiece The Last Judgement (1536–41) has revealed details about the artist’s painting technique. The London Times reports that much of the restoration work dealt with the removal of a layer of white grime that dulled the fresco—salt from dried perspiration from millions of visitors over the years. Once cleaned, the clarity of Michelangelo’s composition allowed for a detailed examination of his brushstrokes.
Paolo Violini, the Vatican’s chief restorer, found that the artist set groups of parallel lines at perpendicular angles to one another, creating a cross-hatching effect. Significantly, Violini saw that even when these brushstrokes wobbled, the entire grouping of strokes wobbled in precisely the same way.
“That meant one thing: Michelangelo was using special brushes with multiple heads, each with a small brush on the end of it, allowing him to produce parallel strokes with one large brush,” Violini told the Times. He believes Michelangelo made different types of brushes himself, “one with three heads and others up to 15 cm wide with up to ten brushes on them.”
These specialized brushes are thought to have allowed Michelangelo to paint faster and to replicate the cross-hatching he achieved with a chisel on his sculptures, “which makes the light on the stone vibrate,” Violini said.
Violini’s findings have been published in a book, Michelangelo 2026: The Extraordinary Conservation of the Last Judgment, which also analyzes a hidden self-portrait Michelangelo painted on a strip of cloth worn by a figure representing death. The face appears on the lower left side of The Last Judgement where the dead are rising from the ground before either ascending to paradise or descending to hell.
“It is the last section of The Last Judgment to be completed by Michelangelo in 1541 after he had started it in 1536, and while painting it he fell off the scaffolding,” said Fabrizio Biferali, curator of the Vatican Museums’ Renaissance department, noting that Michelangelo broke his leg in the fall.
“I believe he then painted his own face among the dead being reborn,” he added, “because he felt reborn after his injury, as well as feeling reborn because he was coming to the end of five years of work.”
