Daniel Sikkema has been sentenced to life in prison for hiring a hit man to kill his estranged husband, respected New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York announced on November 4. The onetime escort had been convicted in May on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country in relation to the January 2024 slaying of Sikkema, which took place in the divorcing couple’s Brazil vacation home amid a bitter custody battle over their teenage son.
“Today’s life sentence holds Daniel Sikkema accountable for a cold, calculated murder-for-hire plot that resulted in the murder of his husband, Brent Sikkema,” said US Attorney Jamie McDonald in a statement. “For months, the defendant manipulated friends, family, and employees to execute a killing driven by greed. His actions demonstrated a profound disregard for human life and the rule of law. This sentence reflects the seriousness of the crime, and it reflects the strength and perseverance of the victim’s community and our law enforcement partners.”
Brent Sikkema was the founder and a co-owner of noted contemporary art gallery Sikkema Jenkins & Co. (now Sikkema Malloy Jenkins), which helped to launch the careers of artists including Jeffrey Gibson, Deana Lawson, Arlene Shechet, Shahzia Sikander, and Kara Walker. He was brutally stabbed to death with a kitchen knife on January 14, 2024, while he slept in his Rio de Janeiro vacation residence.
A manhunt resulted in the capture of Brent and Daniel Sikkema’s onetime security guard Alejandro Triana Prevez at a gas station in Brazil, some six hundred miles away. Prevez, a Cuban national, told authorities that Daniel had paid him to kill the dealer. It was subsequently discovered that Daniel had paid Prevez thousands of dollars to carry out the murder, using the identities of friends, family, and staffers without their knowledge. Daniel denied culpability, claiming that the funds supplied to Prevez had been for back pay for services performed while he and his husband were in Cuba.
The New York Post reports that Daniel’s lawyer, Richard Levitt, told the court that his client maintains his innocence and plans to appeal. Prevez’s case is still pending in Brazil.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/leake.title: Leaked UN report 'establishes conclusively' that UAE hired Colombian mercenaries for Sudan's RSF
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/leake.author: Oscar Rickett
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/leake.text:
Leaked UN report 'establishes conclusively' that UAE hired Colombian mercenaries for Sudan's RSF
A confidential report by United Nations investigators “establishes conclusively” that the United Arab Emirates hired Colombian mercenaries to fight for Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The report, submitted to the UN Security Council last week and obtained by Middle East Eye, details how Global Security Services Group (GSSG), a UAE-based company with close ties to the government, moved the Colombians into Sudan through Libya, Somalia and Chad, where Emirati proxies control large swathes of territory.
The UN investigators also demonstrate that “the UAE-linked Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF) base in Bosaso, Somalia, has been used as a site of transit and/or training for Colombian mercenaries prior to their deployment to Sudan”.
MEE and other outlets have previously reported on the use of Colombian mercenaries and the ports of Bosaso and Berbera by the UAE and RSF, which has been found by the UN and the United States to have committed genocide in Darfur, western Sudan.
Arms and other supplies have been flown in and transported overland to the RSF through territory controlled by the Haftar family and its militias in Libya, through Ethiopia, Chad and two breakaway regions in Somalia with close ties to the UAE: Puntland and Somaliland, which is recognised by Israel.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The UAE and the other entities involved in this network have denied any wrongdoing. The Emirati foreign ministry did not respond to MEE’s request for comment for this article.
But this fourth quarterly update of the UN Panel of Experts on Sudan, which is marked strictly confidential and will not be made public, will be harder for Abu Dhabi to shake off. In a letter included in the leaked report, the UAE said it "rejects any allegations of wrongdoing in relation to the Sudan conflict", and that it "takes allegations about mercenaries very seriously".
'They [Colombian mercenaries] were trained and deployed through a network of facilities and transit routes involving the UAE, Somalia, eastern Libya and Chad'
- UN Panel of Experts report
Those Colombian mercenaries also, according to the report, “played a significant role in RSF military operations in Darfur, particularly in the siege and capture of el-Fasher”.
“The mercenaries provided combat and technical support, including drone operation, artillery and infantry support,” the report says. “They were trained and deployed through a network of facilities and transit routes involving the UAE, Somalia, eastern Libya and Chad.”
Last October, the RSF took the city of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, after a siege that lasted more than 500 days.
Victims and eyewitnesses told MEE that during this operation, RSF fighters raped, executed and extorted thousands of civilians. They also set up makeshift clinics where they took blood from detained victims.
The mercenaries were trained, according to UN investigators, in Abu Dhabi, Ghayathi and al-Wathba (all in the UAE), and at the PMPF base in Bosaso, which is in the semi-autonomous region of Puntland, Somalia.
“The UAE military financed, trained, and supervised the PMPF,” the report says.
Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE's UN candidate
This conclusive evidence of Emirati involvement in Sudan’s war, which has raged since April 2023, comes as Lana Nusseibeh, one of the Gulf country’s top diplomats, campaigns to become the next secretary-general of the UN.
Sudan’s ambassador to the UK, Babiker al-Siddig al-Amin, told MEE that Nusseibeh’s candidacy should not be used to “whitewash” the UAE’s support for the RSF in Sudan.
“Those who have the blood of the Sudanese people on their hands should not be leading international institutions,” the ambassador said.
“The UN should be very careful, because if Nusseibeh succeeds, it would be a significant blow to its credibility. The UN’s role should not be taken so lightly.”
'Those who have the blood of the Sudanese people on their hands should not be leading international institutions'
- Babikir al-Siddig al-Amin, Sudanese ambassador to the UK
Born in Abu Dhabi into a well-known Palestinian family, Nusseibeh attended a private boarding school in England before attending the University of Cambridge and then Soas University of London.
She became the UAE's first female permanent representative to the UN in 2013 and served until 2024. During that time, she served as vice president of the General Assembly, president of the UN Women executive board and twice president of the Security Council.
Nusseibeh played a key part in the UAE’s official normalisation of relations with Israel in 2020, and Colin Shindler, a former teacher of hers at Soas, said in 2020 that she had written some “wonderfully insightful and incisive essays on Zionism and Israeli history”.
Nusseibeh has for years denied reports detailing Abu Dhabi’s involvement in the war. Asked in recent interviews whether she could be impartial on Sudan as UN secretary-general, she said she could, without directly addressing Emirati support for the RSF.
“I have been clear that the atrocities committed by the RSF must be subject to accountability, and that I would support the work of UN fact-finding mechanisms,” Nusseibeh told Politico this week.
Security Council ties to the UAE
The UN is due to install a successor to incumbent Antonio Guterres by the end of the year. The five nations on the Security Council that wield vetoes - the P5, made up of the US, UK, France, Russia and China - all maintain significant economic and diplomatic relations with the UAE.
Until October, the race to succeed Guterres was dominated by centrist or left-leaning Latin American candidates. But US President Donald Trump, who has called the UN prone to “a far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats”, rejected them all.
Nusseibeh is behind other candidates in the straw polling for the job, with Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan currently in the lead.
But the UAE is a close strategic ally of - and major investor in - the US, France and the UK. Abu Dhabi’s ruler, Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whom President Donald Trump calls a “warrior”, has committed $1.4 trillion in investment to the US, including in artificial intelligence.
The UAE has pledged billions of euros to France, while hosting a French military base and a branch of the Louvre in Abu Dhabi.
It has also poured billions of pounds into the UK, where its vice president, Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, owns Manchester City Football Club, as well as a significant chunk of Manchester itself. The city’s former mayor, Andy Burnham, is now the UK’s prime minister.
China is the UAE’s biggest trading partner and Russia has been able to circumvent western sanctions imposed on it in the wake of the Ukraine war by going through Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
Pressure on the UK to back the UAE
Diplomatic sources have told MEE that the US, Russia, France and the UK are all leaning towards supporting Nusseibeh’s candidacy, with China not in favour of her.
Multiple sources in the UK’s Labour Party and in New York and Washington-based humanitarian organisations told MEE that David Miliband, head of the International Rescue Committee (IRC), has told his brother Ed, Britain’s foreign secretary, that the UK should support his friend Nusseibeh’s candidacy.
The IRC denied the allegations, saying that neither the organisation nor David Miliband had taken a position on UN secretary-general candidates.
A British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson told MEE last week: “The UK’s priority is to find the candidate best equipped to lead the UN in tackling our shared global challenges.
“Our focus is on the merit of the candidates to secure the most qualified candidate for the next UN secretary-general. We will not be publicly commenting on individual candidates.”
The British government has previously been accused by Nathaniel Raymond, executive director of Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab, which monitors the war in Sudan and briefs several governments, of not calling out the UAE’s support for the RSF.
In April 2024, the UAE cancelled meetings with British ministers because they were angry that the UK was not jumping to Abu Dhabi’s defence at a UN Security Council meeting on Sudan’s war.
One British government source told MEE that a UK minister flying to the UAE at the time had to have their plane turned around mid-flight. The source also said Britain had not intended to leave the UAE undefended at the meeting.
UN annual report blocked
The UN investigators’ quarterly report, which will remain confidential, follows another report drafted this year. That report also asserted that the UAE had supplied mercenaries to the RSF and that those fighters had taken part in the assault on el-Fasher.
After investigators presented their evidence to the UN Security Council in July, the UAE’s UN ambassador demanded that they “immediately remedy the serious defects” in the report.
Bahrain, a close UAE ally and a non-permanent member of the council, has blocked the report for months.
In September, Anthropic established with “high confidence” that the UAE was behind an influence operation targeting UN experts and critics of its role in Sudan.
GSSG, the company that deployed the Colombian mercenaries, was founded by a senior official in the Emirati presidency, The New York Times reported on Thursday. On its website, the company is described as “a preferred security provider” for the UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Presidential Affairs.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Mee User
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Gaza records more birth defects in nine months than in all of 2022, Wafa reports
The number of birth defects recorded among newborns in Gaza during the first nine months of 2026 has exceeded the total reported for the whole of 2022, the year before Israel’s war on the territory began, the Palestinian news agency Wafa has reported.
A medical source in Gaza told Wafa that 260 cases were recorded between January and September, compared with 184 cases in all of 2022.
The source said 322 cases were recorded in 2025, a 75 percent increase on the 2022 figure.
Possible contributing factors include maternal malnutrition, exposure to environmental pollutants and disruptions to prenatal care during the war, the source said, calling for an independent international scientific investigation.
The source cautioned that the figures alone do not establish the rate of congenital anomalies among newborns or determine their causes.
A January 2025 report by Human Rights Watch said pregnant women in Gaza faced serious health risks because of the war, the blockade, damage to health facilities and shortages of food, water and medicine.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/deadl.title: A deadly raid tests a revolutionary town’s faith in Syria's new government
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/deadl.author: Natacha Danon
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/deadl.text:
A deadly raid tests a revolutionary town’s faith in Syria's new government
Driving north from Damascus, I made my way toward the Lebanese border, through barren apple and cherry orchards, up into the Qalamoun mountains.
As the town of Rankous came into view, 33-year old Abu Jad, a former member of the Free Syrian Army (FSA) who fought against former ruler Bashar al-Assad, was waiting for me on the main street. He waved at me from the darkened window of his SUV and greeted me with a grim smile.
“Welcome to Rankous, the capital of the revolution in Qalamoun,” he said.
Early in the morning of 22 October, the town’s habitual calm was shattered when Syrian security forces stormed homes and shops, rounding up 45 people and killing five.
According to the Ministry of Interior, the victims had links to the Islamic State (IS), held “extremist ideas,” and had “declared the Syrian state as infidel”.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Three of the victims were unarmed at the time, while two opened fire on the security forces, killing two of its members, according to residents.
For three consecutive days, hundreds of residents and visitors converged on the town square, where a collective wedding was supposed to be held in less than two weeks’ time.
Instead of celebrating life, they were left mourning their sons who had lost their childhood to the war, only to be killed after it finally came to an end.
For the people of Rankous, the latest bloodshed has deepened a sense of loss and injustice in a town that gave hundreds of lives to the revolution. Many feel that their community has been left on the margins of the post-Assad order, with little representation in state institutions or support to rebuild.
As Syria approaches the second anniversary of Assad’s fall, grievances are quietly growing among many war-scarred communities across the country, with groups like IS poised to exploit them.
Descending from his car, Abu Jad extended his left hand to give me a firm handshake, while holding the other tightly against his chest. In 2014, he lost the use of his right arm from a bullet wound.
Today, he serves as the media spokesperson for Firas al-Bitar, who founded the FSA-affiliated Sham Liberation Brigade after defecting from the Syrian army in 2012.
A native of Rankous, Bitar rallied hundreds of men from the town to fight against the Syrian regime, leading to its withdrawal in late 2012. In 2014, he and his men fought tooth and nail once again, this time against the Lebanese group Hezbollah, who entered Syria to defend Assad's administration.
Overwhelmed by the militia’s firepower, his troops withdrew from the town and were transported to the rebel stronghold of Idlib on the regime’s notorious green buses.
But on 8 December 2024, Bitar and his men made a triumphant return to Rankous, cruising in on trucks from northern Syria as Assad’s army crumbled before them. They rode on euphoria for months, until they found themselves sitting at home utterly destitute.
A historic rival of the rebel faction that took power in December 2024 - the now officially dissolved Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) - members of FSA factions found themselves sidelined by the new Syrian army being built.
According to some media reports, Feras al-Bitar flagged the young men to the authorities due to their connections to Jamal Zainia (nom de guerre Abu Malik al-Talli), a former HTS member still under international sanctions. Abu Jad denied that the raid was linked to a higher-level dispute between him and Zainia. Zainia has also publicly denied involvement in any sort of disagreement.
General security raid
I got into Abu Jad’s car and we drove to the house of Ahmad al-Khattib, the father of one of the victims, 21-year-old Youssef al-Khattib.
He greeted me respectfully at the door and accompanied me to a modest living room, where a dozen men were seated in silence paying him their respects.
At 6 o’clock in the morning, the security forces had burst into Youssef’s home, shoving his wife aside as she opened the door.
'He used to dance at weddings and play taekwondo. Plus, I smoke and my son never once reprimanded me - would someone who belongs to IS have been that way?'
- Ahmad al-Khattib
“Youssef and two friends were seated in the living room drinking matte together after returning from dawn prayers,” his father told me, relaying his wife’s version of the events, who declined to speak to me.
“There was an exchange of fire and all three were killed.
“We didn’t expect those who carried out the raid to be General Security; we thought they were from Hezbollah perhaps, which explains why my son must have resisted the raid,” Ahmad told me, adding that his home had been occupied by Hezbollah during the war.
“He used to dance at weddings and play taekwondo. Plus, I smoke and my son never once reprimanded me - would someone who belongs to IS have been that way? The five boys, my son included, merely had faith in God, nothing more.”
Prior to the fall of the Assad regime, Youssef had been providing intelligence to the rebel factions in Idlib.
“He was communicating with and supporting Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham from behind the front lines; I didn’t even know until he took up arms the day of the liberation, which gave me great happiness,” his father said, a smile spreading on his face. “However, he only received limited compensation from the state.”
Youssef’s younger brother Majd was also an informant for Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham.
In 2020, Assad forces raided his home, killing six of his friends and injuring him in his back. “I didn’t feel anything when I was injured because Youssef was by my side; he would carry me around the house,” he told me. “My accident pushed him to also become an informant.”
When Assad fell in December 2024, Youssef joined the new Syrian army, but he only lasted a few months because he was deployed to another province and the salary was low.
Another knock came at the door, and the men stood to greet Muhammad Suleiman, father of 25-year-old Majd Suleiman, and Muhammad Faraoun, father of 22-year-old Ahmad Faraoun. Majd Suleiman was killed that fateful morning at the small supermarket where he worked in a shootout with the security forces.
“He was with the revolution from the age of 10, when he would attend protests with his friends,” his father recalled. Majd spent much of the war hiding at home, as he was wanted by the government for mandatory military service.
'We want justice for the blood of our sons, we want to see those responsible held accountable in court. We joined the revolution to live in freedom and dignity'
- Muhammad Faraoun
However, Majd, like many other young men of Rankous, was not accepted into the army, citing a lack of available positions.
“He wasn’t accepted into the army so, unemployed, he committed himself to [going to] the mosque," he said.
His father says he had a good reputation, with no criminal record, and practised taekwondo in his free time. In mid-November, he was supposed to have his wedding, alongside several other young couples.
“The wedding was supposed to be in the same square where the funeral is now taking place,” his father said, eyes hollow with grief.
“We ask for the spies and informants to be exposed. There are informants now like there were at the time of the regime - nothing has changed, only the accusations,” he added, his voice wavering with anger.
The Assad regime maintained a staggering network of informants, who provided real or fabricated intelligence on their coworkers, friends, and even family members.
“We want the truth to be revealed and the identities of the informants who are creating social divides to be exposed,” Muhammad echoed.
“Our hearts are with the government, but those who wrote security reports [on our sons] and acted on unreliable information are at fault,” chimed in Muhammad Faraoun, father of 22-year old Ahmad Faraoun, a fifth-year student studying information technology.
“We want justice for the blood of our sons, we want to see those responsible held accountable in court. We joined the revolution to live in freedom and dignity."
Tipping point
Ahmad offered to accompany me to the town cemetery, where his son has been laid to rest. We drove to the top of a hill, where hundreds of graves overlook a valley surrounded by the Qalamoun mountains. His grave was unmarked, the brown earth upturned and the tombstone not yet engraved.
He pointed to graves further afield belonging to “the martyrs of the revolution,” he said.
He looked stoic, with deep wrinkles etched into his sun-tanned face, his grief all too familiar to the residents of Rankous. Over 600 people of the town were killed under the siege or detained by the regime, with some 60 men disappearing into the depths of Saydnaya prison, a 15-minute drive away.
He pointed to a blue-domed mosque, which overlooks the cemetery from the top of another hill.
“It was converted into a regime military base during the war and was rebuilt by our sons when the war ended,” he told me. He said the new government has not done anything to rebuild the town or provide basic services, with a trace of reproach in his voice.
I bid Ahmad farewell and made my way to the town square where dozens of mourners had started to gather. Chairs lined both sides of the street leading up to the funeral tent, where pictures of the "martyrs" had been strung up and the Qur'an was playing on loop. I then encountered Nihad al-Shahin, head of the local development committee.
The committee was formed in early 2025 to carry out basic repairs using donations from local residents amid the paralysis of the state, which lacks resources to rebuild the country on the massive scale that is needed. The World Bank estimates that $216bn is required for reconstruction.
“We are from the revolution, but the state has provided nothing in return,” Abu Jad said. “We have footed the bill for basic services and reconstruction, from street lighting and roads to schools and mosques.”
Frustration had been building since the fall of Assad, but the latest events constituted a tipping point. “The outcome of what happened at the hands of the internal security forces has left a deep wound in one of the most prominent incubators of the revolution in the Qalamoun region,” al-Shahin told me.
“Those who lived through 14 years of war naturally seek peace and stability, and this is a sentiment shared by all our people in Rankous.”
Al-Shahin demanded that the authorities undertake an investigation and present evidence to residents that the young men were in fact linked to the Islamic State. But he says that even if the evidence is legitimate, a raid of such a magnitude was unjustified.
“The raid was flawed in the manner it was conducted - it never warranted this level of violence,” he said, indignance flickering across his face. “There are numerous ways to resolve such issues and prevent bloodshed among our people.”
In former rebel strongholds like Rankous, the recent events have reopened old wounds and triggered memories of the former regime.
“There remains an inherited security mindset that requires review and must be rebuilt anew,” al-Shahin added.

US and Iran edge closer to potential breakthrough in talks to end war, Bloomberg reports
The United States and Iran are moving closer to a possible breakthrough in efforts to end the war, with Tehran considering proposals on its nuclear programme that it had previously been unwilling to discuss, Bloomberg reported, citing a diplomat familiar with the talks.
The diplomat said Iran was studying proposals on its nuclear activities presented by Qatar, the main mediator.
Any concession could help to advance negotiations, which have stalled since the collapse of an interim agreement reached in June.
Reuters and The New York Times have also previously reported on Iran’s willingness to compromise on the nuclear issue.
US President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani about efforts to de-escalate the conflict and secure a comprehensive agreement, the emir’s office said on Friday.
Qatari officials have been shuttling between Doha and Tehran to help bridge differences, including over Iran’s nuclear activities and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.title: Here’s How Major Galleries’ UK Operations Performed in 2025
https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.text:
The good news: The United Kingdom is still the world’s second-largest art market by value, according to the latest Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report. The not-so-good news? Since 2009, UK sales have grown just 14 percent, while the United States market has grown 51 percent.
The art market seesaw keeps tilting. This fall, many galleries with UK branches filed their annual reports with Companies House, the UK government agency that keeps records for businesses registered in the country. Some, like David Zwirner, Lisson, and Sprüth Magers, saw their turnover (the UK term for revenue) grow, while others, like Hauser & Wirth, Sadie Coles HQ, and Pace, saw it drop. There was no one-size-fits-all story for the UK market in 2025.
ARTnews pulled the filings for 10 of these galleries to get a sense of how the trade is doing.
- Pace Pace’s 2025 report showed that its international business posted a $5.6 million loss in 2025. The figures cover The Pace Gallery Limited, the London-registered company that operates the gallery’s London space and owns its subsidiaries in Hong Kong, Beijing, Seoul, Geneva, and Berlin. They do not include Pace’s US or Tokyo operations. Turnover fell 2.6 percent, from $67.7 million in 2024 to $65.9 million in 2025. Meanwhile, cost of sales rose 12 percent, gross profit dropped $7.4 million to $12.8 million, and year-end cash on hand fell from $34.8 million in 2023 to $24.1 million in 2024 and $11.1 million in 2025. CEO Marc Glimcher told ARTnews that the gallery is “all off the bottom” and said it had a record performance at Art Basel Paris in October, though he did not offer specifics. “We’ve done a lot of internal reengineering of the way the companies work together. The successes we’ve had in Berlin and Japan have been very, very instructive, and we have had an extremely profitable year already in Los Angeles,” Glimcher said. “The things we’ve done are already bearing fruit, and they’re bearing fruit because the market has substantially changed.”
- Lisson Lisson’s 2025 financial year ended on January 31, 2026. In the filing for its parent company, Art Holding Co. Limited, the group reported a 9 percent increase in turnover, to $130 million (£97 million) from $119.42 million (£89 million) in 2024. The group described the period as a “year of encouragement despite the wider art market continuing to face many macro-economic driven challenges.” The gallery attributed its recovery to “a couple of challenging years coupled with a renewed focus on stock and secondary sales activities.” Lisson added in the filing that the risks and uncertainties facing the business continue to relate to “inherent volatility in the contemporary art market,” and that it mitigates that risk “as far as possible by offering work from a diverse spread of artists across a wide price spectrum to a broad range of private and institutional collectors, both in the UK and internationally.” A spokesperson for Lisson told ARTnews that while the audit shows a decrease in profit for both Lisson Gallery London Limited and Art Holding Co. Limited, Lisson’s global gross profit has increased six percent year-on-year and the losses were largely due to non-trading foreign exchange movements. “Lisson has been able to maintain this and recover efficiently due to a number of factors, including a renewed focus on secondary sales activities and securing distribution fees (despite significant upward inflationary pressures on freight costs),” said the spokesperson.
- Hauser & Wirth Hauser & Wirth’s turnover fell 13.1 percent, from $90.82 million (£68.29 million) in 2024 to $78.93 million (£59.35 million) in 2025. However, the company remained profitable in 2025, with profit up 51 percent year on year, totalling £403,318 profit for 2025 against 2024’s £266,539. In the filing, the company said its directors “have a strong belief in the future of the company and are pleased to report continuing profitability during a period of art market fluctuations.” In the filing, the gallery also noted that the UK “represented a small element of the annual program in 2025,” with nine exhibitions and two art fair presentations there, compared with 58 exhibitions and 13 fair presentations worldwide. At Frieze London and Frieze Masters in 2025, the gallery sold just under $21 million worth of works. “As a global business, the UK company’s results are not indicative of the gallery’s overall performance, which includes larger markets such as Switzerland and the US,” a Hauser & Wirth spokesperson told ARTnews. “The gallery has a strong commitment to the UK, reflected in the major project underway to create a new London flagship on South Audley Street in Mayfair. 2026 has been a year of significant growth and investment for the gallery globally, including new spaces in Palo Alto, the Hauser & Wirth Publishers HQ in Zurich and Stockwell House the community-led space in Somerset as well as five new artists and estates joining the roster.”
- Goodman Gallery At Goodman Gallery, which has locations in Johannesburg, Cape Town, New York, and London, turnover for the UK business rose 7 percent in 2025 to $47.3 million (£35.26 million), while pre-tax profit soared 60.8 percent to $6.37 million (£4.75 million). Cost of sales fell 2.3 percent to $31.95 million (£23.82 million). “We anticipate healthier financial performance in the 2026/2027 financial year,” Liza Essers, owner and director of Goodman Gallery, told ARTnews. The gallery is celebrating its 60th year in business, and the anniversary has helped drive sales, according to Essers. She added that the gallery’s most recent William Kentridge exhibition, which opened in September in London, has “surpassed expectations,” with films selling for $485,000 and works on paper priced from $250,000 to $850,000. Essers noted that the gallery had a strong showing at Art Basel Paris, including several significant sales to long-term clients from Europe, North America, and Asia. This year the gallery also launched Goodman Gallery Advisory, a secondary-market arm focused on 20th-century artists ranging from Alexander Calder to Yayoi Kusama.
- Pilar Corrias Pilar Corrias saw its turnover fall 42.7 percent, from $25.76 million (£19.2 million) in 2024 to $14.75 million (£10.99 million) in 2025. In the filing, the gallery said its main challenges were supply chain issues, market volatility, digital security, logistics such as shipping, the recoverability of debts, and foreign currency fluctuations. Looking ahead, the gallery said that for 2026 and beyond it would focus on reaching more collectors worldwide by showing at major international art fairs, investing in digital infrastructure to grow its online presence and improve security, and strengthening its relationships with private collectors, institutions, and museums. The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.
- Sprüth Magers Monika Sprüth & Philomene Magers Limited, the holding company of Sprüth Magers gallery, returned sharply to profitability in 2025, reporting a pre-tax profit of $1.83 million (£1.36 million) after a $2.34 million (£1.75 million) pre-tax loss in 2024. Turnover rose 66.2 percent to $24.77 million (£18.46 million). The accounts also broke down turnover by region. UK turnover more than doubled, to $139,047 (£103,643) from $63,938 (£47,689) in 2024. Turnover from Europe rose 74.1 percent to $17.31 million (£12.9 million), while turnover from outside Europe rose 49.3 percent to $7.32 million (£5.45 million). “Based on the performance in 2025 and current trading, the directors consider the company to be in a strong financial position as it enters 2026,” the filing said. “The outlook for 2026 is positive and the directors expect a similar level of performance to 2025, while recognising that results remain sensitive to market conditions and the timing of high-value transactions.” The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.
- Sadie Coles HQ Sadie Coles HQ’s turnover fell 10 percent in 2025 to $34.63 million (£25.81 million), but the gallery’s pre-tax profit rose 57.2 percent, from $536,279 (£399,731) in 2024 to $843,063 (£628,401). “Careful curation of the gallery programme and the addition of new represented artists means that the company is continuing to attract new collectors and to expand its business,” the gallery said in the filing. It noted that turnover was slightly lower than in 2024, despite a significant increase in the total number of sales. In fall 2025, Sadie Coles HQ opened a new space on Savile Row, which the gallery said has helped it “attract new artists of calibre.” The gallery added that it “is confident of continued success.”
- Timothy Taylor Timothy Taylor reported turnover of $23 million (£17.21 million) in 2025, up 3.7 percent from $22.26 million (£16.59 million) in 2024. Cost of sales rose 5.9 percent to $17.4 million (£12.96 million), while gross profit fell 2.5 percent to $5.68 million (£4.24 million). In the filing, the gallery said it “intends to continue strengthening its brand presence in the UK, the US and Asia.” The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.
- Thaddaeus Ropac 2025 marked Thaddaeus Ropac’s ninth year of trading in the UK, and the gallery’s founder recently told ARTnews that he had renewed its lease on Dover Street for another 10 years. The gallery’s 2025 turnover fell 4.9 percent to $46.58 million (£34.72 million), while pre-tax profit fell 7.3 percent to $3.32 million (£2.47 million). In the filing, the gallery said that 2025, like 2024, reflected “uncertainties around economy and sociopolitical upheavals,” but that it remained “profitable in this climate, a reflection of its strong engagement with its customers and artist and close control over costs.” The gallery’s UK staff grew from 23 in 2024 to 25 in 2025. That year, Thaddaeus Ropac also opened a space in Milan, adding to its locations in London, Paris, Salzburg, and Seoul. A spokesperson declined to comment.
- David Zwirner According to David Zwirner’s 2025 filing with Companies House, the gallery’s turnover rose 56 percent, from $49.72 million (£37.13 million) in 2024 to $77.51 million (£57.89 million) in 2025. The gallery attributed the $27.79 million (£20.8 million) jump in sales revenue to “increased art fair sales as well as revenue recognition timing.” At the 2025 edition of Frieze London, the gallery reported sales led by a Chris Ofili painting for $700,000. It also sold a painting by Steven Shearer for $550,000, two paintings by Lucas Arruda priced from $320,000 to $350,000 each, a work on paper by Elizabeth Peyton for $300,000, a work on paper by Lisa Yuskavage for $180,000, and two works by Wolfgang Tillmans priced from $115,000 to $250,000. The gallery also sold works by Kerry James Marshall, Christopher Williams, Huma Bhabha, Sosa Joseph, and Frank Walter for undisclosed five-figure sums. The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.

Middle East conflict weighs on British Airways owner IAG's profits
6 November 2026 13:34 GMT
International Airlines Group (IAG), the owner of British Airways and Iberia, said its third-quarter net profit fell by more than 12 percent as fuel costs rose and the conflict in the Middle East disrupted flights.
Profit after tax fell to 1.23 billion euros ($1.37bn) in the July-September quarter, compared with 1.4 billion euros a year earlier. The group said fuel costs rose by more than 30 percent during the quarter.
“Strong pricing was offset by lower capacity, the impact of one-off disruption events and in particular by higher jet fuel prices,” the company said.
IAG also cited cancellations linked to the Middle East conflict, aircraft availability issues involving engines and air traffic control disruptions.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/trending/c.text:
'Is this a joke?': Centcom podcast mocked as Iran war drags on
The Pentagon has entered its podcast bro era, and viewers have widely derided its debut.
As the cost of the US-Israeli war on Iran spirals for American taxpayers, US Central Command (Centcom) launched its official podcast on Thursday.
The first episode of Inside Centcom pairs Admiral Brad Cooper, who leads the US command overseeing the war, with Fleet Master Chief Lateef Compton.
In the 12-minute episode on YouTube, Cooper jokes about stealing French fries from Compton’s lunch. The pair touch only briefly on the deeply unpopular war, now in its ninth month. Centcom turned off comments on YouTube.
The podcast looks like an attempt to reach young men who might one day fight Washington’s wars in the Middle East.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
"It's called service for a reason. You're going to give more than you're going to get. But if you find satisfaction in giving, you'll have no greater satisfaction than serving in the United States military in particular," claimed Cooper.
"It’s been a busy year," Compton joked at the start of the episode, a passing nod to a war that has killed thousands in Iran and left the US mired in another Middle East conflict.
Cooper said nothing about the US strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February, the first day of the war.
Amnesty International said the strike killed 156 people, including 120 children, and concluded that the US violated international humanitarian law by failing to take all feasible precautions to protect civilians.
UN human rights experts said in September that there were "reasonable grounds" to believe the US committed war crimes in Iran.
“For sure, no one could have imagined the trajectory of events that we would be on, but through it, everyone has been doing a fantastic job,” Cooper said.
'Shitshow'
On X, viewers were less forgiving. The clip drew more than two million views, and one user called it a “shitshow”.
“Is this a joke? Its completely undignified. The host should ask him for his reflections on killing 168 schoolchildren and teachers in Minab,” journalist Murtaza Hussain wrote.
“Why the fuck are top US military officials podcasting?” another user posted.
“Thank you CENTCOM, we definitely needed this! I’m so excited for the second episode! Maybe they’ll get a good guest like Jake Paul or Nicki Minaj, ooo, or maybe even Netanyahu!” another wrote.
Trita Parsi, a US-based expert on Iran, wrote on X: “I am all in favor of Centcom abandoning the needless-wars-in-the-Middle-East business and going all in on podcasting…”
Christopher K Mellon, a former US deputy assistant secretary of defence for intelligence, was equally scathing.
“I’m sorry, the American public does not need to become personally familiar with the idiosyncrasies of our CENTCOM commander; the American people need our CENTCOM commander to execute his or her duties somberly, professionally, and excellently,” Mellon wrote.
Democratic congresswoman-elect Elaine Luria wrote on X that Cooper’s job “is to win wars, not record podcasts…read the room”.
The Pentagon’s latest estimate to Congress puts the cost of the war at $47.1bn. Brown University estimates that American consumers have paid more than $153bn in additional fuel costs.

Mohammed Hijab suggests UK counter-terror police tried to recruit him as informant
Prominent British YouTuber Mohammed Hijab has claimed that counter-terrorism police tried to recruit him as an informant after seizing his devices.
Hijab, whose legal name is Mohamed Hegab, describes himself as a philosopher of religion pursuing a PhD in the subject at the University of Birmingham.
He has more than a million subscribers on YouTube and frequently takes parts in debates on religion, as well as political issues.
In a post on X on Wednesday, Hijab said: "I want this on the record.
"In May, counter terrorism police stopped me without explanation, seized my devices and read more than ten thousand messages. My phone came back on 11 September. No further questions."
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Hijab added: "Their notes, disclosed through my subject access request. One line reads 'Doesn’t want to be an informant.'"
He posted a screenshot of a page marked "REDACTED EXCERPT - Unrelated content removed" which has the Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) logo on it and the heading: "Examining Officer's Notes - Continued".
All the notes in the screenshot are redacted apart from a handwritten line which says: "Doesnt want to be an informant."
It is unclear whether the entire document was redacted by the police, or whether Hijab blacked it out himself to protect sensitive information.
I want this on the record. In May, counter terrorism police stopped me without explanation, seized my devices and read more than ten thousand messages. My phone came back on 11 September. No further questions. Their notes, disclosed through my subject access request. One line reads “Doesn’t want to be an informant.”
— Mohammed Hijab (@mohammed_hijab) November 4, 2026
Hijab shared a second screenshot of a letter purportedly from "Gatwick Borders Team", referring to Gatwick airport, which is part of Counter Terrorism Policing South East.
The letter, dated 18 May, says: "Further to your examination under Schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act which was conducted at Gatwick airport on the 12th May 2025, I am writing to inform you of a change in power used to retain the property that was seized from you."
Two paragraphs below it are redacted. The letter then reads: "This does not necessarily mean you are currently under criminal investigation.
"We will endeavour to return your items to you at the earliest opportunity."
MEE contacted CTP London for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.
Schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act 2000 gives the police the power to detain and question people at airports without needing prior grounds to suspect them of terrorism.
Hijab said in a recent YouTube video: "I was recently called in for a police interview under caution. I wasn't arrested but it was a criminal investigation and still is one. And it's one that relates to, I would call it, obviously from my perspective, activism.
"The questions were essentially questions that were for the most part related to anti-Israeli activism, actually."
He said he believed Israel was trying to "interfere" with him. Hijab did not provide evidence for these claims.
Hijab has participated in public debates on Israel, including on broadcaster Piers Morgan's show.
He recently debated Jonathan Conricus, a former international spokesperson for the Israeli military, on Morgan's show.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/fake-.title: Fake Iranian accounts ‘campaigned for Netanyahu’ ahead of Israeli election
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/fake-.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/fake-.text:
Fake Iranian accounts ‘campaigned for Netanyahu’ ahead of Israeli election
A network of 1,653 X accounts posing as Iranian users amplified Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s election campaign ahead of last week’s vote, Haaretz reported on Friday.
The accounts posted messages in Hebrew urging Israelis to vote for Netanyahu “on behalf of the Iranian people”.
The accounts, which claimed to belong to Iranians living in Iran or abroad, appeared to coordinate their activity. Their operators remain unidentified.
Activity intensified on election day, when multiple accounts published identical messages and responded to posts in coordinated bursts.
Two accounts, for example, shared 109 identical posts, compared with just four expected through organic activity, according to Haaretz’s analysis.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
They also responded simultaneously, or within five minutes of each other, to 232 posts by 53 different accounts.
On election morning, two accounts posted the same Hebrew message about an hour apart: “We call on you to support Benjamin Netanyahu to finish the job”, accompanied by the hashtag #IsraeliElections2026.
“Tomorrow, vote only for the Likud party,” one account wrote in response to a Netanyahu post at 10pm on the eve of the election.
“Vote for Benjamin Netanyahu,” another posted twice within two minutes after midnight.
“Dear people of Israel, if you want to be protected from the Islamic Republic and the Axis of Resistance, vote,” read another message, published in Hebrew and English at around 2am.
Haaretz reported that the findings were based on research by Expose, a social media monitoring company that specialises in tracking digital influence operations and disinformation.
The investigation follows an earlier Haaretz report that found accounts previously linked to an influence campaign targeting Iran’s government had begun engaging with Israel’s election campaign and amplifying Netanyahu’s videos.
The Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter subsequently filed a petition with the Central Elections Committee over the accounts identified in the investigation.
Expose found that around 1,600 of the accounts had been identified last year as part of an influence operation promoting Reza Pahlavi, the son of Iran’s last shah, who was overthrown in 1979, as an alternative to the Iranian government.
As Israel’s election campaign gathered pace in July, 185 of these accounts began interacting with Netanyahu’s social media profiles, including by sharing posts attacking his political opponents.
According to Haaretz, the network returned to its usual focus on Pahlavi after the election concluded last week.
Some of the findings were submitted to the Central Elections Committee in October as expert evidence in a petition brought by the Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter against Netanyahu, Likud and the Prime Minister’s Office.
The committee’s chairman, Judge Noam Solberg, rejected the petition on the eve of the election.
Solberg ruled that the network’s activity was subject to election advertising transparency requirements and appeared, on the face of it, to violate the law.
However, he said the committee could not reach a definitive ruling because the identities of those operating the accounts were unknown. He ordered the evidence to be referred to the police.
In response to the investigation published in October, the Prime Minister’s Office and Likud denied any connection to the accounts.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Cornell faculty declares ‘no confidence’ in school leaders in fallout from alleged gang-rape
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Cornell University’s faculty senate approved a resolution on Friday declaring “no confidence” in the school’s top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student’s lawsuit saying she was gang-raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to members of the faculty senate on Friday afternoon.
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, and other administrators handled the woman’s allegations properly and whether they’ve done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
While the faculty body has no power over the university’s top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell’s trustees to urgently address what they viewed as longstanding institutional failures.
Voting took place electronically over more than a week, with the results released on Friday.
The Cornell community has been in a state of distress and dismay since mid-September, when a former student filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All of those men have denied her allegations, saying that either the sex was consensual or they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter, and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several of the accused students after a months long Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by the New York Times.
Kotlikoff also convened a taskforce to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.
Some faculty members have been furious with Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school’s disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

https://gothamist.com/news/republican-je.title: Republican Jeff Van Drew concedes NJ congressional seat in surprise victory for Democrats
https://gothamist.com/news/republican-je.author: Mike Hayes, Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/republican-je.text:
Four-term Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew has conceded to small-town Jersey Shore mayor Zack Mullock in a race that, just weeks ago, was a long shot for Democrats trying to win back the House.
The Associated Press had not called the race as of 11:20 p.m., but preliminary results show Mullock leading by nearly 5 points, with 70% of the votes counted.
Mullock, a 41-year-old business owner, former pro golfer, and Cape May mayor, won New Jersey's 2nd Congressional District two years after Van Drew, who switched parties in 2019, carried the district by a healthy 17 points in 2024.
Van Drew said he called Mullock to concede.
“I wish him the very best. I wish him success. His success is our success,” he said during a speech to supporters in Sea Isle City that was streamed on NJ PBS.
“I’m not going to blame Donald Trump,” he said, adding that he wasn’t sure what he was going to do next. “I made decisions in my life and I’m proud of them.”
The surprise victory was the latest victory for Democrats who were on the verge of making historic gains in the House of Representatives. Fairleigh Dickinson University politics Prof. Dan Cassino said Van Drew’s defeat goes beyond a “wave election” for the Democratic Party.
“ That is apocalyptic, end of the party, cats and dogs lying down together, mass hysteria sort of stuff happening,” he said, channeling Bill Murray in the first Ghostbusters movie.
Van Drew’s loss will likely leave Republicans with just one of 12 congressional seats in the state. In the 7th Congressional District, Republican Rep. Tom Kean, Jr. was also defeated by first-time Democratic candidate Rebecca Bennett. In the neighboring 4th Congressional District, Republican Rep. Chris Smith has won re-election for a 24th consecutive term.
New Jersey Democrats have been musing about toppling Van Drew since last year. In the 2025 governor’s race, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill turned several counties in the 2nd District from red to blue.
In the June Democratic primary, Mullock defeated three other challengers for the nomination. Like many Democrats this year, Mullock ran on affordability, often touting how he hasn’t raised taxes in Cape May in his six years as mayor. He also focused on electability, arguing his ability to win three straight local elections in typically conservative Cape May proved he could beat Van Drew.
A key topic of debate in the race was a controversial $17 billion dollar data center in Vineland, New Jersey, in a central part of the district. Mullock joined other Democrats in criticizing the large facility, which is owned by DataONE and backed by Microsoft. He argued for a federal moratorium on data centers while more research is done into their effects on the environment and the electrical grid.
Van Drew tried to distance himself from the data center. In March, his campaign manager posted on Van Drew’s Facebook page that the project had “no federal component” and Van Drew wasn’t involved in its approval. In April, Gothamist reported that the Republican received $19,000 in campaign donations from the owners and other executives connected to the Vineland facility.
In September, Sherrill fined DataONE a record $1 million for illegally operating dozens of generators to help power the 2.6 million square-foot facility. Her administration said it was the largest fine ever handed down to a data center for illegally powering a facility.
Only in the last few weeks did the national Democratic Party throw sizable financial support behind Mullock’s campaign. Mullock has raised less than $1 million since January, according to his FEC filings. Van Drew raised a reported $2.5 million this year, according to his filings.
In the week before Election Day, a super PAC tied to Democratic opposition research firm American Bridge 21st Century spent a reported $1.5 million on an ad attacking Van Drew.
Van Drew was first elected to Congress as a conservative Democrat in 2018. Before entering Congress, he worked as a dentist in South Jersey for 30 years and held several local and state offices.
Van Drew gained national attention after his first win in 2018 in the middle of Trump’s first term. He became a media fascination as an apparent rare Democrat who could win in a conservative, very pro-Trump district. But a year later, Van Drew switched his allegiance to the Republican Party, just before he voted against impeaching Trump. The President endorsed Van Drew’s re-election as a Republican a year later.

https://taz.de/Regisseur-Andrei-Swjaginz.title: Regisseur Swjaginzew über „Minotaurus“: „Das Gezeigte entspricht den Gegebenheiten in Russland“
https://taz.de/Regisseur-Andrei-Swjaginz.author: Tobias Obermeier
https://taz.de/Regisseur-Andrei-Swjaginz.text:
Regisseur Swjaginzew über „Minotaurus“: „Das Gezeigte entspricht den Gegebenheiten in Russland“
Regisseur Andrei Swjaginzew erzählt in seinem Thriller „Minotaurus“ von Untreue und Misstrauen. Der Überfall auf die Ukraine ist im Film allgegenwärtig.
In seinem Film „Minotaurus“, der im Mai in Cannes den Großen Preis der Jury gewann, erzählt der russische und mittlerweile in Frankreich lebende Regisseur Andrei Swjaginzew von einem skrupellosen Ehemann, der von seiner Frau betrogen wird. Gleichzeitig wird er in die Mobilmachung für den russischen Angriffskrieg hineingezogen. Er soll als Firmenchef für die Teilmobilisierung eine Liste entbehrlicher Angestellter anfertigen. Langsam zerfällt die Ordnung seines streng kontrollierten Lebens. Im Interview spricht der Regisseur über seinen düsteren Thriller, den Reiz der französischen Filmvorlage und darüber, was er Kritikern seines Films entgegnet.
taz: Herr Swjaginzew, Sie wären 2021 beinahe an Covid-19 gestorben, lagen 40 Tage im Koma und konnten Ihre Gliedmaßen über Monate hinweg nicht mehr bewegen. Wie geht es Ihnen mittlerweile?
wurde 1964 in Nowosibirsk geboren. Er absolvierte dort eine Schauspielausbildung, die 1986 in Moskau fortsetzte. 2000 begann er für das Fernsehen und auch als Regisseur zu arbeiten. Sein Spielfilmdebüt „The Return – Die Rückkehr“ lief 2007 in Venedig und gewann dort den Goldenen Löwen. „Leviathan“ lief 2014 in Cannes.
Andrei Swjaginzew: Ich kann nicht behaupten, dass ich komplett geheilt bin. Das war eine unglaubliche Erschütterung für meine Gesundheit. Ich hatte einen sogenannten Zytokinsturm, bei dem das Immunsystem anfängt, den eigenen Körper zu zerstören. Hinzu kam, dass ich auf der Intensivstation von einem Keim infiziert wurde, der 92 Prozent meiner Lungen angegriffen hat. Dieser Keim war resistent gegenüber allen Antibiotika. Am Ende wurde sogar eine Transplantation angedacht. Die Erfolgschancen einer solchen Operation sind sehr gering. Meine Prognose lag bei 60–40. Glücklicherweise fand ich einen Arzt in Deutschland, der mich mit einer Bakteriophagen-Therapie rettete. Ein Wundermittel, das in Deutschland noch nicht lizensiert ist. Wenn man in so eine Situation gerät wie ich, sollte man wissen, dass es diese Rettung gibt.
Der Film
„Minotaurus“. Regie: Andrei Swjaginzew. Mit Dmitriy Mazurov, Iris Lebedeva u.a. Frankreich/Lettland/Deutschland 2026, 141 Min.
taz: Ihr neuer Film „Minotaurus“ basiert auf Claude Chabrols „Die untreue Frau“ (1969). Was macht den Film für eine Neuinterpretation so interessant?
Swjaginzew: Das Sujet des Films ist hervorragend aufgebaut. Wenn ein Zuschauer an der Kinokasse steht und den Titel sieht, denkt er zunächst, dass damit der ganze Film verraten wird. Doch man erfährt bereits zu Beginn des Films, dass der Protagonist seine Frau verdächtigt, untreu zu sein. Im Grunde ist der Titel also kein Spoiler. Denn was dann passiert, ist das Interessante. Wir als Zuschauer beobachten, wie sein Verdacht wächst, wie er beginnt, seine Frau zu beobachten. Diese verschachtelte Beobachtung ist wie eine Matrjoschka. Sie ist das Wesen des Films. Zugleich ist das Beobachten auch die Natur des Kinos.
taz: Wie weit treibt der Film dieses Spiel?
Swjaginzew: Bis zu dem Kulminationsmoment, ab dem nur noch die Zuschauer beobachten und der Protagonist nicht mehr. Es folgen 20 Minuten lang sehr detaillierte Szenen, in denen viel passiert, aber kein Wort gesprochen wird. Keine Sprache. Das ist ein Traum eines jeden Filmemachers: Einen Film zu machen, in dem man nur mit der Sprache der Bilder alles erzählen kann. In jenen Szenen zeigt sich, was in dem Protagonisten vorgeht, als er versucht, die Spuren des von ihm begangenen Mordes zu beseitigen. Der Mord ist die treibende Kraft des Films.
taz: Wie haben Sie Ihren Cast gefunden? Eine Zusammenarbeit mit Schauspielerinnen und Schauspielern, die in Russland leben, dürfte nicht möglich gewesen sein.
Swjaginzew: Für einige Schauspieler, die infrage kamen und in Russland leben, war es nicht möglich. Sie haben das Drehbuch gelesen, mussten aber ihre Teilnahme absagen. Es gibt genügend russische Schauspieler überall auf der Welt, in Argentinien, Israel, Paris, London oder auf Zypern. Die Schauspieler mussten uns zuerst selbstgemachte Proben auf Video schicken. Dann wurde die engere Auswahl nach Riga eingeladen, wo wir den Film drehten.
taz: Sie versetzen die Geschichte nach Russland im September 2022. Als Leiter eines Unternehmens in einer russischen Provinzstadt wird Ihr Protagonist vom örtlichen Bürgermeister aufgefordert, eine Liste von 14 Angestellten zu erstellen, die für die „militärische Spezialoperation“ zwangsmobilisiert werden sollen. Was macht ihn zum titelgebenden Minotaurus?
Empfohlener externer Inhalt
Wir würden Ihnen hier gerne einen externen Inhalt zeigen. Sie entscheiden, ob Sie dieses Element auch sehen wollen:
Trailer „Minotaurus“
Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung
Swjaginzew: Der Filmtitel hat zwei Dimensionen. Die eine ist die politische und soziale Dimension, die auf den antiken Mythos des Minotaurus und seiner Menschenopfer verweist. Die zweite bezieht sich auf einen sehr interessanten Text von Honoré de Balzac aus dem Jahr 1829. Er heißt „Physiologie der Ehe“. Darin vergleicht er die Ehe mit einem Labyrinth, in dem der Ehemann umherirrt und seine Frau beobachtet. Er beobachtet ihr Schweigen, ihre Geheimnisse, ihre Auslassungen, ihre Zweideutigkeiten und schließlich schöpft er Verdacht, dass sie einen Liebhaber hat. Balzac sagt, dass in diesem dunklen Labyrinth die Unruhe des Ehemanns wächst und er erwartet, dass im nächsten Moment der Liebhaber auftaucht und ihn „minotaurisiert“, also in das kretische Ungeheuer verwandelt.
taz: „Minotaurus“ ist ein Thriller über Untreue, Misstrauen und Mord. Gleichzeitig erzählt der Film von Russlands Elite, die sich sehr schnell mit der neuen Kriegsrealität arrangiert. Der Überfall auf die Ukraine ist dabei allgegenwärtig, aber immer nur als eine Art Hintergrundrauschen wahrnehmbar. Es gibt Stimmen, die diesem Film genau das vorwerfen. Dass er eben nur eine russische Innenschau zeigt und die Brutalität des Krieges zur Nebensache wird. Was antworten Sie dieser Kritik?
Swjaginzew: Es ist mir egal, was man dem Film vorwirft. Niemand kann einem Künstler vorschreiben, wie er über eine Sache spricht. Es ist sein Privileg und seine Wahl, wie er über das spricht, worüber er sprechen möchte. Der Film drückt Ideen aus, die für mich wichtig waren, und er sagt das, was ich sagen wollte. Die Kriegsgräben zu zeigen, wäre vielleicht einfacher gewesen als die indirekte Sprache meines Films. Aber das Gezeigte entspricht den realen Gegebenheiten in Russland. Die Atmosphäre in den russischen Städten war genauso, wie man sie im Film sieht. Ich habe das so gemacht, wie ich es für richtig gehalten habe. Für mich war es wichtig, einen Menschen zu zeigen, der vor einer moralischen Wahl steht. Ich möchte an dieser Stelle einen römischen Spruch zitieren: „Ich habe gemacht, was ich konnte, mögen die es besser machen, die dazu imstande sind.“
taz: Sie gewannen in Cannes den Großen Preis der Jury. In Ihrer Dankesrede adressierten Sie Wladimir Putin und forderten ihn auf, das Blutvergießen endlich zu beenden. Im September wurden Sie von der russischen Regierung auf die Liste ausländischer Agenten gesetzt. Was macht das mit Ihnen?
Swjaginzew: Ich möchte Leere nicht kommentieren. Das hat für mich keine Bedeutung.
taz: Ihre Filme wie etwa „Leviathan“, „Loveless“ und auch „Minotaurus“ sind von einem großen Fatalismus durchzogen. Sie zeigen ein moralisch verkommenes Russland, das korrumpiert ist von Machtstreben, Gewalt und Patriarchat. Wo sehen Sie einen Lichtblick in diesem Land?
Swjaginzew: Den Lichtblick sehe ich darin, dass ich darüber reden kann. Dass wir das Zeugnis der Zeit ablegen könne. Dass wir diese Zeit festhalten können und das in der Sprache tun können, die zu uns passt, die angemessen ist. Das ist die Hoffnung. Dass man sprechen kann und Gehör findet. Das klingt vielleicht pathetisch, aber anders kann ich das nicht formulieren.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-fran.title: Trafic aérien, mobilisation des forces de sécurité… Ce que l’on sait de la nouvelle vague d’alertes à la bombe
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-fran.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-fran.text:
Une série de fausses alertes à la bombe agite l’Europe vendredi, après des dizaines d’alertes similaires cette semaine, visant des vols commerciaux mais aussi des médias et mobilisant les forces de sécurité.
L’histoire se répète, depuis le début de la semaine. Au moins une vingtaine de vols civils – pour la plupart de compagnies low cost – ont été visés par de fausses alertes à la bombe jeudi 5 novembre. Ces avions, partis notamment d’Italie, ont été escortés par des avions de chasse. Rebelote vendredi, tandis que onze vols au départ ou à destination de Prague et de Sofia ont fait l’objet d’une alerte à la bombe.
Quatre nouvelles alertes à la bombe ont été également émises vendredi sur des avions survolant le territoire français, qui ont atterri « sans encombre » et sur lesquels les services de déminage « procèdent aux inspections de sécurité », ont annoncé les services du premier ministre.
Un vol de la compagnie Ryanair qui devait partir de Lisbonne en direction de Rome vendredi matin a aussi été visé par une « menace de bombe » qui s’est avérée sans fondement, d’après les autorités portugaises. Le secteur des médias a également été ciblé vendredi en Irlande. Les locaux de plusieurs médias irlandais dont le groupe audiovisuel RTÉ ont été évacués vendredi matin après avoir reçu une alerte à la bombe.
« Opérations hybrides » ?
« Nous ne savons pas encore s’il s’agit d’une personne derrière cette opération ou d’une action coordonnée », a déclaré le vice-Premier ministre Simon Harris à la radio, évoquant une « situation très sérieuse et évolutive ». Cette série de fausses alertes, difficiles à attribuer, a pour conséquence de mobiliser les services de sécurité et de semer la peur, à zéro coût, soulignent les experts.
Sans préjuger de l’identité des auteurs, « il faut le voir dans le cadre des opérations hybrides contre les États européens », a réagi auprès de l’AFP Jean-Marc Rickli, directeur des risques globaux et émergents au Centre de Politique de Genève. « Ça ne coûte rien à celui qui le fait mais ça a un impact important au niveau logistique et bien sûr sur la perception des populations. Les autorités ne peuvent ignorer ces alertes car si une se matérialise, elles seront tenues pour responsable », fait-il valoir.
Le flou entourant les auteurs de ces alertes rend d’autant plus difficile de trouver une parade. Des revendications envoyées jeudi aux aéroports de Rome et de Sofia émanaient des « combattants de l’État masculin ». Cela semble renvoyer au nom d’un mouvement ultranationaliste russe, sans qu’il soit possible de vérifier le lien.
Les Européens accusent régulièrement la Russie et l’Iran de conduire des opérations de déstabilisation contre eux sur leur territoire, qu’il s’agisse de campagnes de désinformation, de sabotage ou de cyberattaques. Des menaces propices à l’escalade, « L’Otan continue de surveiller la situation et de se coordonner étroitement avec les alliés », a ainsi commenté l’organisation de défense transatlantique.
« Éviter de surréagir »
Ces dernières années « ont émergé des situations d’affrontements intermédiaires, sous le seuil des conflits armés, qui impliquent des États dans la conduite d’actions hostiles et de déstabilisation envers d’autres États », parfois au travers de proxys, souligne une source sécuritaire européenne, en citant « actions cyber, manœuvres informationnelles, d’intimidations, ou encore l’instrumentalisation des flux migratoires ».
Selon le chef de la police londonienne, Mark Rowley, il va s’agir de garder la tête froide. « Nous avons déjà connu cela par le passé. Quand nous faisions face aux menaces terroristes liées à l’IRA (groupe paramilitaire irlandais, N.D.L.R.), il y a des décennies, nous parlions de + terrorisme à 10 pence + : un faux appel annonçant une bombe pouvait perturber toute une ville. Nous avons dû apprendre à vivre en faisant la part entre ce qui était un canular et ce qui était réel », a-t-il déclaré vendredi sur la radio BBC 4.
« Dans ce nouvel environnement de menaces, avec des acteurs malveillants aux quatre coins du monde, parfois téléguidés par des États hostiles, nous allons devoir adapter cette même méthode, pour éviter de surréagir à chaque message que nous recevons en ligne ».
Les armées européennes en escorte
L’armée de l’Air française a escorté un avion Aer Lingus qui reliait Dublin et Rome. Récalcitrant, le pilote « aurait refusé » de rejoindre la base militaire d’Évreux, « préférant un aéroport civil ». La justice a ouvert une enquête. Les 151 passagers ont « atterri en toute sécurité », a informé la compagnie.
Des vols de la compagnie finlandaise Finnair pour Rome et Vienne ont aussi été visés par une fausse alerte à la bombe. Celui en direction de la capitale italienne a été escorté par la chasse italienne vers l’aéroport de Fiumicino. Un vol WizzAir Milan-Varsovie et un Varsovie-Bruxelles ont aussi fait l’objet d’alertes.
L’armée de l’air bulgare a escorté trois avions Ryanair, eux aussi « visés par des alertes à la bombe », a informé le ministère de la Défense à Sofia. Quatre avions qui se sont posés ce jeudi matin à Prague ont vécu la même chose.
« Toute menace contre des civils est inacceptable », a dénoncé Apostolo Tzitzikostas, commissaire européen aux Transports qui estime qu’il est « trop tôt pour tirer des conclusions sur le fait que ces incidents » soient liés aux attaques hybrides russes contre l’Europe. Début octobre, plusieurs aéroports de la région de Moscou avaient été fermés dans le cadre.
En Italie, c’est un courriel, signé d’un groupuscule russe masculiniste et homophobe, les « combattants de l’État masculin », envoyé à l’aéroport et à des sociétés aéroportuaires qui a déclenché l’alerte, informe le porte-parole d’Aéroports de Rome.
« Vous êtes tous complices d’un complot criminel. Nous voulons vous anéantir pour cela (…). Votre régime féministe s’en souviendra à jamais. L’explosion se produira dans 60 minutes. Aujourd’hui, votre ciel sera rouge », était-il écrit dans le courrier électronique. L’AFP n’a pas pu confirmer que le groupe russe « État masculin », dissout par le tribunal de Nijni Novgorod en 2021, était bien à l’origine du message masculiniste.
Être le journal de la paix, notre défi quotidien
Depuis Jaurès, la défense de la paix est dans notre ADN.
- Qui informe encore aujourd’hui sur les actions des pacifistes pour le désarmement ?
- Combien de médias rappellent que les combats de décolonisation ont encore cours, et qu’ils doivent être soutenus ?
- Combien valorisent les solidarités internationales, et s’engagent sans ambiguïté aux côtés des exilés ?
Nos valeurs n’ont pas de frontières.
Aidez-nous à soutenir le droit à l’autodétermination et l’option de la paix.
Je veux en savoir plus !

Après cet été, une première partie de Championnat des Nations plutôt réussie, les Bleus entament le deuxième acte de cette nouvelle compétition avec de nouveaux objectifs et schémas de jeu. Le XV de France affrontera Les Fidji, samedi 7 novembre, à 21h10, sur la pelouse du Groupama Stadium de Décines-Charpieu à Lyon.
Derrière ce France-Fidji, première rencontre de la série d’automne du Championnat des Nations, se cache de nombreux enjeux pour les Bleus dirigés par Fabien Galthié. Outre le fait de terminer fin novembre en « ramenant le trophée à la maison », ce qu’a expliqué dans la semaine le deuxième ligne Mickaël Guillard, c’est aussi une énorme revue d’effectif et de plans de jeu qui sera effectué.
En raison des nombreuses blessures qui touchent le camp tricolore — Marchand, Flament, Meafou, Jegou, Jalibert et Ramos sont hors...

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Gérald Rossi,Samuel Gleyze-Esteban
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Dans la sélection de l’Humanité cette semaine : un conte séduisant pour les jeunes et les autres, une traversée intérieure de l’écoanxiété, et un épisode intime de la libération des camps nazis.
« L’Oiseau bleu » enchanteur pour petits et grands
D’un lit posé sur la scène s’extirpent deux enfants, Tyltyl et Mytyl. Frère et sœur. Le jour n’est pas encore levé, et les deux gamins, en vérité, magie de la poésie et du théâtre, dorment toujours. Mais les voilà prêts pour un rêve extraordinaire. Tel est le fil conducteur de cette pièce mise en scène par Marjorie Nakache.
Écrit par Maurice Maeterlinck L’Oiseau Bleu, adapté au théâtre, au cinéma et même en BD, a été jouée pour la première fois à Paris en 1911 après sa création en 1908 à Moscou. C’est aussi en 1911 que Maeterlinck est lauréat du Nobel de littérature.
Il y est question « d’appendre à voir, de réfléchir au-delà...

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: « Crime et châtiment » d’Aki Kaurismäki, une adaptation du classique de Dostoïevski sur grand écran
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Vincent Ostria
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
En 1983, le Finlandais Aki Kaurismäki débute sa carrière en s’attaquant à un monument de la littérature, « Crime et châtiment », dont il propose une transposition très personnelle, qui brille par sa retenue et sa mélancolie rentrée.
Dès son premier long-métrage, Aki Kaurismäki, phare du cinéma finlandais, est en totale possession de ses moyens. Il va d’entrée de jeu imposer un regard à la fois nostalgique, poétique et ironique dans une adaptation moderne du classique de Dostoïevski Crime et châtiment.
Une version très libre du récit, dont le cinéaste éradique la dimension psychologique ainsi que de nombreuses...

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/cair-.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/cair-.text:
Cair shuts down Florida office as judge declines reversal of terrorist designation
The Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair) has shut down its operations in Florida after a judge declined to reverse the terrorist designation of the group that the state legislature and the governor had imposed earlier this year.
Chief Judge Allen C Winsor of the US District Court for the Northern District of Florida made his decision on Wednesday, while acknowledging Florida's “novel - and perhaps unprecedented" new law allowing for terrorist designations of non-profit groups without due process.
But ultimately, he said Cair's emergency request did not adequately prove that the group was suffering a criminal punishment.
Winsor did, however, say Florida officials cannot prevent Cair from accessing legal services. Florida officials also pledged not to prosecute Cair's board, its staff, or its third-party associates.
Cair has said it will now appeal the decision.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
A visit to the website CairFlorida.org on Friday only produced the following message on a dark backdrop: "We have suspended our operations in Florida because of Governor [Ron] DeSantis and other state officials’ baseless and unconstitutional enforcement of the state’s unprecedented new 'domestic terrorist organization' laws against us. The ACLU, SPLC, and their partners are representing us in a federal lawsuit challenging this designation on First Amendment and due process grounds."
In a statement, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement called Winsor's ruling "the right call for the safety of Floridians" and said it "remains vigilant against threats and committed to keeping Floridians safe".
Cair's national deputy director, Edward Ahmed Mitchell, mourned the loss of its operations in the state.
"For the first time in over twenty years, Florida Muslims cannot call their community’s leading civil rights organization for help if they experience a hate crime at their mosque, illegal discrimination in the workplace, violent bullying in school, or any other acts of bigotry," he said in a statement.
"The unprecedented notion that Governor DeSantis has the power to punish an American civil rights organization for its speech and unilaterally force the closure of its doors without due process is an affront to the Constitution."
Multiple designations
In July, Cair sued the governor of Florida for designating it a "domestic terrorist organisation" alongside some of the most deadly drug cartels in the Americas.
Cair filed the lawsuit in partnership with non-profits The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC).
The designation opens up Cair to "immediate and irreparable harm, including the shuttering of all their operations and advocacy in the state", the group said in a statement.
Florida has further listed the Muslim Brotherhood, which has no known operation in the US or a centralised headquarters globally, as a terrorist organisation, as well as "antifa", which is short for the anti-fascist movement. It also has no defined scope or location.
"Officials can brand nonprofit corporations with debilitating stigma and then use an array of state authorities to immediately silence and incapacitate the organization, its employees, its members, and a wide range of others associated with the group through extraordinarily broad and severe criminal, civil, and administrative penalties," Cair said at the time.
The designation stems from HB 1471, which the Florida legislature passed in March. DeSantis signed it in April, and it went into effect on 1 July.
DeSantis had previously tried to go it alone, signing an executive order in December to blacklist Cair, but a federal judge blocked it earlier this year.
After the legislature adopted the bill, Cair sought an emergency injunction to stop the enforcement of HB 1471.
HB 1471's language indicates that providing support to designated terrorist groups will lead to criminal liability, and ensures that religious codes - sometimes protected by the First Amendment - do not supersede Florida law.
Cair and its partners said in the lawsuit that the designation model "contains no requirement that notice to the designated group include all the reasons for the designation and all the material evidence - inculpatory and exculpatory - that state decisionmakers may rely on to make or approve the designation. It does not require the State to prove or even provide evidence that the organization violated any law".
