https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new White House chief of staff?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new White House chief of staff?
Miller has been a close confidant of Trump since 2016 and an architect of the president’s hardline immigration policies.
United States President Donald Trump has tapped his longtime adviser Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff.
The move on Friday represented a doubling down on Trump’s most controversial policies following his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing earlier this week.
Democrats will take control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in January, and are widely expected to launch investigations into Miller’s role in the White House.
The 41-year-old Miller has been one of Trump’s most vocal defenders and is widely seen as an architect of the president’s mass deportation campaign.
In his post on Truth Social, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors”, saying he would take over the role from Susie Wiles on Monday.
An early adherent
Miller had built a reputation as a conservative activist long before entering Trump’s orbit.
At Santa Monica High School, he cut his teeth railing against what he described as liberal school policies on local radio shows.
At Duke University, he led the Duke Conservative Union and became a staunch advocate for three of the school’s lacrosse players after they were accused of rape.
After college, he moved to Washington, DC, where he worked as a legislative aide to Republican members of Congress and Republican Senator Jeff Sessions.
He joined Trump’s initial presidential campaign in January 2016, where he was credited with shaping the president’s messaging and caustic political stylings.
“I think he and Trump hit it off from the very beginning,” former Trump adviser Steve Bannon told The Associated Press news agency in 2017. “I think he helped Trump find his voice.”
What was his role during Trump’s first term?
Following Trump’s surprise victory in the 2016 race, Miller assumed the role of presidential adviser and speechwriter.
He served as an influential voice in shaping Trump’s most strident actions related to immigration, often framing the issues as an effort to protect Western “civilisation”.
During that period, Democratic lawmakers accused Miller of perpetuating white nationalist rhetoric. In 2019, the Southern Poverty Law Center released emails allegedly showing the Trump adviser supporting white nationalist websites and ideologies.
He is credited with shaping the Department of Justice’s 2018 “Zero Tolerance” policy at the US border, which called for the arrest of nearly every adult crossing into the US without legal documentation.
The scheme resulted in widespread family separation, with children barred from being housed in criminal detention facilities along with their parents. Trump later changed the policy via executive order, amid widespread outrage.
As an adviser to Trump, Miller campaigned to end Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), a programme that allowed individuals brought to the US as children without documentation to receive legal paperwork for education and employment. The programme stopped accepting new applicants in 2021.
Miller also drove wide-scale visa restrictions during Trump’s first term, including a 2017 travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries, which came to be known as the “Muslim travel ban”.
The initial order blocked citizens of Syria, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen from entering the US for 90 days. An adjusted version of the policy was eventually upheld by the US Supreme Court.
He later became a top proponent of Trump’s unfounded claims that the 2020 election was stolen, supporting a scheme for Trump to be certified as the victor.
Trump 2.0
Miller remained by Trump’s side as the former president staged a political comeback ahead of the 2024 presidential vote. He became Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser when the administration retook office in January 2025.
Since then, he has helped to orchestrate Trump’s mass deportation drive, which has seen immigration enforcement agents flood communities across the country, increasingly targeting individuals with no or only minor criminal records.
In May 2025, Miller told Fox News the administration had “set a goal of a minimum of 3,000 arrests for ICE every day, and President Trump is going to keep pushing to get that number up higher each and every day”.
He has also been a vocal defender of increasingly violent tactics by immigration agents. He initially defended the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January. He initially called both Good and Pretti “terrorists” before walking back the statement about Pretti.
In his return to the White House, Miller also unsuccessfully sought to end birthright citizenship, while becoming an increasingly vocal defender of Trump’s military actions in the Western Hemisphere.
He endorsed the US abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and told CNN in January that the US had a right to seize Greenland based on its military might.
“We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world … that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” he said.
“These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.”
What does a chief of staff do?
It was not immediately clear how Miller’s new role would affect his influence over Trump.
The chief of staff is typically tasked with overseeing White House staff and hiring, maintaining the president’s calendar, and advising the president on policy.
Some insiders refer to the role, which largely controls information flows, as the “gatekeeper” to the presidency.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/why-n.title: Why nearly 100 Muslims won national, local races in the US midterm elections
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/why-n.author: Yasmine El-Sabawi
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/why-n.text:
Why nearly 100 Muslims won national, local races in the US midterm elections
At least 97 Muslim Americans have won their races in this week's midterm elections, encompassing the federal, state, and local levels, according to the Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair).
It's hard to imagine that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's landslide win last year didn't have an impact on his fellow Muslims who hadn't entertained the possibilities.
More than a dozen other candidates are still awaiting the full ballot count - depending on individual county rules and the way mail-in votes are handled - but they are ahead of their opponents as of Friday morning.
They come from a pool of 168 Muslim-American candidates who made it past the primary stage of their races, which is when they compete within their own party to earn the nomination.
Seven Muslim Americans are headed to Washington, DC.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Six are going to the House of Representatives, including incumbents Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, Andre Carson, and Lateefah Simon; and they will be joined by freshmen Adam Hamawy and Darializa Avila Chevalier.
If Aisha Wahab secures her win, which had not been decided by Friday morning local time, she would also join the incumbent House members.
One Muslim American is going to the Senate: Abdul El-Sayed. He will be the first to ever serve a six-year term in the upper chamber.
Cair has tracked 39 other statewide offices where Muslim Americans won, ranging from attorney general to the state legislature and the state senate.
At the county and municipal level, there are 16 winners, and education and school boards saw 27 Muslim-Americans elected.
Eight were elected to be judges.
The wins make for an all-time record, and come as anti-Muslim sentiment and rhetoric, particularly among Republicans, is at its highest in a generation, according to groups like Muslim Public Affairs Council (Mpac), the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSO), and the Institute for Social Policy and Understanding (ISPU).
Policy over party
Muslims make up just one percent of the US population, at some 5.5 million people. But they receive an outsized amount of media scrutiny and online attacks.
Mpac had warned prior to Tuesday's elections that voter intimidation tactics may also keep Muslim American voters from going to the polls.
But Muslim voter registration rose by at least 25 percent over the past year, and at least one survey showed a 93 percent turnout to the ballot box.
Eighty percent said they primarily voted for Democrats, compared with six percent for Republicans, Cair found.
'Muslims tend to vote more based on policy than party lines'
- Urooj Ali, Georgia Voter Project
NBC's exit polling takes that further and shows that it was Muslims, out of all the faith groups or none at all, who voted the most for Democrats.
For comparison, in 2024, the ISPU said more than 20 percent of Muslim Americans voted for Donald Trump, as he pledged to end all wars and boost affordability.
"From our field programme... we are seeing that Muslims tend to vote more based on policy than party lines. So a lot of them actually identify as independent rather with the Democratic Party or with the Republican Party," Urooj Ali, the communications director for the non-partisan Georgia Voter Project, told Middle East Eye.
Georgia is a highly coveted swing state in the American South, and as of Tuesday, it has two Democratic senators and a Democratic governor - the first black woman to win the office.
"Georgia actually broke a midterm election record for early voting this year, so it was the highest voter turnout for early voting in a midterm election," Ali said. "Around 30,000 Muslims voted early this election cycle, and for context, in 2022, only 36,000 Muslims voted total, including election day."
Of the four hijab-wearing Muslims who are now state senators-elect, Georgia's Ruwa Romman is among them.
In the US, citizens have to be registered to vote, and in most cases before election day - otherwise they will be turned away. Some states, like Michigan, allow for same-day registration.
Defiant
Over the last month, there have been several anti-Muslim incidents across the US, ranging from vandalism featuring explicit graffiti across several buildings in California to threats to shoot hijabi women in Illinois and even one shooting at a Mosque in California that killed a security guard.
That mosque shooting came shortly after CSO issued a 36-page report entitled "Manufacturing the Muslim Threat", revealing that "Republican elected officials built a coordinated anti-Muslim campaign involving 1,111 social media posts, eight bills, and a 62-member congressional caucus" in 2025, meeting the criteria of "speech likely to inspire violence".
Cair's survey showed that Islamophobia was a key factor in moving Muslim Americans this election cycle, with 70 percent saying that anti-Muslim sentiment motivated them to vote.
The ISPU, which created the National American Islamophobia Index, showed a steady rise in such sentiment in its latest findings from 2025, saying that on a scale of 0 to 100, the index jumped from 25 in 2022 to 33 in 2025.
The jump was most pronounced among white Evangelicals (15 points), Catholics (12 points), and Jews (11 points), the ISPU said.
But the incidents have not had the intended effect of scaring Muslims away.
Sameerah Munshi, who was the sole Muslim woman to serve on the Advisory Board of Lay Leaders on Trump's Religious Liberties Commission before she resigned in protest in March, told MEE that the changing demographic of Muslim Americans means this generation is more emboldened and defiant.
"I'm basically Gen Z, so I didn't really get a full understanding of the 9/11 aftermath and how things were," she said. "I think this generation of us who have grown up with that in mind... we didn't really, I think, experience the hopelessness that a lot of Muslims who were adults or who were voting at that time felt, and I think that's kind of pushed this generation to really be politically engaged."
Munshi insisted that the way popular culture has come to challenge pro-Israel, anti-Palestinian language and laws over the past three years has also encouraged Muslim Americans to take a stronger stand.
Cair's survey showed that 76 percent of voters named Gaza and Palestinian human rights among their most important issues, and 80 percent specifically said Israel's assault on Gaza, which the United Nations and Holocaust scholars call a genocide, was a "major influence" on their vote.
"We've been seeing on our social media platforms that big people like Tucker Carlson have flipped," Munshi said. "All these establishment Democrats are slowly making way for these progressives who are pro-Palestine, and who are very adamantly against the state of Israel."
Former Vice President Kamala Harris famously lost her bid for the presidency in part because of a refusal to abandon her unconditional support for Israel as it was killing up to 300 Palestinians a day in Gaza - most of them civilians.
Intersectional values
When Munshi resigned, it was in protest against a crackdown on a Catholic colleague's defence of Palestinian rights.
'At James Talarico’s victory speech, you had people holding ‘Love Thy Neighbor’ signs. That is the same as saying “alhamdulillah” on stage. That’s the same expression'
- Haris Tarin, Vice President MPAC
Carrie Prejean-Boller was removed from the panel, whose members are appointed by Trump himself, by Texas Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick, chairman of the Religious Liberty Commission.
Patrick lost his re-election bid on Tuesday after 12 years in office. He was handily defeated by the first Democrat to take up the post in nearly three decades, and the first woman in the state's history.
Deep-red Texas, from the governor down, went almost wholly blue this week. Senator Ted Cruz, who has often engaged in anti-Muslim rhetoric, remains the only Republican in a senior role in the state.
Despite being a self-described Christian, Cruz has attacked two Democrat preachers who have been newly elected to the Senate, specifically for their inclusion of Muslims and Palestinians in their religious positions.
Cruz's new colleague and the other senator from Texas, James Talarico, has said that Islam, like Christianity, is an "equal pathway to truth". He has also said that "seeing what's happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being" on actor Ilana Glazer's podcast.
Adam Hamilton, the first Democratic senator to be elected in Kansas in nearly a century, has said he believes Christians will meet Muslims in heaven, leading to Cruz's outrage. And shortly after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, Hamilton, who has longstanding connections to Palestinian Christians, highlighted in an interview the "underlying problem that keeps these kinds of things (violence) coming to the surface - that also needs to be understood if ever there’s going to be peace".
Both Hamilton and Talarico, much in the same vein as senator-elect Sayed, have honed in on their religious lifestyles rather than shying away from them to run for a party that has typically eschewed outward acts of faith.
"Sometimes progressives get that we are a faithful, religious nation," Jamiah Adams, a communications expert and founder of Believers Consulting, told MEE.
Religious Americans of all faiths, she said, "are values-based people... [and] our values are not being meted out right now."
"Those candidates who uplifted their faith and talked about how their values align with what they want for their constituents, they were successful because they spoke in that values conversation."
Sayed's fiery victory speech in the early hours of Wednesday morning began with an "inshallah" and then an "alhamdullilah", and his campaign was centred on his religiosity as a Muslim who takes a break five times a day to pray.
"Historically, Democrats didn't know how to talk about faith," Haris Tarin, vice president for policy and programming at Mpac, told MEE.
"They were scared to talk about faith. They actually tried their best to run away from talking about faith. What [Tuesday] showed was that the Democrats who actually lean into their faith, whatever their respective faith may be, it works, because Americans want authenticity and they want people who actually believe in who they are themselves."
"At James Talarico's victory speech, you had people holding 'Love Thy Neighbor' signs. That is the same as saying "alhamdulillah" on stage. That's the same expression," Tarin added.
Identity politics
While Muslim Americans specifically see Islamophobia and Palestine as core issues at election time, they still mainly vote just like the vast majority of their compatriots: on the economy and job creation, according to polling carried out by the ISPU.
And just like voters, candidates who identify as Muslim make that, for the most part, just a slice of who they are.
Mamdani ran a mostly secular campaign, and then somewhat leaned into his faith after he was elected. Sayed, on the other hand, has said he is devout and that his commitment to his religion is why he felt fit to run.
Not all Muslims are progressives or Democrats at all.
Abe Hamadeh, who was just re-elected to the House of Representatives, representing Arizona, is a Republican who has received Trump's endorsement. The Republican Party, under this president and the influence of The Heritage Foundation, is staunchly pro-Israel and has assumed a largely anti-Muslim stance.
In a written statement provided to MEE by the non-partisan Muslim Americans in Public Service, its chair, Ahmad Maaty, said he is "incredibly proud to witness the growing number of Muslim Americans stepping into public service and positions of leadership across our country".
"Seeing members of our community increasingly represented in elected office and civic institutions is both inspiring and meaningful. These victories reflect years of community engagement, perseverance, hard work, and the growing participation of Muslim Americans in shaping the future of our communities and our country. They are a reminder that our voices matter, our participation matters, and we have a meaningful role to play in the decisions that shape our lives."
Junaid Ahmed, who identifies as a Muslim progressive and lost the Democratic primary in Illinois' 8th District in March, said the slate of newly elected Muslim officials from this week represents a win for diversity more than anything else, given that Muslims are a plethora of races, ethnicities, and points of view.
"[This] just takes it to the next level, right? The people of colour... I'm very hopeful. I'm very excited," he told MEE.
"Hopefully, what this House and Senate does is show the American people that when we say 'America First', that starts showing in the policy."
Ahmed told MEE he is planning a bid for the House of Representatives again in 2028.
Ali, with the Georgia Muslim Voter Project, said there is no "agenda" rooted in the actual identity of being Muslim American, other than "leading with the community care aspect".
Being Muslim is more of a way of life rather than an identity," she told MEE.
"It's more... to ensure that like we are leaving the world a better place than we received it."

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Protesters break into Microsoft data centre site in Amsterdam
Data centres face protests across Europe due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use.
Protesters in the Netherlands have broken into a construction site for a new Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, the latest action in a growing movement sweeping Europe.
Several hundred activists occupied the site in the Sloterdijk district on Friday, responding to a call for a two-day protest across Europe against data centres, which handle the large processing workloads associated with artificial intelligence (AI). Demonstrators clashed with police as some climbed a crane and set off flares.
Nathan Timmer, of the protest group Geef Tegengas – which translates as Push Back – told local broadcaster AT5 that demonstrators were occupying the site in an effort to stop construction.
“We don’t want it to be built. Nobody needs it,” Timmer said. “The only thing this will be used for is AI slop. AI warfare, data surveillance and committing genocide. We don’t want that.”
Pro-Palestinian activists also joined the demonstrations in the Dutch capital. By late afternoon police were escorting activists off the construction site, though some remained, local media reported.
Dutch police said they detained 150-200 people suspected of trespassing during the protest.
Microsoft said it was aware of the Amsterdam demonstration.
“We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully,” a spokesperson said. “However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
Data centres face resistance around the world due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use. Activists argue that the boom in facilities serving cloud computing and AI is moving faster than public consultation and environmental oversight.
Dozens of civil society and grassroots groups have said they will join the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday in 15 European countries, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom, organisers said.
In Germany, a dozen protesters gathered in front of a data centre on the outskirts of Berlin on Friday.
“We want to put a stop to this blind construction of data centres around Germany, regardless of any environmental concerns,” said protest spokeswoman Caro Weber. “This is really, really dangerous for our future.”
About 100 people also protested against data centres in front of the Polish parliament, representing communities around Warsaw where new centres are planned.
In Italy, the fast-growing data centre industry is facing an equally rapid rise in grassroots opposition, particularly in the northern Lombardy region, the country’s main hub for digital infrastructure.

Yemen's Houthis granting ships safe passage via email: Report
Yemen’s Houthis are controlling maritime transit of the Red Sea through a system under which vessels can request safe passage via email, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.
The Houthis, who control swaths of Yemen, declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia earlier this year, after which some ships began contacting them before transiting the Red Sea, the Journal reported.
If the Houthis reply, they typically do so within 24 hours, the newspaper said, citing crew member accounts and emails it reviewed.
The Journal included one email in which the master of an unnamed ship declared it “has no connections with Israel, the United Kingdom and the United States of America” and said “we kindly request your confirmation for safe passage.”
Vessels allegedly linked to those countries have been repeatedly targeted by the Houthis.
In another email, the Houthis responded to a separate request from a Chinese container ship: “We hope you are keeping well. We are glad that you understood the criteria for the scope of the vessels ban,” they said.
The Houthis said the ship had a permit for transit that is valid for seven days, adding: “We also invite you to subscribe to our email alert service to receive the latest news and updates.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Meghan Markle’s father arrested in US over alleged child sex abuse photos
US authorities found sexually explicit photos that appeared to show Thomas Markle with prepubescent girls.
The estranged father of Britain’s Prince Harry’s wife, Meghan Markle, has been arrested in the United States on a charge of possession of child sexual abuse material.
The US Department of Justice on Friday announced that Thomas Markle Sr was arrested in Florida after law enforcement officers discovered “sexually explicit photographs” of him with prepubescent girls in two storage units, located in the Los Angeles area, that he rented for nearly two decades.
“Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions”, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel said on Thursday.
According to the Justice Department, authorities learned in October that an individual signed an affidavit stating they had discovered child sex abuse material among Markle’s possessions in the Philippines.
Law enforcement interviewed a separate individual who told them the 82-year-old had rented a storage unit near Los Angeles since 2008. Information gathered from the first individual led to the discovery of a second unit.
After receiving warrants, the Justice Department said FBI agents searched the two units registered to Thomas. Inside, they found 78 items, including photos, film negatives and books that contained explicit imagery of him with underage girls.
The affidavit described three of those photographs. Two showed a man, who a witness identified as Thomas, with a nude prepubescent girl. The third photo shows a nude underage girl in what appeared to be a Philippine hotel room.
Officials, according to the affidavit, also found photos that appeared to show Thomas with “children in various stages of undress”.
Thomas was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the US.
‘Deeply distressed’
Meghan issued a statement to The New York Times in October, saying she first learned of the allegations against her father in 2018, when a letter detailing them was sent to the unit of London’s Metropolitan Police that was handling her security then.
“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours,” the duchess of Sussex wrote to the Times in an apparent reference to reports by the Sun, a British tabloid, on the allegations. “My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.”
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them,” she added.
The arrest of Thomas comes as President Donald Trump’s administration has been criticised for its handling of cases related to the abuse of children, particularly the release of files on the investigation into convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.
Last year, King Charles stripped Prince Andrew of his princely title as he tried to shield the royal family from the scandal surrounding his brother’s relationship with Epstein.
Meghan, Prince Harry and their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, relocated back to the United Kingdom in August.
The Associated Press tried to reach Meghan’s representative on Friday but has not yet heard back.
Thomas Markle is expected to appear in a Florida court on Friday. If convicted, the Justice Department said he could face a maximum sentence of 20 years in a US federal prison.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/us.title: US midterms: A blue tsunami has rebuked Trump. Will it end Washington's wars?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/us.author: Sami Al-Arian
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/us.text:
US midterms: A blue tsunami has rebuked Trump. Will it end Washington's wars?
The political tsunami that swept across the US on 3 November was extraordinary in both its scale and implications. The electoral flood that overwhelmed the Republicans was not simply another midterm correction.
It was a sweeping rejection of Donald Trump's presidency: his economic policies, his wars, the corruption charges against his administration and his increasingly confrontational use of presidential power.
But the more consequential question is what happens next. Will this upheaval produce a fundamental reassessment of American foreign policy, particularly towards Israel, Palestine, Iran, and the wider Middle East? Or will the Democratic establishment try to restore the familiar bipartisan consensus that helped produce the very crises now confronting Washington? The answer will shape American politics throughout 2027 and beyond.
The scale of the Republican defeat exceeded expectations. Democrats captured both chambers of Congress. They flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa, North Carolina, Ohio and Maine, bringing their total to at least 54. The count in Alaska favours the Democrats, and Mississippi could still elect its first Democratic senator since 1982.
Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since 1932, and Texas, which Republicans had dominated in statewide elections for decades, elected Democrat James Talarico. South Carolina and Iowa, long Republican strongholds, delivered extraordinary upsets.

Among the losers were several candidates Trump had personally picked, in an election he had sought to nationalise around his name.
Democrats also made substantial gains in the House, with a distinct possibility of reaching 258 members, a gain of more than 40 seats, while governorships won in traditionally Republican states, including Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada, showed that the backlash extended well beyond Washington into the Republican Party's geographical and demographic foundations.
The price of the Iran war
The national exit poll found that nine in 10 voters considered government corruption a major or crucial factor in their decision, that 63 percent regarded the decision to attack Iran as wrong, and that 87 percent worried about the price of fuel.
The same poll found that nearly three-quarters of voters said the war was a crucial or major factor in their decision, and about a third called it crucial. Nearly eight in 10 said inflation was causing their families hardship, and only 38 percent approved of Trump's performance.
Trump had promised peace, prosperity and an end to costly foreign entanglements. Americans got mounting economic pressure and Trump's war of choice
The war on Iran may not have been the sole cause of the Republican collapse, but its military, economic and political consequences contributed greatly to the backlash.
By late October, average petrol prices had reached about $4.27 a gallon, more than a third higher than when Trump returned to office less than two years earlier. Diesel had climbed even more sharply, to about $6.35. Disruptions to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damage to regional infrastructure were the main reasons.
Vice President JD Vance attributed the Republican defeat directly to the war. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance declared, adding that Trump himself had acknowledged its electoral consequences. Trump subsequently conceded that the conflict and higher fuel prices had damaged Republican prospects.
Vance's admission went to the heart of the contradiction between Trump's promises and his record. He had promised peace, prosperity and an end to costly foreign entanglements. Instead, Americans got mounting economic pressure and Trump's war of choice. Trump had squandered much of the political capital that enabled his return to power in 2024.
Michigan and Texas
The deeper implications of this election were clearest in Michigan. The victory of Abdul El-Sayed over Republican Mike Rogers was significant not simply because it preserved a Democratic Senate seat, but because it challenged assumptions about the viability of candidates openly critical of American support for Israel.
Sayed, a progressive Egyptian American physician and former public health official, became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. His victory followed a contentious Democratic primary in which establishment figures questioned whether his progressive positions, particularly his opposition to Israel's assault on Gaza, would sink him in a competitive state.
Michigan's electorate proved more complicated than those calculations suggested. The state contains substantial Arab and Muslim communities, particularly around Detroit, alongside organised labour, African American voters, progressive activists and other constituencies whose priorities cannot be reduced to a single issue.
In 2024, anger over the Biden administration's support for Israel's war on Gaza had opened a profound rupture between sections of these communities and the Democratic establishment, and the "Uncommitted" movement gained national prominence in Michigan.
Sayed's victory demonstrated that a broad electoral coalition can be built without abandoning criticism of Israeli policies or accommodating every demand of Aipac and the pro-Israel political machine. This does not mean that Michigan has become uniformly pro-Palestinian, or that Gaza determined every race. It means that the political boundaries surrounding the Palestinian question are shifting.
Talarico's victory in Texas, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1988, pushed the same boundary further.
Talarico made his position on the Israel lobby and Gaza explicit: "I've never taken money from Aipac, and I'm not taking money from Aipac in this campaign. Seeing what's happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being."
For years, Democratic leaders operated on the assumption that unconditional support for Israel was both strategically indispensable and politically necessary. The emergence of winning candidates who openly reject Aipac's money and criticise Israel's conduct suggests that this assumption is becoming untenable.
The significance of Talarico's victory is not merely that a Democrat won in Texas. It is that a Democrat could win in Texas while openly challenging one of the most entrenched orthodoxies of American foreign policy.
The Democrats' contradiction
Sayed and Talarico will enter the Senate as critics of their own party's record on Gaza. President Joe Biden's administration armed Israel during its genocide in Gaza and defended it at the UN.
In December 2023, the administration bypassed congressional review to sell Israel tank shells and vetoed a resolution in the UN Security Council calling for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire. The Democrats' victory over Trump cannot erase that shameful record.
According to Brown University's Costs of War project, Washington provided at least $21.7bn in military assistance to Israel in the two years after 7 October 2023, under Biden and Trump.
Yet the Democratic Party is increasingly divided over the very policies its last administration pursued. This election produced at least 11 newly elected members of Congress, two senators and nine House members, who have publicly advocated for Palestinian rights, criticised Israel's conduct in Gaza or opposed aspects of American military assistance to Israel.
Some have called for ending military assistance altogether, while others demand conditions, accountability or a reassessment of the relationship.
They join established congressional critics such as Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, while figures such as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani represent a broader political challenge to Israel's defenders. Together, they expand a constituency willing to challenge longstanding assumptions about the influence of the Israel lobby and unconditional American support for Israel.
None of this means that the Democratic Party has abandoned its traditional commitments to the Zionist state. Its establishment remains closely connected to the foreign policy institutions, influential donors and strategic consensus that regard Israel as a central American ally. A Democratic congressional majority should not be confused with an antiwar majority, much less a consensus in favour of Palestinian liberation.
The election results were not simply a repudiation of Trump and his war on Iran, conducted in partnership with Israel. They were also a challenge to the Democratic establishment of Biden, Antony Blinken and Jake Sullivan, whose policies enabled and sustained Israel's assault on Gaza.
The question is whether the dissenters remain a minority or become part of a more fundamental transformation of the party. The electoral victory has created an opening, but it has not resolved the struggle over the party's direction on Palestinian self-determination and freedom from occupation.
What changes in January
When the new Congress convenes on 3 January, the balance of power in Washington will shift dramatically. For the first time in Trump's second presidency, both chambers will be controlled by the opposition, which will substantially weaken his ability to pass legislation, secure senior appointments and avoid scrutiny.
Democrats will have considerable power to obstruct, investigate and expose administration policies, but much less power to impose an alternative foreign policy
Democratic committees will acquire the power to investigate, subpoena and hold hearings on the Iran war, military spending and arms transfers, and Congress's powers over appropriations could be used to condition support for Israel.
Trump nonetheless retains constitutional authority over diplomacy and military command, and overriding his veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats do not possess.
The outgoing Republican Congress is under pressure to pass the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) and associated appropriations during the lame-duck session, while it still controls both chambers. That could fold Israel's massive military funding into broader defence and intelligence legislation.
For Israel, this period deserves particular scrutiny. The existing military relationship includes long-term assistance arrangements, weapons contracts and the War Reserve Stockpile Allies-Israel programme, whose authorisation runs to 1 January 2027. Any attempt to renew or expand these arrangements before the transition could constrain the incoming Congress's ability to exercise real leverage over dangerous Israeli policies.
Democrats will therefore have considerable power to obstruct, investigate and expose administration policies, but much less power to impose an alternative foreign policy. The immediate consequence is likely to be institutional confrontation rather than a new strategic direction.
A turning point, not a revolution
For Palestine, the election has created opportunities but offers no guarantees. A larger congressional bloc critical of Israel could increase scrutiny of arms transfers, settlement expansion and the treatment of Palestinians under an entrenched system of apartheid and military occupation.
Congressional hearings could give greater visibility to first-hand Palestinian testimony and independent investigations, and Democratic leaders could face pressure to reconsider the longstanding practice of shielding Israel from accountability.
The relationship is nonetheless deeply institutionalised. According to the Council on Foreign Relations, Israel has received more than $300bn in American assistance since its founding, adjusted for inflation, underpinned by military cooperation, intelligence arrangements, domestic political networks and decades of bipartisan commitments. These structures will not disappear because of one election.
On Iran, the implications may be more immediate. Congressional investigations into who authorised the war, what it cost and what it achieved could constrain further escalation and strengthen demands for diplomacy.
Vance's admission matters here. When a sitting vice president identifies a foreign war as the principal cause of his party's defeat, he is acknowledging that military intervention has become a serious domestic liability.
Opposition to Trump's war does not, however, imply support for a different approach to Iran: many establishment Democrats share Republican positions on Iran's regional influence and nuclear programme, even when they disagree over the use of force.
Washington's strategic relationships with regional authoritarian regimes, including Saudi Arabia, the Gulf states, Egypt and Jordan, are equally unlikely to change suddenly. The coming debate will be about the methods, costs and sustainability of American dominance in the region, not its abandonment.
The November elections have produced three developments. First, they have delivered a sweeping repudiation of Trump and weakened his ability to govern without institutional resistance. Second, they have shown that criticism of American support for Israel is no longer confined to the margins of Congress.
Third, they have exposed a visible contradiction between the Democratic establishment's record and the demands of a growing constituency seeking accountability, restraint and a different relationship with the Middle East.
Electoral change is not necessarily structural change. The system that produced bipartisan support for Israel's assault on Gaza remains largely intact, and its military institutions, lobbying networks and strategic assumptions continue to exercise enormous influence.
The question for the next two years is whether the new congressional balance will merely constrain Trump or begin to challenge the deeper foundations of American foreign policy.
The flood may have swept away Republican control of Congress. It has not yet swept away the structures that sustain America's wars or its blind support for Israel.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay starting 12-day Latin America tour
The 71-year-old pontiff is visiting three countries despite undergoing surgery to remove a tumour last month.
Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Uruguay as he begins a 12-day tour of South America, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.
The 71-year-old head of the Roman Catholic Church touched down in Montevideo on Friday after a 13-hour flight from Rome, telling reporters he feels “fairly good”.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place,” Leo told reporters on board the papal plane. “I had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward. And I am very happy to say praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistance, I’m here today, I think in fairly good shape.”
On his trip, the pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades.
His packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay – the region’s least Catholic and most secular country – will include a visit to a neighbourhood with heavy gang violence, a mass in Paysandu, about 375 kilometres (230 miles) from Montevideo, and another mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometres (60 miles) from the capital.
Cardinal Daniel Sturla, archbishop of Montevideo, told the AFP news agency that there was “widespread interest in the pope’s visit that goes well beyond the confines of the Catholic Church”, with tickets for masses in Paysandu and Florida quickly running out.
The regional trip is somewhat of a homecoming journey for Leo, as he will finish in Peru in three weeks, where he served for almost two decades as a missionary, forming a deep attachment to the continent.
The trip will take the pope to the former Inca capital of Cusco and the Amazon rainforest, and he will also revisit his old diocese of Chiclayo for a private visit to a chapel he helped rebuild.
Leo said on Wednesday that he was looking forward to returning to a region “so dear to me”.
The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics said he hoped the trip would “strengthen faith, renew hope, and rekindle the fire of charity” in the countries he is visiting, which face rising inequality and violence, as well as a decline in Catholic followers.
Despite undergoing an operation on October 13 to remove a cancerous tumour, doctors have given him the all-clear to travel, and the Vatican said no special medical measures were necessary beyond the standard care on papal trips.
“His stamina is fantastic. The way that he’s singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief. She noted that Leo had passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his surgery and was eager to get on the road.

Harmeet Dhillon, who led anti-Israel campus protest crackdown, resigns
Several senior US Justice Department officials have resigned, including Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon who was one of the department’s leads in the administration’s efforts to crack down against anti-Israel protests on college campuses.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump, announced on Thursday that he had accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon.
According to Democracy Now, Dhillon spent her 19-month tenure "gutting" civil rights, and diversity, equity and inclusion protections in education, and led the campaign to target dozens of universities nationwide over student-led pro-Palestine activism and campus protests.
It added that under Dhillon, the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division stopped investigating accusations of systemic racism and sexism.
Dhillon was also directly involved in unsuccessful attempts to obtain voter registration lists from some 30 states ahead of this week's midterm elections that dealt heavy defeats to Trump's Republican Party.
In her resignation letter, cited by US media outlets, Dillon said that she submitted it in October and agreed to remain in her position until the election.
Blanche also announced on Friday the resignations of Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg, and Jason Reding Quinones, US attorney for the Southern District of Florida.
Quinones oversaw an investigation into former intelligence officials whom Trump accused of seeking to remove him from power.
The Justice Department under Trump has pursued cases against a number of perceived enemies, and several prosecutors have lost their jobs over their reluctance or inability to bring charges.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: USA women throttle Switzerland 7-0 to open hockey worlds amid jersey dispute
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The United States opened their defense of the women’s ice hockey world championship with a 7-0 victory over Switzerland on Friday in Esbjerg, Denmark.
Hannah Bilka and Laila Edwards scored twice each, while Kirsten Simms, Hilary Knight and Casey O’Brien also found the net as the Americans pulled away after a competitive opening period. Caroline Harvey contributed three assists.
Bilka broke the deadlock nine minutes into the game, but Switzerland goaltender Andrea Brändli kept the favorites at bay for the remainder of the first period. The Americans took control in the second, with O’Brien doubling their lead before Edwards converted a power play just 15 seconds after a Swiss penalty.
The US outshot Switzerland 15-3 in the second period before adding four more goals in the third, including Bilka’s second and a solo effort from Simms.
Knight, the United States’ longest-tenured player making her 16th world championship appearance, scored midway through the final period to extend her tournament records to 68 goals and 121 points in 88 games. The 37-year-old is the competition’s all-time leader in both categories.
Aerin Frankel earned the shutout in goal, stopping all eight shots she faced as the Americans improved to 14-0 all-time against Switzerland, bronze medalists at February’s Olympics.
All but one member of the American roster, forward Joy Dunne, plays in the Professional Women’s Hockey League.
Canada opened their tournament by easing past Sweden 5-1 on Friday in Herning.
The youngest Canadian team since 2013, with an average age of 26, jumped to a 3-0 lead in the opening period with goals from Eldridge, Emily Clark and Rebecca Leslie.
Kendall Cooper added the fourth on a power play midway through the second period.
Hanna Thuvik pulled one back for Sweden on a power play in the final period before Eldridge completed the scoring with her second goal.
Canada goaltender Ann-Renée Desbiens stopped 13 shots in the Group B game.
In Group A, the Czech Republic rallied to beat Austria 4-1. Austria are playing in the top division for the first time. Katerina Mrazova led the Czechs with two goals and an assist.
Last year’s bronze medalists Finland faced hosts Denmark in Herning later Friday.
The US and Canada are the tournament favorites, continuing a long-standing cross-border rivalry. Canada have won 13 world titles, followed by the US with 11 across the previous 24 championships.
The Americans have won 10 of the past 14 world championships and arrived in Denmark as reigning world and Olympic champions, having claimed the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.
Finland are the only other team apart from Canada and the US to reach the final, doing so in 2019.
The 11-day, 10-nation tournament in the Danish cities of Esbjerg and Herning is the first to take place in November after the IIHF moved it to begin before the PWHL season.
Rather than having the top five teams grouped together as before, the field has been split into two groups of five based on rankings, with the US leading one group and Canada the other.
The top four from each group qualify for the playoffs, with the final set for 16 November. The bottom two will play a relegation game.
Canada and the US are wearing generic jerseys without their national logos, mandated by the International Ice Hockey Federation and designed by IIHF supplier True Hockey.
Hockey Canada and USA Hockey have their own apparel and jersey contracts with Bauer and CCM, respectively.
The two federations are suing the IIHF over the dispute in a Swiss court.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
More than half of New Zealand’s voters cast early ballots in the tightly contested race.
Polls have opened on the final day of voting in New Zealand against a backdrop of concerns over the rising cost of living and the broader state of the economy.
Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and close at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).
Voting already began on October 26. More than 1.6 million voters, out of nearly 3.8 million in total, had cast their ballots by the end of Thursday, according to the country’s Electoral Commission.
The country has strict laws banning any talk of politics on election day.
The 19-hour election day blackout, which ends when polling places close on Saturday evening, bars everyone, including political parties, news outlets and social media users, from commenting on likely election outcomes, campaign issues and anything else that might encourage or discourage people from voting in a particular way.
Billboards and advertising must be removed. Bumper stickers, T-shirts and even social media profile pictures are also covered by the law.
Breaches of the law can incur a fine of up to 20,000 New Zealand dollars ($11,000).
Opinion polls ahead of the tightly contested election suggest the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.
New Zealand elections
Most parties are campaigning on the economy, but their suggested solutions differ widely.
The National Party is pledging to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme.
The Labour Party is focusing on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport.
Recent polls show no clear winner. A handful of seats either way could decide who governs.
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.
Voters do not elect a leader of the country but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.
Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

Iran's health ministry denies report on iodine distribution over US strike fears
Iran's health ministry has denied a report by The Times of London that it was distributing iodine tablets near its nuclear sites to prepare for possible US strikes.
"No Ministry of Health official has spoken to The Times, and the quote attributed to the ministry is false," Hossein Kermanpour, head of the ministry's public relations and information centre, wrote on X.
He said the health system was prepared for various scenarios and threats from "an enemy that does not even spare children". But he added that declaring a state of war was not within the ministry's authority.
He called publishing unverified reports at such a time "irresponsible".
The Times of London had cited an unnamed health ministry official who said Iran was handing out iodine tablets to communities near its nuclear facilities.
The official was quoted as saying, “Trump can no longer be trusted. He may go through with this crime," and that in every war, Iran had tried to distribute the tablets, which help protect the thyroid gland from radiation, within two to three kilometres of its nuclear sites.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: EU tells TikTok to fix ‘harmful’ For You feed, threatens fines
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
EU tells TikTok to fix ‘harmful’ For You feed, threatens fines
TikTok’s algorithm ‘leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from’, European Commission says.
The European Union has ordered TikTok to change the algorithm powering its For You feed, threatening the social media platform with large fines.
On Friday, Brussels accused TikTok of violating the EU’s Digital Services Act over the “harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect” by feeding users similar video clips based on what they’ve previously viewed or liked, even if they are “triggering”.
“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same, leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” European Commission Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen, who oversees tech sovereignty, said in a statement.
“Today’s preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ well-being, including those of minors.”
The algorithm, according to the EU, results in the “endless” exposure of users to “content about sadness, isolation or body image.”
The EU said that although TikTok had made some changes to mitigate the risks highlighted by the commission, the tweaks were not enough.
TikTok rejected the EU’s findings, saying they are “fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety”.
TikTok has “a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience”, a spokesperson for the tech giant said.
Brussels’ fines on the Chinese-owned platform could increase by up to 6 percent, according to regulators, unless the platform resolves the issue. The company will have a chance to respond before the commission issues its final decision.
Recent efforts in countries like France, Spain and England have focused on protecting minors on social media platforms from predatory behaviour, cyberbullying, deteriorating mental health and eating disorders. Several countries introduced social media bans for children below the age of 15.
Earlier EU findings
In February, the EU found that TikTok did not “adequately assess how these addictive features could harm the physical and mental well-being of its users, including minors and vulnerable adults”.
Whereas the EU’s February findings focused on features such as the impact of notifications, Friday’s order went after the algorithm itself, a senior EU official told the AFP news agency.
In July, the bloc accused TikTok of exposing children to risks like cyberbullying and predatory behaviour.
In the same month, Brussels ordered Meta to change Facebook’s and Instagram’s feeds in an investigation into the platforms’ violations of the bloc’s Digital Services Act.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: ‘We’re still cool’: Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd confirm split and reject WNBA draft speculation
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd have confirmed they ended their romantic relationship more than a year ago, with the Dallas Wings star backcourt tandem rejecting suggestions that their relationship influenced the team’s decision to select Fudd with the No 1 pick in this year’s WNBA draft.
The former University of Connecticut teammates announced their breakup on Friday’s episode of Fudd’s podcast, and asked fans to stop sending hostile messages to them and their families.
“Before we continue with anything else, Paige and I have something that we want to share with everyone,” Fudd said. “We are no longer together. I don’t know how else to say that.”
Bueckers confirmed the split, saying the two had been separated for more than a year, well before Fudd joined her in Dallas in April.
“We were not together before she got drafted,” Bueckers said. “So all of those narratives can go to bed. She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She’s an amazing human, amazing basketball player. And we’re still friends. We’re still cool.”
Fudd’s selection in April had prompted considerable attention to her relationship with Bueckers, who was herself the first overall pick by Dallas in 2025. The pair became the first college teammates to go No 1 in consecutive WNBA drafts since fellow UConn standouts Tina Charles and Maya Moore in 2010 and 2011.
Fudd, an Associated Press All-American and one of the country’s top outside shooters, helped UConn win the national championship in 2025 before being selected first overall in a draft without a clear consensus top prospect. She quickly made her mark in Dallas, hitting six three-pointers against the New York Liberty in May to break the franchise’s rookie single-game record previously held by Bueckers.
The attention surrounding Fudd’s arrival in Dallas reflected a broader trend in the WNBA, where players’ romantic relationships have become subjects of intense social media speculation, at times overshadowing their accomplishments on the court.
At the Wings’ media day in April, Bueckers addressed questions about their relationship and denied having any influence over Dallas’s draft decision.
“Quite frankly, I believe me and Azzi’s personal relationship is nobody’s business but our own, and what we choose to share is completely up to us,” she said.
“Azzi Fudd was a No 1 draft pick because she earned it, and it had nothing to do with me and everything to do with who she is as a human being, who she is a basketball player, her resilience, her strength and her career-best year at UConn,” Bueckers added. “She should be celebrated as such.”
The pair first met at a USA Basketball camp in 2017 and played together for four seasons at UConn, helping the Huskies end their nine-year NCAA title drought in 2025. Their relationship became public in July of that year, when Bueckers referred to Fudd as her girlfriend during an interview with the TikTok show WAG Talk.
On Friday, Bueckers said the speculation surrounding their relationship had led to negative messages directed at both players and people close to them.
“We’ve seen a lot of negativity. We’ve seen a lot of hate,” she said. “We’ve had stuff sent to us. We’ve had stuff sent to our family, our friends.”
“I hate that we have to address this, but just to control the narrative, there’s been some crazy things said about us,” she added. “Sometimes in life, there’s just seasons. And sometimes in life, two people are just at different points of their life.”
Bueckers said their separation had not affected their ability to play together, noting that they had already spent an entire season as teammates after breaking up.
“We’re the utmost professional,” she said. “We care about basketball and we’re still friends.”
Dallas finished the regular season with a franchise-record 27 wins, a 17-game improvement from the previous year, and reached the playoffs for the first time since 2023. They gave the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries a first-round scare, pushing the series to a deciding third game.
Bueckers earned her second consecutive All-Star selection, while Fudd averaged 13.1 points in 30 games as a rookie and shot 39.7% from three-point range. Fudd’s season ended prematurely because of a right knee injury that required surgery.
Bueckers said the two would continue to support each other as friends and teammates.
“We still support each other. We are still going to be great friends. We are going to be great teammates. We are going to be professionals,” she said. “At the end of the day, we still care about each other and want the best for each other.”

Macklemore says US venues rejected his Free Palestine tour
American rapper Macklemore said on Friday that major US concert venues, including New York's Madison Square Garden, refused to book his Free Palestine tour that just concluded three dates in Europe.
The rapper launched the effort after he was removed as the opening act on musician Ed Sheeran's concert tour in August, because the stadium owners had objected to him saying "Free Palestine" on stage.
Since then, nine US venues declined to allow him to book available dates through the end of the year, Macklemore said on social media. The venues included Madison Square Garden and the Kia Forum in Los Angeles.
"The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues," he said in a post. "In over 20 years of touring, I've never experienced anything like this."
Macklemore played Free Palestine shows in Dublin, Paris and London to raise funds for organisations that support Palestinians. The musician said he would work with other artists and organisers to do more performances for the cause.
"We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech," he wrote. "Yet we've reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending."

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
Trump-Xi Busan deal aimed to ease tariffs and tech restrictions; progress hinges on China’s fulfillment of commitments.
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to urge Beijing to immediately implement commitments under the Busan trade agreement.
“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions. He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement announcing the discussions on Friday.
The announcement refers to a trade deal negotiated between Washington and Beijing in which US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions amid tit-for-tat tariffs imposed first by Washington and then by Beijing.
On Thursday, China said it was open to buying more US farm goods if the world’s two largest economies agreed to implement the reciprocal tariff cut.
“China has consistently been open to expanding purchases of agricultural products from the US, but only on the condition that the two sides implement their agreed ’30 billion for 30 billion’ reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement,” Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson Huang Ling said in a statement.
The move follows a September meeting between Trump and Xi, when the White House proposed $60bn in cuts, including $17bn worth of US farm goods.
In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy $17bn of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made last October to buy US soya beans.
“Secretary Bessent reiterated the Trump Administration’s commitment to pursuing trade and economic policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen U.S. economic and national security,” the Treasury added.

Attacks, raids and forced demolitions mark another day of Israeli violence in West Bank
Israeli forces and settlers carried out 20 attacks on Palestinian olive pickers in six West Bank governorates on Friday, according to the Palestinian Wall and Colonization Resistance Commission.
The attacks included detentions, assaults, uprooting of trees and theft of crops, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing the commission. Farmers were also blocked from their fields.
West of Jericho, Israeli settlers entered farmland in ad-Duyuk at-Tahta with their sheep. They destroyed crops and greenhouses, resident Mustafa Fheidat told Wafa.
He estimated the damage at hundreds of thousands of shekels.
East of Ramallah, Israeli forces raided the Abu Fazaa Bedouin community for more than three hours, smashing vehicles, assaulting residents and detaining one man.
In Hebron, Israeli forces closed several Old City neighbourhoods for Jewish holidays, including the Ibrahimi Mosque, which will stay closed to Muslims until Saturday night.
Forces also detained three Palestinians, including a journalist, in Hebron and Masafer Yatta, assaulting a fourth.
Among them was Mohammad Yousef Makhmareh, a man with a disability, who was detained in Khirbet al-Markaz after soldiers tried to take his sheep. He lost a hand years ago to a landmine left by Israeli forces.
In occupied East Jerusalem, two Palestinians were forced to demolish their own homes, which housed 18 people, in Jabal al-Mukabber.
The families had paid 25,000 shekels trying to prevent the demolitions.

Chuck Schumer dismisses opposition to his leadership from progressive Democrats
US Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is facing opposition from progressives and a new group of Democratic lawmakers-elect to become Senate majority leader, in a rift that underscores the party’s divide on Israel.
Senators-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Troy Jackson of Maine, and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan all said on the campaign trail that they will oppose Schumer as Senate majority leader.
Meanwhile, progressive groups have said the Democrats’ sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday should start the process of new lawmakers leading the party.
“Voters made it very clear that they want a new generation of Democratic fighters,” Indivisible, a progressive Democratic group, said this week. “We need a Leader in the Senate who is capable of leading that fight. It’s time for Senate Democrats to choose new leadership.”
One key difference between the 75-year-old Schumer and the new cohort of Democratic lawmakers is his position on Israel. Schumer is a longtime supporter of military aid to Israel and has manoeuvred to stop bills in Congress that would condition military assistance.

In February 2026, Schumer said that one of his most important jobs as Senate minority leader was to “fight for aid to Israel”.
“I have many jobs as leader… and one is to fight for aid to Israel, all the aid that Israel needs,” he told a group of pro-Israel Jewish leaders at the time.
“As long as I’m in the Senate, this programme will continue to grow from strength to strength, and we won’t let anyone attack it or undo it,” Schumer said, even referring to US taxpayer aid for Israel as his “baby”.
Schumer is Jewish-American and has received support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). But recent polling shows that he is out of step with the majority of Jewish voters in the US, who lean heavily Democratic.
A supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and Aipac’s actions are increasing antisemitism in the US, a poll commissioned by J Street and published this week found.
Still, the division on Schumer reflects a wider ideological divide within the Democratic Party. Senator-elect Sayed represents members who want to end the US’s support for Israel amid the genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank. Other senators, like John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, are staunchly pro-Israel.
But Schumer is likely to return as Senate majority leader, partly because no senior Democratic senators have expressed interest in the role.
Schumer on Thursday dismissed talk of a rift within the party after a historic victory.
"The bottom line is: first... we’ve had a very, very strong finish here, and I have worked really hard to get the results we got. But second, the issue is not me,” he told MS Now. “The issue is unity, fighting together. We still have a big job to do.”

Houthis and Yemeni government blame each other for Taiz market attack that killed 30
Yemen’s Houthis and the internationally recognised government have blamed each other for a deadly attack on a market in Taiz province earlier on Friday.
The Houthis said Saudi aircraft carried out the strikes, while the government accused the group of firing a ballistic missile at the market and called the attack a “war crime”.
“Saudi enemy aircraft targeted the market in Al-Waziya city with several strikes,” Houthi health ministry spokesman Anis al-Asbahi said, according to the Houthi-run Saba news agency.
The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the aircraft had taken off from Saudi Arabia’s Khamis Mushait base.
Meanwhile, local authorities in Taiz blamed “indiscriminate Houthi missile fire” and denied any air strikes had taken place.
The Houthi health ministry put the toll at 30 dead and eight wounded, and said rescue teams were still searching for bodies under the rubble at the market, which lies in a Houthi-held area of the province.
Government forces said on Friday that they had recaptured several areas of Taiz from the Houthis. The province lies near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key oil shipping route.
