https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Eurovision’s Asia experiment gets under way in flamboyant Bangkok
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Oliver Holmes
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Thailand is about to get a glitz-infused injection of pop culture, with crews starting construction of a large stage in Bangkok as part of an extravagant attempt to transplant Eurovision to Asia.
Organisers have promised the world’s longest-running music competition will launch “a new chapter in Asia” next weekend, when 11 contestants from across the region will sing and dance for votes.
How much notice an Asian audience has shown in the experiment to replicate the beloved contest is yet to be seen, although organisers will hope it sets off a Eurovision-mania chain reaction. Several competitor countries, such as the Philippines and South Korea, already have avid Eurovision fanclubs.
Still, a week before the grand final ample tickets remained on sale for entry to the concert hall at One Bangkok Forum, which sits near the city’s celebrated Lumphini Park.
Eurovision’s official Instagram account has been promoting its Asian sister account to its 2.3m followers. So far, about 65,000 accounts have followed. Bulgaria’s Eurovision 2026 winner, Dara, is getting flown over to perform her electro-dance earworm, Bangaranga, during the interval.
Dean Vuletic, author of Postwar Europe and the Eurovision Song Contest, said the nascent show would face an uphill battle to “capture the attention and fascination of the local audience”.
Vuletic, an academic who taught the world’s first university course on Eurovision, attributed the contest’s extraordinary success in part because it emerged in the late 1950s during the rise of television, and at a period of postwar European integration. “So there’s a reason why Eurovision is peculiarly European, and why I think it would struggle to succeed elsewhere,” he said.
Another spin-off version, titled American Song Contest, received poor viewing figures in 2022, facing stiff competition from more established shows such as American Idol.
Despite his reservations, Vuletic travelled to Thailand for the final show. He said: “This is another chapter in that history that I think I have to see.”
In what appears to be an attempt to hold on to the name association of the world’s largest live music event, the show has not rebranded itself as “Asiavision” but gone with the spin-off title “Eurovision Song Contest Asia”, leading to some geographic confusion.
However, such regional melding is not unusual in Eurovision’s 70-year history. The competition is run by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which despite its name is not location-specific, meaning broadcasters outside Europe take part, including those from Israel and Australia. Next year’s Eurovision will feature a Canadian act for the first time.
In the rush to lock down competitors, not all of Asia is covered, with India and China absent. The 11 announced performers are from Bhutan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam.
The hosting nation’s own entrant is a collaboration including a solo female artist and local T-Pop (Thai Pop) star, Mang. She joins Daou, who gained national fame through winning a survival-style Thai TV show and his role in a short-lived boyband called LAZ1.
Anyone in the world can view the live show on YouTube, and even vote, although under a complex voting system their voice will not overrule national juries and public votes in participating countries. Eurovision onlookers have been wondering if political allegiances will affect results, as they have for the main event, where friendly neighbours often appear to engage in bloc voting. Thailand and Cambodia were at war last year, which could play out in the tallies on the night.
Eurovision attracts more than 100 million viewers every year. The competition has been overshadowed by accusations that Israel should be excluded over its war in Gaza. Critics say its continued inclusion is at odds with the banning of Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and several broadcasters have pulled out.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: ‘One less gang leader’: Haiti’s prime minister celebrates police operation
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
‘One less gang leader’: Haiti’s prime minister celebrates police operation
Haiti’s National Police announced that alleged gang leader Mathias Saintil was killed in an exchange of gunfire.
Haiti’s National Police (PNH) has confirmed that a gang leader known as Mathias Saintil was “neutralised” as part of a recent law enforcement operation.
In a social media post shared on Friday, officials described Saintil as the leader of the Boston gang, named for a neighbourhood in Cite Soleil, an impoverished part of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
Saintil was reportedly struck by “multiple bullets” during a law enforcement operation, and a police source said he died later in the hospital.
Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime celebrated the news with a social media post of his own.
“One less gang leader,” he wrote in a mix of French and Haitian Creole. “The battle to liberate the country from the grip of bandits continues with determination. The gangs won’t be able to sleep!”
Haiti has struggled with a surge in gang violence for years, most notably after the assassination of then-President Jovenel Moise in 2021.
The assassination left the country in crisis, and no national elections have been held in the years since. Amid the political turmoil, organised crime in Haiti sought to expand its influence, claiming large swaths of territory.
As much as 90 percent of Port-au-Prince has fallen under gang control, including key roadways and maritime ports. At least 26 gangs operate in the area in and around the capital, according to the United Nations.
Haiti has long struggled with political instability, economic decline and successive natural disasters. It has been ranked as the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere.
The country’s gangs often recruit young people with the promise of food, income and protection. The UN estimates that half of the country’s gang members are children and teens under the age of 18.
The violence, however, has led to a spiralling humanitarian crisis. At least 1.4 million people have been displaced from their homes, particularly in the capital area.
Some 1,123 Haitians were killed in the violence between July and October of this year, according to the UN. Another 440 people were injured during that time period, and rates of sexual violence remain high: Between July and August, there were 689 cases of gang-involved rape.
The crisis has prompted widespread outcry. In April, members of a new international Gang Suppression Force (GSF) began arriving in Haiti, with a mission to “neutralise, isolate and deter gangs”.
Its 12-month mandate was renewed in September, with the UN Security Council granting an extension until March 2027.
But the GSF has encountered many of the same setbacks that faced its predecessor, the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support (MSS) — namely, insufficient resources and staffing.
Proponents of the GSF have called on the international community to fulfil its commitments by funding the force to the fullest extent.
Members of the GSF have also come under attack as part of their clashes with Haiti’s gangs. On October 18, for instance, four Salvadoran aviation technicians involved in the GSF were kidnapped.
El Salvador has responded by surging as many as 2,000 troops to Haiti. Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele described the deployment as a rescue mission.
“We have one single objective: to ensure our four compatriots return home alive and unharmed,” Bukele wrote on October 21, sharing a video of armoured vehicles patrolling Haitian streets, some firing guns.
“But I want you — the gang leaders — to understand one thing very clearly,” Bukele added. “Today’s attack is nothing compared to what is coming if you do not return all four hostages alive.”
He has since called on Haitians to “rise up” and “reclaim control of your communities”. He also insisted that his forces are not “invaders”.
Human rights watchdogs have criticised Bukele for his heavy-handed approach to gang violence in El Salvador, which he has addressed in part through mass arrests and mass trials.
Bukele has warned he is “capable” of deploying the same tactics against Haiti’s gangs. In his latest post on Friday, Bukele interacted with a social media user who suggested they had identified the residence of a prominent Haitian gang leader.
“Where is this house located?” Bukele asked. “Give us the exact address, and we will destroy it.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: COP31, Asean, Mercosul, G20: Lula aproveita reveses da extrema direita para fortalecer multilateralismo
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Rodrigo Chagas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) inicia na próxima semana uma série de compromissos internacionais: a COP31, na Turquia; a cúpula da Associação de Nações do Sudeste Asiático (Asean), nas Filipinas; o Mercosul, no Uruguai; e o G20, nos Estados Unidos. Reeleito para um quarto mandato, Lula pretende aproveitar os encontros para fortalecer o multilateralismo, em meio às derrotas eleitorais do presidente estadunidense Donald Trump.
A avaliação de fontes do Palácio do Planalto ouvidas pelo Brasil de Fato é que a vitória de Lula no Brasil e a derrota dos republicanos nas eleições legislativas dos EUA abriram uma oportunidade para recuperar a cooperação internacional, enfraquecida pela política unilateralista de Trump.
Somam-se ao cenário de reveses, ainda, o resultado das eleições em Israel, em que Benjamin Netanyahu não conseguiu formar maioria para seguir governando, e a renúncia de Santiago Peña, no Paraguai, um dos aliados mais fiéis à política estadunidense na América Latina.
O governo brasileiro também identifica condições mais favoráveis para normalizar as relações diplomáticas com os estadunidenses e para abertura de novos mercados a partir de relações bilaterais.
A defesa do multilateralismo marcou o discurso do ministro das Relações Exteriores, Mauro Vieira, na Cúpula Ibero-Americana, realizada nesta quinta-feira (5), em Madri. Representando Lula, o chanceler criticou as políticas de hegemonia e as esferas de influência, defendeu uma ordem internacional baseada na cooperação e condenou o bloqueio estadunidense a Cuba. “A era das arrogâncias unilaterais, dos protetorados e da diplomacia da força já passou”, afirmou Vieira.
Clima e Ásia serão prioridades do quarto mandato
A primeira viagem internacional de Lula após a reeleição será à COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. O presidente participará da cúpula de líderes nos dias 11 e 12 de novembro, quando o Brasil encerrará sua presidência da conferência climática, exercida desde a COP30, realizada em Belém (PA).
O discurso de Lula deverá enfatizar a importância da ciência, do financiamento climático e do cumprimento dos compromissos internacionais. O governo brasileiro pretende defender instrumentos como o Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre (TFFF), as metas de redução de emissões e o combate ao desmatamento.
Na terça-feira (3), a presidência brasileira da COP30 apresentou dois mapas do caminho, com propostas para acelerar a transição para longe dos combustíveis fósseis e interromper a devastação florestal. Os documentos serão levados à conferência na Turquia como parte do legado brasileiro.
Depois da COP31, Lula seguirá para as Filipinas, onde terá uma agenda bilateral com o governo local e participará da cúpula da Asean, prevista para começar no dia 15. A visita integra a estratégia de diversificação das relações comerciais e diplomáticas do Brasil.
Segundo avaliações compartilhadas no Planalto, a aproximação com a Ásia deverá ser uma das prioridades da política externa no quarto mandato. O interesse brasileiro vai além da abertura de mercados para produtos agropecuários e inclui cooperação em ciência, tecnologia e inovação.
Planalto vê oportunidade para normalizar relações com os EUA
A derrota dos republicanos nas eleições legislativas é interpretada pelo governo brasileiro como um fator de enfraquecimento da estratégia de Trump para a América Latina. A avaliação é que, passada a eleição presidencial brasileira, a continuidade das hostilidades contra o governo Lula traria poucos benefícios políticos ao presidente estadunidense.
A expectativa, porém, não é de uma mudança imediata na política externa dos EUA, mas de uma normalização pragmática das relações bilaterais. O Planalto considera que os interesses convergentes entre os dois países são maiores do que as divergências e não identifica motivos estratégicos para uma nova escalada de tensões.
Entre os problemas que o governo brasileiro pretende superar estão as restrições à concessão de vistos e à circulação de autoridades, agravadas durante os ataques do governo Trump ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e ao processo eleitoral brasileiro. A situação também envolve o tratamento dispensado à embaixadora brasileira em Washington, Maria Luiza Viotti, e a autorização para que Daniel Perez assuma a embaixada dos EUA em Brasília.
O ministro Mauro Vieira participará, nos dias 9 e 10 de novembro, de uma reunião de chanceleres do G7, em Paris, na França, onde há possibilidade de uma conversa bilateral com o secretário de Estado estadunidense, Marco Rubio, que poderá contribuir para a retomada da normalidade diplomática.
As negociações comerciais, por outro lado, continuaram mesmo durante os momentos de maior tensão. A última reunião oficial entre representantes dos dois governos sobre o tema ocorreu em setembro, nos EUA.
Lula e Trump estão confirmados na agenda internacional de dezembro, quando ocorrerá a cúpula do G20, em Miami, nos dias 14 e 15. Até quinta-feira (5), nenhum dos governos havia solicitado formalmente uma reunião bilateral entre os presidentes.
Integração regional enfrenta obstáculos
Antes do G20, Lula deverá participar da cúpula de chefes de Estado do Mercosul, marcada para 4 de dezembro, em Montevidéu, no Uruguai. A reunião ocorrerá em meio às dificuldades de integração do bloco, especialmente pelas divergências entre o governo brasileiro e o presidente argentino, Javier Milei.
No Planalto, a avaliação é de que, mesmo com as travas impostas por Milei, a integração sul-americana precisa avançar a partir de interesses comuns, mesmo entre governos com orientações políticas distintas. A cooperação no combate ao crime organizado, na segurança das fronteiras e na proteção da Amazônia e outros biomas compartilhados aparece entre as possibilidades para fortalecer as relações regionais.
A aprovação da PEC da Segurança Pública pelo Senado, na terça-feira (3), também deve fortalecer essa dimensão da política externa brasileira. A proposta, que aguarda promulgação, amplia a atuação da Polícia Federal em crimes de repercussão internacional e a coordenação do governo federal no setor. Na avaliação do Planalto, o enfrentamento às organizações criminosas que atuam além das fronteiras brasileiras exige maior cooperação policial e diplomática com os países vizinhos.
De acordo com as fontes ouvidas pelo Brasil de Fato, o governo brasileiro também não trabalha com a expectativa de uma mudança radical na política dos EUA para a América Latina após as eleições legislativas. A aposta é preservar relações pragmáticas, ampliar parcerias comerciais e fortalecer os mecanismos de cooperação internacional sem abandonar posições brasileiras sobre soberania, democracia e mudança climática.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Eurovision is heading to Asia: here’s what to expect
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul and Natasha May
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text: Aina Abdul will represent Malaysia at Eurovision Asia on 14 November. Photograph: Eurovision Song Contest View image in fullscreen Aina Abdul will represent Malaysia at Eurovision Asia on 14 November. Photograph: Eurovision Song Contest Explainer Eurovision is heading to Asia: here’s what to expect The first foray into Asia for the song contest will see 11 countries vying for the trophy, but will it have the same feel as its European predecessor? The Eurovision song contest is being brought to Asia, with 11 countries competing in a single final in Bangkok on 14 November, in what organisers intend to be the first of many regional editions. So, which countries will be belting their hearts out? Will there still be tactical voting? Will the contest’s gloriously camp traditions survive the journey across to Asia? Here’s all you need to know. Which countries are taking part, and which ones aren’t? Bhutan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. All 11 acts have been chosen, including some who are already big names at home, including Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên and Malaysia’s Aina Abdul. Negotiations with China and Japan ran past the production deadline, according to the show’s executive producer, Assaf Blecher, who says he is “very, very optimistic” both will take part next year. Will the format be the same as the European Eurovision? The format essentially follows the European original. Each country sends one act, performing live, for a maximum of three minutes and with up to six performers on stage. Blecher says the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which owns Eurovision, approves every song and lyric, and that political songs are barred in the same way as in Europe. National juries score a dress rehearsal the night before, and the public votes on the night. Viewers in the competing countries can vote, but not for their own country, and votes from everywhere else are pooled into a 12th territory. Voting is through a QR code or the website, with eight free votes per viewer, which must be spread across at least three songs. A further 10 votes can be bought at prices that vary by country. View image in fullscreen Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên is already a big name in her home country. Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty Images for VIFW The final will be streamed on Eurovision’s YouTube channel and is carried by a broadcast network in each competing country. The winner receives a trophy and no prize money. One key difference is that the winner will not automatically gain hosting rights, at least at first, on the grounds that smaller countries lack the infrastructure. In terms of which flags will be allowed in the arena, a question that has repeatedly caused rows in Europe, spectators may bring one each, subject to Thai law, while delegations may carry only their own national flag on stage and in the flag parade. Will neighbours vote for each other? Bloc voting, where countries award high scores to their neighbours, is a long-running tradition in Europe. Blecher says it is too early to know whether Asia will follow suit, while Dave Goodman, the EBU’s head of communications for the contest, says viewers will be encouraged to spread their votes across several countries. Mutual support could come from Himalayan neighbours Nepal and Bhutan, while close linguistic and cultural ties exist between south-east Asian nations such as Thailand and Laos. However, host Thailand may not want to rely on votes from neighbouring Cambodia, given the recent fighting on their shared border where a territorial dispute remains unresolved. The EBU rule barring winners in conflict from hosting does not apply in Asia, Goodman says, because hosting does not pass to the winner. View image in fullscreen Fans hold signs bearing the face of Filipino singer Carmelle Collado who will compete for the Eurovision Song Contest Asia. Photograph: Basilio Sepe/AP While other tensions in the region exist - such as water security along the Mekong River and overlapping claims in the South China Sea between Malaysia, Vietnam and the Philippines - they are not open hostilities and unlikely to affect voting. Will the show still retain Eurovision’s camp overtones? It is not yet clear whether Asia will fully embrace all the traditions of its European predecessor. Blecher feels it may not yet be the same “full campy” experience as this year’s competition in Europe but noted that the latter had evolved over 70 years Bettina Miski, a PR expert who runs a YouTube series connecting Asian artists with global audiences, says it’s not certain the contest’s queer culture will automatically transfer. “While the host country, Thailand, has marriage equality and globally visible queer media, we have to keep in mind all the other countries, with potentially more restrictive media, where it will be on air,” she says. Malaysia and Bangladesh, for example, are both competing but criminalise same-sex relations. View image in fullscreen Junhee is a k-pop veteran and represents South Korea. Photograph: H&P Entertainment, PAN Entertainment Why is this happening now? This is not the first attempt to export the format. The American Song Contest, in which US states competed rather than countries, ran for one series in 2022 and was not renewed. Goodman says: “One of the reasons for doing the format … in other territories is also, yes, to make sure that we can keep the Eurovision song contest, the original one, sustainable for the future.” Reports of budget cuts and production changes in October prompted organisers to release a public statement reaffirming the contest would go ahead as planned. Explore more on these topics Eurovision Asia Pacific Thailand explainers Share Reuse this content

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: US Treasury sanctions eight Canadian money exchange firms over Iran ties
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
US Treasury sanctions eight Canadian money exchange firms over Iran ties
US Treasury claims firms helped sanctioned Iranian entities and handled funds linked to alleged drug trafficking boss.
The United States has imposed sanctions on eight Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping Iranian entities circumvent financial sanctions.
The US Department of the Treasury announced the measures on Friday as part of what it calls “Operation Economic Outcast“.
The Treasury said some of the businesses also laundered their proceeds by converting Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets such as cryptocurrency, adding that some of the businesses helped an alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.
“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
According to the Treasury, the businesses are based in Ontario and British Columbia, and they include Million Exchange, Amin Exchange and Cryptoyal.
The sanctions effectively cut the firms off from the US dollar-based financial system, freezing any assets they hold in the US and barring them from transactions with American people or entities.
Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) issued a statement shortly after the US Treasury’s announcement, saying that it worked with the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) to impose the sanctions against the money service businesses.
“FINTRAC works regularly with foreign financial intelligence units to combat money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion,” the statement said on Friday. “Through bilateral agreements, the Centre is able to disclose intelligence to financial intelligence units worldwide.”
In a separate statement on Friday, the US Treasury said FinCEN, its anti-money laundering unit, issued an order targeting the money exchanger MEXC Global.
FinCEN said the order prevents US financial institutions from processing fund transfers involving Seychelles-incorporated MEXC Global, which it says has facilitated at least $16bn in illicit transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia, as well as transactions with other sanctioned actors.
More pressure on Tehran
According to the US Treasury, its sanctions campaign aims to “sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime” and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which Canada also lists as a terrorist organisation.
On Wednesday, the US Treasury sanctioned a network in India and Turkiye that it accuses of helping Iran evade restrictions on its oil exports and airlines. The network is run by Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, who are based in the northern Indian city of Chandigarh, the US Treasury said.
The US claimed last week that the campaign had pushed Iran’s rial to new lows and driven inflation to about 90 percent.
Below is a list of the identified businesses in Canada:
- Diverse Trade Inc, doing business as Million Exchange in Ontario
- 1380079 BC Limited, doing business as Amin Exchange in British Columbia
- Top PC Technician Inc, operating in Ontario
- NIA Nations Currency Ltd, based in British Columbia
- 2397639 Ontario Ltd, doing business as Farah Exchange
- CCC Inc in Ontario
- B Galaxy Inc, doing business as Cryptoyal, from the same Ontario location as CCC Inc
- Darvish Exchange in Ontario

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Vivemos uma dicotomia entre uma vitória e uma não-derrota’, diz Don L; rapper volta ao Recife neste sábado (7)
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Rostand Tiago
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Cerca de um ano após sua última passagem pela capital pernambucana, o rapper Don L volta ao Recife neste sábado (7), na Concha Acústica da UFPE, trazendo pela primeira vez em muito tempo um show solo, fora de festivais. O cearense apresentará os arranjos e as encruzilhadas do capitalismo tardio no Brasil de seu último disco, “Caro Vapor Vol. 2: Qual a Forma de Pagamento”, lançado em 2025, e revisitará outros momentos de sua trajetória em uma noite especial.
Em conversa com o Brasil de Fato PE, Don L afirma acreditar que a energia de seu show certamente será influenciada pela energia política que seu público pernambucano vive. Declaradamente de esquerda radical – “sou mais guerrilheiro do que MC”, diz um verso seu – ele acredita que será uma noite contaminada pela euforia de uma plateia embalada pela sensação local de dever cumprido, em um estado que elegeu sem-terras e comunistas para a Câmara Federal e um senado destoante daquele escolhido pela maioria do país.
“Vivemos momentos muito tensos. Sinto que teremos essa energia de descompressão e vontade de celebrar a vida no show. Por mais que nossas conquistas, pontuais e táticas, ainda sejam insuficientes para mudar nossa vida agora, elas já são uma não-derrota”, declara Don L.
O rapper coloca em perspectiva: o triunfo precisa ser celebrado, mas os caminhos de luta ainda são longos. “Elegemos o Congresso talvez mais à direita da história desde a ditadura, mas aprendemos também que só a mobilização popular muda algo de forma estrutural no país. Então vivemos essa dicotomia entre uma vitória e uma não-derrota”, afirma.
No palco, o enfoque será seu último álbum, que trilha por arranjos e batidas brasileiras para narrar as ferramentas de sedução e contradição do país, entre bets, big techs, exôdos, lifestyles e amores. O artista também revisitará outros trabalhos com um tempo de apresentação que a sua turnê por festivais não permitia. Um momento, de certa forma, de transição da formatação de seu show.
Don L teve sua passagem pelo projeto Tiny Desk Brasil celebrada, tornando-se o segundo mais visualizado da história. Ele apresentou seu trabalho acompanhado por uma banda e novos arranjos, experiência que pretende levar para as apresentações do próximo ano.
Contudo, Don L destaca que seu atual formato, no qual vem acompanhado pelas vozes de Alt Niss e Terra Preta, além do DJ Roger nas picapes, também é dono de uma energia que alcança a vivacidade de uma banda a partir da abertura ao improviso. “Quando estou com DJ, ele não é apenas um cara que dá play nos instrumentais. Ele é uma banda, trabalhando em cima dos pads e performando muita coisa ao vivo”, elabora o rapper. Com picapes ou instrumentos, os rumos são os mesmos: organicidade e dinamismo. “Vivemos um momento de esgotamento, sobretudo com as IAs atuando em criações engessadas. Então a imperfeição e o improviso têm cada vez mais valor por serem humanos”, complementa.
É também um momento em que Don L observa os rumos do rap no país, suas lutas e suas possibilidades de futuro. Por mais que tenha observado algumas movimentações de infantilização no ritmo recentemente, ele acredita que tal fenômeno não chegou a se concretizar e o hip-hop brasileiro segue ocupando seu lugar de contracultura, graças à histórica capacidade de autodefesa de sua comunidade. O artista encontra possibilidades estéticas para muito além de um caráter panfletário.
“Eu não gosto que categorizem meu rap como ‘consciente’ ou ‘de mensagem’. Eles me parecem muito panfletários e pouco sedutores. E eu busco o sedutor. Cantar não uma orelhada, mas um estilo de vida e uma forma de ver o mundo. E isso vem de tudo o que eu ouvia e me formou, como Racionais, Marcelo D2, Chico Science. Algo na borda da cultura, que você ouve e vê possibilidades de festa, amor, visão de mundo e estilo”, conclui Don L.
O show de Don L é a principal atração do Baile do Andrew, que ainda contará com o DJ Iury Andrew recebendo a rapper Bione, Zoe Beats com Relikia e Léo da Bodega, além das discotecagens de Mau Lopes e Afrobeat. Os ingressos estão disponíveis na plataforma Sympla.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I have flung myself headfirst into Sarah J Maas’s romantasy universe and I find myself a changed woman | Johanna Cosgrove
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Johanna Cosgrove
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Fitness influencers love to inform us that “summer bodies are built in winter”, and boy oh boy have I spent the last three colder months in the southern hemisphere in a deep phase of preparation. I had a meticulous spreadsheet. I tracked everything with military precision. I committed to my grindset and sacrificed for my goals.
However, my end result wasn’t a six-pack of abs and a back strong enough to carry a dinner convo with the most punishing of acquaintances. It was to consume the entire back catalogue of Sarah J Maas – 16 books in total (including the novellas) – in anticipation of the long-awaited sixth book in the A Court of Thorns and Roses series.
I have flung myself headfirst into the Maasverse and like many readers I find myself … a changed woman.
Unless you have been living under a rock, or are Nobel prize for literature recipient Anne Carson (who mostly reads books written in 500BC), it has been impossible to miss the chokehold that the romantasy genre has had over (mostly) millennial women for the last several years. Characterised by blending elements of fantasy and romance together and catapulted into our hearts and nethers by its wild popularity on BookTok, romantasy is all over our bestseller lists and our social media.
Sarah J Maas is expected to crack 100m copies sold after this week’s release of A Court of Splintered Harmony and is arguably romantasy’s biggest superstar. Unfortunately, this feels exceptionally radical in 2026, with global literacy rates at an all-time low. (The vice-president of the US failed to pronounce “English proficiency” at a recent press conference, and Alix Earle, an influencer, proclaimed two weeks ago she has “never read a book … maybe Dr Seuss”.)
The flipside of the coin is the category of readers I affectionately call “The Man Bookers”. Their tastes are academic, bordering on performative; they do not read for pleasure, but for knowledge and masochism. They’ll have as many opinions on the Booker prize and the state of contemporary literature as tote bags full of physical media; their bookshelves are stacked with volumes from Fitzcarraldo Editions, the New York Review of Books and Dalkey Archive.
I adore Man Bookers in all their pretentiousness. My boyfriend falls into this category and politely informed me this morning – in an extremely performative male final boss move – that he has read “approximately eight single sentence novels” which is a shocking thing to hear at any time, let alone when one is half asleep and still in bed.
These literary consumers are generally the No 1 haters of romantasy lovers. They see us as basic and are quick to sneer and chide us for chugging down “faerie porn” on our Kindles.
To this I say: what the hell is wrong with you? Genre fiction is exceptionally important! Why is it globally acceptable to be a massive fan of Tolkien or George RR Martin or Frank Herbert, and yet Sarah J Maas is met with derision?
Obviously we all don’t have to like everything (as you will no doubt remind me in the comments) but when a subgenre dominated by female authors and consumers is judged for the same things male authors are celebrated for (rabid fanbase, elaborate world-building, scantily clad magical females), I cannot help but cry misogyny.
Speaking of, it only takes one look at the news to see why it’s no wonder women are turning to fictional faeries for entertainment. On TikTok and Reddit there is an entire theory (with many videos) on the supposed ACOTAR-to-divorce pipeline. Quite simply, the theory goes, women are reading these books, observing the complicated yet ultimately healthy relationships depicted in them, and leaving their shitty husbands. Shocking to realise that being treated with kindness and adoration is a fantasy in 2026!
My friend Rosie Dent – a prominent Maasverse expert and BookTok sensation – says, “Reading romantasy is actually an act of rebellion in this puritanical hellscape.” Rosie is among multiple BookTokers who have entire treatises on this series; her musings are articulate, insightful and thorough and probably researched enough to warrant a PhD. I messaged her throughout my strict reread and was grateful for her deep knowledge of the lore.
I have never been a part of an adult fandom before and this one is spectacular. I’m currently in a romantasy book club with some of New Zealand’s most successful and intelligent comedians. Surprise! The smartest and funniest women you know are reading smut!
And so, as I finally dive into A Court Of Splintered Harmony (after months of hard work), I can’t help but notice I’m a bit more excited, a bit more alive and a bit more connected than when I started. The power of fiction! I’m now reading nonstop. Every day. And definitely enjoying my literary wares more than my significant other (it’s not a competition but it’s true).
As my favourite fit man Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson says: “Success isn’t always about greatness. It’s about consistency.” And to that I say – consistent reading for pleasure? Not a fantasy any longer.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘I didn’t expect to be a main character’: Abdul El-Sayed heads to the Senate with a mandate – and a spotlight
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Detroit, Michigan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Abdul El-Sayed said he did not expect to be “a main character of this midterms”, but the first Muslim elected to the US Senate in history will take his seat in January after a vitriolic campaign that cast him as the central villain of the president and his party.
By October he told the Associated Press he was “not shying away” from those rightwing fixations. “What are you implying?” El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, replied when a town hall attender asked if he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood, in a now-viral exchange.
On Tuesday, Michigan voters helped the pugnacious progressive cap off a transcendental blue wave nationwide, defeating his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, by about seven points, 52.5% to 45.5%.
“My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed,” he said at the beginning of his victory speech in downtown Detroit on Tuesday night, as the crowd erupted in cheers. He then thanked the voters of Michigan, for taking a “chance on the unlikeliest of candidates”.
He won with majorities among Black voters and Jewish early voters, and with a larger share of the vote than Kamala Harris or senator Elissa Slotkin in 2024 in Wayne, Oakland and Macomb counties, despite Republican attacks on his faith and objections from some Jewish leaders to his stance on Israel. Now he takes that mandate to Washington as one of the most visible Democrats to have emerged from this election cycle.
“He is a charismatic, social media-savvy politician, so he will come to DC with a lot more initial interest than most freshman politicians,” said Matt Grossmann, director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research. “He won’t be able to say he had some sort of unique vision that worked above all others, but he will be able to say people said he couldn’t win in a swing state, and he did. I think that will matter.”
The test, according to Shekar Narasimhan, founder and chair of the AAPI Victory Fund, a Super Pac focused on Asian American and Pacific Islander political power, is less about identity than delivery.
“I think the onus on Abdul is less about being the first Muslim senator. Obviously, there is a weight for that, but it’s more about how he represents Michigan given the $165m that was thrown at him in both the primary and the general election,” Narasimhan said. “I think he does have to carry an agenda, and I think the caucus is going to give him some leadership position to be able to carry it out.”
For many Arab and Muslim Americans, the result was vindication. Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute, called voters’ rejection of the attacks on El-Sayed “tremendous” for “every little boy named Abdul, every little girl named Zainab”, arguing that the question at stake was whether the country supports an inclusive democracy.
Donald Trump and other Republicans repeatedly used Islamophobia to target his faith. At a rally in Port Huron on 25 October, the president baselessly called El-Sayed a jihadist and a Muslim Brotherhood member, said he was “on the side of the terrorists”, and claimed he would “have to go through a metal detector” before entering the Senate. John Kennedy, the senator from Louisiana, said El-Sayed “sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey”, while Ted Cruz, the senator from Texas, called him a “jihadist leprechaun”, and JD Vance called him “evil”.
Campaign mailers paid for by the Senate Leadership Fund, a prominent Republican Super Pac, and seen by the Guardian would link El-Sayed with Sharia law, with text that said his specific views “dictates how women dress”, “requires women have a guardian” and “prohibits women from divorcing”.
El-Sayed dismissed those attacks, quipping that he supported “shawarma law”.
On election night, Dearborn’s mayor, Abdullah Hammoud, said voters chose El-Sayed “regardless of the direction in which he prays”. He called it “a beautifully American story”.
Some Jewish leaders, such as the Detroit community director for the American Jewish Committee, Amy Sapeika, said El-Sayed’s rhetoric, and even his victory speech, made many in the community “feel excluded as Jews and as people who support Israel”.
While exit polls and preliminary analyses show that a majority of Michigan Jews voted for El-Sayed, his margins in heavily Jewish communities trailed other Democrats in the state, such as the governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson. In West Bloomfield, where a synagogue attack took place in March, Rogers’s share of the vote rose to 46% from 42% two years ago, when he ran against Slotkin for the Senate.
El-Sayed would reach the same parity with Black voters as Slotkin’s win in 2024, where he won about 86% compared to her 85%, according to an exit poll by NBC.
On Israel, El-Sayed has not changed his position since being elected. On election day morning, Trump said on Fox & Friends that roughly $4bn in annual US military aid to Israel would be “cut off at the end of the year”, citing “lunatics like an El-Sayed”. El-Sayed, who campaigned on ending the aid, welcomed the announcement and called for an end to arms sales as well.
While Congress appropriates the aid, Grossmann said Trump had “basically credited Abdul with changing his position on aid to Israel”, giving him an early win. Narasimhan called the announcement “a good starting point”. He said efforts by Bernie Sanders and other Democrats to restrict offensive weapons were “as far as he’s going to get in this environment on Israel”.
Asked on CNN on Thursday about working with the president and vice-president, El-Sayed made clear he was not softening his tone. He said he would “take every opportunity” to “differentiate between what JD Vance says and what JD Vance does”, and that he finds the pair “odious” in how they behave outside their official roles.
But he also said he would work with them. “I’ll work with anybody to serve the people of the state of Michigan,” he said. “If they’re serious about doing that, let’s get some stuff done.”
