The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture, C. D. Dickerson III and Andrew Sears, Chicago University Press, 240pp, £40 (hb)
The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture explores the enduring fascination with fractured statues, focusing on the “power dynamics of iconoclastic dismantling and defacement, and how various cultures treat broken statues”, says a publisher’s statement. Highlights include Michelangelo’s terracotta Model of a Nude Woman (around 1533), which new research suggests may have been intentionally created incomplete. The publication accompanies a wide-ranging and eclectic exhibition spanning more than 4,500 years of global history, which opened in September at the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence before it travels to the National Gallery of Art in Washington DC next year.
Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Nancy Spector, Phaidon, 352pp, £39.95 (hb)
This newly revised and expanded edition assesses the relevance today of the influential conceptual artist Felix Gonzalez-Torres who died from an Aids-related illness in 1996. “Almost two decades after its original publication, the monograph accompanying Gonzalez-Torres’s 1995 retrospective at the Guggenheim Museum is still the canonical text on the artist,” says a publisher’s statement. Gonzalez-Torres is known especially for his famous sweet installations, which are usually mounted in piles in the corner of rooms. “The candy pieces, like all his works, encourage a wealth of meanings, and can be everything from stridently political to gently lyrical,” writes the critic and host of The Art Newspaper’s podcast, Ben Luke.
The Voice of the Artist(s): another vocabulary, Gabriela Galcerán (editor), Sternberg Press, 360pp, £23.50 (pb)
This publication grew out of a video project devised by the cultural producer Gabriela Galcerán in which 26 artists chose a word, one for each letter of the alphabet, and responded to it in their own way. The five thematic chapters, including “Power + Politics” and “Agency + Language”, subsequently draw connections between their ideas. Contributors include Lynn Hershman Leeson, Lawrence Abu Hamdan and Gary Hill. “They all made me flinch, each for a different reason. I love the wide range of tones and registers that make up this choral effort. Some are intimate, some political, some humorous or oblique,” says Galcerán in a statement.
Faces and Phases, Zanele Muholi, Renée Mussai (editor), Mack, 464pp, £65 (hb)
For more than 20 years, the South African artist and activist Zanele Muholi has been documenting Black lesbian and bisexual women, along with queer, trans, non-binary, and gender fluid people for the project Faces and Phases. This new volume of the work, released to mark the project’s 20th anniversary, has been updated to include new sitters in locations such as São Paulo, Salvador, London, Porto and Los Angeles. “These striking photographs are often accompanied by participants’ testimonies, sharing their personal stories, feelings, and lived experiences,” says a publisher’s statement. Muholi was born in Durban in 1972 at the height of apartheid in South Africa. In the early 2000s, the photographer began to raise awareness of the hypocrisies and hate crimes that remain prevalent against the LGBTQ+ community within the country.

https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyns-hak.title: Brooklyn's Hakeem Jeffries is poised to lead a Democratic House. Will his party follow?
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyns-hak.author: Brigid Bergin
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyns-hak.text:
Hakeem Jeffries is en route to become the first Black Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives and one of the most powerful Democrats in the country.
But a scene from primary night back in Brooklyn this June illustrates the challenges he’ll face in managing a left flank that is at least partly responsible for Democrats taking back Congress this week.
Supporters of then-congressional hopeful Claire Valdez and other democratic socialist candidates were basking in a string of primary-night wins in Bushwick when Jeffries’ image appeared on the screen.
“You’re next!” the crowd chanted. The exuberant, audacious primary threat reflected the attitude of many young DSA enthusiasts who view the Democratic leader as too centrist and too supportive of Israel.
With the Associated Press projecting Democrats will now control the House and Senate, Jeffries could be joined by fellow Brooklynite and Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer in controlling both houses of Congress. Both are seen as “establishment” Democrats who have been reluctant to embrace the democratic socialist wing of the party.
Now Jeffries is poised for the first time to take the gavel as a leader of a restive party struggling to define itself as more than just an opposition party to President Donald Trump.
The fight over Democrats' future is playing out in Jeffries’ hometown and his home district. On one side are Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s progressive politics. He and his incoming allies in Congress have surged on a message of affordability, taxing the rich and support of the Palestinian cause. On the other side are politicians like Jeffries, who has deep ties to the more centrist Brooklyn political establishment and a long history of steadfast support of Israel.
“The first big question a lot of the folks are asking is what does it mean to be a Democrat today?” said Democratic strategist Basil Smikle, a professor of practice at Columbia University’s School of Professional Studies and the former executive director of the New York State Democratic Party. “ In many ways, Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker of the House could help define that term and chart a course for Democrats for the next 20 to 30 years potentially.”
While Jeffries has earned the respect of colleagues, constituents and even former adversaries, there will be real challenges within the Democratic caucus. Two newly elected members from the New York City delegation — Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier —are on record repeatedly withholding their support for his leadership unless he changes the party’s priorities.
“For me, it really comes down to, are we going to have strong leadership that is going to really push for the things that working people across this country have been demanding for ages, whether that is abolishing ICE, Medicare for All, the John Lewis Voting Rights Act, making sure that we are fighting for universal childcare, investing our tax dollars in our babies here and not in bombs abroad,” Avila Chevalier said in an interview ahead of the election.
A spokesperson for Jeffries did not respond to a request for comment as the Democratic House leader stumped for Democrats in competitive contests across the country and in New York.
Jeffries signaled Tuesday night that he plans to build on the affordability agenda that fueled Mamdani’s campaign last year and became a standard talking point for Democrats across the country during the midterms.
“ We're gonna fight for an affordable America, we're gonna end this national nightmare, and we're gonna continue America's long, necessary, and majestic march toward a more perfect union,” Jeffries said at his own victory party.
Jeffries first ran for office in 2000 at 29 years old. He challenged 20-year incumbent Assemblymember Roger Green, whom Jeffries accused at the time of being out of touch with his constituents and “backed by the Democratic machine,” according to the New York Times.
He was then an attorney at the white-shoe law firm of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison. Jeffries lost to Green twice, in 2000 and again in 2002. He won the seat in 2006 after Green retired.
“He’s more mature now,” Green said of his one-time opponent. The 77-year-old former lawmaker lives in the congressional district and remains in contact with Jeffries. Green said Central Brooklyn contains a growing number of DSA supporters and is a prime example of the economic inequality that has become their rallying cry during recent elections.
“This is a district where you see a lot of young folks that are part of ‘the precariat,’’ Green said, describing young people fresh out of college who are failing to find entry or mid-level work in the tech industry because of the artificial intelligence boom. “Then the district still has a large concentration of people of color in areas that have been really impacted by a tradition of intergenerational social and economic inequality, particularly in the housing projects.”
The district features higher rates of unemployment, food insecurity and childhood poverty than national averages, according to the Congressional District Health Dashboard compiled by NYU Langone Health. The demographics of the district have also changed dramatically in two decades, with a steep drop in Black residents and an increase in white, Latino and Asian residents.
“I think if Hakeem seizes this moment to pull the Black body politic together and align it with our progressive allies in the white community and the Latino community to bring about a Roosevelt-type moment, then we’ll be okay,” Green said, referring to the economic policies of President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal.
That won’t be any easy task and there are other elected officials within the district who don’t believe Jeffries understands the party’s current zeitgeist.
State Sen. Jabari Brisport, a DSA member whose district overlaps with Jeffries, said in his six years in office, he has never had a single conversation with the congressmember. He said he has spoken to Jeffries’ staff, but never to Jeffries personally. Brisport traced the perceived animosity to around 2018, when rumors circulated that the DSA might try to primary Jeffries.
Jeffries briefly faced the threat of a primary in the fall of 2025 when City Councilmember Chi Ossé, another DSA member, filed paperwork to run for the same congressional seat. Ossé pulled the plug on his primary challenge at the urging of Mayor Mamdani
Brisport is not optimistic about Jeffries as House speaker.
“ I would say he is wildly out of touch with the district and also the Democratic Party, at large, most glaring being his pro-Israel stance three years into the genocide,” Brisport said. He cited Jeffries lack of support for Medicare for All and the support he receives from the real estate industry and Wall Street.
Queens Borough President Donovan Richards, a Jeffries supporter, said he felt emotional waking up on Election Day knowing that he was on the verge of making history.
“People try to label him as establishment, but that’s not who he is,” Richards said.
Civil rights activists nationally and within the district say they’ll defend Jeffries. At the same time, there is a growing appetite for Black leaders who reach leadership positions to do more to improve conditions for Black Americans.
“ It is also going to be up to us to make sure that he has the backup so that he can address the issues that Black New Yorkers care about, that Black Americans care about,” said L. Joy Williams, president of the NAACP New York State Conference and former president of the Brooklyn Conference. “But then also make sure we got a lighter on hand and that if we need to light a little fire under his butt, we have no hesitation with doing so.”
Some voters in Jeffries' district see new advantages to his history-making ascent. Mollie Wormser, 29, said the symbolism alone of the first Black speaker was cause for celebration, as she cast her vote for Jeffries at P.S. 256 in Bedford-Stuyvesant on Tuesday.
“ I think the first Black speaker of the House would be probably bring back some kind of the Obama-era type optimism that I think I'm hoping for,” she said.
Benjamin Davis, 70, credited Jeffries with pushing back against the Trump administration, even while he was in the minority. He also said it was good to have a moderating voice leading the party.
“ I'm a diehard Democrat,” said Davis. “But I don't think we need to go to the extreme.”
Brittany Krigstein and Elizabeth Kim contributed reporting.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mamdani-midt.title: Last Night’s Victories Were Made Possible by Zohran Mamdani
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mamdani-midt.author: Corey Robin
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mamdani-midt.text:
Last Night’s Victories Were Made Possible by Zohran Mamdani
Zohran Mamdani understood something no one else did: most Donald Trump voters had their reasons for going for Trump, and those reasons were economic. Mamdani saw that, and he saw a path to winning them back. He gave it a name: affordability.
If there’s one person who saw yesterday’s repudiation of the right coming long before everyone else did, it’s Zohran Mamdani. In one way or another, he and the movement that created him are the architects of the Democrats’ victory.
Two years ago, the day after the 2024 election, the mood was grim; the future was bleak. Nobody saw the possibility for regrouping. What did Mamdani do? Just one week after Donald Trump’s victory, he went out and interviewed Trump voters all across the city. He spoke to white, black, brown, Muslim, Asian, but above all working-class men and women and, above all, in the Bronx and Queens.
Everyone now thinks of Mamdani’s victory a year later, first in the primary and then in the general election, as a foregone conclusion, a New York thing that had no meaning beyond New York. It wasn’t. The reason it wasn’t is that Mamdani understood something no one else understood: Trump voters had their reasons for going for Trump, and those reasons could be explained and understood. Not the hard-bitten right-winger, mind you, but the people who put Trump over the top. That reason was economic. Mamdani saw that, and he gave it a name: affordability.
And lo and behold, what did one Texas voter, who’s voted Republican all his life, say last night about how and why he voted for the Democrats for the first time?
No one can afford anything anymore. Our water and air is the dirtiest and our education is horrible.
Mamdani spoke to that sentiment with his use of the term “affordability.” It’s not just a strictly economic word; as this Texas voter suggests, it’s almost a spiritual term, a sense of the enshittification of life, the grinding worsening of material and therefore cultural conditions. Water is dirty; education is horrible; it’s all going to shit. That’s what Mamdani spoke to, and he said, “We can do something about that.”
So many politicians now use that word “affordability” that we forget it was Mamdani who, less than two years ago, made that the word. And what every other Democratic politician across the United States, whether they’re Democratic Socialists of America or not, saw is that those Trump voters, those swing Trump voters, are gettable — if you can speak about the economic and cultural catastrophe that has been visited upon ordinary citizens. Whether we’re talking about the Latino men who shifted right toward Trump along the border in Texas or the farmers in the Midwest who’ve voted Republican their whole lives till yesterday, or the Solid South.
Look at the voters who shifted from Republican to Democrat yesterday and the demographic trends. Remember those young people who voted Trump and were declared lost for a generation to the tradwives and the manosphere? They saw the largest shift left of any demographic group. Voters eighteen to twenty-nine years old saw a 32-point shift to the left. White noncollege voters, which is how this addled nation codes “white working class,” saw a 14-point shift to the left. Latino voters saw a 28-point shift to the left.
It took a Muslim socialist, born in Uganda, raised in New York City, to give the American heartland a new kind of language to wage political battle against the Right. Just as it was Jewish socialists a century ago, many of them immigrants and raised in New York City, who gave America during the 1930s and 1940s, in politics and culture, in the wake of one of the first anti-immigrant backlashes the country had ever seen, a new language for itself.

https://gothamist.com/news/trump-urged-v.title: Trump urged voters to pretend he’s on the ballot. In NY and NJ they listened.
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-urged-v.author: Jon Campbell, Elizabeth Kim, Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-urged-v.text:
President Donald Trump made a simple request when he headlined a rally for New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman last month.
“Just pretend I’m on the ballot,” he told the crowd in Syracuse.
New York voters obliged — and Democrats are ecstatic with the results.
The blue wave that swept the nation Tuesday washed over the Empire State, where Democrats up and down the ballot outperformed already high expectations en route to significant victories across the state.
The same occurred in New Jersey, where Democrats picked up two key House seats that had been held by the GOP.
In both states, Democrats repeatedly linked their GOP opponents to Trump, knowing that polls show voters in both states largely view the Republican president unfavorably.
“Well Mr. President, you got your wish,” Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said in her victory speech Tuesday night.
The bigger-than-anticipated Democratic victories in New York and New Jersey started with the top of the ticket, with Hochul scoring a 22-point lead over the Republican Blakeman with 76% of the vote counted, according to the Associated Press.
Her performance was in stark contrast to 2022, when Hochul won her first full term by a slim 6-point margin. That year, Hochul’s relatively lackluster win in a state that has twice as many Democrats as Republicans helped lead to down-ballot losses in four key races that helped the GOP win control of the House.
That wasn’t the case this time around.
In the Hudson Valley, Democrat Cait Conley scored a victory over Rep. Mike Lawler, a Republican congressmember who had been one of the Democrats’ top targets for two straight cycles.
On Long Island, Democratic Reps. Tom Suozzi and Laura Gillen held leads of 15 and 16 points, respectively, over their opponents with roughly half the vote counted.
In New Jersey, Democrat Zack Mullock denied Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew a fifth term in Congress in a surprising upset in South Jersey, winning by roughly five points. First-time Democratic candidate Rebecca Bennett defeated embattled Republican incumbent Tom Kean in New Jersey’s 7th district, taking home nearly 60% of the vote in a race that was expected to be far closer.
The wins, coupled with Democratic victories across the country, led to Democrats controlling the House of Representatives and the Senate, according to race calls by the AP.
That would put two Brooklyn Democrats — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Charles Schumer — in position to become speaker of the House and Senate majority leader, respectively, come January.
“Are we gonna kick some ass tonight or what?” New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who headed the Senate Democrats’ election efforts, said as she took the stage at Hochul’s victory party at the Hilton Hotel in Midtown. “The country looks very blue tonight.”
Since 2022, Hochul has partnered with Jeffries, Schumer and Gillibrand to raise tens of millions of dollars for the state Democratic Party to help fund a coordinated campaign designed to bolster turnout for candidates up and down the ballot.
A moderate, Hochul also leaned on Democrats who are much further left than she is — most notably New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — to drive up voter turnout among younger voters, whom the 68-year-old governor otherwise struggled to reach on her own.
Jasmine Gripper, state director of the left-leaning Working Families Party, said Hochul’s partnership with Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez shows that “she knows who she needs to be with in order to win.”
“Hochul is governing well but she's also building the right coalition,” Gripper said.
Republicans, meanwhile, were largely resigned to defeat with one significant exception.
In New York’s 21st congressional district, Republican Anthony Constantino — an entrepreneur and political newcomer who aggressively courted Trump’s support — held a 2-point lead over Democrat Blake Gendebien with three quarters of the vote counted. Public-opinion polls showed Gendebien with a slight lead heading into the race.
The Republican at the top of the ticket — Blakeman, the Nassau County executive — vowed to work with Hochul and Democrats going forward.
“ You win some, you lose some,” he said in his concession speech. “The fact of the matter is that now we pull together, we move forward, we have the best interests of the people in our heart.”
In a victory speech late Tuesday, Jeffries — who could become the first Black person to serve as House speaker – said Tuesday marked a “dramatic change election.”
“We understand as House Democrats that we have to deliver dramatic change,” he said. “House Democrats are committed to making life better for you beginning on Day One.”
Includes reporting by Michael Hayes.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.title: The Donald Trump Era in American Politics Is Ending
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.author: Paul Heideman
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.text:
The Donald Trump Era in American Politics Is Ending
The takeaways from the midterms are clear: no amount of billionaire spending could overcome the fact that Donald Trump’s dominance is coming to a close, the Left has much more room to grow, and we have entered a period of new possibility in US politics.
The American people delivered an absolute rout against Donald Trump and the GOP last night. Here are five takeaways from the midterm results:
1. Trump Owns This Defeat
Everything about this defeat points to a different way Donald Trump has weakened the Republican Party.
In Texas and South Carolina, he pushed his preferred candidates, Ken Paxton and Darline Graham, for the Senate above the first choices of the state parties. Both were terrible candidates and terrible campaigners who made the Democrats’ job vastly easier. In Florida, he pushed an aggressive gerrymander that energized Democratic voters while failing to net any additional seats for Republicans. Nationwide, the nakedly criminal war on Iran combined with his refusal to even humor voters’ anger at the cost of living weighed down every Republican in the country.
Over the last few weeks, Trump implored voters to pretend he was on the ticket. They followed his advice.
2. Billionaire Money Wasn’t Enough
One reason Trump and the rest of the party felt empowered to simply ignore clear signs from the electorate was their massive financial advantage.
A few dozen billionaires, including Elon Musk, Miriam Adelson, the Winklevoss brothers, and Ken Griffin, poured truly staggering amounts of money into Republican super PACs. Trump’s personal super PAC, MAGA, Inc., had over $400 million in its account. That was more money than the Democratic Senate super PAC, House super PAC, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, and Democratic National Committee combined. Most of the Republican financial advantage was spent on the Senate, where the GOP outspent Democrats by about 50 percent.
Republicans expected to be able to use this golden hoard to simply crush Democrats in states like Texas. It wasn’t nearly enough — a fact that should be heartening to anyone dismayed about the undemocratic effects of big money in politics.
3. The Knives Are Going to Come Out for Trump
Because of the previous two points, Republican politicians are going to turn on Trump quickly.
The writing is on the wall for 2028. There is no reason to think that a president whose connection to reality is visibly attenuating with each passing week will be able to turn his popularity around in the next two years. Any Republican with ambitions for the future will be racing to create distance between themselves and the administration.
The few Republicans who openly opposed Trump in the last few years, like Ron DeSantis, are already blaming Trump for the defeat and calling for a new direction for the party. Determining that direction will be a messy, conflictual process, with open conflict among different elements of the party. But with every passing day, there will be fewer and fewer reasons for members of the party to continue their obeisance to Trump.
4. Democrats Won the Biggest Overall Congressional Majority for Either Party Since the GOP in 2014
The size of the Democratic majority is striking. As of Wednesday morning, most projections have the Democrats winning about 245 seats in the House, and fifty-four or fifty-five seats in the Senate. This puts the Democrats in a similar position to the Republicans in 2014, when the GOP expanded on its majority in the House and finally recaptured the Senate from the Democrats.
Since the Trump era began, no party has had majorities of this size in both the House and the Senate.
In both the House and the Senate, this vastly decreases the leverage available to small minorities of the caucuses. In the Senate, John Fetterman will not be able to block progressive legislation the way Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema were during the Biden administration. Similarly, in the House, even the expanded team of socialist legislators will not come close to providing the margin of victory for the Democratic majority.
In this context, Democratic politics will likely reflect the center of gravity of the caucus in each chamber, rather than the power of a few legislators holding strategic veto points.
5. The Left Is Continuing to Rise
Across the country, this was a fantastic night for the Left.
Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates, as expected, won their general elections in places like New York, Colorado, and Michigan. Moreover, DSA candidates won election to the state house in close races in Kentucky and Florida. Candidates like Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed, who are often associated with DSA despite not being members, also won races that were widely seen as tests for the progressive wing of the Democratic Party. Angie Nixon, a DSA member who won an upset victory in her primary for Florida’s senate seat, came within a few points of winning in a state most liberals had written off as irredeemably red. Exit polls, meanwhile, showed that three times as many young voters described themselves as democratic socialists as MAGA.
DSA’s project has clearly not hit its ceiling yet, and these results show that it is time to take the fight to new battlegrounds.

https://gothamist.com/food/can-opening-a.title: Can opening a restaurant in a New York museum turn the food into a work of art?
https://gothamist.com/food/can-opening-a.author: Joshua David Stein
https://gothamist.com/food/can-opening-a.text:
On a recent Friday night, in the basement of the towering Brutalist building that was once known as the home of the Whitney Museum, bejeweled women in angular dresses and tan men with perfect stubble cut into delicate turbot and sipped martinis out of hand blown glasses. Long tapered candles flickered, illuminating freshly baked baguettes and mounds of French butter. The tablescape could all have been a Renaissance still life, save for all the life abounding around it.
“This is the poireaux de poire poivre,” announced a white-blazer-clad server to the table next to me, as he delivered a $29 dish of leeks with peppercorn-poached pears on the table. It’s a very elegant tongue-twister, but a tinkle of laughter and bonhomie rose like a mist from the table.
This is Marcel, the glamorous new restaurant named after the architect Marcel Breuer, in whose namesake building it is housed. Opened this spring and operated by Sotheby’s, in partnership with the design firm Roman & Williams, it is just the latest in a wave of restaurants cohabitating with art institutions. Around the city, restaurants are installing themselves like creative barnacles within the walls of galleries, museums and, like Marcel, auction houses.
Manuela, a Soho restaurant owned by the gallery Hauser & Wirth, opened in 2024, joined hotspots like Kappo Masa, co-owned by gallerist Larry Gagosian, to offer dinner with a side of blue-chip art. At Manuela, diners enjoy halibut in the shadow of Cindy Sherman, Louis Bourgeois and Philip Guston.
On the Bowery, the shimmering OMA-designed wing of New Museum is home to a buzzy restaurant called Oberon. Across the river, Ned Baldwin’s strange seafood palace Zoli opened within Amant, a sprawling arts campus nestled into the warehouses of East Williamsburg. And in the fall, MoMA PS1 will open a new French-African cafe helmed by the Jamaican-American chef Devonn Francis.
The commingling of art and dinner is nothing new, of course. The Russian Tea Room was founded by members of the Imperial Ballet in 1926, and quickly became a refuge for Picasso and Dali. FOOD, the legendary SoHo restaurant, was an installation project by artist Gordon Matta Clark, and more recently reincarnated by the late artist Lucien Smith. Howard Chandler Christy’s murals at the Cafe des Artistes have survived countless openings and closings. But those were art in restaurants: come for dinner, stay for the decoration. These days the relationship is more symbiotic. Museums depend on restaurants; restaurants on museums: Each nourish the other.
We are in a delicate and tense time for the public museum.
“Museums broadly have been facing a multi-decade decline in attendance,” said Stephen Reily, who heads the think tank ReMuseum, which focuses on promoting innovation in art museums. “COVID was a cliff that some but not all have come back from.”
There’s also new competition. As social-media-forward ersatz museum-ish experiences like the Balloon Museum and the Museum of Ice Cream — neither mission driven nor non-profit — threaten to bodysnatch visitors, public funding has also evaporated. This all leaves administrators looking for ways to bring new bodies into the doors.
“Museums are in a Darwinian moment, an industrial revolution is happening behind the scenes and the toxicity is forcing the moths to change color,” said Rayme Silverberg of Paradigm Shift, a start-up dedicated to safeguarding the financial sustainability of museums.
A restaurant, particularly a well-regarded buzzy one, helps a museum bring in new visitors and reframe itself within a community. Restaurants, meanwhile, are facing rising food costs, rising labor costs, ever increased competition and outrageous rents. Nestling inside a larger institution, especially one with wealthy donors, space to spare and a built-in audience should relieve at least some of that pressure.
Plus, you know, it’s fun. At Oberon, for instance, diners can enjoy tomato and stracciatella salads and a roasted half chicken while taking in an agentic AI installation behind the bar under a strange fuzzy roof that looks like the inside of Kenny Powers’ mullet. The comfort food, by Brooklyn stalwart chef Henry Rich of Rucola and Rhodora, seems at odds with the modern art but the frisson is unmistakable. What roasted half chicken with fig leaf and preserved lemon doesn’t taste better under avant-garde light fixtures by Minjae Kim? The after-dinner treats, dark mint chocolates with wrappers designed by artist Laurie Anderson, don’t hurt either. They read, “I was thinking of you. And I was thinking of you. And I was thinking of you. And then I wasn’t thinking of you anymore.”
Each art cantina serves a slightly different purpose. Marcel, where the menu is pricey but nothing compared to the art on the wall, the restaurant is, as Sotheby’s chairman Lisa Dennison told Gothamist, “a natural extension of the Sotheby’s experience. It is a space where our clients, visitors, and the wider community can engage with art in a different and more intimate way, whether they're visiting our galleries, meeting friends for breakfast or lunch, or enjoying dinner surrounded by an array of exceptional works.”
The exceptional works Dennison mentions include a large Willem DeKooning hanging over the banquets. In the vitrines on the way to the restroom, patrons pass Franz Kline’s striking blue Venus statue, a tangle of painted steel by John Chamberlain. Marcel hums along with the pleasant bustle of commerce. The art can be bought (price on request); the omelette can be bought ($34); even the forks, knives, spoons, chairs, and those handmade martini glasses can be purchased ($300), part of the Marcel collection by designers Roman & Williams.
Even if you are among the rare diners who can’t afford a de Kooning, eating among a masterpiece gives just enough of a soupçon of affluence.The ten course tasting menu at The Modern seems pricey at $285, but overlooking the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, it's a pittance to cosplay as a plutocrat art patron.
Of course, not all of these spaces swim in the monied deep end of the art world. Zoli, deep in East Williamsburg, is as far away fromthe profit-minded Sotheby’s is to the non-profit Amant. Whereas Marcel’s chef, Marie Rose Aude, channels haute Parisien cuisine, Zoli’s Ned Baldwin goes weird and weirder still. As Baldwin, a trained artist (Yale, MFA, sculpture), explains to me,
“I curate the menu like a group show,” said Balwin
The offerings are eclectic and strange. Duck hearts are skewered and Kombucha-glazed. An oyster lurks inside a beignet. Rock shrimp are served with husk cherries. The steak is bison and smoky; the cheesecake is Taleggio and funky. But it fits the space perfectly. The food is complemented by the three large aquariums full of genetically modified fish, bizarre crustaceans and detritus from Brooklyn canals by the artist Pierre Huyghes that divide the space. Little shrimps silently gaze out at the diners from their installation. Though the experience is less tony and more experimental than Marcel, the feeling is similar: the restaurant and the artist are in symbiotic dance. It is delightfully unclear where the aquarium ends and the red shrimp with husk cherries begin.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.title: ICE Was Secretly Ordered to Stop All Immigration Raids on Election Day
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.author: Karl Loftus
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.text:
Orders for what one official called a “national no enforcement day” began circulating on Monday inside U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement.
Handed down through ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division through internal group chats and verbal commands, the directive called for a halt to all immigration enforcement operations on Election Day, according to ICE officials across the country who spoke to The Intercept.
“We were told all operations are canceled for Election Day,” said one ICE immigration official, who operates in the south and requested anonymity to protect their livelihood. “Word of mouth from our first-line supervisors, no official email notice.”
According to multiple ICE officials who spoke to The Intercept, the orders were handed down quietly to avoid media attention.
“Yesterday was the least amount of activity observed from ICE ERO throughout the entire year so far,” said Sherman Austin, the creator of StopICE.net, a crowdsourced platform tracking reported ICE activity across the United States. “You can kind of tell like from the morning. Usually, ICE gets started really early, and there’s a huge spike in activity between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m. That spike wasn’t there on Election Day.”
Another ICE official, who works in the Great Lakes region, confirmed the orders ahead of Election Day, referring to it as “National No Enforcement Day.”
“We were told to do ‘admin’ shit,” the official said. They said that ICE deportation officers who regularly do street-level operations were diverted to administrative office work: “I’ll be drinking coffee at the office for the first time in a year.”
In total, ICE officials working in four areas of responsibility — ICE’s jurisdictional regions — coving parts of the northeastern, midwestern, northern, and south-central U.S. regions told The Intercept that they had received orders to stand down on Election Day.
“Something Unusual Was Going On”
StopICE, the tracking website, which has roughly half a million subscribers, did record some ICE activity on Election Day, according to Austin, although most of the reports stemmed from sightings unrelated to any immigration enforcement activities.
“There were a few reports that came in about ICE being at usual spots like the jails,” Austin said, “or seen driving in certain areas in in the city, but it wasn’t the same type of activity that’s usually seen on the site. It was pretty clear that something unusual was going on.”
AntiFreeze, another crowdsourced ICE-tracking platform that allows users to report and receive real-time alerts about ICE raids, also saw abnormally low levels of ICE activity on November 3, according to Josh, the creator and developer behind the site, who requested to keep his last name anonymous.
“On Election Day, our network only logged about 56 reported ICE sightings nationwide, which is one of the quietest Tuesdays we’ve ever seen,” Josh said. “We did get about three sightings that did report ICE activity near polling stations, but most of the reports were observations of vehicles associated with ICE. We barely got any reports about actual ICE arrests yesterday.”
Local activists also observed a low level of ICE activity on the street level.
“There was no evidence of street abductions,” said an activist working with the rapid-response network in Minnesota’s Twin Cities.
“ICE, in some capacity, was still out and about, but we did not see any reports of off-the-street detainments by ICE or attempts at detainments,” said the activist, who said they got word of ICE arrests at jails, but not targeted operations among the general public. “There were a lot of folks, probably more than usual, observing, and so I think we can be pretty confident that this wasn’t due to lack of observation.”
Leo Martinez, who volunteers with VC Defensa in Southern California, told The Intercept that no one in his rapid-response group reported any sightings of ICE activity on Tuesday.
It is still unclear exactly where the orders to halt immigration enforcement operations on Election Day originated from, although some ICE officials believe the orders stemmed from ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations leadership — and not directly from the White House.
“Nobody from the SDDO level” — a reference to Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer, part of ICE’s upper management — “expected it to happen until the very last moment,” said another ICE official familiar with the matter. “But I think some of us caught on that senior leadership was making this call with fears of us being at the polls.”
The official said, “It’s crazy that The White House didn’t catch on.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

In Last Night’s Midterms, the Left Proved It Can Win
Democratic voters have long sided with socialists on policy but feared they were a liability in elections. Last night’s results finally proved that wrong.
The Left has been so conditioned in the Trump era to look aghast and horrified at election results that it is still hard to fully believe the outcome today. Yet the historic events of last night really did happen: Donald Trump and Republicans suffered a historic rebuke from voters, handing Democrats wins up and down the ballot all across the country, flipping both chambers of Congress in their favor, and handing them the largest congressional majorities they’ve had since Barack Obama’s election.
In many ways, the result is simple. Across poll after poll leading into the election and exit poll after exit poll leading out of it, the message from voters was the same: they think the economy sucks, they think prices are too high, and they’re angry at Trump and blame him squarely for this entire situation. To send this message, voters turned out in droves to hand power to a Democratic Party that these same polls show they have very little love for, sometimes viewing the Dems even more dimly than they do Trump.
Democrats were expected to take the House. They were not expected to win a majority of more than 250 seats in it, as current estimates have them winning. Nor were they expected to win a Senate majority, let alone a Senate majority of at least fifty-four seats. And they were not expected to flip deep red seats across the country, to sweep Republicans from control of Texas at nearly every level of power, and to win a majority of the country’s governorships, achieving wins and trifectas in states they’ve been practically locked out of for sometimes decades. Obama referred to his 2010 midterms rout as a “shellacking.” Last night was an annihilation.
This is not just good news for Democrats. For the Left, which operates within these Democratic majorities at both the state and federal levels, the results present a historic opportunity to turn its political priorities from words into tangible reality across the country, further building the power it has patiently and, for a long time, quietly been constructing from the ground up these past ten years.
That includes at the federal level. Even though Trump has two more years in the White House, and Democrats are threatening to zealously turn their powers of oversight on the vast record of abuse and criminality he’s racked up during that time, there is some, extremely slim reason to believe something could actually get done.
Trump phoned Politico last night to make clear he was open to working with the Democrats and didn’t “want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” The last time Trump was in the White House with a Democratic Congress, the pandemic, the United States saw the largest expansion of the welfare state in decades. Trump’s ideological malleability and the fact that he is currently looking at a legacy as a historic failure presents at least the possibility of an opening for something better to happen.
It’s an opening the Left will be able to take advantage of, too. The Left will enter this new Congress with far more formidable numbers than it’s had in decades: at least seven members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), creating the historic opportunity to for the first time form a distinct socialist caucus in Congress and a Squad-like progressive “Bloc” that could have as many as twenty members.
The massive Democratic House majority means “the Bloc” will not have the expected leverage of being able to block House Democratic leader’s Hakeem Jeffries’s bid for Speaker, or to hold up legislation Freedom Caucus–style. But it will have influence. Much of the generous pandemic policies of 2020, including both Trump and, later, Joe Biden’s stimulus checks, originated with the public demands of socialist and progressive members of Congress that later found their way into legislation on the back of their clear public need and popularity.
This time, the Left will be making these arguments in a world in which socialists have already transformed the way even centrist Democrats talk about politics. The party’s years-long obsession with “norms” and rescuing democracy having largely faded into the background in favor of the affordability-focused and anti-billionaire rhetoric popularized by, respectively, New York’s socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and the socialist duo of Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.
Just as importantly, it’s a world in which the Left, thanks to a spate of major wins last night, has thoroughly discredited the arguments used to marginalize and dismiss its basic case.
Earthquake in Michigan
No left-wing victory last night was bigger than Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan Senate win over Republican Mike Rogers by a whopping 7 points. It was the exact, hefty margin El-Sayed himself had promised he would win by back in May and defied the incessant predictions that he would end up badly underperforming.
There was arguably no more important race this year than for the purple state’s Senate seat: for the Left, which sought to prove progressives could run and win outside of blue strongholds; for corporate Democrats, a segment of whom feared losing the ability to fearmonger about supposedly risky left-wing candidates; for the pro-Israel lobby, which feared that the success of a stridently pro-Palestinian message would obliterate its claim that blind fealty to Israel was “good politics”; for Trump and the MAGA movement, whose loss of the key state could be a harbinger of even worse political defeat to come.
El-Sayed’s win has confirmed all of these. It represents not just a failure for MAGA, in the form of now two-time loser and career-long warmonger Mike Rogers. It’s an absolute disaster for the pro-Israel lobby and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) in particular, which blew tens of millions of dollars over the course of both the primary and general to defeat El-Sayed and tried every trick in the book to defame and make voters, particularly Jewish ones, fear him.
Instead, both exit polls and voting data indicates El-Sayed comfortably won Jewish voters despite this ugly, Islamophobic campaign against him. He outperformed Kamala Harris in the heavily Jewish Oakland County, the home base of his Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, who humiliated herself trying to kneecap him in the final days of the race.
Catastrophically for the pro-Israel lobby, he did all this while maintaining an unabashed opposition to further US aid to Israel, proving unambiguously that left-wing criticisms of Israeli policy are not only broadly shared by voters in battleground states, but that they are shared by Jewish voters, too.
That he managed this is especially impressive given that, unlike his Democratic colleague running for governor, El-Sayed had to overcome not only an avalanche of big money spending but also members of his own party working around the clock to sabotage him, from Stevens’s last-minute endorsement of Rogers to Rep. Hillary Scholten’s support for a write-in campaign against the Democratic nominee in the final days.
Democratic defectors to the GOP had a variety of motives, but at least some of them made publicly clear they hoped El-Sayed’s defeat would nip the growing Democratic opposition to US aid to Israel in the bud — something they were willing to elect a candidate who included actual antisemites in his campaign to do, as well as to empower an administration that makes common cause with literal neo-Nazis and white supremacists. Instead, they lost and disgraced themselves for nothing.
El-Sayed also did it on a progressive platform of Medicare for All and taxing the rich, two ideas that, when Bernie Sanders first popularized them in 2016, the public was told were too controversial with swing voters and risky to run on. A decade later, these ideas have such widely understood, popular support that Republicans didn’t even bother attacking them. Instead, they put all their eggs in the race-baiting basket, making El-Sayed’s Arab ethnicity and Muslim faith the overwhelming focus of their attacks in what turned out to be one of the most shockingly racist election campaigns this century — and another disgraceful failure.
Wins and Losses
El-Sayed’s win wasn’t the only bright spot for the Left last night. There was also Troy Jackson’s win in Maine, who succeeded where four others had failed in unseating the seemingly untouchable thirty-year Republican incumbent Susan Collins from her Senate seat. Though Jackson, an eighteen-year state legislator and former state senate president and Democratic leader, was far from your typical image of a left insurgent, he quickly consolidated socialist and progressive backing after former nominee Graham Platner’s personal scandals pushed him out of the race.
Though not a socialist, Jackson’s genuine working-class background — as a fifth-generation logger who entered politics to win collective bargaining rights for his fellow woodworkers — and robust progressive record made him closer to the kind of candidates the Left hopes to see in power. In the end, Jackson was able to secure victory by neutralizing Collins’s ability to run up big scores in otherwise blue-voting areas.
The other major progressive win was by James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Texas seat in thirty-eight years, part of a historic blue sweep across Texas that saw Democrats end nearly three decades of GOP rule of the state. Talarico is not a socialist, despite old comments criticizing capitalism that briefly became a campaign issue, and like El-Sayed, he took pains to insist that he was a capitalist. Even so, he was backed by groups like More Perfect Union and the Progressive Change Campaign Committee and drew support from prominent socialists like Hasan Piker, who has said that the Left was “the force that backed him early on” and “allowed him to win.”
Maybe more important, Talarico ran on a class-based message decrying “billionaire mega-donors” — one of whom, Elon Musk, lit at least $47 million on fire trying and failing to beat him — and insisting that the fundamental political divide in the United States was “top versus bottom,” a more progressive message than many Democrats ran on even in solid blue states. So his emphatic 12 point victory over the scandal-plagued Ken Paxton is a victory for the kind of populist message the Left has long advocated, even as Talarico did things like refusing to back Medicare for All and declining to campaign with Bernie Sanders when he visited the state.
Speaking of Sanders, as of the time of writing, seventeen of the twenty-one candidates endorsed by the socialist senator have won their races, while only two have lost, and two are in races that are still to be called. Sanders’s endorsements were less straightforwardly left-wing than those of organizations like DSA or Justice Democrats. They included candidates like El-Sayed and Jackson, but they also included more establishment candidates like Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, who beat corporate-friendly rivals in their primaries. They ran the gamut from DSA candidates like New York’s Claire Valdez and Colorado’s Melat Kiros to candidates like Rebecca Cooke, the less progressive candidate in her primary but someone who flipped a Trump-voting, rural Wisconsin district that for decades was represented by a Democrat.
They also included William Lawrence, the Sunrise Movement cofounder who has flipped a swing district in the swing state of Michigan despite having one of the more left-wing résumés of any Democratic candidate — something that, like El-Sayed, we were told would make him a guaranteed loser. The fact that Lawrence left DSA mid-campaign and had to distance himself from old tweets that included calls to nationalize the fossil fuel industry should not take away from the magnitude of his win. On the back of a progressive populist campaign that pushed a data center moratorium and Medicare for All, Lawrence won a purple district that used to belong to the Democrats’ patron saint of centrism, former CIA analyst Elissa Slotkin.
Even some of the defeats were surprisingly good for the Left. In ruby-red Florida — where Republicans outnumber Democrats by 1.5 million and a Democrat hasn’t won statewide office since 2012 — DSA member Angie Nixon lost by less than 3 points, little different from the 2 point losing margin of the ex-Republican candidate who Democrats ran for governor. The state’s last three Democratic losing margins for Senate are 13, 16, 0.2, and 8 points. And that’s after being outspent nearly four-to-one and getting no help whatsoever from the national Democratic Party, which should be kicking itself for missing the opportunity to win another gettable Senate seat.
That a DSA member would even be competitive in Florida — the heartland of right-wing Cuban extremism and the home of both Marco Rubio and now two Bolsonaro sons — would have sounded laughable five years ago, or even five months ago. That Nixon could do this well with this little help will, together with El-Sayed’s win, make it that much harder to argue that the socialist label is an inherent electoral liability.
It should spark some soul-searching among the Democratic establishment and its decision to preemptively write off the race as a foregone loss. But it will no doubt also spark debate within the socialist movement, too, given Nixon’s result was built partly on distancing herself from alienating positions like defunding the police and abolishing prisons. Her strong showing, along with the success of other left-wing candidates who similarly moderated or eschewed contemporary left orthodoxy on some issues, points to the benefits of DSA candidates having the flexibility to tailor campaigns to local electorates.
The Left also suffered a defeat of sorts in Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn fell short at a second tilt at a Senate seat in a state where a Democrat hasn’t won statewide election for twenty years. Osborn, a union leader who led a successful 2021 strike against Kellogg’s over planned benefit cuts, was something of a proof of concept for the Left: that, as per research from the Center for Working-Class Politics, the way to win in such states is to run genuine working-class candidates with populist platforms outside of the Democratic Party brand.
To some extent, both of Osborn’s campaigns proved this true. The last four Democratic losing margins in Nebraska Senate races were 41 points, 19 points, 24 points, and 16 points; by contrast, Osborn has fallen short by roughly the same, single-digit margin of 7 points both runs. Clearly, if pro-working-class candidates are going to flip a deep red state like Nebraska, Osborn’s campaign is a model for how to do it.
But a losing margin is still a loss. Despite combining left-populist policies like “right to repair” with centrist messaging on issues like immigration — Osborn famously ran ads declaring he backed Trump’s border wall — the former union leader was unable to shake attacks that he was a secret Democrat. A particularly damaging set of “scandals” had Osborn on tape bashing the border wall and other Trump policies and using insulting language about his voters. On top of an avalanche of outside spending aimed against him, it proved too much to overcome.
These are on top of a few other stinging defeats for the Left, including Justice Democrats–backed Justin Pearson’s razor-thin loss in Tennessee’s Ninth District, who looked like he might be able to overcome a Republican gerrymander thanks to a surge in black voter turnout.
Socialists may instead be heartened by the victory of Scott Houldieson over a Trump-endorsed candidate in the Republican-held Indiana First Senate District. Houldieson, a union autoworker who cofounded and led the reform effort within the United Auto Workers that resulted in Shawn Fain’s leadership of the union, easily flipped the seat with a 14 point victory on the back of an affordability-focused campaign. Though not DSA-backed or a statewide race, it is to some extent a vindication of the kind of approach the Left believed would see success in Nebraska.
The Local Game Continues
Meanwhile, as usual, socialists and progressives continued their steady accrual of elected office at the state and local levels.
As of the time of writing, DSA has notched 130 wins in everything from state legislatures and city councils, to mayor’s offices and ballot measures, with forty-two losses and fifty-eight races still to be decided. While Angie Nixon fell short of her Senate bid, environmentalist Ashley Herrmann became only the second socialist to win elected office in Florida and the first to be elected to its state legislature in more than a century, flipping a swing district that the Republican incumbent had won with 58 percent of the vote two years earlier. Other notable socialist wins included Robert LeVertis Bell’s election to the Kentucky state house and Mathewos Samson’s election to the Georgia General Assembly, which, together with Gabriel Sanchez’s reelection, makes him one of two socialists in the state legislature.
Particularly notable are several mayoral races that were foregone conclusions after the primaries. Janeese Lewis George is now officially Washington, DC’s first socialist mayor, having won on the back of an affordable housing plan that combines “abundance”-style reforms with expanding rent stabilization. In Providence, Rhode Island, socialist David Morales has similarly cruised to an expected win and, together with a socialist-led city council, will now work to pass a robust rent control measure in the housing-crisis-stricken city — a measure the incumbent mayor he successfully primaried had vetoed.
More complicated is the Los Angeles mayor’s race, where socialist City Councilor Nithya Raman is currently on track to unseat Karen Bass as Los Angeles mayor. Raman’s candidacy was the subject of some controversy, after she was endorsed by the local DSA chapter despite not fully embracing the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement against Israel and not being questioned about it, leading the DSA’s National Political Committee to nearly strip her of the endorsement, an effort that failed by one vote. If Raman does win, she’ll be the first candidate to unseat an incumbent LA mayor in twenty-one years.
This is on top of a host of progressive ballot measures pushed through by majorities of voters countrywide: the defeat of an abortion ban ballot measure in Missouri, a successful ban on dark money in elections in Montana, and divestment from Israel in Providence, to name a few. Maybe most notably, ballot measures restricting the construction of data centers have so far won overwhelmingly around the country, thirty-eight to one, with eight still to be counted — a clear public vindication of a position championed and popularized by the broad Left.
What’s Smart Is What’s Right
For the past decade, socialists and progressives have often had good election nights even when the Democratic Party has suffered, and they have had bad nights while Democrats rejoiced. Last night may be the first one where both the Left and the centrist party establishment have seen historic wins in tandem.
Over the past two years, the Left showed it was the force most willing to fight against Trump’s right-wing assault and to come up with an effective argument — affordability and fighting oligarchy — to do it. Last night finally proved left policies and rhetoric are not the electoral liability Democratic voters have been told for decades it is.
For decades, Democratic voters have had to make the agonizing decision every election to choose between their heads and their hearts. The Left may have just freed them of it.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Hong Kong artists create a poetic moment in Venice
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, the Hong Kong-born artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui are training visitors’ attention on the quiet moments and subtle details connecting both cities. The exhibition, marking the 25th anniversary of Hong Kong’s first participation in the Venice Biennale, is curated by the Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA) and continues until 22 November. It is housed in a historic Venetian residential building in the floating city’s Campo della Tana neighbourhood, a setting that underlines the meditative, lived-in quality to the works.
“What we hope visitors take away from the exhibition is a moment of reflection,” says Dr Maria Mok, the director of the HKMoA. “Through Kingsley and Angel’s attention to everyday details, we hope visitors feel invited to slow down and become more attentive to their surroundings, even within the hustle and intensity of urban life.”
One of Kingsley Ng’s installations, for instance, Laundry Nocturne (2026), consists of a projection and soundscape that evoke the play of light across laundry hung between buildings. It was inspired by the artist’s experience visiting Venice, where billowing laundry on clotheslines is still common, though for Ng it also evoked memories of Hong Kong.
“The laundry becomes a point of entry into a wider soundscape of nighttime labour: recordings from a wastewater treatment plant, a newspaper-printing facility and a postal sorting centre evoke the work that continues while much of the city sleeps,” Ng says. “These modest, often overlooked processes that keep a city alive do not only connect Venice and Hong Kong. They are like a low hum in almost every city, to be picked up by an ear that doesn’t only listen to loud grandeur.”
For her installations, Angel Hui shines a spotlight on humble features of Hong Kong’s everyday life, including goldfish in plastic bags and a neighbour’s ornate but faded window frame. In her magical rendering, glowing plastic bags embroidered with goldfish motifs are suspended overhead, while a handwrought iron window made by Hui and traditional metalsmiths rotates slowly in the gallery.
“In Hong Kong, a goldfish bag is an everyday object; in Venice, it seemed almost precious—delicate and exposed,” Hui says. “The experience reminded me that a work does not need to be grand to hold meaning. Sometimes, its poetry lies in inviting us to look more attentively, and to meet the familiar with tenderness.”
Both artists, through their site-specific installations, encourage visitors to mark a pause while heightening their attention to details of light, sound, colour and texture. This invitation to contemplation is echoed in the exhibition’s title, Fermata, which is a type of musical symbol instructing a performer to hold a note or a pause for an extra moment, and the term for the places where Venetian vaporettos stop to let off and pick up passengers. For Hui, this title and its dual meanings resonate across the exhibition’s disparate locales.
“The difference in pace is pronounced: Hong Kong often presses forward, while Venice seems to make room for pause,” she says. “This is why Fermata—a moment of stopping, of stillness—felt so resonant. In both cities, the ordinary endures, and in that endurance, everyday objects acquire a quiet radiance.”
The exhibition’s title and installations also complement the theme of this year’s Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys, set by the late curator Koyo Kouoh.
“I come to see the works as experiences to return to and live alongside,” Ng says. “For me, that is one meaning of In Minor Keys: making time for the ordinary and immediate—the air, light and weather around us—and becoming more attentive to our presence within them.”
The artists’ ability to turn familiar objects and moments into tableaux where time pauses and senses are heightened is key to the exhibition’s power. It allows their installations to resonate across localities, from the Venetian Lagoon to Hong Kong’s cityscape.
“The artworks merge into the Venetian neighbourhood, from laundry hanging across nearby alleys and above our courtyard exhibition space to the view of the neighbourhood outside Kingsley’s Laundry Nocturne gallery, to wrought-iron windows that echo Angel’s work,” Dr Mok says. “All these details are blurring the boundary between the exhibition and its surroundings. They also show how small moments of daily life can quietly synchronise across different cities and audiences.”
- Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, Campo della Tana, Castello 2126, 30122, Venice, until 22 November 2026

https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-man-wak.title: Bronx man wakes up to a $39K nightmare after online meetup at hotel, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-man-wak.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-man-wak.text:
A man who used a social media app to meet someone at a Bronx hotel told police he believed he was drugged and was robbed of nearly $40,000 in cash, along with his car and cellphone.
The NYPD is asking for the public’s help identifying a person shown in surveillance images wearing a hot pink dress, with tattoos on their chest and silver earrings.
The incident took place on Aug. 24 at the Tremont Hotel in the Bronx.
The 31-year-old man met the person there around 10 p.m. that Monday, police said, after previous meetups. At some point during the encounter, he fell asleep and two other men entered the room, according to police.
When he woke up, his car, cellphone, about $39,507 in cash and other belongings were missing, according to police. The two men were later identified, but the person in the pink dress fled on foot, police said.
The man's car was later recovered, police said.
Emergency medical workers took the man to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he was listed in stable condition, according to police. The man told investigators he believed he had been drugged, police officials said Wednesday.

https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.title: Keeping Taíno Culture Alive: Bronx Exhibit Celebrates the Legacy of Bobby González
https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.text:
Share This Article
A new exhibit at the Museum of Bronx History explores the life of the Puerto Rican poet, storyteller and educator who dedicated nearly four decades to preserving Indigenous culture and challenging stereotypes about the South Bronx.
For Bobby González, preserving Indigenous history began close to home: inside his family’s bodega in the South Bronx.
Growing up near the Melrose Houses, González encountered people from different Indigenous backgrounds who visited the neighborhood store owned by his parents. Those conversations helped shape his understanding of his own Taíno heritage and inspired a lifelong commitment to educating others about Indigenous history.
Now, three years after his death, his work is being remembered through a new exhibition at the Museum of Bronx History.
“From the South Bronx Reservation: Bobby González, Taíno Indian,” which opened Oct. 8 and runs through March 2027, explores the life of the Puerto Rican poet, storyteller and educator who dedicated nearly four decades to preserving Indigenous culture and challenging stereotypes about the South Bronx.
Born in 1951, González grew up in a Puerto Rican family whose parents migrated to New York after World War II. His father worked as a short order cook before opening a bodega in the 1970s, where González and his brothers helped run the family business.
According to Stephen Payne, director of the Bronx County Historical Society, the bodega played an important role in shaping González’s identity.
Visitors included people with Cherokee, Quechua, Lenape and other Indigenous backgrounds. Their conversations encouraged González to learn more about Indigenous communities across the Americas and explore his own ancestry.
That experience later influenced the phrase “South Bronx Reservation,” which González used to describe the neighborhood’s Indigenous presence.
Payne explained that the phrase also reflected similarities between the South Bronx and some Native American reservations, including struggles with pollution and limited resources.
For González, the neighborhood was more than a place where he grew up. It became the foundation of his writing, poetry and cultural activism.
His widow, Maria Aponte González, remembered him as someone who remained deeply connected to his community.
“He was a very gentle spirit,” she said. “Never yelled, never raised his voice.”
She described her late husband as approachable, calm and someone to whom community members frequently turned for advice.
González co-founded the cultural organization Taíno del Norte, organized the annual Bronx Native American Festival and wrote several books, including “The Last Puerto Rican Indian.” He also traveled across the country, speaking at schools, colleges and museums about Indigenous history.
Some of González’s belongings, via the Bronx History Museum.
His mission was to challenge the belief that Taíno people—a native group that originally inhabited the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico—had disappeared centuries ago.
“We are Taíno, we are still here,” Payne said, recalling a phrase used by the organization González helped establish.
Payne explained that the exhibition highlights how Indigenous identity continues to shape Puerto Rican communities, particularly in the Bronx, where González became an important figure in the Taíno cultural revival movement.
The exhibition also arrives at a time when the Bronx is experiencing demographic changes. Payne said rising living costs have contributed to Puerto Rican residents leaving the borough or city, making it increasingly important for community members to share their stories now.
“It’s very important to preserve that part of the history while there still are people in the community who can speak to it,” he said.
The exhibition brings together personal belongings, writings and other materials preserved by González throughout his lifetime.
Aponte González, who co-curated the exhibition alongside documentary filmmaker Edwin Pagán, selected the objects from their home.
“Everything that you’re going to see in the exhibit is Bobby’s work,” she said.
Rather than focusing on how others described her husband, she wanted visitors to experience his legacy through the materials he created himself.
Among his contributions were poetry workshops, including a spoken word series that helped emerging poets develop their voices. He also used puppetry and storytelling to introduce children to Indigenous history and cultural traditions.
Aponte González launched the Bobby González Legacy Project in 2024, following conversations she had with her husband about preserving his work before he became seriously ill.
She described the exhibition as a project that took two years to develop, with support from Pagán and the Bronx County Historical Society.
For Payne, the exhibition also reflects a larger challenge facing historical institutions: preserving the experiences of working class communities whose personal records and belongings are often lost because of housing instability or limited financial resources.
He explained that families who have experienced eviction or frequent moves may no longer have access to photographs, documents and other materials that help tell their histories. In those cases, institutions often rely on oral histories and archival research to recover stories that might otherwise disappear.
González’s collection offered a different opportunity because he had preserved much of his own work, which his widow has made available through the Legacy Project.
Beyond celebrating his accomplishments, both Aponte González and Payne hope the exhibition encourages younger generations to learn about their cultural backgrounds.
“Young people need to make space in their heads. And be open to learn things,” Aponte González said.
For Payne, the larger message is that Indigenous history should not be understood only as something belonging to the distant past.
He hopes visitors recognize that Native American communities continue to preserve, reclaim and develop their cultural traditions today.
Through González’s writing, storytelling and activism, the exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to explore that living history through the experiences of a man who dedicated his life to sharing it.
The exhibition is on display at the Museum of Bronx History, located at 3266 Bainbridge Ave. in the Bronx, through March 2027.

Amidst the blue wave, few across the country will notice that a YouTube rapper was elected to Congress last night. Republican Anthony Constantino will represent New York's 21st district in Congress in January, a seat formerly represented by one-time gubernatorial candidate Elise Stefanik before her mysterious flame-out in 2025, finally giving federal representation to white boys with bars.
But this previous January, Constantino's full-length rap album "Thank You President Trump" was released. "Thank You President Trump" is a project with a concept, organized around nine voice notes issuing personal thank yous to President Trump, including from Constantino himself, golfer John Daly, former NFL star with an increasingly alarming TikTok account Antonio Brown, and other people who I assume are famous, but who I just wouldn't know about for lifestyle reasons.
In the wake of Constantino's victory, the Hell Gate staff took it upon ourselves to once again collectively review a piece of art, and our opinions were as complicated and diverse as the great state of New York itself.
