https://gothamist.com/news/ny-appeals-co.title: NY appeals court strikes down Nassau County's ban on transgender athletes
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-appeals-co.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-appeals-co.text:
A New York appeals court on Wednesday struck down Nassau County's ban on transgender girls and women participating in certain sports competitions at county-owned facilities, marking a turning point in a years-long legal battle.
The local law prohibited teams designated for women and girls from using county-owned sports facilities if they allowed transgender women and girls to compete.
The ban, backed by Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, had been subject to multiple legal challenges.
Both the New York Civil Liberties Union and Attorney General Letitia James filed separate lawsuits, arguing that the ban violated state laws protecting against discrimination based on gender identity.
Wednesday's ruling reversed a lower court decision that had upheld the ban. The appellate court found that Nassau County could not enact a local law that conflicted with the state's antidiscrimination protections.
The ban had already been temporarily blocked by the same appeals court in October 2025 while litigation continued.
But Nassau County did not consider the legal battle over.
“We are reviewing the decision with the intention to continue the appeals process,” county attorney Thomas Adams said.
That may be easier said than done, according to Gabriella Larios, an attorney at the NYCLU, which filed its lawsuit on behalf of the Long Island Roller Rebels, a women's roller derby league.
“The court made it abundantly clear that any attempt to ban transgender girls from public spaces across our state is prohibited by New York's anti-discrimination laws,” Larios told Gothamist. “So this is a massive victory, not just for trans people in sports, but for trans people everywhere.”
Larios said Nassau County could seek to appeal to New York's highest court, but there is no guarantee the court would agree to hear the case.
“It is an uphill battle for them, and they would be flying in the face of very clear state law in pursuing that appeal,” Larios said.
The Roller Rebels said they continue to welcome transgender women to join their league.
The appeals court also ruled in favor of the attorney general in a separate lawsuit challenging the same ban.
“Transgender athletes have the right to play on the court or field like everyone else,” James wrote on X Wednesday.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: 8 Takeaways From Progressives’ Biggest Night in a Generation
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
8 Takeaways From Progressives’ Biggest Night in a Generation
Polls did fail to capture something: the scale of the Democratic wave.
In the days leading up to Tuesday’s election, prognosticators issued the obligatory warning that polls could be subject to systematic error. And indeed, polls did fail to capture something: the scale of the Democratic wave.
Not only did Democrats win the House (as expected), and the Senate (as seemed possible), but they secured a majority of governorships for the first time in 20 years. They swept at least five of the six Senate seats rated as toss-ups by The Cook Political Report (with votes still being counted in Alaska), and even picked off a seat in South Carolina that had been in Republican hands since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964.
Not since the waning days of George W. Bush’s disastrous second term has there been a Republican collapse of this scale, nor such a clear set of opportunities to lead for the Democratic Party. The results have upended much of the conventional wisdom that has dominated American politics since Donald Trump himself tore up the rulebook a decade ago.
While the meaning behind the results will surely be debated through the next election, it was a decisive enough evening for a few stories to come into focus almost immediately.
Democrats can—and should—compete everywhere. The party swiftly picked up Senate seats in five states—Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas, and South Carolina—where Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024. But perhaps more remarkable were the states where Democrats came unexpectedly close: In increasingly ruby-red Florida, democratic socialist Angie Nixon fell short of winning a Senate seat by just three points. Even closer was Jamie Davis in hyper-polarized Louisiana—and, as of writing, Scott Colom’s race in Mississippi is still too close to call. All three were Black candidates who put up historic results despite limited investment from the national party. As successful a night as the party had in deep-red territory, Democrats may have approached a supermajority with a little more investment in races dismissed as unreachable.
The generational shift in the Democratic Party is here, and it’s populist. Seven battleground states elected Democratic senators under the age of 50, in Peggy Flanagan (47), Josh Turek (47), Chris Pappas (46), Annie Andrews (46), Abdul El-Sayed (42), Jon Ossoff (39), and James Talarico (37). And it’s not just the candidates themselves that are fresh and new; it’s their ideas. In Colorado’s First Congressional District, 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros became the first woman from Generation Z elected to Congress. And in Montana, it looks like Sam Forstag, a union leader and former wildland firefighter, will flip MT-1. It’s a far cry from the Democratic Party that, two years ago, hoped to invigorate the youth vote with the vim and vigor of Joe Biden. And the depth of the bench is no accident: It was cultivated by organizations like Run for Something, which not only notched nearly a hundred local victories and counting Tuesday but planted the seeds for statewide wins by backing candidates like Talarico starting nearly a decade ago.
The GOP’s gerrymandering gambit backfired. In Texas, Florida, North Carolina, and Ohio—all of which redrew their maps mid-decade to marginalize Democratic voters—Democrats held on to seats they were projected to lose, and in some cases even picked up seats. What’s more, in another blow for disenfranchisement, Black voters showed up in droves in the wake of the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act. Among other victories, they helped elect the first Black woman governor in American history. In spite of everything, voters continue to choose their politicians; not the other way around.
Americans do care about foreign policy. President Trump made a surprising final pitch to voters on Election Day, with a dubious vow to suspend $4 billion in aid to Israel and an admission that his administration’s financial support of the country is “a bad talking point” for Republicans. It was an acknowledgment of Americans’ deep opposition to his international agenda—and, with more strikes on Iran potentially coming after the midterms, it’s also a reminder to newly empowered Democrats that voters are demanding a break with the foreign policy status quo. It was just under 20 years ago that Senator Barack Obama launched a presidential campaign built around his opposition to the Iraq War; that could be instructive.
Voters vented their AI agita. Voters weighed in on at least 40 data center measures nationwide, and, overwhelmingly, communities from Maine to Ohio to Kansas voted to regulate and restrict data center construction. Data center industry darling Darline Graham and infamous AI flip-flopper Greg Abbott faltered. Meanwhile, Big Tech already has its eyes on the presidential matchup ahead: “We already know the number-one issue of the 2028 presidential election,” reads a memo by a leading industry lobbyist: “AI.” (One potential candidate—Jon Ossoff—directly addressed those risks in his victory speech.)
Money doesn’t change everything. This was the most expensive midterm election in US history—and no single donor gave more than the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, who funneled huge sums to Republicans in his home state of Texas. Democratic hopefuls James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa made Musk’s attempts to buy their races a centerpiece of the joint rally that closed their campaigns. “Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people?” asked Hinojosa, “Or this is the billionaires’ world and we just live here?” In the end, Texans picked the people, not the plutocrat.
MAGA may have reached the end of the line. Many of the issues top of mind for voters amounted to a referendum on Trump’s governance. Gas prices, affordability, and national security have been squeezed by the profoundly unpopular Middle East war he promised he’d never start. His naked self-dealing has thrown the wealth gap into stark relief and made political corruption one of voters’ chief concerns. And with countless jobs and the health of the economy riding on the whims of a few increasingly unaccountable tech companies, Trump’s failure to regulate AI has sounded yet another sour note with the public. He also handpicked a number of disastrous candidates who fumbled winnable races: the corrupt Ken Paxton, the shameless Vivek Ramaswamy, the grossly underqualified Darline Graham, and on and on. In stripping his party of both the House and Senate in such dramatic fashion, Americans may have just rendered their final verdict on Trump—and the MAGA movement at large will stand trial in 2028.
Every party faction had something to celebrate. It remains to be seen if that unity can last. From the insurgent left to the moderate middle, hardly any candidate up or down the ballot underperformed on Tuesday. The factional divides faded away in favor of an unambiguous rebuke of Donald Trump; a rising blue wave lifted all boats. But for a Democratic Party that remains historically unpopular, approaching what will be the first presidential election in 13 years without Trump on the ballot, hard work lies ahead. As one of the new progressive House members texted me late last night, “Wow Wow! I hope Hakeem and Chuck understand how much this is anti-establishment, populist, fed-up energy for change.”
As Robert Reich said before any votes were counted, “We’re going to have to continue to organize, mobilize, and energize everyone around us to put pressure on Congress—even a Congress controlled by the Democrats—to protect and strengthen our democracy.”

https://gothamist.com/news/four-takeaway.title: 4 takeaways after Democrats’ big night in New York
https://gothamist.com/news/four-takeaway.author: Walter Wuthmann, Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/four-takeaway.text:
Tuesday night’s blue tsunami fortified Democrats' dominance in New York — and boosted their influence around the country.
Gov. Kathy Hochul cruised to re-election over Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman with the widest margin for a New York governor since 2018, according to unofficial results. Democrats expanded their already large majorities in both the state Senate and state Assembly. And Mayor Zohran Mamdani saw his “affordability” message successfully deployed by Democrats to score historic wins from Texas to Maine.
Here are four takeaways from election night:
1) Hochul quieted the naysayers
The governor has spent the last four years dogged by criticism that she dragged down the Democratic ticket with her narrower-than-expected win in 2022, when she defeated Lee Zeldin by just six points. But Hochul silenced those critics Tuesday night, with unofficial results showing a 20-plus-point drubbing of Blakeman. That included winning Blakeman’s own Nassau County.
Hochul bet big on her key alliance with Mamdani, that delivering on their shared promise to expand free childcare would energize the party’s young, progressive base. At the same time she cast herself as a moderate and level-headed foil to President Donald Trump, pushing back on his hardline immigration enforcement and trade war with Canada.
Hochul now goes into her second full term with goodwill, a robust fundraising machine and a mandate. It remains to be seen whether her margin of victory changed her political calculus on top progressive priorities like taxing the rich.
2) The night also belonged to Mamdani
Over at Hochul’s victory party in midtown Manhattan, the star speaker of the night wasn’t the governor, but Mamdani.
Mamdani praised Hochul for embracing progressive policy ideas like universal childcare, and for her willingness to partner with him. But he drew a direct connection between Democrats’ triumphs across the country on a message of affordability and his own election last year.
“We have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to working people once again,” he said.
3) NY Republicans will be looking for a fresh playbook
There was an obvious sign New York Republicans knew they were in for a bad night at the Long Island banquet hall where Blakeman held his election party: no TVs broadcasting election results. Instead, Frank Sinatra’s “My Way” blasted over the speakers.
Afterward, Blakeman delivered a brief concession speech, and some attendees continued to chat and order drinks at the bar as if nothing happened. Others sank into denial. “There had to be some shenanigans,” said Rosalie Cancellarich of Floral Park. “Am I saying it was rigged? I don’t know.”
The party has a steep uphill climb back to power — Republicans haven’t won statewide office in New York since Gov. George Pataki was re-elected in 2002. The GOP playbook focused on crime and illegal immigration — which Rep. Mike Lawler and Blakeman both used — was a dud. The party is in for some soul-searching ahead of 2028.
4) All eyes on AOC
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said she would wait until after the Midterms to decide whether to run for president or Senate. Tuesday night’s blue tsunami undoubtedly strengthens a case that she has a path to the White House. The congresswoman previously said that Abdul El-Sayed’s election in Michigan would portend a huge win for progressive movement, and that it could "break open the entire political calculus in America.”
Adding to the intrigue, Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign released a memo on Tuesday touting her accomplishments and concluding that the congressmember has “proven herself to be one of the most effective voices in the country for America’s working class.“
Ocasio-Cortez stayed out of the spotlight on election night, but she’ll now be fielding a lot of questions about her future. She won her fifth term in office with a commanding margin over her Republican opponent Diamant Hysenaj.
Some of her constituents were already mulling whether it might be the last time she asks voters to return her to the House.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The American People Just Kicked Donald Trump’s Ass
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The American People Just Kicked Donald Trump’s Ass
An epic defeat turns the president into a lame duck—and hopefully marks the beginning of the end of the MAGA era.
Donald Trump wants to make one thing perfectly clear: The epic defeat suffered by the GOP in Tuesday’s midterms wasn’t his fault.
As it became clear that the GOP was not only losing both houses of Congress, as well as countless local races, but doing so at levels not seen in generations, Trump posted on Truth Social: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”
Trump spent much of the evening that way—searching for anything that could explain the humiliation he was suffering. He blamed Fox News for having too many Democrats on. He blamed far-right Republican politicians like Texas Governor Greg Abbott, resoundingly defeated in his bid for a fourth term, for supposedly straying from the righteous path of Trumpism. He proclaimed to Fox News that the results weren’t actually about him. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he said, adding, “It was a point in time. I shouldn’t feel guilty.”
Almost nobody believed the man who has now morphed from a onetime political colossus to a widely loathed lame duck. (As if to underscore his newfound irrelevance, the White House posted a picture of Trump on Wednesday morning with the desperate-sounding caption, “PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT.”) That’s because the verdict of the American people was as unmistakable as it was accurate. Across the country, voters said the same thing: Trump’s entire second term has been a catastrophe, and he deserves to be punished, along with the party that has aided and abetted him for the last 10 years.
It is not hard to understand how we got here. Trump won in 2024 only because he faced a fatally weak opposition. The Democrats nominated Joe Biden, who was visibly in cognitive decline, committed to supporting a genocide in Gaza that revolted many Democratic voters, and maddeningly indifferent to the affordability crisis caused by Covid and the Ukraine War. By the time Biden finally ended his campaign, the damage had already been done (particularly since the new Democratic nominee, Kamala Harris, was unwilling to distance herself from Biden). Trump told voters he would focus on lowering the cost of living and keep the United States out of new wars overseas. That was enough to get him a second stint in the Oval Office. But instead of sticking to the promises he’d made, Trump misinterpreted the election as a mandate for a hard-right, untrammeled MAGA presidency, with himself as an imperial, untouchable king. He unleashed ICE to deploy gestapo tactics on American streets, enriched himself and his friends with corruption that dwarfed the graft of the Gilded Age, and launched a ruinous tariff war. Then, to top it all off, he launched an illegal war of choice in Iran that destabilized the global economy and sent the price of just about everything soaring.
Voters were rightly fed up. Given a chance to express themselves in the midterms, they handed the GOP a defeat that is truly historic. Metaphors of a blue wave or blue tsunami hardly do the midterms justice. The scale of the Democratic Party’s victory was far larger than other modern midterm defeats, even the “thumping” suffered by George W. Bush in 2006, Barack Obama (a “shellacking”) in 2010, or Donald Trump in 2018.
Instead, the 2026 midterms were the type of wipeout that a party suffers once in a generation. In terms of scale, it is comparable to the 1974 midterms, where the GOP was devastated by the Watergate scandal and the resignation of Richard Nixon.
Sean Trende, one of the smartest Republican political strategists, noted, “If you are watching this and just have a passing familiarity with elections, just understand you’re seeing something special, a 100-year flood. Easily the worst election for a party since 1974.”
The Democrats are on track to win the popular vote in House races by 13 percentage points. As New York Times columnist David Wallace Wells notes, “The 2010 margin was 6.8 points, an election remembered as a generational wipeout. Tonight is expected to almost double that. 2008 was 10.5 and 2006 was 8.0. A thirteen point win would be the biggest congressional margin in fifty years.”
Even more impressive than the size of the victory was where the Democrats won. They didn’t just sweep the swing states but also made unprecedented incursions into red states—or what should now be seen as formerly red states. The Solid South is no longer solidly Republican. Texas now has a Democratic senator and governor. Georgia has two Democratic senators and a Democratic governor. South Carolina has a Democratic senator. Mississippi is too close to call but could have a Democratic senator. Angie Nixon, who wasn’t supported by the national Democratic Party, came agonizingly close to flipping Florida.
The victories in the South inaugurate a new era of politics: If Texas is a purple state, then Democrats have many more paths to forging a national victory in presidential elections.
It’ll take a few more weeks to have a full vote count, but Democrats are looking at roughly 255 seats in the House and 54 or 55 Senate seats.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The Democratic victory is all the sweeter because Republicans ran a disgracefully bigoted campaign, playing to racism, Islamophobia, transphobia, and homophobia. Despite this, Keisha Lance Bottoms, who won in Georgia, will become the first Black woman governor in American history. Abdul El-Sayed, who won handily in Michigan, will be the first Muslim senator in American history. Chris Pappas, who won in New Hampshire, will be the first openly gay male senator in American history.
These victories also bode well for the future: The Democrats, if they can address the economic problems that have fueled voter rage, have a chance to govern as a multiracial, multicultural, and socially liberal majority party.
One of the bizarre features of the election was how focused Donald Trump was on the human posterior. He repeatedly praised the “ass” of Ohio Senate candidate Jon Husted (who lost his race) and singer Nicki Minaj. Republican operative Todd Gillman told Politico: “Honestly, we need to move as far away from Trump as we can. I think Republicans might be screwed all the way until ’30. Talking about Nicki Minaj’s fat ass. All that stuff is just wearing people out.”
Trump’s crude way with words perhaps gives us the best metaphor for the midterms. Trump and the GOP have received a once-in-a-lifetime ass-kicking.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-wins-cour.title: NYC wins court fight over rollout of pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-wins-cour.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-wins-cour.text:
New York City has won a legal battle over its new tax on luxury second homes, potentially clearing a hurdle for Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to collect hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenue.
On Wednesday, a state appeals court reversed a lower court's ruling that had given property owners temporary relief from the new surcharge and dismissed their lawsuit against the tax.
The new pied-à-terre tax is intended to raise revenue from certain high-value properties used as second homes. While Mamdani has said the tax would help fulfill a campaign promise to tax the rich, its rollout has faced significant political and legal hurdles.
The tax has been subject to three separate legal challenges, including claims that the city's rollout would cause “mass confusion” for property owners and that the surcharge unfairly discriminates against wealthy residents.
In September, a Staten Island judge ordered the city to redo notices it had mailed to property owners who might be subject to the surcharge.
Wednesday's ruling marked a victory for the Mamdani administration against the lawsuit, filed by property owners who argued that the new pied-à-terre tax hadn't been properly rolled out.
The appeals court found that the property owners lacked standing to sue because they hadn't shown they suffered a concrete injury from the city's actions. The judges said receiving a tax notice or appearing on a public list of properties potentially subject to the surcharge was not enough to establish such harm.
The court did not determine whether the city had followed every procedure correctly, and the decision does not resolve separate legal challenges to the tax.
In a statement Wednesday, Mamdani celebrated the decision, saying the appeals court had rejected an attempt by wealthy property owners to avoid paying their fair share.
“The pied-a-terre surcharge asks those who can afford luxury second homes to contribute toward the safer streets, cleaner parks and essential public services that every New Yorker deserves,” Mamdani said.
He added that the city would continue defending the tax against ongoing legal challenges.
But Mamdani's claim that the tax will bring in $500 million a year remains in question. The city's Department of Finance has already granted more than 8,800 exemption requests.
Earlier this year, city Comptroller Mark Levine estimated that the tax could generate up to $380 million from roughly 11,200 properties.
David Brand contributed reporting.
This story has been updated with new information.

https://gothamist.com/news/cornell-alum-.title: Cornell alum, ‘Diddy’ prosecutor tapped to investigate allegations of campus gang rape
https://gothamist.com/news/cornell-alum-.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/cornell-alum-.text:
A former federal prosecutor who oversaw the sex trafficking case against Sean “Diddy” Combs is now leading an investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Wednesday that Jacqueline Kelly will serve as outside counsel in the high-profile case.
“The Office of the Attorney General is committed to a thorough investigation guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law,” James said in a statement, describing Kelly as a “seasoned prosecutor who has overseen numerous cases from investigation through trial.”
She added: “With her criminal legal experience, commitment to public service and judicial experience, I am confident that she will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
An unnamed former student filed a lawsuit in September accusing seven men of pressuring her to consume drugs and alcohol, then raping her while she was intoxicated. The civil complaint prompted protests at Cornell and reignited a decades-long debate about how to prevent sexual assault on college campuses, as well as how to address the limitations of New York’s sexual assault laws.
A spokesperson for the university said the administration fully supports a special prosecutor’s appointment and is committed to an independent review of how it has handled the case. The spokesperson, who declined to be named, also said the university supports efforts to change the state’s rape laws.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said last month she would remove Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten from the case after he declined to bring criminal charges. The governor signed an executive order that appointed the attorney general’s office to investigate the woman’s allegations. Kelly will lead that team, which James said is tasked with gathering evidence, reviewing records from previous investigations, interviewing witnesses and assessing whether any laws were broken.
“All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case,” Kelly said in a statement. “I look forward to lending my years of experience as a federal prosecutor to the Office of the Attorney General as we examine all available evidence.”
Kelly is a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, where she represents sexual assault victims, as well as companies facing investigations, according to a biography on the firm’s website.
Before going into private practice, she served as the first chief of the civil rights unit in the criminal division of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York. In that role, she supervised the prosecutions of Combs, a doctor accused of sexually abusing dozens of patients, and the CEO of a clothing company charged with sex trafficking.
Kelly is a Cornell University alum and went to law school at Columbia University.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: When turning back the clock means going under an NYC sidewalk
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Time waits for no man — except Gilo Vintimilla, the master jeweler whose expertise is required to turn back the hands on the only clock embedded in a New York City sidewalk.
“There?” he asks his phone in a lilting Ecuadorian accent as he balances on top of a ladder beneath the sidewalk, carefully adjusting the clock’s minute hand from below.
“No, no, too far, come back,” responds Brianna Thompson, as she observes the clockface from street level. Thompson is marketing director for William Barthman Jeweler — the very company that installed the clock here on the corner of Maiden Lane in 1899 as a novelty advertisement in front of the business's original location. “Wait, no, too far, come forward.”
Of the many New York City clocks that don’t automatically update for daylight saving time, few require as much manual care as the Financial District’s pavement timepiece. But despite the hassle, Vintimilla has been loyally descending into this basement since 2001 every time the clock needs a fix.
“It's a labor of love. The clock is his baby,” Thompson explains after we ascend to the street and Vintimilla flits away to William Barthman’s current location a few blocks away. Meanwhile, the Wall Street lunch crowd appears none the wiser about time’s mechanical passage, as people rush past and periodically over (and on) the clock.
It’s a tough baby to love: Some 50,000 people a day walk over its sapphire crystal cover. In addition to adjusting for daylight saving, Vintimilla must periodically jiggle the face to get off dirt, lest it get in the mechanisms. Around 2014, a hand truck rolled over the clock and broke the glass. In 2001, the force of the Twin Towers’ collapse sent a crack through the sidewalk, the clock and the adjacent building. Vintimilla fitted the clock with a fresh new face and cover; the crack is still visible in the sidewalk and building.
Recently, the residential conversion of that building, 174 Broadway, turned the basement in which the clock is powered into a wreckage-filled pit of broken beams and rubble. Vintimilla plans to readjust the clock face soon to make sure it’s level, an endeavor that will likely require temporarily removing it from its subterranean perch.
When he’s not fixing the clock, he’s fixing just about everything else, from eyeglasses and jewelry to handbags and shoes, or doing custom jewelry design. Though he’s trained by various vendors, including Rolex, he’s mostly self-taught.
Since the William Barthman company installed the timepiece here over 120 years ago, maintaining it has always been a challenge met by impassioned jewelers. When its original designer died in 1917, no one could maintain the mechanical oddity, and so it was replaced with a version that could be. Today, the clock may be fixed in history and concrete, but its upkeep is dependent on Vintimilla and whoever pays 174 Broadway’s Con Ed bill.
Its preservation, however, is spiritually important, says clock enthusiast and recently licensed NYC Tour Guide Suzanne Dirks, handing me a sheet of custom clock stickers as we stand under scaffolding, gazing at the clock’s stalwart — if grime-spotted — compass.
“The clock is a window in time. A relic of time. It's seen so much change,” she waxes as tourists stumble by, intermittently looking up and at their phones.
In our digital world, such analog heirlooms are no longer necessary to determine the hour, but, Dirks says, "I think we still desperately need them because they’re reminders that there’s an IRL world where we are connected by these anchors, that time is shared amongst New Yorkers.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/m.title: Mamdani Continues Crackdown On Illegal E-Motos With Brick-And-Mortar Sweep
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/m.text:
Illegal e-motos are common on city streets. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Dozens of businesses were hit with more than 130 violations for selling illegal e-bikes and scooters in a two-month enforcement blitz to protect consumers against fire-prone and overpowered micromobility devices.
Inspectors for the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection visited 229 retail shops across the five boroughs between Aug. 1 and Sept. 20 and found 136 individual violations that resulted in more than 75 summonses, each carrying a $1,000 fine. Three stores were shuttered.
“New Yorkers deserve to feel safe knowing that the devices they see in their communities meet the City’s safety requirements,” said DCWP Commissioner Sam Levine, whose agency ensures that stores sell only UL-certified e-bikes and batteries, display e-bike fire safety materials in their storefronts, and don’t sell illegal e-motos and scooters that have too much power and speed capability. “Our citywide sweep sends a clear message that businesses cannot put New Yorkers at risk just to make a profit.”
In addition to the three closures, Levine’s agency worked with another five shops to bring them into compliance with the law, the agency said. Stores remain closed until all outstanding fines are paid to DCWP, the department said.
Since e-bikes and scooters started growing in popularity during the pandemic there has been misplaced ire from politicians. Confusion over which devices are legal on city streets and bike lanes led to a fervent backlash to all electric bikes.
E-scooters are illegal in New York City if they exceed 20 miles per hour or weigh more than 100 pounds. E-bikes are legal if their motors don’t exceed 750 watts and their top speed is 25 mph.
The law defines a “motorized scooter” as a two-wheeled powered device that can’t be registered with the Department of Motor Vehicles, like, say a legal moped, and also doesn’t fit the city’s street-legal definitions of an e-bike or stand-up scooter. DCWP can give summonses to businesses selling these out-of-class devices, known as e-motos.
These devices, which far exceed the city’s limits for power and speed, are often sold online and in stores as legal devices.
But the tides are shifting. Two high–profile deaths involving New Yorkers riding non-street-legal e-motos and scooters sparked long-overdue action from city and state politicians.
In August, the city Law Department sent cease-and-desist letters to 42 online retailers selling the so-called e-motos, which are illegal to ride on city streets and bike lanes.
The cease-and-desists brought large retailers like Amazon, Temu, and Walmart into compliance. Such companies now block orders by geography so consumers can’t ship these devices to their New York City homes. But many small direct to consumer brands are still shipping flagrantly illegal e-motos and scooters and marketing them for city use. Aniioki, a brand that Streetsblog sees out on the streets daily, sells bikes online that can hit over 50 miles per hour.
DCWP said it also issued more than 85 cease-and-desist orders and 41 summonses to online sellers for battery safety violations.
And in July, Attorney General Letitia James issued a consumer alert to warn perspective buyers of the shady market. So far her office has received three relevant complaints.
State lawmakers are also pushing legislation to officially bar the sale of e-motos online and in stores, closing a loophole that has allowed retailers to sell devices that are illegal to ride on roadways but are legal to own for private use.
State Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D-Long Island City) introduced the bill to establish a clear definition for these overpowered vehicles, and explicitly prohibit companies from not only selling them, but from falsely advertising them as legal, a common practice that results in unsuspecting consumers purchasing devices they can’t legally use.
The driver, Timothy McVey, 41, of Staten Island, turned himself in at the 62nd Precinct station house and was booked for failure to yield and failure to exercise due care

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.title: How Democrats Changed Everything
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.text:
The size of the Democrats’ victory Tuesday night shattered records and even the most optimistic expectations, handing the party a governing mandate with a clear demand for change.
But what do voters want that change to look like? This week on The Intercept Briefing, politics reporter Jessica Washington and managing editor Maia Hibbett break down Tuesday night’s election and hear from voters in Maine, Michigan, and Texas about what drove them to the polls in the midterms that saw a so-called “blue tsunami.”
“The rich get richer, the poor get poorer,” said one voter in Maine. In Michigan, a voter told The Intercept that politics “feels like a game that the rich play sometimes.” A Texas voter expressed anger that President Donald Trump was “spending taxpayer money to renovate the White House and turn it into this gold sanctuary.”
Frustration with wealth inequality and money in politics came up again and again in The Intercept’s conversations with voters. So did a desire for more social welfare spending, Medicare for All, freedom for Palestinians — and responses to transphobic and Islamophobic fearmongering on the campaign trail.
“When Democrats win so far across the board, you can make an argument that any faction of the Democratic Party has the mandate,” said Hibbett, “because Democrats of all stripes won Tuesday night.”
In any case, the results indicated a clear disapproval of the way the Trump administration is governing and the use of fearmongering as a tactic of distraction.
“One lesson maybe for Democrats is there’s no point in attempting to placate people when it comes to bigotry,” said Washington. “The thing that’ll motivate voters is if you can convince them that you’re going to make their lives better, not if you can convince them that you’re playing the middle on an issue of civil rights.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Bruce Bryan: We’re just hoping that people step up and tell Washington to go fuck itself.
Jessica Washington: Welcome to the Intercept Briefing. I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter at The Intercept.
Maia Hibbett: And I’m Maia Hibbett, managing editor here.
JW: Over the past few days, Intercept reporters hit the ground in key states to speak to voters about the issues driving them to the polls. We went to Texas.
Jermiah Robinson: The food prices, for one, and the gas prices.
Darryl Moore: Gotta work two jobs just to make it.
Tiffany Williams: I never really understood, like, how important it is for the minority to vote.
Lenna Tasby: This election is important because this election is going to make or break whether we have a vote or not. There’s a reason why they’re shutting down these polling places.
Intercept reporter Akela Lacy: What are the issues that motivated you this cycle?
Charles Senter: Well, I love Trump.
Helen Dexter: Red ticket all the way. The stop of the Muslim influx.
Lenna Tasby: If you’re spending taxpayer money to renovate the White House and turn it into this gold sanctuary, that’s money that can be used for our military veterans. That’s money that can be used to help with this homeless population. The government needs to be held accountable.
MH: We heard from voters in Michigan.
Erin Horne: The election this year is very critical because Trump’s got two more years.
Zouheir Alawieh: Our democracy is in danger.
Noora Iskander: I believe in Medicare for All. People have a right to self-determination, especially in Palestine.
Wendy: There’s a lot of concern about, of course, the economy, but the data centers, our children’s education.
JW: And we spoke to voters in Maine.
Intercept reporter Noah Hurowitz: What mattered to you as a voter this election?
Tyler Echard: Cost for the most part. Everything keeps going up.
Bryan Golay: The rich get richer, the poor get poorer. At least 30 years ago, there was like a veneer of caring, and now there’s just blatant corruption and greed.
JW: So Maia, what a night.
MH: Yeah, it’s honestly embarrassing if you’re a Democrat and you did not win. They swept the House and the Senate by just about the biggest margins that the pollsters could have predicted. So luckily, the audience I’m concerned about, the pollsters, can rest easy. As of 11:00 a.m. [ET] on Wednesday morning, they had 228 seats in the House, Democrats did. They only needed 218 for a majority, so obviously that is more, and they’re expected to pick up some more seats as some more races get called. They had 54 seats in the Senate, which means that they have a big enough margin that they can’t be stopped from legislating by one lone senator, if one senator wanted to gum things up.
JW: And not at all surprising. The White House tried to spin Republican losses on Trump not being on the ballot and the quality of candidates, despite the fact that Trump repeatedly said at rallies across the country, “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”
Donald Trump: We’re going to ask you to pretend I’m on the ballot, because when I’m on the ballot, this has nothing to do with ego, I just get 49.2 percent more vote. And if we get even a good percentage of that, we’ll have the biggest victory that you’ve ever seen.
MH: He’s saying, “We’ll have the biggest victory ever” — and it was a very historic night. I think people will hear the word “historic” a lot in the coverage in the coming days because of this huge blue wave, not the kind of history Trump wanted, but also because there are some really surprising major firsts.
One of them was that last night, very early, like at 2:30 a.m. [ET], Abdul El-Sayed became the winner of the Senate race in Michigan, which means he will be the first ever Muslim U.S. senator.
Abdul El-Sayed (acceptance speech): To all the kids who watched this last month, to all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocked someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost.
JW: That race was filled with Islamophobia, both in the primary and in the general election. His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, just peddled in a million different Islamophobic tropes. Voters told our colleague, Matt Sledge, who was out in Michigan speaking with them, that they really didn’t like hearing all of this hate speech.
Zouheir Alawieh: They don’t have any programs for our economy, for our health, for our future. So that’s why they are attacking us as Muslims and as human beings.
Tea Edwards: Just, like, all of the Islamophobic hate campaigns that have been going around will probably sway a few people. The people who are actually researching what will be good for communities I think will see right through it.
MH: This was a campaign that was defined by so much panic about El-Sayed being Muslim. The race ended 25 years after 9/11, and there were all of these really kind of vitriolic Islamophobic tropes. It reminded me a lot of the campaign against [Mayor] Zohran Mamdani here in New York last year. There’s all this fear of the left and this fearmongering suggesting that there’s no way a Muslim candidate could represent American interests.
And of course, one of the big differences between El-Sayed and Mamdani is that El-Sayed is not a socialist.
JW: Say that again for the people in the back, because they are not going to believe you. El-Sayed has described himself as a capitalist who understands how capitalism works, so definitely not a socialist.
I’ve heard him described as much more of a [Sen. Elizabeth] Warren than someone in the Bernie Sanders mold.
MH: But he still faced millions of dollars in outside spending in this race, mostly because of his stance on the United States relationship to one other country.
We’ve heard in some of these deep-blue districts in the House races where socialists were elevated in the primaries, there was a lot of rhetoric on opposing Israel’s genocide in Gaza and fighting U.S. weapons flows to Israel. But it’s pretty rare to hear that from a U.S. Senate candidate, and now from a senator-elect.
JW: It also caused some really ugly drama with his former primary opponent, Haley Stevens.
MH: Do you want to try to recap that as fast as we can, or should I?
JW: I’ll get started and see if you can add in anything that I miss.
So essentially, on the Friday right before [Election Day], Haley Stevens released a statement condemning an ad that was not even created by the El-Sayed campaign, calling on him to condemn the ad, which he did disavow. She also asked him to take back his statements on Israel.
Now, things seemed fine for a second. Haley Stevens had all of these Democratic surrogates going on air saying that she promised to support him. While Haley Stevens’s staffers were at an event for El-Sayed, Haley Stevens popped up at an event supporting the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, giving him her endorsement.
Maia, is there anything that I missed in that?
MH: Jessie, I think the only thing you missed was just how baffling and strange this episode was. So you mentioned this ad that kicked it off. It was produced by this outside group Rebellion PAC, which is the group headed by Cenk Uygur, who some listeners might know from The Young Turks. He is also famously Hasan Piker’s uncle.
Haley Stevens, as she was struggling to explain why she switched from El-Sayed to the Rogers camp, kept citing Hasan Piker and the “uncle.” It was this kind of almost incomprehensible move where Anderson Cooper, the CNN host, was pressing her at one point, saying, well, you cite his affiliation with Hasan Piker and this part of the Democratic Party you don’t like, but you knew about this before — so what changed?
It really seemed strange. So we sent Matt Sledge out in Michigan to ask some voters what they thought of it, and if they thought that this was a politically savvy move that would have any resonance. And here’s what they said.
Kathleen Britton: I’m so disappointed in Haley Stevens. I gave her serious consideration during the primary.
Jesse Craft: She fought against Mike Rogers, then said somehow he earned her vote. I don’t really understand it. I kinda think it’s career-ending for her.
Wendy: How embarrassing to use an African American church. How embarrassing for you to use our votes and then disregard them because of your own personal issues.
Intercept reporter Matt Sledge: So you don’t think it’s gonna help Mike Rogers?
Kathleen Britton: I do not.
Erin Horne: No, I think she actually helped Abdul.
[Break]
JW: Maia, before the break, you started talking about money and politics, and I want to get into how that shaped the midterms. Last week, we talked about how this election cycle became the most expensive on record. Midterms ad spending is expected to reach north of $11.6 billion. Mega-donors overwhelmingly gave to Republican candidates, including Elon Musk, who spent nearly $450 million, with large sums of that directed at boosting Ken Paxton in Texas, who, by the way, lost to James Talarico. Now, for context, the next highest donors under Musk are a Republican couple [Richard and
Elizabeth Uihlein] who spent $150 million, mostly in Wisconsin and Illinois. 
Jesse Craft: We all see where money is coming from. It’s coming from very, very wealthy billionaires. I don’t think we should be able to buy elections.
Tea Edwards: Politics, it just feels like a game that the rich play sometimes. Kind of feels hopeless when you’re just looking at all of these people and corporations giving money to each other.
MH: You hate to see Elon Musk throw away almost half a billion dollars. It only leaves him so many billions to go.
JW: Heartbreaking.
MH: But, I mean, in Texas, as you mentioned, that money really did not pan out. It didn’t seem to sway voters. It seemed like if anything from the voters who talked to our reporters in Texas, in Michigan, and in Maine, which we’ll get to later, people were really mad about outside election spending and don’t like the idea that billionaires or corporations can buy their elections.
And in Texas, a lot of that money went to propping up this anti-trans panic campaign that Paxton was running. But all that money was not enough to save Paxton from James Talarico. Paxton was a pretty bad candidate: He was mired in too many scandals to keep track of, including a 2015 grand jury indictment on felony securities fraud charges.
In 2020, eight of his top deputies reported to the FBI that he was potentially abusing his office to do favors for a donor and friend. And just earlier this year, he offered a plea deal in a child sex abuse case that seemed to anger Texans and voters.
Remember, this is the era of the Epstein files and people being very concerned about child sex abuse. It did not seem like the wisest calculation for Paxton to offer this while running for Senate.
JW: As it turns out, there is not enough money in the world to buy Ken Paxton out of being Ken Paxton and voters recognizing that. But Republicans tried this cycle to spend big on transphobia and to blanket the airwaves with these anti-trans advertisements.
Elon Musk’s Texas PAC spent $78 million on anti-transgender ads in Texas, which actually accounted for nearly half of all ad spending in support of Paxton. Republicans’ big play in Texas was transphobia — and that play failed.
While clearly it didn’t sway the election, some of those messages did appear to trickle down to voters. Our colleague, Akela Lacy, talked to voters in Dallas and the surrounding areas, and she did come across some voters who said they wanted to support Talarico or even some voters who did support Talarico but were concerned about his stance on trans rights, an issue that Republicans really fearmongered on this cycle yet again after doing it in 2024.
Akela Lacy: When you said you saw some stuff about James Talarico that made you unsure about voting for him, can you say more about that? What did you see, and what’s your impression of him?
Jermiah Robinson: I think I seen something about the LGBTQ+ community? I mean, I don’t really care about it, but I don’t know. People were saying a lot of bad stuff. I think they said something about him —
Canvasser: Encouraging sex change.
Jermiah Robinson: Yeah, on the children. I don’t really stand for that.
Maia Hibbett: The watchdog group Media Matters also put together a montage that showed just how much Republicans really leaned into this transphobic rhetoric.
Danielle Buck: He wants to trans our kids. He believes that there are six genders.
Andrew Kolvet: They wanna indoctrinate your kids. They wanna trans your kids.
Adam Sosnick: They’re gonna trans your kids. They’re gonna Talarico your kids.
Donald Trump Jr.: Trans kids back in school, trans agendas back in school, in your classrooms, with your children.
JW: Clearly, some of that rhetoric did trickle down to voters based on Akela’s conversations, and some people even believed the misinformation being spread in those ads.
But fearmongering was just clearly not persuasive enough to distract people from their lived reality, and that lived reality is that gas prices are up, rent is unaffordable, and grocery prices are up.
I think one lesson maybe for Democrats is, there’s no point in attempting to placate people when it comes to bigotry. The right can and will distort your messages, and so you can stand in your values or not, but the thing that’ll motivate voters is if you can convince them that you’re going to make their lives better, not if you can convince them that you’re playing the middle on an issue of civil rights.
MH: We saw a parallel to this in some ways in Michigan as well, where a lot of the Republican argument was based on this perception of Islamophobia and fearmongering. Ultimately, that was not enough to elevate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed. In Texas, there’s also, of course, the strong anti-immigrant sentiment that Republicans frequently run on, and I think the statewide results showed us that that narrative really fell apart this cycle.
JW: To your point, clearly, attacks on trans people, attacks on immigrants didn’t work in Texas. Democrats had an amazing night. Gina Hinojosa toppled three-term incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. The state has not had a Democratic governor since 1990.
MH: And speaking of toppling long-term incumbents that have been hard to get out of office, our colleague Noah Hurowitz was in Maine, where Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins last night after many Democratic attempts to get her out of office.
This issue of disillusionment with money and politics came up quite a bit when he was talking to Maine voters.
Sharon McDonnell: It’s immoral. It is immoral to have people worried about their fuel and have that much money coming into this. It’s just wrong.
Tyler Echard: The amount they spent on just mailers, not handed at the door but in the mail, is especially, it seems, on the Republican side of things, has been absolutely insane. The amount of money is more than I will probably make in my lifetime, spent in this election.
Charlie Dingman: It’s been extraordinary in Maine, the amount of spending in this race, particularly in the Senate race. I think there’s a lot of fatigue. I think people are tired of it. I have had some conversations with voters at the doors that lead me to think that the extremely negative and extremely untruthful ads may be backfiring.
JW: It seems like those ads backfired. The last voice you heard was Charlie Dingman, Maine Democratic Party chair.
Collins campaigned on her record of securing federal investments for state infrastructure, such as rural hospitals, and she really prided herself on being a moderate Republican who apparently breaks rank with President Donald Trump. But the reality of the situation is quite different.
The Congressional Quarterly Roll Call found that her votes aligned with Trump 90 percent of the time in both of the president’s first and second terms, and voters really noticed that. They understood the difference between what she said she was, a political moderate, and her voting record, which aligned with the really far-right Donald Trump. And that’s something that Noah heard from voters as well.
Sharon McDonnell: She has had this persona of moderate cross-party stuff that’s just really eroded. If you read every article about her, it’s like, “Moderate Susan Collins.” Like, wait a minute, she’s voted with Trump. She hasn’t used her power.
MH: Collins really used that line about her being a moderate and being an independent voice in Washington as a go-to for her campaign.
In past cycles, it has worked. As we alluded to a little bit earlier, the Democrats have mounted challenges against her before. In 2020, they ran a candidate named Sara Gideon, who looked somewhat likely to oust Collins. And I think this cycle, there were a lot of reasons for Democrats to be nervous about this race.
Troy Jackson, the nominee, is a former state senator, and he ran on lowering costs, really centering working-class interests. But he had jumped into the race kind of hastily. If you remember Graham Platner, Jessie, he was the former nominee for Senate in Maine for the Democratic Party, and he was really considered a rising star, but had to drop out because of a series of scandals, and Jackson had to jump in last minute and fill his place.
But ultimately, Jackson pulled it off.
Troy Jackson (acceptance speech): We did it. Working people did it.
JW: Clearly, Jackson had a disadvantage going into this race. There were people who complained and said that he wasn’t as charming as Platner, he wasn’t as polished. But in this election, the ideas and running on affordability seems to have won the day in Maine and really throughout the country.
Collins had a reputation of delivering for the state, but clearly that wasn’t enough to overcome this blue wave across the country and some frustrations with Collins as well.
But Maia, taking a step back to look at the full scope of Democratic wins, what do you make of their gains on Tuesday? Are there other races that stood out to you? What stood out to you overall?
MH: Well, there’s the spin about the spin, which is that everybody is going to be framing this election and these results in their own interests. When Democrats win so far across the board, you can make an argument that any faction of the Democratic Party has the mandate, because Democrats of all stripes won Tuesday night.
But to my view, it’s hard to see how this is a world where there isn’t a clear demand for some kind of transformational change. So I’m wondering what Democrats do with their mandate now, especially as we think ahead to 2028.
If you recall 2020 and the last time the U.S. elected a Democratic president, you might remember that the Biden campaign was the sort of centrist, moderate return to normalcy choice, but they got there after a lot of left momentum in the primary and a really serious showing of support for Bernie Sanders, who remains one of the most popular politicians in the country.
Once Biden got into office, he arguably tried to give some of that kind of left, dare we say, populist economic message some service. There was the Build Back Better plan that had a lot of social safety net spending and Covid relief. There were climate infrastructure projects. There was the elevation of Lina Khan [to Federal Trade Commission chair].
For a little while, Biden was getting called the most progressive president since FDR, and then he threw it all away supporting the genocide in Gaza and really lost the support of the left, and then lost the support of the country when he was kind of visibly melting on the debate stage and refusing to drop out of the race.
So I’m curious what Democrats have learned from the Biden years and how that will convert into the next congressional term and the next presidential election.
JW: It really feels like I’ve lived a million lives in between now and that debate that really tanked Joe Biden’s entire political career at the end there.
I will say to your point, we’re already seeing Hakeem Jeffries, who’s likely to be the House Speaker, calling for unity and saying that people don’t want to fight. But you don’t really get a blue wave like this or a political wave like this when people don’t want to fight.
Clearly, there’s anger at Republicans. There’s anger at the cost of living. There’s anger at the war. If Democrats don’t deliver, they’re likely to see a red wave come the next cycle.
But I did want to take just a little bit of a step back and talk about Black voters and what’s happened in the aftermath of the Supreme Court voting rights decision. Black voters in this election really delivered historic victories in southern states for Democrats, but Black representation in Congress thus far appears to have been slightly reduced in this election. Now, for those who remember our discussion earlier this year about the Supreme Court decision to gut the Voting Rights Act, there were a lot of deep concerns that the decision would crater Black political representation, and so far that hasn’t come to bear, but it’s worth paying attention to in cycles that are less blue, where we’ve seen really massive redistricting.
I will shout out, there was one historic victory for Black Americans: Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, won her race for governor, becoming the first Black female governor in the country.
MH: We’ve talked a lot about these historic wins, but we would be remiss to not mention a close call in Florida, where Angie Nixon narrowly lost.
Nixon is a Black woman who’s a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and had a really shocking primary upset when she defeated the establishment favorite to get the Democratic nomination. The Democrats didn’t invest very much in her Senate race in Florida. The conventional wisdom says Florida’s not flippable, but conventional wisdom also says that South Carolina’s not flippable — and they did that.
Nixon ended up coming within about 2 [percentage] points to Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, who just won a full term after being appointed to hold the seat that used to belong to [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio. A lot of people on the left side of the Democratic Party are wondering what would have happened if Democrats had invested in a DSA candidate running statewide in Florida, which is kind of a crazy statement to make if you think of just two years ago.
JW: I mean, I listened to her [concession] speech, she is an incredible speaker, but obviously, that’s not enough to win elections. You need money, clearly, and investment from the party.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-accused-o.title: Man accused of pushing ex-girlfriend and baby from Bronx balcony pleads not guilty
https://gothamist.com/news/man-accused-o.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/man-accused-o.text:
Domestic violence survivors and advocates wearing purple filled a row of seats in a Bronx courtroom Wednesday for the arraignment of a man accused of pushing his ex-girlfriend and their 8-month-old daughter off a 15th-floor apartment, killing the woman.
Police found Nathaly Ramirez, 23, and her baby on the ground outside their Olinville Avenue apartment on Oct. 6, according to the Bronx district attorney’s office. Ramirez died from her injuries. The baby suffered critical injuries and is still in the hospital.
Angel Carrasco, 31, pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to second-degree murder, first-degree attempted murder and other charges. When he entered his plea, several women wearing purple socks, purple sweatshirts and T-shirts that said “Stop Domestic Violence” and “Domestic Violence Survivor” in purple lettering murmured and sighed. Purple is associated with domestic violence awareness.
Prosecutors did not share additional details in court about what may have prompted the pushing. In a statement, District Attorney Darcel Clark said the shoving had “outraged the city.”
“His callous disregard for life has left a young mother dead and his own daughter forever altered because of his heinous actions,” she said. “He now faces justice for the heartbreaking loss of Nathaly Ramirez.”
Several of Ramirez’s loved ones sat quietly in the back of the courtroom and did not speak with reporters after the arraignment. Carrasco’s defense attorney, Nathan Karnovsky with Bronx Defenders, also declined to comment outside the courtroom.
Carrasco is not expected back in court until mid-February. Justice Alvin Yearwood told members of the public in the courtroom that it would take time for the case to wind its way through the system, in order to protect Carrasco’s constitutional rights.
“I ask you to be patient and to understand that we’re working on this,” he said.
Carrasco made his first court appearance virtually from a hospital bed in a psychiatric ward. In court on Wednesday, his attorneys did not request additional psychiatric testing.

https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.title: Rain in NYC and NJ will end weeks-long stretch of beautiful weather
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.text:
It’s about to rain on New York City’s good weather parade.
Nearly three weeks of beautiful, clear-skied, mild weather days are coming to an end as a weather system moving through the area Thursday and Friday will bring cloudy skies and rainfall, according to the National Weather Service.
Local weather account New York Metro Weather, gives a daily weather vibes rating on X from 0 to 10. The account's been doling out 8s, 9,s and 10s from Oct. 19 through Nov. 3, with Wednesday receiving a 7 — an indication of the vibe shift to come.
John Homenuk, who runs the account, said that’s due to a persistent high pressure system that’s hung out over the area which no storm has yet been able to push away.
“When you have a stretch like this, it really is enjoyable,” he said. “It's not just one or two days and you have to kinda force yourself outside to go do something, you know? You have some options and the forecast is good for a while. So it's really nice, and you get to spend quite a bit of time outside. ”
Conditions are expected to stay dry through Wednesday with temperatures approaching 70 degrees in some parts of the city, but the National Weather Service predicts cloudy skies by the evening. A low pressure weather system approaching the area will likely bring showers in the first half of Thursday, which will be mostly cloudy with a high near 74, according to the National Weather Service.
Homenuk said he doesn’t expect “anything crazy” but the system will bring more humidity to the area and slightly cooler temperatures this weekend.
Things get a little more bleak Friday, with showers and possible thunderstorms after 1 p.m., and a high near 70 degrees, according to the NWS. The total rainfall will likely be under half an inch, which helps the area get closer to normal for the season after getting just half the normal amount of rain for October, NWS meteorologist John Murray said.
“ It could potentially be some heavy rain at times, it is possible Friday and into Friday night,” he said. “Could have some minor flooding here and there especially in your poor drainage, low-lying areas.”
But nothing lasts forever, even cold November rain. Conditions will be drier through Saturday and Sunday, though the chances of rain won’t be completely gone, and temperatures will remain unseasonably warm throughout the weekend, Murray said.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/b.title: Election Recap: Street Safety and Transit Won Big Across the Empire State on Tuesday
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/b.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/b.text:
New York backers of mass transit, livable streets and cities won big on Tuesday, as Democrats vanquished foes of congestion pricing, sent street safety champions to Congress and re-elected a governor who has enthusiastically embraced transit.
Congestion pricing’s mightiest haters turn out to be extremely meek
Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman and U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-Hudson Valley for a couple more months) made a big show of opposing congestion pricing. Blakeman promised to end the toll and attacked the MTA throughout his campaign. Lawler, for his part, spent the past few years lying and whining about the same toll.
Neither politician survived Tuesday’s wave. Blakeman couldn’t even find enough voters in Nassau County who were mad enough about congestion pricing to lift him to victory on his home turf, and Lawler conceded to his opponent Cait Conley before midnight — even before election workers in Westchester County could hand-count a quarter-million ballots in the Democratic stronghold.
Elected officials should remember this fact about congestion pricing: fewer than 300,000 people drive cars into Manhattan’s Central Business District every single day from around this vast metropolitan area. There are simply not enough drivers whose opposition to congestion pricing would propel you to higher office.
Gov. Hochul, America’s transit champion, must build Nassau County II
In 2023, Gov. Hochul dreamed of solving New York State’s housing crisis by upzoning certain parts of the New York City metropolitan region that had spent decades refusing to build new homes. Her commendable ambition died on the rocks of her own inexperience and the catchy but evil chant, “Local control, not Hochul control.”
But that was three years ago. Get ready to learn Hochul control, not local control. In addition to trouncing Bruce Blakeman across the Empire State, America’s most prominent Bills fan won Nassau County — her opponent’s home and a longstanding metonym for NIMBYism.
If there was ever a time to go big on transit-oriented development and finding a way to fit one million more people into Nassau, this is the time to push it through. Nearly 80 percent of New York State voters support the construction of multifamily housing around transit stops.
Furthermore, Hochul now has time to fulfill an impressive slate of pending projects, including the Interborough Express, the second phase of the Second Avenue Subway, the 125th Street crosstown subway, Penn Access and the joint city-state plan to speed up buses. Hochul will oversee the creation of one more MTA capital plan during her new term, when the agency publishes its 2030-2034 five-year plan. She’ll be responsible for the headache of funding that plan, too.
Southern Brooklyn gets the blues
Recent election cycles have seen southern Brooklyn going increasingly Republican, as Democrats wrote off the region and conservatives made inroads among immigrant populations frustrated by crime or prices. But, as in so many states across the country, Republicans managed to completely alienate those voters by rewarding these them with ICE raids and tariffs that made their lives here harder and more expensive.
Republican State Sen. Steve Chan and Assembly members Lester Chang, Alec Brook-Krasny and Michael Novakhov all lost to Democratic challengers in districts that encompass neighborhoods including Bensonhurst, Sunset Park, Bay Ridge, Midwood and Sheepshead Bay.
Streetsblog readers may remember Novakhov as the pol who essentially defended speeding after a recidivist speeder struck and killed a mom and two children on Ocean Parkway. He later signed on to the “Stop Super Speeder” bill that passed in Albany earlier this year.
It’s a bird! It’s a plane! It’s a supermajority!
In January, Democrats will control at least 46 out of 63 seats in the state Senate, giving them a historically comfortable supermajority in the upper chamber of the legislature. That provides a big cushion if legislators want to override Hochul’s veto on any of their priorities, and leaves room for defections from bills that certain members might find unpalatable.
For Streetsblog purposes, the supermajority will include two new street safety champions into the senate: Nyack Mayor Joe Rand and Dutchess County Legislator Lisa Kaul. Both stressed their livable streets bonafides in office and on the campaign trail. Rand wants to make his district more walkable and bikeable and also wants better MTA operations west of the Hudson Valley, while Kaul has talked about dragging the New York State Department of Transportation’s attitude out of the car-centric thinking of the 1950s and 1960s.
The safe streets route to Congress
With the formality of the election out of the way, New York’s Congressional delegation will add at least three new members with a real interest in street safety. Micah Lasher told Streetsblog in June that he believes the federal government should make street safety a condition for getting transportation funding, and locally he said that he welcomed the 72nd Street bike lane proposal.
Brad Lander is an extremely well-known quantity on street safety. As a City Council member, he devised the Dangerous Vehicle Abatement Program in order to give the city’s automated camera enforcement some teeth, and constantly provided oversight of the city’s failure to properly implement it. Lander supported the Ninth Street protected bike lane, the redesign of Fourth Avenue and answered the Dave Colon Open Challenge in 2025. In Washington, he’ll push to create a 50-50 split between highway and transit funding for surface transportation rather than the current 80-20 split towards highways.
The pair will head to the capital with Claire Valdez, who will succeed Nydia Velázquez in Congress and penned an ambitious vision for federal involvement in transportation for Streetsblog. Valdez wants to pursue ideas like funding the QueensLink, giving more federal money to cycling infrastructure, sending money from the FHWA directly to cities instead of routing the money through state DOTs and directing more federal money to mass transit accessibility projects.
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, meanwhile, seems poised to run for higher office — either the senate or presidency. Ocasio-Cortez talked about changing the 80-20 split, and a lot more, on a bike ride with Streetsblog earlier this year:
Mamdani voters delivered for Hochul
Gov. Hochul ran up the score big time in New York City, capturing 76 percent of Gotham’s vote. Even though he wasn’t on the ballot this time, Mayor Mamdani can claim some credit.
Analyst Michael Lange found that in the Mamdani-friendly Commie Corridor, Hochul’s vote share rose by 38 percent, compared to 18 percent in the rest of the city.
Two of Mamdani’s big campaign promises, free buses and universal childcare, will require state help to come to fruition. That means Hochul must either raise taxes or find a couple billion dollars in the state’s couch cushions.
Between the Assembly and state Senate, Mamdani and the Democratic Socialists of America sent 11 legislators to Albany to support the mayor’s agenda. Next year, Hochul and Mamdani will find out what each can get out of the other when neither has to worry about an election.
Mamdani’s show of force also had some closer-to-home implications: All five of ballot initiatives passed, including Proposal 1 to speed up outdoor dining approvals and Proposal 3 to clear bureaucratic hoops that slow bike lane and bus lane implementation.
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.

https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.text:
Despite an unceremonious, sudden, and possibly illegal eviction, it seems like the young barn owls of upper Manhattan will be OK.   
A parliament of barn owls had been nested in a hole in the roof of the rickety water tower of an Upper West Side apartment building—but late last week, birders noticed workers doing construction on the roof of the water tower, destroying the nest that the owls had built.  
Birder David Lei told Hell Gate that the fledglings being raised in the disrupted nest began roosting out in the open on nearby buildings last week, which was unusual, he explained. 
"That owl should have been roosting in a more sheltered location, like on an air conditioner windowsill, something like that," Lei said. "But it was out in the open, fully exposed. Songbirds had been bothering it during the day, just natural behavior. But you know, a hawk could have seen it and attacked it."
Lei said that management at 15 West 75th Street had told the residents that they were doing "scheduled maintenance" on the water tower. The building's management did not respond to Hell Gate's request for comment by publication time, but we will update this story if they do.
