https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.title: Reichsbürger | Königlich oder kriminell?
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.author: Joachim F. Tornau, Düsseldorf
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.text:
- Politik
- Reichsbürger
Königlich oder kriminell?
Zu Beginn des Prozesses gegen die Reichsbürger-Sekte »Königreich Deutschland« präsentiert sich der selbsternannte Monarch Peter Fitzek unverbesserlich.
Die Verhandlung hat noch gar nicht begonnen, da hält der König zum ersten Mal Hof. Peter Fitzek, Gründer und selbsternannter »oberster Souverän« der 2025 verbotenen Reichsbürger-Sekte »Königreich Deutschland«, genießt die Kameras, die im Hochsicherheitssaal des Düsseldorfer Oberlandesgerichts auf ihn gerichtet sind. »Unsinnig« sei die Anklage, lässt der 61-Jährige die versammelte Presse wissen, seine Untersuchungshaft »menschenrechtswidrig«. Nebenbei holt er Akte um Akte aus einem blauen Müllsack.
Seit Freitag muss sich der Mann mit der hohen Stirn, dem dünnen Zopf und dem unerschütterlichen Sendungsbewusstsein vor dem Staatsschutzsenat verantworten. Die Bundesanwaltschaft wirft ihm und drei Mitangeklagten vor, die Führungsspitze des 2012 in Lutherstadt Wittenberg gegründeten »Königreichs Deutschland« (KRD) gewesen zu sein. Und damit: Rädelsführer einer kriminellen Vereinigung.
Das KRD sei ein »auf Steuer-, Wirtschafts- und Urkundsdelikte gerichteter Gegenstaat« gegen die Bundesrepublik Deutschland gewesen, trägt der Oberstaatsanwalt vor, der ironischerweise Kaiser heißt. »Das KRD«, sagt Ingo Kaiser, »verfolgte das Fernziel, sein Gebiet auf das Gebiet des Kaiserreichs von 1871 auszudehnen.«
Fürs Erste beschränkte sich das Staatsgebiet, auf dem die Gesetze der Bundesrepublik nicht gelten sollten, auf eine Handvoll Immobilien – und auf rund 700 Unternehmen bundesweit, die sich per Aushang zum Bestandteil des »Königreichs« erklärten. Einige firmieren heutzutage noch so. In Sachsen verfügte das KRD immerhin über drei schlossähnliche Anwesen, im Harz über ein baufälliges Hotel.
Das dafür nötige Geld zog Fitzek seinem »Volk«, das nach seinen Angaben zuletzt rund 6000 Menschen zählte, auf verschiedensten Wegen aus der Tasche. »Seminare zum Systemausstieg« gab es für 374 Euro, Ausweisdokumente für 440 Euro, eine Peter-Fitzek-Büste für 300 Euro. Er versprach Unternehmen, sich der bundesdeutschen Steuer- und Abgabenpflicht entziehen zu können, wenn sie sich dem KRD anschlössen. Eine solche »Umstellung« ließ er sich nach Angaben des brandenburgischen Verfassungsschutzes mit bis zu 24.000 Euro vergolden.
Die Bundesanwaltschaft legt dem gelernten Koch und seinen Mitangeklagten aber vor allem zur Last, dass sie eine »Königliche Reichsbank« – zuletzt unter dem Label »Gemeinwohlkasse«, mit Filialen in Dresden, Ulm, Menden und Lutherstadt Wittenberg – sowie eine Kranken- und Unfallversicherung betrieben. Ohne Erlaubnis versteht sich. Insgesamt habe das KRD damit von 2020 bis 2025 etwa zehn Millionen Euro eingenommen. Zudem seien rund zwei Millionen Euro Steuern und Sozialabgaben hinterzogen worden. Das Ausstellen von Ausweisen, die das »Königreich« als Personalausweisalternative vergab, wertet die Anklagebehörde als Urkundenfälschung.
Vor Gericht spricht Fitzek von sich im Pluralis Majestatis als »Wir«, hält sich noch immer für »Peter I.«, den rechtmäßigen Souverän seines Königreichs. Den mehrfach vorbestraften Überzeugungstäter als Spinner und Geschäftemacher abzutun, greift jedoch zu kurz. Der rechtsesoterische Guru und Verfechter antisemitischer Verschwörungsmythen ist seit Langem im Rechtsaußen-Milieu zu Hause. Er drehte Propagandavideos mit einem verurteilten Holocaust-Leugner, ist freundschaftlich verbunden mit den rechtsextremen Freien Sachsen und bekam in der Untersuchungshaft Besuch von der AfD-Bundestagsabgeordneten Christina Baum. Diese erklärte anschließend, sie hoffe auf einen Freispruch. »Unser Land braucht mehr denn je solche innovativen Köpfe.«
Verteidigen lässt sich Fitzek unter anderem von dem Anwalt und Publizisten Björn Clemens, der für die Verteidigung von Rechtsextremen bekannt ist und selbst in der politischen extremen Rechten in Erscheinung tritt. Zum Prozessauftakt sprach dieser von einem »Missbrauch der Strafprozessordnung für politische Ziele«. Ganz anders reagierte seine Anwaltskollegin Christin Konrad, die den Mitangeklagten Martin S. verteidigt und auch Fitzek schon vertreten hatte: mit einem Gebet. »Mein geliebter göttlicher Funke«, rief sie mit zitternder Stimme. »Bitte sorge dafür, dass am Ende Liebe und Freiheit siegen.«
Für den Prozess sind gut 50 Verhandlungstage bis September 2027 angesetzt.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Crushed Trump. Here’s What They Should Do Next.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel, John Nichols, The Nation
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Crushed Trump. Here’s What They Should Do Next.
Seeking facile compromises with Trump is a fool’s mission—and voters who are hungry for change will not accept half-measures.
Donald Trump made one thing crystal clear to Americans who have been suffering because of his failed economic policies, disastrous wars of whim, and rampant corruption: that the 2026 midterms should be seen as a referendum on his presidency. Time and time again, on campaign swings to try and boost hapless Republicans from Ohio to Texas, the president told voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”
The voters listened—and on November 3, they delivered an epic rebuke to Trump and his scandal-plagued party.
Democrats did not just win the House, where they are projected to win as many as 258 seats as this issue goes to press—a majority similar to the one a newly elected Barack Obama enjoyed when he and then–House Speaker Nancy Pelosi enacted the Affordable Care Act. They flipped at least seven seats in the Senate as well, taking control of a chamber that, during the first two years of Trump’s second term, had rubber-stamped such noxious cabinet picks as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. And they made these gains not just in reliably blue territory, but with dramatic victories in state after state where Trump had prevailed just two years ago—including Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas—and in at least one state (Kansas) where they hadn’t won a Senate seat since the 1932 election that saw Franklin Roosevelt defeat Herbert Hoover.
Coupled with statehouse wins that put Democrats in charge in all seven of the swing states that backed Trump in 2024, and the victories of a multiracial, multiethnic slate of Democratic governors in states where the party has not prevailed in decades—including Texas and Georgia—this is truly a national mandate. It gives congressional Democrats the authority at the federal and state levels to check and balance a historically unpopular president—the Pew Research Center put Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 30 percent just before the election—and to develop a robust alternative to Trumpism, that toxic blend of authoritarianism, bigotry, corruption, unnecessary wars, tax cuts for the rich, surrender to AI oligarchs, and a cruel neglect of human needs.
The winners tell the story. From coast to coast, voters backed Democrats who called for more than just status-quo politics with a little blue coloring. Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who overcame Trump’s vicious attacks on his Muslim faith, won with a motto of “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All”—as well as an outspoken opposition to the genocide in Gaza and AIPAC’s influence on American politics. James Talarico beat Trump’s “Talafreako” labeling and a $158 million attack campaign by Elon Musk to become the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988. In his victory speech, Talarico called for “a new kind of politics: a politics rooted in a deep love—for our state, for our country, and most importantly, for all of our neighbors,” one that “requires that we stand between the bullies and the bullied.” The senator-elect wasn’t alone; Lone Star voters, long known for dashing Democrats’ hopes, went straight-ticket blue, handing Democrats every statewide position on the ballot and electing Texas’s first-ever Latina governor, the anti-corruption campaigner Gina Hinojosa.
In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation’s first Black woman to win a governorship. In Ohio, Amy Acton triumphed over the hateful politics of the Republican right. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the country’s first Native American woman governor, while Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan will go to the US Senate as a proud member of the White Earth Nation in northwestern Minnesota, as well as a former head of the Children’s Defense Fund–Minnesota and—along with El-Sayed and Troy Jackson in Maine—a close ally of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders.
Many newcomers to the House are unapologetic progressives who ran with support from Sanders and the surging Democratic Socialists of America, including New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros in Colorado, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. And a proud economic populist, Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, will return to the Senate as an unabashed advocate for breaking up monopolies, regulating banks, strengthening unions, taking on Big Tech, regulating data centers, and going after Trump’s corruption.
The scope and character of this rebuke to Trump is vitally important: It gives the new Congress a mandate to check and balance “the most dangerous president in the history of the United States,” as Sanders referred to him during the midterm campaign.
Trump is indeed dangerous, and he will remain so in the last two years of his presidency. He retains the much-abused powers of his office—including the ability to unilaterally launch wars abroad—and he will no doubt redouble his efforts to bypass Congress, ignore the courts, target enemies, and obstruct meaningful progress.
But he will do so now as a more diminished and discredited figure than ever before. Voters everywhere appeared repelled by Trump: His corruption and self-dealing finally became an albatross around his neck, with Democrats moving the issue to the top of the political agenda. “While the crook president and his crook family rake in billions from around the world, you pay more for everything,” Senator Jon Ossoff told Georgia voters as part of a scorched-earth campaign that saw the Democrat—a potential 2028 presidential contender—finish with 59 percent of the vote.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a key campaigner along with Sanders for progressives across the country, drew thunderous applause on election eve when she argued against “playing nice with people who are committed to the destruction of our democracy” and declared: “There must be accountability for crimes that have been committed and wrongs that have been done against the country and the people of the United States of America.”
To do that, Democrats need smart accountability strategies—such as those of Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the presumptive chair of the House Appropriations Committee—that follow the money and connect the costs of the self-dealing by Trump and his cronies to oligarchical wealth, the affordability crisis, and lousy healthcare. Accountability and affordability can go hand in hand, but it will happen only if Democrats make a true break with the rotten status quo. A failure to reject Trump’s foreign policy—particularly when it comes to the war with Iran and his near-total support of Israel, two issues that Vice President JD Vance quickly identified as liabilities for the GOP—will send exactly the wrong message to voters. And pulling punches on economic issues will only raise questions about whether Democrats are sufficiently distinct from Republicans.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Democrats need to recognize that seeking facile compromises with Trump, who vows that he’ll be “Mr. Veto” on the issues that matter, is a fool’s mission—and voters who are hungry for change will not accept half-measures.
Unfortunately, some Democrats still don’t get it. Before the election, Hawaii Senator Brian Schatz suggested that Democrats should avoid “aspirational” agendas. “I do not think it is time to propose things that the president of the United States is guaranteed to veto,” Schatz said.
That’s the wrong take.
Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar of Texas has wisely warned, “We cannot be the party of nervous lawyers who just tinker around the edges.” Casar was spot-on when he said that Democrats “have to show we’re more than anti-Trump. That starts with cracking down on corporate greed to bring down the cost of health care, housing, child care, groceries, and gas…. If Donald Trump chooses to veto our popular, pro-affordability policies, the fight is far from over. We’ll run on them in 2028 and pass them in 2029.”
Democrats must counter Trump’s self-enriching schemes, crude abuses of power, and ugly theatrics with big ideas and clarity about how to implement them. Where to begin?
take on big money
The 2026 midterms saw record election spending—roughly $12 billion, according to OpenSecrets. Close to a half-billion dollars came from Musk alone. Republicans had an overwhelming money advantage. Democrats beat the money this time, but the party needs a comprehensive legal, legislative, and state-based strategy to address the crisis.
regulate ai
Democrats should follow the lead of Peggy Flanagan, who proposed an independent federal body to provide AI regulation and oversight. They should also encourage states to lead as “laboratories of democracy”: Polls show that 80 percent of Americans favor laws that choose humanity over machinery.
let abdul el-sayed lead on medicare for all
When Barack Obama campaigned in Michigan, he said that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American.” Yes! El-Sayed proposes to “finish the job” by “[expanding] Medicare to cover all necessary healthcare, including vision, dental, and hearing, and extend it to every single American from cradle to grave without premiums, copays, or deductibles.” El-Sayed is the right leader to join Sanders, who is expected to head the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, in fighting for an agenda that—as the midterm results make clear—is seen by the electorate as radical common sense. It is high time to ignore the establishment’s hand-wringing over the populist energy that was key to winning the midterms, to reject Trump’s corruption and his billionaire allies and declare, as Troy Jackson did at the finish of his campaign: “We’re not from the left, we’re not from the right, we’re from the bottom, and we’re rising!”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Budapest exhibition explores Van Gogh and Gauguin's artistic excursion to Montpellier
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
After Paul Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888 to stay with his friend Van Gogh, the two artists would go out to paint together and then socialise and discuss art in the evenings over a glass of wine. Their very different personalities, however, soon led to tensions. Living together in the confines of the Yellow House and sharing a small room as a studio, they began to row. As winter approached, and the weather made it impossible to work outside, the situation only worsened.
In mid-December, in an attempt to clear the air, Gauguin suggested that they should make a trip to Montpellier, 70 km west of Arles. Their goal was to visit the Musée Fabre, renowned for its fine collection of paintings.
The artistic result of this trip forms a central part of a major exhibition on Gauguin which opened this week at Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts. Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin: The Circles of Post-Impressionists and Symbolists (until 28 February 2027) provides a wide-ranging exploration of the art of Gauguin and his associates. The show’s title comes from a key painting by the artist inspired by the Montpellier visit, Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889).
Van Gogh and Gauguin travelled from Arles to Montpellier by train, which took around four hours. Although it has long been assumed that they made a day trip on either 16 or 17 December 1888, it is arguably more likely that they spent the night there and stayed for both days. The Musée Fabre had over 800 paintings on display, so they would surely have wanted time to savour the works. Many of the finest pictures were French, given by Alfred Bruyas, a local collector and patron of Gustave Courbet.
For Gauguin, the highlight of the museum was Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854). This landscape composition includes the figure of Courbet himself, laden with his equipment and holding a walking pole. He is greeting Bruyas, who is accompanied by a bowing servant.
Gauguin, who was impressed with the Courbet, painted a work in response, a year later, in the Brittany fishing village of Le Pouldu. The main figure in this work is Gauguin himself, facing a Breton woman on the other side of a gate.
Superficially, the Gauguin painting bears little resemblance to the Courbet. Stylistically, Courbet’s smoothly painted picture contrasts with Gauguin’s rough brushwork. The compositions appear to have little in common, other than showing an artist encountering other people—and being greeted with a “good day” (and, incidentally, both scenes also include a dog).
The moods seem very different. Courbet appears thrilled to greet his patron and friend. Gauguin’s encounter with the Breton woman, however, is fleeting, as they happen to pass each other at a gate. The Budapest exhibition’s lead curator, Judit Geskó, sees the Gauguin picture as representing “the artist as a solitary wanderer”.
But despite the differences, Gauguin’s decision to entitle his work as he did shows that he was directly acknowledging the source of his inspiration, the Courbet. Gauguin’s title is actually inscribed on the painting, in the lower-left corner.
Gauguin made two versions of his composition: the one on loan to Budapest from the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and the other (which was unavailable for borrowing) at the National Gallery in Prague. The Hammer picture, which was the original, was created to display on the dining room door in the small inn where he was staying in Le Pouldu.
As for Van Gogh, the Dutchman was particularly struck in the Musée Fabre by the portraits by Courbet. These included a self-portrait, The Man with the Pipe (around 1849), which may well have inspired Van Gogh one month later to paint his Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe (January 1889).
Bruyas was depicted by a range of artists and these portraits were also much admired by Van Gogh in the Montpellier museum. Vincent described Bruyas’ appearance to his brother Theo as “a gentleman with a beard, red hair, who looks damnably like you or me”.
Electric discussions
Both Gauguin and Van Gogh were great admirers of Courbet, who was very well represented in the Musée Fabre. Although they agreed about Courbet, their tastes for other artists were often rather different. Vincent wrote to Theo that their artistic discussions in Montpellier had been “excessively electric”. He explained: “We sometimes emerge from it with tired minds, like an electric battery after it’s run down.”
Despite these animated discussions, the inspirational visit seemed a success. Vincent reported back to Theo the day after their return that in the museum they had been “right in the midst of magic”. He added: “Gauguin said to me this morning, when I asked him how he felt: ‘that he could feel his old self coming back’, which gave me great pleasure.”
Sadly, the reconciliation did not last long: just four days later Van Gogh severely mutilated his ear. Although the trigger was probably news he had just received that Theo had become engaged (which Vincent feared would threaten his brother’s support), tensions with Gauguin were also a contributing factor.
Van Gogh in the Gauguin show
Budapest’s Gauguin exhibition is ambitious, with 80 works by the French master and 70 by other artists. Although financial valuations for exhibitions are rarely revealed, The Art Newspaper can report that its total insurance value is €1.5bn.
The show includes three works by Van Gogh: the landscape painting Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) and two rarely-displayed drawings from the collection of the Budapest museum, The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888).
The Budapest exhibition has two Gauguin paintings dating from his stay with Van Gogh in Arles: the landscape Les Alyscamps (October 1888, Musée d’Orsay, Paris) and the portrait Madame Roulin (November-December 1888, Saint Louis Art Museum). Both of these subjects were also tackled by Van Gogh.
Among the other Gauguin highlights in the show is Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901, Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich). This is one of four still-life paintings inspired by Van Gogh’s favourite motif—sunflowers. Gauguin painted these in the Marquesas Islands (north of Tahiti), with flowers grown from seeds he was sent by a friend from Paris.
The museum estimates that the Gauguin exhibition could see up to 350,000 visitors, a huge number for a medium-sized European capital. However, even this won’t match Geskó's Van Gogh show in 2006, which attracted 486,000 people to the museum to see the Dutch painter's works.

https://gothamist.com/news/skeletal-rema.title: Skeletal remains found in backyard of West Village building, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/skeletal-rema.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/skeletal-rema.text:
Construction workers discovered part of a 19th-century human skeleton behind a building in the West Village on Thursday, according to the NYPD.
Officials said a construction crew excavating the backyard of 79 Christopher St. called 911 around 11 a.m. after finding several bones and part of a skull, buried 4 to 7 feet below the ground.
The city medical examiner determined that the bones were historic, and likely buried when the plot of land was used as a cemetery for the neighboring church in the mid-1800s, according to the NYPD. The property is adjacent to St. John’s Lutheran Church, which dates back to 1855.
Police said no foul play was suspected, and that it was not immediately clear if the remains belonged to a woman or a man.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.text:
- Kommentare
- Koalitionsverhandlungen
Gegner von Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin als Steigbügelhalter der Faschisten
In Berlin wird gerade über eine Koalition aus Linke, Grünen und SPD verhandelt. Das passt einigen Sozialdemokraten gar nicht. Unser Kolumnist weiß, warum.
Schon wieder. Sigmar Gabriel, Karl Lauterbach und diverse andere Sozialdemokraten haben nichts aus der Geschichte gelernt. Vor rund 100 Jahren haben sich Sozialdemokraten und Kommunisten wechselseitig mit atemberaubenden Vorwürfen bekämpft. Und so haben sie den Aufstieg der Faschisten begünstigt; manche würden sagen, dass sie ihn überhaupt erst möglich gemacht haben. Und heute schwingen sich Sozialdemokraten wieder dazu auf, Die Linke und Bündnisse mit ihnen wie jetzt Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin zu diffamieren und zu bekämpfen. Bemerkenswert ist, dass es sich – wie man aus Kreisen der SPD hört – bei den Unterzeichnern überwiegend um Anhänger des Seeheimer Kreises, also einer rechten Parteigliederung, handelt. Und unterzeichnet haben vorzugsweise nicht in Berlin lebende Genossen.
Für die nächste Bundestagswahl ist vollkommen klar: Wer den Aufstieg der Faschisten ins Kanzleramt, wer Alice Weidel (AfD) als Kanzlerin verhindern will, der muss nach alternativen Bündnissen suchen. Und Rot-Grün-Rot ist genau so ein Projekt. Nicht nur für Berlin, sondern perspektivisch für die ganze Republik. Umgekehrt gilt: Wer dieses Bündnis bekämpft, macht sich perspektivisch zum Steigbügelhalter der Faschisten.
Michael Schlecht ist Gründungsmitglied von WASG und Die Linke. Nach 30 Jahren verschiedener hauptamtlicher Tätigkeiten als Gewerkschaftssekretär für die IG Druck und Papier sowie Verdi wurde er 2009 in den Bundestag gewählt. 2017 schied er aus und war zuletzt wirtschafts- und gewerkschaftspolitischer Sprecher der Linke-Bundestagsfraktion.
Der von Union und SPD im Bund beschlossene und geplante Sozialabbau wird zur weiteren Verbitterung, Verzweiflung und Wut bei noch mehr Menschen führen. Damit droht einerseits die weitere Stärkung der AfD und andererseits auf Seiten der Union eine Fortsetzung des Zerfallsprozesses, aus dem heraus Teile bereit sein werden, sich einer blau-schwarzen Koalition zur Verfügung zu stellen.
All die Vorwürfe gegen die Berliner Linke wie Antisemitismus und mangelnde Fähigkeit, die innere Sicherheit zu gewährleisten, sind vorgeschoben und aufgebauscht. Die Gefährdung der inneren Sicherheit in Berlin etwa durch die organisierte Kriminalität ist in der jüngsten Vergangenheit unter einer sozialdemokratischen Innensenatorin überhaupt erst virulent geworden. Und die Bekämpfung des Antisemitismus ist durch Mittelstreichung bzw. Zweckentfremdung eines CDU-geführten Senats behindert worden. Für Linke, auch für die Berliner Linke, ist das Existenzrecht Israels unverhandelbar. Der Staatsrechtler und Jude Philippe Sands – jüngst erhielt er den Friedenspreis des Buchhandels – hat bemängelt, dass die Kritik an der israelischen Regierung wegen des Krieges gegen die Palästinenser hierzulande nur mit ohrenbetäubendem Schweigen vorgetragen wird. Wer dieses Schweigen durchbricht, ist nicht antisemitisch.
Nein, im Kern geht es darum, eine Regierung unter Führung der Berliner Linken zu bekämpfen, die durch Eingriffe in kapitalistische Eigentumsverhältnisse die Wohnungs- bzw. Mietenkrise nachhaltig lösen will. Es geht um die Sicherstellung der Bezahlbarkeit des Lebens.
Wenn bei einem ehemaligen sozialdemokratischen Parteivorsitzenden das Denken durch Mitgliedschaft in diversen Aufsichtsräten korrumpiert ist, dann ist die Verantwortungslosigkeit seiner Positionierung noch naheliegend. Und wenn sich abgehalfterte sozialdemokratische Mandatsträger, allen voran der ehemalige Berliner Oberbürgermeister Michael Müller und die zuletzt als Wirtschaftssenatorin amtierende Franziska Giffey an einer politischen Giftspritzerei beteiligen, ist das menschlich sogar noch verständlich. Aber bei vielen jüngeren, zum Teil aktiven Sozialdemokraten ist die geschichtliche Vergessenheit schlicht erschreckend.
Auch auf Seiten der Linken gibt es Parteigänger, die den Geschichtsunterricht verdrängt haben. Sozialdemokraten werden von ihnen generell ins gegnerische Lager gestellt. Deshalb bekämpfen sie ebenfalls ein rot-grün-rotes Bündnis und versuchen, mit provozierenden Aussagen zum Nahost-Konflikt, die von der Parteilinie abweichen, und mit einer Zusammenarbeit mit Terrorunterstützern den Koalitionsprozess zu sabotieren. Erfreulich ist, dass der Parteitag der Linken am 31. Oktober diesen Bestrebungen eine klare Absage erteilt hat: 90 Prozent der Delegierten stimmten für Koalitionsverhandlungen zur Bildung von Rot-Grün-Rot unter Führung der linken Bürgermeisterin Elif Eralp.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.

https://gothamist.com/news/supreme-court.title: Supreme Court case could affect admissions reforms for NYC specialized schools
https://gothamist.com/news/supreme-court.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/supreme-court.text:
As Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces mounting pressure to boost the numbers of Black and Latino students gaining admission to New York City’s specialized public high schools, a new case before the U.S. Supreme Court could sharply narrow his options, education experts say.
The high court recently agreed to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a challenge to the test- and lottery-based admissions system used by the Maryland county for its public magnet middle schools.
The case comes amid the recent rekindling of decades-old debates over integration of New York City Public Schools, one of the most racially segregated school systems in the country. Many of the calls for reform have centered on the city’s prestigious and highly selective specialized high schools, where Black and Latino students are sharply underrepresented.
As with his predecessors, Mamdani has been pressed to articulate a specific plan to address underrepresentation of Black and Latino students to the specialty schools, with students, parents, past school officials and members of the City Council sounding the alarm.
But the Supreme Court, which has steadily eroded affirmative action initiatives, even those where race receives no mention, could further narrow and define what options are available for policymakers in New York City and other school systems facing similar challenges.
“It might freeze in time the racial makeup of every screened program in New York City,” said David Bloomfield, an education professor at Brooklyn College and the CUNY Graduate Center, who has publicly opposed the entrance exam for the city’s specialized high schools.
Here’s what to know about the Montgomery County case and its potential ramifications for New York City.
What is the issue before the Supreme Court?
The admissions lottery under scrutiny, based on successful test-takers in specific neighborhoods, was added during the pandemic and with an eye toward increasing the enrollment of Black and Hispanic students in the magnet schools.
Policy experts said the case centers on a narrow but consequential question: How do challengers of an admissions policy prove harm to a particular race when the policy makes no mention of race?
Under Supreme Court precedent, a so-called race-neutral policy can be found to be racially discriminatory — and a violation of the constitution’s equal protection guarantee — if challengers can prove two things: that the intent of the policy and its effect are discriminatory.
The challengers there are arguing that the lottery admissions policy is racially discriminatory in part because the share of Asian and white students admitted to the county’s magnet schools decreased after it was implemented. The challengers argue that individual Asian and white students were harmed.
“If a program is racially discriminatory and it hurts a single student of that race, that should be enough to bring a lawsuit to challenge it,” said Dean McGee, a lawyer for the Pacific Legal Foundation, who has brought similar cases in the federal courts.
But lower courts found that the lottery admissions system for Montgomery County magnet schools isn’t racial discriminatory, because the share of Asian American students admitted to the schools is still larger than the share of Asian American students in the applicant pool. In similar cases elsewhere, the First and Fourth Circuit courts of appeal have arrived at similar conclusions.
Why is this case being watched beyond Maryland?
The Supreme Court’s decision guidance could affect outcomes in similar admissions cases in the federal pipeline, including an action brought by a parent in New York who alleges a special admissions initiative discriminates against Asian American students.
If the Supreme Court sides with the parent challengers in the Montgomery County case, the justices could broaden what constitutes racial discrimination, opening the door for similar challenges of school admissions policies.
Liberal and progressive education experts say such a ruling could also deter education officials from pursuing admissions reform for selective schools, out of fear of incurring more lawsuits.
The court’s guidance could also affect reforms not just aimed at changing the racial makeup of selective schools, but also the economic diversity of such schools, said Richard Kahlenberg, an education and housing researcher for the Progressive Policy Institute, who has opposed race-based affirmative action programs but supported economic-based affirmative action.
A ruling for the plaintiffs, Kahlenberg said, could make it easier for conservatives to sue school districts over economic race-neutral affirmative action programs.
He added: “That’s the worry — that you freeze in an unfair status quo, and any reform that negatively impacts white or Asian students would be cause for concern among those on the right.”
But McGee, the Pacific Legal Foundation lawyer, said a ruling for the challengers wouldn’t necessarily halt admissions reform.
Policymakers, he said, would have to ask, “How do we benefit individual students? How do we fix failing schools? It would prohibit them from viewing (reforms) through a strictly racial lens and implementing policies for specific racial goals.”
How are admissions to New York City’s specialized high schools determined?
New York City has eight specialized high schools that currently determine entrance offers based on a student’s score on the Specialized High Schools Admissions Test, or SHSAT.
A portion of seats are also allocated to students who score slightly lower on the exam and attend a summer preparatory program.
At the eight test-based specialized high schools only 3.5% of students admitted this year were Black and 6.5% were Hispanic. The majority, 56.5%, were Asian and 23.5% were white, according to city education department data.
At Stuyvesant High School, only three of the 777 admitted students were Black. At Staten Island Tech, only one of the 294 admitted students was Black.
State law requires the SHSAT be the sole determinant for admissions to three of the city’s top specialized high schools.
What has Mamdani said about the situation in NY?
On the campaign trail, Mamdani promised to keep in place the SHSAT, after previously opposing it. At once, he has also vowed to address school segregation.
After the writer Nikole Hannah-Jones recently published a widely discussed article about the fallout from her decision to send her daughter to the city’s segregated public schools, Mamdani has repeatedly been asked how he plans to address the issue. He has vowed to tackle the issue, but offered scant specifics.
“We are exploring every single tool that we have at our disposal to ensure that this is going to be a very different school system moving forward than the one that we have inherited,” Mamdani said on The Brian Lehrer Show.
When pressed about the specifics of any integration plan at a recent town hall with Hannah-Jones, the schools chancellor Kamar Samuels promised to improve integration but offered no specifics or timeline for acting.
City council members have also urged the Mamdani administration to act.
Specifically, the members have pushed changes to the admissions policies at the five other specialized schools not explicitly cited in the state law, suggesting the schools instead rely on other factors in addition to a student’s SHSAT score, such as essays, teacher recommendation, and an applicant’s “background.”
But the policy experts said those reforms, if enacted, could also be the target of future racial discrimination lawsuits.

https://gothamist.com/news/south-bronx-e.title: South Bronx, East New York lead NYC in littering and panhandling tickets, analysis finds
https://gothamist.com/news/south-bronx-e.author: Ben Feuerherd, Carol Chen
https://gothamist.com/news/south-bronx-e.text:
NYPD officers are issuing criminal tickets for low-level offenses like loitering, panhandling and littering in the South Bronx and in East New York, Brooklyn at higher rates than anywhere else in the city, according to a new data analysis.
In 2025 and the first half of this year, more than 60% of the criminal summonses the NYPD issued for loitering were written by officers in just one of the city’s 78 police precincts — the 40th, in the South Bronx — according to an analysis published earlier this week by the Data Collaborative for Justice at John Jay College.
Audrey Martin, a spokesperson for the New York Legal Aid Society, said the new data shows that police are unfairly targeting neighborhoods where many low-income people of color live.
"Policing strategies like saturating neighborhoods with summonses fail to change anything except for how much time our neighbors spend fighting tickets or how much money they pay out of their pockets,” Martin said.
Residents of the neighborhoods who spoke to Gothamist had mixed opinions about such enforcement, with some supportive of the NYPD and others critical of low-level ticketing.
The analysis comes as Mayor Zohran Mamdani has faced intense criticism about his handling of policing issues, including for allowing the NYPD to continue a crackdown on what the NYPD calls quality-of-life crimes and violations. As a candidate for mayor, Mamdani said police should focus on solving more serious crimes, but quality of life enforcement has continued at a similar rate as the final year of the Eric Adams administration.
NYPD spokesperson Bradley Weekes said in a statement that NYPD officers in the South Bronx and East New York precincts are responding to increasing numbers of 311 calls. He said in the 40th precinct, in the South Bronx, 311 calls have increased 215% since 2015. In the same period, they’ve increased 556% in the 75th precinct. He did not immediately say whether there are disproportionately more 311 calls about low-level offenses in those precincts than in others.
Weekes added that the number of summonses citywide has not grown over time. The overall number of criminal summonses currently being issued by officers is at similar levels to what they were during Bill de Blasio’s administration, not counting the years during the pandemic, he said.
He said that in the South Bronx and East New York, the number of criminal summonses being issued by officers is down this year compared to the same period last year. Officers in the 40th precinct in the South Bronx have written 20% fewer criminal summonses, and officers in the 75 precinct in East New York have issued 15% fewer, he said. The analysis notes criminal summonses are on track to decline slightly in 2026, with officers on pace to issue 101,192 in 2026.
Police officers issue criminal summonses for violations that could be covered by lesser civil tickets — like open container violations — for a variety of reasons, according to the NYPD patrol guide. If someone is a recidivist, has a warrant or if an officer finds a "legitimate law enforcement reason” to do so, they can issue the more serious criminal summons.
Few are convicted
The vast majority of the criminal tickets that NYPD officers issue wind up being dismissed, according to a previous study by the same John Jay College group. In 2024, judges who heard criminal summons cases threw out 65% of them because of paperwork issues or because they were legally insufficient.
In the end, only 9% of the criminal tickets issued in 2024 ended in convictions, according to the study. The researchers found that even if people end up getting their tickets dismissed, they are punished anyway because they often lose time and wages fighting a ticket in court.
Racial disparities in summons enforcement have also persisted for years, according to the most recent analysis. In the first half of 2026, nearly 82% of criminal summonses were issued to Black and Hispanic New Yorkers, according to the data.
Michael Rempel, a researcher at the Data Collaborative for Justice and an author of the dashboard, said violations like having an open container of alcohol or loitering, are ones where police officers have the most discretion.
They are not the kind of offenses officers respond to after getting 311 complaints, Rempel said. “Clearly it's a choice to issue those types of summonses in large numbers,” Rempel said.
Residents have mixed feelings
More than a third of the city’s panhandling complaints from 2025 through the first half of this year were issued in the 40th precinct, in the South Bronx.
Antigone Raynaud said she comes to a busy shopping district called The Hub in that area regularly to make extra cash selling her blood plasma at a medical office. Raynaud said drug use and homelessness seem like understandable reasons for police to patrol the area. But, she added, a criminal summons for loitering could turn into an arrest warrant if the person doesn’t pay it — and she said that seems like too severe a punishment for a low-level offense.
“To be standing somewhere and get a ticket, not show up, and then now you're getting arrested, I think that's a bit excessive,” Raynaud, 30, said when she heard the area led the city in such tickets.
Malaika Holder, 32, is a lifelong resident of the Bronx who lives in Mott Haven, another neighborhood in the 40th precinct. In an interview earlier this week, she said she was not surprised residents there are ticketed at high rates for something like loitering — but said she found it sad.
“I do feel like the residents of the Bronx do have this very tense relationship with police and law enforcement, especially because in the Bronx, a lot of the community and what the culture is just loitering and just hanging out in different spaces,” she said. “A lot of our third spaces are stoops.”
Holder added that even though there may be an issue with people using drugs in the area, she thought that should be addressed with resources other than the police department.
“I don't think we should be criminalizing people who are looking to substitute their hard times with vices,” she said.
In Brooklyn, officers in East New York issued 855 criminal summonses for alcohol in public in 2025 through the summer of 2026, the most out of any precinct in the city. The tickets accounted for 8% of the citywide total, the data shows.
East New York residents offered a variety of opinions on the enforcement.
Das Angshu, 57, a plumber who lives in the neighborhood, said he welcomes the police presence.
“I see the police all the time right around here. They are doing a public service. I don’t see them doing a lot of ticketing,” Angshu said. “ I see them, I feel more safe. They are very fair.”
Kenneth Willis, an 18-year-old student, said he supports the police in stopping serious crimes, but said he’s concerned low-level enforcement will pit police against residents.
“ It's gonna create tension within the neighborhood, especially you already have people that don't like cops,” he said. “You're making it so people have to go to court, people have to pay money, people have to pay money that they don't have, it's gonna cause problems.”

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.title: Parlamentswahlen in Neuseeland | Qiulae Wong: Königsmacherin mit roten Linien
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.author: Barbara Barkhausen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.text:
- Politik
- Parlamentswahlen in Neuseeland
Qiulae Wong: Königsmacherin mit roten Linien
Die 38-jährige Qiulae Wong ist Vorsitzende der Opportunity Party in Neuseeland, die für die Regierungsbildung entscheidend werden könnte.
Am Anfang stand das Jobportal Seek. Dort schrieb die neuseeländische Opportunity Party im vergangenen Jahr den Vorsitz aus. Die damalige Unternehmensberaterin Qiulae Wong erfuhr davon, bewarb sich und bekam die Stelle, obwohl sie zuvor nie ein politisches Amt innehatte.
Vor den Parlamentswahlen am 7. November wird die 38-Jährige nun als mögliche Königsmacherin gehandelt. Ihre Partei könnte entscheiden, wer nach der Wahl in Neuseeland die Regierung bilden kann. Nicht zuletzt wegen ihres »kometenhaften Aufstiegs« haben Medien sie bereits mit der früheren neuseeländischen Regierungschefin Jacinda Ardern verglichen.
Wurzeln in Fidschi, Erfahrungen in London
Wong wurde in Fidschi geboren. Rund acht Jahre lang arbeitete sie in London, zunächst in der ethischen Modebranche, unter anderem für ein Start-up, das Unternehmen wie Vivienne Westwood bei der Umstellung auf nachhaltigere Geschäftsmodelle unterstützte. Dann kehrte sie nach Auckland zurück, Neuseelands größte Stadt auf der Nordinsel, wo sie bereits als Kleinkind aufgewachsen war. In die Politik trieb sie nach eigener Darstellung die abrupte Kehrtwende der Regierung beim Klimaschutz. Aus nächster Nähe habe sie erlebt, wie das Vertrauen der Unternehmen in Investitionen und Planbarkeit litt. Das sei »der letzte Tropfen, der das Fass zum Überlaufen gebracht« und veranlasst habe, dass sie sich nach anderen Wegen umsah.
Wong tritt in Mount Albert an, einem Wahlkreis, den einst Premierministerinnen wie Jacinda Ardern und Helen Clark hielten. Sie zielt auf die Stimmen jener Wähler ab, die von beiden großen Parteien – den konservativen Nationals und der linken Labour Party – enttäuscht sind.
Steuer auf Land, Geld für alle
Das Herzstück ihres Programms ist eine umfassende Steuerreform mit einer Bodenwertsteuer. Wong will damit das Horten von Bauland unattraktiv machen, Wohnen bezahlbarer machen und das Steuersystem Schritt für Schritt von der Einkommensteuer wegführen. Die Einführung soll nach Parteiangaben über zehn Jahre gestaffelt erfolgen.
Mit dem Geld soll ein bedingungsloses Grundeinkommen finanziert werden, das die Partei »Citizen’s Income« nennt. Es würde 19.400 Neuseeland-Dollar im Jahr betragen, gut 370 Dollar pro Woche – umgerechnet sind dies rund 9800 Euro jährlich. Damit sollen die wichtigsten Sozialleistungen, darunter die Altersrente, ersetzt werden. Für Rentner, Eltern, Alleinerziehende oder Menschen mit Behinderung sind ergänzende Zahlungen vorgesehen. Wong sieht darin auch ein Sicherheitsnetz für Angestellte der Mittelschicht, sollten ihre Jobs durch künstliche Intelligenz ersetzt werden.
Wong nennt fünf rote Linien
Politikwissenschaftler wie Stephen Levine von der Victoria University of Wellington beobachten mit Interesse die Aufmerksamkeit, die die Opportunity Party selbst im Ausland erhält. Die Partei, die ihren Namen vom Plural »Opportunities« in den Singular änderte, habe zuvor nie ernsthaft Aussicht auf Parlamentssitze gehabt. Nun hänge womöglich die Regierungsbildung von ihr ab.
Der amtierende Regierungschef Christoper Luxon von den Nationals schließt aktuell eine Zusammenarbeit mit der Partei aus. Wong dagegen will zuerst mit der Partei verhandeln, die die meisten Sitze holt. Ihre fünf roten Linien hat sie folgendermaßen formuliert: Preise senken, Politik säubern, das Gesundheitssystem reparieren, die Ozeane schützen und Glaubwürdigkeit beim Klimaschutz zurückgewinnen. Deswegen steht ihr das Lager aus Labour, Grünen und Te Pāti Māori wohl näher als die konservativen rechten Parteien.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://taz.de/Greenpeace-warnt-fuer-Deu.title: Greenpeace warnt vor Rechenzentren: Mega-Datenfabriken verursachen Mega-Wasserstress
https://taz.de/Greenpeace-warnt-fuer-Deu.author: Kai Schöneberg
https://taz.de/Greenpeace-warnt-fuer-Deu.text:
Greenpeace warnt vor Rechenzentren: Mega-Datenfabriken verursachen Mega-Wasserstress
Einige geplante Rechenzentren in Deutschland könnten so viel Wasser wie eine Kleinstadt verbrauchen, warnt Greenpeace. Das gefährde die Versorgung.
Große Rechenzentren können in trockenen Regionen Deutschlands zu Wasserstress führen. Laut einer Kurzstudie des Öko-Instituts im Auftrag der Umweltorganisation Greenpeace verbrauchten die hiesigen Serverfarmen im Jahr 2025 rund 13 Milliarden Liter Wasser zur Kühlung. Bis 2030 könnte dieser Bedarf durch neue Mega-Datenfabriken auf bis zu 27 Milliarden Liter pro Jahr anwachsen – was dem Trinkwasserverbrauch einer Großstadt mit rund 580.000 Einwohnern entspricht, etwa so viel wie Essen.
„Das kann lokal durchaus desaströse Effekte haben“, sagt Greenpeace-Expertin Linda Klapdor der taz. Bereits im vergangenen, besonders heißen und trockenen Sommer habe es in einigen Kommunen Beschränkungen der Wassernutzung und historische Tiefstände in Flüssen und Seen gegeben. Greenpeace fordert von der Bundesregierung verpflichtende Wassergutachten vor Genehmigungen, ein Verbot wasserintensiver Anlagen in Trockengebieten und konsequente Sanktionen bei Verstößen gegen behördliche Meldepflichten.
Die Bundesregierung plant bis 2030 eine Verdoppelung der Rechenzentrums-Kapazitäten in Deutschland. Während bisherige Anlagen meist weniger als 5 Megawatt Anschlussleistung haben, entstehen nun Anlagen mit über 1 Gigawatt, mehr als 200-mal so viel. In Deutschland sind aktuell knapp 30 Riesenprojekte mit mehr als 100 Megawatt Serverleistung in Planung.
Die Studie modelliert deren jährlichen Wasserbedarf auf jeweils bis zu 930 Millionen Liter pro Jahr, etwa den Trinkwasserverbrauch einer Kleinstadt mit 20.000 Menschen. In bereits trockenen Regionen könnten die neuen Datenfabriken „akuten Grundwasserstress, Verteilungskonflikte mit steigenden Belastungen für die Menschen in den betroffenen Gemeinden und Schäden am lokalen Ökosystem verursachen“, heißt es in der Studie. Problematisch sei zudem der hohe Strombedarf.
Digitalwirtschaft hält Wasserverbrauch für „sehr gering“
Diese Berechnungen stehen im Kontrast zur Darstellung der Digitalwirtschaft. Der Branchenverband Bitkom hatte den Wasserbedarf von 65 Prozent der deutschen Rechenzentren jüngst als „sehr gering“ eingestuft. Fast zwei Drittel der hiesigen Anlagen verbrauchten maximal 0,1 Liter Wasser pro Kilowattstunde IT-Stromverbrauch, heißt es in einer in dieser Woche erschienenen Bitkom-Untersuchung.
Das Öko-Institut kommt nach der Bereinigung von zum Teil unvollständigen Datensätzen aus dem behördlichen Rechenzentrumsregister hingegen auf einen gewichteten Mittelwert von 0,67 Liter Wasser pro Kilowattstunde IT-Stromverbrauch. Bereits der aktuelle Jahresverbrauch deutscher Rechenzentren von 13 Milliarden Litern entspreche dem Wasserinhalt des Berliner Wannsees.
„Das Problem ist die fehlende Transparenz der Betreiber“, erklärt Klapdor die unterschiedliche Darstellung. Weniger als die Hälfte der rund 1.200 meldepflichtigen Rechenzentrumsbetreiber in Deutschland hätten überhaupt Daten an die Behörden geliefert, nur 139 Meldungen seien für die Studie verwertbar gewesen. Auch laut Bitkom erklären sich die unterschiedlichen Werte „möglicherweise durch die unterschiedlichen Berechnungsansätze und die zugrunde liegende Datenbasis“, heißt es in einer Stellungnahme für die taz.
Zudem widerspricht Greenpeace einem zentralen Argument der Betreiber, wonach niedriger Stromverbrauch technisch zwangsläufig durch einen höheren Wassereinsatz erkauft werden müsse. In der Praxis lasse sich kein statistischer Zusammenhang zwischen Strom- und Wassereffizienz nachweisen. Eine hohe Energieeffizienz könne komplett ohne Wasserkühlung realisiert werden. Eine moderne Trocken- oder Kompressionskühlung könne den Wasserverbrauch der Serverfarmen sogar vollständig auf null senken.
Börsen brechen nach Ankündigung von Bernie Sanders ein
Während es in Deutschland erst wenige Proteste gegen neue Datenzentren gibt, waren sie in den USA eines der wichtigen Themen im Wahlkampf zu den Midterms. Laut einer am Mittwoch veröffentlichten Umfrage von Nachrichtenagenturen waren für 56 Prozent der Wähler*innen die Themen Datenzentren und künstliche Intelligenz ein entscheidender Faktor für ihr Votum. Viele demokratische Kandidaten warben damit, den Bau von Rechenzentren stärker zu regulieren. In drei der Bundesstaaten, die die Demokraten den Republikanern bei den Senatswahlen abgenommen haben, gibt es besonders viele geplante Datenzentren: Texas, Ohio, Iowa.
In den USA sind sie nicht nur wegen ihres hohen Energie- und Flächenverbrauchs umstritten, sondern auch wegen der Luftverschmutzung. Aus Mangel an Netzkapazitäten bauten die Betreiber vielfach Gaskraftwerke zur Stromversorgung in die Nähe.
Das hat auch einen negativen Klimaeffekt. Nach einer Untersuchung der Umweltorganisation Sierra Club verursacht die Energieerzeugung für die derzeit in den USA bis 2030 geplanten Datenzentren 618 Millionen Tonnen CO2. Zum Vergleich: Deutschland verursachte im vergangenen Jahr 649 Millionen Tonnen. Vielerorts scheiterten US-Rechenzentrumsprojekte an örtlichen Protesten der Bevölkerung, allein 45 waren es im zweiten Quartal 2026.
Unter anderem die Forderung des demokratischen Senators Bernie Sanders nach einem US-weiten Moratorium für den Bau von Rechenzentren sorgte am Donnerstag und Freitag für Unruhe an den Börsen weltweit. Vielerorts brachen Aktien rund um die Chipbranche ein, die als Profiteure des KI-Hypes gelten.
Das war auch in Deutschland zu spüren. Der deutsche Leitindex DAX sackte am Freitag um 2,3 Prozent auf 25.706 Punkte ab. In Japan brach der Nikkei-Index in der Spitze um 7 Prozent ein, in den USA war der Index der Technologiebörse Nasdaq am Donnerstag um 5,5 Prozent abgestürzt. „Die Angst vor einer rigorosen KI-Regulierung nach dem Erdrutschsieg der US-Demokraten löste an der Wall Street und in Asien regelrechte Panik aus“, sagte ein Analyst zur Nachrichtenagentur Reuters. Bereits im Vorfeld der Wahlen hätten KI-Aktien an Anziehungskraft verloren.

Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.title: Neurologie | Gehirngesund durch Prävention
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.author: Ulrike Henning
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120371.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Neurologie
Gehirngesund durch Prävention
Viele Risiken für Erkrankungen wie Demenz oder Schlaganfall lassen sich beeinflussen, aber die Umsetzung im Alltag fällt häufig schwer.
Die Familie nicht mehr erkennen, die Adresse vergessen und den Heimweg nicht mehr finden, sich in den Zeiten verirren – das kann eine Demenz mit sich bringen, und das fürchten Menschen in Deutschland besonders. Ebenso wie einen Schlaganfall, der in vielen Fällen eine Behinderung zur Folge hat. Unter anderem Lähmungen sowie Schluck- und Sprechstörungen können dabei sein.
Was die Furcht befeuert, ist der mit den Erkrankungen verbundene Verlust der Gehirngesundheit. Das heißt, dass Lernen, Kreativität, Produktivität und soziale Teilhabe schwieriger oder gar nicht mehr möglich sind. Aber das Risiko für beide Krankheiten ließe sich durch Prävention deutlich senken.
Dieser Präventionsgewinn ist nicht neu, aber er ist immer besser belegt. Darauf machten jetzt Neurologen im Zusammenhang mit dem Kongress der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Neurologie in Berlin in dieser Woche aufmerksam. Gerade für den Schlaganfall liegen mehrere Studien vor.
In zwei neueren unter diesen lag der Einfluss von Risikofaktoren auf die Krankheitslast bei gut 80 Prozent. Die Interstroke-Studie von 2016 mit Teilnehmern aus 32 Ländern zeigte, dass zehn beeinflussbare Risikofaktoren mit 90 Prozent des Schlaganfallrisikos assoziiert waren. Die Ergebnisse beschreiben allerdings das Präventionspotenzial auf Bevölkerungsebene, schränkt DGN-Präsidentin Daniela Berg ein. Das heißt, so die Neurologin vom Universitätsklinikum Schleswig-Holstein in Kiel, dass hier nicht die Wahrscheinlichkeit beschrieben wird, mit der sich ein Schlaganfall im Einzelfall verhindern lässt.
Zu den genannten Risiken für einen Schlaganfall zählen Bluthochdruck, Bewegungsmangel, zu hohe Blutfettwerte, Rauchen, Diabetes mellitus, ungesunde Ernährung, übermäßiger Alkoholkonsum und Vorhofflimmern. Viele dieser Faktoren tragen aber genauso dazu bei, dass das Risiko etwa für Herz-Kreislauf-Erkrankungen oder Krebs steigt. Es kann also nicht falsch sein, sich damit zu befassen und vielleicht die eine oder andere Gewohnheit infrage zu stellen. Die eher medizinischen Risikofaktoren gehören unter ärztliche Kontrolle.
Es bleibt aber etwas, das als individuelle »Lebensstildissonanz« bezeichnet werden kann. Den Begriff prägten Neurologin Berg und ihr Team selbst: die Lücke zwischen dem genauen Wissen über einen gesunden Lebensstil und der Alltagsrealität. Folgt man dem Konzept, scheitern gesundheitliche Vorsätze quasi aus biologischen Gründen.
Für Berg geht es deshalb darum, die Gehirntätigkeit besser zu verstehen: »Das Gehirn braucht Zeit zum Lernen. Und es kann auch lernen.« Aus der Evolution des Menschen stamme die Erfahrung, dass energiereiche Ernährung fast immer nötig war – und Joggen eher nicht. »Wer Prävention will, muss sie ermöglichen«, sagt die Neurologin und fordert hierfür auch politische Unterstützung. Weil das Belohnungssystem im Gehirn schneller sei und das Denken länger brauche, müssten Menschen eher in Sachen Prävention ermutigt werden, als ihnen nur die Schuld am falschen Verhalten zuzuschreiben.
Prävention ist aber nicht nur Verhalten, das dazu beitragen soll, Krankheiten zu verhindern. Gesundheitswissenschaftler und Mediziner haben neben dieser Primärprävention zwei weitere Dimensionen eingeführt: Die Sekundärprävention meint hier die Früherkennung von Krankheiten, wozu etwa regelmäßige Blutdruckmessungen oder Krebsfrüherkennung mit verschiedenen Verfahren gehören. Bei der Tertiärprävention wird versucht, bei bereits vorhandenen Krankheiten Folgeschäden oder Rückfälle zu minimieren – das kann unter anderem in einer Reha erfolgen.
Der letztgenannte Bereich ist bei der Versorgung von Schlaganfällen wichtig. Schon jetzt leben in Deutschland 1,5 Millionen Menschen, die einen solchen überlebt haben; 70.000 Patienten kommen jährlich mit einer Neudiagnose dazu. Götz Thomalla, Neurologe und leitend am Hamburger Universitätsklinikum Eppendorf tätig, sieht als Problem hier, dass es in der Nachsorge noch zu wenig Kontinuität gibt. »Es gibt hier mehrere Ansprechpartner, viele Themen und mehrere Fachdisziplinen und Berufe, die beteiligt sind, dazu die Sektorenaufteilung – Krankenhäuser, Reha-Einrichtungen und die ambulante Versorgung.«
Einen Unterschied in der Nachsorge macht wohl auch, wie aktiv sich Patienten (oder auch Angehörige) um die nötigen Therapien kümmern können. Jedenfalls ist bei Schlaganfällen wichtig, weitere Ereignisse dieser Art zu vermeiden, und bei der Reduzierung der Folgen auch den psychischen Teil nicht zu vernachlässigen.
Die Nachsorge ist umso wichtiger, als dass es neue Erkenntnisse gibt, dass nach einem Schlaganfall Entzündungsprozesse in den Blutgefäßen zunehmen. Diese Entzündungen auch im Gehirngewebe selbst könnten über Jahrzehnte nachwirken. Sie könnten zu kognitiven Beeinträchtigungen führen – bis hin zur Demenz. Somit wäre eine Minimierung dieser Vorgänge wiederum nützlich dafür, Folgeerkrankungen zu vermeiden.
Wie das ganz konkret aussehen kann, zeigt eine neue Kampagne der DGN: Prävention wirkt. Hier wurden nicht nur nützliche Informationen zu Parkinson, Demenz und Schlaganfall zusammengetragen, sondern es berichten auch Patienten über ihren Krankheitsverlauf.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.title: Amtrak's Penn Station plan could funnel taxpayer money to new venue for James Dolan
https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.text:
Amtrak’s proposal to rebuild Penn Station could lead to heaps of taxpayer money being used to subsidize a new entertainment venue for the Madison Square Garden Company.
The plan to overhaul the station calls for Amtrak to purchase the Infosys Theater at MSG, demolish it and convert the site into a grand light-filled entrance on Eighth Avenue. Previous estimates have put the cost of purchasing the theater at hundreds of millions of dollars.
During an investor’s call Wednesday, MSG’s chief financial executive David Collins fielded questions about the potential sale of the theater, which has a capacity for roughly 5,600 people. He noted the move would take away a revenue source for the company — but said the money from the sale could be used to fund a new venue, potentially in the five boroughs.
“The primary way for us to minimize the tax leakage would be to reinvest all of the potential proceeds in another domestic venue. … I would say that we are not limited to just the New York City market,” Collins said. “However, I would also say that New York City is our core operating market and with us having one less theater here, we would definitely most likely look to the New York market first.”
He did not say whether the Garden would look to buy an existing venue or build a new one.
In recent years James Dolan, the billionaire owner of MSG and the New York Knicks, has struck gold with his Las Vegas Sphere. That cutting-edge venue has a capacity for 20,000 people and has been so successful that Dolan is building another sphere at National Harbor on the Potomac River, just outside of Washington, D.C.
Amtrak special adviser Andy Byford, who is leading the redesign effort of Penn Station, has repeatedly said that the national railroad is looking to get us much money in federal grants and before potentially seeking funding from New York and New Jersey. That means if Amtrak's plan goes through, taxpayers would likely be on the hook to purchase the Infosys Theater — and in turn to fund MSG’s new theater elsewhere.
Representatives for MSG and Amtrak did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
MTA Chair Janno Lieber has repeatedly criticized Amtrak’s plan and has declined to sign on as an official partner for the rebuild, stating the work could interrupt Long Island Rail Road service at the station. Lieber has said Amtrak has refused to disclose the full details of its plan unless the New York transit agency agrees to join the project.
The MTA was planning its own rebuild of Penn Station — which is owned by Amtrak — until President Donald Trump took over the project last year. Lieber in 2023 said he did not want taxpayer money to be used to purchase the theater, saying he thought “the Dolans have gotten a pretty good deal from New Yorkers so far.”
While the MTA’s plan was under consideration that year, a private developer with ASTM Group estimated at a public hearing that the cost of purchasing Infosys was “substantially less” than $1 billion. The estimate came from Peter Cipriano, who is now CEO of Penn Transformation Partners, which was selected by the federal government to redevelop the rail hub.
Dolan supported Trump’s 2024 election campaign and this year backed Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, who lost this week to Gov. Kathy Hochul.
MSG’s latest Securities and Exchange Commission filing lists the redevelopment of Penn Station as having a potential impact on its financial outlook, including the “potential transfer” of the Infosys Theater.
The Trump administration has set a tight deadline to begin work on the redevelopment of Penn Station. Officials said they expect shovels in the ground by the end of 2027.
Collins said during MSG’s investor call that executives “expect ample time to determine the appropriate path forward” on selling the theater.

https://hyperallergic.com/pablo-helguera.title: Pablo Helguera to Helm the New School’s Vera List Center
https://hyperallergic.com/pablo-helguera.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/pablo-helguera.text:
Pablo Helguera to Helm the New School’s Vera List Center
Upon his appointment, the artist reflected on the urgency he feels to “make sense of rapidly unfolding events, question prevailing narratives, and imagine alternative futures.”
Artist, educator, and writer Pablo Helguera has been appointed as the new director of the New School's Vera List Center for Art and Politics (VLC), succeeding Senior Director and Chief Curator Carin Kuoni, who steered the arts-driven research center for 22 years. Helguera was also tapped as the director of the university's art collection, which consists of over 2,000 postwar and contemporary works.
Having entered the new role this Monday, November 2, Helguera takes the reins after six years of serving as an assistant professor and director of the Arts Management and Entrepreneurship graduate program at the New School's College of Performing Arts. Helguera was previously the director of adult and academic programs at the Museum of Modern Art for over a decade.
As an artist, Helguera centers social engagement through public performance and installation, archival findings, pedagogical practices, and traditional media. Among his most famous projects is “The School of Panamerican Unrest” (2006), a cross-continental road trip from Anchorage, Alaska, to Ushuaia, capital of Argentina's southernmost Tierra del Fuego province, that culminated in over 100 public engagement events across 25 cities in 20 countries. Helguera is also known for developing Librería Donceles, a traveling used bookstore with thousands of Spanish-language texts that visited 13 countries.
The social, ideological, and cultural frameworks of language are prominent themes that Helguera explores in his practice, which coalesces with his roles in education and public programming. He became a Guggenheim Fellow in 2008, and additional recognitions include support from the Franklin Furnace Archive, Art Matters, and Blade of Grass; a Creative Capital grant; and an honorary doctorate from the Kansas City Art Institute.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.title: Republicans Are Desperate to Pretend They Never Supported the War With Iran
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.author: Alain Stephens
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.text:
Alain Stephens is an investigative reporter covering gun violence, arms trafficking, and federal law enforcement.
To say that Americans were pissed off is an understatement.
On Tuesday, Democrats didn’t just seize control of both houses of Congress. They redrew the American political map, capturing offices that had remained reliably Republican for generations, from the Deep South to Kansas and Texas. The Lone Star State alone, with its 40 Electoral College votes, now raises the possibility of a seismic shift in the calculus of future presidential elections.
The sheer scale of the historic Democratic surge delivered an unmistakable rebuke to America’s supposedly populist president. The message was clear and simple: We do not like you.
Much of Americans’ rapid disillusionment with the Trump administration can be traced to a single word — Iran — and the cascading economic hardships Americans have endured as the war has dragged on.
For the GOP, the threat is existential. The war has gone from a Republican loyalty test to a political albatross for many of its former supporters, one that many Republicans are now jettisoning themselves away from to salvage their own political futures.
By Wednesday, it had become the chief explanation for the party’s sweeping electoral defeat, with Vice President JD Vance declaring unequivocally on X that “the reason we lost is the war.”
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he wrote. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Coming from Trump’s own vice president, it was a striking about-face.
The tirade also raised an awkward question ahead of the 2028 presidential race: How does a potential successor to the MAGA mantle campaign against a war waged by his own administration?
Trump, however, has not gone nearly as far as his VP. Although the president acknowledged the war hurt Republicans, he still defended it on its merits. Speaking with reporters Wednesday after expounding at length about his White House ballroom, Trump said, “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it.”
Where Did All the Warmongers Go?
But on the campaign trail, Republicans were not completely oblivious to Americans’ collective frustration with the Iran war.
In September, ABC News identified 17 Republican lawmakers and candidates who had called for ending the war through public statements or votes. Much of the pressure came in competitive midterms races, as the conflict’s effects on oil, diesel, and fertilizer prices reached American households.
In Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson called for a “successful and immediate end” to the war in September, warning that voters were paying the price at gas pumps and grocery stores. Yet she voted six times against House measures directing Trump to halt the attacks. During an October 25 ABC interview, Hinson said she would not rule out a post-election U.S. offensive and said she trusted Trump and the military to choose the right timetable. Despite the president praising her weight loss at a recent rally, tepidly breaking with Trump wasn’t enough to get Hinson over the line, and she lost to Democrat Josh Turek by 4.5 percentage points.
Michigan also had its share of Iran backtrackers. Republican Senate hopeful Mike Rogers described Iran as an “imminent threat” when the bombing began on February 28. In May, he called the conflict a potential “win-win-win.” But with the midterms fast approaching, Rogers released a campaign ad declaring “the war with Iran needs to end” quickly and warned Michigan families could no longer afford the economic fallout.
Rep. John James, the Republican candidate for Michigan governor, likewise praised Trump’s use of force early in the war, saying the president “had the balls” to “assure the survival and success of liberty.” He voted against six House war-powers resolutions, including as recently as September. Days after that vote, he said the war needed to wrap up “quickly.” He went on to declare in an interview, “the position has always been, I hate war.”
Both Rogers and James lost their races.
Even Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a possible contender in the Republican Party’s next presidential contest who could reportedly be up for Pete Hegseth’s job, warned Monday that the war was a “big, big drag” on his party. Trump, DeSantis pointed out, campaigned against another Middle Eastern war. Now voters are dealing with higher fuel costs, and Republicans who refuse to acknowledge the connection are “gaslighting” them. But back in spring, DeSantis defended the strikes on Iranian leadership, describing its government as “a fanatical, apocalyptic, militant Islamist regime.”
The polling helps explain the Republican panic. An Associated Press poll found roughly 6 in 10 voters believed the U.S. made a “wrong decision” in attacking Iran. And it’s not as though Republicans weren’t warned. A handful within their own ranks, including Thomas Massie and Rand Paul, opposed the war from its earliest days and backed efforts to rein it in. But those criticisms seemed to fall on deaf ears.
A Hasty Retreat
With plenty of blame to go around, the criticism has gone beyond candidates and into the conservative media ecosystem.
During the network’s primetime Election Night coverage, Fox News host Sean Hannity told his colleague Bret Baier that the results would have been different without the Iran war. Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the war a betrayal of America First principles, demanded new Republican leadership, and labeled the conflict a “catastrophically stupid decision.”
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene called Trump breaking his promise not to start another foreign war his “biggest betrayal” and said “Americans are fed up with it.”
Other commentators placed the responsibility squarely on Trump himself for sucking his own party into a political quagmire. In The Federalist, senior editor John Daniel Davidson blamed the party’s collapse on Trump’s undermining of a GOP coalition built upon rejecting the interventionist politics of the George W. Bush era.
Some prominent Republican operatives are sure to be thrown under the bus by their own party in the retreat. The first to get the boot may be none other than Hegseth, America’s chief “warfighter,” who has been one of the war’s most enthusiastic, and public, cheerleaders. The defense secretary responded to the criticisms in a nearly six-minute-long video posted online on Thursday, in which he seemed to make the case for keeping his job, touting his elimination of the “Marxist ideology” of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and tarring transgender troops as having a “mental illness.”
“Regardless of how people care about the war, which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon, we need to continue, as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military,” he said. “This is not about me, but of course, the other side, in case you noticed, they’re obsessed.”
Already facing growing Republican dissatisfaction and a ballooning roster of disgruntled and ousted senior military officials, Hegseth now faces the prospect of investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress and an impeachment effort led by Massie. And while Trump has so far publicly defended his defense secretary, he has also reportedly consulted allies about whether to hit the ejector seat on Pete.
But while Republicans and Democrats read polls and calculate the political currency of war and economic hardship, the human cost cannot be measured in votes. At least 3,636 people had been killed in Iran as of early April, including 1,701 civilians and 254 children, according to human rights monitors. More fighting has followed and likely driven that number far higher.
At least 23 American service members have died in operations connected to the war, with almost 900 wounded by enemy fire. But these are estimates, and the Trump administration has worked to actively obfuscate the true casualty rates of the war. These are not electoral statistics. They are lives lost, families shattered, and consequences that will endure long after administrations swap office spaces.
For Republicans now scrambling to distance themselves from a deeply unpopular war, the political consequences may be harder to escape than their own voting records. Tuesday’s results show voters are increasingly willing to hold politicians accountable for needless wars, and the suffering inherited from them.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
