https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Às vésperas do Dia Internacional pela Eliminação da Violência contra as Mulheres, celebrado no dia 25 deste mês, dados da Defensoria Pública do Distrito Federal (DPDF) mostram como a violência doméstica pode continuar mesmo depois do fim de um relacionamento. Disputas pela guarda dos filhos, falta de pagamento de pensão alimentícia e retenção de patrimônio estão entre as situações enfrentadas por mulheres que procuram assistência jurídica no DF.
Entre janeiro e julho de 2026, o Núcleo de Promoção e Defesa dos Direitos das Mulheres (Nudem) realizou 6.683 atendimentos e protocolou 276 ações judiciais. Do total de atendimentos, 1.945 foram relacionados ao Direito de Família, equivalente a 29,1%. Outros 1.628 envolveram medidas protetivas de urgência e situações de descumprimento, correspondentes a 24,4%.
Os dados fazem parte do relatório de atividades do Nudem, divulgado pela Defensoria nesta sexta-feira (6). O levantamento mostra que o enfrentamento à violência também passa por garantir condições de sobrevivência, autonomia financeira, moradia e proteção aos filhos.
Para a coordenadora do Nudem e defensora pública Rafaela Mitre, as demandas acompanhadas mostram que a violência está associada a diferentes situações de vulnerabilidade. “Os casos apresentados no relatório mostram como a violência se combina com falta de renda, insegurança de moradia, adoecimento e ausência de apoio para cuidar dos filhos. Por isso, proteger uma mulher também significa criar condições para que ela possa se sustentar e reconstruir sua vida com segurança”, explica a coordenadora.
Violência que continua
Entre os atendimentos relacionados ao Direito de Família, as ações de alimentos lideraram os registros, com 503 casos, seguidas pelas demandas de guarda, com 502. Também foram contabilizados 235 atendimentos relacionados a divórcio, 142 a união estável e 123 a execução de alimentos.
Na avaliação de Mitre, essas demandas não podem ser compreendidas apenas como conflitos familiares. “As demandas de guarda, pensão alimentícia e divórcio são parte fundamental da proteção das mulheres, porque a violência pode continuar mesmo depois da separação. Os vínculos familiares e econômicos podem ser utilizados para praticar novas violências, como deixar de pagar a pensão para comprometer a subsistência da mulher e dos filhos, usar a convivência com as crianças para ameaçar ou vigiar a mãe, reter patrimônio ou criar obstáculos ao encerramento da relação”, afirma.
A defensora destaca que a formalização do divórcio e a regulamentação da guarda, da convivência e da pensão alimentícia são medidas importantes para reduzir os espaços de controle e estabelecer regras que considerem a segurança da mulher e dos filhos.
O relatório também apresenta casos acompanhados pelo Nudem que ilustram a relação entre violência patrimonial e dependência econômica. Em um deles, uma mulher que havia criado uma empresa de locação de brinquedos infantis teve equipamentos e veículos retidos pelo ex-companheiro, que descumpriu uma medida protetiva patrimonial. Os bens eram a principal fonte de renda da família.
Sem recursos para manter a própria subsistência, a mulher sofreu um Acidente Vascular Cerebral (AVC) enquanto relatava as violências na Delegacia da Mulher. A Defensoria ingressou com pedido de alimentos compensatórios. A liminar concedeu o pagamento provisório de 1,5 salário mínimo mensal, e a decisão foi proferida cinco dias depois do ajuizamento da ação.
Dependência econômica
O relatório aponta que a atuação do Nudem envolve demandas que ultrapassam o atendimento jurídico. Entre janeiro e julho, foram registrados 325 atendimentos psicossociais e 308 encaminhamentos à rede de proteção e a outros setores.
A equipe própria do núcleo é composta por uma assistente social e uma psicóloga, que trabalham de forma integrada à assistência jurídica. Entre as atividades estão acolhimento, avaliação de vulnerabilidades, identificação de fatores de risco, elaboração de relatórios técnicos e encaminhamento para serviços de saúde, assistência social e acolhimento institucional.
Para Rafaela Mitre, a dificuldade de romper o ciclo de violência está relacionada à combinação de diferentes fatores, que muitas vezes atingem as mulheres simultaneamente. “Os obstáculos envolvem medo, ameaças, dependência econômica, sofrimento psicológico, isolamento e preocupação com os filhos. Muitas mulheres precisam enfrentar tudo isso ao mesmo tempo, sem moradia segura, renda própria ou uma rede de apoio”, diz a defensora.
A defensora também chama atenção para as formas de violência que não envolvem necessariamente agressões físicas. “É fundamental ampliar a compreensão de que a violência não começa com a agressão física. Humilhações, isolamento, controle do dinheiro, vigilância e ameaças muitas vezes são naturalizados ou confundidos com ciúme e cuidado, mas já são formas de violência e podem se agravar ao longo do tempo”, afirma.
Rede de proteção e acesso aos serviços
Além da assistência individual, o Nudem desenvolve ações para aproximar os serviços de proteção das mulheres em regiões periféricas e rurais. Uma das iniciativas é o projeto Entrelace, realizado desde março de 2025, que já alcançou aproximadamente 500 mulheres no Distrito Federal.
O projeto promove rodas de conversa, atividades de educação em direitos, orientação jurídica e atendimento psicossocial. As ações são organizadas a partir de demandas identificadas por lideranças comunitárias, com participação de instituições parceiras. A iniciativa busca facilitar o acesso à informação sobre a Lei Maria da Penha, medidas protetivas, direitos familiares e autonomia econômica. O núcleo também realiza capacitações para profissionais da Defensoria e da rede de atendimento, com o objetivo de qualificar o acolhimento.
Para a coordenadora, um dos principais desafios é garantir que os diferentes serviços funcionem de maneira integrada e que os encaminhamentos resultem em atendimento efetivo.
“A mulher não pode ser responsável por articular a própria proteção, percorrendo sozinha diferentes instituições para conseguir segurança, moradia, assistência social, saúde e orientação jurídica”, afirma Rafaela Mitre.
O relatório também registra o monitoramento de decisões de indeferimento de medidas protetivas e reclamações relacionadas ao atendimento. A partir desse acompanhamento, o núcleo busca identificar obstáculos à proteção, aperfeiçoar os pedidos judiciais e reunir informações para fundamentar a atuação institucional.
A avaliação de risco é outra frente de trabalho. O Nudem utiliza o Formulário Nacional de Avaliação de Risco (Fonar) para identificar fatores associados ao feminicídio e à reincidência da violência, subsidiando pedidos de proteção e estratégias de segurança construídas com as mulheres atendidas.
“As medidas protetivas salvam vidas. Garantir sua efetividade exige acesso rápido, avaliação cuidadosa do risco, acompanhamento e resposta aos descumprimentos. Essa proteção deve estar articulada às políticas de moradia, renda, saúde e cuidado com os filhos, criando condições concretas para romper o ciclo de violência”, conclui a coordenadora do Nudem e defensora pública Rafaela Mitre.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Whitney Museum selects a staff curator and a stage director to lead 2028 biennial
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Benjamin Sutton
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Whitney Museum of American Art has selected Meg Onli, a curator at the museum, and Zack Winokur, a choreographer and director for the stage, to curate the 2028 edition of the Whitney Biennial. It is due to open in March 2028.
“Every Whitney Biennial springs from a distinct curatorial alchemy,” Scott Rothkopf, the Whitney’s director, said in a statement. “Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art. Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial.”
The 2024 Whitney Biennial: our review
Onli is one of the Whitney’s star curators, having joined the institution as a curator-at-large in 2023, then as a curator in 2024. She co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, titled Even Better Than the Real Thing, with fellow Whitney curator Chrissie Iles. Most recently she co-curated the museum’s current Roy Lichtenstein retrospective (until 10 May 2027).
“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about,” Onli said in a statement. “I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead.”
Winokur’s work spans dance, music, visual art, opera and theatre. He is the co-founder and artistic director of the performing arts collective AMOC* (American Modern Opera Company), which last year staged a five-week takeover of the Lincoln Center campus on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. He was previously the artistic director of Little Island, a park and cultural event space designed by Heatherwick Studio and MNLA that rises out of the Hudson River not far from the Whitney. His projects for the stage and screen have included directing productions at Opera Philadelphia and the Santa Fe Opera, and working on the expanded version of The Wizard of Oz currently showing at Sphere in Las Vegas.
“I’m honoured to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur said in a statement. “Our shared desire to centre objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring. As an artist, what excites me most is being in service to other artists, and I’m delighted to have the opportunity to do so in the context of the Whitney.”
The 2026 Whitney Biennial, which was organised by staff curators Marcela Guerrero and Drew Sawyer, closed in October. It was seen by more than 550,000 visitors, according to the museum’s figures, around 75% of whom identified as either Millennials or Gen Z, making it the youngest audience since the Whitney started tracking visitors’ ages.
The exhibition’s 2026 edition was also remarkably controversy-free, though the exhibition is often a lightning rod for debates, protests and political statements. The 2019 edition was led by Whitney curators Jane Panetta and Rujeko Hockley, and came to be known colloquially as the “tear gas biennial” due to weekly protests and participating artists’ threatened withdrawals over the Whitney’s vice chairman at the time, Warren Kanders, who was the chief executive of Safariland, a defense and security contractor that manufactured tear gas canisters that had been deployed against asylum-seekers at the Mexico-US border, among other materials. Kanders eventually resigned from the museum’s board; he is currently the chairman and chief executive of Cadre Holdings, a Florida-based manufacturer of security and law-enforcement equipment.
The 2017 Whitney Biennial, which was co-curated by Christopher Y. Lew and Mia Locks, was largely overshadowed by the wide-ranging debate over a single painting in the exhibition: Dana Schutz’s Open Casket (2016), in which the artist portrayed the famous image from 1955 of 14-year-old Emmett Till lying in an open casket following his brutal abduction, mutilation and murder. The artist Hannah Black wrote an open letter criticising the work’s inclusion in the biennial and calling for its destruction, sparking protests inside and outside the museum and arguments about censorship, identity and cultural appropriation.
The 2028 Whitney Biennial will be the 83rd edition of the exhibition, which started out as a series of medium-specific exhibitions before becoming the Whitney Annual in 1937, then transitioning to its every-other-year format in 1973. It remains the most closely watched recurring exhibition of contemporary art in the Americas.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.title: President Trump Moves to Make Oval Office a Public Monument
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.text:
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday seeking to designate the Oval Office and the adjacent Cabinet Room national monuments, saying that the new designation would prevent future administrations from making major modifications without Congressional approval. In his second term, Trump made it a priority to redecorate both, turning the previously restrained presidential working spaces into extravagantly gilded interiors in the style of Louis XIV.
In the wake of this week’s midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered historic defeats, Trump appears to be self-soothing by focusing on the many renovation projects he has initiated at the White House and across Washington, D.C. At the White House, in addition to his makeover of the Oval Office, these have included the construction of a granite helipad on the White House’s South Lawn and, most notoriously, the demolition of the building’s East Wing to make way for a 90,000-square-foot, $600 million ballroom. (On Wednesday, in his first public appearance after Tuesday’s Republican wipeout, Trump led a media tour of the ballroom construction site.)
Around the nation’s capital, Trump has embarked on a fraught, $14 million repair of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, begun the redevelopment of a popular public golf course by cutting down hundreds of trees, and proposed a 250-foot-high triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Apparently worried that incoming Democrats would block construction of the arch, Trump asked for hastened approval of the project, which was granted Wednesday by his hand-picked planning commission; that evening, Judge Tanya Chutkan stopped construction for fourteen days.
It is not clear how designating the Oval Office a national monument will prevent another president from simply revising, or ignoring, the designation—the White House is already designated a National Historic Landmark, which has not stopped Trump from building his ballroom. Nevertheless, speaking from the now gold-saturated Oval Office, Trump told reporters, “When completed, and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it’ll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.title: New York Republicans Are Ripping Each Other to Shreds
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.author: Holly Pretsky
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.text:
New York City's Republican of the Moment Curtis Sliwa is DEFINITELY NOT demoralized by the absolute shellacking his party got on Tuesday.
"I view this complete tsunami, this blue tsunami, especially when it relates to the 62 counties of New York, as Liberation Day for Republicans who no longer feel that if they're not MAGA, they don't exist," Sliwa told Hell Gate. "You know, 'We're RINOs.' Well, guess what? I'm a proud RINO." (In case you've never seen Fox News, that's a Trumpworld pejorative that stands for "Republican In Name Only.")
The losses went far beyond GOP candidate Bruce Blakeman's double-digit defeat by Governor Kathy Hochul. Republicans lost at least six state Senate seats, at least seven Assembly seats, a major congressional seat in the Hudson Valley, all three statewide races by double-digit margins, and they barely hung onto a seat in the deep red North Country with a pretty embarrassing candidate.
Still, Sliwa's feeling…optimistic.
"This is a perfect opportunity for Republicans to organize and mobilize. The people united will never be defeated," he said. "That's a phrase that is very left-wing, very progressive. But this is what Republicans, if they want to save their party, must begin to do: Stop complaining, stop moaning and groaning. Your whole campaign was to basically call Zohran [Mamdani], you know, attaching him to Hochul, a communist, a socialist, a jihadist, and an Islamist. I don't even think they understand what a communist is. I don't think they understand what an Islamist is. But then again, they just attached it all together, and when all was said and done, Zohran helped Hochul, and Trump helped destroy Team Blakeman and other Republicans who were running under that MAGA mantra."

“Across the line, then in line, then out of line: This was my progression through WAR”
MILES GREENBERG ONCE walked without respite on a conveyor belt for twenty-four consecutive hours, save for a twenty-three-minute loss of consciousness around hour eighteen. This durational performance, Oysterknife, 2020, had been an outlier in the Canadian artist’s body of work, its staging and premise owing less to the canon of Western sculpture Greenberg typically engages than to the conventions of performance art itself (think of Senga Nengudi and David Hammons’s collaborations, or Pope.L’s crawls). It had been an outlier, that is, until the debut of WAR at the former Eighty-Sixth Street Cinema on October 29, Greenberg’s first performance in New York City in more than three years and his largest to date. Entailing forty performers walking for six continuous hours, it was also the first piece since Oysterknife to feature the motorized belt.
As I passed under the marquee and into the erstwhile theater turned active construction site, I was already expecting Greenberg to deviate from the sculptural sensibility for which he is best known. “It does what a painting does,” the artist had written in announcement of WAR on his Instagram, setting his iron sights on sculpture’s sister art, away from things like Roman marbles. In my mock Michael Fried voice, I thought, “Surely it does what a bad painting does”—though at that point, I did not yet know that Greenberg had taken as his model precisely the kind of French history painting that Fried disparaged for being overly posed, chief among such works Jacques-Louis David’s The Intervention of the Sabine Women, 1799. Armed with the absorption/theatricality paradigm, I was simply curious to discover how Greenberg would bring painting and performance together in this crumbling cinema.
I went up some stairs, through a kind of foyer done up with an open bar, and then entered the theater proper to join a crowd of onlookers beneath the projection booth soffit, all gazing out at the spectacle occupying the rest of the hall. I saw four rows of ten semi-undressed performers, two flanking a central runway, each performer striding barefoot on a conveyor belt. At the far end of the room, a mirrored backdrop extended the phalanxes indefinitely, and where the runway intersected with the backdrop was an LED screen glowing a cold white light. A stone lay directly in front of the screen. Altogether, the arrangement formed a kind of tableau vivant: Greenberg had staged two opposing factions on the verge of battle. I noticed the music next, an original score by Chino Amobi composed of atmospheric chanting, intermittent sirens, and explosive percussion like something out of a violent video game. Every ten or so minutes, in phase with the looping score, the white light flashed red. This was Greenberg’s cue to break ranks, hop off his treadmill, and strut fiercely down the runway in surveillance of his company. Throughout the six hours, he acted as an overseer.
There was more to describe—for instance, the team of stagehands running around in boiler suits, switching out exhausted performers like spent bullets, or the various video cameras and photographers documenting every detail—but what struck me was the audience. For a start, it was the kind of fashionable crowd that made me keenly aware that I should have worn more black. This sense of being out of place was heightened by the fact that, little by little, people were stepping out onto the runway, crossing the implicit proscenium between performance and world. They would walk to the stone and back, gawk at the performers, and maybe take some photos, all the while looking terribly self-conscious themselves. If the timing was right, the light would flash red and Greenberg would have to march through the people clotting his path.
It took a tequila or two from the bar to steel me for a turn down the runway. When I reentered the theater, Greenberg was patrolling the rows of performers with a 3D scanner in hand, wielding it over body after body, capturing the shapes of future sculptures. With the thought in mind that the word per-formance signifies a passage through form, I set foot into the scene. Suddenly, the opposition between absorption/theatricality seemed utterly to dissolve, if only for a moment. The sensation was something like I imagine it would be to walk through Walter De Maria’s Mile-Long Parallel Walls in the Desert, 1961–63, when the visual field suddenly flattens into a diagram of linear perspective. “I wanted it to feel like you were standing in a gigantic oil painting,” as Greenberg put it to me the following day. “It’s about the physical relationship between the viewer and the artwork, being able to traverse this straight through the panel.” I found the extent to which WAR was successful along this line to hinge on the stone at the end of the runway. Walking directly toward it, straining to keep my focus on its silhouette against the effulgent screen behind, it appeared as a vanishing point, impossibly distant, everything converging there.
And then the illusion was gone, for I was standing there myself, looking back through the rows of performers to the crowd I had abandoned. Now among the all-Black cast, my pallor felt a great deal more conspicuous than my clothing had at the other end of the room, especially as I had to step out of the way of Greenberg’s patrol. Indeed, the knowledge of being an object in everyone’s sight was so overwhelming, I could not be certain that I had ever really felt absorbed into the scene, even as I played an active part in it. Across the line, then in line, then out of line: This was my progression through WAR, and it gave me to understand just how, in posing as painting, the boundary between presence and representation becomes an irresolvable problem: “I wrote WAR as a response to the news, but I didn’t feel like I could make an artwork about one particular conflict or genocide which doesn’t physically affect me,” Greenberg said. “This was a kind of petri dish to put the feelings that do apply to me in, and to see what happens.”
Traipsing back up the runway, I knew that neither rejoining the audience nor drinking any more tequila would dispel my confusion between definite responsibility and limited agency. After all, what could be a better emblem of this tension than the motorized belts all around, demanding as they did one step after another, only to foreclose forward movement? Compared with the Covid-era Oysterknife, though, the difference here was that WAR implicated cast, crew, and crowd equally in the performance of this confusion, even while thematizing the very difficulty of sharing it—a vital reminder, especially when getting the news or looking at a painting can feel like such a private experience.
Julian Stern is a critic who lives in New York.

https://taz.de/Ansage-der-Berliner-Links.author: Uwe Rada
https://taz.de/Ansage-der-Berliner-Links.text:
Ansage der Berliner Linkspartei: Mit Emde soll Ende sein
Die Linkspartei in Berlin beschließt, die umstrittene Abgeordnete Emde zum Verzicht ihres Mandats aufzufordern. Zusätzlich droht ihr der Fraktionsausschluss.
High Noon war es nicht, als die beiden Landesvorsitzenden der Berliner Linkspartei den Beschluss bekannt gaben, aber die Verkündung kam noch rechtzeitig für die „Tagesschau“ zur Prime Time. „Wir vertrauen ihr nicht mehr“, erklärten Kerstin Wolter und Maximilian Schirmer am Freitagabend nach einer Sitzung des Landesvorstands der Hauptstadt-Linken.
Die, der die Spitze der Landespartei nicht mehr vertraut, ist die umstrittene Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde. Mehrfach hatte sie das Existenzrecht Israels geleugnet, hat sich mit Ibrahim Ibrahim fotografieren lassen, einem Sympathisanten des Hamas-Terrors. Emde soll, das hat der Vorstand nun beschlossen, ihr Mandat als Abgeordnete der Linksfraktion im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus abgeben.
„Sie hat sich wiederholt und bewusst über unsere gemeinsamen Beschlüsse hinweggesetzt“, sagten Wolter und Schirmer am Freitag zur Begründung. Ein Mandat sei keine Ich-AG. „Mandate werden kollektiv errungen: durch die Arbeit und die Stimmen von Kandidierenden, Mitgliedern und der gesamten Partei. Daraus erwächst Verantwortung für das eigene Handeln.“ Am Ende stand die unmissverständliche Ansage der beiden Landeschefs: „Es reicht, genug ist genug.“
Der Druck auf die Linkspartei, endlich das Ende vom Emde einzuleiten, war in den vergangenen Tagen noch einmal größer geworden. In der taz hatte die Linken-Bundestagsabgeordnete Katalin Gennburg bereits am Mittwoch Emde zum Rücktritt aufgefordert. „Für mich ist ein Punkt erreicht, an dem ich denke, jetzt reicht’s“, hatte Gennburg gesagt.
Emde, die in Neukölln ein Direktmandat geholt hatte, hatte zuvor nicht nur ihre Aussage wiederholt, Staaten hätten kein Existenzrecht. Während des Parteitags am vergangenen Samstag, auf dem die Linke beschloss, Koalitionsverhandlungen mit Grünen und SPD aufzunehmen, hatte sie vor dem Tagungsort auch gegen die eigene Partei demonstriert. „Gewählt für Palästina. Verraten für den Senat“, lautete das Motto der Kritiker eines rot-grün-roten Bündnisses aus den Reihen von palästinasolidarischen Gruppen.
Eine kleine Tür bleibt offen
Zuletzt hatte sich auch noch Parteiikone Gregor Gysi zu Wort gemeldet. „Ich hoffe, dass wir sie ausschließen“, hatte Gysi im Podcast von Paul Ronzheimer gesagt. Emdes Äußerungen nannte er „antisemitisch und vor allen Dingen indiskutabel für meine Partei“.
Ob Vanessa Emde ihr Mandat tatsächlich zurückgibt, ist offen. Tut sie es nicht, könnte sie aus der Linken-Fraktion im Abgeordnetenhaus ausgeschlossen werden. Diese tagt am Dienstag. Sollte der Fraktionsvorstand beantragen, Emde aus der 44-köpfigen Fraktion rauszuwerfen, könnte am Dienstag darauf darüber abgestimmt werden. Nötig für einen Ausschluss ist eine Zweidrittelmehrheit.
Dass diese zusammenkommt, gilt inzwischen als immer wahrscheinlicher. Wie aus Kreisen der Fraktion zu hören ist, hätten einige der Abgeordneten, die neu in der Fraktion sind, sich zunächst ein eigenes Bild machen wollen. Emdes Auftritte, nicht zuletzt ihr Auftritt während des Parteitags, hätten aber viele Abgeordnete davon überzeugt, dass es keine Vertrauensgrundlage für eine Zusammenarbeit mehr gebe.
Mit der Aufforderung, ihr Mandat niederzulegen, und einem möglichen Antrag auf Ausschluss aus der Fraktion kommt die Linke auch einer Forderung der Berliner SPD entgegen. Deren Fraktions- und Landeschef Steffen Krach hatte erklärt, dass es mit Vanessa Emde als Teil der Linksfraktion kein Linksbündnis geben werde.
Allerdings haben die beiden Linken-Vorsitzenden Emde noch eine kleine Tür offengelassen. „Vanessa Emde hat eine Woche Zeit, zu uns zurückzukehren“, fügten Wolter und Schirmer hinzu. „Dazu soll sie ihren Instagram-Beitrag löschen, sich für ihren Auftritt am Rande des Parteitags entschuldigen und eine konstruktive Zusammenarbeit auf Grundlage unserer Beschlüsse zusagen.“
Ob Emde durch die Tür geht? Unwahrscheinlich.

Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.title: On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.author: Alec MacGillis
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.text:
Jacob Hawk leaned over the plastic fencing to get Vivek Ramaswamy’s attention as the Republican candidate for Ohio governor moved down the line shaking hands at the Ohio University branch campus in Chillicothe, six days before the midterm elections. Hawk held onto Ramaswamy’s hand and started trying to tell him everything he was dealing with, everything he wanted the Republican candidates gathered there to help him with.
Hawk, 39, told him that he was a self-employed landscaper who was having a hard time with the high cost of fuel. He told him that he was raising three young kids from two different moms, mostly on his own. He told him of his worries for his 9-year-old son, who was autistic and underweight and suffered from a two-year delay in brain development.
Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, nodded and offered some token reassurance and moved down the line, toward the arena where he would soon be appearing with President Donald Trump and Sen. Jon Husted and the rest of the Republican slate in a state that Trump had won by 11 percentage points two years ago, and which the party had dominated during the era of Trump. I had been at many Republican events in the state over that time, including a rally in an airplane hangar outside Dayton in March 2016, where a giant crowd had roared as Trump’s jet had rolled into view and where he had declared that he had come to save Ohio. “Our jobs are being sucked away,” he said then. “It’s unbelievable what’s happening.”
This event was different. Ten years had passed, and gone was the fierce bravado of Trump the conquering hero, bristling with retribution and promises. This rally was populated largely by the same sort of voters who had been particularly drawn to Trump all along, working-class Midwesterners who had not been engaged in politics before he came on the scene. But there were fewer of them — the campaign had chosen an arena that held only 2,000 — and their devotion had been subsumed by uncertainty. They were still with Trump, but they weren’t sure how to reconcile their own difficulties with the fact that he was the president during this trying time.
Take gas prices, which “are beating the hell out of me,” Hawk told me. He was trying his best not to hold them against Trump and his decision to go to war against Iran, instead faulting Congress for limiting domestic oil drilling. “The president has to go find oil in another country because Congress won’t let him find it in our country,” he said, overlooking the fact that Trump’s party has controlled both houses of Congress during his second term.
Nearby, Debbie Shock, a 57-year-old mail carrier, blamed the high fuel costs on “the stock exchange, the markets — they’re the ones that control it.” “We have oil right here in the U.S.,” she said. “Why are we buying it from other countries to begin with?”
Shock fit a profile I had gotten to know well in 2016: an Obama-Trump voter. She was loyal to Trump — “I like the man. Nobody’s perfect, you know what I mean?” — and told me she would never go back to Democrats now. Why not? I asked. “They’re covering up the child molestation,” she said. What did she mean by that? “I’ve heard stories about the sex trafficking. The Clintons are involved in it, Disney World, you know, all that.”
It would be easy to ridicule such murky talk, yet it was not much less coherent than what soon emerged on the arena stage, which was streamed on a large screen for the few hundred of us who were out on the lawn outside the arena. Trump has never been known for structured oratory, but it is hard to overstate the extent to which his digressive style has advanced since 2016, and to convey how surreal it is to experience firsthand, as the reality of what presidential communication has come to in 2026.
The rally opened with the customary introductory video of late-era Trump, an explicitly messianic framing: “God said, ‘I need someone who will be strong and courageous,’” the voice-over intones. “So God made Trump.”
Thus introduced, Trump opened his remarks with a lengthy disquisition on Husted’s body, which had newly become part of his routine. “I looked at Jon and studied his physique,” he cooed, after referring to his recent comments on Husted’s “ass.” “I studied the feet, the legs, the shoulders. I tapped him on the shoulder, and it was like hitting a piece of steel.”
When a protester inside the arena started shouting something — those of us outside couldn’t hear what — and was removed, Trump bid him good riddance: “Now he goes home and his boyfriend gets upset with him.”
There were protesters outside, too, and things were starting to heat up between them and the supporters. “What are you talking about, ‘boyfriend?’” shouted one protester, a young man. “He was just talking about Jon Husted’s ass! That’s not gay??”
A supporter in front of me, a bearded man in his 50s, stewed as he watched the protesters. “You’re going to see someone dropping like a bad habit,” he growled, as he started to move toward them, before being held back by the woman who was with him.
A moment later, Trump had moved on to Jeffrey Epstein, saying that the Democrats had protected him for years. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” he declared. “I was the one who was totally exonerated from him. But they use it, because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”
This set off a new round of shouting outside, as cries of “pedophiles!” flew back and forth.
Suddenly, one Trump supporter near me rushed hard at a protester and knocked him to the ground, his head landing with such a thud on the blacktop that I initially thought it might be a suppressed gunshot. Dozens of officers swarmed to the spot. Cameras flashed.
A few moments later, a couple other protesters, also young men, began railing against the war against Iran. “We’re going to be the ones sent off to die for Israel,” one shouted. “‘America First,’ and you want me to die in the Middle East?”
Trump touched on the war — “they’re getting beaten very badly” — but spent far more time on his home renovations. “The White House has to be beautiful outside, it needs that exterior plaster. The bricks were falling, the stone was broken, the monuments were coming off, the beautiful windows were cracked, it looked terrible, and I fixed it very inexpensively, and now it’s more beautiful than ever,” he said. “And President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness, who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalks, who doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing, we’d like to have granite and marble we’d like to have it look nice, you don’t use asphalt, you use asphalt for your streets. …”
On the ramble went. To the Haitians in nearby Springfield: “The town went from no crime to high crime,” but “they’re being moved out.” To a riff on Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling her a liar, in apparent reference to Acton’s having accused her stepfather of raping her when she was 12, as he was subsequently charged with doing. The ad had met with widespread opprobrium, but Trump defended Ramaswamy. “The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she is no good. … How the hell is that his problem?” To “O Canada, which has been ripping us off for years,” and Somalia, “which isn’t even a country,” and “transgender mutilization,” and his plan to rename the Strait of Hormuz for himself.
Finally, Trump ceded the stage to Husted and Ramaswamy. But by then, the lawn had emptied out as people drifted home, Jacob Hawk among them. A vendor was shouting out discount prices on his MAGA merchandise. “$10 special on hats! All the hats are $10! These are normally $25 hats. That’s a good hat for $10.”
The next day, the full Republican slate of statewide candidates appeared, sans Trump, at a small pep rally inside a former Delphi auto-parts factory in Vandalia, outside Dayton. It is an enormous building that employed more than 100 prior to its closing in 2009 and is now being used as a warehouse by a company that sells air conditioners, employing only 10 or so; Delphi announcements still remained on the bulletin boards, adding a ghostly feel.
The setting was an unintentional reminder of what Ohio has been through. Between 2000 and 2025, the state lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs, a devastation that had made it highly susceptible to Trump’s message in 2016. But Republicans have been in charge of the state since 2010, and so it was the task of the candidates gathered there, with an audience of just a few dozen, to cast the state as being on an upswing. Complicating this challenge is the fact that so much of the state’s recent growth has been concentrated in the Columbus area: countless data centers, defense contractor Anduril, a massive Intel plant under construction.
The bigger challenge, though, was the nationwide pall that hung over the event: the reality of stubbornly high inflation and high gas prices, the latter a direct consequence of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. He had stood against costly foreign entanglements when he ran in 2016, in opposition to his party’s recent record, and carried that same banner again in 2024. But another aspect of his political persona had prevailed: a heedless swagger that, in this case, had been fanned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It had led him into this drawn-out conflict that has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion.
And it had left a long row of Republican candidates standing in this giant building stacked high with made-in-China air conditioners all but pleading the small assemblage to save them from the political climate. “You can’t give up,” Husted said. “This is a Republican state, and the only way Democrats can win is if Republicans don’t vote.”
Five days later, I was in York County, Pennsylvania, which Trump had won by 25 points in 2024, and which was home to one of four Republican-held House districts targeted by Democrats. I chose to go to a precinct on the outskirts of York, thinking it would offer a diverse cross-section, in between more Democratic York proper and more Republican rural areas. But over 90 minutes of conversations, I didn’t encounter a Republican voter until I was about to call it a day.
The first person I spoke with, Bill, a 52-year-old state government employee who asked that I not use his last name for fear of losing his job, had voted for Trump three times. He hardly considered himself MAGA but was drawn in 2016 to Trump’s “drain the swamp” rhetoric and his disavowal of the war in Iraq. He voted for him again in 2020 and 2024 because he didn’t think much of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.
But on this day, Bill was coming to vote against his Republican representative, Scott Perry, because he was too “Trump adjacent.” Bill had finally had enough of Trump, especially when it came to all the revelations of self-dealing involving his family and cronies. “I will not be falling for him again,” he told me. “Drain the swamp, no wars. … It was all a lie.”
He said he couldn’t understand how Trump had gone from America First to seemingly letting the country’s foreign policy be dictated by Israel. He said that he was voting for the Democrats mainly just for the sake of “gridlock,” as deliberate blockage. “Someone’s got to stop this,” he said. “It’s getting out of control.”
Each Democratic voter I spoke with after that was coming with their own motivation for voting against the Republican slate, like the cast of “Murder on the Orient Express.”
For Annie (who also asked that I not use her last name), it was for Trump’s social-welfare cuts, which had cost her and her disabled husband $300 per month in SNAP benefits and nearly cost them their Medicaid coverage.
For Desiree Edmonds, an elementary school teacher, it was high inflation, which was translating into anxiety among the working-class children in her classroom.
For Mark Castillo, a 19-year-old ironworker, it was for the sky-high cost of diesel.
For Jacqueline Jimenez, a native Puerto Rican who worked as a home-health aide, it was for the excessive harshness of ICE arrests.
For Shiri Kramer, a warehouse worker, it was for the general meanness emanating from the administration, which made her think of her grandfather, a Jewish American who had extended mercy to German POWs during World War II. “My grandfather would be writhing right now,” she said. “Nothing happening in our country is OK.”
By night’s end, Republicans had lost this Pennsylvania district by 10 points, as well as the other three in the state and more than 40 nationwide. They had lost at least seven Senate seats, even in states where Democrats hadn’t prevailed in decades — Kansas, Texas, South Carolina. Incredibly, even Mississippi was on the verge. In Ohio, Republicans lost the race for Senate and governor — only one of the seven statewide candidates on stage at the warehouse emerged a victor — as well as two Republican-held House seats, a stark reversal in a state that had seemed to be trending away from Democrats for good. In all, Democrats flipped five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers. The Democratic popular-vote margin in congressional races nationwide was 13 percentage points — nearly double the Republican margin in their own wave years of 2010 and 1994, and approaching the scale of the historic Democratic rout in the post-Watergate election of 1974.
The particularly stunning loss of the South Carolina seat brought to mind a warning issued in May 2016 by Lindsey Graham, whose death this July left the seat vacant. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will deserve it,” Graham tweeted in 2016. For years, the Republican Party had avoided the catastrophic reckoning he warned of — through Trump’s narrow win in 2016, through the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol, through Biden’s fateful insistence on running for reelection at age 81 in 2024. Along the way, much of the party, including Graham himself, had accommodated itself to Trump. One way of looking at the 2026 results was that the warning had finally come true. The reckoning had been delayed by a decade, but it had gathered more force over time, like a boulder rolling downhill.
There was a hint of such a reckoning in the words that Bill, the three-time Trump voter, left me with in York. After he returned from voting, he bade me farewell with a parting regret.
“You see what’s going on,” he said, “and you’re like, ‘What the hell did I do?’”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Hochul Wants More Power Over State Education Dept. Amid Move to End Regents Requirement
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
New York’s slow-moving transition away from requiring Regents exams to graduate has a new critic: Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Hochul, who decisively defeated her Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman on Tuesday, has raised concerns that state education officials are moving to eliminate existing graduation exam requirements without a clear plan for what will replace them, potentially weakening the value of a New York diploma.
Those concerns have also prompted Hochul to renew her call to give the governor’s office more control of the state Education Department, which answers to a board chosen by New York lawmakers rather than the chief executive.
“People see in the articles, ‘New York State abandons Regents,’” Hochul said last week on the Max Politics Podcast. “They think I’m New York.” She added: “The buck should stop with me, given that we are the funder of education.”
Hochul’s comments come as state education officials have yet to spell out what will replace Regents exams as a graduation requirement. The class of 2027 is the last crop of students required to pass Regents exams under the state’s current timeline. The 17-member Board of Regents, which sets state education policy and selects the education commissioner, will determine what comes next.
Hochul spokesperson Jonah Allon said that the governor is concerned about “the lack of clarity about what will replace” the Regents exams. “The Board of Regents have a responsibility to preserve academic rigor and ensure clear, consistent graduation standards across the state.”
The clock is ticking. This year’s seniors generally must still pass a series of standardized Regents exams in English, math, science and social studies to graduate. But the state Education Department is developing new diploma requirements for future graduating classes. New York City officials said that for the next three years, students will only have to pass their classes to earn a diploma.
What Hochul would do with more control over state education policy remains a question mark. A spokesperson did not respond to questions about whether she thinks the Regents exams should remain in place or whether she supports alternative requirements.
Hochul has previously clashed with state education officials on other issues, including a school cellphone ban. State Education Department Commissioner Betty Rosa favored giving school districts more control to set their own policies, but Hochul pushed for a statewide approach and signed a ban into state law last year.
A spokesperson for the state Education Department did not respond to questions.
Giving the governor control could help create a stronger vision for schools across the state — and clarify who is responsible for education policymaking, supporters say.
“There is no single, clear line of accountability for the quality of education New York’s children receive,” Dan Weisberg, a former top official in New York City’s Education Department, wrote in the publication Vital City. “When a governor is clearly in charge, there’s real potential for serious leadership on education.”
There is some precedent for such a move: California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently mounted a successful push to consolidate power over state education policy.
But taking control of the Education Department comes with political challenges, too.
Hochul could face criticism of New York’s academic performance, which is middling even as the state leads the nation in education spending.
And if she moves forward with changes to graduation standards — including hands-on projects, work-based learning and dual enrollment envisioned by state officials — she would also be responsible for their consequences. Other states offer cautionary tales about how difficult such changes can be to pull off.
State lawmakers may also be reluctant to cede some of their power over state education policy to the governor.
“It’s great that the governor would like to take a more hands-on approach to education,” state Sen. John Liu told Politico. “The state Education Department is structured the way it is due to law as well as the state constitution so the governor will need to work within those confines.”
Arlen Benjamin-Gomez, executive director at the advocacy group EdTrust-New York, said it is a “big deal” that the governor is weighing in more strongly on the graduation requirement changes. Her organization recently called for a two-year pause on changes to develop a clearer vision and give schools more time to prepare.
Benjamin-Gomez emphasized that giving the governor more power could help elevate education policy issues, which received little discussion during the gubernatorial race.
“If she had control over the education system, she would be running on an education agenda that she could develop and then be held accountable to implement,” Benjamin-Gomez said.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

https://citylimits.org/new-jerseyans-acc.title: New Jerseyans Accused of Stealing NYC Rental Assistance Money, And What Else Happened This Week In Housing
https://citylimits.org/new-jerseyans-acc.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-jerseyans-acc.text:
Share This Article
Three New Jersey residents were arrested Wednesday night on charges that they stole over $1 million from New York City’s One Shot Deal program by using fraudulent identities, according to the Department of Investigation.
The city’s Department of Investigation alleges that scammers stole over $1 million from a pool of city money designated to help people facing eviction and homelessness.
The scammers used fake identities and front companies posing as landlords to swindle the city’s New York City’s Human Resources Administration (HRA), the complaint claims.
Tenants behind on rent due to hardship like the loss of a job can apply to New York’s “One Shot Deal” program, which will pay up to six months of back rent and help stave off eviction or homelessness. Allegedly, the defendants used false identities to submit 170 applications to HRA, with the agency approving 94 of them.
The agency rejected most rental assistance applications so far this year, according to Gothamist, often sending them back for resubmission.
In a statement, the Department of Social Services, which oversees HRA, said that its “integrity review process identified these suspicious applications and referred the matter to the Department of Investigation two years ago, exactly as our oversight systems are designed to do.”
The defendants—Erica Williams, Kareem Canty, and Tajizhanae Whitaker—were arrested Wednesday night in New Jersey and charged with conspiracy, wire fraud, and aggravated identity theft. The city’s Department of Investigation investigated alongside the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, which is prosecuting the case.
“These defendants allegedly manipulated sensitive personal information as well as the City’s One Shot Deal application process to fraudulently divert emergency rental assistance payments,” said DOI Commissioner Nadia Shihata in a statement.
With One Shot Deals, HRA pays landlords directly on behalf of eligible renters. The city issued 54,343 one shot deals in the last fiscal year that ended in July. The year before, the city spent $555 million on the deals, with an average of $9,700 each, according to the New York Housing Conference.
The funds were “intended to keep the most vulnerable New Yorkers in their homes,” said Shihata.
In one instance, investigators allege that Williams submitted a One Shot Deal application from her home IP address in New Jersey. The application listed an address in Rego Park, Queens and included copies of a birth certificate and passport, “belonging to a certain individual that was purportedly Applicant-2 but in fact belonged to someone else,” the charging documents read.
The applicant, who prosecutors allege was Williams, listed the property manager as ALC Development LLC. But the LLC does not own or operate any housing in New York City, according to investigators, and was controlled by Williams. In June 2022, HRA sent seven checks totaling $14,000 to ALC Development LLC’s bank account.
Williams, Canty, and Whitaker allegedly submitted 170 applications from New Jersey computers, using falsified identities and naming three LLCs registered in New Jersey and controlled by Williams as the property managers, the complaint says. Williams then used the LLCs to transfer funds to the personal bank accounts of Canty and Whitaker, the alleged co-conspirators.
Attempts to reach the defendants were unsuccessful.
Here’s what else happened in housing this week—
ICYMI, from City Limits:
- The tallest mural in the U.S. debuted recently in the South Bronx, spanning all 29 stories of a building at NYCHA’s Morrisania Air Rights development.
- Nine homeless New Yorkers who died of hypothermia during last winter’s brutally cold weather were laid to rest this week in Manhattan, after advocates stepped in to claim their remains, which were initially headed for burial at the city’s potter’s field on Hart Island.
- City Hall released a long awaited plan to increase the number of public restrooms across the city, but homeless advocates—who’ve pushed the issue for years as part of a “Free to Pee” campaign—say it lacks detail and funding commitments.
ICYMI, from other local newsrooms:
- The Mamdani administration intervened to try and halt an eviction in Brooklyn which advocates say is a case of deed theft, according to The City Reporter.
- City Hall scored a court victory this week in one of the legal challenges to the mayor’s pied-à-terre tax on pricey second homes, Gothamist reports.
- The Sunset Park home where a fire killed six people this week had previous violations for illegally subdividing apartments, according to Pix 11.
- A Queens man was convicted under a New York State law targeting deed theft, the New York Times reports.
- Property owners are pushing state lawmakers to tackle rising property insurance costs in Albany this year, according to The Real Deal.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-democ.title: Israel’s Shaky Democracy Continues to Crumble
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-democ.author: Jared Hillel
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-democ.text:
Israel’s Shaky Democracy Continues to Crumble
From military rule over Palestinians to apartheid in the occupied territories, Israel has never been a democracy for Palestinians. Efforts to restrict expat voting ahead of the elections showed how barriers to democracy can reach Jewish citizens, too.
In July 1950, speaking at the annual Zionist Organization of America convention, US Vice President Alben W. Barkley asserted that Israel was “an oasis of liberty in the desert of despotism,” articulating a precursor to the oft-repeated adage “Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East.” While the expression cannot be traced to a singular person, the sentiment that Israel — a nation with free elections and civil liberties — stands alone amid a sea of authoritarian regimes has been cultivated by Western institutions and Israeli leaders since the state was founded.
From the outset, Israel’s earliest laws legalizing persecution against Palestinians showed the incompatibility between Jewish supremacy and democracy. But the subjugation of one group is rarely self-contained, and throughout history, illiberal nations have almost always turned against a portion of their citizens, often as violence against the outgroup reaches its peak.
In the midst of the bloodiest three years in the country’s history, and particularly during the election campaign, this tendency began to play out. Israel has disenfranchised voters, at times even contradicting its own discriminatory laws, in efforts to marginalize Jews perceived as a threat to Benjamin Netanyahu and his increasingly violent political agenda.
Barriers to the Ballot
In the past three years, emigration from Israel has reached record heights. According to a study published by Tel Aviv University, 270,000 citizens have left the country in the past three years. Between 2013 and 2015, the corresponding period in the previous decade, the number sat at 183,000. Like much of the American Jewish diaspora, those who have left in recent years have become deeply critical of Benjamin Netanyahu.
While Israel guarantees every citizen over the age of eighteen the right to vote, it has never permitted absentee ballots. With the exception of diplomats, emissaries, and Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldiers occupying territory in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria, voters must be in the country on Election Day. With this election largely seen as one of the most consequential in the nation’s history, a survey taken before the election estimated that up to 67,000 expats could be returning home to vote.
On October 27, Likud won twenty-seven seats, and Gad Eisenkot’s Yashar party won twenty-one. Netanyahu’s bloc took fifty-three seats, against forty-eight for the Jewish opposition bloc and nineteen for the Arab-led parties. No bloc won the sixty-one seats needed for a majority. The results have left the country facing uncertain coalition negotiations.
Leading up to the vote, Likud tried to stop Israelis outside the country from coming back. In September, Likud petitioned the Central Election Committee, demanding it block Fly & Vote, an initiative by the nonpartisan American-Israel Democracy (AID) Coalition, which sought to help Israelis abroad return and cast a vote.
Offering logistical help, including eligibility checks and passport renewals, the organization also coordinated six group flights and helped search for commercial flights. While participants were still required to pay their airfare, Likud argued the initiative violated financing laws and constituted election bribery.
While the petition was ultimately dismissed, the AID Coalition agreed to not subsidize tickets, organize any additional group flights, or provide transportation and accommodation.
This summer, a second spat broke out when hundreds of Israelis living abroad discovered they had been stripped of their voting rights after being classified by the Interior Ministry as nonresidents. The designation, known as Code 51, excluded citizens from the voter registry altogether.
Petitioning the Supreme Court, the expats argued that they were not notified of their status change, with several only realizing when checking their electoral eligibility. The courts dismissed the case on procedural grounds, stating the claim was filed too late.
While there is no definitive proof linking Likud to the Code 51 scandal, it is clear that the party has repeatedly tried to curtail the expat vote. Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that informal discussions were held between senior Transport Ministry officials about the possibility of restricting designated landing slots at airports, making it more difficult to fly into the country.
Similar to the proposed judicial reforms of 2023, where Netanyahu sought to weaken the power of the Supreme Court, this democratic backsliding has prompted furor among the Israeli left. But as is often the case with liberal Zionists, the far greater repression affecting Palestinians remains largely ignored.
Defending the Ethnocracy
The AID Coalition describes itself as a group “strengthening, and preserving the democratic foundations of the State of Israel.” While a valiant objective, a more honest statement would be about preserving an ethnocracy. Israeli Professor Oren Yiftachel describes this form of governance as one that “promotes the expansion of the dominant group in contested territory and its domination of power structures while maintaining a democratic facade.” This dynamic has been present since the state’s founding.
While the 150,000 Palestinians who remained in their homeland after the Nakba were declared citizens and granted the right to vote from the beginning, the community also faced systematic discrimination from the outset. From 1948 until 1966, Palestinian citizens of Israel were placed under military rule, which included measures that restricted their movement, prohibited political organizing, and imposed arbitrary curfews. Simultaneously, the government confiscated hundreds of thousands of dunams of land, uprooting farmers from their livelihood and forcing many to turn to low-wage labor to survive.
In 1967, a year after lifting the military administration, Israel would turn their attention toward Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza after occupying both territories in the Six-Day War.
Assuming control of around one million Palestinians, residents of the newly occupied territory were placed under military rule. This time citizenship and the right to vote were withheld from them, since such incorporation would threaten the Jewish demographic majority.
As Jewish settlers moved into the occupied territories, aided by generous Israeli government subsidies, an apartheid regime took shape, as authorities applied separate laws, courts, and democratic rights to Palestinians and Israelis living in neighboring areas.
Although Israel disengaged from Gaza in 2005, it lay siege to the Strip two years later, imposing a crushing blockade. After the October 7 attacks, it returned yet again as the occupying power, this time unleashing a genocide that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. In the West Bank, the apartheid regime continues, as roughly 500,000 settlers, excluding those in East Jerusalem, live with full rights outside of Israel’s internationally recognized border, beside Palestinians who cannot vote, travel freely, or even build on their ancestral land.
Amid the dire situation in the West Bank and Gaza, the plight of Palestinians living inside Israel is largely forgotten. Yet these 2.1 million residents continue to live as second-class citizens.
In 2018, the Israeli Knesset passed the quasi-constitutional Nation-State Law, stipulating that self-determination is unique to the Jewish people, without guaranteeing equality for its other citizens. Furthermore, Palestinian citizens of Israel continue to face entrenched discrimination in urban planning, economic development, and educational opportunities.
The Authoritarian Turn
In 2024, the Varieties of Democracy Institute downgraded Israel from a liberal to an electoral democracy. The demotion followed Netanyahu and his coalition’s attempt to overhaul the judiciary, their accusations the Supreme Court was “left-leaning,” and deterioration in protections against torture. This classification did not take into account the active atrocities that Israel was perpetrating in Gaza and the West Bank at the time.
Yet since this reclassification, Netanyahu has shed more of the democratic facade he has long sought to uphold.
More than five hundred humanitarian workers have been killed since the war in Gaza began. In December 2025, Israel attempted to bar thirty-seven nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) from operating in the West Bank and Gaza. The Supreme Court froze the ban, allowing the organizations to continue operating pending a final ruling.
More recently, numerous foreign journalists have been turned away at the border during the election campaign, with others facing arduous interrogations and detention before being allowed entry.
Perhaps most revealing is the government’s willingness to break long-standing supremacist laws, which uphold Jews as a privileged class in Israel.
Starting in 2025, several Jewish activists were detained and deported for engaging in protective presence, a form of nonviolent solidarity work in which civilians deter violent settlers from harassing Palestinian communities. Earlier this year, a Jewish American academic on a three-year residency visa was denied entry after being accused of being a “left-wing anarchist.”
After the backlash prompted by the film NAZA, in which IDF soldiers admitted to knowingly killing innocent civilians in Gaza, Netanyahu announced plans to introduce a bill that would strip those who defame the IDF of their Israeli citizenship.
Last month, it was reported that two Jews were denied citizenship for having previously partaken in anti-occupation activism in the West Bank. This was the first known case of the state violating the Law of Return, which stipulates that every Jew is entitled to immigrate to Israel.
Many saw Gad Eisenkot as the last chance to halt the country’s authoritarian drift. The election has left open the possibility that he could still lead the government, but he has no clear path to power. While he might reverse the emerging trend of discriminating against Jews and Israelis deemed insufficiently patriotic, none of his proposed policies address the core issues that make Israel an ethnostate.
The election has not changed the reality for Palestinians, with or without Israeli citizenship, or the refusal of every major party to address these injustices. What Eisenkot may offer is merely a return to the illusion of democracy.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.title: Israel | Nach der Israel-Wahl hängt viel von palästinensischen Parteien ab
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.author: Nimrod Flaschenberg
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.text:
- Kommentare
- Israel
Nach der Israel-Wahl hängt viel von palästinensischen Parteien ab
Die hohe palästinensische Wahlbeteiligung in Israel erwirkte, dass die rechte Opposition mit den boykottierten palästinensischen Parteien rechnen muss.
In den letzten Tagen des Wahlkampfs brachte die hebräischsprachige Kampagne der Vereinten Liste – ein Parteienbündnis, das die arabisch-palästinensische Minderheit in Israel und Israels kleine jüdische radikale Linke vertritt – in Zentralisrael einige Transparente mit der Aufschrift »jüdisch-arabisch und demokratisch« an. Der Gedanke dahinter ist, dass der Begriff »arabisch« eingefügt weden soll in die sonst übliche Beschreibung Israels als jüdisch und demokratisch. Damit würden die jüdische Vorherrschaft sowie der ethnokratische Charakter des Staates – oder, wenn man so will, der Zionismus – infrage gestellt.
Die folgenden Wahlergebnisse fielen gemischt aus: Einerseits ging Benjamin Netanjahus Likud-Partei als stärkste Kraft in der Knesset hervor, und sein rechtsextremer Block ist größer als der zionistische Oppositionsblock. Das bedeutet, die Mehrheit der jüdischen Israelis unterstützt eine Politik der rassistischen Hetze, des Völkermords und des militärischen Expansionismus. Andererseits gingen die palästinensischen Staatsbürger in noch nie dagewesenem Ausmaß zur Wahl.
Nimrod Flaschenberg ist ein in Berlin lebender Analyst und Aktivist sowie Mitbegründer von Israelis for Peace. Während des Wahlkampfs war er in Tel Aviv und beteiligte sich an der Kampagne der Vereinten Liste.
In der neuen Knesset stieg die Vertretung der Parteien, die palästinensische Bürger repräsentieren, von 10 auf 19 Sitze. Die Vereinte Liste erhielt elf Sitze und Raam acht (von 120 Sitzen). Dieses Ergebnis rückte eine beständige Wahrheit ins Blickfeld, die jeder anerkennen muss, der in Israel oppositionelle und progressive Politik betreiben will: Der einzige Weg, die extreme Rechte zu besiegen, besteht darin, eine jüdisch-arabische politische Partnerschaft zu fördern, die letztlich zu einer Friedenspolitik im Nahen Osten führen könnte.
Nach drei Jahren Militarismus, Völkermord, grassierender krimineller Gewalt und einer ultrarechten Regierung, die politischen Dissens unterdrückte, gingen die palästinensischen Bürger in einem Akt der Selbstverteidigung in Scharen wählen. Dieser Schritt könnte den Israelis Hoffnung auf eine andere Zukunft geben, wenn sie sich nur dazu entschließen, eine andere Vision anzunehmen.
Der Ball liegt nun bei der zionistischen Opposition. Dabei sollte man sie nicht zu etwas machen, was sie nicht ist. Außer Jair Golans Demokraten sind im Grunde alle anderen Oppositionsparteien prinzipiell gegen eine Zusammenarbeit mit arabischen Parteien – sie lehnen eine gemeinsame Regierungsführung mit der moderaten Raam ab, ganz zu schweigen von der linkeren und national-palästinensischen Vereinten Liste.
Doch Oppositionsführer Gadi Eisenkot und seine Partner stehen vor der Wahl: Sie können sich entweder von Netanjahu in eine neue Wahlrunde hineinziehen lassen und zum fünften Rad am Wagen in einer neuen Ausprägung der aktuellen faschistischen Regierung werden, oder aber sie treiben die Bildung einer Regierungskoalition voran, die sich doch auf palästinensische Stimmen stützt.
Sollten sie letztlich eine Regierung bilden, die mit der Vereinten Liste zusammenarbeitet, würde dies weder die Besatzung beenden noch illegale Siedlungen verschwinden lassen. Es würde jedoch die grundlegenden politischen Strukturen und Formen der Zusammenarbeit schaffen, die notwendig sind, damit sich die israelische Politik zu einem späteren Zeitpunkt – wenn der internationale Druck zunimmt – in Richtung Frieden bewegen kann. Damit es in Israel zu einem echten Wandel kommt, braucht es sowohl Bewegung auf internationaler Bühne als auch innerhalb der israelischen Politik.
Selbst wenn eine Regierung mit palästinensischer Unterstützung dieses Mal nicht zustande kommt und es Neuwahlen oder eine Einheitsregierung gibt, wird dieser Moment jenem Teil der Gesellschaft, der von den liberalen Kreisen Israels noch übrig ist, ein für alle Mal klarmachen, dass die jüdisch-arabische Partnerschaft das politische Projekt ist, das sie vorantreiben müssen.
Politischer Wandel vollzieht sich sehr, sehr langsam, bis er plötzlich ganz schnell kommt. Dies könnte ein solcher Moment sein. Es könnte ein entscheidender Zeitpunkt sein, der maßgeblich über die Zukunft von Israel und Palästina bestimmt.
Gleichzeitig ist zu bedenken, dass die Drohung einer Eskalation im Iran oder in Gaza stets Netanjahus bevorzugtes Mittel ist, um jede Chance auf Wandel im Keim zu ersticken. Direkt nach den Zwischenwahlen in den USA besteht daher ein hohes Risiko für eine solche Eskalation.
Nochmals: Jeder wirkliche politische Wandel in Israel und Palästina muss auch über einen politischen Wandel im israelischen System führen – und über einen Wandel in der jüdisch-israelischen Gesellschaft. Genau das ist das durchaus revolutionäre politische Projekt der Vereinten Liste: der Aufruf zu echter Gleichberechtigung in diesem Land. Man sollte es nicht unterschätzen.

Let the Investigations Begin!
In this week’s Elie v. US, our justice correspondent demands subpoenas, subpoenas, subpoenas of Trump and his cronies. Plus: Elon Musk gets hoisted by his own petard.
There are a lot of individuals, communities, and, yes, special interests that had a hand in the Democrats’ taking control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. All of those people will now expect their particular issue to be championed by the upcoming Congress. Democrats will be expected to do all the things.
I also have my pet issues and priorities, but I am here to be reasonable. I do not expect Democrats to center the thing that is most important to me. I don’t expect them to lead with it. I don’t expect Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer to spend a lot of time on CNN talking about it. What I do expect is a constant, rolling drumbeat of subpoenas, investigations, and indictments. Give everybody else their requested legislation. Force Donald Trump to use his veto pen so often that his tiny hands start to cramp up. That’s what everybody wants. But for me, just give me… justice. Give me accountability.
Jeffries has already said that the Democrats will not be out for “revenge.” He’s said that they are not interested in “retribution.” Some have interpreted these statements as an indication that the Democrats in Congress will not try to hold the Trump administration accountable for what it’s done.
I have a more charitable read on Jeffries’s statements, which is that “revenge” and “retribution” are different from accountability. I think “revenge” and “retribution” are indeed wrong. We have lived through that, and it sucks. I don’t want to see the Democratic version of Trump’s prosecutorial persecution of Hunter Biden or James Comey or John Bolton or (wait, I’m not done) Leititia James or Jack Smith or Ilhan Omar. The Trump administration investigates people because they dared to dissent. He uses the law to bully his enemies and intimidate others into silence. I don’t want the Democrats to engage in any bit of that.
What I want is for the Democrats to investigate criminal acts—from the ones that have taken place in plain sight to the ones where the criminals think they’ve gotten away with it because Trump approves of their crimes. I don’t want Jared Kushner to be investigated because he’s the president’s son-in-law. I want him investigated because he’s potentially laundered and embezzled $2 billion dollars in funds from the governments of Saudi Arabia and the UAE. I don’t want Stephen Miller investigated because he’s a racist ghoul who’s at the center of the Trump brain trust. I want him investigated because he’s a racist ghoul who has violated the due-process rights of millions of people and, potentially, directly violated court orders. I don’t want Pete Hegseth investigated because he’s a toxic psychopath who is unqualified to lead America’s military forces. I want him investigated because he’s a fucking murderer who needs to spend the rest of his life in jail, either in this country or The Hague.
If Trump pardons all of these cronies, I want there to be enough public evidence available that these people can’t take a Carnival freaking Cruise without being scooped up by Interpol.
And don’t even get me started on the Epstein files. I’m finna sound like Marjorie Taylor Greene when it comes to the Epstein files.
It doesn’t have to be what the Democrats lead with. It doesn’t have to be what the Democrats tout as they’re trying to show the people they are delivering on what they voted for. It just has to be something the Democrats do. Wake up, issue a subpoena, release information on who is a pedophile, then get in front of the cameras and talk about gas or eggs or Iran or whatever. They can talk about whatever the hell they want to, as long as the subpoenas and indictments keep rolling in.
The incoming head of the House Oversight Committee (which will have the authority to conduct most of the investigations I wish for) is likely to be California Democrat Robert Garcia. On election night, after they called the House for the Democrats, I was on a show and about to launch into a polemic about how Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez should really get that position instead of Garcia. But then Garcia issued a two-word statement: “Lawyer Up.” I swallowed my AOC rosary (for the briefest of moments) and said to a friend (off-camera, of course), “Sheet, negro, that’s all you had to say.”
The Bad and the Ugly Bold and the Beautiful
- In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola holds a slight lead over Republican Dan S. Sullivan in the race for the Senate. We’re still waiting for the cross-country skiers to deliver more ballots to be counted, but it seems that most of the outstanding ones are early or absentee ballots. Peltola has been overperforming with people who voted by mail or placed their votes in a barrel attached to a Saint Bernard.
- In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom remains ahead of incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by roughly 1,800 votes. The race will likely come down to around 15,000 provisional ballots, which are cast by people when their eligibility is in some type of question, and a smattering of ballots that were mailed on time but arrived after Election Day. What I find interesting here (I mean, beyond “HOLY SHIT MISSISSIPPI IS IN PLAY”), is that Republicans are ideologically committed to throwing away any ballot they can. Mississippi Republicans literally took a case all the way to the Supreme Court specifically asking to throw away ballots that arrive by mail after Election Day. But if Hyde-Smith is losing (and she is losing right now), she’ll likely want those provisional ballots and late-arriving ballots to count if she’s going to have any chance of closing the gap. So, you know, expect a lot of rank hypocrisy from Republicans from the Delta.
- In Kansas, where 98 percent of the precincts have been counted, Democrat Cindy Holscher leads Republican Ty Masterson by about 7,000 votes in the state’s gubernatorial race. Holscher has declared victory, but when the margin is within 1 percent (which it appears to be), Kansas law calls for an automatic “close audit” of 10 percent of the precincts, which means 10 percent of the vote will be recounted by hand to look for any discrepancies. Masterson also has the right to demand a recount if the margin remains this close.
- In Los Angeles, democratic socialist Nithya Raman has defeated Democrat Karen Bass in a close-as-nails run-off between the top two vote-getters from the city’s open primary in June. That means DSA-backed candidates now run NYC and LA. It also means a person who has been critical of Israel’s atrocities in Gaza will be the mayor that hosts the world at the 2028 Summer Olympics. What a time to be alive.
