Inspired Takes Bitter Assholes
- Maine Senator Susan Collins lashed out at Trump as well as at voters after her defeat on Tuesday, claiming that her efforts to break from the president were “never enough” to satisfy voters and that they were more impressed by rhetoric than results. She sounds… concerned. Perhaps even… disappointed. Hopefully, Susan Collins has finally learned her lesson.
- Vice President JD Vance blamed the Republicans’ loss on the Iran War and other factors that lead directly back to his boss. Trump said that Vance’s analysis was “fine.” Friends, when Trump shrugs off a direct attack from one of his underlings as “fine,” consider it your first indication that the dear leader is running out of Kool-Aid.
- After doubling down on her endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers even after he lost to Abdul El-Sayed, Haley Stevens said that she hoped the Democratic Party would be “big enough for more than one viewpoint”—which is a wild thing to say given that she, not El-Sayed, abandoned her party’s nominee because he didn’t share her viewpoint. Stevens then canceled a scheduled appearance at George Washington University on Thursday, where she was supposed to join Representative Jamie Raskin for post-election analysis. I’m looking forward to Stevens’s future career as discount Tulsi Gabbard, but I hope she doesn’t get too comfortable in her pariah chair, because she’s gonna have to make space for John Fetterman very, very soon.
Worst Argument of the Week
I was going to skip this section this week because, I mean, WE WON IN TEXAS, Y’ALL. But SCOTUSblog editor Sarah Isgur decided to unleash a take so bad I had to put down my peace pipe and pull out my keyboard.
It involves Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito. Before the election, Alito said he would not retire during the lame-duck Congress, even if Republicans lost control of the Senate. After the election, Alito reiterated his pledge. This means that Alito likely cannot retire at all during the next and last two years of the Trump presidency, because Democrats now have the strength to block his replacement from being confirmed (and Democrats will block another Trump appointment to the Supreme Court or, so help me God, I will start shooting myself up with gamma radiation until I turn green).
But Isgur sees another way out. She wrote on the apartheid social media app: “Alito won’t retire in the lame duck and he doesn’t need to. Trump can nominate someone to the Supreme Court and the senate can confirm without a vacancy. Then Trump can wait to sign the commission any time in the next two years. The question isn’t Alito, its [sic] Cornyn/Tillis/Thune.”
What she’s saying is that Trump can nominate Alito’s replacement now, before the new term, and have him confirmed by the Senate now, by the lame-duck Senate—and then hold that appointment in waiting for up to two years, until Alito decides to actually vacate his position.
This is wrong. It’s completely wrong. There’s no constitutional mechanism to nominate a person for a vacancy that does not exist. It’d be like a president nominating someone to a position that has not yet been created: “I think we should have a department of puppies, and, if we ever do, I nominate Snoopy to lead it, because he’s a very good boy.” That’s not a nomination; it’s a pointless mouth-noise, and no one is bound to respect it. There’s nothing for the Senate to confirm if the position or vacancy doesn’t exist.
As usual, when it comes to Republicans, the concept that seems to flummox them is consent: who is authorized to give consent, for what purpose the consent is given, and how long the consent lasts. The Senate has the power to “advise and consent” on presidential appointments, and that consent should lapse at the end of the Senate’s term, should the president not fill the vacancy. Starting on January 3, 2027, we have a new Senate. Any consent given by the old one is moot if there are vacancies that haven’t been filled by then. Trump cannot hold the consent of the old Senate in his pocket for two years. He could, at most, hold it for two more months before the new Senate convenes in January.
Isgur is not the first person to have this wild and stupid thought. It’s long been understood that the idea of a “vacancy” on the court is a little loose—the exact temporal moment a “vacancy” comes into being can be open for interpretation—and could be manipulated by bad-faith actors (like Isgur or Trump) to play all sorts of games with the appointments process. Hell, the seminal Supreme Court case, Marbury v. Madison in 1803, essentially arose because both John Adams and Thomas Jefferson were playing a game of dick-measuring with the Appointments Clause.
But the reason nobody has really tried to exploit this existential conundrum is that it fairly quickly leads to total system failure and mutually assured destruction. If presidents, along with a sympathetic Senate, can make replacement appointments in perpetuity, even when no actual vacancy exists, then there’s no reason for them not to do it for every judge and commissioner in the entire federal system. But if an outgoing president did that, there would be no reason for an incoming president to honor any of those appointments (again, see Marbury v. Madison, where Adams tried to make a bunch of lame-duck appointments and Jefferson told those people to go jump into the nearest lake). And you pretty quickly end up with President Jon Ossoff ordering the National Guard to remove “Justice” Jeanine Pirro from the office she’s squatting on First Street.
Hmm… come to think of it, I’m not totally opposed to that scenario. Go ahead and listen to Sarah Isgur, Trump, and ensure that Democrats pack the court so hard in 2029 that it will be unconstitutional to so much as look at a gun without a favorable FBI psychological profile. [Obi Wan-Kenobi voice]: “If you strike me down, I will become more powerful than you can possibly imagine.”
What I Wrote
For two years, we were told that Democrats could not win unless we supported the worst kinds of policies. We were told to sacrifice trans kids. We were told to deport our neighbors. We were told to embrace toxic masculinity. We were told if we did not do these things, we would never win an election outside of New York, San Francisco, and Chicago.
The people who told us this were wrong. I wrote about why.
In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos
In 2020, Elon Musk moved from California to Texas.
In 2021, Musk relocated Tesla’s headquarters to Texas.
In 2024, Musk relocated the headquarters of SpaceX and Twitter to Texas.
Musk made all of these moves to escape regulators in California as well as an ongoing workplace-discrimination lawsuit regarding rampant alleged racism at Tesla.
In 2027, Musk, Tesla, SpaceX, and Twitter will fall under the jurisdiction of Texas’s new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, and new Democratic attorney general, Nathan Johnson.
Life comes at you fast.

https://gothamist.com/news/intoxicated-q.title: Intoxicated Queens driver killed baby after running stop sign, indictment says
https://gothamist.com/news/intoxicated-q.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/intoxicated-q.text:
A Flushing man has been indicted on charges including manslaughter after he allegedly sped past a stop sign while on cocaine and THC, then struck and killed a 1-year-old boy in a stroller.
Elvin Rivera, 57, was driving in a residential area of Flushing around 8:35 a.m. on Oct. 11 when he ran through a stop sign on 32nd Avenue, traveling northbound on Murray Street, according to the indictment.
He then sped through the intersection and struck the stroller, which was being pushed by the 1-year-old’s nanny, authorities say.
The Queens District Attorney’s Office said Rivera remained on the scene, where he failed drug sobriety and field tests. A blood test later confirmed the presence of THC and cocaine, the DA’s office said. Rivera had also been driving in violation of restrictions resulting from a DWI case in April, according to the DA’s office.
The child, 1-year-old Justin Hu, was rushed to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, according to Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz.
“Our thoughts are with Justin’s family as they mourn this unimaginable loss,” Katz said in a statement Friday.
The indictment charges Rivera with 12 counts, including manslaughter, vehicular manslaughter, assault, driving while impaired, failure to exercise due care and failing to stop at a sign.
He could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted of the top charge, and is scheduled to return back to court on Jan. 7.
Attorney information for Rivera was not immediately available.

https://hyperallergic.com/meg-onli-and-z.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/meg-onli-and-z.text:
Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial
Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company.
Meg Onli, an organizer behind some of the Whitney Museum of American Art's signature exhibitions, and Zack Winokur, a performing arts director and co-founder, are the co-curators for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, the museum announced today, November 6.
“Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art," Scott Rothkopf, director of the Whitney, said in a statement. "Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial."
The news comes just two months after the 2026 Biennial closed and a month after unionized staff at the museum dodged a full-blown strike ahead of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, a blockbuster retrospective co-curated by Onli. The Whitney union was one of four New York City museum unions under United Auto Workers 2110 — along with the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum — that voted to strike amid drawn-out contract negotiations over low compensation, benefits, and workplace conditions. Hours before the planned strike, unionized staffers ratified their second contract and secured a new wage floor, increased parental and bereavement leave, and stronger safety provisions, among other amendments.
First joining the museum as curator-at-large in 2023, Onli co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, Even Better Than the Real Thing, with Chrissie Iles. That same year, Onli was promoted to Nancy and Fred Poses Curator to lead the Whitney’s painting and sculpture acquisition committee, bringing her previous experience as director and curator of the Underground Museum in Los Angeles and associate curator at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania.
“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about," Onli said in a statement. "I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead."
Winokur is the co-founder of the American Modern Opera Company, an interdisciplinary collective comprised of 17 singers, musicians, dancers, and other performing artists. He also served as artistic director for Little Island on Pier 55 and NYPopsUp, a statewide initiative aimed at opening performing arts spaces after COVID-19.
“I’m honored to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur added in a statement. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring."
Dating back to 1932, the Whitney Biennial remains the longest-running survey of American art, with more than 3,600 artists participating in the exhibition to date. The 83rd edition is slated to open in March 2028.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/pent.title: Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/pent.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/pent.text:
Replacements for embattled War Secretary Pete Hegseth are increasingly being discussed at the Pentagon, according to current and former defense officials. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is at the top of many lists. Mike Waltz, the disgraced former national security adviser at the center of the 2025 Signalgate messaging scandal and currently U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, has also been mentioned.
Those and other names have emerged as Hegseth is facing down a bipartisan impeachment effort as early as next week and is in a mad scramble to hold onto his job.
Officials acknowledged that both DeSantis and Waltz were dismal choices, but all who spoke with The Intercept said even the most problematic picks would be preferable to Hegseth, who has been excoriated at the Pentagon and beyond for Signal-gate, his purge of top military leaders, his inability to defeat Yemen’s Houthis in 2025 or win the Iran war in 2026, his campaign of extrajudicial killings in attacks on so-called drug boats, his efforts to weaken transparency and scuttle accountability, and his obsession with troops’ testosterone levels, among other distractions.
In the wake of an election rout that handed Democrats firm control of the House and the Senate, Hegseth is in the crosshairs of lawmakers whom he has treated with contempt for two years. “Dead man walking,” said one official in an exposé published by The Intercept Thursday. Hours after publication of that report, Hegseth launched a desperate bid to stave off his ouster, employing his Fox News-host-honed skills at fanning culture war flames to air his grievances and whip up the support of his boss and the MAGA faithful.
In a video posted on X, the self-styled secretary of war pulled out the stops: “He literally took a bullet for this nation,” Hegseth said amid obsequious flattery of Trump. “He shook his fist and said ‘fight, fight, fight,’ and so will we.”
The chief of what he recently called “the most powerful, most lethal and most prepared military on the planet,” Hegseth cast himself as a besieged victim and tied himself to Trump in a naked attempt to save his job. “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth carped in a video filmed outside the Pentagon.
Hegseth was referring to outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who said Wednesday that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment for high crimes and misdemeanors when the House is back in session next week. Numerous Democrats have indicated a desire to join Massie’s effort to oust Hegseth since their midterm election landslide, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to be the next speaker.
Hegseth’s missive to Trump hit many hot-button issues that Americans seemingly repudiated in Tuesday’s electoral landslide. He boasted about driving “the weird and the woke” out of the military and took aim at his and Trump’s enemies. “Why do the Democrats and the deep state radicals really hate us? Because we tore down their sacred cows one by one and without apology,” said Hegseth, who rattled off a list of things he has torn down, such as diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives; military efforts to combat climate change; the rechristening of military bases named for Confederate leaders; and the rights of trans service members.
Hegseth’s video rant was part of a doomsday plan coordinated by chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, first reported by CNN and corroborated by a defense official who spoke with The Intercept. It was accompanied by a coordinated campaign of social media posts by Pentagon underlings trying to tie Hegseth’s fortunes to the president, consisting of photos of the war secretary posturing accompanied by the text, “STAND. FIGHT. DEFEND THE REPUBLIC.”
While it was a brazen attempt to cast any future effort by Trump to cut him loose as an enormous defeat for the president, officials said Parnell’s Hail Mary could succeed. “It’s sad. But it may work because Trump is so easy to manipulate,” said one defense official. “Hegseth knows he is dealing with a president with the mind of a three-year-old.”
During the Pentagon’s Thursday afternoon social media blitz, one of those Hegseth underlings messaged this reporter a clip from the 2013 film “The Wolf of Wall Street,” in which Leonardo DiCaprio’s stockbroker character pivots mid-way through announcing his resignation and a deal with the Securities and Exchange Commission, declaring: “I’m not fucking leaving! … They’re gonna need a fuckin’ wrecking ball to take me outta here!”
The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. In neither case did the Senate vote to convict. Should Massie’s lame-duck impeachment measure succeed in the House, it would likely languish in the Senate where Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., would have little incentive to bring it to a vote, said a congressional staffer for a member on the Armed Services Committee. Still, some pundits predict Hegseth may not survive the weekend, much less the month or the year.
If and when Hegseth is ousted, there will be no shortage of people jockeying to take his place. In addition to DeSantis and Waltz, other names bandied about at the Pentagon or on Capitol Hill include Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst, a retired military officer who chose not to run for reelection this year, as well as failed Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who was defeated by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. Some of those names were mentioned in a Thursday post on X by James Stavridis, a retired four-star Navy admiral, former supreme Allied Commander of NATO, and partner and vice chair of Carlyle, a global investment firm with deep Pentagon ties. Stavridis also named Mike Pompeo, Trump’s former secretary of state.
While DeSantis and Trump had been bitter rivals during the 2024 Republican presidential primary campaign, the outgoing Florida governor and assumed 2028 GOP presidential hopeful has since vocally supported Trump’s crackpot initiatives. To advance Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda, DeSantis hastily constructed (and then quickly shuttered) “Alligator Alcatraz,” a detention hellhole that the Department of Homeland Security’s watchdog found did not comply with a slew of federal and state standards. The Florida governor was also the first official to use Trump’s renamed “Gulf of America” for the Gulf of Mexico, in an official document.
Amid the rubble of a devastated Republican Party, DeSantis — a longtime culture warrior who rode what he called what he called “woke gender ideology” to national prominence — quickly pivoted. “The ground shifts and the emphasis, then, is on different things,” he said on Wednesday. “Four years ago, we were in that peak woke era. … Now, the issues are different and Republicans, it seemed like, in some of the ads I was seeing, with how much money they were spending, they really were fighting yesterday’s battle.”
DeSantis also has a troubling military background. As a lieutenant in the Judge Advocate General’s Corps — a role akin to that of a first-year associate at a law firm — he served at the notorious American prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. He also served in the failed forever war in Iraq, as a senior legal adviser to the commander of SEAL Team One in Fallujah.
Asked about DeSantis’s standing within the Pentagon, an official said: “Anything is better than Hegseth.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Indígenas denunciam corte de água que abastece comunidade no Parque do Mate, em Campo Largo
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Karina Ernsen
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O curso de água que abastece a comunidade indígena do Parque do Mate, em Campo Largo (PR), na Região Metropolitana de Curitiba, está seco há cinco meses. As famílias da retomada indígena kaingang, que ocuparam o espaço desde 2022, denunciam a irregularidade do abastecimento hídrico. Esse córrego existe desde o antigo engenho, no fim do século 19.
O Parque Histórico do Mate, também conhecido como Antigo Engenho de Mate da Rondinha, é um remanescente da economia ervateira paranaense. Construído por volta de 1870, o conjunto preserva a tecnologia dos engenhos hidráulicos que utilizavam a água do Rio Rondinha, desviada por um canal, para movimentar a roda d’água e acionar o maquinário.
Tombado pelo Estado do Paraná em 10 de julho de 1968 (Processo 19/68) e pelo Instituto do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico Nacional (IPHAN) em 1985, o local é um patrimônio histórico. Após anos de abandono pelo poder público, encontrou na comunidade indígena kaingang da aldeia Kógunh Já Má seus atuais guardiões.
O açude que abastecia o parque e a comunidade está seco. A água vem do Rio Rondinha, através de um desvio artificial que abastecia o antigo engenho. Esse desvio, que alimentou o desenvolvimento econômico do Paraná, foi interrompido, deixando a comunidade indígena sem acesso à água.
Omissão que enfraquece a luta indígena
O cacique Jafé Cassemiro, liderança da aldeia, relata que, quando chegaram, o açude estava cheio de peixes e o rio alimentava não apenas a comunidade com comida, mas também com lazer. “A água descia para o açude. As crianças se banhavam, pescavam, a gente irrigava as hortas. Agora não dá nem para jogar uma linha de anzol”, lamenta.
Ele conta que a interrupção não é a primeira, mas tem sido a mais longa e dolorida. Vivem ali 38 famílias, incluindo mais de 60 crianças.
O abandono do Parque do Mate antecede a ocupação indígena. De acordo com a professora Emi Lorenzetti, do curso de Tecnologia em Agroecologia do Instituto Federal do Paraná (IFPR) – campus Campo Largo, o local estava inativo e sem manutenção há mais de uma década, com a estrutura se deteriorando.
Desde 2022, os indígenas que ocuparam o local têm mantido o território. A comunidade realiza a limpeza da área, o plantio árvores nativas, como as araucárias, e a manutenção do espaço. Jafé relata o acordo feito com o governo para assumir o cuidado com o espaço: “A gente fez várias reuniões com o estado, com o município, em que eles afirmaram [a permissão] de ficar aqui, com um termo de compromisso, de cuidar aqui do Parque do Mate”, explica.
Enquanto cuidam do território, sofrem com o corte de água, que atinge diretamente a segurança alimentar e nutricional da comunidade. “Sem essa fonte, fica inviável qualquer projeto, até mesmo para a sustentabilidade do local”, afirma a professora Lorenzetti, que acompanha a retomada indígena desde o início. Ela lembra que os peixes que habitam o lago estão morrendo na lama: “Onde há água, há vida. E hoje a comunidade está sendo privada disso.”
O que diz o poder público?
Em janeiro de 2026, o Centro de Apoio Operacional das Promotorias de Justiça de Proteção aos Direitos Humanos do Ministério Público do Paraná (MPPR) fez uma visita institucional à aldeia Kókhun Já Má, no Parque do Mate, a convite da própria comunidade. A visita teve como objetivo conhecer as condições de moradia e planejar ações futuras de infraestrutura coletiva, incluindo saneamento, iluminação e acesso à água e energia elétrica.
Na ocasião, foi produzido um relato formal ao órgão com a necessidade de regularização do fornecimento de água e energia elétrica para as moradias. As demandas foram registradas pelo MPPR para análise e eventual articulação institucional.
Procurado pelo Brasil de Fato Paraná, o MPPR esclareceu que a 4ª Promotoria de Justiça de Campo Largo, responsável pelo acompanhamento da questão hídrica, tem um procedimento administrativo em curso para monitorar os impactos ambientais na aldeia. No entanto, segundo o órgão, “até o momento não chegou à Promotoria notícia relacionada ao citado esvaziamento de um açude devido ao bloqueio de um desvio do Rio Rondinha.”
O MPPR informou ainda que, na 1ª Promotoria de Justiça, tramita o Procedimento Administrativo nº MPPR-0023.23.000778-5, que acompanha as tratativas de formalização da reivindicação territorial e outras diligências estruturantes.
A prefeitura de Campo Largo informou que o caso é de responsabilidade do governo do Paraná e do Instituto Água e Terra (IAT), entidade autárquica vinculada à Secretaria do Desenvolvimento Sustentável e do Turismo.
Procurado, o IAT respondeu, em nota, que localizou no sistema oficial três “Declarações de Uso Insignificante” para captação superficial no Arroio Rondinha, afluente do Rio Verde, destinadas à irrigação de olerícolas. Segundo o IAT, a licença é para “pequenas parcelas de água” e uma equipe de fiscalização deve ir ao local verificar irregularidades. O órgão não explica como captações “insignificantes” teriam o poder de secar um açude histórico e deixar a comunidade sem água.
A atuação da Funai e o Grupo de Trabalho
O indigenista Mauro Leno Silvestrin, servidor da Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) e que acompanha o caso, esclarece que a situação do Parque do Mate é tratada por um Grupo de Trabalho (GT) interinstitucional, que reúne diversas secretarias estaduais, órgãos federais (como o próprio IAT, a Funai e a Defensoria Pública da União), o MPPR, a Defensoria Pública do Paraná, a Universidade Federal do Paraná (UFPR) e o IFPR. Segundo ele, todas as decisões relativas ao parque e à comunidade indígena passam por essa instância colegiada.
Silvestrin explica que é necessário um processo de desassoreamento do rio para restabelecer o fluxo da água — o que já foi encaminhado pelo GT. A execução dos mutirões de limpeza depende da compra de Equipamentos de Proteção Individual (EPIs) para garantir a segurança dos voluntários.
Segundo ele, a Secretaria de Cultura do Estado e o IAT ficaram responsáveis por tentar adquirir esses equipamentos, e a Defesa Civil foi consultada sobre a possibilidade de doação. “Estamos aguardando a compra desses equipamentos de proteção para poder fazer os mutirões e desassorear o rio”, afirma o indigenista.
Jefé conta que as famílias já subiram o córrego para desassorear o curso em duas ocasiões, mas que, dessa vez, o poder público pediu para a comunidade aguardar medidas do Estado.
Como se deu a denúncia
A denúncia sobre a seca do açude que abastecia o parque foi feita pelos próprios indígenas durante um encontro da Rede EcoAção Socioambiental RMC, projeto executado pelo Centro de Formação Urbano Rural Irmã Araújo (Cefuria), em parceria com a Itaipu Binacional.
A rede aplica questionários e se reúne com catadores, agricultores familiares, povos originários, comunidades tradicionais, organizações da sociedade civil e instituições de ensino. A partir dos dados, um dos objetivos da iniciativa é consolidar “diagnósticos participativos” e articular comunidades e grupos da Grande Curitiba.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: French court orders restitution of Pissarro painting sold at Sotheby’s for £1.2m to heirs of Jewish banker
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Vincent Noce
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A French court has ordered the cancellation of the Sotheby’s London sale of a landscape by Camille Pissarro, and its immediate restitution to the heirs of Jewish banker Salomon Flavian, on the grounds that it was looted in Paris in 1941. According to the 5 November ruling, Sotheby’s has two months to reveal the “complete identity” of the buyer, subject to a daily penalty of €1,000 for any delay.
Entitled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne (fishing dock and Duquesne basin, 1902), this view of the port of Dieppe in Normandy, was sold at Sotheby’s London on 25 June 2024 for £1.2m.
The Sotheby’s catalogue did mention it had been owned by Flavian from 1935 and was registered in the Répertoire des biens spoliés (repertory of looted art) released by the French government in 1947. Nevertheless, it indicated that the work was “offered for sale pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian”. Their consent, Sotheby’s explained in court, had been obtained by the Mondex Corporation, a Toronto-based company specialised in the return of looted art.
At a court hearing on 18 September, Corinne Hershkovitch, the lawyer for seven heirs of Flavian, said this agreement had been signed by only two relatives and the others were not consulted. In court, Mondex and Sotheby’s endorsed a study which concluded that the painting had been acquired in the late 1930s by the British artist and collector Edward Le Bas, from the dealer Paul Rosenberg, and therefore was no longer part of Flavian’s collection seized in 1941 by the Nazis.
The court judged otherwise, considering that there was “no direct and convincing evidence” of these alleged transactions. On the contrary, the Flavian family’s research produced “a set of precise, serious and concurring elements demonstrating that Pissarro’s work was indeed looted during” the Second World War, according to the judges.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Sotheby’s London said it is “disappointed by the judgement regarding the restitution”. However, the auction house “welcomes the decision to dismiss all claims against Sotheby’s”. “The history of the artwork is complex”, the spokesperson adds, and “we fully recognise the profound losses suffered by the Flavian family during the Nazi era and, from the outset, have approached this matter responsibly and with the care and respect it deserves.”
“It is a very important ruling, which opens the way to a restitution that the Flavian family has demanded since the war,” Hershkovitch tells The Art Newspaper. “It shows Mondex’s failure in its mission, and now Sotheby’s has to bear the responsibility for having sold a looted artwork.”
Mondex’s lawyer, Melina Wolman, says the company intends to appeal a judgement that, she says, is “posing major difficulties in regard with historical factors”. She adds that the name of Le Bas, who owned the Pissarro painting in the 1950s, appears on an entry in the catalogue raisonné edited by Paul Rosenberg in 1939. But the court ruled that this was only one among “contradictory elements” and that Sotheby’s and Mondex “did not support this hypothesis by any direct proof of such sales, at a time when France was at peace and the art market well structured”.
In court, Remi Sermier, a lawyer for Sotheby’s, also disputed the court’s jurisdiction on a sale made in London. But the court stated that, under French law, the annulment of the 1941 dispossession acts makes all subsequent sales of the work null and void. However, the court chose not to cancel the agreement signed between Mondex and the two heirs who had waived all their rights to the painting just before the sale, in exchange for a share of the sale price.
The ruling could trigger a cascade of ligitation internationally. Sotheby’s is “considering whether to join the appeal”, a spokesperson says, stressing that “client confidentiality is of paramount importance” for the company and it is not ready to willingly disclose the identity of the painting’s buyer. The spokesperson adds: “There is a procedure that will need to be followed in order to enforce the decision in the UK.”
In case of success, the Flavian family will have to face the current possessor, who can demand compensation from Sotheby’s. For its part, the auction house could turn against Mondex and the consignor of the work, because, according to sources close to the case, the settlement agreement Mondex and the seller signed contains an indemnity clause of which Sotheby’s is the beneficiary.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.title: Andy Warhol’s ‘Camouflage’ Portraits Inspired Piaget’s New Limited-Edition Watch
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.text:
Andy Warhol amassed quite the watch collection during his life—including a piece or two from Piaget (around seven, to be exact). And now, the maison has collaborated with the Andy Warhol Foundation for Visual Arts to bring an homage to the artist to your wrist.
Meet the Camouflage watch, a creation inspired by Warhol’s Camouflage self-portraits, which the artist crafted in 1986. As such, just 86 pieces of this iteration of the Andy Warhol watch will be made. Piaget takes the bold colors splashed across the American creative’s face in the series and plops them right on the dial. Here, sodalite and turquoise stones are the stars in waves of blue, paired alongside satin-finished gold and polished rose gold to add texture and dimension to that camouflage look. Piaget uses 27 pieces in all to make the dial, which it took over 100 hours of R&D and craftsmanship to come to life, into a blend of blue and warm hues.
Beating away inside the gadrooned white-gold case lies Piaget’s 501 P1 caliber, an automatic movement that powers those dauphine hands and offers up a 40-hour power reserve. Flip the watch over, and you’ll catch a glimpse of Warhol’s engraved signature, as well as the number of watches in the series.
“Our objective is to take inspiration from Andy Warhol’s creations without strictly reproducing each of his works on a dial,” Stéphanie Sivrière, artistic director of Piaget, said in a press statement. “The direct connection between Andy Warhol and Maison Piaget is color, particularly through the use of ornamental stones, which remains the common thread of this very distinctive timepiece.”
This isn’t the first time the duo has teamed up, either. In 2024, Piaget was given the go-ahead by the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts to rename its Black Tie watch (itself a reinvention of the iconic Ref. 15102, a 45 mm cushion-shaped timepiece Warhol owned) in Warhol’s honor. Under the new license, the maison was also able to craft one watch annually that pulled from the artist’s oeuvre. As a result, Piaget dropped the limited Collage timepiece back in 2025, home to blocks of pink opal, green chrysoprase, and yellow serpentine on the dial, now followed by the 2026 iteration (price available upon request). We’ll just have to wait and see what’s in the cards for 2027, then.
	As part of Art Week NYC, a citywide gathering celebrating contemporary art, Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, is speaking with ARTnews senior editor Maximilíano Durón about Warhol’s love of timepieces and the watchmaker’s collaboration with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts that grew out of it. The talk takes place at the PMC Studio on Saturday, November 14. RSVP here.

Art Basel Miami Beach has unveiled a “Premium Discovery” pass. Available for one- and two-day increments, and priced at $3,600 and $4,500, respectively, the pass promises a “Signature Experience” at the event, which will launch in previews December 2–3 before opening to the general public December 4–6. Despite its many perks, the Premium Discovery pass will not gain visitors entry to the fair’s inaugural preview day, and will only get them into the three-hour vernissage on the second preview day.
Those purchasing the single-day pass may attend the December 3 vernissage, from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m., and enjoy a “curated journey” on December 4 or 5. Buyers of the two-day pass can expect the “ultimate Art Basel Miami Beach Immersion” on both December 4 and 5 and may also attend the vernissage. Holders of both single- and two-day passes can attend all three public days with early entry. Other benefits include concierge service during the public days, access to the collectors’ lounge, invitation to select VIP events, a guided tour of the show conducted by director Bridget Finn, and an “exclusive Art Basel gift.”
Those seeking a slightly less expensive experience can purchase the “Premium Connection” pass ($2,600) or a “Premium” pass ($1,250). The former comes with concierge service and the aforementioned gift; the latter does not, but both guarantee entry to the vernissage and the collectors’ lounge.
For those of more modest means, a single-day standard ticket will get you into any one of the public days for $92—one forty-ninth (1/49th) the price of the Premium Discovery pass.

Generalstreik in Frankreich: Sie hoffen, dass das nur der Anfang ist
In 207 Städten wurde in Frankreich gestreikt. Unterwegs mit der Lehrerin und Vorsitzenden der Bildungsgewerkschaft Nara Cladera.
Die Schüler*innen laufen ganz vorn, klar, sagt Nara Cladera. Dann die Gewerkschafts-Chef*innen, auch klar. „Und dann kommen wir schon.“ Die Lehrer*innen. Bei der größten Demo in Frankreich seit Jahren wollen auch sie vorn dabei sein. Alles hat ja an den Schulen angefangen. „Und dann kommt Planète Boum Boum.“ Planète Boum Boum? „Wie erklärt man das jetzt?“, fragt Cladera ihre Kollegin, die neben ihr am Donnerstagmorgen in der Garage des Gewerkschaftshauses im 10. Pariser Bezirk steht und Flugblätter in einen Transporter lädt. „Techno-Demo-Kollektiv“, ist die Antwort.
Cladera, 57, ist Grundschullehrerin und eine der Vorsitzenden der Bildungsgewerkschaft SUD éducation. Sie arbeitet südlich von Paris, im Département Val-de-Marne. Dort liegt der Vorort Créteil, wo die großen Bildungsproteste Mitte September begonnen hatten.
Premierminister Sébastien Lecornu will 2027 rund 10 Prozent des Regierungsbudgets einsparen. 1.800 Lehrerstellen sollen wegfallen, 2026 waren bereits 4.000 gestrichen worden. Als die Sparpläne bekannt wurden, protestieren zuerst Lehrer:innen des Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in Créteil gegen fehlendes Personal und unbesetzte Stellen. Ihre Schüler:innen schlossen sich an. „Und von da aus ging es immer weiter,“ sagt Cladera. „Es breitete sich aus wie ein Tropfen Öl, der ins Wasser fällt.“
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Sieben Mal gab es seitdem landesweite Proteste. Für den 5. November haben praktisch alle Gewerkschaften des Landes zum Streik aufgerufen.
Bis zu 20 Prozent ihrer Schüler:innen seien depressiv
Cladera steigt auf den Fahrersitz, eine Kollegin setzt sich neben sie. Draußen staut sich der Verkehr. Viele Pendler sind auf das Auto ausgewichen, rund die Hälfte der Regionalzüge fällt streikbedingt aus. „Das ist doch schon mal was“, sagt Cladera. Sie lenkt den Transporter durch den Pariser Nordosten.
„Der Druck“, sagt ihre Kollegin, „der hat viele Schüler:innen aufgebracht“. 37 Stunden pro Woche verbrächten Gymnasiast:innen in der Schule, die Aussichten auf einen Studienplatz seien völlig ungewiss. 15 bis 20 Prozent ihrer Schüler:innen seien depressiv, sagt Claderas Kollegin.
Jetzt sind sie am Place de la République angekommen, wo die Demo starten soll. „Die haben den Verkehr immer noch nicht gesperrt, das darf nicht wahr sein“, sagt Cladera. Sie parkt den Transporter auf dem Fahrstreifen.
Es sei auch die Repression, die Schüler*innen auf die Straße treibe, sagt sie. „Die Polizei hat sie direkt vor den Schulen angegriffen, mit Tränengas beschossen.“ Einschüchterung, um die Mobilisierung zu ersticken. „Aber sie haben das Gegenteil erreicht. Das wird groß heute.“
Haushalt ohne Zustimmung
Am Mittwoch hat die Nationalversammlung über Macrons Haushaltsentwurf abgestimmt: 458 Abgeordnete stimmten dagegen, 0 dafür, obwohl Macrons Fraktion 90 Abgeordnete hat. Die Verfassung erlaubt ihm jedoch, den Haushalt auch ohne Parlamentszustimmung aufzustellen. Seit 2022 macht Macron das jedes Jahr so. Geht es nach den Gewerkschaften, soll der erste Generalstreiktag deshalb nur der Anfang einer langen Protestwelle sein.
Die Gewerkschaftsleute um Cladera pumpen große Ballons auf und zurren sie auf dem Dach des Transporters fest. In den umliegenden Cafés liegt die Tageszeitung Le Parisien. „Die Liste der 200 heruntergekommensten Gymnasien Frankreichs“ ist die Titelgeschichte. Ordner legen Binden an, die Straße füllt sich. Sophie Binet, die Chefin der Gewerkschaft CGT, bedankt sich bei allen, die trotz der Gewalt der Polizei der vergangenen Wochen auf die Straße gegangen seien. „Die Frage ist nicht, ob wir gewinnen, sondern wie viel“, sagt Binet.
Doch seit 1990 hat die französische Industrie ein Drittel ihrer Arbeitsplätze verloren. Chinesische Autobauer übernehmen französische Fabriken, die nicht mehr gebraucht werden, um dort Elektroautos zu bauen – mit einem Bruchteil der früheren Belegschaften. So sind nur noch rund zwei Millionen Französ*innen Gewerkschaftsmitglieder, keine acht Prozent der abhängig Beschäftigten. Anders als in Deutschland liegt die Rolle der Gewerkschaften in Frankreich vor allem darin, sozialpolitischen Druck auf den Staat zu machen. Doch der ist heute so hoch verschuldet wie nie zuvor. Fast 116 Prozent der Wirtschaftsleistung waren es 2025, 3,5-mal so viel wie 1990.
Als sich der sozialdemokratische Präsidentschaftskandidat Raphaël Glucksmann an die Demospitze stellt, wird er ausgebuht. Es sei ihm „völlig egal, ob Aktivisten meine Anwesenheit nicht gefällt“, sagt er Reportern – geht dann aber. Bejubelt wird hingegen der Linkspopulist und EU-Skeptiker Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Überall sind die Plakate der von ihm hierarchisch geführten Partei La France insoumise (LFI, Unbeugsames Frankreich). Junge Frauen tragen Schilder: „LFI statt LBD“. LBD sind die Gummigeschoss-Gewehre der Polizei, mit denen diese in den vergangenen Wochen demonstrierende Schüler:innen verletzt hat. In einem Straßencafé lässt sich der linke Autor Didier Eribon mit Mélenchon ablichten und postet das Foto stolz.
Palästina allgegenwärtig
Feuerwehrleute in Uniform sind auf der Straße, in Frankreichfahnen gehüllt wie in einen Mantel. Andere tragen die Fahnen wie Bürgermeister über der Brust. Eine alte Frau hält ein Schild hoch: „Endlich wieder 17 sein“. Schüler:innen halten Plakate: „Mehr Lehrer, weniger Faschos.“ Palästina ist allgegenwärtig: „Finanziert Schulen, keinen Genozid“. Ein Mann hat einen Stand aufgebaut, er verkauft Frankreichfahnen, Palästinafahnen und Kufijas für 10 Euro. Viele nehmen auf ihren Schildern Bezug auf zurückliegende Wahlen: Ungarn, Serbien, Israel, Brasilien, USA, sie hoffen auf den Vibe-Shift, einen antipopulistischen globalen Stimmungswechsel, der auch in Frankreich ankommt und im nächsten Frühjahr Marine Le Pen von der Macht fernhält.
Ein Anarchisten-Block hält sich nicht an die Marschordnung. Er stellt sich vor die erste Reihe. Tiefschwarz, vermummt, die Fäuste oben. Ein riesiges Transparent: „Wir werden nur das haben, was wir uns zu nehmen wissen“. Die Fotografen halten drauf, als hätten sie ein seltenes Tier entdeckt. Nach ein paar Minuten kommen Hundertschaften der Polizei. Ohne Vorwarnung stürmen sie in den Block, prügeln auf die Demonstranten ein, reißen das Transparent mit der unerhörten Plünderungs-Propaganda herunter und schleifen einige Schwarzgekleidete davon.
Cladera will losfahren, aber der Transporter kommt nicht vom Fleck. Zehntausende strömen aus allen Richtungen auf den Boulevard Voltaire und ziehen wie ein wabernder Teppich zum Place de la Nation. Es dauert mehr als zwei Stunden, bis die Wagen, die eigentlich an der Demospitze fahren sollten, sich in Bewegung setzen können.
Es gehe „um die Umverteilung des Reichtums, um soziale Gerechtigkeit“, sagt Cladera. „Schon die Schüler:innen sagen: Wir sehen, dass unseren Eltern das Geld nicht bis zum Monatsende reicht.“
1,6 Millionen Demonstranten
Am Donnerstag zeigt sich, wie groß der Einfluss der Gewerkschaften noch ist. Im ganzen Land wird gestreikt, in 207 Städten seien insgesamt 1,6 Millionen Menschen zu den Demos gekommen, meldet die CGT am Abend. 350.000 seien es allein in Paris gewesen. Das Innenministerium spricht von 600.000 landesweit, es blieb fast überall friedlich. Die Frustration über den neoliberalen und autoritären Macron, die Angst vor einer Präsidentin Le Pen, die Wut der Jugend über die Bildungsmisere – viele hoffen, dass die Verzahnung der Schüler*innen- und der Sozialproteste eine neue politische Dynamik auslöst und die Gewerkschaften eine womöglich tragende Rolle spielen.
Die Lehrer*innen von SUD éducation wissen jedenfalls, was die jungen Leute hören wollen. Das von ihnen eingeladene Planète-Boum-Boum-Kollektiv liefert ab, spielt seine Kirmestechno-Version des Sowjet-Hits „Katjuscha“, „Alles was wir wollen ist Generalstreik“ als Refrain. Mit brennenden Bengalos zieht der Block am Abend auf den Place de la Nation.
„Wir hoffen, dass das heute nur der Anfang ist“, sagt Cladera. „Die Regierung ist nervös, wir dürfen nicht nachgeben“, schreibt die SUD abends. Was das genau heiße, das werde man dann sehen, sagt Cladera. Es sei immer „ein Mysterium, wie so eine politische Dynamik weitergeht“.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-lula-.title: Austerity Is Now the Central Conflict in Brazilian Politics
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-lula-.author: André Singer, Catarina Príncipe, Aldo Cordeiro Sauda
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-lula-.text:
Austerity Is Now the Central Conflict in Brazilian Politics
Lula da Silva beat Flávio Bolsonaro to win a fourth term as Brazil’s president. Political scientist André Singer says the hardest fight is still ahead: Brazil’s bourgeoisie wants harsh austerity, and Lula’s coalition is split over it.
- Interview by
- Catarina Príncipe
- Aldo Cordeiro Sauda
On October 4, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election nearly two points ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Three weeks later, Lula turned the result around and won a fourth term in the October 25 runoff. In between, left-led demonstrations filled the streets of hundreds of Brazilian cities. The government also banned online betting, backed a forty-hour workweek, and raised the benefit of Bolsa Família, the cash-transfer program for poor families that Lula created in 2003.
Few analysts know Lula’s political project better than André Singer. A professor of political science at the University of São Paulo, Singer served as Lula’s spokesperson from 2003 to 2007 and press secretary from 2005 to 2007. He developed the concept of Lulism in Os sentidos do lulismo (2012) and O lulismo em crise (2018), and his new book, Impasse: O Brasil diante da onda reacionária, came out in August.
After the runoff, Singer spoke with Catarina Príncipe and Aldo Cordeiro Sauda for Jacobin about Bolsonarism as autocracy with a fascist bias, the Brazilian bourgeoisie’s silence during the campaign, and why the second-round mobilization was not populism. He also discussed the fight over austerity that awaits Lula’s fourth term.
- Catarina Príncipe You’ve written about the idea of an “autocracy with a fascist bias” to understand the phenomena of Donald Trump in the United States and Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil. Could you explain this idea further?
- André Singer Honestly, I can’t speak directly about Trumpism, because I don’t have enough expertise. So I’ll talk about Bolsonarism, the experience from which I formulated the idea of an autocratic tendency with a fascist bias. Studying the Bolsonaro presidency of 2019–2022, one can show empirically that he tried to reshape Brazil’s institutions in the direction of an autocratic regime. One of the major conflicts during his term was over the independence of the Federal Police. For an American audience: The Federal Police is equivalent to the FBI. It is a national police force for the country’s major security problems, because everyday problems fall to the state governments. But the big questions of corruption, organized crime, drug trafficking, and arms trafficking are all the Federal Police’s business. That is why a convention that successive presidents have observed since the return to democracy in the 1980s is so important: guaranteeing the Federal Police’s independence. The president of the republic appoints the director, but presidents have made a practice of appointing directors who have a certain independence from themselves. Bolsonaro made a point of violating that convention and appointing a Federal Police leadership at the service of his own political interests. I’m describing this because it is the most evident case of all: he tried to manipulate the Federal Police to concentrate power. Why do I say this autocratic tendency has a fascist bias? Because I find in it certain elements in common with historical fascism. Why don’t I say it’s fascist tout court? Because there are many elements that don’t correspond. Let me give one element in common: the activation, through propaganda, of the unconscious of the masses. It is a kind of advertising that aims to hook the voter, the citizen, and the supporter through unconscious identification rather than rational argument. That doesn’t mean there aren’t also arguments of a material nature, material interests; I’m not saying it is merely a technique aimed at the unconscious. But I think this is very typical of fascism and not of the nonfascist right. What isn’t in common with fascism? For example, there is no political party organized into militias, as in Italian fascism and then German Nazism. There is also no warlike rhetoric, in the sense of external war: Bolsonarism has a very strange nationalism of submission to the United States — something hard to understand. But it has no rhetoric of confrontation with other countries or of territorial expansion, an important element of historical fascism. Since some elements are in common and many are not, I proposed a way of understanding the Bolsonaro phenomenon. We are facing an autocratic tendency — that is proven — with a fascist tendency that we still need to test. Meanwhile, there is a more general theoretical problem: the concept of fascism isn’t well defined. Strange as it may seem, that is the problem we have to face: arriving at a concept of fascism that lets us understand the present situation. Obviously we are interested in understanding history, but with a view to the present and the future.
- Catarina Príncipe In an interview, I heard you distinguish between fascism from below and fascism from above. Which class does this autocracy with a fascist bias mobilize most?
- André Singer Marxist-inspired thought has already made clear the characteristics of historical fascism, and one stands out: fascism is a movement that comes from below, not from above. Leon Trotsky first made that contribution, in his writings on Germany, and it still holds; it is a fundamental distinction. Bolsonarism has this characteristic: it comes from below; it is not a movement of the ruling class. It draws in the middle strata, but it quickly spreads to intermediate popular layers, which form its backbone. So in Brazil today, the far right penetrates from below.
- Catarina Príncipe How do you analyze the relationship between the ruling class and politics, given the existence of what you call two cross-class coalitions: the Bolsonarist “confederacy” and the Lulist “concertación”? What is the composition of these two coalitions?
- André Singer I call one the “confederacy,” by a certain analogy with the nineteenth-century American case, and the other the “concertación,” by analogy with Chile after Augusto Pinochet. I developed these two hypotheses to understand the 2022 election. So I’ll answer with 2022 in mind, then briefly go through the changes in 2026. The idea of the confederacy was that a coalition of agribusiness entrepreneurs and service sector entrepreneurs in the cities formed. Certain evangelical denominations, which represent a kind of Brazilian Bible Belt, joined them. These denominations account for about 30 percent of the Brazilian electorate, and Bolsonarism has repeatedly won 70 percent of their vote. In the 2022 election, the whole of the security forces joined these two components, the entrepreneurs and the evangelical Bible Belt, from the armed forces down to the regional (state) police forces. These forces represent a large contingent. Besides everyone formally engaged in security work, Brazil has an enormous army of private security guards, because public security can’t cope with the very serious crime problem. These three tracks of the confederacy, so to speak, created an enormous corridor through the interior of the country. It runs from the north of Rio Grande do Sul to the south of the North Region, through the interior of São Paulo and Minas Gerais, the country’s most industrialized states. That corridor aligned with Bolsonarism, which largely explains its significant electoral power. In addition, the evangelical Bible Belt gives Bolsonarism a very strong bridgehead in Brazil’s large metropolitan regions. In 2026, there was a change: because of the failed coup attempt, the armed forces pulled back. They had been very important because Bolsonaro, a former army captain, went through the military academy with the men who, by coincidence, made up the high command when he took office. He brought them into the government, and so the armed forces were deeply committed to the Bolsonaro government. That is no longer the case. You can’t identify anyone of note from the armed forces in the campaign of his son Flávio Bolsonaro. But we know that the police forces backed that candidacy discreetly, rather than explicitly, as they had with Jair Bolsonaro’s government. I call it a confederacy, although it has no connection with slavery. But it does have this connection: it divided Brazil. It united the interior, as if against the big cities, even though, I repeat, the evangelical denominations have influence in the big cities. You also notice a certain prejudice against the Northeast and an underlying ideology that a more modern Brazil would be better off rid of a more backward Brazil. It is a kind of implicit ideology, which sometimes shows up more, sometimes less. As for the concertación: the name came to me because, to build the coalition that sustained him, President Lula made an alliance with sectors of the old Brazilian Social Democracy Party (PSDB). Until 2018, the PSDB had been the main rival of Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT). The current vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, headed the sectors willing to join. The PSDB as a whole has shrunk to a small party, and it stayed neutral: it backed Lula neither in 2022 nor now. But the alliance with Alckmin represented a union with former PSDB sectors willing to form the democratic front. So, as in Chile, the two great adversaries came together: in Chile, the Socialist Party and the Christian Democratic Party; in Brazil, the PT and the PSDB. Along with this party coalition, there was an important class coalition. Lulism represents the base of the Brazilian social pyramid, as everyone knows. But the alliance with this faction of the PSDB also brought in what I call the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie, the most modern sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which backed President Lula in the second round of 2022, not the first. That was very important both for his victory and for the future of the government. In this 2026 election, that sector of the bourgeoisie did not speak out; it stayed neutral and backed neither Flávio Bolsonaro nor President Lula. João Moreira Salles — founder of Piauí magazine, an important filmmaker, and an heir to one of Brazil’s biggest banking families — wrote a very powerful article on the importance of that silence. The consequence of that silence was the acceptance, practically until the last minute, of a Flávio Bolsonaro victory. An extraordinary movement reversed that in this year’s second round. To conclude for now: the cosmopolitan sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which stayed silent, is no longer explicitly present in the concertación.
- Catarina Príncipe You define Latin American populism as a mass phenomenon: in certain circumstances, classes take the form of multitudes with little or no class organization, connecting people and leader directly. Was this type of populism what secured Lula’s victory? And how can we reconnect this expression of the multitude with more sustained class organization?
- André Singer I think the concept of populism doesn’t apply to the second-round victory. It’s a very interesting question, and it’s going to give me some work, because I’ll have to develop something more sophisticated to account for the phenomenon. But at first sight, I think we had a social explosion — let’s call it that — without the characteristics of populism. It was more organized and more conscious of its aims than the populist phenomenon implies. To be clear, my theoretical framework is Ernesto Laclau’s old definition, from 1978, not that of the so-called second Laclau. It is a good one for thinking about populism in Latin America and, of course, in Brazil too. Why do I say the explosion is more conscious and more organized? More conscious because it aimed, first, to stop the far right. Flávio Bolsonaro won [the first round] by 2 percentage points and immediately began putting together his government and saying he would change the Constitution. That was a tactical error, even from his own standpoint: it had such an impact that the democratic sectors of Brazilian society immediately began to speak out and organize. That is one side of the phenomena. The other is a feeling that President Lula needed a fourth term, because the government itself began to change during the campaign. It isn’t obvious, but President Lula changed the campaign in mid-September without saying so: he began to take measures. One event seems revealing to me. On September 11, at a rally in Porto Alegre, he said, “I know you are finding products expensive at the supermarket,” referring to coffee and beef. That is very significant, because until then the government had not addressed the population’s material needs directly. From then on, the president not only spoke to those needs but began taking measures. For example, he raised the Bolsa Família benefit, which the government had not adjusted in four years, and he banned online betting, the “bets.” Remember that Brazil is living through a triple crisis: a cost-of-living crisis, a crisis of household indebtedness, and, on top of it, an epidemic of bets. People began gambling wildly, partly to earn extra income to pay off debts. Since betting companies design bets so that the great majority lose, people ended up worse off. President Lula faced great resistance to the ban. First, many companies are involved, and long-term legal contracts were already in place; second, soccer clubs, which are very popular and important in Brazil, depended to some extent on sponsorship from those companies. The other very important decision was the switch from six workdays and one day off (6x1) to five and two (5x2), cutting the workweek from forty-four to forty hours: probably the greatest labor victory since the 1988 Constitution. Congress passed it, but everyone knows it was the president’s initiative and that he committed himself to it. Structurally, of course, it is even more important than the betting ban. But the ban has symbolic meaning, because the president decided on it during the campaign: an act of boldness and courage in defense of the popular economy. Alongside it, the government took two measures to restructure the debts of the popular classes, and others such as free public transit on weekends, which speaks directly to the young people who took to the streets. What I mean is that all this is not populist rhetoric; these are actions. It is what I call a change in the character of the government. Finally, these sectors that took to the streets are not completely disorganized. The demonstrations took place in hundreds of cities, but the largest, and most unprecedented, were in São Paulo, the country’s biggest metropolis. I have been comparing the two October demonstrations in São Paulo, on October 11 and 24, with the great right-wing demonstration for the impeachment of President Dilma Rousseff in March 2016. There had been no demonstration of this kind for at least ten years. The Left led these demonstrations, although they were not only of the Left. They formed a democratic front, with centrist sectors and possibly even a democratic right: individually, people may have gone out to defend democracy. But the leadership clearly belonged to the Left, and these are possibly the largest left-wing demonstrations in Brazil’s history. The Brazilian left has organizations: the PT, the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), the Communist Party of Brazil (PCdoB), the student organizations, the cultural associations, the unions, the neighborhood associations, and the popular movements, especially the Landless Workers’ Movement (MST) and the Homeless Workers’ Movement (MTST). On the center left, you have the Socialist Party of Brazil (PSB) and the Labour Democratic Party (PDT). In short, Brazil has an organizational structure, and it mobilized. So, from these two angles, I wouldn’t describe this as a populist phenomenon; something different happened.
- Aldo Cordeiro Sauda This year, you observed a pendular movement by the cosmopolitan wing of the bourgeoisie toward the far-right candidacy, the opposite of its support for Lula’s election in 2022. Internationally, US foreign policy shows the same pendular movement: sympathy for Lula under Joe Biden in 2022, explicit support for Bolsonarism under Trump in 2026. To what extent does the Brazilian ruling class’s shift toward Bolsonarism express mere deference to Washington?
- André Singer As far as I understand, the sector I call cosmopolitan — in the American case, the big technology companies — backed Biden in 2020. In 2024, it wasn’t very clear to me what they were doing, but they didn’t seem to back Trump either, with the exception of Elon Musk. Yet when Trump took office, all of them were there. In the Brazilian case, though, it seems plausible that a conversion of the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie to the far right influenced the Brazilian bourgeoisie. Until the last minute, there was a certain expectation that this sector might speak out in favor of President Lula. That sector committed itself to democracy in 2022, in a movement broader than support for President Lula. In August 2022, at a demonstration in São Paulo, those business leaders issued a letter. They said they would not accept, under any circumstances, a refusal to recognize the election result — exactly what the White House said. Those two positions were very important in keeping most of the armed forces from joining the coup, because the military knew it could not govern without that support. So you see: there is a Brazilian phenomenon. A link to a transformation in the United States is a possible hypothesis.
- Catarina Príncipe Our understanding of the question is that the Brazilian cosmopolitan bourgeoisie is staying neutral now because of the political change in the United States from Biden to Trump. At the time of the coup attempt, the Biden presidency was very important in stopping it from going forward. Now, with Trump, there might be some attempt at direct intervention in Brazilian politics. So, part of the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie doesn’t want to take a position today, to avoid a falling-out with US policy and with a possible Bolsonaro victory. It’s less a direct mirror between fractions of the bourgeoisie.
- André Singer Then I’ll take advantage of your interpretation to add something that makes the problem more complex. The major point of division between that sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie and Lula’s third government is the fiscal deficit. That sector demands a big cut in public spending, which in its view would have to fall on pension benefits, and it wants to delink them from the minimum wage. The Brazilian Constitution links the two, so raising the minimum wage in real terms also raises all benefits. The other target is the constitutional floor for health and education: the Brazilian Constitution requires that a certain share of annual tax revenue go to health and education, and this cannot go down. The bourgeoisie’s aim is to remove that floor from the Constitution, so that this spending falls. So, we have a very serious issue: on one side the pension system, all the retirees; on the other, the two main social policies that form the social core of the 1988 Constitution, health and education. That is the main problem. We still don’t know whether there is also a certain caution or a desire to align with the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie.
- Aldo Cordeiro Sauda National sovereignty took center stage in the campaign, perhaps for the first time since the return to democracy. What role did this issue play in the second-round turnaround against Flávio Bolsonaro?
- André Singer The Trump administration’s offensive against Brazil — the tariffs and its direct or indirect intervention in the elections — has put national sovereignty on the agenda. Trump justified the first tariffs by saying that Brazil was persecuting his preferred candidate, Jair Bolsonaro. Brazil today does not have a very strong nationalist current. A nationalism is now starting to grow, because the global situation has changed and the country faces political-economic aggression — let’s call it that. So nationalism has come onto the agenda, but in my opinion — and I may be wrong — it has still not become a central issue.
- Catarina Príncipe Lula wants to transform the Brazilian economy by investing in the green economy, infrastructure, and artificial intelligence (data centers) and by using Brazil’s resources in rare metals and minerals. How much room for maneuver does he have to do this, given the New Fiscal Framework, the Lula government’s 2023 fiscal rule capping annual spending growth at 70 percent of revenue growth? How should we think about his government’s relationship with the bourgeoisie in this fourth term and the new balance of forces? Do you believe the bourgeoisie will tend to deepen its conflict with the PT, intensifying the pendular movement? And in this context, what happens to the mass mobilization from below that we saw in the second round?
- André Singer I think this is the central point regarding the fourth term: what the outcome of this conflict will be. The stock market fell nearly 14 percent the day after the election. As I have been saying, the market has no vote, but it has money, and its message is clear: if you don’t cut public spending, we’re leaving. The question of fiscal adjustment is truly central, because the bourgeoisie is demanding harsh austerity. In my opinion, the demand for austerity is the fundamental issue in Brazilian politics today, but in general nobody puts it openly: it remains an implicit debate. That is partly because we are not managing to politicize the problem, to make the popular classes, the working class, aware that this is what is at stake. This is the main confrontation. This organizes Brazilian politics. In my recent book, Impasse: O Brasil diante da onda reacionária, I tried to show that this issue splits the democratic front in two. It is, as Americans say, an elephant in the room: everyone treats it as if it didn’t exist. I felt that my role was to bring it to the surface; obviously I can’t do that alone, but I can contribute to some extent. The conflict is immediate, because the transformation Brazil needs, which runs through reindustrialization, is a gigantic task. Brazil is an enormous country, and you don’t change a structure of this order without major investment. This transformation can’t rely on public investment alone; there must also be private investment. But we have to think with the instruments we have. Perry Anderson says Keynesianism no longer works, so we need to create new mechanisms; but until we have them, I’ll use the old ones. The state will have to induce this development process, although it also has to bring in other investors. There is, therefore, an incompatibility between the country’s needs and this radical cut in public spending, which goes in the opposite direction. This is the central point. Even if the terms of the debate were not clear, I think the large demonstrations in hundreds of Brazilian cities point toward the government having this commitment. We’ll have to follow events to see how it unfolds.
- Catarina Príncipe Your earlier book defined Lulism as “combating poverty without confronting capital.” Can Lulism go beyond itself, and does it want to? Is there room to do so today, given the current party arithmetic in Congress? And how can the Brazilian left organize to force it to take measures that go beyond welfarism?
- André Singer I’ll start with Congress, which I think is simpler. In the Congress that takes office in 2027, the far right has grown, not at the expense of the Left but of other forces on the Right. In the Chamber of Deputies, it went from 91 to 121 deputies, out of 513 seats. That is significant: since the return to democracy, we would hardly find such a large single-party caucus. But it decides nothing on its own. What we will have is permanent negotiation, which is already happening: Lula’s third government already negotiated permanently with what we in Brazil call the Centrão. To be clear, the Centrão is the established right, the traditional right, so to speak. It generally holds the majority in Brazil’s National Congress, because the Brazilian electoral system reproduces small local oligarchies that tend to dominate legislative elections. This is structural in Brazil, and it will continue. President Lula has specialized in negotiating with those sectors. The third term was the most difficult in this respect, because Congress gained power from what we in Brazil call the “secret budget” (orçamento secreto) [budget amendments through which lawmakers steer federal funds without disclosing who requested them]. Even so, the president managed to pass his two boldest proposals. The first was the income-tax exemption for those who earn up to R$5,000 (about US$940) a month, offset by a levy on those who earn more than R$50,000 (about US$9,400). The Chamber of Deputies approved it unanimously. The second was the change of the work schedule from 6x1 to 5x2, which we have already discussed. The Chamber had already approved it unanimously, and the Senate has just passed it by an overwhelming majority. This shows that such negotiation is possible. The traditional right makes concessions on one side and concessions on the other. Its concession to the far right is an effort to reduce the sentences the courts imposed on Jair Bolsonaro and on everyone they convicted of taking part in the 2022 coup attempt, and that effort will expand. It will probably have real consequences: the far right will try to make it possible for Bolsonaro to run in 2030. I think that is its outlook. I repeat, it won’t achieve this without the support of the Right, but depending on the back-and-forth negotiations, it could happen. I now turn to the problem of the Left. The Left should not leave the democratic front. The central problem in Brazil, as in many countries around the world, is to isolate the far right and reverse its advance toward power everywhere. Looking at the long term, we are witnessing a gradual, slow, but constant advance of the far right, sometimes faster, sometimes slower. If the far right comes to power and consolidates itself around the whole world, the working class will suffer a tremendous setback in every respect. Our task, then, is to avoid this by isolating the far right and defeating it as an alternative for power in Brazil. For that, we have to stay in the democratic front. But two incompatible economic programs divide the democratic front. We have to fight explicitly inside this democratic front for our position to win a majority. I’m convinced that democracy depends on the majority of the population recognizing in it an answer to their problems; if it doesn’t, it won’t last. That is the best contribution the Left can and must make to the defense of democracy. Lulism, as I characterized it, is a movement that seeks to combat poverty, which is fundamental in Brazil, without confronting capital. I stand by that definition. But political reality is dynamic. We and all the other actors are facing new situations, so new things are bound to happen. As you know, we can’t predict the future; we can only see tendencies. I would end by saying that a popular commitment is in Lulism’s nature: it depends on a popular base; it is a popular movement. Beyond that, only the political process will tell.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.title: US-Sanktionen gegen Havanna | USA kehrt in Kuba zurück zum Kolonialismus des weißen Mannes
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.author: Christian Klemm
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.text:
- Kommentare
- US-Sanktionen gegen Havanna
USA kehrt in Kuba zurück zum Kolonialismus des weißen Mannes
Washington erlässt neue Sanktionen gegen den Inselstaat. Der Verlust von Menschenleben ist dabei einkalkuliert. Ein Kommentar.
Die Bösartigkeit dieser US-Administration ist kaum noch zu toppen. Nachdem die Regierung von Donald Trump mit einer Seeblockade Kuba von internationalen Öllieferungen fast vollständig abgeschnitten hat, holt Washington zum nächsten Schlag aus – diesmal gegen die kubanische Elektroindustrie: Am Donnerstag (Ortszeit) gab das dortige Außenministerium bekannt, erstmals zwei chinesische Elektronikunternehmen auf die Sanktionsliste zu setzen. Sie werden beschuldigt, der kubanischen Armee Elektronik und Sicherheitskomponenten zu verkaufen. Die Begründung ist ein Meisterstück antikubanischer Rabulistik aus dem Weißen Haus: Die »herrschende Elite« in dem Karibikstaat eigne sich Energieressourcen und maritime Transportmittel an und lasse »das kubanische Volk mit Stromausfällen, Treibstoffknappheit und einer darbenden Wirtschaft zurück«.
Für die aktuellen Stromausfälle, Treibstoffknappheit und die großen Wirtschaftsprobleme Kubas ist jedoch nicht die »herrschende Elite« dort verantwortlich, sondern einzig und alleine die »blonden Bestien« (Augusto César Sandino) aus dem Norden. Die verfolgen nämlich ein großes Ziel: die Karibikinsel wieder zu dem machen, was es zur Zeit der Batista-Diktatur war, die von der Revolution 1959 hinweggefegt wurde: ein Spielerparadies und Bordell vor allem für US-amerikanische Touristen mit haufenweise Dollars im Gepäck.
Unser Kollege Johannes Hecht befindet sich zurzeit auf Kuba. Seine Eindrücke von der Karibikinsel könnt ihr hier in einem Kurzvideo sehen.
Die neuen Sanktionen sind vor allem ein Problem für die kubanische Solarindustrie, weil Havanna beim Aufbau seiner Solarparks auf chinesische Technologie angewiesen ist. Die Volksrepublik in Fernost hat sich seit Jahren zu einem zuverlässigen Handelspartner für die Genossen in der Karibik erwiesen. Wenn sie nun durch die USA sanktioniert werden, ist das für Peking wirtschaftlich leicht zu verkraften. Für Kuba allerdings ist das eine Verschärfung seiner chronischen Energieknappheit. Durch sie ist beispielsweise schon jetzt die Gesundheitsversorgung der Bevölkerung betroffen. Auch die Nahrungsmittelproduktion ist auf Strom angewiesen. Das heißt in der Konsequenz: Die Trump-Regierung kalkuliert für ihr politisches Ziel, die Insel von »den Castros zu befreien« (Nota bene: Einer lebt schon nicht mehr.), den Verlust von Menschenleben mit ein.
Der ehemalige US-Präsident Barack Obama hatte eine vorsichtige Annäherung zwischen den USA und Kuba begonnen. Donald Trump hat diese nicht nur abgebrochen, sondern die Entwicklung durch seine beinharte Hinterhofpolitik in Lateinamerika umgekehrt: Der weiße Mann aus dem industrialisierten Norden gibt wieder den Ton an. So wie zu Zeiten des Kolonialismus.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.
