https://gothamist.com/news/man-arrested-.title: Man arrested in NYC on accusations of sexual assault, rape on Cape Cod, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/man-arrested-.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/man-arrested-.text:
A former rowing coach was arrested Thursday in the Bronx on allegations of sexual assault and rape stemming from his time coaching on Cape Cod, according to law enforcement officials.
Guy Monseair, 57, was taken into custody on City Island around 7 a.m. by officers from the NYPD and Homeland Security Investigations Human Trafficking Task Force, officials said. According to the Barnstable, MA Police Department, he is charged with four counts of aggravated statutory rape of a child and one count of indecent assault and battery on a child under 14.
Police said all of the alleged incidents took place between 2008 and 2011 while Monseair was a rowing coach at several different clubs on the Cape. Barnstable Police said they were made aware of the allegations last month.
It was not immediately clear when Monseair moved to the Bronx. NYPD officials said he started the City Island Rowing group between 2012 and 2014, though officials couldn’t say if he was still involved in the organization. There have not been any allegations against Monseair from his time in New York, according to the NYPD.
An undated online profile page lists Monseair as the head coach and executive director of City Island Rowing. The profile says that he grew up in Zimbabwe and moved to the U.S. to pursue his coaching career full time.
“At City Island Rowing, Monseair’s coaching philosophy emphasizes both athletic and personal growth, with a focus on resilience, teamwork, and discipline. Under his leadership, the program has grown to support a large team of athletes, many of whom have achieved national and collegiate success,” the page reads.
The organization did not immediately respond to several messages seeking comment.
In a statement, a spokesperson for USRowing said the organization revoked Monseair’s membership rights as soon as they learned about the allegations on Thursday. That means he is prohibited from participating in all competitions and activities under their jurisdiction.
USRowing also reported the matter to the U.S. Center for SafeSport, and urged other abuse survivors to come forward either online or by phone at 833-5US-SAFE (833-587-7233).
According to the Barnstable Police Department, Monseair will be extradited back to Massachusetts, where the case will be prosecuted by the Cape and Islands District Attorney's Office.
Information for his lawyer was not immediately available.
This is a developing story and was updated with new information.

https://hyperallergic.com/dc-protesters-.title: DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch
https://hyperallergic.com/dc-protesters-.author: Emma Cieslik
https://hyperallergic.com/dc-protesters-.text:
DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch
A group of 50 used puppets and a fake arch to deliver the point that Americans are against the "Arc de Trump."
WASHINGTON, DC — South of Memorial Circle, within eyeshot of the Lincoln Memorial and John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, more than 50 protesters gathered yesterday, November 5, to oppose Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch ahead of the National Capital Planning Commission’s (NCPC) final meeting to vote on the project.
Hours after the NCPC approved the arch in an 8–4 vote, a district court judge granted the District of Columbia and Virginia a 14-day restraining order to halt construction.
At the event organized by Third Act DC, an environmental and pro-democracy action group for area residents aged 60 and up, two Virginia Congressional representatives, an Arlington County Board member, and Greg Werkheiser, an attorney with Cultural Heritage Partners, spoke about how the arch would infringe on the architectural and spiritual purpose of the space. He was one of two people associated with lawsuits that the District of Columbia and Virginia, the Arlington County Board, as well as Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed against the National Park Service and Department of the Interior in opposition to the arch.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/demo.title: Is There a Left Candidate for President?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/demo.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/demo.text:
The race for 2028 is already starting, and progressives are all asking one question: Who will take up the left’s mantle in the next presidential election?
An obvious first choice for many self-described leftists, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., has said she is seriously considering a run. Ocasio-Cortez laid the groundwork for a potential presidential bid rooted in economic populism and “fighting oligarchy” while campaigning alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., for midterm candidates around the country this cycle.
Democratic strategists, however, have pointed out it would be far easier for Ocasio-Cortez to run for Democratic New York Sen. Chuck Schumer’s seat in 2028; and it’s even possible the 75-year-old presumptive majority leader will retire.
There isn’t a clear pick for another Democratic candidate with star power who could mount a truly progressive campaign — presenting the left with the threat of losing the momentum that fueled a democratic socialist wave during the primaries and animated campaigns across the ideological spectrum on Tuesday.
That, said her former spokesperson Lauren Hitt, is not Ocasio-Cortez’s problem.
“I think the wrong reason to run would be because nobody else is running in the progressive lane,” said Hitt, who now advises progressive and moderate candidates. “She has made a lot of good investments in the midterms and in helping build up the progressive bench, but it was not her job to make sure we had another person to run.”
(Representatives for Ocasio-Cortez did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
So if Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t run from the left, who will?
The Field So Far
Candidates exploring potential presidential bids include a few newer faces alongside a very similar cast of moderates who campaigned for the Democratic nomination in the 2016 and 2020 primaries.
Names like New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and even the party’s former nominee Kamala Harris are making the rounds; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has also laid the groundwork for a run. The recently reelected Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has long been viewed as a potential contender, as has Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, though he said last month he’s not planning on a run.
None of them are people you would necessarily liken to someone like Ocasio-Cortez or the grandfather of the movement behind her, Sanders himself.
Rep. Ro Khanna of California is so far the most “progressive” person openly considering a run. Khanna served as national co-chair of Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign, and he’s long been a voice for an anti-interventionist foreign policy. He drew the ire of tech billionaires for supporting a wealth tax in California.
Yet there’s a palpable skepticism around Khanna among leftists, even if they can’t quite put their finger on why. Some weren’t impressed when he defended his support for funding Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system after publicizing an arrest in the West Bank earlier this year. (Khanna later came out against funding the Iron Dome). And as a multimillionaire, he’s also drawn criticism from the right and the left for his personal wealth.
Like Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna has said he will back Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., for House Speaker despite pledges from other candidates to withhold their support for either Jeffries or Schumer, both moderates, for leadership positions next session.
Leveraging Economic Populism
It’s still incredibly early, but there’s one unifying theme emerging from Tuesday’s results for whichever candidate decides to try to court the progressive vote.
“All I know is that the populist lane is wide open for someone to seize it,” said Ravi Mangla, the spokesperson for the Working Families Party.
Victories over the past two years, from Zohran Mamdani’s election as mayor of New York City to the clutch of democratic socialists and progressives heading to Congress in January, show that Democrats can marshal discontent with Donald Trump and the far right to elect candidates running on progressive policies.
”Voters were very clear: People are very, very angry,” said Greg Krieg, a progressive Democratic strategist who works with Slingshot Strategies and is the spokesperson for the pro-Palestine super PAC American Priorities. “There is a focus on economic populism that transcends the ideological splits in the party.”
With the rising cost of living, and candidates tapping into that populism, the question for progressives is how to best wield the blue version of economic populism against the right-wing version that powered Trump’s rise.
“Right-wing populism didn’t really defeat left-wing populism, it just ran against a kind of corporate slop for many years,” Krieg said.
This era’s new “kitchen table” issues are a constellation of economic woes that voters are increasingly connecting to the forces concentrating wealth and political power in the hands of the few. Democrats should respond to that by fighting, visibly, against the things that take money out of people’s pockets, corruption and price-gouging among them, Krieg said.
“I think that the American people, if they are presented a choice of right-wing populism and left-wing populism, will opt for the left-wing populism,” Krieg said. “And I think that’s quadruply true now that we’ve done the right-wing populism experiment and it’s been such a fiasco — so let’s give them that option.”
The factors influencing how Democrats approach 2028 are taking shape now. They include the debate over who will lead the party in the House and Senate, though any effort to stop Schumer or Jeffries from leading roles would face long odds. And how Democrats fare in the next presidential race will depend in large part on what they do with their control of Congress during the last two years of Trump’s final term in office.
DSA Endorsement?
Then there is the group that helped power the rise of Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani, the next mayors of Washington and Los Angeles, and the largest incoming bloc of socialist members of Congress in history: the Democratic Socialists of America.
Any candidate that gets buy-in from DSA will have to support policies like Medicare for All, taxing the rich, a Green New Deal, and an embargo on U.S. arms to Israel. DSA, which endorsed both Sanders’s 2016 and 2020 primary bids, is running a presidential exploratory committee that will eventually vote to endorse a candidate after collecting input from its members.
DSA passed a resolution to explore a 2028 endorsement at its national convention last year. And there isn’t necessarily a consensus among its members — more than 125,000 people across 130 chapters in 43 states — on whether or not they want to see Ocasio-Cortez run, said Ella Teevan, who chairs the group’s presidential exploratory group and sits on its National Political Committee.
“The Bernie case feels just a little bit different because I think the membership was a little bit more united around Bernie, although by no means unanimously,” Teevan said. “If and when we do consider an AOC endorsement, hers will be a little bit more contentious. But like I said, that’s the beauty of DSA.”
Though Ocasio-Cortez is no shoo-in, DSA members haven’t coalesced around any other candidate — and it’s not clear they will.
“I know that there are other quote-unquote progressives who might be considering a presidential run in 2028, but I think it’s really clear for us that they need to support DSA’s core demands that most people in the United States support,” Teevan said.
“If a candidate were to come along who supported those policies, I think a considerable portion of membership would think about whether we should endorse them,” she said. “But yeah, I don’t think that there’s a natural other person with name recognition in the field that, at least, I can think of right now.”
And there may yet be candidates who enter the race who aren’t yet on the radar, said Hitt, Ocasio-Cortez’s former spokesperson: “It’s totally possible there’s a progressive champion who could fill that lane that we aren’t even thinking of yet.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

Como as plataformas digitais mudaram a disputa política, o jornalismo e a democracia no Brasil? A pergunta atravessa “Redes e rumos: jornalismo e sociedade transformada na era dos distúrbios informacionais”, livro de Sandra Bitencourt lançado na Feira do Livro de Porto Alegre.
A obra, organizada em seis partes, discute as transformações nas relações entre jornalismo, política e democracia no momento de expansão das plataformas digitais. Entre os temas estão as plataformas como arena pública, a “política das emoções” e a “batalha pela verdade” em tempos de desinformação.
Na conversa, a entrevistada analisa o Brasil que saiu das urnas em 2026. Ela comenta a atuação do “Exército do Lula”, comandado pelo deputado André Janones, e a ocupação das redes na reta final da eleição. Também fala sobre o papel do jornalismo na cena política.
Sandra Bitencourt é jornalista e doutora em Comunicação Social pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Judge puts Trump's arch project on hold despite commission's approval
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Helen Stoilas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Moments after the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC)—a review panel stacked with Trump administration appointees—approved plans for a Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, on Thursday night (5 November), a federal judge blocked construction on the project for 14 days.
The move obstructs the government’s stated aim of starting work on one of US president Donald Trump’s pet building projects immediately, despite lawsuits and public protests, and allows a court case brought by a Vietnam War veteran and the attorneys general of Washington, DC, and Virginia to continue.
In her 33-page decision, Judge Tanya S. Chutkan outlined the government’s shifting justifications for building the arch, which have included a desire to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, a more than century-old congressional act to commemorate the end of the Civil War, and even supposed national security concerns. “These arguments are unavailing,” she wrote.
She also found that “harm is certain” to be inflicted on both Washington, DC, and Virginia if construction on the arch is allowed to go ahead, as it would interrupt traffic at a vital artery into the capital for years and result in unknown damage and expense.
Trump has pushed to fast-track the project, so that it could be mostly completed before he leaves office in 2028. His efforts to leave his mark on the capital include the bulldozing of the historic East Wing of the White House to make room for a 1,000-seat ballroom, a slapdash relining of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall, and plans to paint the Eisenhower Executive Office Building white.
In another move to secure his design legacy, Trump signed an order on Thursday that aims to make the Oval Office—which he has decorated with gilded adornments—into a national monument. “It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters without a trace of irony. Presidents can create national monuments, based on the 1906 Antiquities Act, but this refers to federal lands set aside for preservation.
Trump’s grand plans have so far been helped by the fact that the committees overseeing preservation and design review for the capital are packed with appointees loyal to the president. This was most evident in Thursday’s meeting of the NCPC, where chairman Mark Paoletta—who also serves as general counsel of the Office of Management and Budget and deputy director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau—continually presented the government’s legal arguments in favour of building the arch.
When a smaller contingent of non-administration commissioners, led by DC city council chair Phil Mendelson, moved to delay the vote on the arch to December, vice chair Stuart Levenbach—who also works in the Office of Management and Budget as chief statistician—noted that "the project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today".
No explanation was given for what that time constraint involved however. In the end, the NCPC voted along loyalist lines, with the eight administration-appointed members voting to approve the arch plans and four voting against.
The vote came at the end of more than eight hours of public comments from more than 100 speakers, including public officials, veterans and families of fallen soldiers—many of them calling in from an all-day protest taking place at Memorial Circle.
Most of their testimony was excoriating, and many urged the commission not to kowtow to the self-aggrandising whims of the president. Congressman Jared Huffman, the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, said the arch lacks congressional authorisation and goes against the Height of Buildings Act and other preservation laws. He warned that those working to move forward with the arch “will put themselves at legal risk".
"I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," said Huffman, referencing the outcome of the recent US midterm elections.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ga.title: Miami Beach Dealer Faces Another Lawsuit from Artist Alleging Non-Payment
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ga.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ga.text:
Gabriel Kilongo, the dealer behind the Miami Beach–based gallery Jupiter, is facing another lawsuit from a third artist who alleges that he is withholding money from the sales of her art.
Yirui Jia, a young painter who had a solo show at Jupiter’s Miami Beach location in 2025, sued Kilongo in September in the Supreme Court of the State of New York, alleging that he had only paid her $2,000 of a $42,000 sum owed for the sales of five paintings.
It is one of four lawsuits filed in the past two years against Kilongo, whose gallery also formerly operated in New York. Others, as first reported by Urgent Matter, have centered around allegations of nonpayment, damage to art, and withheld artworks. The lawsuit regarding the damaged artwork appears to have been settled, while the others appear to still be pending.
According to Jia’s lawsuit, she received written assurances from Kilongo that he would pay her. He told her that he was “managing a very tight cash flow,” per an exchange quoted in the lawsuit, and stated that he was “waiting for a few things to clear on the gallery’s end” in order to remit payment. But he did not do this, the suit alleges, and therefore defied the consignment agreement they had signed.
The suit includes a sales report produced by Jupiter that notes that all five paintings had sold for values between $2,000 and $32,000. Two went to a Vancouver-based buyer named Bing Zhang, the document states, while the other three went to Bradley Chubb, the Buffalo Bills linebacker who was traded from the Miami Dolphins earlier this year.
“The complaint speaks for itself,” said a lawyer for Jia in a statement to ARTnews. Kilongo has not responded to the complaint at this time of writing.
He did not respond to ARTnews’s request for comment on Jia’s lawsuit specifically. But, responding to the four lawsuits facing the gallery, he said, “These are distinct proceedings, involving different circumstances and procedural histories, and should not be presented as a single narrative of wrongdoing.”
The dealer founded Jupiter in 2022, having previously worked at New York’s Mitchell-Innes & Nash gallery as an associate. The gallery has regularly shown at notable art fairs, including Untitled, Expo Chicago, and Zona Maco, and has even continued doing so as Jupiter has faced lawsuits, most recently appearing in the Independent New York art fair this past May.
Kilongo has previously touted his relationship with Jia, whose work was the subject of a solo show at Mitchell-Innes & Nash in 2024, the second to last exhibition there before the gallery transitioned to an advisory. “We have successfully placed works by artists—like Yirui, for instance—in prominent collections, including those of some museum trustees,” Kilongo said in an interview for Artnet’s Gallery Network program. “It’s always incredibly gratifying to see how her work holds up along other historical artists while still maintaining Yirui’s distinct and recognizable identity.”
Urgent Matter reported in May that Kilongo surrendered his New York gallery to his landlord and agreed to pay $25,000. It is unclear, however, whether Jupiter continues to operate in Miami Beach. The gallery’s website states that the most recently staged exhibition, a two-person show for George Clinton and Gerasimos Floratos, closed in Miami Beach this past February.
In Artnet News, Kenny Schachter reported that Jupiter was administratively dissolved on September 25, exactly one day after Jia’s lawsuit. Kilongo told ARTnews that this was not true and “does not accurately reflect [the gallery’s] current standing.”
Schachter’s column also stated that Kilongo, who was born in Democratic Republic of Congo and was raised in Israel, was detained by ICE and has since been released. Schachter attributed confirmation to James Snyder, director of New York’s Jewish Museum, but ARTnews could not establish a clear connection between Kilongo and that institution beyond the dealer having served on a host committee for a young collectors event held at the museum this past October. A database on ICE’s website that allows users to track detainees does not contain an accessible record for Kilongo.
Schachter did not mention in his column that he had himself exhibited with Jupiter in 2025. Others to have exhibited with the gallery include Emmanuel Louisnord Desir, Baseera Khan, Marcus Leslie Singleton, and Travis Fish.
The first of the lawsuits against Kilongo’s business was filed in 2025 by Jade Thacker, who alleged that she was owed $204,000 because he failed to pay her out for one sale and return works shown in 2024 that did not sell. Kilongo has not responded to Thacker’s lawsuit.
That lawsuit was followed by one in February 2026 from Location Incorporated, a New York entity based in the East Village that claimed Kilongo’s gallery had inflicted $1.6 million in damage to a sculpture shown at the Untitled Art, Miami Beach fair in 2024. Though the lawsuit did not identify the artist or work, Jupiter brought a work that year by New York–based artist Izhar Patkin. That lawsuit was dismissed and later settled, according to Urgent Matter.
And in March 2026, artist Stephanie Pierce sued Kilongo, echoing Thacker’s allegations by claiming that she was owed money for works sold in 2023 and that he withheld artworks. She sought $100,000 in damages. In this case, Kilongo responded by denying the allegations. Serving as his own legal representative, he said that “payment relating to the works has been made and that the return of the remaining works is actively in progress, with a majority already returned.”

https://www.artforum.com/news/meg-onli-a.author: Polly Watson
https://www.artforum.com/news/meg-onli-a.text:

The Whitney Museum of American Art has named Meg Onli and Zack Winokur as the curators of the 2028 Whitney Biennial.
Onli, who currently serves as the museum’s Nancy and Fred Poses Curator, co-organized the 2024 Biennial, “Even Better Than the Real Thing,” as well as the blockbuster retrospective “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New,” on view at the Whitney through spring 2027. She is the founder of the Black Visual Archive project, which documents and reviews contemporary Black culture.
Winokur, the onetime artistic director of New York’s Little Island, is a director of theater, dance, and opera widely known for his genre-defying productions. Winokur also cofounded AMOC* (American Modern Opera Company), and served as the artistic director of NYPopSUp, a statewide initiative aimed at resurrecting the performing arts post-Covid.
“Every Whitney Biennial springs from a distinct curatorial alchemy, and I couldn’t be more excited to bring Meg and Zack together to lead the 2028 edition,” said Whitney director Scott Rothkopf in a statement. “Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art. Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial.”
In a statement, Onli described herself as “thrilled” to be co-curating the event. “From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about,” she said. “I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead.”
Winokur was equally enthusiastic about partnering with Onli. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration,” he said. “It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring. As an artist, what excites me most is being in service to other artists, and I’m delighted to have the opportunity to do so in the context of the Whitney.”

https://taz.de/Union-will-Aigner-als-Bun.title: Union will Aigner als Bundespräsidentin: Es ist keine Schwäche, sich hinter eine starke Frau zu stellen
https://taz.de/Union-will-Aigner-als-Bun.author: Anna Lehmann
https://taz.de/Union-will-Aigner-als-Bun.text:
Union will Aigner als Bundespräsidentin : Es ist keine Schwäche, sich hinter eine starke Frau zu stellen
Ilse Aigner soll Bundespräsidentin werden. Das verdankt sie nicht Friedrich Merz, der erneut nicht wie ein Antreiber, sondern ein Getriebener wirkte.
E s scheint festzustehen, Ilse Aigner soll Bundespräsidentin werden. Auch die CDU stellt sich nach übereinstimmenden Medienberichten hinter sie. Die offizielle Bestätigung steht noch aus, aber zuletzt lief alles auf die bayerische Landtagspräsidentin zu. Es gab in den vergangenen Tagen kaum noch eine Politikerin in Union und SPD, die sie nicht für eine „hervorragende“ Kandidatin hielten, auch die Grünen funkten Zustimmung.
Alle warten nur noch darauf, was Friedrich Merz sagt. Der Kanzler und CDU-Vorsitzende will sich nach bisheriger Planung am Montag äußern, nach einer Sitzung des Präsidiums. Die CDU-Führungsebene, darunter auch zwei Frauen, deren Namen ebenfalls im Laufe der Debatte als mögliche Kandidatinnen aufploppten, trifft sich bereits am Sonntagabend zum Abendessen. Der Austausch darüber, wen die CDU, die formal das Vorschlagsrecht hat, als Nachfolgerin von Frank-Walter Steinmeier aufstellt, dürfte kurz werden.
Interessanter ist die Erörterung, warum Merz auch dieser Findungsprozess mal wieder komplett entglitten ist und er sich von Markus Söder so vorführen ließ. Der CSU-Chef hatte Aigner bereits im April zum ersten Mal vorgeschlagen. Der Kanzler hielt sich lange bedeckt, legte sich zuletzt lediglich darauf fest, dass eine Frau Bundespräsidentin werden soll. Wieso nutzte Merz nicht den CSU-Parteitag Ende Oktober, um das Thema abzuräumen? Stattdessen hieß es kurz zuvor, die CDU werde einen eigenen Vorschlag machen und vor zwei Wochen streute sein Umfeld noch den Namen der hessischen Fraktionsvorsitzenden Ines Claus. Ein Testballon oder eine Trotzreaktion?
Jedenfalls keine konsistente Strategie. Der CDU-Vorsitzende hat erneut keine glückliche Figur gemacht und dokumentiert, dass Personalplanung nicht sein Ding ist. Er, der sich selbst gern als Antreiber sieht, wirkte wie ein Getriebener. Aber egal, am Ende ist es kein Zeichen von Schwäche, sich hinter eine starke Frau zu stellen.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anderson-phi.title: Equality Is About Who Rules
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anderson-phi.author: Matt McManus
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anderson-phi.text:
Equality Is About Who Rules
What do we actually mean by “equality”? Few thinkers have answered that question better than Elizabeth Anderson: not identical outcomes but a society where no one gets to dominate anyone else, including at work.
There is a complex debate about the extent to which socialists prioritize equality above the full flowering of each person’s individuality. But you’d have to be quite the contrarian to deny that socialists take equality very seriously; perhaps more seriously than any other major political ideology. Prominent socialist thinkers like G. A. Cohen and Thomas Piketty have dedicated much of their work to defending the philosophical and economic merits of egalitarianism. Socialist Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech put equality at the core of his vision: “that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: ‘We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.’”
That said, the commitment of socialists and other egalitarians to equality can often seem frustratingly vague. It invites accusations of ill-defined “social justice” advocacy or even pursuing the much dreaded “equality of outcomes” through a Harrison Bergeron–like willingness to cut everyone down to size. Of course, many of these charges are lobbed in bad faith, and even the more refined versions ignore how other core principles — like liberty or order — are equally contestable and vague until explicitly defined. But having a firmer grasp on what we mean by equality and what we want would help the Left understand itself better.
Equality of What?
Few living thinkers have done more to answer this question than University of Michigan philosopher Elizabeth Anderson. A former doctoral student of John Rawls, Anderson made her name in the 1990s criticizing contemporary egalitarian philosophy and developing her own version of relational equality. More recently, Anderson has become a vigorous proponent of workplace democracy, contending that there is something deeply tyrannical about the forms of work that exist today. Her most recent book, Hijacked: How Neoliberalism Turned the Work Ethic Against Workers and How Workers Can Take It Back, argues for rehabilitating the tradition of social democratic and socialist political thought as a counter to the Right’s moralizing about work.
From the beginning, Anderson was fiercely critical of many dimensions of contemporary capitalism and its inequalities. Her early book Value in Ethics and Economics (1993) is a careful critique of how market relations and their distinct ways of reasoning about ethical questions are increasingly colonizing many spheres of society. She insisted that realizing many forms of “freedom, autonomy and welfare demands that certain goods be produced, exchanged, and enjoyed outside of market relations or in accordance with non-market norms.” While in this book Anderson typically appeals to ideas of autonomy and welfare rather than strict equality, there is a clear egalitarian undercurrent. She criticizes libertarians’ “fetishism” of property and markets as the sole site of freedom, and how this leads them to be blind to the “social relations of domination that exist prior to market transactions and that condition the choices individuals make there.” For instance, a long history of patriarchal subordination means that women may feel compelled to enter into exploitative contracts, say, in the sex industry, to get by day to day.
In her important paper “What Is the Point of Equality?” Anderson clarifies the role equality plays in inhibiting domination. It opens with a sardonic question: “If much recent academic work defending equality had been secretly penned by conservatives, could the results be any more embarrassing for egalitarians?” She chastises both Marxists like G. A. Cohen for trivializing equality by reducing it to debates about whether we ought to compensate people for being temperamentally gloomy or easily bored, and liberal egalitarians like Ronald Dworkin for proposing an envy-free distribution of resources — implying conservatives are right that the push for equality is ultimately about nothing more than resentment.
Anderson wanted egalitarians to finally get serious and realize that we aren’t, in fact, all that interested in building a society where people get the same bundle of goodies. Inegalitarian societies have built hierarchies whose social relations enabled some people to dominate others, often by insisting that those atop the social hierarchy were intrinsically worth more than those at the bottom. Egalitarians, Anderson argued, are fundamentally committed to undoing those forms of social hierarchy that enabled domination and oppression:
Egalitarian political movements oppose such hierarchies. They assert the equal moral worth of persons. This assertion does not mean that all have equal virtue or talent. Negatively, the claim repudiates distinctions of moral worth based on birth or social identity — on family membership, inherited social status, race, ethnicity, gender, or genes. There are no natural slaves, plebeians, or aristocrats. Positively, the claim asserts that all competent adults are equally moral agents: everyone equally has the power to develop and exercise moral responsibility, to cooperate with others according to principles of justice, to shape and fulfill a conception of their good.
In The Imperative of Integration, Anderson further defined the parameters of what she called the “relational theory” of equality and inequality. It located the “causes of economic, political, and symbolic group inequalities in the relations (processes of interaction) between groups, rather than in the internal characteristics of their members or in cultural differences that exist independently of group interaction.” Anderson emphasizes that in our society what makes people unequal often isn’t intrinsic to them but the result of the social relations in which they are embedded. But to invoke Karl Marx’s language of fetishism, this is very often obscured by ruling ideologies, which redirect the source of inferiority from social relations onto the individuals and groups themselves. Someone sold into slavery is described, in Aristotle’s terms, as a “natural slave” rather than someone who has been trapped in an oppressively hierarchical social system. Moreover, to reinforce hierarchy we often impute still worse forms of inferiority upon those at the base of the pyramid. For instance, when Senator John C. Calhoun called slavery a “positive good” because slaves were racially inferior, and the best thing for everyone was their paternalistic subordination to the superior race.
There is a lot to commend in Anderson’s relational equality. It helped steer egalitarians away from arguing about whether people with highfalutin tastes should be supplied with plovers’ eggs and truffle oil and back toward the hierarchies of oppression that it is the Left’s job to confront. If there is a limitation to her approach, it’s an enduring ambiguity about what a flourishing life ought to look like. This is a necessary part of making the case for equality; namely, why and how would people live better lives if they were more equal through being free of domination. Here Marx provides us with a helpful clue in the third volume of Capital, where he posits that under socialism the cooperative development of human powers and capabilities will become an end in itself for the first time, rather than just a means of training more efficient workers. The development of human powers to foster a rich individuality in community with others ought to be on our horizon, and doing so will mean transcending capitalism.
The Tyranny of Private Government and the Conservative Work Ethic
In her more recent work, Anderson has become one of the sharpest critics of both capitalist practices and ideology. In Private Government, she asks us to imagine “a government that assigns almost everyone a superior whom they must obey.” This government offers routines but no rule of law: orders can be arbitrary, can change without notice, and can’t be appealed. Worst of all, the bosses answer to no one below them. “They are neither elected nor removable by their inferiors.” Most of us, Anderson point out, don’t have to imagine this. It’s what most of us encounter every day when we go to work. And yet, despite the oppression it entails, we are often told that not only is there no alternative, but that such a system is nothing less than freedom itself.
Anderson’s point is well taken. If we were told that tomorrow the federal government was going to tell most Americans when to wake up, what they were going to wear, when they could go to the bathroom and eat lunch, how and when they were going to talk to others, there would be riots in the street. Everyone with a “Don’t Tread on Me!” flag would be making liberal use of their Second Amendment rights, Rand Paul would be weeping on live television, and the Daily Wire would proclaim this the Communist States of America. And yet Anderson observes this is the reality for millions of Americans subject to “private government” every day. She rejects the claim that that the modern commercial firm is a realm of individualism, as opposed to the collectivism of the state. Anderson notes that in the “great contest between individualism and collectivism regarding the mode of production, collectivism won, decisively. Nearly all production is undertaken by teams of workers using large, indivisible forms of capital equipment held in common.” Firms are collective enterprises, where the social relations grant capitalists and managers enormous domineering powers at the expense of their workers. She recommends that the way to respond to these forms of domination is to extend the liberal and democratic norms we already apply to statist collectives to private government: allow workers more democratic rights, greater protections, and the right to assemble and check unaccountable private power.
In Hjjacked, Anderson examines some of the ideological reasons many on the Right consider this unacceptable. She points out how from the beginning of the modern era there have been fierce debates over the work ethic and who deserved greater power and rewards: workers or capitalists. Anderson shows how socialists and a surprising number of liberals argued a “progressive work ethic” holding that, since workers did most of the work under capitalism, they were getting a raw deal. But they were always confronted by capitalists advocating a “conservative work ethic” that “stressed discipline, frugality, and asceticism for workers, while reaping the lion’s share of productivity gains for themselves in their capacity as capital owners.” The spirit of this conservative ethic was well captured in Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises’s letter to Ayn Rand, congratulating her on the publication of Atlas Shrugged:
You have the courage to tell the masses what no politician told them: you are inferior and all the improvements in your conditions which you simply take for granted you owe to the effort of men who are better than you. If this be arrogance, as some of your critics observed, it is still the truth that had to be said in the age of the Welfare State.
Anderson thinks that there are several ways we can confront this ideology. One is by reconstructing and re-canonizing the work of socialist and social democratic thinkers who tried to conceive of better ways to organize the economy. Anderson quips that it is “telling that in the history of political thought, no social democrat has been canonized, despite the huge influence of social democracy in many wealthy capitalist countries.” This is something of an exaggeration outside the United States, where left-wing economic thought has gained more traction, but her point still stands. A major goal of left-wing philosophers ought to be reintroducing large numbers of people to the rich and thoughtful tradition of socialist and social democratic thought, to help inspire thinking about where to go in the future.
Anderson is esteemed in academic circles but deserves a much wider popular audience. The times are certainly ripe for her message: in his second administration, Donald Trump has gone on a warpath against workers’ rights and needs, making it harder for public sector employees to engage in collective bargaining. Recently, he even went as far as to adopt an explicit “Let them eat cake” attitude toward rising costs to pay for his siege of Iran: “We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare.” Anderson offers us ways to both criticize these forms of domination and think through how to envision a better future where workers take back the world they built.
But above all else, Anderson reminds us that equality is about more than who gets what. Fundamentally, it’s a question of who rules and who is ruled. For most of us, for most of our waking hours, the answer is that the boss rules and we are ruled. Anderson’s work is an invitation to change that answer.

- Frankreich
Seite an Seite gegen die Regierung
Der machtvolle Streik- und Demonstrationstag ist noch nicht zu Ende. Gewerkschafter, Schüler und Gelbwesten machen vereint mobil gegen die Sparpolitik.
Nach einem weiteren Protesttag mit mehreren hunderttausend Teilnehmern hat die französische Regierung eine Erhöhung des Mindestlohns auf 1500 Euro in Aussicht gestellt. Es sei wichtig, »diese Schwelle zu überschreiten«, sagte Arbeitsminister Jean-Pierre Farandou am Freitag dem Sender TF1. Derzeit liegt der Mindestlohn in Frankreich bei rund 1478 Euro netto. Lohn- und Gehaltserhöhungen zählen zu den zentralen Forderungen der Gewerkschaften, die zu den Protesten am Donnerstag aufgerufen hatten.
Die französischen Gewerkschaften hatten der Regierung mit einem massiv befolgten Streik- und Demonstrationstag offen den Kampf erklärt. Im Mittelpunkt stand die Forderung nach höheren Löhnen und der Sicherung der Kaufkraft sowie darüber hinaus nach mehr sozialer und Steuergerechtigkeit. Die dringend nötige Sanierung des Budgets und der Abbau der Staatsschulden dürfe nicht allein auf Kosten der sozial schwächsten Franzosen gehen. In diesem Zusammenhang werden die im Haushaltsentwurf für 2027 vorgesehenen Einsparungen in Höhe von zusammen 54 Milliarden Euro kategorisch zurückgewiesen.
Dazu passte die im Laufe des Tages bekanntgewordene Meldung, dass in der Nationalversammlung der Haushaltsentwurf der Regierung für 2027 keine einzige Stimme bekommen hat und somit de facto einstimmig abgelehnt wurde. Selbst die Abgeordneten des Regierungslagers verurteilten den Budgetentwurf als »unrealistisch«.
Insgesamt nahmen nach Angaben der linken Gewerkschaft CGT an 260 Demonstrationen 1,6 Millionen Menschen teil, davon 350.000 allein in Paris. Das Innenministerium hat landesweit 575.000 und in Paris 65.000 Demonstranten gezählt. Bis auf einige wenige Störversuche gewaltbereiter Schläger, die aber in keinem Verhältnis zu den Ausschreitungen und Plünderungen vom 17. Oktober standen, verliefen alle Aktionen des Tages ruhig und friedlich.
»Es war ein riesiger Erfolg«, schätzte am Abend CGT-Generalsekretärin Sophie Binet ein. »Wir haben deutlich gemacht: Wenn die Regierung nicht auf unsere Forderungen eingeht, droht sich die soziale Krise und damit die Konfrontation noch wesentlich zu verschärfen.« Dass Premierminister Sébastien Lecornu die Gewerkschaften und die Unternehmerverbände für kommenden Montag zu einer Gesprächsrunde über die Löhne eingeladen hat, wollen die Gewerkschaften als »Zeichen einer beginnenden Einsicht« werten.
Sie warnen aber vor einem Scheitern, sollte die Regierung nur einer Anhebung des gesetzlichen Mindestlohns SMIC um wenige Euro anbieten.
Heute beträgt er 1478 Euro netto (1867 brutto) bei einer 35-Stunden Woche und die Gewerkschaften CGT und CFDT fordern, ihn umgehend um 150 bzw. 100 Euro netto zu erhöhen. Dieses Thema, so ist schon abzusehen, wird auch die verbleibenden sechs Monate bis zur nächsten Präsidentschaftswahl bestimmen.
Dabei wollen auch die Gelbwesten mitmachen, die 2018 als spontane Bewegung des Protests gegen die Inflation und vor allem – auch seinerzeit schon – der dramatisch gestiegenen Treibstoffpreise entstanden war. Nachdem sie einige Monate lang Präsident Emmanuel Macron, die Regierung und die Ordnungskräfte in Atem gehalten hatte, war sie danach im Sande verlaufen. Die Gelbwesten verfügten nie über eine Organisationsstruktur; sie wollten unpolitisch bleiben und sich von keiner Partei manipulieren lassen.
Zu ihren Anhängern, die man seinerzeit auf 300.000 bis 1,3 Millionen geschätzt hatte, zählten besonders viele Wähler der rechtsextremen Partei Front National und ihrer Nachfolgeorganisation Rassemblement National, die sich seit jeher stark auf unzufriedene Bürgermassen stützt. Von 2018 bis heute sind offenbar einige Aktivisten der Gelbwesten im Verborgenen aktiv geblieben, denn als Mitte September – ausgehend von einem Gymnasium in der Pariser Region – spontan die Proteste von Oberschülern gegen Lehrermangel und schlechte Arbeitsbedingungen an vielen Schulen aufflammten, bekundeten nach den Gewerkschaften und linken Parteien oder Organisationen auch die Gelbwesten ihre Solidarität. Sie nutzten ganz offensichtlich die Protestbewegung, um wieder Flagge zu zeigen und als politische Akteure wahrgenommen zu werden.
Die Gelbwesten hatten sich inzwischen ein Leitungsgremium mit neun Sprechern und Vertretungen in vielen Regionen und Departements des Landes gegeben. Mit jedem Aktionstag der Oberschüler wuchs auch ihre Bedeutung. Sie haben auch an politischem Profil gewonnen, und ihre Erklärungen den Medien gegenüber zeugen davon, dass sie heute politisch dem linken Lager zuzuordnen sind.
Beim Streik- und Demonstrationstag der Gewerkschaften spielten sie bestenfalls eine Rolle am Rande. Das hinderte sie aber nicht daran, zu einer Fortsetzung bis zum kommenden Samstag aufzurufen, an dem die Gelbwesten selbst eine große Demonstration auf dem Pariser Concorde-Platz durchführen wollen. Was aus diesem ehrgeizigen Plan wird, bleibt abzuwarten. In den vergangenen Wochen hat die Polizei den Gewerkschaften wiederholt Demonstrationen auf den traditionellen Routen durch das Stadtzentrum verweigert und sie an den Stadtrand verbannt. Dabei verfügen die Arbeitnehmervertretungen über einen geschulten Ordnungsdienst und Erfahrungen bei der Abwehr gewalttätiger Ausschreitungen. Daran fehlt es den Gelbwesten, die seit 2018 in den Akten der Ordnungskräfte immer noch als gewaltbereite und potenziell terroristische Bewegung geführt werden.
Über die Frage hinaus, wie viele Menschen am Samstag mit einer gelben Weste durch Paris ziehen werden, wird es interessant sein zu beobachten, ob und wie aus verschiedenen Protestmilieus heraus eine neue und länger anhaltende soziale Bewegung entsteht.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: D.D. Guttenplan
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Organizing Brought Us to This Moment
Voters across the country have given the keys to Democrats. But can the party get in gear?
Victory has a hundred parents, as President Kennedy would doubtless have put it if he’d lived to our more enlightened times, but defeat is an orphan.
Tuesday’s stunning electoral tsunami was big enough, and blue enough, to allow everyone from Chuck Schumer (who recruited Janice Mills to stop Graham Platner in Maine, and also backed Haley Stevens to block Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan) to Our Revolution (the Bernie Sanders–aligned group that pushed Maine Democrats to pick Troy Jackson, rather than a more anodyne centrist, as their candidate after Platner withdrew) to claim a share of the credit. This wave was also wet enough to water whatever pet theory you had ready, whether that was The New York Times’ incessant evangelizing for “moderate Democrats” or journalist David Sirota’s claim that “Bernie Sanders’ form of anti-oligarch populism is now the real center” of the Democratic Party. In the blinding light of this new electoral dawn, even Mamdani strategist Morris Katz’s rash prediction that “the Rahm Emanuel Democrat hardly exists anymore” had a kind of crazy plausibility—though this old leftist is keeping my hammer, stake, and garlic ready to hand.
Still, while we’re handing out trophies, here are my four nominees for PVP (Particularly Valuable Player) in Tuesday’s election victories:
- Howard Dean: As chair of the Democratic National Committee from 2005 to 2009, the Vermonter pressed hard for a 50-state strategy. Even though Dean’s spadework prepared the ground for Barack Obama’s presidency, his argument that no state should be abandoned as “unwinnable” by the national party was roundly dismissed by his successors and the party hierarchy. Even Wikipedia complains that Dean’s approach “requires a campaign to spend resources in a rival’s strongest states, when those resources could be concentrated in swing states.” With not only Texas and South Carolina but Kansas and Iowa and even Mississippi now very much in play, Dean is looking much more like a prophet than a crank.
- Stacey Abrams: Like Moses, Abrams herself might not have made it into the promised land (or the governor’s mansion in Atlanta), but does anyone believe that Jon Ossoff or Raphael Warnock would be in the Senate without her leadership organizing the fight against voter suppression? Or that Keisha Lance Bottoms would not only have won but won so convincingly, if Abrams hadn’t made straight the way in 2018 and 2022?
- The Texas Organizing Project: While the dream of a Democratic revival in the state that once produced crusading progressives like Maury Maverick, Lyndon Johnson, and Barbara Jordan has been gestating since 1994 (the last time Democrats won a statewide election), it wasn’t until 2009 that two women, Ginny Goldman and Michelle Tremillo, started to do something about it. Focusing their work on Black and Latino Texans, and running toward, rather than away from, fights on climate justice, immigrant rights, healthcare, and education, the TOP’s Movement Voter Project ran trainings and did the hard fieldwork in races all the way down the ballot, from Gina Hinajosa and James Talarico down to the Texas agriculture commissioner and numerous contests for the state legislature.
- Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement: It’s been 10 years since Hugh Espy, a CCI organizer, sat me down in his Des Moines office and explained why, for most of Iowa’s working class, Republican and Democratic politicians were “two sides of the same coin: They do the bidding of corporate power. They don’t want to take on Big Ag, the Farm Bureau, Monsanto.” Things got so bad in the state that, as Art Cullen, legendary editor of the Storm Lake Times-Pilot put it just last year, “Nowadays, people who do not believe in banning books or Black history call themselves ‘Concerned Citizens of Sac County’ and not ‘Sac County Democrats.’” Yet all that time Espy and his comrades kept on doing the work of seeding democracy—at picket lines, Farm Aid forums, country fairs, and public hearings. Something big happened in Iowa on Tuesday. But as in Texas, the ground had to be cultivated for a long time before bearing fruit.
The Nation’s late and much-lamented strikes correspondent, Jane McAlevey, always insisted there are “no shortcuts” in politics, and whatever else it does or doesn’t prove, Tuesday’s unexpected redrawing of the electoral map ought to remind us that with sufficient organizing no cause need be regarded as hopeless. I donated money to three candidates this cycle: Brad Lander (because I live in his district, and know him to be a mensch), Dan Sullivan (the Alaska “spoiler” who made the Times clutch its pearls—because why should the other side have all the fun?), and Scott Colom, who at the time seemed like the unlikeliest of the three (despite some of the best ads in this or any political season). If bare-knuckled, profane economic populism can win statewide in Mississippi, it can win anywhere.
But will it be given the chance? Will Chuck Schumer, the “senator from Wall Street,” who is almost certain to run unopposed for majority leader, really pursue economic policies that will make a difference to working families? Will Hakeem Jeffries start harmonizing with the Squad just because it is in the nation’s interest? The politics of dislodging either are not encouraging—at least in the short term. Rather than recruiting sacrificial candidates to oppose them, congressional progressives might consider adopting a “short leash” approach to the Democratic leadership—and a short list of legislative demands to test their good faith.
As Corbin Trent, one of the cofounders of Justice Democrats (a group that also deserves considerable credit for never buying the Trump “vibe shift” fairly tale) put it on NBC, “We’ve been given the keys by the American people, and it’s time to drive the car to a better place.”
What does that look like—especially when Donald Trump still has two more years left in office? As my colleague Robert Borosage notes, “Americans want their leaders to focus attention and resources at home.” This means bold action to end the war with Iran—starting now, not (as the infinitely patient Schumer proposes) waiting until next year. It means ending military aid to Israel, and making clear to whoever forms that country’s next government that America will no longer be complicit in genocide or the slow strangulation of Palestinian hopes for justice and self-determination.
But in an election where voters told pollsters their top three concerns were the economy, the future of democracy, and healthcare, it is domestic matters that will rightly preoccupy Democrats. Clawing back GOP handouts to the Epstein class (and redistributing them downward), restoring the Affordable Care Act subsidies eliminated by Trump, and banning stock trading by sitting government officials and members of Congress would all signal the kind of change in direction Americans just voted for. Vetoing any of these measures would also be an albatross Democrats could hang around the necks of Republicans for the next two years and beyond.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
As would my own favorite policy proposal: a phased transition to Medicare for All. From El-Sayed in Michigan to Annie Andrews in South Carolina, fixing our broken healthcare system is an issue that cuts across both state and party lines, with 65 percent of Americans saying they would be in favor. The details of getting there may be “gnarly,” but bold action by the next Congress on healthcare cost and access—making Trump and his GOP loyalists the defenders of the status quo—would be smart politics now, and potentially transformative later.
Speaking of smart politics, what about accountability? No matter how richly he may deserve it, anyone with a functioning memory should be wary of devoting too much time and energy pursuing yet another futile impeachment of Donald Trump. But that needn’t deter Congress from using its oversight powers to illuminate the depths of Trump and his family’s corruption and profiteering from office—or from investigating the tech oligarchy’s cozy relationship with the Trump White House. A full reckoning with Elon Musk (anyone else for nationalizing Starlink?), or Jeff Bezos, or Mark Zuckerberg, may have to wait until there’s a (social) Democrat in the White House. But can we at least stop the fawning?
Because that breeze we’ve all felt since Tuesday night is the Overton window blowing wider open than it has been in decades. Let’s not waste the moment.

https://hyperallergic.com/jordan-poorman.title: Jordan Poorman Cocker’s Vision of Global Indigeneity
https://hyperallergic.com/jordan-poorman.author: Petala Ironcloud
https://hyperallergic.com/jordan-poorman.text:
Jordan Poorman Cocker’s Vision of Global Indigeneity
The curator, who just organized a major rehang of Indigenous art at Crystal Bridges, reflects on the ways institutions can create space for Native artists to flourish.
BENTONVILLE, Ark. — On October 16 and 17, before a room full of Indigenous artists, curators, and scholars at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art’s symposium on contemporary Native art, Jordan Poorman Cocker opened with a land acknowledgment. Founded by Walmart heiress Alice Walton, the museum sits on the ancestral homelands of the Osage Nation, Quapaw Nation, and Caddo Nation, who were forcibly relocated in the 19th century. Poorman Cocker, a Kiowa and Tongan citizen, was hired as the museum’s Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) officer and first full-time curator of Indigenous art in 2023. She makes the hour-and-a-half drive in from Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the Cherokee Nation’s capital and home to several nations coerced there during the removal era.
The two-day gathering coincided with the reinstallation of contemporary Native art in the museum, which Poorman Cocker spearheaded alongside Ashley Holland (Cherokee Nation) as a way to showcase the diversity of style, medium, and living Native artists across Indian Country, including works by citizens of the ancestral Tribes in Arkansas. Choctaw and Cherokee multi-disciplinary artist Jeffrey Gibson delivered a keynote address, and later spoke to an audience with Poorman Cocker while beading; Diné weaver Melissa Cody traced the lineage of her work in dialogue with her mother Lola Cody; and Lehuauakea delivered a workshop based in her traditional kapa practice.
Poorman Cocker’s own curatorial practice draws on her background in museum studies at Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand and the global spirit of Indigeneity, which rejects the divisive borders of colonial nation-states. Like many Native curators, she cites the groundbreaking 2019 exhibition Hearts of Our People: Native Women Artists at the Minneapolis Institute of Art as a major source of inspiration. That sentiment was echoed by Kiowa beadwork artist Terri Greeves, who spoke at the symposium alongside other Kiowa Tribe members and matriarchs. Poorman Cocker is also a beadwork and textile artist herself, rooted in Kiowa and Tongan beadwork and textile conventions.
In an email correspondence with Hyperallergic, Poorman Cocker shared more about a recent landmark commission, telling a fuller history of Native art, and what it means to bring Kiowa voices into the museum. The interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.
Hyperallergic: Tell me more about what the reinstallation at Crystal Bridges represents for Indigenous art in this moment. What is it trying to change? How did the 114,000-square-foot expansion inform the museum’s capacity to provide ongoing opportunities to collaborate with the featured artists?
JPC: The impetus is to recenter two primary areas: the Indigenous art collection and the craft collection. Native American and Indigenous art are foundational to every American art collection. Over the years, I have written acquisition proposals for artworks sourced from the gallery system and annual markets, with an emphasis on artist commissions. Crystal Bridges is better positioned to nourish the art ecosystem, including many artists — particularly those whose work aligns with intergenerational art forms, who need financial support for artist apprenticeships, community classes, and other art education efforts that sustain artist communities and knowledge systems.
Indigenous and Native art makes up about 3% of Crystal Bridges’s permanent collection. The museum sector writ large has a long way to go to better present Indigenous artists and stories.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Anistia às Ligas Camponesas da Paraíba: Estado pede desculpas e movimento cobra reparação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Um marco na história da luta camponesa na Paraíba: em 5 de novembro de 2026, a Comissão de Anistia aprovou, por unanimidade, o requerimento de anistia coletiva apresentado pelo Memorial das Ligas e Lutas Camponesas, de Sapé, em parceria com a Defensoria Pública da União (DPU). A decisão é resultado de uma mobilização iniciada entre 2022 e 2023, que enfrentou idas e vindas, ameaças e fragilidades institucionais até chegar à votação.
Na sessão, houve pedido oficial de desculpas em nome do Estado brasileiro, conforme o relato de Alane Lima, coordenadora do Memorial das Ligas e Lutas Camponesas de Sapé.
“O que vivenciamos hoje foi um dia de muita emoção. Ver reconhecida a trajetória de um movimento autônomo de luta, como foram as Ligas Camponesas, e ter reconhecido que seus integrantes e suas organizações sofreram perseguições e violações por parte do Estado é motivo de esperança. É uma demonstração de que estamos no caminho certo e de que seguiremos em luta”.
Reparação além do gesto simbólico
Alane Lima afirma que as recomendações apresentadas incluem o reconhecimento dos lugares de memória relacionados à trajetória das Ligas Camponesas, o acompanhamento psicológico contínuo das vítimas e de seus familiares, a garantia de uso vitalício da sede do Memorial pela organização e o apoio dos governos federal e estadual à manutenção do espaço. Nos cinco hectares que integram o Memorial, também há produção de alimentos destinados à comunidade.
“Entre as recomendações, está o reconhecimento de todos os pontos de memória que fizeram parte da história das Ligas Camponesas. Também solicitamos acompanhamento psicológico contínuo para as vítimas e seus familiares, considerando que os impactos da violência e das violações não atingiram apenas aqueles que sofreram diretamente a repressão, mas também seus familiares e as gerações seguintes”, destaca.
A representante também defende que o reconhecimento seja acompanhado de condições materiais para a continuidade das atividades do Memorial, incluindo condições dignas de trabalho para as pessoas da comunidade e do território que atuam no espaço. Segundo ela, o desafio agora é garantir que as recomendações sejam efetivamente cumpridas pelo Estado brasileiro.
“Outra solicitação diz respeito à garantia de uso vitalício do espaço que abriga a sede do Memorial das Ligas e Lutas Camponesas pela organização. Defendemos, ainda, a responsabilidade do Estado brasileiro e do Estado da Paraíba na colaboração para a manutenção do Memorial e na garantia de condições dignas de trabalho para as pessoas da comunidade e do território que atuam nesse espaço”, explica.
Ao final da sessão, a Comissão de Anistia, vinculada ao Ministério dos Direitos Humanos e da Cidadania, realizou um pronunciamento oficial em reconhecimento às graves violações de direitos humanos, perseguições e violências sofridas pelos trabalhadores rurais e suas lideranças. Em pé, os representantes da Comissão dirigiram um pedido público de desculpas aos camponeses e às camponesas das Ligas Camponesas da Paraíba:
“O Estado brasileiro não só pede desculpas pelas violações, como lhes agradece pela luta, pela resistência, pela democracia e por vocês ainda continuarem lutando. Muito obrigado e parabéns a todos vocês, os camponeses e as camponesas das Ligas Camponesas da Paraíba. Muito obrigada”.
Assista aqui o pedido público de desculpas aos camponeses: https://www.instagram.com/p/DfYDSLOnysC/?img_index=2
Ação e contexto nacional
Alane Lima também destaca a ação civil pública ajuizada pelo Ministério Público Federal (MPF), em parceria com organizações sociais, universidades e memoriais, contra a União e o Estado da Paraíba. A iniciativa busca responsabilizar o poder público pelas violações cometidas contra trabalhadores rurais entre 1964 e 1981. Entre as medidas solicitadas estão pedido de desculpas, abertura de arquivos, busca por desaparecidos e preservação de lugares de memória.
Na Paraíba, as Ligas Camponesas ganharam força no final dos anos 1950, mobilizando trabalhadores pela reforma agrária e por direitos sociais. A repressão ao movimento se intensificou após o golpe de 1964.
No cenário nacional, a CPT registrou 1.593 conflitos no campo e 26 assassinatos em 2025. Já a Lei nº 10.559/2002 estabelece medidas de reparação para vítimas de perseguição política, fundamento jurídico das políticas de anistia.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A new contemporary art hub nestled among the ruins of a medieval monastery is due to open in northern Italy next September. The Fondazione Vezza project, founded by the Piedmontese entrepreneur Sandra Vezza and her son Charley, will be based in Monforte d’Alba in the Langhe wine region, around 60 kilometres southeast of Turin.
The pair plan to develop a trail over the next decade through the woodland on Colle San Pietro hill; two site-specific large-scale works by the US artist Kathleen Ryan and the Italian sculptor Alessandro Pessoli will inaugurate the project next autumn. The trail will include the ruins of the monastery of San Pietro, an early medieval complex first documented in 1014.
Flavio del Monte, formerly director of institutional relations at Massimo de Carlo gallery in Milan, will oversee the Fondazione Vezza project. “Each year, one or more artists will be invited to engage with the site, its woodland, its paths, existing architecture and history. Over approximately ten years, the works will shape a route that will continue to grow and change without losing the site’s original character,” says a project statement.
Sandra and Charley Vezza will fund the production of the works; budget costs remain confidential. Asked if the foundation will own the pieces produced, a spokesperson said: “Yes, they will be installed permanently onsite. The target audience is really everyone, the widest possible audience.” The site will be open to the public and free to enter.
“With its opening in 2027, the Foundation will begin a long-term exploration of the relationship between contemporary art, the landscape, and the Vezza family’s vision, shaped by the artists invited to contribute to the site over time,” adds the statement. Project supporters include the Comune di Monforte, the Comune di Milano and Gagosian Gallery.
Sandra and Charley Vezza founded the Italian Radical Design Group in 2022, a Barolo-based company established with “the specific aim of preserving and promoting historic Italian design brands”, says the company website. The same year the group acquired Memphis Milano, the 1980s post-modern design collective. In 2012, the Vezzas bought Gufram, an Italian radical design brand founded in the 1960s, known for its pop art-inspired furniture.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ca.title: Carsten Höller’s Spiraling Silver Slides Appear in Mexico City as a Permanent Installation
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ca.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ca.text:
Belgian artist Carsten Höller’s giant, spiraling silver slides have made their way to Arte Abierto Polanco in Mexico City as part of a permanent installation.
The large-scale installation, titled Mexico City Slides (2026), features four spiral slides integrated into Antara, an upscale open-air shopping mall that houses retail, dining, entertainment, offices and public space. Höller’s installation was commissioned by Arte Abierto and Sordo Madaleno Arquitectos and can be seen from Antara’s gardens, plazas and pedestrian promenade.
The Mexico City Slides installation ranges from 39 to 125 feet in height and 102 to 295 feet in length. All four spiral slides are open to the public and allow four people to ride simultaneously from various entrances such as the family-style restaurants, the Google offices, the Rosewood Hotel, and the Arte Abierto Art Space. All four slides end at the same exit. The artist said he wanted the installation to be an “equalizer” and a “voluptuous panic upon an otherwise lucid mind” for participants and viewers. In 2015, Höller told The Guardian that it’s “impossible to travel down a slide without smiling.”
Höller’s installation is part of a work-in-progress franchise that he started in 1998. Different variations of the slides have appeared across the world, from Test Site (2006) at Tate Modern in London, Victoria Slide (2011) at the New Museum in New York, Vitra Slide Tower (2014) at the Vitra Campus in Weil am Rhein, Florence Experiment Slides (2018) at Palazzo Strozzi in Florence and DAC Slide (2020) at the Danish Architecture Centre in Copenhagen.

The journal Antiquity has published a new study on a collection of engravings discovered in 2019 within Cova de la Font Major, a cave located near Barcelona in northeastern Spain. The find is one of the largest collections of cave art on the Iberian Peninsula; its 280 Paleolithic engravings include 55 animal figures, as well as nonfigurative designs.
Although more than half of the Paleolithic cave-art groupings recorded in Europe are located in the Iberian Peninsula, the study notes that the northeastern region has generally yielded only fragmentary evidence. The discovery of this extensive collection came as a surprise, particularly since the cave was first excavated in 1957 and it has been part of a tourist route since 1993.
Míriam Salas-Altès, a co-author of the paper, believes these engravings went unnoticed for so long because the cave is dark and, as Scientific American reports, it may have been more difficult to spot the carvings than it would have to see paintings. Additionally, the walls are covered in modern-day graffiti, making it even trickier to make out the etchings.
The study reveals that the majority of markings are nonfigurative: “Among the most frequent representations are straight, parallel lines, arranged in groups of two, three or four, sometimes superimposed over zoomorphic figures … Other, less common motifs include convergent lines, circular or semicircular forms and quadrangular shapes.” One panel contains hundreds of “loop-shaped” etchings.
Representations of fauna include horses, deer, wild oxen, and at least one bear, though identification is difficult due to the limited depiction of details such as eyes, nostrils, hooves, manes, and coats. Most are rendered through simple body outlines.
Tourists’ access has been curtailed in order to protect the engravings, and researchers believe that clearing the years of sediment that has settled in the caves may reveal more art.
