https://taz.de/Hito-Steyerl-Der-Kulturbe.title: Hito Steyerl zu KI und Kunst: „Ich arbeite von innen mit den Dingen gegen die Dinge“
https://taz.de/Hito-Steyerl-Der-Kulturbe.author: Katrin Gottschalk und Sophie Jung
https://taz.de/Hito-Steyerl-Der-Kulturbe.text:
Hito Steyerl zu KI und Kunst: „Ich arbeite von innen mit den Dingen gegen die Dinge“
Die Künstlerin Hito Steyerl über das Aufwachsen in einer Franz-Josef-Strauß-Demokratur, das KI-Chaos und Politik, die in die Künste drängt.
taz: Frau Steyerl, angeblich rottet die künstliche Intelligenz bald die Menschheit aus. Sie haben sich als Medienkünstlerin viel mit KI beschäftigt – was halten Sie von solchen Aussagen?
Steyerl: Ich glaube, es gibt noch ganz andere Möglichkeiten, wie die Menschheit sich ausrotten könnte, KI trägt einfach zum allgemeinen Chaos bei. Um das genauer einschätzen zu können, fehlen aber die Daten. Die Algorithmen sind geheim, die werden auch nicht veröffentlicht.
taz: Das ist jetzt nicht direkt beruhigend.
Steyerl: Ein großer Teil des Hypes um KI ist selbsttragend geworden und funktioniert mit zirkulären Investitionen. Prognosen werden über den tatsächlichen Bedarf hinaus erstellt und führen dazu, dass dafür immer mehr Infrastruktur gebaut werden muss. Diese kommt dann wieder denselben paar Firmen zugute. Aus meiner technischen Erfahrung heraus weiß ich, dass ein Teil dieser Infrastruktur nicht nötig ist. Die KI-Infrastruktur-Branche ist eine Blase.
taz: Welche Teile der Infrastruktur wären nicht nötig?
Steyerl: KI-Modelle lassen sich wesentlich bescheidener mit weniger Energie- und Datenaufwand trainieren, durch algorithmische Optimierung und mit abgespeckten Architekturen. Dann bräuchte man keine neuen Atomkraftwerke, Gaspipelines, fossile Infrastruktur und weiß Gott was, um das alles zu betreiben.
Die Person
Hito Steyerl, geboren 1966 in München, gilt als eine der bedeutendsten Künstlerinnen der Gegenwart, bezeichnet sich selbst allerdings lieber als Filmemacherin und Autorin. In ihren multimedialen Arbeiten bringt Steyerl Gesellschafts- und Technologiekritik humorvoll zusammen. Für ihre Kunst erhielt sie zahlreiche Auszeichnungen. Hito Steyerl lebt mit ihrer Familie in Berlin.
Die Ausstellung
„Hito Steyerl – Deine Mudda macht Show“ läuft vom 30. Oktober 2026 bis zum 29. März 2027 in den Hamburger Deichtorhallen.
taz: Sie begannen in den 1990ern mit essayistischen Dokumentarfilmen, in der Kunstwelt wurden Sie mit medientheoretischen Essays und Videoinstallationen bekannt, 2015 bespielten Sie mit Ihrer immersiven Arbeit „Factory of the Sun“ den Deutschen Pavillon der Kunstbiennale in Venedig. Bis heute befassen Sie sich in Ihrer Filmkunst mit den gesellschaftlichen Auswirkungen des technologischen Wandels. Wie sehen Sie Ihre eigene Rolle? Sind Sie die Beobachterin, die mit dem Material arbeitet, das sie vorfindet?
Steyerl: Ich arbeite von innen mit den Dingen gegen die Dinge. Manchmal auch mit den Dingen für die Dinge. Würde ich mir KI nur von außen anschauen, könnte ich sie gar nicht verstehen. Ich bin von vornherein ein Teil davon. Das ist eine komplizierte, auch kompromittierte Position.
taz: Warum kompromittiert?
Steyerl: Der amerikanische Literaturwissenschaftler Michael Rothberg hat das so genannt: the implicated subject. Genauso ein impliziertes Subjekt bin ich in diesen Technologien. Ich befasse mich mit ihnen und bin gleichzeitig mittendrin. Die meisten sind das, sind sich dessen aber nicht bewusst.
taz: Sie selbst sind sehr zurückhaltend mit Ihren Daten. Sie nutzen keine sozialen Medien, kein Facebook. Wo liegt Ihr Handy gerade, im Kühlschrank?
Steyerl: Nee, das habe ich hier bei mir. Es sind aber viele Funktionen ausgeschaltet. Bis vor vier Jahren hatte ich noch so ein altes Bananenhandy ohne Internet. Während der Pandemie wurde das unmöglich wegen dieser ganzen QR-Codes, die man brauchte. Da habe ich aufgegeben.
taz: Also selbst Sie, die Sie sehr datensensibel unterwegs sind, haben sich dem Smartphone nicht verweigern können.
Steyerl: Ich denke, man könnte sich noch immer verweigern. Aber es ist sehr viel Arbeit, weil alles darauf zugeschnitten ist.
taz: Sie kommen aus München, haben als junger Mensch Häuser besetzt und die Schule abgebrochen. Heute sind Sie eine der bedeutendsten Künstler*innen Deutschlands. Wie sind Sie aufgewachsen?
Steyerl: In einer relativ konservativen, postfaschistischen Franz-Josef-Strauß-Demokratur. Bei uns war alles so, wie es halt damals war in den 70er und 80er Jahren in Bayern.
taz: Also keine 68er-Eltern?
Steyerl: Nein, überhaupt nicht. Meine Eltern waren Wissenschaftler am MIT, dem Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Mit Flower Power und Hippies hatten die gar nichts zu tun.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
taz: Sie konnten im Anschluss ohne Abitur Film in Tokio studieren. Wie kam es dazu?
Steyerl: Das war ein lustiger Zufall. Meine Mutter hatte in München eine japanische Person kennengelernt. Deren Töchter waren beide Schauspielerinnen, haben für den bekannten japanischem Nouvelle-Vague-Regisseur Shōhei Imamura gespielt. Der hatte zufällig auch diese Filmschule besucht und war der Meinung, dass Schulabbrecher besonders dafür begabt seien, Filme zu machen.
taz: Wieso wollten Sie Film studieren?
Steyerl: Spätestens ab 16 war ich eigentlich immer im Kino, ich träumte davon, selbst Filme zu machen, am liebsten Kampfsportfilme. Bruce Lee, Schwertkampf, etwas in der Richtung. Diese Filme faszinieren mich immer noch. Die Eleganz, die Choreografie, die Präzision. Ich habe damals auch Kampfsport gemacht, ich habe sechs Mal die Woche Karate trainiert.
taz: Jetzt nicht mehr?
Steyerl: Nein, aber ich habe mich gerade fürs Boxen angemeldet. Vielleicht vertiefe ich auch Muay Thai weiter.
taz: In Ihrem Kurzfilm „Lovely Andrea“ von 2007 erfährt man, dass Sie damals in Tokio als Bondage-Model gearbeitet haben, also dass Sie sich vor der Kamera fesseln und knebeln ließen. Warum?
Steyerl: Einer meiner Lehrer hatte einen Film über Filipinas gemacht, die für Sexarbeit nach Japan geschmuggelt wurden. Ich wusste, dass so etwas auch in der Pornoszene üblich war, und das wollte ich in einem Dokumentarfilm von innen heraus beleuchten. Den Plan gab ich dann aber sehr schnell auf, war zu gefährlich. Aber die meisten Leute an meiner Schule, also auch die Studierenden, hatten Part-Time-Jobs in der Sexindustrie, sie haben zum Beispiel Pornogeschichten geschrieben. Das ging allerdings nur für die männlichen Studierenden. Für die weiblichen waren die moralischen Grenzen zu rigide.
taz: Aber der Nebenjob als Bondage-Model ging trotzdem?
Steyerl: Nicht wirklich. War sketchy.
taz: In „Lovely Andrea“ geht es auch um Ihre Jugendfreundin Andrea Wolf. Während Sie in München Dokumentarfilmregie studierten und später in Philosophie in Wien promovierten, hat sich Wolf der PKK angeschlossen. Sie wurde 1998 in den besetzten Kurdengebieten getötet. Wie wichtig ist Andrea Wolf für Ihre Arbeit?
Steyerl: Einerseits sehr wichtig. Andererseits ist sie nun schon lange tot, die Erinnerung an sie verblasst allmählich. In ihrem Kielwasser haben sich aber mehrere Frauenfiguren herausgebildet. Kurdinnen, die ich kennengelernt habe, die mittlerweile so etwas wie ihre Rolle für mich eingenommen haben.
taz: Die kurdischen Gebiete tauchen seit 20 Jahren immer wieder in Ihren Arbeiten auf, zuletzt 2025 in der Videoinstallation „Mechanical Kurds“. Warum reisen Sie so häufig dorthin?
Steyerl: Am Anfang wollte ich herausfinden, was mit Andrea Wolf passiert war. Und dann hat sich das verselbstständigt. In den zehner Jahren gab es einen sogenannten Friedensprozess, der das Herumreisen in diesen Gebieten leichter machte. Und es gab mit der HDP in der Türkei eine starke zivilgesellschaftliche kurdische Bewegung. Dann kamen die Schlacht von Kobanê, die Angriffe von Daesh, die Autonomiebewegung in Rojava. Jedes Mal war ich dort, habe versucht was zu lernen.
taz: Verspüren Sie Ihren kurdischen Kontakten gegenüber eine Verpflichtung, deren Geschichte weiter zu erzählen?
Steyerl: Jein. Ich bin Filmemacherin, und da hat man auch eine formale Verpflichtung. Es bringt nichts, irgendetwas zu erzählen, wenn man es nicht gut durcharbeiten kann. Diesem Aspekt bin ich genauso verpflichtet.
taz: Steht die künstlerische Autorität über dem aktivistischen Auftritt?
Steyerl: Ja, ich komme stark aus einer reflexiven Perspektive, nicht aus einer aktivistischen. Und Kurdistan ist mir zu wichtig, um bei der Form zu schlampen.
taz: In „Mechanical Kurds“ begleiten Sie Geflüchtete in Erbil, die für maschinelle Lernsysteme Fotos beschriften, also darauf Häuser, Straßen und Menschen markieren. Was haben Sie in Erbil gesehen, das Sie dazu brachte, die autonome Maschine als Mythos zu bezeichnen?
Steyerl: Diese Arbeit existierte nur für eine kurze Zeit. In den frühen 2020er Jahren kam die Weltbank auf die Idee, dass man Geflüchtete im Nahen Osten für Mikroarbeit einspannen solle, weil dort viele junge Leute mit Handy in den Geflüchtetenlagern waren. Die kannten sich digital aus, brauchten Geld, und so konnte man sie gut ausbeuten. Wir haben mit etwa 15 bis 20 Leuten aus Lagern in Südkurdistan gesprochen. Die wurden dann alle wieder gefeuert, die Maschinen können sich mittlerweile selbst beibringen, wie man Dinge erkennt und annotiert.
taz: Also ist die autonome Maschine kein Mythos mehr, sondern Realität?
Steyerl: Ja und nein. Die eben beschriebene Arbeit ist nicht mehr nötig. Es gibt aber eine neue Form der Mikroarbeit im Bereich Robotik. Die Menschen haben dafür ein iPhone am Schädel, filmen sich beim Wäschefalten oder Müllrausbringen und bringen so den Robotern bei, wie sie sich im 3D-Raum bewegen. Teilweise werden die Leute richtig gut dafür bezahlt, denn es sollen sich auch etwa Zahnärzte bei ihrer Arbeit filmen. Aber die meisten Leute kriegen weniger als den Mindestlohn dafür.
taz: Eine Ihrer frühesten Arbeiten, die Sie jetzt in Ihrer Hamburger Werkschau zeigen, ist die Filmreihe „Normality 1–X“ aus den Jahren 1999 bis 2001. Sie handelt vom alltäglichen Antisemitismus und Rassismus im wiedervereinten Deutschland. Haben die dokumentierten Vorfälle auch mit Ihren eigenen Erfahrungen zu tun?
Steyerl: Klar, was denn sonst, ich bin offensichtlich nicht weiß. Aber ich fühle auch mit, wenn jemand wie Pöbel MC von seinen Erfahrungen im Osten rappt.
taz: Wie beobachten Sie den Umgang mit Antisemitismus heute, insbesondere in der Kulturszene?
Steyerl: Die Kunst war ursprünglich ein Ort, an dem über eingefahrene Lager hinweg diskutiert werden konnte. Das ist jetzt nicht möglich. Auch weil die Politik sich heftigst einmischt. Es müsste zunächst einmal die Autonomie des Betriebs wiederhergestellt werden.
taz: Wie?
Steyerl: Wenn eine öffentliche Diskussion nur noch unter den Maßgaben stattfinden kann, dass irgendeinem beliebigen Kulturstaatsminister gefällt, was da geredet wird, muss man gar nicht erst damit anfangen. Der beschäftigt sich mit T-Shirts, während die Partei, die ihn gestellt hat, gerade mutmaßlich den Beginn der Machtübernahme der AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt zu verantworten hat.
taz: Angenommen, Wolfram Weimer würde sich einen anderen Job suchen, was wäre dann auf der Seite des Kunstbetriebs zu tun?
Steyerl: Es geht nicht um irgendeine Person, sondern um den Vibeshift hin zum Autoritären, zum Kulturdiktat, zur Militarisierung, all diesem Post-Preußenkram, Staatsräson-, Rheinmetall-, Wehrtüchtigkeitsdrip. Darüber hinaus wäre interessant, die Dinge strukturell zu diskutieren, statt nur aus einer rein von sozialen Medien getragenen Aufregungsdebatte heraus. Jetzt ist der Kulturbetrieb teilweise wie ein Blinddarm sozialer Medien, er unterwirft sich nahezu reibungslos dem Plattform-Aufmerksamkeitsmaxxing. Wieder mehr Autonomie zu gewinnen, wäre wichtig.
taz: Die Dinge aus einer formalen Perspektive zu diskutieren, was hieße das konkret?
Steyerl: Form, Infrastruktur, System fokussieren. Vielleicht findet man da auch Poesie wieder.
taz: Sie waren zuvor Professorin an der Universität der Künste in Berlin und sind es heute an der Akademie der Bildenden Künste in München. Was ist Ihnen wichtig, Ihren Student*innen mitzugeben?
Steyerl: Ich möchte ein Klima schaffen, in dem sich die Leute gegenseitig unterstützen. Das ist das Wichtigste für ihre weitere Laufbahn. In Akademien gibt es oft einen absurden Druck, dieses oder jenes zu machen, damit man am Markt reüssiert. Das versuche ich draußen zu halten. Niemand weiß, was morgen passiert und was morgen erfolgreich sein wird, das wusste man kurz vor 1933 auch nicht.
taz: Sie selbst nennen sich Filmemacherin und Autorin anstatt Künstlerin. Warum?
Steyerl: Ich bin nicht sicher, ob das, was ich mache, Kunst ist. Und ich glaube, die Kunst ist sich auch nicht sicher. Wir schauen mal, wie das weitergeht. Momentan wird die Medienkunst wieder rausgeschmissen aus dem Kunstbegriff und dem Kunstmarkt. Wenn Krise ist, zieht sich der Kunstmarkt wieder auf Malerei zurück. Die Institutionen trotteln dann langsam hinterher.
taz: Man hört, Sie fremdeln mit der Kunstwelt insgesamt. Stimmt das? Sie sind ja gut im Geschäft.
Steyerl: Es ist immer wieder erheiternd, was da passiert. Wie eine Komödie mit allen möglichen Darstellern und Nebendarstellern. Und alle versuchen irgendwie klarzukommen, Klassenunterschiede werden auf magische Weise für die Dauer einer Eröffnung einfach so weggebügelt, da parkt einer draußen seine Yacht und ein anderer sein Fahrrad, und alle saufen auf Ruinart sein Nacken. Meistens ist es auch ein sehr ernüchternder Betrieb mit unglaublich viel Betrug und Ausbeutung.
taz: Wann fühlen Sie sich der Kunstwelt zugehörig?
Steyerl: Das weiß ich nicht. Wo bin ich überhaupt zugehörig? Ich habe aufgehört, mir diese Frage zu stellen. Auf mich passt ein Ausspruch des amerikanischen Schauspielers Groucho Marx: „Ich möchte keinem Club angehören, der mich als Mitglied aufnehmen würde.“
taz: Ein unterbelichtetes Thema in der Kunstwelt ist noch immer Mutterschaft. Sie haben selbst eine mittlerweile 21-jährige Tochter. 2016 mussten Sie eine Veranstaltung auf der Berlin Biennale absagen, weil Sie – Zitat Moderatorin – „a successful artist and mother“ seien.
Steyerl: Möglich, dass meine Tochter krank war und ich niemanden gefunden habe, der auf sie aufgepasst hat.
taz: Müsste die Kunstwelt mehr über Mutterschaft sprechen?
Steyerl: Ich weiß nicht, ob es etwas nützen würde. Ganz viele Dinge sind einfach nicht zugänglich. Viermonatige Residencies an entlegenen Orten gehen nicht, weil die Kinder in der Schule oder im Kindergarten sein müssen. Ich empfehle, als Filmkünstlerin zu arbeiten. Da kannst du einfach deinen Film hinschicken und zu Hause bleiben und dem Kind Fieber messen. Das ist ein echter Lifehack.
taz: Aus einigen Ihrer Arbeiten spricht eine gewisse Wut. Im Video „Strike“ zerschlagen Sie mit offenem Haar einen Bildschirm. Der Titel von „Hell Yeah We Fuck Die“ kombiniert Worte, die am häufigsten in Songs vorkommen. Beide Arbeiten teilen auch ein Reproduktionsmoment. Ist das die spezifische Wut einer Frau?
Steyerl: Wallah Krise.
taz: Findet Ihre Wut ihren Ausdruck in der künstlerischen Arbeit?
Steyerl: Ich hoffe doch, dass meine künstlerische Arbeit als eine Art von Sublimierung funktioniert, wo dann nicht nur Affekt hinten rauskommt. Das wäre sonst peinlich. Das ist ja auch der Motor der kapitalistischen Verwertungsindustrie schlechthin. Wahrscheinlich geht es mir darum, mit Wut so lange zu spielen, bis ich eine Form dafür gefunden habe und sie in dieser Form halten kann.
taz: Die aktuelle Ausstellung in Hamburg heißt „Deine Mudda macht Show“. Eine Reminiszenz an den Song „Ja, Ja … Deine Mudder!“ der Hamburger Band Fünf Sterne Deluxe? Und sind Sie die Mudda?
Steyerl: Meine Tochter sagt Deine Mudda hier, Deine Mudda da. Und dann denk ich, Was laberst du, Alte?, das bin doch ich! Überhaupt bekommen Mütter durch diesen Ausspruch ja sehr viel Aufmerksamkeit wenn auch nicht besonders schmeichelhafte. Ich dachte dabei nicht an die Fünf Sterne Deluxe, sondern an eine Zeile der Rapperinnen von SXTN: „Ich ficke deine Mutter ohne Schwanz.“ Das ist Poesie 3000.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: The real race at the NYC Marathon is getting to the front of the toilet line
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
The New York City marathon was the culmination of months, or even years, of physical and mental preparation for more than 60,000 runners who dashed across the five boroughs on Sunday.
But before the run, participants had another important race to complete: the race to the bathroom.
Rows upon rows of purple, plastic portable toilets were stationed around the starting villages on Staten Island, where tens of thousands of runners waited for the race to begin. Doors constantly slammed shut as long lines of people in running shoes and cozy warm-up gear passed in and out of the stalls.
“It’s like the porta-potty company’s Super Bowl,” said Paola Yepez, 26, as she waited for the toilet before running her first marathon.
I was doing the same. My stomach twists in knots when I think about a half marathon I ran a few years ago. I needed the toilet before the race. But the line was so long I had to jump over the gates to get to the start. This time in the toilet line, I wanted to know how other runners were managing their uneasy stomachs and full bladders.
Using the facilities before the race is essential. Urinating or defecating outside of sanctioned toilets can lead to disqualification from the marathon and suspension from future races, according to New York Road Runners, which organizes the event.
One elite athlete went viral earlier this year when she kept competing after soiling herself at a HYROX race in Beijing, prompting outrage, disgust and vicarious humiliation. The pressure was on as runners queued up in front of the portable toilets on Sunday.
“We have a big responsibility on our plate,” said Angelo Martinez, CEO of John To Go, which provided more than 2,000 portable toilets and 46 hand washing stations for spectators and runners.
“When it's game time, [we’re] making sure that they can get ready to run the whole 26 miles and not have to worry about making a pit stop,” he said.
Martinez said John To Go started to prepare for the New York City marathon almost a year in advance. The company spent months investing in more toilets, making staffing plans and mapping out the transportation route. Deliveries started around 10 on Saturday night, he said.
“While the city's sleeping, we're delivering portable toilets and getting ready for the event, where it can be a seamless launch when they start running the race,” he said.
As a longtime runner, going to the bathroom before a race is one of the biggest sources of anxiety for me. I’m always paranoid that I’ll need to go mid-run and either suffer for miles or lose time using a toilet on the course.
As I waited with other runners, they told me about their training, their racing strategies, their goals and all the pre-race fuel sloshing around in their stomachs: gnocchi with pesto, pizza, coffee, bananas, sandwiches, sushi rice.
“After all the carb loading, I'm seriously considering going Keto, because I'm over it,” said Brian Dagliere, 36. “It sounds great, the carb load, but one way to describe it is, to me, it's disgusting. It's just a lot.”
Jodi Renert said her full bladder provided a welcome distraction.
“Waiting in the bathroom to pee is taking away my anxiety to run 26.2 miles,” she said, clutching a big bottle filled with a nutrition-packed drink and resisting the urge to cut to the front of the line.
“ I have to pee so bad,” Renert said. “Like, I shouldn't be drinking this, but it's got, like, all my carbs and electrolytes.”
The whole scene was a little ridiculous. While many New Yorkers were still in bed, we were lining up to flush the nerves — and the waste — out of our systems before we voluntarily ran an absurd distance.
The toilet line leaves a lot of time to marinate on every ache, pain and tummy rumble that could get in the way of achieving a hard-fought goal. Lisa Endrodi said she felt “awful.”
“Scared. Nervous. Yeah, all those emotions. Anxious,” she said.
Marathons have become a mid-life obsession for the 53-year-old, who traveled from the U.K. for her third 26.2-mile race.
“ My husband thinks I'm mad,” she said as she waited in line for the loo.
Going to the bathroom before a race is essential, she said.
“Especially for a female,” she said. “Most definitely. Yes.”
Running 26.2 miles is not a normal thing to put a body through. In my quiet moment of solitude inside the stinky stall, clutching my packet of tissues and bottle hand sanitizer, I remembered I was merely a human with basic biological needs that no amount of training could overcome.
Every person in the toilet line has their reason for running the race. Getting sober. Recovering from cancer. Checking a goal off the bucket list. I was there with my fiance, preparing to run my first marathon. We were racing together three weeks before our wedding, and we had committed to crossing the finish line together.
After multiple trips to the toilet, our starting time arrived, and we had to trust that our bodies were ready. Frank Sinatra’s “New York, New York” serenaded us as we ran side by side across the Verrazano Bridge. That’s when I began to lose a different fluid from my body: tears of joy.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Recife recebe celebração de saberes ancestrais com música, poesia e feira de mulheres empreendedoras
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Fátima Pereira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Ilê Dùn – Culinária e Espaço Cultural Diaspórico, no bairro do Barro, Zona Oeste do Recife, recebe neste sábado (7), das 14h30 às 22h, o encontro “Ebó: Tradições e Resistência”. Com entrada gratuita e classificação livre, a programação reúne música, poesia falada, performance, contação de histórias, artes visuais e uma feira de mulheres pretas empreendedoras. A iniciativa propõe um espaço de valorização das culturas afro-diaspóricas, da memória coletiva e dos conhecimentos transmitidos entre gerações.
Com atrações formadas por artistas pernambucanos, o evento marca a culminância de um projeto cultural que articula diferentes expressões artísticas e práticas tradicionais. Ao longo da tarde e da noite, o público poderá acompanhar apresentações autorais, participar de atividades abertas e conhecer iniciativas de empreendedorismo local. A programação também contará com pintura ao vivo da artista visual Bia, conhecida como MatrizB, durante todo o encontro.
Idealizado pelas produtoras culturais Priscila Ferraz, responsável também pela coordenação, e Tayná Passos, que assina a produção executiva, o projeto busca aproximar arte, educação, gastronomia e ancestralidade. Para Priscila, a proposta é criar oportunidades de circulação e compartilhamento de conhecimentos que permanecem vivos nas comunidades.
“Ebó é um convite à partilha, aprendendo, reconhecendo as raízes e celebrando a riqueza das tradições presentes nos territórios. A gente está juntando diferentes linguagens artísticas a processos de compartilhamento de saberes tradicionais, aproximando assim pessoas, conhecimentos e fazeres ancestrais”, destaca a escritora, arte-educadora e articuladora cultural.
A programação começa às 14h30, com abertura conduzida pela mestra de cerimônia Ana Benedita e contação de histórias para crianças, com Kimberly Fraga. Às 16h, o público acompanha a performance “Òná Ijó – A Dança das Encruzilhadas”, criada pelo poeta e artista multilinguagem Falik. Vinte minutos depois, o Slam das Minas PE promove uma batalha de poesia falada protagonizada por mulheres cis e trans, seguida de microfone aberto para artistas, grupos e demais participantes.
A partir das 18h30, a música assume o palco com o Coco do Rosário, de Jaboatão dos Guararapes. Na sequência, às 20h, a cantora e sambista recifense Maria Pagodinho apresenta seu trabalho. O encerramento fica por conta da cantora, compositora e percussionista Poli, acompanhada de sua banda, às 22h.
Segundo Tayná Passos, culinarista e pesquisadora alimentar, o encontro reúne diferentes manifestações culturais em uma experiência coletiva de celebração e resistência.
“É um encontro em que a oralidade se manifesta na contação de histórias e na poesia falada, os ritmos marcados pelas palmas das mãos nos conectam ao coco e ao samba, e a força coletiva se transforma em axé, presença e alegria”, afirma.
Outro eixo da programação é a feira de mulheres pretas e empreendedoras locais, que estará aberta durante todo o evento. A iniciativa reúne quatro negócios independentes que atuam em diferentes segmentos da economia criativa.
Entre as expositoras estão a Negra Rosa, representada por Marta Soares Gomes de Almeida, com produtos de beleza e autocuidado voltados para a pele negra e os cabelos crespos e cacheados; a Pry Art Crochê, com peças artesanais, moda autoral e amigurumis; a Maria Livreira, livraria independente especializada em literatura étnico-racial infantojuvenil; e a Annigastyle, dedicada à criação de joias autorais.
A feira também dá continuidade ao propósito das atividades formativas realizadas na primeira etapa do projeto, que incentivaram o intercâmbio de conhecimentos, a valorização do trabalho artesanal e a autonomia econômica das participantes.
“Esse movimento ganha continuidade, criando espaço para circulação, comercialização e fortalecimento de pequenos negócios e marcas independentes. Algumas das expositoras também participaram das atividades formativas, como Altayssa, da Annigastyle, que apresenta suas joias autorais. Fortalecer o empreendedorismo das mulheres é ampliar suas redes, sua autonomia e a economia dos territórios”, explica Patrícia Maré, uma das oficineiras.
Antes da celebração deste sábado, o “Ebó: Tradições e Resistência” realizou uma etapa formativa gratuita nos meses de abril e maio de 2026, também no Ilê Dùn. Foram promovidas três oficinas: “Saberes do Milho Branco: Do Sagrado à Mesa”, conduzida por Esmeraldina Pereira, conhecida como Iyá Dindinha D’Osún; “Estamparia Botânica”, com Patrícia Maré; e “Costurando Histórias: Artesania Sustentável”, ministrada por Giselle Silva.
A origem da iniciativa, no entanto, remonta a 2024, quando Priscila Ferraz e Tayná Passos organizaram a primeira edição do “Ebó de Poesia”, no Dùn Ajeun Culinária Afro Diaspórica, no bairro da Boa Vista, área central do Recife. Na ocasião, a proposta reuniu sarau e roda de conversa. A experiência motivou as produtoras a ampliar o projeto e construir novas possibilidades de encontro, formação e fortalecimento comunitário.
A realização de “Ebó: Tradições e Resistência” conta com incentivo do Sistema de Incentivo à Cultura do Município do Recife (SIC), por meio do Fundo de Incentivo à Cultura (FIC), da Fundação de Cultura da Cidade do Recife, da Secretaria de Cultura e da Prefeitura do Recife.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘My reward for waiting in the cold was this painting-like view of the ghat’: Priya Ojha’s best phone picture
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Grace Holliday
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
When Priya Ojha first arrived at Yamuna Ghat in New Delhi, late in December 2021, she was disappointed. She had left her home at 5am especially to capture shots of one of the most sacred rivers in India, but had arrived in dense fog and almost complete silence.
“Visibility was so low that all I could do was wait in the cold,” Ojha recalls. “Around 8am, I heard a voice call out, ‘Dhoop aa gayi’ – the sunrays have come out. They were right. This place that had looked like a graveyard slowly became more lively as local priests started their daily routines and boat riders took out their craft for business.”
Ojha recalls that a young boy appeared at her side and said, “Help me make my first ride and I will show you the ghat.” She agreed: “And that’s how I came across this scene.
“The two boats layered between the foreground and the background give a sense of depth, which makes the photo feel more lively,” she adds. “I liked that I captured not just this majestic place and the hundreds of swirling seagulls, but people just like me who had come to experience its beauty, too.”
When she reflects on the photograph now, Ojha is reminded of her patience that morning. “My reward was this painting-like picture of the ghat,” she says. “Just what I had set out for.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.title: How a Socialist Can Govern a City Under the Thumb of the Trump Administration
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.text:
Socialists will soon govern three of the United States’ most influential cities: Los Angeles, New York City, and the District of Columbia.
Janeese Lewis George joins Zohran Mamdani and Nithya Raman as part of a new wave of socialist local executives. But unlike Mamdani and Raman, Lewis George will govern a city under federal rule.
D.C. is a “federal district,” subject to the whims and micromanagement of the president and Congress. If the federal government doesn’t like the city’s legislation, it can override it. This poses additional challenges if Lewis George wants to change how things are done in the nation’s capital.
Lewis George, a current D.C. city councilmember, has promised to usher in sweeping reforms centered around affordability, including stronger tenant protections, investments in affordable childcare, and long-sought-after reforms on the city’s restrictive zoning laws. She rose to political prominence as the first socialist on the city council, winning her seat on a platform of defunding the police in the wake of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor protests in 2020. (She has since called for hiring additional Metropolitan Police officers.)
For Lewis George to fulfill her campaign promises is “going to require Janeese to use her position and her longstanding reputation as an organizer to convince members of Congress that we can exercise Home Rule and that we deserve the dignity of any other collective body, like a state, in this country,” said Kurtis Hagans, chair of Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America, which endorsed Lewis George in the primary.
All local D.C. bills are required to go through a congressional review period of 30 working days for civil legislation and 60 working days for criminal bills. If Congress doesn’t like the bill, it can either decide to let that review period lapse, allowing the legislation to go into effect, or pass a joint disapproval resolution in both the House and the Senate. If they pass a disapproval resolution, it goes to the president’s desk, where they can choose to veto and let the new law stand or sign it and override the legislation.
Speaking to The Intercept on Election Day, voters said they supported Lewis George because they wanted to elect someone who would fight for everyday Washingtonians.
“I was certainly motivated by wanting really strong leadership for D.C. and people who are going to put D.C. first, in the sense of the residents and the community members and not solely as our role as the capital city,” said Izetta Mobley, a voter in Ward 4, where Lewis George serves as a councilmember.
For Mobley and other voters, that primarily means tackling issues of affordability. “Affordable housing and the rise in unhoused folks, and making sure that unhoused folks have support and city resources …those were very important to me,” said Mobley.
Although Democrats took both houses of Congress on Tuesday, paving a clearer path for the district to flex its autonomy, Lewis George will still have to contend with Democratic leaders like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, both moderates, who are likely to lead the Senate and the House next session. Schumer and Jeffries were often critical of Mamdani when he was running for mayor in their home state of New York, though they seized primarily on his stance on Israel.
Hagans pointed out that Lewis George has the longtime support of former at-large councilmember Robert White, who was elected as Washington’s non-voting delegate on Tuesday. But Hagans said the DC Metro DSA is also preparing to organize residents to put pressure on Congress, given ”the relative powerlessness of the district in the face of Congress.”
Governing Washington has other pitfalls. The district is hamstrung by the fact that the D.C. Council is required to pass a balanced budget and is prohibited from carrying it over into the following year. (Congress also gets to approve it.) The city is already struggling to close a $1.1 billion budget deficit for the upcoming fiscal year — caused by Congress.
In order to achieve her agenda, Lewis George has suggested raising taxes on businesses and the city’s wealthiest residents. For that, she’ll need the support of the city council.
Lewis George is aided by the fact that Tuesday also ushered in a record number of socialists on the city council, adding two, Aparna Raj and Oye Owolewa. “A big part of the vision for the district is to have these organizers on the council as well as an organizer-in-chief at the executive level,” said Hagans.
Aside from bold economic policies, many voters who spoke to The Intercept said they want the new administration to prioritize resistance to the federal takeover of Washington, D.C., and ending the scourge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “We’ve seen ICE raids in our neighborhood, literally where our kids used to go to school,” said Jason Cherkis, another Ward 4 voter. “That’s one reason we voted for Janeese for mayor because she was out front and speaking about ICE in a way our current mayor never did.”
Despite the restrictions placed on a D.C. mayor, immigrant advocacy and civil rights groups concerned about the incursion of ICE in the district are pushing for Lewis George to take a stand.
“We want to see the next mayor doing everything possible to protect these most vulnerable communities from continued attacks,” said Peggy Ramin, policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union of the District of Columbia. “Whether that is legislation or the mayor ensuring that the administration’s agencies are well educated as to what that means in terms of limiting cooperation and even prohibiting cooperation.”
In particular, Ramin said that her organization is calling on the D.C. council and Lewis George to pass legislation that would allow residents to sue any officer — local or federal — who violates constitutional rights.
Ramin is aware of the challenges facing the district to pass this type of legislation without incurring interference from Congress or President Donald Trump — who has personally vowed to oppose Lewis George.
“No matter what Congress ends up doing, whether it disapproves or passes a disapproval resolution or not, I think people here in D.C. are really demanding and asking our council to step up and pass this sort of legislation,” said Ramin.
Aside from federal immigration officials, residents also complained about the National Guard, whose presence was felt even on Election Day. “I have two boys, Black men,” said one voter, Tamika Jackson, “and the harassment is out of control.”
As evidenced by the record number of socialists winning power across the country, Hagans says it’s clear both D.C. and the nation are looking for fighters.
“Democrats have promised a lot for a long time, but they seem unwilling to stand up to Trumpism,” said Hagans. Voters are noticing “this new class of democratic socialists,” he said, concluding, “Maybe I don’t know what that means entirely, but let’s give it a shot.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.title: Texas’ School Voucher Program Could Be “Unrecognizable, If Not Extinct,” Says Democratic Lawmaker
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.author: Lexi Churchill, Jeremy Schwartz
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s vision for education was finally coming together.
This year, the state launched a voucher program that allowed roughly 110,000 of Texas’ more than 5 million schoolchildren to get a private education using taxpayer dollars. Abbott’s loyal appointee at the Texas Education Agency, Commissioner Mike Morath, was leading the state’s largest takeover of public schools in recent history. And the Texas State Board of Education, with Abbott’s support, helped pass a controversial new social studies curriculum that required teaching Bible stories and shifted away from world history to focus on Texas and the United States.
On Tuesday night, as Democrats clinched nearly every office in the state, it all began to unravel.
In a speech after denying Abbott a fourth term, Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa called for a reversal of his education agenda. She pledged to fire Morath and to end the public school takeovers.
Perhaps most significantly, she doubled down on a campaign promise to erase one of Abbott’s biggest accomplishments: school vouchers.
“We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam,” said Hinojosa, who did not respond to requests for an interview.
It is not clear how Hinojosa will deliver on that promise. While Democrats have the ability to restrict parts of the program, eliminating it would require legislative action.
But Hinojosa will have help.
Democrat Sarah Eckhardt, a former state senator who voted against vouchers and will now lead the state office charged with running the program, has said she will push changes to increase accountability and transparency.
Eckhardt, however, acknowledged the limitations of her office, saying that any big overhaul must come from lawmakers.
Democrats won back the Texas House for the first time in 24 years, but Republicans retained a majority in the Senate.
Rep. Diego Bernal, the Democratic vice chair of the House education committee, seemed confident that there is a path toward killing the program, at least as it now exists.
Bernal, whose district is in San Antonio, said some Republican colleagues previously told him privately that they had reservations about the voucher program, but were limited in what they could do because of pressure from leaders who have now been ousted.
“I guarantee that program is not going to be untouched, and it will be probably unrecognizable, if not extinct, by the time we’re done with it,” he said.
Rural Texas Pushes Back
Abbott spent years trying to pass a statewide voucher program. By 2024, he’d grown angry at rural Republicans who repeatedly blocked such legislation because, they argued, public schools were a vital part of their communities. So Abbott shelled out millions of dollars to oust them from office and elect pro-voucher Republicans instead.
He succeeded. And the following year, those Republicans helped pass the $1 billion state voucher program. This week, at least 13 Republicans who Abbott had previously endorsed or helped fund as part of his voucher push lost to Democrats or were trailing in close races.
Abbott’s office declined an interview request, referring ProPublica and The Texas Tribune to his campaign office, which did not respond.
His bullishness on vouchers turned off some Republican voters in rural communities that have historically been strongholds for his party, education experts and politicians said.
A Texas Tribune analysis found Democrats made striking gains in rural and semirural parts of the state, where concern over vouchers, along with issues like data centers, ran high. In rural counties, Abbott’s margin over Hinojosa fell 16 percentage points from his 2022 margin over former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke, and it fell 20 percentage points in exurban counties.
Former state Rep. Dewayne Burns, an anti-voucher Republican from a mostly rural district south of Fort Worth who was defeated by an Abbott-backed primary challenger in 2024, said many of his constituents felt betrayed by the governor’s push for vouchers. “That’s the first time that I think rural Texans really kind of stepped back and said, ‘Are you guys really supporting us?’” he said. “I think they overestimated the loyalty that Texans, especially rural Texans, had to the governor.”
Former state Rep. Steve Allison, who represented a suburban San Antonio district before he was unseated in the 2024 primary, said he remains convinced his constituents never wanted the voucher system. Pro-voucher groups targeted him in a series of ads that attacked him for issues like border security and property taxes but said little about school choice. Polls at the time showed Texans held complicated views on school choice, with one University of Houston poll showing that while two-thirds of Texans supported voucher legislation, an equal number believed that vouchers would funnel money away from already struggling public schools.
“I know what I saw when my staff took very careful notice of what phone calls were coming in and what emails and texts and visits were coming in,” he said in an interview. “It was clear that the overall district was opposed to vouchers.”
Concerns about vouchers became key in several rural and suburban Texas districts this year where Abbott’s selected candidates had won two years ago. One of those races was for Allison’s old seat, which pro-voucher candidate Marc LaHood won in 2024 after Abbott spent at least $700,000 supporting him.
Another was in Bell County in Central Texas. There, the Abbott-backed incumbent, Rep. Hillary Hickland, conceded a close race Wednesday morning. She did not respond to a request for an interview. Her Democratic opponent, Amelia Rabroker, a former teacher, said the Republicans’ heavy-handed push for vouchers spurred her to challenge Hickland.
“A lot of money was pushed into her campaign to make that happen, and she delivered on those vouchers, and it was very upsetting to the people of Central Texas,” Rabroker said. “I think it was a huge concern. The biggest.”
Similarly, LaHood, who did not respond to requests for comment, faced a flurry of questions over his support of vouchers at a candidate forum for the District 121 race in October. His opponent, Democrat Zack Dunn, said vouchers and public education were second only to affordability in the minds of voters he met. On Tuesday night, Dunn defeated LaHood with 54% of vote.
“Across the board, overwhelmingly the sentiment was, ‘We need to fully fund our public schools,’” Dunn said in an interview. “The voucher scam, the voucher scheme, the voucher vote that was taken is hurting us. It’s hurting us definitely across the state, but it’s hurting us in 121. Yes, we heard that over and over and over again.”
What’s Next?
Dunn said he would support measures that ensure more transparency in how taxpayer dollars are used for private schools.
Ultimately, though, he wants to see the program repealed.
Some changes can come through administrative actions by Eckhardt, the new state comptroller. In a news conference the day after her election, Eckhardt said she planned to rigorously audit how taxpayer money is spent and to release more information about the program to the public.
Under her Republican predecessors, the comptroller’s office shielded information that included data detailing how much state funding certain private schools received and how many students most public schools lost to the program. The office argued that it was protecting student privacy.
“As the comptroller, my job is to vigorously follow the money and report back to the Legislature if their investment is not panning out,” Eckhardt said. She added, “That is part of the vigorous audit and performance evaluation of this program that any comptroller should be doing, and I certainly will be doing.”
One key supporter of vouchers in the Senate, the last Republican bulwark in the state, is taking a more measured approach on the program’s future.
Houston Republican Sen. Paul Bettencourt, who led the effort to approve vouchers that had failed in prior years, said the Legislature will need to review the outcomes from the 2026-27 school year and assess the benefits and families’ concerns. He pointed to the fact that vouchers were returned by some parents whose children required special education services.
“I think that it has helped students in many other states,” Bettencourt said. “We need to look at what’s happened here with this first cohort, and we need to make sure that we’re debating not the emotionality prior to passage of a bill, but the facts of what happened after the passage of a bill.”
Scott Schneider, an attorney who represents private schools participating in the voucher program, said the midterm results shocked private school leaders. Some were counting on the state funding to support their business. He said private school leaders could start a lobbying effort to grandfather in the families already benefiting from the program, but schools are also planning for what they will do if the state funding goes away altogether.
“It’s going to be a hot mess,” Schneider said.

https://hyperallergic.com/please-dont-si.author: Hakim Bishara
https://hyperallergic.com/please-dont-si.text:
Please Don’t Sit on the Flowers
Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape goes to auction, Brancusi gets lost at MoMA, interview with Doris Salcedo, and is showing at documenta worth it?
Sitting at September Cafe, I watch the autumn leaves separate from the trees and get carried away gently by the wind. They swirl and twirl, performing a merry little dance in the air before falling to their final resting place.
News has just come in about a sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections, as fierce and awesome as a Gustave Courbet wave. But I see nobody popping champagne bottles in the streets. A pregnant black cat with a hanging belly saunters by.
Lying back in the dentist’s chair, a TV screen in front of me shuffles picturesque views from exotic places. They're idyllic to the point of not looking real. My doctor, a Lebanese, shows me an X-ray of my mouth, which looks like Beirut at the height of the Civil War.
The sky over the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge is gray, and the Harlem River is brooding as I make my way to Taryn Simon’s exhibition Father Country I Do Love You at the Guggenheim Museum. The show tells the heroic tales of an FBI agent whose alleged career intersects with major events in American history. Cold, antiseptic photographs encased neatly in plexiglass make up a detective story linking the protagonist to the explosion of TWA Flight 800, the 9/11 attacks, the bombing of the United States embassy in Nairobi, Bill Clinton’s impeachment, and more. Trudging up the Guggenheim’s spiraling galleries, I wonder whether this patriotic show is organized and sponsored by the US State Department. Simon makes you read a lot, but all that reading is just meant to distract you from thinking.
Jodie Foster narrates the audio guide for those who don’t have the patience to read long-winded wall texts. At the cafeteria, while eating a bikini sandwich, I see a woman who looks exactly like Judi Dench, another actress. “I love storytelling,” she tells a friend before plunging her teeth into a chocolate croissant.
On my way out, I once again resent how this museum forces everyone to exit through the gift shop to encourage commerce, but I buy myself a $5 Guggenheim bag anyway. Outside, in one of the manicured gardens of the Upper East Side, a small sign pleads, “Please don’t sit on the flowers.”
I cross the street into Central Park through Engineers’ Gate, climb the steps past a gilded bust of John Purroy Mitchel, NYC mayor between 1914-1918, and look out over the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir. I think of the Kennedys, of Trump, and of Simon. A worker collects brown leaves in plastic bags and tosses them into a truck wrapped in a photo of green leaves. A mother tries to snap a photo of her child, but the unruly kid refuses to pose for the camera. He throws a fit, falls, and, to her shock, ends up sitting on the flowers.
—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Strange, Empathetic Allure of Andy Beshear
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Grace Byron
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Strange, Empathetic Allure of Andy Beshear
The potential Democratic hopeful for president is not a socialist. But he has a folksy demeanor and moral compass.
Ever since I moved to New York, I’ve become accustomed to watching people’s eyes glaze over when I tell them I went to Indiana University. Many of these East Coast dilettantes who went to Yale or NYU, even some of my friends, cannot point to Indiana on a map. I’ve learned that New Yorkers all have a very different idea of what constitutes the Midwest. My home state borders Kentucky to the south and has plenty of cultural similarities with the Commonwealth. Fried chicken, gravy, and corn are staples throughout Indiana, but especially when you drive south through the hills. I grew up in Mike Pence’s Indiana; I was very aware of what it meant to live in a “red state.” Of course, I had a complicated upbringing, but I tell people they can’t talk shit about the Midwest unless they’ve lived there; These states are diverse. Many kinds of people call the region home.
For Governor Andy Beshear, this is familiar territory. He’s won big in Kentucky, a Republican-majority state, multiple times, rising through the ranks to become a potential Democratic presidential nominee for 2028. He’s yet to announce—and he’s not the only in the area running on an anti-Trump agenda—JB Pritzker seems potentially poised to run too. It’s a crowded race, and there’s a divide between the far and center left. Who will pull the party further? Alexandria O’Casio Cortez seems to be entertaining a run, and it seems Kamala Harris may try her luck again, despite the previous failure of her last-minute entry during the war on Gaza. Gavin Newsom remains a front-runner too. Early as it is, Andy Beshear, a lesser-known candidate who has only recently entered the spotlight, has released his memoir-cum-platform, too, called Go and Do Likewise.
Beshear lies somewhere in the middle among his fellow Democratic hopefuls. He may admire Zohran Mamdani, but he’s not a socialist. He may believe in liberal ideals like accessible healthcare for all and minority rights, but he has some critiques for mainstream MSNBC-loving liberals whose rhetoric abandons the working class. “Not thinking about health care as essential to rural America is not understanding how the economy works,” Beshear told The New Republic last year, before emphasizing affordability as the defining issue that concerned his rural constituents. He believes in protections against climate change, but thinks it is just as important to create new jobs in rural Kentucky and protect farmers from tariffs. He wants a ceasefire in Gaza, but believes Israel is a “critical ally” to the United States and has yet to use the term “genocide” to describe what’s going in Palestine. The author of a profile on Beshear put it this way while reflecting on his Christian faith for Vogue: “But as devout as Beshear is, I note an equally fervent faith in the power of pragmatism.” While some more provocative ideologues like Jennifer Welch and Hasan Piker have become spokespeople for the left, the path seems clear for a more stringent liberal like Beshear. He emphasizes social rights while still appealing to some mainstream Democrats. His local wins have already shown how Democrats can win votes “anywhere.” His upset victory has been heralded as a way forward for the left to win red states and seats—even if he barely won. Sometimes squeaking by is the only option.
Sometime last year, Beshear started receiving the profile treatment in the mold of a Kennedy. It was the black-and-white photos in Vogue that first caught my attention. He seemed like he was trying to seem like a Real American Man, relatable and folksy, with a clear, calm, empathetic, rational plan for the country. In an interview with Tyler Foggatt for The New Yorker’s Political Scene podcast, he spoke about red-state electability and the economy. Now, as Beshear returns for a new press cycle, he’s going after Trump: “He doesn’t give a damn about the Constitution,” he told MS NOW.
While Beshear wants the Democrats to be more than the party of #resistance, his memoir spends a fair amount of time differentiating his faith and politics from the current president’s crass, hawkish version of Christianity. He even nicknames his political foe Matt Bevin “Trump Lite.” According to Beshear, Bevin practices “Us” and “Them” politics and would rather die than admit he’s wrong. In short, he’s a bully—like Trump himself. In Go and Do Likewise, this tactic stands out. Trump is front and center by page two, scrunched between Bible verses and the Parable of the Good Samaritan. Later, Beshear points out that “Trump throws Gatsby parties with his billionaire friends, while Jesus hung out with the exact opposite.” He implies that “Now go and do likewise,” the command at the end of Jesus’s story, “means treating all people as people of God—not dividing the country by party, race, ethnicity, or even sexual orientation.” Empathy, he argues, is “neither liberal nor conservative.” They “certainly aren’t woke—a word that has become a pejorative to some people.” Moving beyond the lingo while still embracing its zeitgeist, he extolls us to “Make America Kind Again.”
For Beshear, the truth is that community is all around us. We don’t have to like our neighbor to care about them. Go and Do Likewise is full of Good Samaritans who don’t ask about pronouns in the face of a flood; they just get to helping their neighbors. It’s a value he sees everywhere he travels in Kentucky. “This is what our faith should teach us—that our own comfort does not have to come at another’s expense,” he writes.
This was not the version of faith that I grew up with; I am more familiar with JD Vance’s vision of the world—preaching one thing and practicing another all with a stern grip on right and wrong. Beshear notes that many Republicans cast faith in “militaristic terms,” rather than as the work of a beloved community. His brand of Christianity is not to make a Christian nation but to inspire through his faith. “God-talk is easy,” he says. “Living it out consistently is tough.”
As the former attorney general of Kentucky, Beshear fought for the rights of the many rather than the few. Even when it wasn’t politically expedient. He wanted everyone to be able to get healthcare and vaccines—including those with preexisting conditions and in rural, underserved areas. Beshear slowly unspools these victories over the course of the book: his achievements as a lawyer, his father’s own legal wins and political aspirations. As attorney general, Beshear took on opioid companies, winning settlements for those who had become addicted to pain pills. When talking about such cases, he likes to be clear. He doesn’t like to use the phrase “substance abuse disorder” but “addiction.” For Beshear, it’s important to use the language of his constituents. He wants to be the kind of candidate you can envision yourself having a beer with and shooting the shit. He’s certainly easier to imagine having a gab session with than Newsom or Harris.
“Candidates don’t sound like normal human beings when they use terms like ‘food insecurity’ when they should say people are hungry,” he writes. “I talked to people, not down to them.” He prefers to say why he is doing something rather than merely use empty rhetoric. Of course, that’s much easier on a state level than a national one, even if Beshear has already faced intense criticism from Republicans for his pro-choice and pro-trans stances. He even took a picture with the infamous drag group Ladies of Perpetual Indulgence at a Pride event. Unlike Newsom, who has consistently folded on trans issues, Beshear has defended trans women in sports, calling the restrictions just plain mean. This folksy, simple down-home talk of right and wrong and acceptance strikes me as a similar recipe to Dolly Parton’s anti-politics politics. She wanted everyone to get along and have a chance at a happy life. The Golden Rule was more important than partisan divides.
Beshear includes plenty of stories about other people in his book, including a Democratic senator from Louisville whose trans son took his own life. “The response? No compassion. No empathy,” he writes in anger. He vetoed the bill that sought to keep trans people out of sports, something he continually gets flak for to this day even as he’s instead sought to move the conversation to things like jobs and affordability. “Don’t tell me the Democratic Party should stop fighting for the rights of all people. Just explain your authentic why, and then get back to focusing on the issues that touch all our lives on a daily basis.” I can’t imagine a Democrat in Indiana saying something like during my teen years: “The moment we fail to see our shared humanity is the moment we let people fall through the cracks.”
It does seem, by and large, that Beshear is walking the walk as much as any politician can in his position. He helps everyone after tornados and floods, not just those who voted for him or adhered to strict Covid protocols. He is comfortable partnering with YouTube maverick and provocateur Mr. Beast for disaster relief fundraising as he is giving a speech at the Martin & Coretta King Unity Breakfast. From healthcare to racial justice, the back half of God and Do Likewise is a chapter-by-chapter breakdown of his more tightly held political beliefs. The “dream is nonpartisan,” he says, and admits that Democrats too make mistakes. Some critics have pointed out he’s a bit cautious when it comes to taking on Republicans like Mitch McConnell. He may be less compromising than someone like Gavin Newsom, but that doesn’t mean he can’t be timid about challenging the Republican establishment. It’s a classic paradox. Everyone has to pick their battles.
The personal stories that Beshear shares—from a friend who died in a mass shooting to a woman who got an abortion after her father sexually abused and raped her—inform his public ideology. He uses these parables to explain his positions. It is difficult to believe any politician fully, but there do seem to be a lot of genuinely held beliefs in Go and Do Likewise. There are a lot of natural disasters stateside, but foreign policy is largely absent—unlike in many other political hopeful’s books. Often, these publications are vanity projects—business cards for those trying to get in the game and do the press circuit. It’s a policy book sprinkled with faith rather than the other way around. JD Vance’s book, on the other hand, Communion, is a book instrumentalizes faith as a back door into his cruel beliefs about immigration and minorities.
Whether or not the kind of empathy Beshear champions takes root, it’s clear that the Democrats need a new strategy. They’re struggling to decide what that means. There are signs the midterms could be a win for liberals, but that hardly guarantees a certain victory. A politics of empathy, that grounds those often betrayed by the establishment—the poor and the downtrodden, people of color and queer people—would be a decisive refutation of mean-spirited MAGA politics. I’m not sure America is ready to become kind again. For many, I worry it is too late. I want to believe that we can still find connection, but in the isolation, misinformation, and division, many seem afraid to befriend anyone who doesn’t look like them. As the public sphere shrinks, we become more terrified than ever to engage with the other. For some, like Andy Beshear, the face of the other inspires compassion. For others, it merely inspires fear.

https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/jeremy-bacch.title: Jeremy Bacchi demande la levée des sanctions administratives contre les lycéens mobilisés
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/jeremy-bacch.text:
Le sénateur PCF des Bouches-du-Rhône Jeremy Bacchi demande l’amnistie pour les « lycéens victimes de sanctions administratives » dans le cadre du mouvement social en cours. Il a écrit au ministre de l’Éducation nationale. « Dans plusieurs établissements, des directions ont prononcé ou s’apprêtent à prononcer des sanctions administratives impliquant l’inscription d’avertissements dans les dossiers scolaires à l’encontre de jeunes ayant participé à des actions de mobilisation ou s’étant trouvés à l’extérieur des grilles de l’établissement malgré des interdictions préfectorales ou de direction », dénonce Jeremy Bacchi dans sa missive à Edouard Geffray.
« Qualifier d’absences injustifiées des actes d’engagements de la jeunesse et les assortir d’un avertissement porté au dossier scolaire constitue une réponse d’une extrême gravité », critique le dirigeant communiste, qui s’inquiète de sanctions « notifiées de manière immédiate » sans « instruction » qui permette « de faire valoir le principe du contradictoire ». Aussi demande-t-il de garantir le respect des procédures.

89 min: Wilson steps across Tonali, who swings an arm to bring him down and picks up a booking.
88 min: Meanwhile, Leeds are doing a marvellous job of containing Spurs, who are trying to respond, but can’t get anywhere near their opponents’ box. Leeds’ xG is now exactly 2 to Tottenham’s 0.28.
87 min: No, is the answer to that. Not a single one.
86 min: TNT are interviewing Nmecha as the game goes on, a box popping up and invading the action. Did any football fan ask for this sort of thing?
84 min: Kudus makes way for the 18-year-old Williams-Barnett. When the game restarts, Calvert-Lewin once again tears clear down the right, but doesn’t back himself to shoot, turning around instead and laying off to Okafor. The move breaks down. That’s a couple of big chances butchered by Calvert-Lewin today.
82 min: Spurs haven’t won any of their last 49 matches in which they’ve gone behind. No wonder Roberto De Zerbi looks thoroughly miserable. That goal was no more than Leeds deserved; they’ve been by far the better team in this second half.
80 min: VAR has a look at a possible handball by Wilson, but there was no touch with his arm. The goal stands!
GOAL! Leeds United 1-0 Tottenham Hotspur (Okafor 79)
Bard throws in from the left. Wilson swivels just inside the box, chesting down and teeing up Okafor, who takes a touch infield before lashing a shot across Kinsky and into the bottom left! Lovely move, and what a substitution!
77 min: Kinsky annoys Longstaff again by pawing his corner clear. Then Leeds make a double change, sending on Wilson and Okafor for Tanaka and Nmecha.
76 min: … but Spurs don’t clear their lines particularly well, and Tanaka strides down the left to win another Leeds corner. Longstaff, who must be wondering how he didn’t score, to take.
75 min: Bogle advances down the right and crosses low for Longstaff, who turns and launches a rising shot goalwards from 12 yards. It’s a superb effort, and heading in, but met by the fingertips of Kinsky. What a save! The ball clears the bar, and nothing comes of the corner.
73 min: Kulusevski and Bentancur combine down the right, but at such slow speed that Leeds close down all avenues to their box. Spurs have not created very much this afternoon.
71 min: From the set piece, Bogle shoots. The ball hits Bentancur. Leeds claim a penalty, but that’s hit Bentancur on the chest. No sir!
70 min: Bard loops down the middle. Nmecha tries to loop over Kinsky, who tips onto the bar. But he was offside. Then Calvert-Lewin fails to hit the target. But Kinsky takes his sweet time over the restart, so the referee awards a corner to Leeds!
68 min: Spurs play some possession stuff. They don’t really go anywhere for a while, but suddenly spring into action, Gallagher bringing the ball down on the edge of the Leeds D before pearling a low drive inches wide of the bottom left. Not entirely sure Trafford was getting to that. Spurs fans thought that was in, so are jeered for their cheer not long after.
66 min: … so Spurs make a triple change, replacing the ineffective Marmoush and Fernandes, plus Porro, who is on one-and-a-half yellows, with Kulusevski, Bentancur and Gallagher. Gray will take over from Porro at right-back.
64 min: Leeds have had seven attempts on goal during this second half. Spurs are yet to generate a single one.
63 min: Calvert-Lewin, Bard and Longstaff combine well down the left. The ball’s rolled infield for Ampadu, who shoots from 25 yards. The ball takes a huge deflection to the left, and had it stayed on target, it was a goal, because Kinsky had committed to diving the other way. But it squeaks out for a corner, which Kinsky claims. Leeds are getting closer and closer.
62 min: Van de Ven again over-eggs his dribble out from the back. This time he loses the ball, allowing Nmecha to enter the box from the left and aim a curler towards the top right. It’s not a good effort, and easily blocked.
61 min: Leeds are romping ahead in the xG stakes. It’s 1.11 to 0.22.
60 min: Porro clips Bard, who was advancing down the left, from behind. It should be a yellow. It’s not, though, presumably because it would have been a second yellow for Porro, and you know how referees process that sort of situation. Porro is now in the last-chance saloon. Meanwhile nothing comes of the resulting free kick.
58 min: The pace doesn’t drop, but passes are no longer sticking. All a bit messy for now.
56 min: Van de Ven over-elaborates when dribbling out from the back, and is nearly stripped by Longstaff. Had the Leeds man completed the challenge, he was through on goal. Van de Ven breathes out.
55 min: Tonali, dropping deep, tries to release Kudus down the right but has to settle for a corner. Kudus ambles across to take it. He exchanges passes with Solanke, then Robertson finally crosses long. Leeds deal with it. A bit of a waste.
53 min: Calvert-Lewin romps into space down the inside-right channel, chasing a fine Longstaff pass. He should shoot upon reaching the area, but lays off to Tanaka instead, who leans back and skies over the bar. Huge chance spurned.
52 min: Porro slides in, over the ball, and catches Nmecha on the shin. It’s a yellow. It should be a yellow. But Bogle’s far worse action in the first half should have been that at the very least. Roberto De Zerbi highlights this inherent contradiction, and is also booked for his trouble. Consistency? Good luck in your search for that.
50 min: Bogle crosses from the right. Calvert-Lewin prepares to sidefoot home from six yards, only for Van de Ven to nip in ahead of him, and slice the ball over his own bar and wide left. Then from the corner, hit long by Longstaff, Calvert-Lewin heads goalwards. Solanke blocks on his own line, then Elvedi heads wide left from close range. It should be 1-0.
48 min: Ampadu throws long from the right. Van de Ven clears. Leeds have had no joy with their long-throw weapon so far.
46 min: Bard’s very first act is to whip in a glorious low cross from his position on the left. Calvert-Lewin is on his heels and can’t connect. That was begging to be rammed home.
Leeds get the second half started. They’ve replaced Gudmundsson with Bard.
Half-time postbag. “Both feet are off the ground. That’s Bogle’s entire weight on Tel’s Achilles. That can lead to a serious injury. Bizarre decision” – Martin Perring
“Why do red cards exist if not precisely to protect players?” – John from Norway
“The most insane thing about VAR, and there are so many insane things about it, is that we have to watch replays of a player OBVIOUSLY doing a red-card challenge one thousand times in slow-motion, and it ends with not even a yellow. The chicken-shit nature of it all, the incompetence, all elevated because of technology. I hate it so, so much” – Øivind Idsø
“There’s overthinking it, as you say, but this is like they’ve been given a task to find a reason for not giving that as a red, rocking and rolling desperately, frame-by-frame. The explanation they release for not giving a red should be a corker. Meanwhile, whatever happened to ‘clear and obvious’? VAR is almost single-handedly turning me into a grumpy old man. I’ll be off out now to shout at some pigeons” – Rob Knap
“I’ve supported VAR from the start. It was always going to have teething issues as it was implemented, and it was never going to 100% eliminate mistakes. Subjectivity is still a thing. But, my word, they don’t half make it hard to defend at times. It should be established now, a mature technology with most of the errors ironed out. If anything, though, It’s getting worse. I’m not in the ‘Bin it’ camp yet, but I’m a lot closer than I was at the start of the season” – Matt Dony
“Committees are an extremely useful method for decision making, especially when people have time to deliberate. But perhaps football refereeing isn’t suited to committees” – Kári Tulinius
“That would have been a red card at Elland Road in the 70s” – Gary Naylor
HALF TIME: Leeds United 0-0 Tottenham Hotspur
Leeds should have had a penalty; they should also have had a man sent off. The players walk down the tunnel. The referee was planning to drive away in his car, but the doors and square wheels have fallen off and there’s all smoke coming out of the radiator.
45 min +5: Ampadu throws long from the left. Van Hecke powers a header miles clear. Ampadu has another go. Van Hecke batters clear again. The xG does not change.
45 min +4: The xG, for what that’s worth, is 0.19 to 0.22. Meanwhile Roberto De Zerbi continues to give the fourth official the what-for. His post-match interview could make for good entertainment.
45 min +2: Fernandes slices a low drive miles off target. After nearly boiling over, this half is now fizzling out, which is probably for the best all round.
45 min: There will be six minutes of additional first-half time, most of which a result of the on-field referee and VAR spending ages failing to make a decision.
44 min: Kudus fizzes a tempting low cross through the Leeds six-yard box from the right. What a ball. But neither Gray nor Solanke respond. Any touch and it was the opening goal.
43 min: Tel limps off. A heavy trudge, he’s in some difficulty. He’s replaced by Solanke.
42 min: Marmoush clips Muharemovic from behind. That should be a booking as well, but the referee has lost control of this with his unwillingness to make any sort of decision whatsoever. Meanwhile Tel goes down, he looks really unhappy.
40 min: Tel is getting dog’s abuse now. He’s also moving very gingerly, having recently had someone stand on his ankle.
39 min: Roberto De Zerbi isn’t happy about that. You can’t blame him. Meanwhile the game restarts, with Bogle, who shouldn’t be on the pitch, crossing for Nmencha, who plants a header straight at Kinsky. Had that gone in, there would have been some wild scenes all right.
38 min: No red card, no serious foul play. That is preposterous enough in itself; that there’s not even a yellow is beyond a joke. The on-field referee should have seen that, at the very least.
37 min: VAR is flapping taking a long time over this. You can overthink these things, you know.
36 min: It’s a really poor challenge, studs landing on Tel’s achilles, the Spurs player’s leg bending. It should be a red card.
35 min: VAR is in fact checking for a red card. The on-field referee, it should be noted, has completely abdicated responsibility.
34 min: Bogle leaves one on Tel, who was in the process of spinning him. It’s a really poor challenge, studs on ankle. A red card wouldn’t be out of the question here; there’s not even a yellow shown.
33 min: A long pass down the left confuses Elvedi into conceding a corner with a misjudged backwards header. One corner leads to another, then Marmoush heads harmlessly wide. To be fair, Trafford has had next to nothing to do as well, if you ignore a couple of long-range shots scuffed straight at him.
