Iran's navy reports that an oil tanker caught fire after colliding with a naval mine while travelling through a "prohibited" area in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
According to the reports, the vessel turned off its navigation systems and ignored “regular warnings”.
No casualties have been reported.
The navy subsequently issued a warning to other ships attempting to cross the contested waterway without Iranian permission.
“This is the fate of all ships and vessels that ignore warnings and travel in prohibited areas,” it said in comments carried by Iran’s semi-official broadcaster IRIB.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Who is Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat poised to become House speaker?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Who is Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat poised to become House speaker?
Likely to become the first Black House Speaker, Jeffries faces pressure from progressives over Trump and Israel.
With Democrats’ decisive victory in the United States’ midterm elections on Tuesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is on the verge of making history as the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives.
For the 56-year-old congressman, it would be the culmination of almost two decades in office, giving him a central role in Democrats’ efforts to rein in Republican US President Donald Trump in the final two years of his presidency.
But as Jeffries celebrated the “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats back into power the day after the election, some within the party were not convinced that the congressman, known for his cautious approach to politics and longstanding support for Israel, was the right man for the moment.
An online petition on Change.org calling on lawmakers to choose another speaker had collected more than 980,000 signatures by Saturday morning, while several newly elected progressive lawmakers have not said whether they will support him.
“We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” the petition reads.
“This is not a foregone conclusion,” it continues, urging others to run for the job.
Jeffries, who has spent years cultivating relationships within the Democratic caucus, now finds himself at the centre of a bigger fight within the party, as its growing progressive wing pushes for a more confrontational approach to Trump and a break with some of the ideas that have defined the Democrats for decades.
From Brooklyn to Democratic leader
Jeffries grew up in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, in the 1970s and 1980s, as the neighbourhood was grappling with the crack cocaine epidemic.
“There was a lot of dysfunction and pain that surrounded the communities that I was raised in, but also a lot of love and compassion from family and friends, and community folks,” he told NYU Law in 2019.
The son of two social workers, Jeffries eventually became a lawyer, tracing his decision to pursue a career in law back to the 1992 riots that erupted in Los Angeles after four white police officers were acquitted in the beating of Rodney King, a Black man.
“It crystallized the fact that we still had a long way to go to eradicate social and racial injustice,” he said.
Jeffries went on to work as a corporate lawyer before entering politics, losing two runs for the New York State Assembly before winning a seat in 2006 and eventually being elected to Congress six years later.
In Washington, he helped broker a bipartisan criminal justice reform law signed by Trump in 2018. Two years later, during Trump’s first impeachment trial, he argued that Trump should be removed from office as one of seven House impeachment managers who presented the case to the US Senate.
Rising quickly through the Democratic ranks, Jeffries became caucus chair in 2019 before making history three years later, when he was unanimously chosen to succeed former Speaker Nancy Pelosi as the party’s House leader, becoming the first Black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress.
Can Jeffries unite his party?
Jeffries and Pelosi have been compared for their distinct leadership styles. While Pelosi was known for her commanding, top-down approach, Jeffries has built a reputation for quietly and deliberately building consensus among his colleagues.
That approach has frustrated some Democrats, who say Jeffries has been too reluctant to take firm positions and who question whether he is prepared to confront Trump and Republicans in Congress aggressively enough.
Those concerns were on display after Jeffries declared after the election that “the American people don’t want us to get even; they want us to get things done on their behalf.”
Among those who pushed back was left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker, who reposted a video of Jeffries’s comments, saying: “No, we definitely ARE looking for justice and accountability.”
Jeffries also faced criticism after reports emerged in August that he had privately met Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who does not have a formal role in the administration but has been involved in diplomatic efforts in the Middle East and in Russia.
Jeffries defended the meeting, saying Kushner had requested it and that he had used it to discuss the affordability crisis. But critics argued that rather than meeting privately with Kushner, Jeffries should have been preparing to investigate his business dealings.
Ahead of the election, Axios reported on a plan by some incoming progressive lawmakers – informally known as “The Bloc” and including Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Melat Kiros of Colorado – to use the upcoming speaker vote to win concessions from Jeffries on issues such as Medicare for All, cutting funding for ICE, and weapons shipments to Israel.
That may be harder now that the Democrats have a comfortable majority, with Jeffries less dependent on progressive newcomers to secure the speakership. But the result also makes it harder for Jeffries to argue, as he has in the past, that Republican control of Congress is hindering the Democrats’ ability to advance their agenda and hold Trump accountable.
Jeffries’s Israel stance divides Democrats
Of all the sources of tension between Jeffries and his party’s progressive wing, the hardest divide to bridge may be over his longstanding support for Israel and ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
At a conference hosted by the group in 2020, Jeffries opposed putting conditions on US aid to Israel and described Jerusalem as New York City’s “sixth borough”.
He has also been one of the top recipients of financial support from AIPAC and its network of donors, earning the nickname “AIPAC Shakur” from New York radio host Charlamagne tha God.
In a celebratory post after the elections congratulating the candidates it had supported, AIPAC singled out Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer by name.
But Jeffries’s steadfast support for Israel throughout its genocidal war on Gaza has put him increasingly at odds with his own party, and he recently signalled that his position may be changing.
In July, even as he voted against an amendment that would have cut $3.3bn in annual military aid to Israel, he acknowledged the need for a reset in US-Israel relations.
“A meaningful change in direction is needed,” he wrote in a letter to colleagues.
Jeffries appears to have the speakership all but secured, with no serious challenger emerging so far.
However, with Trump still in the White House, a party grappling with its own divisions, and voters expecting change on everything from the cost of living to the war on Iran, the bigger test for Jeffries will come once he is on the job.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.title: How Going Blind Made Doris Salcedo’s Art Bigger and Better
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.author: Emily Watlington
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.text:
Doris Salcedo is best known for her moving “anti-monuments,” gigantic artworks—or sometimes negative spaces—that propose new ways to commemorate atrocities. Always, she focuses on the victims’ perspectives. Her best-known work, Shibboleth (2007), installed in Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, comprised one giant, scar-like crack in the concrete, rerouting foot traffic in a manner that evoked the jarring disruption of borders more broadly.
The Colombian artist began working at such a monumental scale only after she began losing her central vision. At age 31, Salcedo was diagnosed with Stargardt disease, a rare genetic condition, and today she is legally blind, with only peripheral sight.
Before her vision started to change, Salcedo made all her sculptures alone. Reflecting on that time during a visit to one of her studios in Bogotá in July, she remembered treasuring “the privacy of improvising and of working directly with the materiality.” But as her condition progressed, she had to give up solitude “little by little” and started working with assistants.
Naturally, she mourned surrendering the spontaneity her independence enabled. At first, Salcedo, now 67, found that “it was a very difficult adjustment, especially losing the privacy.” She also found that she had to “think in a different manner,” since “before, I was improvising; I never had a prior drawing.” When she works with a team, she has to come up with a plan she can clearly communicate: “Things have to be absolutely defined,” she explained. Slowly, though, she found that working collaboratively “gave me the possibility of making better pieces than the ones I was making by myself. A collective statement is far more powerful than a lonely solo voice. It becomes like a chorus, and a really potent one.”
In November, at White Cube Gallery in New York, Salcedo will premiere a sculpture that is the culmination of decades of this collaborative way of working—and huge in a way that could never be accomplished by one person. A full-sized house—at nearly 30 feet—has been woven entirely from human hair. When I visited, dozens of assistants were working across her three studios, tying knots in individual strands, a painstaking process. The resulting pattern resembles chicken wire or a chain-link fence.
Even working with such a big team, the process took three years. “To be thankful is not enough,” Salcedo said of the collective effort, adding that it could have easily taken 20 years to make on her own—and that she couldn’t spare that kind of time at her age.
As Salcedo led me through her studio—her own iconic salt-and-pepper curls rhyming with the looping locks lining the space—she told me that all of her workspaces were designed by the architect Carlos Granada. The two have been working together for 25 years. He is also the architect behind Fragmentos, Salcedo’s 2018 “anti-monument” commissioned by her national government to commemorate the 2016 Colombian peace agreement. Visiting the building in the heart of Bogotá, what at first looks like a typical modernist, single-floor gallery takes on new weight in the feel of its flooring: The textured tiling is made from firearms that once belonged to the Colombian guerrilla group FARC and were later melted down. Visitors walk right on top of these instruments of violence and fear, on tiles Salcedo made in close collaboration with 20 Colombian women who survived sexual violence during the conflict.
The work has an undeniably chilling effect. School groups flock to it regularly. Some critics, though, have found its message misleading, since several splinter factions are still active and thousands of fighters rejected that 2016 agreement. But for Salcedo, Fragmentos is not a static space: She regularly invites other artists whose work resonates to exhibit within its walls. When I visited, a crew was de-installing a sound installation by Hajrah Waheed that filled the space with movingly hummed songs of resistance. The work, titled Hum II (2023), is surprisingly affecting, unifying: You’re made to feel something of the song’s sentiments even if they’re in languages you don’t understand. Fittingly, the title means “we” in Urdu, Waheed’s mother tongue.
Like Fragmentos, Salcedo’s studios boast high ceilings. Her workspaces also feature glass brick walls and floating staircases: These are sparse spaces that enable her and her team to see what they are working on. As she walked me through, magnifying glass in hand, she pointed out that one of her studios is the same shape as the home she is building—a triangle atop a square, as if a kid drew a house. Eventually, we came upon the net-like hair arranged in sections like a gradient, growing darker and denser at the bottom. She let me touch it, and I was surprised to find it so sturdy and lightweight at the same time.
THE WORK-IN-PROGRESS MARRIED a complicated process to a simple shape. As we spoke, I found myself wondering about the latter—why a house? I found a hint in two books sitting on the surface of her desk, both of them scanned so she can see them on a screen in large print: Domicide: The Global Destruction of Home and Dreamhouse: Stories of Art and Shelter.
House is not her first work on the subject of the devastating effects of the global housing crisis. Uprooted (2020–22), her prize-winning work in the 15th Sharjah Biennial (where, as it happens, she met Waheed, a fellow prize winner), repurposed 804 dead trees into a mesmerizing, if uninhabitable, home. At almost 1,000 feet long, the work is meant to speak to the predicament of climate refugees. Her newer work, which takes the same shape, is about more deliberate displacement: specifically, “domicide,” which the authors of one of the books on her desk, J. Douglas Porteous and Sandra E. Smith, describe as the calculated destruction of homes. Explaining the impetus for her piece, Salcedo pointed to current conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, Syria, and Sudan, where people are being violently displaced en masse.
Domicide, she pointed out, has a cascading effect: victims lose not just a structure but their communities. They lose access to privacy and respite, as well as bathrooms and places to cook and sleep. Mental health, studies show, tends to deteriorate rapidly as victims are forced into survival mode.
With House, Salcedo wanted to show that, while the dispossessed are of course vulnerable, they are also resilient. Her meshy nets are fragile and flexible, yet they are also much stronger than they seem. Hair may be ephemeral, but she makes it structural and sturdy. It’s all inspired, she told me, by the ways that spiders make webs of silk, material they take from their own bodies. Pairing hair and home, she evokes the ways that bodies and buildings—like dignity and domesticity—are tightly bound.
SALCEDO LEARNED TO WORK WITH human hair from earlier pieces: “Unland” (1995–98) comprises tables severed and then rearranged such that they depend on dissimilar tables for structural support. As if personifying the balancing act, the artist intricately threaded the surfaces with hair, drilling tiny holes in the tables to insert locks she gathered from a local salon. But for House, given its magnitude, she decided to source hair online, learning to look carefully for certain certificates, as there is a lot of violent crime in the human hair trade.
Hair is not the only tricky material that will feature in her fall show. On an upper floor of one of her studios, more assistants were at work on objects of a smaller scale, all destined for display alongside House at White Cube. They were wearing jeweler’s glasses and using X-Acto knives to meticulously remove the starch from individual grains of rice. A team of architects and engineers looked on, huddled around a computer on a lofted level as they worked out the structure of the sculpture’s shape. “I’ve never had such a large team,” she explained as I took in the scene. At one point, she tried working with a renowned engineer who eventually stepped down, saying the idea was too complicated.
When an artist uses sculpture’s most stalwart materials like wood or bronze—as Salcedo has in the past—“the tools are already designed for you,” she said. House required more trial and error than she’s ever needed before—so it also required her biggest team yet. “I had to fabricate new tools and new ways of working,” she explained as we watched assistants drill minuscule holes in starchless rice grains before passing them along to the next station, where still other assistants would thread individual hairs through those tiny openings. They were assembling a kind of mesh, then forming it around damaged cooking supplies—bowls and pots and pans—to form Grains of Sorrow (2023–26), a reminder of what is lost to domicide besides simple structure.
If this sounds like an incredibly elaborate—and surprisingly elegant—way to speak to tragedy, for Salcedo, both beauty and labor are part of her point. She is cognizant of how her studio might provide jobs to those who need them, employing, for instance, 150 women from the Colombian countryside, where it is difficult for them to find work.
The decision to both scale-up and work elaborately is as conceptual as it is material: “My work has always been labor-intensive because in the Global South, labor is intensive,” she said. “It’s completely different from industrialized countries.” She meant this not only as a way to shine a light on contemporary conditions, but also as a retort to art-historical tropes: Modernity is too often narrated, she said, as if “no single person from the Global South participated. But we know all the labor and all the suffering created modernity.” She wants to combine the forms and traditions of European sculpture with painstaking labor to show the two were always intertwined.
I asked her about the role beauty plays for her; she replied that she’s received a lot of criticism on this matter. She maintained, however, that “in all the violence and terror I’ve been researching all my life, I think the abject part belongs to the perpetrator,” adding that “beauty has a lot to do with dignity”—something she wants to restore as she tells the stories of victims. Elegance is also a way to get people to really look: The stories she’s telling are almost always in the newspapers, but that doesn’t mean everyone stops to soak them in. Salcedo doesn’t want you to divert your eyes from the world’s horrors, so she goes to extreme lengths to make sure you can’t look away.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.title: Soziale Bewegung | Berliner Rechenzentren: Protest gegen den KI-Boom
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.author: Darius Ossami
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.text:
- Berlin
- Soziale Bewegung
Berliner Rechenzentren: Protest gegen den KI-Boom
Zu viel Strom, zu viel Wasser, zu wenig Mitsprache: Am Rand eines Rechenzentrums im Ortsteil Marienfelde forderten Protestierende ein Moratorium.
Am Freitag fand in der Hauptstadt wohl die erste Kundgebung gegen Rechenzentren statt. »Bis vor einiger Zeit war mir noch gar nicht klar, wie bedeutungsvoll Rechenzentren sein werden«, sagte eine Aktivistin in blauer Windjacke ins Mikrofon. »Doch inzwischen weiß ich, wie Rechenzentren aussehen, wie viel Fläche sie brauchen, wie viel Wasser und Energie, dass sie Lärm machen und die direkte Umwelt erwärmen.«
Rund 20 Menschen standen im kalten, schneidenden Wind vor einem eingezäunten Rechenzentrum im Bezirk Tempelhof-Schöneberg, am Rand des unwirtlichen Geländes eines ehemaligen Gaskraftwerks. In der Lankwitzter Straße 25 im Ortsteil Mariendorf befindet sich auf knapp 10.000 Quadratmeter das zweite Rechenzentrum der NTT Global Data Centers EMEA GmbH.
Vor dem Gebäude halten Aktivist*innen Transparente hoch. »Rechenzentren nein Danke« und »Wassergerechtigkeit jetzt«, ist darauf zu lesen. Die Demonstrierenden sorgen sich um den hohen Strom-, Wasser und Flächenverbrauch von Rechenzentren und den zunehmenden Einfluss von KI und Big Tech, andere beklagen fehlende Transparenz beim Ausbau der digitalen Infrastruktur.
Die kleine Kundgebung war Teil des europäischen Aktionstages »Stop Dirty Data Centers«, der gleichzeitig an mehr als 80 Orten stattfand. Eigentlich sollte am selben Tag der »Tag der offenen Rechenzentren« stattfinden. Das Rechenzentrum in Mariendorf blieb für die Öffentlichkeit jedoch gesperrt, angeblich aus Sicherheitsbedenken, wie es auf der Demonstration heißt.
Als das Rechenzentrum im vergangenen Jahr errichtet worden ist, soll es Medienberichten zufolge zu mehreren Brandanschlägen gekommen sein. Auf der linksradikalen Internetplattform Indymedia waren dazu anonyme Bekennerschreiben aufgetaucht.
»Rechenzentren verschwenden Unmengen an Strom und Wasser. Die Bundesregierung will die Rechenzentrumskapazität verdoppeln, der Stromverbrauch könnte sich dabei sogar verdreifachen«, so die Aktivistin Caro Weber in einem Statement. »In Brandenburg sollen Rechenzentren in Gebiete mit akuter Wasserknappheit gebaut werden. Außerdem werden an vielen Orten Rechenzentren zusammen mit neuen klimaschädlichen Gaskraftwerken geplant. Das ist nicht zukunftsfähig.«
Auch in Berlin bauen Unternehmen wie NTT oder Virtus riesige Rechenzentren und vermieten deren Kapazitäten an Unternehmen. An wen, bleibt intransparent. »So sind sie zum Beispiel ein wesentlicher Teil von Geheimdienstaktivitäten, vom Ausspähen und Sammeln von Informationen, deren Verarbeitung und Weitergabe«, kritisierte eine Aktivistin vor Ort. »Sie sind aber auch ein wesentlicher Bestandteil der digitalen Kriegsführung.«
Dennoch boomt die Branche. Die Europäische Union will ihre digitale Infrastruktur ausbauen und die Rechenzentrumskapazitäten innerhalb weniger Jahre verdreifachen. Bundesweit machen Rechenzentren inzwischen 21 Prozent des Auftragsbestands des Baukonzerns Hochtief aus, wie dieser mitteilt. Auf dem Gelände in Mariendorf entsteht gerade ein weiteres Rechenzentrum. Auch in Spandau gibt es ein Rechenzentrum, weitere sind für Lichtenberg und das Umland geplant.
Unter den Protestierenden war auch der Stadtforscher Fabian Halfar von »Cables of Resistance«. Auf die Frage, was an Rechenzentren problematisch sei, seufzte er. »Wir profitieren alle von digitalen Anwendungen, keine Frage, aber was wir jetzt gerade sehen, ist ein Ausbau von Rechenzentren vor allem für KI.« Die Art, wie Big-Tech-Firmen KI verbreiteten, sei nicht mit einer demokratischen, fairen Gesellschaft vereinbar. Zudem »werden Unmengen an Ressourcen verbraucht, es ist ein Top-Down-Ausbau von Infrastruktur, der im Endeffekt nur dazu beiträgt, Arbeitskräfte zu ersetzen.«
Zu den großen Rechenzentrumsunternehmen wie NTT oder Virtus kommen in Berlin laut Halfar neuerdings Projektentwickler aus der Immobilienbranche. »Sowohl in Lichtenberg als auch in Spandau treiben hauptsächlich ehemalige Projektentwickler aus der Immobilienbranche jetzt große Projekte nach vorne, unterstützt von Investmentkapitalfirmen und Pensionsfonds.« Auf dem Immobilienmarkt sei die Gewinnmarge momentan bei Rechenzentren am höchsten, »weil da eine extreme Nachfrage von den großen Big-Tech-Firmen herrscht«. Halfar fordert, dass die Gesellschaft mitentscheiden solle, wie digitale Infrastruktur ausgebaut wird.
»Wir alle erleben Ohnmacht angesichts der Geschwindigkeit, mit der KI in unser Leben dringt«, so Weber: »Dabei haben wir aktuell keinerlei demokratisches Mitspracherecht, was das für unsere Zukunft bedeutet.«
Die Protestierenden fordern ein Moratorium für den beschleunigten Ausbau von Rechenzentren, auch wegen der befürchteten sozialen und ökologischen Folgen. Sie wollen sich nun mit Bürgerinitiativen vernetzen. »Lernen können die Aktivist*innen dabei von den USA: Dort führt der über Parteigrenzen hinweg organisierte lokale Widerstand regelmäßig zum Stopp diverser Bauprojekte«, teilte Aktivistin Caro Weber mit.

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

Die Klima-News der Woche : Braucht die Energiewende wirklich neue Gaskraftwerke?
Empfohlener externer Inhalt
Wir würden Ihnen hier gerne einen externen Inhalt zeigen. Sie entscheiden, ob Sie dieses Element auch sehen wollen:
Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung
Deutschland subventioniert fossile Reservekraftwerke. Artenschutzkonferenz ohne Durchbruch. Immer mehr Abkehr vom Verbrenner-Aus in der EU.
Es gibt Phasen, in denen Windräder und Solaranlagen wetterbedingt kaum Strom liefern – und dann? Bei der ersten Ausschreibung zur Absicherung der Stromversorgung hat die Bundesnetzagentur elf Zuschläge erteilt, und zwar ausschließlich für Gaskraftwerke. Stromspeicher kamen nicht zum Zuge, dabei hatte es auch dafür Bewerbungen gegeben. Warum und ob die Energiewende neue Gaskraftwerke braucht, darüber sprechen Susanne Schwarz und Verena Kern im klima update°.
Klimaschutz und Naturschutz hängen eng zusammen. In Armenien ist jetzt die Weltnaturschutzkonferenz zu Ende gegangen. Sie sollte Bilanz ziehen, wie die Umsetzung des historischen Kunming-Montreal-Abkommens vorankommt. Ein zentrales Ziel: Bis 2030 sollen mindestens 30 Prozent der weltweiten Land- und Wasserflächen wirksam geschützt sein. Die bisherigen Anstrengungen reichen aber nicht aus.
Die europäische Abkehr vom Verbrenner-Aus zeichnet sich immer deutlicher ab: Jetzt hat auch der Umweltausschuss des Europäischen Parlaments für eine Aufweichung der CO2-Regeln für Neuwagen gestimmt. Damit könnten auch nach 2035 neue Autos mit Verbrennungsmotor auf den Markt kommen.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Da luta por educação à revolução: como as mulheres ajudaram a transformar a Rússia em 1917
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Serguei Monin
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Na Rússia czarista, mulheres enfrentaram restrições ao acesso à educação e à participação política, construíram organizações próprias e tiveram papel decisivo no processo revolucionário. A história do Instituto Smolny ajuda a contar essa trajetória.
A Revolução Russa, cujo aniversário é celebrado em 7 de novembro, também foi resultado de décadas de organização e luta das mulheres por direitos, educação e melhores condições de vida. Em 1917, elas estiveram entre as protagonistas das mobilizações que derrubaram o czarismo e participaram da construção do processo revolucionário que transformaria a sociedade russa. Essa trajetória, no entanto, começou muito antes da tomada do poder pelos bolcheviques.
Na Rússia do século 19, o acesso das mulheres à educação era limitado e marcado pela desigualdade de classe. Enquanto meninas da aristocracia podiam frequentar instituições de ensino criadas especialmente para sua formação, a maioria das trabalhadoras enfrentava o analfabetismo, a exploração no trabalho e a ausência de direitos políticos. Ainda assim, a ampliação dos espaços de educação feminina abriu caminhos para a circulação de ideias e para a participação de mulheres nos debates intelectuais e políticos.
Um dos exemplos dessa trajetória é o Instituto Smolny, em São Petersburgo. Fundado em 1764 por iniciativa da imperatriz Catarina, a Grande, foi uma das primeiras instituições estatais de educação feminina da Rússia, voltada inicialmente às meninas da nobreza. Ali, elas estudavam línguas, história, matemática e música, em uma formação destinada a preparar jovens para ocupar posições compatíveis com seu lugar na sociedade imperial.
Mais de 150 anos depois, o mesmo edifício se tornaria um dos principais centros da Revolução Russa. Em 1917, o Smolny abrigou o Soviete de Petrogrado e as estruturas de direção bolchevique. Foi dali que Lenin e seus aliados acompanharam e coordenaram os acontecimentos que levaram à derrubada do Governo Provisório. A mudança de função do edifício sintetiza uma das contradições daquele período: um espaço criado para formar as filhas da elite imperial passava a integrar uma revolução que tinha entre suas bandeiras a transformação das estruturas sociais.
Em entrevista ao Brasil de Fato, a socióloga Tica Moreno, integrante da Coordenação Nacional da Marcha Mundial das Mulheres, observa que a história do instituto ajuda a compreender como a educação feminina se relacionou com a formação de quadros políticos e com o desenvolvimento da luta revolucionária. Algumas das mulheres que se tornaram dirigentes bolcheviques tiveram acesso a uma formação que, embora restrita a determinados setores sociais, contribuiu para sua atuação política.
“Uma primeira coisa que aconteceu na Rússia foi a criação de uma das primeiras instituições de educação de meninas e mulheres, pensando nas meninas e mulheres da nobreza. Não era uma educação para o conjunto das mulheres da classe trabalhadora. E é bem interessante ver como várias das dirigentes bolcheviques eram mulheres que tinham recebido essa educação em economia política e outras áreas”, explica.
Em períodos nos quais o czarismo restringia o acesso feminino ao ensino superior, algumas precisaram buscar oportunidades de estudo no exterior. Esse movimento contribuiu para aproximar militantes russas de correntes socialistas e de organizações da esquerda europeia. A formação das mulheres favoreceu assim a construção de relações com outros setores da sociedade e com organizações políticas de outros países.
A luta das mulheres russas não se restringia às possibilidades de educação de uma parcela da população. Com o avanço da industrialização e o crescimento das cidades, um número cada vez maior de mulheres passou a integrar a força de trabalho, especialmente em setores como o têxtil. As condições de trabalho, os baixos salários, as longas jornadas e a precariedade da vida cotidiana fizeram parte das reivindicações que impulsionaram a organização das trabalhadoras.
A luta por direitos também se desenvolveu em articulação com a oposição ao regime czarista e com os movimentos socialistas. Mulheres participaram de círculos de estudo, organizações políticas, greves e manifestações, construindo formas de organização que relacionavam a emancipação feminina à transformação das condições de vida e trabalho da classe trabalhadora.
Essa presença teve um papel decisivo no início de 1917. Em 8 de março, data que corresponde a 23 de fevereiro no calendário juliano, então utilizado na Rússia, trabalhadoras de Petrogrado saíram às ruas em manifestações contra a guerra, a fome e a carestia. Os protestos deram impulso a uma onda de greves e mobilizações que se espalhou pela cidade e culminou na queda do czar Nicolau II, dando início à Revolução de Fevereiro.
A participação feminina não foi, portanto, um elemento secundário ou circunstancial do processo revolucionário. As mulheres estavam nas fábricas, nas manifestações e nas organizações políticas, contribuindo para a construção das forças sociais que questionavam a ordem imperial. Para Tica Moreno, é fundamental reconhecer essa atuação como parte da própria constituição do sujeito revolucionário russo.
“A Revolução Russa não teria sido a mesma sem a participação das mulheres nesse processo, nessa construção, fazendo parte do que foi o sujeito revolucionário na Rússia. Desde anos antes, já havia um processo intenso de organização das mulheres, estruturado sobretudo em um trabalho permanente com as mulheres trabalhadoras. Um trabalho relacionado às condições de vida e de trabalho, mas também a todo o processo de educação e conscientização dessas mulheres”, afirma.
Meses depois, em outubro, os bolcheviques chegaram ao poder, em um processo que teve no Instituto Smolny um de seus principais centros de articulação. A revolução abriu uma nova etapa de disputas sobre os direitos das mulheres e o papel do Estado na transformação das relações sociais. A ampliação da educação pública, as mudanças na legislação familiar, o reconhecimento de direitos civis e políticos e as iniciativas de socialização do trabalho doméstico passaram a integrar, em diferentes momentos, a agenda soviética.
Essas transformações não eliminaram as desigualdades entre homens e mulheres, tampouco foram lineares. A experiência soviética foi atravessada por contradições, limites econômicos e disputas políticas que afetaram a implementação e a continuidade de muitas dessas medidas. Ainda assim, a incorporação da emancipação feminina ao projeto de transformação social representou uma dimensão importante do legado de 1917.
Para Tica Moreno, a experiência das revolucionárias russas também evidencia que a emancipação feminina não poderia se limitar à conquista de direitos para mulheres das elites. Era preciso enfrentar as desigualdades de classe e as condições de exploração das trabalhadoras.
“Uma coisa é um projeto de classe que tem as mulheres da nobreza, da aristocracia, devidamente formadas, escolarizadas, esclarecidas, e o conjunto das mulheres trabalhadoras mantido numa situação de analfabetismo e de exploração do trabalho. […] É também a disputa política de classe dentro do que vai se constituindo como feminismo socialista”, afirma.
A trajetória das revolucionárias russas, portanto, ajuda a compreender que a luta por emancipação feminina não se desenvolveu de maneira isolada das disputas políticas e sociais de seu tempo. Da reivindicação pelo direito à educação à organização das trabalhadoras, a experiência que desembocou em 1917 foi marcada por alianças, conflitos e pela construção de um projeto que vinculava a transformação da vida das mulheres à transformação da sociedade.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Texas Chose the Willie Nelson Slate
The country singer was an enthusiastic supporter of the Democrats who won every major statewide race in Texas.
There are many factors behind Tuesday’s great-big, Texas-size victories for Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa—and for the rest of the long-beleaguered Texas Democratic Party, which swept the GOP out of power in races up and down the ballot.
Donald Trump won the Lone Star State in 2024 by more than 1.5 million votes and carried 242 of the state’s 254 counties. But by 2026, Texas, like every other corner of the United States, had soured on the president. And this year’s Republican slate was uninspired, not just because of the many scandals associated with Trump-imposed Senate nominee Ken Paxton, but also because once-popular GOP stalwarts, such as Governor Greg Abbott, had messy records on everything from public education to immigration policy to data centers. Clearly, this was fertile territory for a Democratic rout.
But Talarico and Hinojosa also had the advantage of having been vetted by the man who invariably ranks at or near the top of lists of influential, and beloved, Texans.
That would be Willie Nelson.
The 93-year-old country singer has released more than 100 studio albums, won a dozen Grammys (having been nominated 59 times in seven different genres) and continues an endless tour that still fills arenas on his own and with a crowd of outlaw country players, folkies, rockers and rappers. It’s fair to say he has achieved “national treasure” status, as the songwriter who gave us “On the Road Again,” “Always On My Mind,” “Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain” and “Whiskey River.”
Nelson is a savvy longtime observer of the politics of his state and nation. And he speaks up.
Last month, the singer shared a video in which he announced, “I’ve gotten to know James Talarico. He’s a good man who will be a good senator for the state of Texas. Please vote and vote for James Talarico.” The two had indeed gotten to know one another; Talarico joined Nelson at his Austin show celebrating the nation’s 250th birthday, posting a photo of the pair and the message: “Happy Fourth of July from Willie and me!”
On the same day, Hinojosa shared a photo of her with the singer-songwriter and wrote: “Texas in our souls Willie Nelson.”
Nelson formally endorsed Hinojosa on October 3, along with a widely circulated message that urged viewers to visit her campaign website. Hinojosa responded, “We’re one month out from Election Day. Listen to Willie. Vote for change this year.”
As with the Talarico endorsement, Nelson’s Hinojosa backing was covered all over Texas media—along with endorsements of Democrats by other musicians with Texas ties, such as Don Henley of the Eagles and the members of the Chicks.
Nelson also went down ballot, endorsing Texan Vikki Goodwin for the powerful post of lieutenant governor—telling voters, “We need her!”
Nelson is not new to progressive politics. He was an active supporter of former US Representative Dennis Kucinich’s anti-war presidential bid in 2004, and has backed a number of Texas Democrats along the way—in particular Beto O’Rourke, who mounted serious bids for the US Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022. O’Rourke lost to Republican Ted Cruz in the Senate race and, this fall, Cruz snarkily announced, “Willie’s music is great, but historically, this has been the beginning of the end for Democrat campaigns in Texas.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Cruz got it wrong.
Democrats swept statewide contests on Tuesday, producing an epic political shift.
Goodwin beat longtime Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick on Tuesday, and will become the first Democratic lieutenant governor of the state in almost three decades.
Hinojosa will be the first Democratic governor since Ann Richards was defeated in 1994.
And Talarico became the first Democrat to win an election for a Texas US Senate seat since 1998—with 55 percent support and a margin of almost 1.2 million votes over Paxton.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The Trump administration wants underwater datacenters. One Great Lakes non-profit is already preparing
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Stephen Starr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
While Elon Musk has often touted putting datacenters in space, reports suggest that another geographic area may soon become a widespread target: our lakes and oceans.
Two underwater datacenters are already in operation off the coast of China, and recent reports suggest that the Trump administration is considering plans for four proposed underwater, sealed-pod datacenters to be built off the shores of Maine and Alaska.
At a campaign rally in Ohio last month, Donald Trump said of datacenters: “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio … they’ll go to China … we want them.”
Underwater iterations are particularly attractive to tech companies as they largely eliminate community opposition and controversy around datacenters in residential areas on land. In theory, underwater datacenters could also significantly cut down on utility costs, another issue that’s currently riling communities across the country.
A Microsoft project set up off the coast of northern Scotland in 2018 found that after two years, server failures were reduced by 87% compared with on-land datacenter equivalents. Microsoft executives saw the project, which ended after two years, as an unmitigated success.
That makes the cool, salt-free waters of the Great Lakes, home to 30 million people in major cities such as Chicago, Toronto and Detroit, potentially attractive to datacenter companies.
A spokesperson for the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said: “The EPA supports development of data center infrastructure that is essential to remaining the world leader in Super Intelligence while using its statutory authorities to protect water quality.”
But the environmental consequences of any similar project in the freshwater Great Lakes, which those tens of millions of people depend on for drinking water every day, could be significant. Local environmental activists are already worried and sounding the alarm – even though no underwater datacenter projects are currently proposed for the region.
For them, they think it is better to be prepared than surprised, given the high stakes of the ecologically sensitive ecosystem.
“We are concerned because if you think about what a datacenter does, it throws off a lot of heat. Lake Erie already has an issue with harmful algal blooms, and they develop because of heat, not only because of fertilizers and agricultural runoff,” said John Lipaj of the Lake Erie Foundation, a non-profit based in Ohio.
The floor of Lake Erie on the US side falls under the jurisdiction of the state of Ohio. In the past, its state government, where Republicans hold a supermajority, proposed a law making it easier for datacenter companies to discharge wastewater into public waterways. That measure was denied by the state’s EPA last July following a public outcry. Of the eight US Great Lakes states, only New York currently has a temporary state-wide moratorium on datacenter construction. That ends in mid-2027.
“We’re also concerned about the possibility of contamination and leaks. These have not been around a long time,” said Lipaj.
“We are concerned about the types of fluid contained in a datacenter, the batteries and electrical equipment. These are all things that could lead to a catastrophic failure that we don’t want happening in the Great Lakes.”
Lake Erie is home or close to major cities such as Cleveland, Detroit and Buffalo and is already by far the warmest of the five Great Lakes during summer months. It also ranks as one of the most polluted large lakes in the country in large part due to agricultural runoff in its western basin. A number of fish species are under threat due to the lake’s warming trend.
“Warm water can impact aquatic life and ecosystems in a number of ways. One immediate effect is what is known as a thermal shock,” said Helena Volzer of the Alliance for the Great Lakes, an environmental group based in Chicago.
“Aquatic organisms are highly sensitive to temperature changes, and even a small, rapid increase of just 2-5F can be dramatic for the aquatic ecosystem. When a facility releases warm water, it can alter metabolism and increase oxygen demand, reduce dissolved oxygen availability, disrupt food webs [and] force fish to move away from preferred habitats.”
On 3 November, residents of Conneaut, a Lake Erie community of about 12,000 people an hour’s drive north-east of Cleveland, voted in favor of a charter amendment to prohibit the construction of large datacenters in its area.
But the idea of offshore underwater datacenters is not a popular one here.
“Being one of the largest freshwater sources in the world, I would be very much for protecting that resource,” said Mariana Branch, a Conneaut council member who lives a short distance from the Lake Erie shoreline. Branch said she hadn’t previously been aware of the idea of datacenters operating underwater.
“Technology is moving so quickly, it’s difficult for cities to keep up with,” she said.
Still, some suggest that following Microsoft’s lead in Scotland may have some merit considering the public opposition to on-land equivalents; and, unlike the open ocean, there are no large fauna in the Great Lakes ecosystems.
“They require a lot of energy for cooling … one of the biggest advantages of these underwater datacenters is the low cooling cost [associated]. They don’t have to spend a lot to cool the servers,” said Nir Kshetri, a professor of emerging technologies at the University of North Carolina Greensboro.
“Datacenters have been a big issue for communities and in the recent elections. Also, datacenters don’t have to worry about any latency problems because they can be located close to large population centers where they are needed. A lake is a great place to do a datacenter. Cold water is even better.”
However, the Great Lakes are not without significant challenges to any such project.
Last winter saw one of the most extensive Great Lakes freeze-ups in decades, with almost all of Lake Erie and up to half of the four other lakes freezing over up to several feet deep. Experts say it isn’t clear to what extent ice cover could affect underwater projects.
What’s more, a Microsoft spokesperson said: “We have no plans to deploy an underwater datacenter in any location at this time,” and: “Our focus today is on building and operating datacenters responsibly on land.”
A spokesperson for Ohio’s EPA said it had not yet received any applications to permit an underwater datacenter in its part of Lake Erie.
For its part, Lipaj says the Lake Erie Foundation has contacted state representatives and state senators in New York, Ohio and Michigan to discuss the issue.
“Whether or not they happen, [we’re saying] let’s propose to state legislatures in Great Lakes states that they consider that this may be coming down the line and let’s get some regulations in place before the datacenter developers make their proposals and then state legislators are scrambling. That’s what we’re trying to avoid. We’re exercising an abundance of caution,” he said.
“The Great Lakes states should take some leadership in this, get the regulations written so that nothing is forced on them.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: ‘Radical’ or ‘hero’?: France debates leftist candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
‘Radical’ or ‘hero’?: France debates leftist candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon
The hard-left leader has transformed into a real contender in next year presidential elections.
Hard-left French leader Jean-Luc Melenchon has been described as a “radical” by right-wing opponents, a “despot” by former allies and a “hero” by some of the students who have taken to the streets in nationwide protests.
The leader of the France Unbowed (LFI) party has emerged as the strongest contender on the left and potential challenger to far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential election.
On Saturday, Melenchon is presenting his programme at a rally in Le Bourget, north of Paris, a day after it was published online.
Among his proposals, he wants to lower the retirement age to 60 and raise the minimum wage to 1,700 euro ($1,900) a month; pull France out of NATO and renationalise parts of the economy.
He wants the European Central Bank to stop France repaying the debt it holds, effectively transforming the debt instead to a permanent interest-free loan – a move he hopes would give the government more room to spend.
On Europe, he envisions France remaining in the EU, but he wants to refuse rules that conflict with the nation’s social, environmental or economic programmes, setting up a potentially confrontational relationship with Brussels.
‘He is in tune with the demands of the demonstrations’
His party is gaining momentum as protests led by students in mid-September swelled to include several groups angry about failing public services, rising living costs and uncertain futures.
The hard-left leader has been hailed at marches, some of which have seen vandalism and looting.
“His strength is that he is in tune with the demands of the demonstrations: better wages, money in education, a lot of welfare measures, no austerity cuts which appease people who are fed up with the cost of living,” said Jacques Reland, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute. “He is the vote of the protesters.”
But some say his policies are radical and unrealistic.
France’s finances and borrowing are under scrutiny as its budget deficit and debt levels are high, raising further doubts on how Melenchon’s ambitious spending plans, particularly on social programmes and public investment, could be implemented.
Some economists warn that his plans could cause investors to sell French government bonds, making it more expensive for France to borrow and potentially causing losses.
“Borrowing money and deciding not to give it back – that’s called theft,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said in September, regarding such proposals.
LFI says higher taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations – another pillar of Melenchon’s campaign – would finance its spending plans.
His proposals include a minimum 2 percent tax on the wealth of billionaires, restoring France’s wealth tax and increasing taxes on large inheritances.
“Financial capital has benefitted, and it is the one that should pay,” he said in October.
His programme draws on a tradition of left-wing economic interventionism, rooted partly in Keynesian thought, that argues that the state should play an active role in the economy to reduce inequalities generated by the market.
“Because this tradition of state intervention in economic and social affairs has been abandoned by most other political parties, the fact that LFI continues to define itself through such interventionism creates an impression of radicalism,” said political analyst Beligh Nabli, a professor of public law at UPEC-Paris XII. “Yet, this radicalism is only relative – it appears radical when compared to other contemporary political offerings, but from the perspective of the history of social democracy, it is not radical at all.”
Melenchon, 75, was born in Morocco to French parents.
He moved to France as a child where he later graduated in philosophy and modern literature. In the 1980s, he joined the Socialist Party, but distanced himself from it when it shifted towards more liberal economics.
In 2008, he finally quit the Socialists and founded the Left Party, which would later evolve into LFI. The party appealed to working-class voters and marginalised communities and became popular with young people.
According to this week’s polls, the presidential candidate is polling between 17.5 to 18 percent, widening the gap with his rivals in the left camp.
Trailing behind is Raphael Glucksmann, who leads the centre-left Place Publique party and secured the backing of the Socialist Party after winning a joint primary in October. Further back, and running on their own ticket – the Communist Party’s Fabien Roussel, Marine Tondelier’s Greens party and independent Francois Ruffin.
The left-wing bloc is undecided on the LFI.
As Melenchon holds a significant lead, smaller parties are weighing whether to support him to give a left-wing alliance a better shot.
Glucksmann has ruled that out, but others are pondering the situation.
“This will be one of the key debates throughout the presidential campaign,” said Nabil.
Another source of tension across the French left is Melenchon’s strong support of Palestine.
He has repeatedly refused to describe Hamas as a “terrorist organisation” and has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – a term other left-wing politicians, including Glucksmann, have been reluctant to use.
Melenchon has also faced accusations from political opponents on the left that his rhetoric fuels anti-Semitism, claims he rejects.
But Melenchon’s popularity is nowhere close to that of National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen.
The far-right leader, who challenged President Emmanuel Macron in a second round in the past two elections, would easily win in a run-off against Melenchon, leading 70 percent to 30 percent, according to a Toluna Harris Interactive poll conducted in October.
Analysts say his economic programme is not the only obstacle. His combative political style and reputation for confrontation over compromise hinder his chances of broadening support beyond a core base.
“In France, it is often said that to win a presidential election, one must campaign from the centre. Yet, the defining characteristic of the LFI programme is that it is not centrist – that is precisely what makes it disruptive. He seeks victory, but not a victory from the centre,” Nabli said.
His leadership has also been criticised.
Several former allies have said their break with the party was driven by both Melenchon’s management style and political disagreements.
Former LFI candidate Thomas Guenole has described the movement as a “dictatorship” governed by “an autocrat”, while former lawmaker Raquel Garrido said there was a left that agreed with LFI’s programme but not with the party leader’s “methods”.
Former close ally Clementine Autain has likewise accused LFI of becoming “authoritarian”.
“He is the ‘supreme leader’,” said Reland at the Global Policy Institute. “The party is very organised, but it’s not a democratic party at all.”

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.title: Fußball | Der VfL Wolfsburg bleibt voll auf dem Gaspedal
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.author: Frank Hellmann, Frankfurt am Main
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.text:
- Sport
- Fußball
Der VfL Wolfsburg bleibt voll auf dem Gaspedal
In beeindruckender Manier gewinnen die Wölfinnen das Verfolgerduell in Frankfurt – und freuen sich nun auf das Gipfeltreffen mit den Bayern.
Gab es eine Spielerin vom VfL Wolfsburg, die bei Schlusspfiff nicht die Faust ballte? Die Freude bei den Vizemeisterinnen war nach dem mit 3:1 gewonnenen Verfolgerduell bei Eintracht Frankfurt an einem kühlen Novemberabend im Stadion am Brentanobad nur verständlich. Mit einer abgeklärten Leistung untermauerte der Werksverein seine Rolle als zweite Kraft der Frauen-Bundesliga. Es mag in der Autostadt ja einiges in Unordnung geraten sein, aber die VfL-Fußballerinnen denken seit Wochen gar nicht daran, in irgendeinem Wettbewerb vom Gaspedal zu gehen. 7:0 im Europa Cup bei Feyenoord Rotterdam, 8:0 im DFB-Pokal gegen die TSG Hoffenheim – und nun ein weiteres Zeichen der Stärke vor dem Bundesliga-Spitzenspiel gegen den FC Bayern in einer Woche.
Vorweg: Die Begegnung zwischen den beiden Teams, die seit der Saison 2022/23 in schöner Regelmäßigkeit die Plätze zwei und drei belegen, besaß am Freitag vor 4102 Zuschauern ein ordentliches, aber kein überragendes Niveau. Es hat schon Gründe, dass beide Mannschaften die Champions League verpasst haben. Immerhin winkt beiden nun aber der Viertelfinaleinzug im Europa Cup, wo am Ende ein deutsches Finale möglich wäre.
Wolfsburgs neues Selbstbewusstsein
Zuerst aber schaut alles auf den Liga-Gipfel zwischen den ewigen Rivalen Wolfsburg und Bayern, die sich am kommenden Samstag in der VW-Arena duellieren. »Wir haben uns in den letzten Spielen viel Selbstvertrauen angespielt. Das wollen wir natürlich auch mit in das Bayern-Spiel nehmen«, sagte Dauerbrennerin Svenja Huth.
Die Wolfsburgerinnen haben den zweiten XXL-Umbruch in Folge besser weggesteckt als gedacht, weil Trainer Stephan Lerch ein stabiles Gerüst gebaut hat, in dem die deutschen WM-Kandidatinnen Camilla Küver und Janina Minge in Abwehr und Mittelfeld die Fixpunkte bilden. Die Unterschiedsspielerin ist jedoch Ella Peddemors, die in Frankfurt erst einen flotten Konter über Vorlagengeberin Huth herausragend abschloss (13. Minute), dann mustergültig das zweite Tor von Smilla Vallotto vorbereitete (50.), und schlussendlich einen Freistoß direkt in die Maschen drosch (73.). »Ich habe mir gedacht, wenn ich ihn mit ein bisschen Curve spiele und die Torhüterin die andere Seite zumacht, kann es funktionieren«, erklärte die Matchwinnerin, die nicht nur ruhende Bälle mit Effet beherrscht, sondern auch ein herausragendes Passspiel besitzt.
Mit ihren elf Saisontoren stellt die Niederländerin selbst Bayerns Weltklassestürmerin Klara Bühl in den Schatten – und das will was heißen. Seine Spielmacherin sei auf einer »Euphoriewelle« unterwegs, sagte Lerch kürzlich: »Ella hat eine große Zukunft vor sich.« Dumm nur, dass der Werksverein wohl kaum eine Vertragsverlängerung mit der bereits von englischen Topvereinen umworbenen 24-Jährigen hinbekommt.
Frankfurts Anspruch – und Wirklichkeit
Bei Eintracht Frankfurt stellen sich nach dem nächsten verlorenen Topspiel dagegen Grundsatzfragen. Der Saisonstart mag ja in Ordnung gewesen sein, doch gegen hochkarätige Gegner wie Paris St. Germain, den FC Bayern oder Wolfsburg zieht die Eintracht am Ende immer den Kürzeren. Das kann nicht der Anspruch an diesem Standort sein.
Erst kürzlich hatte Axel Hellmann bei seiner Ernennung zum Vorstandsvorsitzenden mit der Mutmaßung aufgeräumt, der Klub würde die Investitionen in die Frauenabteilung zurückfahren. Das Gegenteil sei der Fall. »Wir haben ein höheres Budget als in den Jahren zuvor.« Etwa um eine Million Euro sei der Aufwand erhöht worden, »der Frauenfußball hat also eine größere Kapitalausstattung, was unsere Ambitionen unterstreicht. Wir versuchen, den Kader so zu bauen, dass er uns die Qualifikation für die Champions League ermöglicht.«
Doch der Abstand zum Führungsduo bleibt unter Trainer Niko Arnautis bestehen. Der dienstälteste Bundesligatrainer (seit 2016) irrte gewaltig, als er betonte, es sei angeblich »nur um Kleinigkeiten« gegangen. Wie schon gegen die Bayern (0:1) spielte sich der »ewige Dritte« kaum Chancen heraus. Zur Einfallslosigkeit in der Offensive gesellte sich eine Anfälligkeit bei Ballverlusten in der Defensive. Drittes Kardinalproblem ist die Personalie Laura Freigang, die erkennbaren Ballast mit sich herumträgt.
Freigangs Suche nach Normalität
Frankfurts beste Torjägerin wirkte limitiert und blockiert, die Körpersprache als Kapitänin stimmte nicht. Aber ist das verwunderlich, wenn ihr wegen dreier versäumter Dopingkontrollen eine lange Sperre droht? Der Prozess wird demnächst erwartet, nachdem das Bemühen um eine außergerichtliche Einigung offenbar scheiterte. Bei ihrer überfälligen Auswechslung lief die 28-Jährige hinter die Torauslinie und weinte.
Arnautis stärkte Freigang danach im Interview demonstrativ den Rücken: »Sie ist ein Mensch. Morgen geht es für sie weiter. Das ist alles nicht immer einfach. Wir müssen nicht immer jeden Tag darüber reden, sondern sie einfach Fußball spielen lassen. Das macht sie gut. Ich finde es vollkommen okay, wenn sie dann mal Emotionen zeigt. Ansonsten können wir zuhause bleiben.«
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

Melt-Banana in Berlin: Die Verhältnisse, in Unordnung und damit zum Tanzen gebracht
Der Lärm ist ein Weg zum Glück. Das Duo Melt-Banana aus Tokio betört in einem Berliner Schuppen mit krachigem Schreihalsrock.
A lso zum Beispiel so: Da krümmt sich der Typ um seine Gitarre, ein donnergrollendes Dröhnen ist zu hören, dazu noch ein elektronisches Geballer. Es ist laut. Eine Frau schreit.
Und gleich noch einmal, das nächste Lied: Der Typ traktiert die Gitarre, es dröhnt. Noch ein Stückchen schriller. Lauter. Die Frau läuft dazu mit seltsam abgezirkelten Bewegungen über die Bühne und wedelt mit den Armen. Wie eine einigermaßen überdrehte Flugbegleiterin sieht sie aus mit ihren Gesten, als wolle sie in ihrer Pantomime den Gebrauch der Schwimmweste oder den Weg zum Notausgang erklären.
Aber raus will da niemand an diesem Abend in der Neuen Zukunft. Die Menschen in dem im Schatten der S-Bahn geparkten schwitzig-dunklen Schuppen in Berlin-Friedrichshain wollen es lieber noch ein Stückchen lauter. Der Boden wummert, auch an den Füßen ist er so zu spüren, der Lärm.
Melt-Banana auf Tour
Auf ihrer „SLinGShot Tour 2026“ kommen Melt-Banana nach Stationen in Utrecht (6.11.) und Kortrijk in Belgien (7.11.) am 8.11. auch nochmal mit einem Konzert in Dortmund nach Deutschland.
Der um die Gitarre gekrümmte Typ ist Ichirou Agata. Die Frau, die da schrill und manchmal fast manisch ihre Texte ins Publikum schreit, heißt Yasuko Onuki. Zusammen sind sie Melt-Banana, sie kommen aus Tokio, Japan, und machen seit den frühen Neunzigerjahren so einen Schreihalsrock mit einer durchaus erstaunlichen Roll-Qualität in dem ganzen Noise. Überhören lässt sich diese Musik jedenfalls nicht.
Interessant ist in diesem Zusammenhang dann allerdings doch, dass bei den Verhaltensregeln, die den Touristen bei einem Besuch in Japan mit auf den Weg gegeben werden, ganz oben immer steht, nur ja nicht aufzufallen oder gar zu stören. Weil man eben genau das nicht macht in der so sauber geordneten japanischen Gesellschaft. Laut telefonieren etwa in der Öffentlichkeit, macht man nicht, und sogar das Schnäuzen und Naseputzen gilt in Japan, sobald das jemand mitbekommen könnte, als No-Go. Ein Gipfel von Unhöflichkeit.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Schon klar, dass man da bei solchen gesellschaftlichen Zurichtungen einfach mal schreien möchte.
Eine Menge an lärmender Musik
Jedenfalls gibt es in Japan längst nicht nur Melt-Banana, die der lärmenden Musik frönen. Da findet sich unter dem Stichwort Japanoise (das eine „n“ ist wohl aus Schicknessgründen unter den Tisch gefallen) eine wirklich beindruckend hohe Zahl an Bands und Musiker*innen, die genussvoll mit dem ganzen Krach herumwuchten und am Exzess arbeiten – bitte sehr, die harschen Störgeräusche von Merzbow, die imposanten Gitarrenexplosionen von Keiji Haino oder das psychedelisch durchwirkte Wummern der Boredoms sind wirklich nur ein paar ausgewählte Fingerzeige.
Dass sich auch der Westen mit diesen exaltierten Musiken vertraut machen konnte, dafür sorgten so Menschen wie Thurston Moore von Sonic Youth und vor allem John Zorn, die Zentralfigur der fröhlich mit allen nur möglichen Musiken improvisierenden New Yorker Downtown-Szene. Auch ein Album von Melt-Banana hat der Liebhaber und Botschafter der japanischen Underground- und Noise-Szene produziert – ein Livealbum.
Denn entscheidend ist auf der Bühne. Dabei zeigen sich die Menschen in der Neuen Zukunft richtig vernarrt in die Band, eigentlich gleich vom Fleck weg nehmen sie deren von der Bühne geschleuderte Energie auf, die Menge wogt, findet sich in einen vielgliedrigen Körper, der sich immer wieder nach vorne fallen lässt und dann zurück taumelt … im Hin und Her werden einzelne Menschen ausgespuckt und andere bindet dieser große Körper vor der Bühne ein, alles ist in Bewegung, die Verhältnisse, irgendwie doch einmal zum Tanzen gebracht, im Lärm.
Der nämlich schiebt alles weg. Den Alltag bestimmt. Vielleicht die Pein.
Überall auf den Gesichtern in der wogenden Menge ist es zu sehen: Freude, ein Lachen. Schieres Entzücken. Lärm ist ein Weg zum Glück.
Nach einer Stunde ist es mit dem musikalischen Workout in der Neuen Zukunft vorbei. Und draußen hört man doch ein wenig anders hinein in die Welt.
Vielleicht liegt das aber auch nur an dem sachten Dröhnen in den Ohren.

A edição desta semana traz a primeira visita de um sultão de Omã à China em 48 anos e a queda no apoio à resolução da ONU contra o embargo a Cuba. Internamente, destaca a renúncia da secretária de Habitação de Hong Kong após o incêndio no Wang Fuk Court, a queda no lucro das montadoras apesar do recorde de carros elétricos e o plano chinês de levar astronautas à Lua antes de 2030.
Geopolítica
Sultão de Omã assina swap de moedas na primeira visita à China em 48 anos
O sultão Haitham bin Tarik se reuniu com o presidente Xi Jinping em Pequim, em 2 de novembro, na primeira visita de um chefe de Estado omanense à China em 48 anos. Na ocasião, os dois países firmaram acordos de swap de moedas locais e de pagamentos digitais, além de cooperação em navegação por satélite pelo sistema BeiDou, em cadeias industriais e de abastecimento, e em desenvolvimento verde. Também se comprometeram a alinhar a Iniciativa Cinturão e Rota à Visão 2040 de Omã. Xi afirmou que o Golfo não deve se transformar em palco de disputa entre grandes potências.

ONU aprova resolução contra embargo a Cuba, mas apoio cai de 165 para 130
Pela 34ª vez, a Assembleia Geral da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) aprovou a resolução contra o embargo a Cuba. Foram 130 votos a favor, 17 contra e 25 abstenções, ante 165 votos favoráveis no ano passado. A China apoiou o texto, e o representante chinês na ONU, Fu Cong, declarou que o embargo imposto pelos Estados Unidos há 64 anos viola a Carta da Organização.

Política nacional
Secretária de Habitação de Hong Kong renuncia após falhas que antecederam incêndio mortal
Winnie Ho deixou o cargo de secretária de Habitação de Hong Kong em 29 de outubro, depois que um comitê independente concluiu que quatro departamentos do governo deixaram sem resposta denúncias sobre segurança contra incêndio no Wang Fuk Court, antes do incêndio que matou 168 pessoas no conjunto residencial. Paralelamente, um inquérito da Comissão de Serviço Público tem prazo de três meses para entregar seu relatório. O governo também vai substituir a Unidade de Verificação Independente por uma nova seção de controle de edificações e pretende tornar crime o conluio em licitações de manutenção predial.

Liu Yandong, ex-vice-primeira-ministra da China, morre aos 81 anos
Liu Yandong morreu em Pequim em 28 de outubro. Ela integrou o Bureau Político do 17º e do 18º Comitê Central do Partido Comunista da China, tornou-se conselheira de Estado em 2008 e foi vice-primeira-ministra de 2013 a 2018. Liu foi uma “combatente comunista leal e testada pelo tempo”, afirmou o comunicado oficial sobre sua morte, que também destacou sua atuação na frente única do Partido e na aproximação com grupos não comunistas, além do trabalho nas áreas de educação, ciência e tecnologia, saúde e nas pautas de mulheres e crianças.

Economia
Lucro das montadoras chinesas cai 68% apesar de recorde de vendas de carros elétricos
Em setembro, os veículos de nova energia, categoria que reúne elétricos a bateria e híbridos plug-in, chegaram ao recorde de 61,6% dos carros novos vendidos na China. As vendas somaram 1,82 milhão de unidades, alta de 13,6%. Ainda assim, o lucro combinado do setor caiu 68% na comparação anual, para 14,2 bilhões de yuans (US$ 2,11 bilhões), pressionado pelo aumento de custos e pela guerra de preços, que achatou as margens.

Acordo China-Peru entra em vigor com regras de comércio eletrônico e meio ambiente
Entrou em vigor, em 1º de novembro, o protocolo de atualização do acordo comercial entre China e Peru. O texto acrescenta cinco capítulos, entre eles os de comércio eletrônico, de cadeias globais de abastecimento e de meio ambiente e comércio, e revisa sete dos já existentes. O comércio bilateral chegou a US$ 50,4 bilhões em 2025, quase oito vezes os US$ 6,4 bilhões registrados em 2009. A China é o principal destino das exportações peruanas, e o Peru é o quarto maior parceiro comercial chinês na América Latina.

Agricultura e meio ambiente
Feira de frutos do mar de Qingdao reúne 1.600 expositores de 50 países
A 29ª Feira de Frutos do Mar de Qingdao, realizada de 28 a 30 de outubro, reuniu 1.617 expositores de 50 países e 27 pavilhões nacionais em 117,6 mil metros quadrados. Além de produtos do mar frescos e processados, foram expostos equipamentos de aquicultura e de processamento e soluções de logística de cadeia de frio. A feira aproximou fornecedores do Equador, do Vietnã e da Noruega de compradores chineses e estrangeiros.
Leia mais:
Primeiro Reit de infraestrutura hídrica da China começa a ser negociado em Shenzhen
O fundo Yinhua Yuehai, listado na bolsa de Shenzhen em 28 de outubro, é o primeiro fundo de investimento em infraestrutura (Reit, na sigla em inglês) de oferta pública da China lastreado em obras hidráulicas. Fundos desse tipo são negociados em bolsa, detêm ativos como rodovias com pedágio ou estações de tratamento de água e repassam aos investidores a receita que esses ativos geram. No caso do Yinhua Yuehai, a receita virá dos complexos hidráulicos de Feilaixia e Chaozhou por até 30 anos, e os recursos captados vão financiar o Reservatório de Huangmaoxia e projetos de alocação de água no Golfo de Beibu.
Leia mais:
Ciência e tecnologia
Ecólogo chinês Fu Bojie ganha Prêmio Volvo por pesquisa sobre terras secas
Fu Bojie recebeu o prêmio em cerimônia em Estocolmo, em 2 de novembro. O júri destacou as décadas de pesquisa do ecólogo sobre terras secas, que associaram a recuperação ecológica local ao desenvolvimento sustentável no Sul Global. Entre esses estudos estão os que mostram que a revegetação pode agravar a escassez de água quando as espécies e a densidade do plantio são mal escolhidas. As terras secas cobrem mais de 41% da superfície terrestre e abrigam mais de 2,5 bilhões de pessoas. Fu copreside o Programa Global de Ecossistemas de Terras Secas, lançado em 2017.
Leia mais:
China detalha plano para levar astronautas à Lua antes de 2030 com dois foguetes
Wang Xiang, vice-chefe de projeto do programa espacial tripulado chinês, apresentou a sequência da missão em um simpósio em Pequim. O módulo lunar Lanyue e a nave tripulada Mengzhou serão lançados em foguetes separados e vão se acoplar em órbita lunar. Em seguida, os astronautas passarão para o módulo para descer à superfície e trabalhar no solo lunar. Segundo Wang, o desenvolvimento avança em ritmo estável, e a meta segue sendo o primeiro pouso tripulado antes de 2030.
Leia mais:
Vida e cultura do povo
Após terremoto em Xizang, 1.495 estudantes retomam aulas em Lhasa
Em 22 de outubro, um terremoto de magnitude 7,0 deixou sem condições de uso duas escolas primárias municipais de Nagqu, na Região Autônoma de Xizang (Tibete). Os 1.495 estudantes e 89 professores foram transferidos em três grupos para um campus em Lhasa, onde as aulas recomeçaram em 4 de novembro. Até 31 de outubro, 286 escolas haviam sido inspecionadas em sete condados afetados, e 72 prédios foram classificados como perigosos.

China identifica oito soldados mortos na Guerra da Coreia e chega a 44 identificados
Em 28 de outubro, o Ministério dos Assuntos dos Veteranos identificou oito integrantes dos Voluntários do Povo Chinês mortos na Guerra da Coreia (1950-1953) e localizou seus familiares. Desde 2014, a Coreia do Sul devolveu à China 1.023 conjuntos de restos mortais, em 13 repatriações. Com o cruzamento de dados de DNA, 44 deles já foram identificados.
