https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/a-brest-des-.title: À Brest, des syndicats et la LDH s’alarment contre un possible « fichage » des lycéens mobilisés
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/a-brest-des-.text:
Le sénateur PCF des Bouches-du-Rhône Jeremy Bacchi demande l’amnistie pour les « lycéens victimes de sanctions administratives » dans le cadre du mouvement social en cours. Il a écrit au ministre de l’Éducation nationale. « Dans plusieurs établissements, des directions ont prononcé ou s’apprêtent à prononcer des sanctions administratives impliquant l’inscription d’avertissements dans les dossiers scolaires à l’encontre de jeunes ayant participé à des actions de mobilisation ou s’étant trouvés à l’extérieur des grilles de l’établissement malgré des interdictions préfectorales ou de direction », dénonce Jeremy Bacchi dans sa missive à Edouard Geffray.
« Qualifier d’absences injustifiées des actes d’engagements de la jeunesse et les assortir d’un avertissement porté au dossier scolaire constitue une réponse d’une extrême gravité », critique le dirigeant communiste, qui s’inquiète de sanctions « notifiées de manière immédiate » sans « instruction » qui permette « de faire valoir le principe du contradictoire ». Aussi demande-t-il de garantir le respect des procédures.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: They have gone 10 weeks without answers. Will these families ever know what happened to loved ones missing after Nepal’s floods?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Cait Kelly
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Every day, Nikhila Agastya answers more questions from her two children: has she heard anything about their father? Is he with anyone? Is it snowing in Kathmandu? Is he cold, and does he have warm clothing? Will he come home? The answer is: probably not.
“They know that [their] father is missing,” Nikhila says. “And they are still looking for him. They always wait; every day they wait for him. They won’t give up, they think he will come home.”
Her husband, Gopi Agastya, had travelled from Sydney to Nepal to go on a pilgrimage with the Isha Foundation when a flood hit on 26 August. He did not return home.
It has been 10 weeks since the catastrophic floods wiped away whole villages, reaching settlements as high as 82 metres above the river level.
The number of dead has risen to 1,459. Another 5,285 people are unaccounted for. More than 700 of them are foreigners – including 34 Australians – with families who have had no answers for 10 long weeks.
Nikhila last spoke to her husband the morning of the floods, before he entered the immigration centre at the border with Tibet. Gopi was excited about coming home – he missed their two girls, aged 13 and 7, and wanted to eat a home-cooked meal with them. The two parents planned to take the children on a cruise when he returned.
The days that followed are now a blur to Nikhila. She travelled to India to be with family, while a friend whose husband was also missing went to Nepal and filtered any small pieces of information back: the border was still inaccessible; the Isha Foundation was trying to get in; families were putting up posters of loved ones on hospital walls in a desperate hope they would be found.
Nikhila sent images to Australia’s department of foreign affairs – of the shoes he would be wearing, his jacket, beanie, sun goggles – anything that could help identify him.
“He’s a very lovable person. Everyone likes him. He had good friends. I recently spoke to a friend of his, and he said Gopi is not just his name; Gopi is a brand.”
He was also the sole breadwinner of the family. The pair married 15 years ago and moved to Australia: he worked in IT for a major supermarket chain and she focused on their children. But Nikhila is now looking for work, with a government parenting payment nowhere near what Gopi was earning.
Amid these pressures, she can’t help but hope Gopi might come home.
No answers
Every morning for the last 10 weeks, Linda Govender has sent a WhatsApp message to her daughter. And every day, she receives no reply.
Her daughter, Terricia, was in an immigration centre when the floods hit. Now her mother is running a global campaign on behalf of the families of missing foreigners.
“The uncertainty is unbearable,” Govender says from South Africa. “You wake up every morning hoping for news, checking your phone, reading messages and wondering whether today will finally be the day somebody has an answer.”
Govender travelled to the flood zone in the days after, hiring a helicopter with other families to search by air. She returned home to Isipingo Beach, south of Durban, with no answers.
Realising many others were in the same situation, she then set up Global Voices for the Missing – an online community where families can share information and advocate. She says they want Nepal’s government to keep searching to find the whereabouts of the deceased and to maintain regular communication with affected families.
“We understand that difficult decisions have to be made following a natural disaster,” she says. “But families deserve to know that every reasonable avenue has been explored.
“For the families, the disaster does not end. We are still waking up every morning wondering where our loved ones are. We are still waiting for information.”
Soon after the floods, the government of Nepal sought to help speed up that information and set up DNA testing that could match families with the remains of their loved ones.
More than 2,000 people have given their DNA. At the start of October, only 112 bodies were transferred back to families. The process is slow and the backlog is large.
Governments around the world have also been working with their Nepali and Tibetan counterparts to begin the official process of issuing death certificates.
‘We keep continuing’
In the days after the floods, families from around the world rushed to Kathmandu. They hired 4WDs to take them as far as they could into the flood zones, they spoke to embassy officials and politicians, they visited the hospitals, sticking images of their loved ones up on the walls.
Last month, Nepal officially ended the search-and-rescue operation, moving into the “search-and-rehabilitation phase”, according to Phanindra Paudel, the chief of the National Emergency Operation Centre.
Authorities would no longer actively search for bodies but would recover any remains, property or other valuables found during the rehabilitation process, he said.
For hundreds of families around the world, waiting for any news, it was a blow.
Those who took it upon themselves to search for loved ones have not found it easy. Nepal’s government is still trying to clear debris to get up to the border with China, with many roads still closed. Nepal has said rebuilding will cost close to US$4.78bn (A$6.93bn) and has called for greater support for that mammoth undertaking, which will take years.
Thousands were displaced – now living in centres, tents, monasteries, or with extended family. They do not know when they will be able to return home.
Sagar Pandey is the chief executive of the Himalayan Glacier Company. His company had 47 people – including 15 Australians – in tour groups in Nepal’s north when the floods hit. His brother was guiding one of them.
“It was scary, it was bad,” Pandey says. “But now, people are trying to overcome; people are trying to continue their lives in a new way.
“It’s been really hard; they can’t forget, but also people don’t have a choice.”
Nepal has been reeling from the floods, which hit during one of the country’s peak tourist times. Adding to the impact is the fact that overseas visitors are no longer coming. Last year, the country welcomed more than 1.1 million visitors, contributing about 6.7% to the gross domestic product (GDP): now, the number has dropped off. Pandey has lost almost 80% of his usual bookings for this time of year.
“We have the missing guides’ children we have to support, to pay for the future for their schools. So we keep continuing.”
Anita Cook is among that small group of visitors returning to Nepal. She owns iNeeta cafe, a world away from the Himalayas, and one of the few shops in the small Australian town of Moyhu, Victoria. She has been to Nepal twice, and is now taking her two boys to hike the Annapurna circuit.
“Once you’ve been there, it just really leaves a really strong impact on you,” she says. “The way these people live, they’ve got nothing, but they’re the happiest people on the earth and they would do anything, anything to help you.”
Her cafe is full of plants she is selling to raise funds, while the local pub is contributing $1 for every parma sold. She is taking $12,000 the small community has raised and putting it straight into the hands of the guides she knows well – they’ve lost families, are connected to the community and she trusts they can give the money to the right people. But she says the best thing she can do is get on a plane and trek.
“[When it happened] I would have jumped on a plane and went straight away. But we are going now, because trekking in the mountains is the bread and butter of all these people.”
‘I just hope’
For people who went missing at the border, the process has been harder – determining which country they were in when the flood hit has been difficult.
The family of Renee Spry, a woman from the Sunshine Coast, have been waiting while this process happens along with the 49 other families from her group.
“There was some confusion about where they were lost,” Renee’s sister Jacinta says.
“But at the end of it, Nepal agreed that they were on the Nepalese side, and they would be the ones who would be trying to issue death certificates.”
A fortnight after the flood, Renee’s husband and two daughters travelled to Nepal. They could not get to the border area, but provided DNA samples, put pictures of her up and visited the temples she had gone to before her pilgrimage. They raised the money to travel through GoFundMe and donated $10,000 to the Emergency Action Alliance.
“They were prepared they might go there and not really get any answers,” she says. “I still think it was a therapeutic thing that they did it.”
Jacinta says “it is a funny kind of grief”: to lose someone and have no answers, no physical representation that they are gone. “The uncertainty has probably been the hardest bit,” she says. “Feeling just a bit hopeless about it, feeling removed and a long way away.”
The family want people to keep paying attention to Nepal – on the redevelopment and also the increasing disasters the climate crisis is causing in the small country.
“If you were talking to Renee, she would say there are all these people still trying to live there,” Spry says. “In this ongoing danger, in this evolving climate catastrophe.
“She would be worried about them. She would be like, ‘what’s everyone doing about this?’”
For many families, like Nikhila’s, the lack of information has not extinguished their hope that, one day, their loved ones will be found.
“I always feel like that,” she says. “I just hope, still, something, he might be there, somewhere. I just hope.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Rains flood Gaza displacement camps as Israeli authorities block entry of shelter materials into territory
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Katherine Hearst
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Rains flood Gaza displacement camps as Israeli authorities block entry of shelter materials into territory
Thousands of tents sheltering displaced Palestinians have been flooded by heavy rains overnight, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation.
Scarce aid entering the territory has left tens of thousands of Palestinians in the war-torn enclave exposed to the elements for a fourth winter in a row- with no fuel and nothing but makeshift tents and shelters for protection.
Red Cross spokesperon Amani Al Naouq told Al Jazeera that she has seen footage of “entire families, entire camps” inundated with water and scrambling to drain their tents and protect their belongings and lives.
In October, Director General for the International Organization for Migration Amy Pope warned that nearly all of Gaza's population require shelter assistance, with the combined supply pipeline of humanitarian shelter partners covering barely 17 per cent of identified winter needs.
"Families who have already endured repeated displacement and devastating loss must be able to face the winter in safety and dignity," Pope said. "Shelter materials must enter quickly, predictably and at the scale required."
Israel has continued to tightly restrict the entry of aid into the territory, with shelter items- including tent poles, construction materials and mobile homes- almost completely barred as the Israeli authorities consider them "dual use" items.
IOM said that around 8,600 IOM emergency shelter kits are waiting outside Gaza, but continue to be turned away from crossing points by the Israeli authorities.
This has forced humanitarian workers to repurpose salvaged materials to construct makeshift shelters, as storms turbochared by the strengthening El Niño phenomenon batter the territory.
“The solutions are known, the supplies are ready and humanitarian teams are prepared to deliver,” Pope said. “Immediate and sustained humanitarian access is essential to protect lives, strengthen damaged shelters, and help families move beyond temporary solutions. All parties must facilitate principled humanitarian action and support a response equal to the severity of the crisis.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Buildings damaged in Israeli bombings risk collapse as rain inundates Gaza
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Buildings damaged in Israeli bombings risk collapse as rain inundates Gaza
Floods have swept through Gaza after heavy rain, endangering families and putting war-damaged buildings at risk.
Gaza City – Rana Adnan Hmeida, 29, stands at the entrance to her tent in al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, holding her two-month-old daughter as she tries to keep her warm after rainwater has flooded their shelter overnight. The family’s bedding, blankets and clothes are all soaked, with her children exposed to the cold and wind of Gaza’s latest storm.
Hmeida, her husband and children have been awake since midnight as heavy rain and strong winds swept through the camp. Water seeped into the tent and drenched their belongings. With all their clothes wet, Hmeida had to ask neighbours to help dry their clothes.
“Since midnight, we have been sitting awake. Water came into our tent, and the bedding, blankets and everything else got soaked. In the morning, I found my son and little daughter shivering. My two-month-old baby was freezing,” Hmeida told Al Jazeera.
“What am I supposed to do? Hold my children or try to stop the water? I was trying to keep them warm while carrying my little girl, but the water kept coming in. The wind was so strong that we felt the tent was about to be ripped out of the ground.”
Her husband, Sameh Hmeida, 30, said the family’s tent is particularly exposed due to its close proximity to the sea. It has no tarpaulins or insulating materials that might have helped in the storm.
Heavy rain has flooded camps and cities across Gaza over the past days, where many Palestinians are spending the fourth winter outside their homes since Israel began its genocidal war on the enclave in October 2023.
Water levels have risen by 30 to 40cm (12 to 16in) at several camps in Gaza due to Saturday’s rain, with Gaza’s civil defence agency receiving hundreds of calls.
Rainwater has flooded many tents in al-Mina camp, where about 1,700 Palestinian families live, turning the ground into pools of muddy water.
Raed Abu Amsha, 40, said his tent collapsed on top of his family during the storm. The clothes and blankets of all nine children in his care, four of them from his late brother, were soaked.
“I am responsible for orphans as well as my own children, and I cannot provide for their needs. This storm lasted only two hours, and look what it did to us. We need tents, tarpaulins and anything that can protect our children. How long are we going to keep living like this?” he said.
In Nuseirat, a decades-old camp in central Gaza with permanent structures, rainfall also threatens families living in buildings damaged by Israeli bombardments.
Nasser al-Hajj, 54, lives in a tower block that was hit in an Israeli strike in September 2025. Debris from upper floors fell onto his home, leaving a large hole in the ceiling where water now enters every time it rains.
Although the ceiling has been reinforced with support beams, an engineer has warned al-Hajj that the apartment is dangerous, with the risk of further rubble falling from the building if more bad weather hits Gaza.
During the latest storm, al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home and waited for the debris to stop falling from the roof. Two of his children, who have autism, sleep in the tower block’s guard room, away from the damaged area.
“I am forced to live somewhere that could collapse over our heads at any moment. But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera. “I know how dangerous this place is, but I have no other option,” he added.
According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.
About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.
The Gaza Municipality is also struggling to respond to the storms. About 15 kilometres of rainwater drainage lines and 212 kilometres of sewage networks have been damaged. Eight pumping stations and three main stormwater collection basins are out of service.
The remaining system can handle no more than 20 percent of rainwater under the best of circumstances, according to municipality spokesperson Hosni Muhanna.
“[We] continue to clean drainage systems in preparation for the rainy season,” Muhanna said.
The municipality has deployed workers to clean drains and manholes, remove rubbish and clear water channels, repair damaged sections of drainage lines and operate water pumps.
But Muhanna warns that these efforts cannot restore the network’s capacity amid shortages of fuel, equipment and spare parts.
More than 2,000 buildings in Gaza City alone are at risk of collapse, he said, and the volume of rubble in Gaza City has exceeded 25 million tonnes.
Emergency committees in displacement camps are also struggling with shortages of shelter supplies. Adli Awad, an official with the emergency committee in Nuseirat refugee camp, said his team is trying to distribute tents and tarpaulins, particularly to families affected by the rain. But the number of people in need far exceeds available stocks.
“We are trying to provide as many tents and tarpaulins as possible. We are also helping families dig channels to divert rainwater away from tents and reduce flooding,” Awad said.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.title: Doping | Die Wada im Zahlenrausch der Ermittlungen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.author: Tom Mustroph
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.text:
- Sport
- Doping
Die Wada im Zahlenrausch der Ermittlungen
26.000 Dopingkunden, 90 illegale Labore, 100 Tonnen Substanzen – die Weltantidopingagentur feiert die Erfolge ihres Investigativnetzwerks.
Zum zehnjährigen Bestehen ihres internationalen Investigativprogramms gab die Weltantidopingagentur Wada am Mittwoch durchaus beeindruckende Zahlen heraus. Das Programm mit dem komplizierten Namen Global Anti-Doping Intelligence and Investigations Network, kurz GAIIN, hat in den vergangenen Jahren 260 Polizeiermittlungen eingeleitet, in deren Folge 90 illegale Labore geschlossen und 100 Tonnen leistungssteigernde Substanzen beschlagnahmt wurden. Außerdem seien Namenslisten mit etwa 26.000 Dopingkunden sichergestellt worden, erzählte Chefermittler Günter Younger in einem Videocall.
Was bislang allerdings fehlt, sind die prominenten Sportler und Betreuer unter den Kunden. Da werde man noch ein, zwei Jahre warten müssen, vertröstete der frühere LKA-Ermittler aus Bayern auf Nachfrage von »nd«. »Wir haben die Namen von den internationalen Strafverfolgungsbehörden. Wir helfen ihnen dabei, sie zu identifizieren. Einige Festnahmen gab es bereits. Es ist aber auch herausfordernd, aus den Listen die richtigen Personen herauszufiltern«, erklärte Younger.
Eine Pille hier, eine Spritze da
Diese Diskrepanz ist ärgerlich. Sie unterstreicht einmal mehr das klassische Dilemma des Antidopinggeschäfts. Doping selbst ist eine ziemlich schnelle Sache. Eine Pille hier genommen, eine Spritze dort gesetzt. Die Jagd auf jene, die diese Substanzen zu sich nehmen und sich über Siege, Medaillen und Sponsorenverträge freuen können, ist hingegen eine sehr mühsame Angelegenheit.
Bestes Beispiel ist die Tatsache, dass das Internationale Olympische Komitee (IOC) Anfang dieser Woche neue Olympiaurkunden für einige Athletinnen der Spiele 2022 und 2024 zustellte. Die Koreanerin Yelim Kim etwa durfte sich über die Urkunde für Platz acht in der Eiskunstlaufkonkurrenz in Peking 2022 freuen. Grund dafür war, dass das IOC erst jetzt die Ehrentafel in dieser Disziplin aufgrund des Dopingfalls der russischen Sportlerin Kamila Valieva änderte. Diese war damals Vierte geworden, wurde aber 2024 rückwirkend gesperrt. Alle ab Platz fünf rückten nun vor. Und weil es Urkunden nur bis Platz acht gab, bekam Kim als ursprünglich Neunte nun erst ihr Dokument.
Auch beim Marathonlauf der Frauen von Paris 2024 gab es neue Urkunden, weil nun die zunächst auf Rang sieben platzierte und später des Dopings überführte rumänisch-kenianische Athletin Delvine Relin Meringor aus den Listen gestrichen wurde. Der ganz frische EPO-Dopingfall der Olympiasiegerin von 2021, Peres Jepchirchir, hatte auf die Pariser Urkundenvergabe dagegen keinen Einfluss. Die Kenianerin wurde in Paris nur 14., ihr positiver Dopingtest erfolgte auch erst in diesem Jahr.
Erfolgsquote unter einem Prozent
Der Frust darüber, dass vergleichsweise wenig Athletinnen und Athleten durch Dopingtests auffliegen, war auch Motiv für die Einrichtung der internationalen Ermittlungsabteilung der Wada. Die Erfolgsquote bei Tests liegt seit Jahren unter einem Prozent. Younger ist allerdings überzeugt, dass die tatsächliche Doperquote weit höher liegt. Deshalb begann er vor zehn Jahren, die Abteilung aufzubauen. »Anfangs waren wir zwei Mitarbeiter, jetzt sind wir 15«, blickte er zurück. Aufgeteilt sind sie in das Ermittlerteam und eine zweite Abteilung, die sich ausschließlich mit den Kronzeugen und Hinweisgebern beschäftigt.
Mehrere hundert Whistleblower dürften es inzwischen sein. Younger zeigte sich stolz darüber, dass keiner dieser Namen bisher bekannt wurde, dass ihre Identität also geschützt blieb. Um das zu garantieren, trennte er auch beide Abteilungen. »Die Ermittler kennen nicht die Namen der Whistleblower, bekommen aber die Informationen und Sachverhalte übermittelt«, betonte er.
Im Windschatten der Strafverfolger
Für das eindrucksvolle Ergebnis von 260 Ermittlungen und 90 geschlossenen illegalen Laboren war aber ein zweiter Schritt verantwortlich: Die Überzeugung von Strafverfolgern weltweit, dass es sich lohne, auch in Sachen Doping zu ermitteln. Younger machte dafür vor allem die Tatsache verantwortlich, dass die organisierte Kriminalität (OK) wegen des vergleichsweise geringeren Verfolgungsdrucks den Handel mit Doping-Präparaten in ihr gewöhnlich auf Drogen- und Waffenschmuggel ausgerichtetes Portfolio aufnehme. Das mache Doping-Ermittlungen auch für OK-Spezialisten interessant. Und in deren Windschatten kann die Wada wiederum Netzwerke aufdecken.
Workshops mit Strafverfolgern in mittlerweile 99 Ländern führten zu der Vielzahl von oft länderübergreifenden Ermittlungen. Bestes Beispiel ist die in diesem Jahr erfolgte Schließung einer Fabrik für pharmazeutische Rohmaterialien in China, die auch auf Hinweisen europäischer Ermittler über Vertriebsstrukturen beruhte.
Richtig rund wären die Erfolge aber erst, wenn auch jene Spitzensportler und Betreuer aufgespürt würden, die sich vermutlich noch im Dschungel der sichergestellten Tarnnamen und Kundenlisten verbergen. Es wird Zeit, dass das passiert – auch damit nicht erst Jahre vergehen müssen, bis Olympiaurkunden an die Sportlerinnen und Sportler verteilt werden können, die sie wirklich verdienen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://taz.de/Repraesentative-Befragung.title: Repräsentative Befragung: Fast jeder zweite Erwachsene hält Mittagsschlaf
https://taz.de/Repraesentative-Befragung.text:
Repräsentative Befragung: Fast jeder zweite Erwachsene hält Mittagsschlaf
Der kurze Powernap kann wieder fit machen. Eine Analyse zeigt: Mittagsschlaf ist beliebt in Deutschland. Eines gilt es aber zu beachten.
dpa | Fast jeder zweite Erwachsene in Deutschland hält laut einer repräsentativen Befragung mindestens einmal pro Woche einen Mittagsschlaf. Die meisten gönnen sich ein- bis zweimal die Woche ein Schläfchen, gefolgt von der Gruppe, die täglich einen Powernap macht, wie das Robert Koch-Institut (RKI) berichtet. Nicht erfragt wurde, inwiefern Menschen gern häufiger ein Mittagsschläfchen machen würden, es aber – etwa wegen ihrer Berufstätigkeit – nicht können.
Von rund 8.000 Teilnehmerinnen und Teilnehmern gaben rund 45 Prozent an, in den vergangenen vier Wochen mindestens einmal wöchentlich einen Mittagsschlaf gehalten oder sich hingelegt und dabei nichts aktiv getan zu haben, wie das RKI mitteilte. Bei den Frauen waren es 47 Prozent, bei den Männern 44.
Die meisten gönnen sich ein- bis zweimal die Woche ein Schläfchen, gefolgt von der Gruppe, die täglich einen Powernap macht. Den täglichen Mittagsschlaf halten den Angaben nach vor allem Menschen ab 65 Jahren sowie Menschen mit niedrigen formalen Bildungsabschlüssen.
Einige bleiben mittags gern lange liegen – gut ist das nicht
Ein kurzer Mittagsschlaf von unter 60 Minuten wirke sich positiv aus, hieß es vom RKI. Menschen fühlten sich danach weniger müde und leistungsfähiger.
Ein Viertel der Erwachsenen, die mindestens einmal die Woche einen Mittagsschlaf macht, schläft den Angaben nach 60 Minuten oder länger. Ein so langer Mittagsschlaf ist laut RKI allerdings mit einem erhöhten Risiko für Stoffwechselstörungen, Herz-Kreislauf-Erkrankungen, Demenz und Depressionen verbunden.
Es geht dabei um einen statistischen, keinen ursächlichen Zusammenhang, wie es vom RKI hieß. Die Befragung zeigt also nicht, dass der lange Schlaf die Krankheiten auslöst. Es kann zum Beispiel auch so sein, dass Menschen mit mehr Grunderkrankungen ein höheres Schlafbedürfnis haben.
Frauen unter 45 Jahren machen im Vergleich zu älteren Altersgruppen häufiger mindestens einmal pro Woche einen verlängerten Mittagsschlaf. Dazu schreibt das RKI: „Die erhöhte Belastung durch Care-Arbeit und ein dadurch verringerter Nachtschlaf könnten eine mögliche Erklärung sein.“
Und wie lange schlafen Erwachsene nachts?
Auch dazu hat das RKI tausende Menschen befragt. Das Ergebnis: Die erwachsene Bevölkerung schläft im Schnitt 7 Stunden und 26 Minuten pro Nacht. Unter der Woche schlafen Erwachsene im Schnitt mit 7 Stunden und 15 Minuten etwa weniger als am Wochenende mit 7 Stunden und 53 Minuten. Junge Erwachsene zwischen 18 und 29 Jahren schlafen am Wochenende sogar mehr als eine Stunde länger als an Wochentagen (8 Stunden und 23 Minuten versus 7 Stunden und 20 Minuten).
Nach Empfehlung vieler Schlafmediziner sollten Erwachsene sieben bis neun Stunden pro Nacht schlafen, ab 65 Jahren sieben bis acht Stunden. Dabei wird ausdrücklich betont, dass der individuell benötigte Schlaf sehr unterschiedlich ausfällt.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Eva Corlett in Auckland
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.
On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.
But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.
Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.
With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind.
Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.
Labour, led by Chris Hipkins, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.
Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.
“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour.
The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.
Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition.
Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance.
That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee, will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.
On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.
With all the extra seats, there could be 130 in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.
The country faces a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Luxon said caretaker government conventions would apply in the meantime.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well-established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Yemeni government forces claim attack on Houthi positions in al-Misrakh,  while Saudi attacks on Bani Hashih kill at least 15
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Katherine Hearst
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Yemeni government forces claim attack on Houthi positions in al-Misrakh, while Saudi attacks on Bani Hashih kill at least 15
Yemeni government forces have claimed three air attacks on Houthi positions in the al-Misrakh district of the Taiz governorate.
The city of Taiz- which is government-held- has been subject to an ongoing Houthi siege. The blockade has triggered a spiralling humanitarian crisis in the city, as road closures bar vital supplies, including fuel, from entering.
Laurent Bukera, the United Nations Humanitarian Coordinator for Yemen warned that the city's health system is "close to collapse", while the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said that the conflict has blocked lifesaving assistance from reaching 800,000 people, including 600,000 who depend on aid in the city.
Meanwhile, Houthi media reports that at least 15 people have been killed, mostly women and children, in a series of Saudi strikes in the al-Shariyah area of Yemen’s Bani Hashish district. According to the reports, some 30 others have been wounded.

https://taz.de/AfD-Verbotsverfahren-Hubi.title: Datenleak bei der AfD: Hubig will E-Mails bei Prüfung für Verbotsverfahren nutzen

Datenleak bei der AfD: Hubig will E-Mails bei Prüfung für Verbotsverfahren nutzen
Hunderttausende AfD-E-Mails sind im Internet veröffentlicht worden. Die Justizministerin sieht darin mögliche Belege für die Verfassungsfeindlichkeit der Partei.
dpa | Hunderttausende von im Internet veröffentlichen E-Mails der AfD könnten aus Sicht von Bundesjustizministerin Stefanie Hubig helfen, den Weg zu einem Verbotsverfahren für die Partei zu ebnen. Die SPD-Politikerin sprach sich in der Neuen Osnabrücker Zeitung für eine Bund-Länder-Arbeitsgruppe aus, die die Erfolgsaussichten eines Verbotsverfahrens prüft. Dabei könne sie grundsätzlich alle Erkenntnisse heranziehen, die vorliegen. „Auch die E-Mails könnten also wohl herangezogen werden, wenn sie Belege für die Verfassungsfeindlichkeit der AfD liefern“, sagte Hubig.
Unbekannte hatten kürzlich im Internet nach eigenen Angaben Daten veröffentlicht, bei denen es sich um rund 421.000 AfD-E-Mails handeln soll. Die AfD wird bundesweit vom Verfassungsschutz als Verdachtsfall beobachtet. Einzelne Landesverbände werden vom jeweiligen Landesverfassungsschutz als gesichert rechtsextremistisch eingestuft.
„Ernsthaft und systematisch prüfen“
„Ich bin überzeugt, dass wir jetzt ernsthaft und systematisch prüfen müssen, ob die Voraussetzungen für ein Verbotsverfahren vorliegen“, sagte Hubig. Auch Mecklenburg-Vorpommerns Ministerpräsidentin Manuela Schwesig (SPD) hat sich zuletzt für eine Bund-Länder-Arbeitsgruppe zur Prüfung eines möglichen AfD-Verbotsverfahrens ausgesprochen.
Eine solche Arbeitsgruppe würde nach früheren Angaben Wissen aus Bund und Ländern bündeln und mit Verfassungsschutz und Verfassungsrechtlern kooperieren. Erst danach würde entschieden, ob Bundesrat, Bundestag oder Bundesregierung tatsächlich ein AfD-Verbotsverfahren beantragen. Hubig sagte: „Für mich ist klar: Wenn ein Antrag konkrete Erfolgsaussichten hat, dann muss er auch gestellt werden.“

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

Regierungsbildung in Israel : Eine Chance fürs Land
Die arabischen Parteien haben Oppositionsführer Gadi Eisenkot als neuen israeelischen Premier empfohlen. Die Gegner Netanjahus müssen nun mutig sein.
I n diesen Tagen tobt in den Konferenzräumen schicker Hotels und in der Residenz des israelischen Präsidenten eine diplomatische Schlacht – ohne Rücksicht auf Verluste. Die Gelegenheit ist einmalig, dass die Verhandlungen nach der Parlamentswahl vom 27. Oktober der Ära Netanjahu ein Ende setzen und den Kurs des Landes verändern könnten. Wenn denn nur alle mutig genug sind, die Chance zu ergreifen.
Für die arabischen Parteien, die Gadi Eisenkot gerade als Premierminister empfohlen haben, könnte dies der Fahrschein sein, um aus der Rolle der traditionellen Protestparteien am Rande des politischen Geschehens herauszuwachsen und – selbst wenn sie sich nicht an der Koalition beteiligen – die rechtsextremste Regierung, die Israel je hatte, zu Fall zu bringen. Für die Oppositionsparteien unter Eisenkot eröffnet sich die Möglichkeit, den am längsten amtierenden Ministerpräsidenten in der Geschichte des Landes die Macht zu nehmen. Für Netanjahus Lager geht es daher schlicht ums politische Überleben.
Es ist eine Entscheidung ohne Sicherheitsnetz und mit vielen Fragezeichen: Eine Minderheitsregierung unter Eisenkot mit externer Unterstützung der arabischen Parteien könnte rein rechnerisch funktionieren. Doch bliebe sie auch bei kontroversen Entscheidungen stabil? Ex-Generalstabschef Eisenkot ist nicht gerade ein linker Pazifist. Außerdem lehnt Avigdor Liberman, der konservative Anführer von Yisrael Beitenu, Teil des Oppositionsblocks, eine Minderheitsregierung ab.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Eine Koalition unter Einbezug der arabischen Parteien wäre sicherer, aber ist sie machbar? Die Vereinigte Arabische Liste will nicht mit zionistischen Parteien koalieren – und Liberman nicht mit arabischen Parteien. Eine Alternative wäre ein Bündnis mit den ultraorthodoxen Parteien, aber selbst das ist höchst umstritten. Und könnte eine solche Koalition den Erwartungen der arabischen Bürger:innen, die in Massen an die Urnen geströmt sind, Rechnung tragen? Und was ist mit den vielen Israelis, die für Netanjahus Likud – immerhin stärkste Kraft – und seine Verbündeten gestimmt haben?
Dennoch lohnt es sich, den Versuch zu wagen. Letztlich ist dies vor allem eine Chance fürs Land: um Israels internationales Ansehen aufzubessern, die Umstände des schlimmsten Massakers seiner Geschichte aufzuklären und zu demokratischen Prinzipien zurückzusteuern.
Und um seinen arabischen Bürger:innen zu zeigen, dass ihre Beteiligung nicht umsonst war. Dass man ihre Stimme gehört hat.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Not a pretty sight: Trump’s ‘beautiful’ Republican men flop at midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
It was either a last-ditch considered strategy to win votes, or the ramblings of an increasingly unhinged and increasingly amorous party leader.
Either way, it didn’t work.
Despite Donald Trump spending the last few weeks touting the good looks of Republican midterm candidates, praising asses, shoulders and jawlines, almost all of his roster of “handsome” and “beautiful” men lost their elections on Tuesday, while the Trump-approved hot guys who did win mostly limped over the line.
Take Jon Husted, the Ohio senator.
“I examined his ass,” the president, 80, said of Husted in late October. “And then I looked at his shoulders. I looked at his feet. I looked at his hand. I looked at his jawline. Studied him. He’s got a jawline.”
Trump’s lasciviousness continued: “I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”
This unusual sales pitch – “vote for this hot guy” – failed to break through with Ohio residents. Husted lost by five points, in a state which Trump won by 11 points in 2024.
It didn’t work in Georgia either, where Trump spent time campaigning for, and seemingly lusting after, the Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins.
“Mike Collins is a good-looking man – and he’s all man,” Trump told a crowd in the state before the election. He lost to the Democratic senator Jon Ossoff – (Trump: “I don’t think he’s a good-looking man”) – by 18 points.
Trump’s idiosyncratic closing message didn’t go unnoticed. Anderson Cooper, the CNN host, dubbed Trump the “assman-in-chief” as he played clips of his comments on air.
“There’s nothing at all unusual – and certainly nothing gay – about a president who dances daily to YMCA and who publicly pined for a reprise of Betty Buckley in Cats,” Cooper, who is gay, said.
Unfortunately, the candidates Trump had admired continued to record poor results.
“I actually think that Rick Jackson’s a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy,” Trump declared in the run-up to the election. Jackson, 72, had been favored to win but lost to Keisha Lance Bottoms in the Georgia governor’s election by about 8.5 points. Bottoms became Georgia’s first Democratic governor since 2003, and the country’s first Black female governor.
Some fared better. Ed Gallrein, a 68-year-old farmer, was described by Trump as a “perfect man”. Trump picked Gallrein earlier this year to run against the Republican congressman Thomas Massie, whom Trump does not like.
“I needed somebody good, and this guy walks through the door,” Trump said of Gallrein. “I said, look at this beautiful guy.”
Gallrein won his congressional district in Kentucky, 54% to 40%, but this was a much smaller margin than the 64% of the vote Trump himself collected in 2024. Likewise, the Republican Bill Hagerty, whom Trump has described as “a very handsome guy”, retained his Senate seat in Tennessee, but only by about half the margin with which he won in 2020.
What about the others?
Trump branded a group of men “Oklahoma studs” during one campaign rally last month, but they weren’t running for office. It’s unknown how the unnamed men have fared since winning Trump’s praise.
Others might want to be careful of Trump taking a shine to them. Asked by the New York Post days before the election to name the “best-looking member” of his administration, Trump singled out Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, as “a good-looking guy”.
If reports are to be believed, Hegseth and his good looks might be sacrificed in the coming weeks, potentially blamed for the Trump-led Iran war, which contributed to the historic Republican losses.

Trump claims 'minor strikes' on Iran's Qeshm Island, but says talks ongoing
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the American military carried out a new round of "minor strikes" on Iran's Qeshm Island, which he claimed "knocked out" Iranian air defence systems.
Iranian state media reported that two blasts were heard in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which lies in the Strait of Hormuz, the contested waterway which has been disrupted since the US launched its assault on Iran in February.
The Iranian army said in comments carried by state broadcaster IRIB that their air defences downed a US drone over the island.
But Trump told reporters shortly after that the attacks "knocked out" the air defence systems "in about 15 minutes, maybe five".
Responding to reports of the explosions, US Central Command (Centcom) said that the situation is "relatively calm".

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Pro-Russian hackers leak Italian foreign minister’s data on dark web
The prime minister blames pro-Russian hackers for the leak, as her top diplomat says the cyberthreat was ongoing.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blaming pro-Russian hackers for the leak.
Tajani announced in a social media post on Saturday that “for days now, cybercriminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation”.
The threats against Tajani, who is also vice prime minister of Italy, come amid a spate of hoax bomb threats across Europe that have forced flight diversions, security alerts at broadcasters, and attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems.
“They are also targeting my family; they are willing to pay for more details about me and my loved ones,” Tajani added in his X post. “My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way.”
‘Matter of grave concern’
Meloni expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data”.
She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination”.
Tajani added in his statement that Italy’s “position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted: defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation’s democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities”.
He also suggested that the cyberthreats may also be a reaction to the Italian government’s efforts to strengthen the Foreign Ministry’s digital defences.
Tajani did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.
He added that the ministry was taking the threats seriously and was coordinating its response with allied countries.

Journalistische Entgleisungen : Ein bisschen mehr Respekt, bitte!
Die Berliner Wahlsiegerin Elif Eralp steht seit Wochen unter Beschuss. Dahinter steckt auch die Angst vor linken Frauen.
E ine strahlende Frau, die von „Liebe und Gerechtigkeit“ in der Bundeshauptstadt spricht und dabei für Bildung, günstige Mieten und Migranten streiten will: Dieses Leuchtbild der Berliner Wahlsiegerin Elif Eralp war schnell erloschen. Schon bald wurde die Bürgermeisterkandidatin der Linken zur Symbolfigur für radikale Randgruppen ihrer Partei – obwohl sie selbst gegen diese vorgegangen war. „Linke Clan-Bürgermeisterin“, „tief judenfeindlich“, „erpressbar“: Spekulationen, im besten Fall Indizienketten reichten, um sie in zahlreichen Medien abzustempeln.
Derart diffamierende Schlagzeilen rufen Erinnerungen an andere freudige Wahlsiegerinnen wie Andrea Ypsilanti hervor. Auch die hessische Sozialdemokratin musste 2008 eine „Tsunami-Welle von demagogischer Raserei“ (Tom Schimmeck) ertragen. So verschieden die Voraussetzungen sein mögen: Ein Vergleich ist auch 18 Jahre später erhellend. Er zeigt nicht nur, dass antilinke Ressentiments erneut publizistische Entgleisungen und ein geradezu auffälliges Desinteresse am sachlich-demokratischen Ringen zu rechtfertigen scheinen. Das Problem scheint zudem die linke Frau zu sein.
Christiane Grefe ist freie Autorin, unter anderem für Die Zeit, wo sie 25 Jahre lang als Reporterin und Redakteurin gearbeitet hat. Sie schreibt über soziale und ökologische Themen. Zuletzt erschien ihr Buch (mit Tanja Busse) „Der Grund“ über Zielkonflikte bei der Flächennutzung.
Zur Erinnerung: In einem Wahlkampf, der (wie bei Eralp) von Gerechtigkeitsthemen getragen wurde, hatte Ypsilanti über 36 Prozent der hessischen Bürger von der SPD überzeugt. Doch ganz knapp verfehlte sie die Chance, den CDU-Ministerpräsidenten Roland Koch allein im Bund mit den Grünen ablösen zu können. Zerrissen zwischen zwei Wahlversprechen – nicht mit Koch oder den Linken – überzeugte Ypsilanti letztlich ihre Fraktion davon, die Linke für die Duldung einer rot-grünen Koalition zu gewinnen. Darauf zogen – assistiert von einem medialen Trommelfeuer (egoistisch, machtversessen, „Dilettanti“, „Lügilanti“) – vier Abtrünnige wenige Stunden vor dem letzten Votum ihre Unterstützung zurück. Ihre als Gewissensqual verkleidete Intrige führte zu Ypsilantis Sturz.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
So muss es bei Elif Eralp nicht kommen, aber auch ihr wird voreilig die Regierungsfähigkeit abgesprochen, weitere Parallelen sind frappierend. In beiden Fällen gab es höchst ungewöhnliche journalistische Regelverstöße. Die Spiegel-Redaktion veröffentlichte vergangene Woche Korrekturen eines Interviews, die Eralp im Vertrauen auf solche Autorisierungsprozesse erbeten hatte. Dass die Politikerin – auf Anraten des LKA – den Namen eines mit der Hamas sympathisierenden Palästina-Aktivisten streichen wollte, um ihre Familie zu beschützen, fiel ebenso der Indiskretion anheim wie eine Randnotiz an linke Kollegen, die ihr Büro versehentlich mitgesendet hatte. Darin hatte Eralp ihre persönliche Angst benannt.
Déjà-vu: Im Fall Ypsilanti hatte der damalige hessische Ministerpräsident Kurt Beck einer Journalistenrunde verraten, als Bundesvorsitzender der SPD werde er eine Duldung durch die Linke akzeptieren. Er tat das in einem Hintergrundgespräch, was eine Veröffentlichung ausschließt. Doch die Meldung ging sofort raus – und mobilisierte eine Kampagne rechter Sozialdemokraten und Wirtschaftsvertreter gegen die Wahlsiegerin.
Man kann solche gängigen Absprachen zwischen Medien und Politik mit guten Gründen infrage stellen. Doch wenn beide Seiten sie akzeptieren: Was legitimiert dann, sie einseitig zu brechen? Ist es tatsächlich Verantwortung? Eher wohl handelten die Journalisten aus Hybris und bewirkten damit, was in der Branche als tabu gilt: Sie machten selbst Politik.
Und das gerade bei Frauen? Man könnte die Frage als verschwörungstheoretisch abtun, wären nicht damals wie heute platte Weiblichkeitsklischees im Spiel. Nur ein Beispiel ist ein Kommentar des FAZ-Feuilletons über einen Auftritt Eralps: Angesichts einer Gruppe von Parteifreunden, die hinter ihr standen, „fast hätten wir Clan gesagt“, stellt er die Frage, ob die Herren wohl „zur moralischen Unterstützung oder eher als Aufpasser“ mitgekommen seien.
„Überforderung“, „Marionette finsterer Mächte“: solche Attribute gleichen jenen für „diese kleine, hesselnde Frau“, die „frühere Stewardess“ – Ypsilanti. So einer konnte – und nun geht es zur Sache – ihr geplantes ambitioniertes Energiewendeprogramm nur „aufgedrückt“ worden sein. Viel mehr hatte das schwache Geschlecht mit der Berufung des sozialdemokratischen Vordenkers für erneuerbare Energien, Hermann Scheer, zum designierten Wirtschaftsminister sowohl Mut bewiesen als auch politische Witterung. Scheers praktische Vision einer dezentralen „Energie des Volkes“ entpuppte sich als ein Geheimnis der erfolgreichen Wahlmobilisierung in Hessens Kommunen.
Doch damit schwamm das Team Scheer-Ypsilanti gegen den Strom der fossilen Mehrheit ihrer Partei. Namentlich der damalige Finanzminister Peer Steinbrück und Wolfgang Clement aus NRW konnten ihren Spin vom verantwortungslosen, illusionären Projekt der „Amateurin“ in den Medien bemerkenswert monochrom durchsetzen. Dabei spricht eine Menge dafür, dass wir heute beim Klimaschutz weiter wären, hätte sich das Experiment in Hessen durchgesetzt.
Zugegeben, es ist spekulativ, wenn man vermutet, dass hinter den Tiraden gegen Elif Eralp auch die Verteidigung des Status quo gegen ein komplexes Reformprojekt steht. Gemeint ist die von der Linken geplante und von den Berlinern in einer Volksbefragung geforderte teilweise Vergesellschaftung großer Immobilienkonzerne. Beim Widerstand dagegen fällt zumindest auf, dass persönliche Diffamierung und inhaltliches Desinteresse Hand in Hand gehen. Ernsthafte Auseinandersetzungen mit dem Versuch, kommunalen Einfluss auf die Mietpreise zurückzugewinnen, geschweige denn mit dem wohnungspolitischen Gesamtpaket der Linken, findet man jedenfalls höchstens mit der Lupe, obwohl das lange aufgeschobene Thema Wohnen sozialen Brennstoff birgt.
Man muss die Ideen, für die Elif Eralp steht, nicht für das Nonplusultra halten. Sicher ist aber: „Wahnsinn“ oder „neidgetriebene Verliererpolitik“ (Ulf Poschardt, Die Welt) sind keine Argumente. Dergleichen spalterisches Karacho sägt vielmehr weiter am Ast der Demokratie, die seit 2008 immer brüchiger wird – und umso mehr auf Respekt auch von politischen Gegnern angewiesen ist.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Will Pete Hegseth be the blue tsunami’s next victim? | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Can you smell the schadenfreude in the air?
Watching some of the worst people in the world get their comeuppance this week has been deeply satisfying. And the show isn’t over yet. While the midterms have wrapped up, the blame game is only just getting started, with Republicans desperate to find scapegoats for their shellacking.
He may be a big, strong, testosterone-obsessed warrior, but I suspect Pete Hegseth is panicking right now. When it comes to scapegoats, the defence secretary (or “war secretary” as he prefers to identify as) is an obvious choice. The disastrous US-Israeli war on Iran played a key role in the midterm upset, as even JD Vance has admitted, and Hegseth was one of its main architects.
The Democrats have already declared war on the former Fox News personality. “In the majority, one of the first things we’re going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Hakeem Jeffries announced at a campaign rally before the midterms.
It’s not just the Democrats; many of Hegseth’s peers are eager to give him the boot.
The outgoing Republican senator Thom Tillis told CBS News on Tuesday night that Hegseth has a “reckoning” coming. Meanwhile, the (also outgoing) Republican congressman Thomas Massie told Bloomberg News he will “definitely” reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth next week. (Massie has already tried to impeach Hegseth for starting the war in Iran without congressional approval.)
In a Wednesday post on Twitter/X, Massie wrote: “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”
There is little chance that Hegseth will unilaterally decide to make a dignified exit. On Thursday, the defense secretary posted a longwinded video in which, after rambling about DEI and trans people, he asserted that he wasn’t going anywhere.
“A disgruntled, defeated congressman [aka Massie], along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
This little performance did not quieten his critics.
“@PeteHegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos,” Tillis wrote on social media in response. “This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.”
There have been rather a lot of shameful and embarrassing episodes in Hegseth’s career, haven’t there?
There are all the allegations about his previous drunk and disorderly conduct, for example. And the settlement he paid to a woman who accused him of raping her in 2017. And the time his own mother called him an “abuser of women”. (He’s denied any wrongdoing.) And the New Yorker’s report that, in 2015, Hegseth was accused of drunkenly chanting “Kill All Muslims! Kill All Muslims!” (Hegseth’s lawyer told the New Yorker that they weren’t going to comment on these “outlandish claims”.) And the time he accidentally sent top secret war plans in a Signal group chat that included a reporter from the Atlantic. And then, of course, there are all the alleged war crimes he’s responsible for.
Hegseth loves to rail against “DEI hires”, but imagine for a moment if a woman was texting classified information to the wrong people and battling scandal after scandal. There’s no way she’d still be heading up the Pentagon. As has been widely observed, Trump seems to like getting rid of his high-level female officials when they embarrass him, while holding on to his mediocre men.
Indeed, while the secretary of war may be on the defensive now, there’s always the depressing possibility that his sex – and his sycophancy towards the president – may end up saving him. Particularly as Trump is publicly standing by his man for the moment.
When asked on Wednesday if he was considering replacing Hegseth, Trump told reporters: “No, I think he’s doing a very good job.” Behind the scenes, of course, it could be a different story. NBC News reported on Wednesday that Trump has told some of his allies that he’s considering replacing the defense secretary.
But even if Hegseth is able to cling on to the sinking ship until it finally goes down, I take solace in the fact that he must be feeling very uncomfortable right now. And I am clinging on to hope that he will have a very public downfall.
This is, let’s not forget, a man who wanted to livestream an execution via firing squad. While that thankfully never happened, perhaps we’ll all get to watch a live stream of Hegseth getting fired.
Navy admiral fired by Hegseth flips South Carolina seat
Nancy Lacore was in the navy for 35 years before the three-star admiral was ousted by Hegseth without cause amid a broader purge. In response, she mounted a bid for Congress that made Hegseth’s incompetence a key talking point. At the time of writing, the race hasn’t been officially called, but it looks like she’s managed to flip a traditionally Republican seat. Wouldn’t it be poetic if she plays a part in firing Pete?
Young white men abandoned the Republicans at the midterms
“Eighteen- to 29-year-old young white men with no college degrees swung 40 points to the Democrats, and I don’t think it’s all because they’re socialists,” the podcaster Tim Pool told Fox News. “I think it’s because many of them want to burn the Republican party down.” Go ahead, guys!
Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
Part of Brand’s defence was the claim: “Not one of [the victims] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave.” Speaking after the trial, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, emphasized how dangerous these sorts of misconceptions about sexual assault are. “The idea that rape victims must scream, physically resist or immediately report an offence is a well-established rape myth, rooted in outdated and harmful assumptions about how victims are expected to behave,” she said. “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”
Amtrak wants to let passengers bring guns on trains
Just when you think the US is getting a smidgen more sane, you see something like this.
West Bank school on high alert after settler violence
Israeli militants killed five teenage students at al-Mughayyir school in the West Bank last academic year, one at the school gates. In response to parents being afraid to send their kids back to the classroom, the school has had to build bigger fences. Meanwhile, “settlers” continue their violent pogroms on the village, and far too many US politicians continue to excuse and enable this violence.
How ‘Crunchy Moms’ became ‘the most dangerous group on Facebook’
A Guardian investigation has found that groups such as Crunchy Moms (which has more than 490,000 members) are hives of anti-vaccine content and medical misinformation. Most alarmingly: Meta “appears to have helped spread such ideas by promoting Crunchy Moms into users’ feeds, even when they do not seek it out”.
The week in pawtriarchy
While the midterms were on everyone’s mind this week, an alligator in North Carolina was just thinking about brunch. Surveillance cameras caught the creature strolling into the back of a bagel shop, startling the customers. The police were called and the gator was removed. The gator insists he did nothing wrong and is the victim of a schmear campaign.
- Arwa Mahadwi is a Guardian columnist

Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: La Liga – predictions, team news, lineups
Barcelona and Atletico clash on Sunday in a blockbuster encounter which could upend the La Liga title race this season.
Who: Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona
What: La Liga, match day 12
Where: Riyadh Air Metropolitano, Madrid, Spain
When: Sunday, November 8, at 9pm (20:00 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 17:00 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream
A top-of-the-table clash headlines Sunday’s La Liga action, with Barcelona looking to retain their top spot before the international break as they face challengers Atletico Madrid.
With only two points separating the teams, the blockbuster clash could well be the turning point in the 2026-27 title race should Atletico upset Barcelona.
Diego Simeone’s side have been in terrific form all season and take on Barcelona, bolstered by a seven-game winning streak in the Spanish top flight.
Atletico’s striker Julian Alvarez struggled to find his feet early in the campaign, with a dramatic transfer saga involving Barcelona adding to the uncertainty. But the Argentinian has since rediscovered his form, scoring in each of his last two league outings.
If Atletico have been impressive, Barcelona have been irresistible.
Hansi Flick’s team have netted an incredible 46 goals in just 11 league games; the only team to score more in their first 11 matches of a campaign were Athletic Club in 1930-31 (49).
Raphinha and Lamine Yamal have been the architects of Barca’s lethal attack, with the Brazilian winger leading the goal-scoring charts this season with 15 league goals in 10 games. He is just the second player to reach this tally within 10 games at the start of a campaign after Real Madrid icon Cristiano Ronaldo, who did so in 2014-15 (18 goals in 10 matches).
Ahead of Atletico vs Barcelona, here’s everything to know:
How have Atletico played this season?
Atletico are second in the La Liga standings, with 28 points from 11 games. They have won nine matches, lost once and drawn as many.
How have Barcelona played this season?
Barcelona lead the La Liga points table with 30 points from 11 games. They have won 10 games and lost only once, suffering a 2-1 Clasico defeat to bitter rivals Real Madrid last month.
Raphinha thriving where Barca envisaged Atletico’s Alvarez
Raphinha is back to his devastating best as Barcelona’s centre-forward, suggesting the Catalan giants have little reason to regret missing out on Atletico’s Alvarez this summer.
The Argentina international tried to force his way out of Atletico to join Spanish champions Barca, whose attempts to engineer a deal angered the Rojiblancos. Barcelona were fined about 600 euros ($675) for their approach for striker Alvarez by the Spanish football federation in October.
Alvarez stayed and later apologised to Atletico fans to try and rebuild bridges, while Barcelona moved on fast, with winger Raphinha developing into an unstoppable force in a previously unfamiliar number nine role.
Raphinha’s form has made the chances of Barca returning for Alvarez next summer remote, and, after penning a new contract until 2030 on Thursday, he will look to underline that against Atletico.
With the Brazilian firing on all cylinders, Flick’s side won 11 games straight across all competitions at the start of the season.
Currently, he has 19 goals in 13 games across all competitions, including a brace each in the last two games.
After joining Barcelona from Leeds United in 2022, the winger grew frustrated under coach Xavi Hernandez, who did not seem to trust him completely.
However, Flick’s arrival and his high-pressing game suited Raphinha to the ground, and the winger has gone from strength to strength, becoming one of the team’s most influential players and one of the captains.
What happened the last time Atletico played Barcelona?
The last time the teams met was in a 2025-26 Champions League knockout game on April 14.
Although Barcelona defeated Atletico 2-1 in Madrid that day, Atletico edged their Catalan opponents 3-2 on aggregate and reached the semifinals.
Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Predictions
Opta’s supercomputer gives Barcelona a 49.3 percent chance of winning, while Atletico’s probability of a win stands at 27.5 percent. There is a 23.3 percent chance of a draw.
Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Head-to-head
Atletico have won two of their last five games against Barcelona in all competitions (L3), all of which have taken place in 2026.
The teams faced off twice in the Copa del Rey semifinals in March, with Atleti grabbing a solid first-leg 4-0 win at home before holding on for a 4-3 aggregate triumph, while they also won 2-0 at Camp Nou in the Champions League quarterfinals in April, going through 3-2 on aggregate on that occasion.
In La Liga, though, Barcelona have won in each of their last four trips to the Metropolitano. They are bidding to become just the third team in La Liga history to clinch five straight away wins over Atletico, after Athletic Club in 1955 and Real Madrid in 2013 (both runs of six).
Form guide
(Last five games in all competitions; latest match first)
Atletico: L-W-W-D-W
Barcelona: W-W-L-L-W
Team news
Atletico Madrid
Cristian Romero is out with a muscle injury.
Predicted starting XI:
Jan Oblak; Marcos Llorente, Marc Pubill, David Hancko, Alejandro Grimaldo; Giuliano Simeone, Obed Vargas, Morten Hjulmand, Alex Baena; Kang-in Lee, Julian Alvarez
Barcelona
Barcelona midfielder Rodri has been ruled out of Sunday’s clash because of a hamstring injury. He was substituted at half-time of Barcelona’s 3-0 Champions League win over Aston Villa on Tuesday.
Spanish media have reported Rodri could miss up to a month.
Jules Kounde (sprained ankle), Xavi Espart (ankle), Dani Olmo (thigh) and Roony Bardghji (knee) are also sidelined with injuries.
Predicted starting XI:
Joan Garcia; Brian Farinas, Pau Cubarsi, Frenkie de Jong, Joao Cancelo; Gavi, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Fermin Lopez, Karim Adeyemi; Raphinha

https://taz.de/Staats--und-Finanzkrise-i.text:
Staats- und Finanzkrise in Paraguay: Haftbefehl gegen abgesetzten Präsidenten
Paraguays Parlament entmachtet Santiago Peña. Wenig später wird gegen ihn Haftbefehl erlassen. Was ist los in dem lateinamerikanischen Land?
dpa | Die turbulente Finanz- und Staatskrise im südamerikanischen Paraguay hat sich weiter zugespitzt. Das Parlament tauschte am Abend den Staatspräsidenten des Landes aus. Der Senat votierte einstimmig für die Amtsenthebung des bisherigen Staatschefs Santiago Peña, nachdem die Abgeordnetenkammer zuvor dasselbe getan hatte, wie im paraguayischen Fernsehen zu sehen war. Wenig später erließ die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft Haftbefehl gegen Peña. Ihm wird eine Verwicklung in den derzeitigen Bankenskandal vorgeworfen.
Neuer Staatschef ist der bisherige Vizepräsident Pedro Alliana, der kurz nach Peñas Absetzung im Kongress im Amt vereidigt wurde. Er lenkt zunächst bis August 2028 die Geschicke Paraguays, das derzeit durch eine Finanz- und Staatskrise erschüttert wird.
Nahezu gleichzeitig mit der Vereidigung Allianas leitete die Justiz Schritte gegen Peña ein. Gemäß der Anordnung der Staatsanwaltschaft muss dieser unter Hausarrest bleiben, bis er der Fachabteilung für Wirtschaftskriminalität und Korruptionsbekämpfung vorgeführt wird. Das soll laut lokalen Medien am Samstag passieren.
Das Online-Portal „abc“ übertrug Aufnahmen, die Einsatzkräfte der Polizei vor dem Haus Peñas zeigen. Ein Haftbefehl wurde auch gegen Zentralbankchef Carlos Carvallo erlassen.
Amtsenthebung statt Rücktritt
Die Senatoren waren sich während der Sitzung zur Amtsenthebung einig, dass Peña sich der Pflichtverletzung im Amt schuldig gemacht habe. Dieser war selbst nicht zur Anhörung im Senat erschienen und ließ sich durch seine Anwälte vertreten.
Zuvor hatte er vergeblich um einen Aufschub des Termins um 72 Stunden gebeten. Peñas Anwälte argumentierten, das Amtsenthebungsverfahren laufe ins Leere, da Peña zuvor seinen Rücktritt erklärt hatte.
Peña hatte so versucht, dem Amtsenthebungsverfahren zuvorzukommen. Senat und Abgeordnetenkammer nahmen sein Gesuch aber nicht an. Wäre der Kongress Peñas Ansinnen gefolgt, wäre er als ehemaliger Präsident Senator auf Lebenszeit geworden – was parlamentarische Immunität bedeutet hätte.
Bankenkrise stürzt Land in Krise
Paraguay wird in diesen Tagen von einer Finanzkrise mit politischen Folgen erschüttert. Millionen Menschen fürchten um ihre Ersparnisse, seit die im Mittelpunkt eines Skandals stehende Ueno Bank faktisch insolvent ist. Die Zentralbank leitete ein Abwicklungsverfahren gegen das Geldinstitut ein, nachdem dessen Eigenkapitalquote unter die Hälfte des vorgeschriebenen Mindestwertes gefallen war. In der Folge konnten Kunden zeitweise nicht mehr auf ihre Konten zugreifen. Die Digitalbank war in den vergangenen Jahren zu einer der größten Banken Paraguays gewachsen.
Peña unterhielt bis März 2025 Geschäftsbeziehungen zur „Grupo Vázquez“, zu der die Ueno Bank gehörte. Der Politiker hatte Vorwürfe möglicher Interessenkonflikte stets zurückgewiesen. Die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft leitete am Donnerstag nun mehrere Ermittlungen gegen Peña ein. Dabei geht es um die Aufsicht über die Bank, deren Abwicklung und die Bereitstellung öffentlicher Mittel für das Geldinstitut.
Die Staatsanwaltschaft bestätigte Festnahmen von Führungskräften der Bank. Zentralbankchef Carlos Carvallo musste seinen Posten räumen, nachdem ihm wegen seiner früheren Tätigkeit bei der Ueno Bank ebenfalls ein Interessenkonflikt vorgeworfen worden war.
Ihre Rücktritte erklärten auch Innenminister Enrique Riera, Kabinettschef Javier Giménez und Roberto Moreno, der Rechtsberater des Präsidentenamtes.
Der 52-jährige Alliana gilt als wirtschaftsliberal und konservativ. Der Kaufmann gehört wie Peña der traditionellen Colorado-Partei an, die das Land über Jahrzehnte führte.
