https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.title: In defense of feral children
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.author: Mira Ptacin
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.text:
On the Maine island where I live, childhood ends when you’re old enough to catch the 7.15am ferry to school.
We live year-round on Peaks Island, a small island accessible only by boat about 3 miles off the coast of Portland. There is an elementary school here, but no middle or high school. So, once island children reach sixth grade, they begin commuting to the mainland by ferry. In many ways, it is a rite of passage.
When my son Theo started middle school, I was thrilled for him – and a little heartbroken. Suddenly, he was across the bay all day, reachable only by boat or cellphone (which he didn’t have). Theo has always belonged to our island as much as he has belonged to me. After years of rinsing sand from his socks and pulling twigs from his hair, sending him away each morning felt a little like prying him loose from his natural habitat.
Now his school days stretch from the 7.15am ferry until the boat deposits him back on the island at 7.35pm, after sports practice. That means less time roaming the woods and shoreline, and more time indoors being shaped into someone civilized. I have always subscribed to Henry David Thoreau’s idea that “all good things are wild and free”, and lately I find myself wanting my children to stay that way a lot of bit longer.
Fortunately, my son’s daily commute across Casco Bay suggests he has not yet been entirely domesticated.
The ferry is essentially our island’s school bus, except that tourists, commuters, construction workers, dogs, bicycles and people hauling groceries share the ride. Each morning, my son and his gaggle of friends pile into a corner of the cabin with their backpacks and cereal-bar wrappers, trading jokes and half-awake grievances at a volume best described as gull-adjacent. One of the boys is deaf in one ear, so the others naturally speak louder to make sure he doesn’t miss the plot.
It is a bright, goofy and very noisy pocket of preteen life. At least, that is how I see it.
But for a while, another regular passenger saw things differently. The boys didn’t know her name, so inevitably they nicknamed her “Ferry Karen”. My son began coming home with reports of their latest encounters with her. She sat rigidly in her seat, neck craned forward like a heron preparing to strike, and shushed them with clockwork regularity. Too loud! Too boisterous! Too much!
The ferry engine groaned. Gulls shrieked overhead. Waves slapped the hull. And somehow it was the children who were making too much noise.
The boys, good-hearted as they are, tried to lower their voices. Before long, they boarded each morning already bracing themselves, their joy bridled by the expectation that someone would tell them to quiet down before they had even warmed their hands.
When I heard about this, something defiant sparked in me. Maybe it was the mother in me. Or maybe it was the recognition that the world these children are inheriting is already asking an awful lot of them. School shootings, artificial intelligence, political turmoil, economic anxiety, academic pressure … we have handed children a frightening world, and then somehow still have the nerve to ask them to be quieter in it.
These kids already spend most of their weekdays indoors, where bells regulate their movements and adults regulate their voices. The ferry ride is one of the few unsupervised stretches left in their day: 20 minutes on the ocean suspended between island and mainland when they can be loud, loose, ridiculous and wholly themselves. Meanwhile, the adults complaining about kids these days are frequently staring into their phones as though doom-scrolling were a civic duty.
If anyone commuting is modeling questionable behavior, perhaps it isn’t the children being exuberantly alive. Perhaps it’s the grownups hunched over their screens like Dickensian clerks auditing the apocalypse.
To be clear, I am not arguing for children swinging from the ferry rafters or terrorizing commuters before coffee. Kids should learn that public spaces belong to other people, too. But that lesson works both ways. Lately I’ve been wondering whether the problem isn’t simply that parents have forgotten how to let children go. Maybe the rest of us have forgotten how to let children arrive.
Parents worry about their kids’ safety, anxiety, loneliness, resilience, their dependence on phones, their inability to tolerate boredom. We lament that children don’t roam neighborhoods or knock on doors or disappear on bicycles until dinner, the way children supposedly once did. So we tell them: get off your phones! Go outside! Be independent! Figure things out! Take risks!
And then, when they actually appear in the world without us, the rest of the world tells them to quiet down.
Children used to occupy much more of public life: sidewalks and buses, corner stores and vacant lots, parks and stoops and malls. Increasingly, childhood happens in places specifically designated for children – schools, camps, organized sports, scheduled playdates, bedrooms – or on screens. Their lives are supervised, programmed and transported from one adult-approved location to another.
That isn’t entirely the fault of anxious parents. Parents are responding to the world around them. Giving a child independence requires a surrounding culture willing to receive that child. But we seem to want independent children who somehow don’t inconvenience anybody with their independence. We want children in the world, provided they don’t take up too much of it. That may be the contradiction we need to examine.
Years ago, my neighbor May told me something I have carried with me ever since. “When a child is born on Peaks Island,” she said, “it is all our child.” (She was only about 15 herself at the time when she said this.) What she meant was that children here are raised not only by their parents but, in small ways, by everybody. Like the neighbors who let them cut through their yards. The deckhands who hold the ferry as they kids are racing to catch the morning boat. The checkout clerk at our little grocery store who know which candy they’ll choose before they even reach the counter (and remind them to brush their teeth). There is very little anonymity on an island of 1 sq mile.
Paradoxically, this watchful web of familiarity gives children tremendous freedom. Because everyone knows them, everyone is quietly looking out for them. Kids can roam freely, and roam freely they do. Island kids climb rocks and trees, they jump from docks and poke around tide pools without helicopter supervision. “Good thing we live on an island,” we parents say to one another when they wander home with wet sneakers and pockets full of mussel shells, they tear around on bicycles and disappear into the woods only to return when they’re hungry or when the sun has set.
They are gloriously feral. But they are also startlingly capable. By middle school, many of them know how to talk to adults without shrinking, how to read a ferry schedule, how to navigate a city bus, how to get themselves from point A to point B without an adult narrating every step like a GPS with anxiety.
When May told me that every island child was “all our child”, she was giving the adults around her a job, even if these kids weren’t biologically or legally “theirs”. Perhaps that job isn’t always to correct them; sometimes the job is simply to make enough room and to protect the spark that makes children tear down the road on bicycles at speeds that terrify their neighbors. To let them get muddy. To let them argue and reconcile without immediately refereeing. To allow them to grow in every direction, not just the polite ones.
And maybe this isn’t only an island proposition. Maybe wherever children live – in apartment buildings or suburbs, on city blocks or dirt roads – the adults around them can choose to create a little more territory in which childhood is allowed to remain untamed.
So the next time you encounter a cluster of children laughing too loudly on a bus, a sidewalk or a subway platform, consider it less a nuisance than a small daily miracle, the sound of children alive and unedited, the future refusing to sit still, lips sealed.
Look up from our phones, look out the window, and remember what it felt like to be on the verge of everything.

Why are oil traders refusing to buy Russian diesel after Trump-Putin deal?
Zero Russian diesel has reached the US under the deal as buyers fear legal action, with Congress’s ban on Russian energy imports still in place.
At least three tankers carrying Russian diesel to the United States have changed course, casting doubt over US President Donald Trump’s October deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.
Nearly a month after Trump agreed to let Russia release diesel stocks to the US and global markets, despite existing sanctions, zero diesel has reached the US, where prices have nearly doubled since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Russia has sent out a total of four tankers loaded with diesel since the deal was agreed.
Here’s what we know.
What’s happened to tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US?
The Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone-flagged Leruo left the Baltic port of Primorsk last month, with the US East Coast as their declared destination.
As of Thursday, however, one was heading towards Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to marine analytics firm Kpler and the vessel-tracking site MarineTraffic.
A third tanker, still in the North Atlantic, has changed its destination from New York to “for orders”, leaving its unloading point open.
The Financial Times also reported that Beast, a sanctioned Seychelles-owned tanker that was loaded at the Russian port of Primorsk in late October, has set sail towards the US and is currently signalling “Atlantic”.
What did Trump and Putin agree?
A deal big on numbers, but scant on details.
Trump first announced the agreement following a call with Putin on October 9. He said Russia would make more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel available immediately to US and global markets.
Long-range product tankers, which carry diesel supplies, can carry up to about 100,000 tonnes of diesel at a time.
Another 500,000 tonnes would follow in November, then 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The agreement Trump brokered with Putin allows Russian diesel to be sold, delivered, unloaded and imported until April 7. It came after Trump blamed Ukraine for causing diesel shortages by targeting Russian energy facilities amid the Russia-Ukraine war.
It also reversed years of US policy after Washington banned imports of Russian energy following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the US Department of the Treasury has since issued a temporary sanctions exemption, much to the ire of a cross-party group of lawmakers in the US Congress who passed a new sanctions package in the name of the late, pro-Ukraine Senator Lindsey Graham in September.
In a statement to the AP news agency, the Treasury said the exemption was “in compliance with all applicable laws”.
Russia announced its first shipment of diesel during a visit to St Petersburg in October by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.
Yet much about the deal remains unclear.
Neither the White House nor the Kremlin has said whether the agreement was put in writing, and neither has revealed the price to be paid for the diesel, the payment terms or which companies are involved.
How much Russian diesel is now waiting to be sold?
It’s not clear exactly, but it’s less than was promised.
The volumes involved have not been made public, but analysts say the first shipment is unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to US consumers.
US retail diesel prices topped $6 a gallon ($1.59 per litre) in September – nearly twice their pre-war levels – and have remained elevated.
“The reported shipment is equivalent to roughly two hours of US distillate consumption,” Aarathi Krishnan, CEO of Raksha Intelligence, told Al Jazeera, referring to the first tanker to be dispatched by Russia.
“Even if it arrives as planned, it will make very little difference to national supply,” he said.
Why don’t traders want to buy Russian diesel?
Because of the legal risk.
Despite the US Treasury temporarily authorising Russian diesel sales that would normally fall under sanctions, Congress’s ban on Russian energy imports remains in place, leaving a high level of uncertainty for traders.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill wrote to port and terminal operators in her state on Monday, telling them to turn away ships carrying the fuel.
She warned that “any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”
Sherrill argued the Trump administration had no authority to override the ban.
Lawmakers have also warned banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that handling the imports could expose them to civil or criminal liability, as well as future congressional investigations.
The Trump administration claims the exemption is lawful, and no court has ruled on the dispute.
“It’s clear there’s hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so,” Matt Smith, an analyst at Kpler, told AP.
Where will the diesel go now?
Probably not to the US, experts say.
The first two diverted tankers are heading towards Brazil and the Mediterranean, according to Kpler data, and the third tanker could follow.
“Because of regulatory [and] sanctions concerns, we may not see this cargo discharge on the US Atlantic coast,” Smith told AP.
Moscow, however, insists the deal is on track.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said “all the diesel will find its buyers.”
Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, went further, writing on X that the reports were “fake” and “tankers destined for the US continue on course.”

Neuseeland hat gewählt: Knappes Rennen zwischen Konservativen und Sozialdemokraten
Regierungschef Luxon oder sein Herausforderer Ex-Premier Hipkins? Ersten Ergebnissen zufolge wird für beide die Regierungsbildung schwierig.
dpa | Nach der Parlamentswahl in Neuseeland zeichnet sich erwartungsgemäß ein äußerst knappes Rennen zwischen der konservativen Regierungspartei National Party und der sozialdemokratischen Labour-Partei ab. Ersten Ergebnissen zufolge könnte sowohl für Regierungschef Christopher Luxon (56) als auch für seinen Herausforderer und Vorgänger Chris Hipkins (48) eine Regierungsbildung schwierig werden.
Rund 3,8 Millionen Menschen waren zu den Urnen gerufen, die Wahllokale schlossen um 19.00 Uhr Ortszeit (07.00 Uhr MEZ). Umgehend danach begann die Auszählung. Für eine Regierungsmehrheit sind im Parlament mit 120 Sitzen mindestens 61 Mandate erforderlich. Überschattet wurde die Abstimmung von teilweise heftigen Unwettern. Betroffen war vor allem die Metropole Auckland auf der Nordinsel.
Die Bevölkerung des Pazifikstaates leidet derzeit vor allem unter hohen Lebenshaltungskosten, Inflation und steigenden Benzinpreisen infolge des Konflikts im Nahen Osten. Luxons Regierung ist unter Druck. Mögliche Entlastungen für die Haushalte dominierten dementsprechend den Wahlkampf.
Kleinere Parteien als Zünglein an der Waage?
Bereits im Vorfeld hatten Umfragen ergeben, dass beide großen Parteien unter die 30-Prozent-Marke stürzen könnten. Eine Schlüsselrolle dürfte damit kleineren politischen Kräften zukommen. Wochenlange Koalitionsverhandlungen könnten bevorstehen.
Zudem werden in den kommenden Wochen noch Hunderttausende sogenannte Sonderstimmen ausgezählt. Dazu gehören unter anderem Stimmen von Neuseeländern im Ausland und von Wählern, die außerhalb ihres eigentlichen Wahlkreises abgestimmt haben. Das endgültige Ergebnis wird für den 27. November erwartet.
Luxons Nationalpartei führt seit 2023 eine Koalition mit der rechtsliberalen ACT-Partei und der populistischen New Zealand First und hofft auf eine zweite Amtszeit. Auch bei der letzten Wahl war er gegen Labour-Chef Hipkins angetreten. Medien sprechen mit Blick auf den gleichen Vornamen seither vom „Duell der beiden Chrises“.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New ‘high safety’ chemicals in plastic food packaging linked to lower birth weight, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Exposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, which could cause serious health problems later in life, a new peer-reviewed study found.
As the health risks in exposure to common phthalate plasticizers became clear over the last few decades, industry began switching to a new type of chemical, called Dinch, that it claimed was a “high safety”, nontoxic alternative. It is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, and is found in children’s toys, medical devices, some textiles, flooring and other consumer goods.
But it may not be as safe as industry has claimed, the New York University Langone Health analysis of federal US health data suggests. There is a dearth of research into Dinch health risks, though what exists points toward the chemicals being hormone disruptors that can impact kids’ development.
The new paper is the first to link Dinch to lower birth weights and birth lengths. Fetal growth problems can raise the risk for heart disease, learning difficulties, obesity and other issues that can echo into adolescence and adulthood, the authors wrote.
“Chemicals should be properly tested for their safety before they become a widespread exposure for unwitting people in the general public,” said Leonardo Trasande, a lead author on the NYU paper.
The chemical is formally named 1,2-cyclohexane dicarboxylic acid diisononyl ester. It is used to make plastic more flexible and durable, and is found in common kitchen products such as cling film and plastic wine corks.
Researchers looked at data for over 6,600 pregnancies collected as part of the National Institutes of Health Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (Echo) Program. Up to 70% of women showed Dinch in their urine, and higher levels increased the risk of the child being classified as “small for gestational age”, or below the 10th percentile for babies born at the same stage of pregnancy.
Each tenfold increase in Dinch exposure resulted in a 27-gram reduction in newborn birth weight. An average newborn weighs about 3,400 grams (about 7.5lbs). Hispanic mothers or those with lower education levels were more likely to have children affected by Dinch, the study found.
Previous research on animals and human cells has found that Dinch by-products can interfere with the hormones in a pregnant woman that guide fetal development, and may trigger inflammation that affects how nutrients and oxygen reach the baby, NYU’s authors wrote.
The paper appears to expose yet another classic example of industry replacing one dangerous chemical with a compound that has similar health effects. This resets the regulatory and research process, even though the new chemical is very similar in structure or has the same health risks.
After the US and EU regulators began taking action in the aughts over toxic phthalates such as DEHP, industry began increasing the use of Dinch. German chemical giant BASF is among Dinch’s major producers and overall global production volume jumped from 25,000 tons in 2002 to 400,000 tons in 2024.
This process is called “regrettable substitution”, and is common. For example, many chemical companies and goods producers replaced the most dangerous Pfas “forever chemicals”, such as Pfoa, with GenX compounds. But after years of research, the latter have been found to be more toxic.
Researchers with the Switzerland-based Food Packaging Forum said they are concerned about Dinch and the lack of health information around it. But there is evidence that it migrates from food packaging into food, and levels in the EU population have been increasing across recent decades. The Food Packaging Forum is currently conducting health research on DINCH.
The NYU findings “raise pretty serious concerns about regrettable substitution”, Trasande said.
“These results underscore the need for stronger oversight of chemicals used in food packaging and other household products by requiring they be tested before they are introduced to the market, instead of after they are connected to health concerns,” Trasande said, noting that the plastics treaty under negotiation at the United Nations is an opportunity to establish better policies.
Women can protect themselves and their children by buying plastic-free products as much as possible, including clothing and toys. Look for food at the grocery store that comes in glass packaging, and use glass or wood storage and utensils in the kitchen.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Qeshm island and Hormuz hit, as mediators try to prevent US-Iran escalation
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Qeshm island and Hormuz hit, as mediators try to prevent US-Iran escalation
US strikes have continued on Iran after more ships in the Strait of Hormuz were attacked.
Tehran, Iran – The United States has bombed Iran after vessels were targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, as mediators continue to try to prevent large-scale fighting between the two countries.
Two projectiles hit Iran’s Qeshm on Friday night, the latest in a series of air strikes on the southern island over recent weeks targeting Iranian air defences and launchers. President Donald Trump called them “minor strikes”, amid increasing concerns of a potential escalation in the war between the countries.
Iran’s army said in the early hours of Saturday that it destroyed a US-made MQ-9 drone using an unnamed new system. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) separately claimed on Friday that its air defences intercepted an MQ-1, reportedly the 16th aircraft of this model to be destroyed since the start of the war.
At least 11 ships were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the week ending on November 6, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which said three of them sank. The Western military intelligence agency has recorded 88 projectile strikes since hostilities resumed in early July, although it has cautioned that most attacks are going unreported.
UKMTO’s weekly report also identified 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits in the Strait of Hormuz, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. Most of the vessels that travel with their transponders switched on are using the Iranian route to the north. But many ships are still attempting the southern route near Oman with their tracking systems offline to shuttle oil out of the waterway.
Iranian armed forces also claim that, in addition to being hit with missiles and drones, tankers and commercial vessels using “unauthorised” routes also run the risk of being hit by naval mines.
The Iranian military’s naval force said on Saturday that a tanker with its transponder turned off caught fire in the eastern area of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine. Washington says the mines have been cleared.
No range limit on missiles
For years, the IRGC maintained that it was limiting the range of its ballistic missiles to about 2,000 kilometres (1,240 miles) to reassure European countries that they would not be targeted.
But with Trump threatening to resume extensive air strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure, commanders say nothing is off limits now.
“This limitation has been lifted for us,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told reporters during an event on Saturday, in reference to missile range constraints.
His comments came after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered an unrestrained military response to any future threats from Israel and the US. Iran’s aerospace division of the IRGC has prepared “surprising defence achievements” that will be deployed in action if another wave of major attacks starts, he added.
“The operational unveiling of these [advanced] achievements in case of new conflict will not only frustrate and fascinate enemies, but will further solidify Iran’s military authority on the global stage, make the resistance front happy, and fully neutralise aggressors’ calculations,” Mohebbi said.
The spokesman said the IRGC plans to unveil another underground “missile city” soon, and will deploy some combat systems to public spaces so the people can personally inspect them.
Mohebbi added that if the Islamic republic decides to alter its nuclear doctrine and build a bomb, the necessary preparations will be made.
On state television’s war-focused Be Vaght-e Iran (At Iran’s Time) programme over the weekend, presenters and analysts said Iranian armed forces had their fingers on the trigger and were especially eyeing any movement from Israel.
“Our military information about the strategic chokepoints of Israel is complete. If our water, electricity and natural gas is cut off, they will also be plunged into darkness and lack of water,” one analyst said. “This is not a bluff, but a serious warning.”
‘Pendulum swing between war and talks’
Over recent weeks, diplomatic efforts by mediators to avoid attacks that could damage the entire region have picked up, although with limited gains.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that he held talks with 12 foreign ministers over the past 48 hours, including top diplomats from Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
He said he explained the “fundamental positions” of Tehran, including the seven demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and stressed the need to form “regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers”.
Security chief Mohsen Rezaei reportedly emphasised the same conditions to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a visit to Moscow on Thursday, which was also aimed at delivering a message from Khamenei.
Developments between Iran and the US resemble a “constant pendulum swing between war and negotiations” that is increasingly leaning towards conflict, according to political analyst Mostafa Najafi, who is said to be close to Iran’s security chief.
“What is clear for now is that the movement of this pendulum will continue; a conflict whose ending is much more complicated and time-consuming than imagined,” he wrote on X. The historic defeat for Trump and the Republicans in US midterm elections this week may further complicate the picture, he added.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said three factors increase the risk of war in the short term after the elections, unless negotiations lead to a breakthrough.
The political cost of high fuel prices, brought about largely due to the war on Iran, has already been paid, he said, and there won’t be another point on the political calendar soon for Trump to worry about this issue.
“On the one hand, the pressure to get a deal will dissipate,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pressure from pro-war hawks will also escalate significantly because they will be constrained in their efforts to step up the conflict after the Democrats take control of Congress in early January. The appointment of far-right, pro-Israel hawk Stephen Miller as chief of staff also hints that Trump might not be ready to wind down the war.
“Finally, there is a new psychological element to Trump’s mindset following this humiliation: Trump’s desire for vengeance. There has been a vindictive element to his calculations in the past weeks because of his anger over how Iran – in Trump’s mind – has ruined his presidency,” Parsi said.

https://taz.de/Neuer-Stabschef-im-Weisse.author: Hansjürgen Mai
https://taz.de/Neuer-Stabschef-im-Weisse.text:
Neuer Stabschef im Weißen Haus: Extremist Stephen Miller rückt auf
Nach dem Midterms-Debakel muss Trumps Stabschefin Susie Wiles gehen, Miller wird sie ersetzen. Das zeigt: Trump wird von seiner Politik nicht abrücken.
Nach der katastrophalen Wahlniederlage der Republikaner bei den diesjährigen Zwischenwahlen ist im Weißen Haus der erste Kopf gerollt. US-Präsident Donald Trump gab am Freitag bekannt, dass seine bisherige Stabschefin Susie Wiles ihren Posten verlassen wird. Ihr Nachfolger wird Stephen Miller. Trump bezeichnete ihn in einem Post auf Truth Social als „einen meiner zuverlässigsten Berater“.
Die Neubesetzung der Stabschef-Position ist die erste größere personelle Umstrukturierung innerhalb seiner Regierung infolge des Wahlfiaskos bei den Midterms. Mit der Entscheidung für Miller zeigt der Präsident, dass er trotz der deutlichen Wahlklatsche keinen Anlass sieht, seine Politik groß zu verändern.
Miller ist ein langjähriger Mitarbeiter des Präsidenten und Mitgestalter des „Project 2025“, das eine Blaupause zur Umgestaltung der exekutiven Gewalt darstellt. Erklärtes Ziel dieses Werks ist die Zerstörung von demokratischen Institutionen und die Machtkonzentration in der Person des Präsidenten.
Er gehört außerdem zu den Architekten einiger umstrittenen Maßnahmen: darunter die aggressive Einwanderungspolitik sowie das militärische Vorgehen gegen mutmaßliche Drogenboote in der Karibik und im östlichen Pazifik.
„Ewige Flamme der MAGA-Bewegung“
Miller selbst würdigte Trump in einem Post als „die prägendste politische Führungspersönlichkeit“ in der Geschichte der USA. Er erklärte, dass dieser habe „im Alleingang Amerika vor denjenigen gerettet, die es zerstören wollten“. „Die Mission ist jetzt klarer denn je: Wir müssen mit unserer ganzen Seele dafür kämpfen, unseren Präsidenten zu unterstützen und diese großartige Republik zu verteidigen“, fügte er hinzu.
Kurz nach der Wahlniederlage erklärte Trump, dass er womöglich mit Demokraten zusammenarbeiten wolle. Die Ernennung von Miller als Stabschef und seine Selbstinszenierung als „Mister Veto“ in den sozialen Netzwerken lassen jedoch anderes vermuten.
Laut US-Medien gehe es Miller nicht um Kompromisse, sondern darum, die infolge des Wahlausgangs geschwächte MAGA-Koalitaion wieder zu stärkten. „Stephen ist und war schon immer die ewige Flamme der MAGA-Bewegung – er setzt die Worte und die Politik des Präsidenten in die Tat um“, erklärte Millers ehemaliger Mitarbeiter Hunter Morgen gegenüber der New York Times.
„Ich wollte eine Veränderung“, sagte Trump gegenüber Journalisten. Wiles habe „großartige Arbeit“ geleistet, so Trump, doch „manchmal im Leben muss man eben Veränderungen vornehmen“.
Beziehung mit Wiles begann zu bröckeln
Obwohl Trump in seinen öffentlichen Aussagen Wiles' Arbeit verteidigt, soll es hinter den Kulissen Risse zwischen den beiden gegeben haben. Die 69-jährige Wiles, die am Montag offiziell ihren Hut nehmen wird, war mit einer Amtszeit von 21 Monaten die am längsten amtierende Stabschefin unter Trump.
Sie hatte maßgeblichen Anteil an Trumps erfolgreichen Wahlkampf im Jahr 2024 und seiner Rückkehr ins Weiße Haus. Ihr wird außerdem nachgesagt, dass sie für Stabilität und Zusammenhalt innerhalb der Regierung gesorgt hatte.
Zwar ist die Entscheidung, sich von seiner Stabschefin zu trennen, auf die Wahlschlappe zurückzuführen, doch auch jüngste Personalentscheidungen des Präsidenten, wie die fehlgeschlagene Ernennung von Katie Zacharia als Pressesprecherin gegen den Willen von Wiles, soll dem Verhältnis zwischen den beiden geschadet haben.
Wie US-Medien berichten, soll Trump unter anderem Wiles für die Niederlage der Republikaner verantwortlich gemacht haben, die er auf eine falsche Strategie zurückführt. Wiles, bei der während ihrer Amtszeit Brustkrebs diagnostiziert wurde, wird eine neue Position außerhalb der Regierung antreten, aber weiterhin zu Trumps politischem Umfeld gehören.
Weitere Änderungen im engsten Mitarbeiterstab möglich
Der Präsident ließ am Freitag zudem durchblicken, dass dies nicht die letzte Änderung sein werde. Auf die Frage, ob er beabsichtige, Mitarbeiter zu entlassen, antwortete er mit einem knappen „Ja“. „Ich liebe mein Kabinett. Ich halte es für gut. Aber ich werde vielleicht ein paar Änderungen vornehmen. Wer genau, möchte ich noch nicht sagen“, so Trump.
Zu den weiteren Personen, die nach der Niederlage bei den Zwischenwahlen ihre Posten verlieren könnten, zählen Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth sowie Admiral Brad Cooper, der Befehlshaber des US-Militärkommandos CENTCOM. Beide sollen Treiber des Irankrieges gewesen sein, der in der US-Bevölkerung äußerst unbeliebt ist und dadurch zum Wahlsieg der Demokraten beigetragen hat.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: A ‘customer success story’: leaked documents show Cisco doubled down on Israeli military deals during Gaza war
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Alice Speri
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
A year into the war in Gaza, the networks of Israel’s military intelligence community were plagued with technical problems. There were major, multi-hour outages to their systems, and repeated crashes. Built-in debugging mechanisms failed.
The problems, which started as intelligence operations were undergoing updates to digital infrastructure, became so persistent as to undermine the “confidence” of Israeli intelligence agencies in one of their top network providers: the multinational tech conglomerate Cisco.
“This series of events happened during the period of war, deeply impacting customer sentiment,” warned a confidential memo drafted by Cisco and obtained by the Guardian. “During a period of national conflict, these repeated outages severely impacted critical operations.”
The September 2025 draft memo was part of a trove of internal documents leaked by Cisco workers furious with the company’s ties to Israel’s military three years into the war, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians.
Cisco, one of the largest tech companies in the world and at one point the single most valuable, is often described as selling the “plumbing” of the internet. It provides the routers, servers and communications systems that move data for companies, governments and militaries around the globe. While its business ties to the Israeli military have received less scrutiny than those of other tech giants, the company has worked with the Israeli security state for years. Israel’s military intelligence contracts alone generated about $67m in business in three years, according to a 2025 document reviewed by the Guardian.
While Cisco’s involvement with Israel’s military before and since 2023 has been documented before, the leaked documents obtained by the Guardian reveal the lengths the company went to in order to preserve and expand the relationship as the war in Gaza dragged on. They also show that earlier this year, Splunk – a Cisco subsidiary platform that can process and analyze massive volumes of machine-generated data – made a pitch to join the controversial cloud computing contract between the Israeli government, Google and Amazon known as Project Nimbus.
Cisco pursued these opportunities as the mass killing of civilians in Gaza was amply documented, international organizations and governments began to refer to Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide, and the company itself was roiled by internal turmoil over its own role in the war.
Cisco did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Israeli military wrote in a statement to the Guardian: “The [Israel Defense Forces] is assisted by services provided by a range of companies to meet its ongoing needs and objectives. The IDF does not intend to comment on matters relating to contracts or services provided by other entities.”
Members of Bridge to Humanity, a group of current and former Cisco workers who have objected to the company’s role in the Gaza war, called the company’s work with Israeli intelligence a “shocking and complete contradiction of values Cisco sells to us employees and externally to its customers, investors, and the public”. They said the company, which pitches itself internally and to the public as an ethics-driven company, had become “an instrument of genocide”.
“Cisco has been able to skate under the radar because they sell hardware and software,” the group wrote in a statement to the Guardian, adding that its business with Israeli intelligence made it “no different to an arms company that is supplying the bombs and fighter jets”.
Earlier this year, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) found reasonable cause to believe that, following the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on southern Israel, and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, Cisco oversaw a hostile work environment rife with racist rhetoric that violated the rights of Palestinian, Arab and Muslim employees. Cisco previously told the Guardian that it disagreed with the EEOC’s findings and that it is committed to being an equal opportunity employer.
The Bridge to Humanity members alleged that the treatment they endured was linked directly to Cisco’s business interests.
“While Cisco leadership was constantly dismissing our concerns about how it was enabling the horrors we were witnessing,” they wrote, “they were behind the scenes going above and beyond to actively continue to expand their business relationship with the Israeli military and ensure they did not lose a cent of business.”
‘Never let a good crisis go to waste’
When repeated technical failures presented a “risk to operations” during the war, Israeli intelligence leaders threatened to cancel their business.
Cisco went into crisis mode.
In the documents obtained by the Guardian, Cisco referred to its client as the Israel Intelligence Force, or IIF, a body it described as responsible for “delivering critical network infrastructure for various intelligence departments within the Israeli Ministry of Defense”. Several branches of Israel’s government and military are dedicated to intelligence operations, but the IIF appears to be a reference to the IDF’s military intelligence directorate, known as Aman in Israel.
According to Cisco workers familiar with the technical issues, the outages and blackouts endangered intelligence forces’ access to military data.
The leaked documents also reveal that the company activated senior staff in an effort to salvage what it described as a “critical” account, and that it mobilized multiple internal teams over several months to fix the bugs. Cisco also sent staff to meet on site with a secretive Israeli military unit, known as Sapir, which since the 7 October attacks has reportedly been responsible for moving Israel’s intelligence apparatus underground. According to the Cisco documents, fixing the technical issues and training the customer “required site visits by Cisco under extreme security due to ongoing war”.
Cisco’s goal, according to the documents, was to restore “customer confidence” and reverse “negative sentiment”. After fixing the technical issues and helping Sapir return to “business as usual”, between 2024 and the summer of 2025, Cisco noted the client was satisfied and billed the damage control effort as a “customer success story” in an internal presentation.
The leaked documents detail dozens of deals Cisco worked on in 2026 with different Israeli government clients, including the intelligence community, air force and navy, many of which were tagged as “AI” deals. They include evidence that executives for the Cisco-owned Splunk platform sought to join Project Nimbus, though it is not clear whether the deal went through.
Watchdogs that document the private sector’s involvement in Israel’s occupation have found that Cisco has long provided Israel with technological support for its surveillance of Palestinians. Earlier this year, Drop Site News cited Cisco documents which noted that investment in technology had become as important to the military “as the focus on aircrafts, tanks, and any other essential military tools”. It also reported on a company presentation featuring the quote: “Never let a good crisis go to waste.”
Cisco is only the latest tech giant to face the anger of its employees over work with Israel’s military. Since October 2023, tech workers across the sector have denounced what they view as their employers’ complicity in Israeli crimes enabled by the tech products they develop and sell.
“At the same time, we’ve seen more and more reporting coming out showing that a lot of these companies have increased their revenue streams through larger military contracts with the Israeli military,” said Eric Sype, a US-based organizer with the Palestinian digital rights non-profit 7amleh, which has documented several companies’ repressive response to workers’ activism. “The tech sector is moving more and more aggressively into military contracting, and these companies are becoming weapons manufacturing companies.”
Cisco in particular has come under increasing public pressure over its role in the war. A group of investors has called on the company to commission an independent human rights assessment of its business with the Israeli military, and shareholders are expected to vote on a proposal requiring the company to do so at its upcoming general meeting this month.
While Microsoft, Google and Amazon have faced far more scrutiny and backlash over their business with Israel’s military, those companies’ contracts “would mean nothing without the physical hardware and infrastructure that Cisco provides”, Sype said.
“Cisco is at the foundational level facilitating all of these atrocity crimes that are happening and should be talked about and referenced in the same way.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Dozens killed as humanitarian crisis mounts in Yemen: What next for war?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Dozens killed as humanitarian crisis mounts in Yemen: What next for war?
Government forces reclaim key territories in Taiz and Lahij but face setbacks under Houthi resistance in certain areas.
Dozens were killed in Yemen on Friday when a missile struck a market in Taiz governorate, with each side of Yemen’s brutal war blaming the other for the attack.
It has been a month since Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched its “Dawn of Yemen” offensive on the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group after it took swaths of territory along the country’s Red Sea coast.
As the fighting continues, the humanitarian crisis is only intensifying, with hundreds of thousands displaced so far.
Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council has said the government will continue with its “irreversible” drive to dismantle Houthi military capacity and restore sovereignty, meaning the war may get worse before there is any resolution, observers say.
Here’s what we know.
What is Operation Dawn of Yemen?
The operation was launched by the head of the Presidential Leadership Council of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Rashad al-Alimi, on October 5.
Its aim is to recapture areas under Houthi control and liberate the capital city of Sanaa, which has been under the rebels’ control since September 2014.
The operation has relied on air support from the Saudi-led coalition, as well as ground operations carried out by government military coalitions and units to weaken the Houthis’ military capabilities.
In the Red Sea corridor, breaking the Houthis’ maritime chokehold and securing the Bab al-Mandeb strait has been an essential goal after the group captured the strategic port city of Mocha (Mokha) in September.
How much territory have the government forces taken back?
After launching the operation, the government said its forces recaptured positions around Dhubab and Bab al-Mandeb the same day, though the extent of their gains could not be confirmed.
It also said they captured mountain positions in Haifan, western Taiz and around al-Waziiya.
By October 13, fighting spread to Marib, where the government forces claimed gains around the Maas camp and north of Harib.
It did, however, lose territory in Taiz governorate, which led to a Houthi siege that continues to suffocate the city as it reaches its first month.
On Friday, the government forces said they had recaptured many areas in the governorate, including al-Nidani village, Shaab al-Sarari, large parts of the Sanamat area and the Ribat al-Qarn area in Dhi al-Barh in Taiz governorate.
Government troops and coalition fighters also secured the Tavat Wathib and Habil al-Saram hills along the Al-Aqroud front.
They announced the execution of 1,211 operations against Houthi positions on the different battlefronts, as they confirmed control over new positions on the Tur al-Bahah front in the Lahij governorate.
However, government forces are far from being able to take back Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, Thomas Bonnie James, an assistant professor in politics and international relations at Aberdeen University in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.
“[Defeat] won’t happen if it means taking back Sanaa and ending Houthi rule. Not any time soon,” he said. “The government’s forces look big on paper, but they are spread across too many fronts and use old equipment.
“Sanaa is surrounded by mountains, which makes it easy to defend. A much stronger Saudi-Emirati coalition tried from 2015 and never came close,” he explained.
What else has the government achieved since the operation began?
James told Al Jazeera that Dawn of Yemen’s aim is to apply pressure to, rather than achieve the total defeat of, the Houthis.
“Dawn of Yemen is better understood as a way to apply pressure than as a bid for total victory,” he said. “The aim is to make the war more costly for the Houthis and to give Saudi Arabia a stronger position before any peace deal.
“What happens in the next three months matters more than the slogans.”
The Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council announced on Thursday that the armed forces have carried out 40,761 military operations since the beginning of Dawn of Yemen.
The council also said the attacks resulted in the “neutralisation” of about 20,000 Houthi leaders and elements, and more than 5,000 vehicles.
Previous announcements from the military command said they conducted 17,000 targeting operations during their first weeks and daily figures ranging between 951 and 1,272 operations throughout the month.
Last month, the Yemeni government also said its forces were able to kill or wound 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours.
Last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.
The Houthis did say that the total number of attacks the group has been subjected to since the beginning of the escalation reached 3,930 raids and missiles up until early November.
Al Jazeera has not been able to verify these figures.
How are the Houthis striking back?
The Houthis, who are also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have caused hundreds of casualties since the beginning of the escalation.
Yemen’s government forces have blamed the Houthis for an attack on the al-Hadara market on Friday in the Taiz governorate that killed and injured dozens, mostly civilians.
Government military spokesperson, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the “terrorist” Houthis hit the market with ballistic missiles, calling it a war crime.
The Iran-backed Houthis rejected the accusation and said Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemeni government, was responsible for the attack.
After taking the capital and state institutions in 2014, the Houthis have had access to a large number of weapons that once belonged to the Yemeni military.
Analysts say with the external support from Iran and their reliance on international black markets, the Houthis’ military capabilities continued to advance.
Their increasingly long-range missile strikes have allowed them to reach many areas across Saudi Arabia and even Israel in June.
One of the Houthis’ latest deadly attacks killed at least 70 government security recruits in Shabwah.
How is this affecting people in Yemen?
As the government and the Houthis continue fighting, the humanitarian situation in Yemen is heading towards catastrophe.
More than 323,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the escalation began in August, with Taiz governorate taking in most of them, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported on Friday.
More than two in five of the internally displaced in Yemen are in Taiz, where the Houthi blockade continues to encircle the city, cutting off supplies to about 800,000 people.
The UN Human Rights Office has reported 281 civilian casualties since August, with 69 people killed and 212 injured. Children make up more than one-third of casualties.
In Taiz, Salah Ahmed Ghaleb al-Majidi, acting director of the governorate’s Siege Affairs Department, described the situation to Al Jazeera as “catastrophic”.
Essentials, including medical supplies, food, fuel and water, are unable to reach the governorate due to the Houthi blockade.
An Al Jazeera report found that the remaining diesel stocks in the city have dwindled and have less than 48 hours left to run.
Hospitals are warning that once they run out of fuel, departments and medical centres will have to shut down, including emergency services.
Taiz’s deputy governor for health affairs, Ilan Abdul Haw, told Al Jazeera that about 40 percent of hospitals have closed, while those still open are operating at 50 percent capacity due to the lack of fuel.
What next for this war?
James told Al Jazeera that as the winter approaches in Yemen, and the siege on Taiz tightens, conditions will only worsen for Yemenis caught in the conflict.
“The biggest worry is the people of Taiz. More than 800,000 of them have been cut off from aid since the Houthis surrounded the city in early October,” he said. “Winter is coming, aid money is short, and the city is under siege. That is what more fighting will mean for ordinary Yemenis.”
The war has also spread beyond Yemen, as the Houthis continue strikes on Saudi airports and oil sites.
“The Houthis are firing at Saudi almost every day. Saudi Arabia is now openly bombing inside Yemen again for the first time since 2022,” James said. “Both sides are hitting where it hurts most, and that is how wars get bigger”.
Other fighting in the region could also pull Yemen into a wider war, and vice versa, as the US-Israel war on Iran remains in a deadlock, James told Al Jazeera.
“Yemen is now tied to the wider conflict with Iran. If the US strikes Iran again, Iran will want to use the Houthis to put more pressure on Saudi Arabia,” he said.

https://taz.de/Tod-von-Hubert-Aiwanger/!.title: Tod von Hubert Aiwanger: Warum er fehlen wird
https://taz.de/Tod-von-Hubert-Aiwanger/!.author: Dominik Baur
https://taz.de/Tod-von-Hubert-Aiwanger/!.text:
Tod von Hubert Aiwanger: Warum er fehlen wird
An Hubert Aiwanger konnte man viel kritisieren – und das haben wir getan. Doch eines muss man ihm lassen: Ein Hund war er schon, manchmal sogar ein cooler.
Natürlich gibt es da die lustigen Begebenheiten, die einem einfallen, wenn man an die Auftritte von Hubert Aiwanger denkt. Als er beispielsweise versuchte, die Corona-Regeln im Biergarten zu erklären: „Wenn sechs bis acht Leute, jeder mit seinem Kumpel kommt …“ Die Handreichung ging viral.
Oder 2019, als er auf der angesagten Gründermesse „Bits & Pretzels“ auftrat. Die Halle war voll, wenig später würde Barack Obama die Bühne betreten. Doch zuvor durfte noch der bayerische Wirtschaftsminister ein Grußwort sprechen. Das tat er – minutenlang und auf Englisch. Ein Englisch, das dem niederbayerischen Idiom Aiwangers recht anverwandt zu sein schien.
Es dauerte nicht lang, da prasselten in den sogenannten Sozialen Medien die hämischen Kommentare gebildeter deutscher Weltbürger darnieder. Über diesen niederbayerischen Bauernbub, der des Englischen so gar nicht mächtig sei. Und der damit, so viel Unterstellung sei erlaubt, seinen Kommentatoren ermöglichte, ihre vermeintliche Überlegenheit auszuspielen.
Ganz anders die Reaktion des überwiegend internationalen Publikums in der Halle: Den Gesichtern der Zuhörer konnte man entnehmen, dass sie diesen Mann da vorne zwar als etwas exotisch empfanden, aber doch auch als ziemlich cool. Einer, der sich, wie man in Bayern sagt, nix scheißt. Aber auch gar nix.
Populismus an der Grenze des Appetitlichen
Auch in der Politik wurde Aiwanger immer wieder belächelt, sogar von den eigenen Leuten. Etwa als er die Freien Wähler in den Landtag führen wollte. Die ausschließlich in der Kommunalpolitik verwurzelten Freien Wähler? In den Landtag? Schon klar!
Jetzt sitzen sie seit 18 Jahren dort, und seit acht Jahren auch in der Staatsregierung. A Hund war a halt schon, der Aiwanger, um eine weitere bayerische Redensart zu bemühen. Ein Hund zu sein, muss man wissen, ist eines der größten Komplimente, die man hierzulande bekommen kann.
Wir wollen hier nicht aus falsch verstandener Pietät der alten Regel gehorchen, wonach man über Tote nichts als Gutes sagen dürfe (für obige Weltbürger: „De mortuis nihil nisi bene“). Deshalb sei noch mal daran erinnert: Hubert Aiwanger hat oft einen rechten Schmarrn dahergeredet – was durchaus auch zweideutig verstanden werden darf. Sein Populismus bewegte sich manchmal sehr dicht an der Grenze des Appetitlichen. Besonders übel wird sein Umgang mit der Flugblattaffäre in Erinnerung bleiben, als er sich nicht zu schade für eine plumpe Täter-Opfer-Umkehr war und Kritikern allen Ernstes vorhielt, sie würden die Shoah instrumentalisieren, um ihn als Person zu vernichten.
Und doch wird der Niederbayer – und das ist nun keine Floskel, wie sie gerade alle von Schwarz bis Grün in die Mikrophone sprechen – fehlen. Denn Aiwanger war: echt. Ungekünstelt. Authentizität, es tut fast weh, diesen abgenutzten Begriff noch einmal zu benutzen, wird allenthalben gefordert. Ist dann aber tatsächlich mal einer er selbst, passt es auch nicht. Es sei denn, es ist zufällig ein Selbst, das genau ins eigene Weltbild passt.
Authentisch zu sein erfordert Mut. Wer er oder sie selbst ist, riskiert etwas. Kein Wunder also, dass viele Politiker dann doch lieber zum PR-Sprech greifen, sich von Journalisten auch ja jedes einzelne Zitat zur Freigabe vorlegen lassen und den Wählerinnen und Wählern lieber eine so weit wie möglich durchchoreographierte Inszenierung ihrer selbst vorsetzen als ein ungeschminktes Bild. Man kann es ihnen nicht verübeln.
Ein Denksprecher
Aiwanger war der Beweis, dass es auch anders ging. Er sprach in seinem besonderen Dialekt, der stets für Spott herhalten musste. Opfelsoft! Es gab Leute, die es zu wissen vorgaben und kenntnisreich erläuterten, warum Aiwangers Sprache noch nicht einmal „normales“ Niederbayerisch war, sondern ein ganz besonderer Aiwanger’scher Inseldialekt, den außer ihm praktisch niemand sprach.
Doch aller Spott über seine Sprache und unfreiwilligen Bonmots konnte nicht darüber hinwegtäuschen, dass Aiwanger rhetorisch vielen seiner Politikerkolleginnen und -kollegen voraus war – ob nun im Bierzelt oder im Landtag.
Manuskripte benutzte Aiwanger fast nie. Eine Stunde lang frei zu reden war kein Problem für ihn. „Ich bin eben ein Denksprecher oder Sprechdenker, wie auch immer man das nennt“, erklärte er der taz einmal. „Ich denke während meiner Rede mit und schaue, wo ist der logische weitere Schritt. Man beginnt mit dem Kern des Themas und baut dann immer mehr Zwiebelschalen drumherum.“
Ob zwischen Zwiebelschalen oder in der Fußgängerzone: Aiwanger sprach die Sprache der Leute, in vielerlei Hinsicht. Inseldialekt hin oder her. Immer wieder fischte er zwar mit populistischen Parolen im rechten Sumpf, wetterte allerdings auch mal gegen das Großkapital und verfolgte selbst in der Migrationspolitik trotz markiger Sprüche einen eher pragmatischen Kurs. In einem unterschied er sich aber völlig von den echten Rechtspopulisten: Aiwanger stand tatsächlich auf der Seite der einfachen Leute.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

Le sénateur PCF des Bouches-du-Rhône Jeremy Bacchi demande l’amnistie pour les « lycéens victimes de sanctions administratives » dans le cadre du mouvement social en cours. Il a écrit au ministre de l’Éducation nationale. « Dans plusieurs établissements, des directions ont prononcé ou s’apprêtent à prononcer des sanctions administratives impliquant l’inscription d’avertissements dans les dossiers scolaires à l’encontre de jeunes ayant participé à des actions de mobilisation ou s’étant trouvés à l’extérieur des grilles de l’établissement malgré des interdictions préfectorales ou de direction », dénonce Jeremy Bacchi dans sa missive à Edouard Geffray.
« Qualifier d’absences injustifiées des actes d’engagements de la jeunesse et les assortir d’un avertissement porté au dossier scolaire constitue une réponse d’une extrême gravité », critique le dirigeant communiste, qui s’inquiète de sanctions « notifiées de manière immédiate » sans « instruction » qui permette « de faire valoir le principe du contradictoire ». Aussi demande-t-il de garantir le respect des procédures.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Flip voters discovered that Trump’s racism and xenophobia are expensive
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Saida Grundy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
For the first time in a decade, election predictions far exceeded public expectations. What pollsters anticipated as a blue wave billowed into a blue tsunami. Wins that held ground for already blue seats eased nerves, and the flips of swing states like Michigan, Georgia, North Carolina and Ohio energized the blue base. But red-belt-busting wins in Republican strongholds like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas alongside pending races in Alaska and Mississippi left mouths agape. The explanation was that Democrats turned out far more supporters than their regulars, and that the “regret voter” (both swing voters and partisan Republicans) expanded the wave across districts Trump previously won. Elation and sighs of relief rolled over consistently Democratic voters who suffered multiple sucker punches from recent years of Republican upsets. Regret voters, who run the gamut from gen Z men to Latinos, farmers and the white working class, hope a different party can deliver on the economy Trump promised them.
Blue voters look at the dismantling of democracy, multiple wars, mass deportations and Trump’s unchecked power in these last two years and see how it all could have been avoided. Regret voters, however, either co-signed or conceded to Trump’s naked racism and brutish bullying of marginalized people, but switched their votes as soon as the consequences hit their pockets. While some of the president’s backers may have been turned away by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) gunning down American citizens, the final straw for most wasn’t ICE’s brutality, but rather the price of eggs. Some may have been upset by the Tomahawk missile assault that killed 120 schoolgirls in Iran, but most fumed at the rocketing costs at the gas pump that followed. Few demanded answers for the nearly 60 deaths of innocent people detained in DHS detention centers since the start of 2024, but many felt scorned by lost immigrant labor that cut into owners’ profit margins. Maga’s regret voters were all-in for Trump’s racism. Then they found out they couldn’t afford it.
Since Trump’s arrival in 2016, political discourse has been dominated by a narrative that the president galvanized particularly white voters whose economic anxiety went ignored by the left and much of the elite political establishment. It wasn’t completely true. Researchers found that status threat anxiety derived from an increasing majority-minority demographic shift also anchored their voting choices. In the 2026 Maga exodus, however, brass-tacks items like affordability, tariffs and rising inflation are consistently top of mind over other concerns.
Through focus groups across hundreds of Trump’s supporters, political consultant and former Republican Sarah Longwell spotted the immediate trend. “The first thing we do is ask people: how do you think things are going in the country?” Longwell said. “And every focus group, every single time, doesn’t matter – whether left, right or center – right now, people say: bad. And then they immediately start talking about the prices of something.” Underlying economic angst even determined the degree of attention and priority regret voters gave to other issues like the Trump family’s corruption. “Everything comes back to people’s relationship to the economy,” Longwell said. “Trump voters and more low-information voters would probably let Trump get away with corruption. In fact, we know they would – he was doing a lot of corrupt things in his first term.”
Maga voters looked past unchecked government corruption and abuses of power until it affected them financially. While voters were magnetized by Trump’s campaign promises to lower prices, the effects of his economic plans worsened affordability for moderate- to low-income Americans and cut $1tn from essential social safety net services like Snap. He simultaneously pushed a unilateral increase in tariffs, which policy wonks and economists insisted had “no basis in economic reality” and would drastically increase the cost of goods.
His pitches to his base two years ago sounded an awful lot like he murmured “lower prices” and barked his priorities to mass-deport immigrants, gut research and diversity initiatives, and wage an all-out war against gender-nonconforming Americans, including children. Trump’s rhetoric that immigrants take American jobs, access social services such as healthcare for free, and are a drag on the economy are tried-and-tested conservative dog-whistle tactics that mask deliberate xenophobia and anti-immigrant violence as a commonsense protection of Americans’ bottom lines. That dog-whistling further conditions those who embrace Maga ideologies to mark racialized groups as threats to the economic resources to which they feel entitled.
At an ICE job fair in Arlington, Texas, on 2 September 2025, an IT specialist named Aaron Ely told a Washington Post reporter that his private-sector career stalled because the job market was crowded with cheaper and higher-skilled south Asian candidates. Maga and ICE’s racial profiling, surveillance and harassment of immigrants provided an easy solution for eliminating the competition. “I keep seeing these memes where Indians are bragging about taking our tech jobs,” said Ely, 36, while explaining his motivations for joining the agency. “Well, I’m going to work with guys that are going to arrest you, slam your face on the pavement, and send you home.” It wasn’t the price of milk, but a chance to milk state-sanctioned racial violence for his personal advantage that drew Ely to Trump’s policies.
But regret voters’ financial motives also provide Democrats a valuable lesson, one that the most successful social movements against the most ironclad regimes learned long ago: economic exigencies transfer power from governments to everyday people. When the anti-apartheid movement strategized their first boycotts in 1959, Black South Africans knew that the white Boer regime that occupied and brutalized them was first and foremost a capitalist enterprise. The human-rights atrocities of apartheid were meaningless to its profit motives. Over the course of 35 years, Black South Africans organized the “Apartheid Kills – Look at the Label” campaign, in which everyday consumers and vendors were asked to boycott products and goods from South Africa. After a union of Black longshoremen in California refused to offload South African cargo in 1984, the boycott electrified globally and turned the Boers into bad business, bringing apartheid to its knees a decade later.
The economic motive behind millions of regret voters’ actions on Tuesday should remind us that what hits their pockets will hit the polls. Targeting the economics behind the politics is echoed in movements today, even those that seem daunting and impossible to win. “I don’t believe that our people power comes from moral arguments,” said Randa Abdel-Fattah, an Australian lawyer and Palestinian human rights advocate. “Black people have proven that to us … It’s about making genocide unprofitable.”
Millions of Americans are fired up by the blue tsunami. It’s the largest and perhaps only comprehensive, nationwide gain many of our collective populist movements for social justice, civil liberties and human-rights causes have seen in a decade that has been a reign of terrorfor us, and just a financial setback for others. Racism, “wokeness” and Islamophobia alone never changed their hearts and minds, nor are they even the main reason they regret their votes. “Hearts and minds” don’t shift balances of power, but power always shifts when it no longer pays.

https://www.aljazeera.com/video/101-east.title: Nepal’s fight to rebuild after flood disaster
https://www.aljazeera.com/video/101-east.text:
101 East
Nepal’s fight to rebuild after flood disaster
101 East reveals Nepal’s efforts to save lives and rebuild communities after a devastating natural disaster.
On the morning of August 26, 2026, a devastating flash flood of rock and ice thundered from a high Himalayan mountain through Nepal’s valleys, sweeping away homes, villages and bridges.
At least 1,400 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing.
It was the latest in a series of natural disasters that have battered Nepal in recent years as climate change accelerates.
This programme follows the rescuers risking their lives to search for the missing and those providing aid and refuge for traumatised children and families.
101 East reveals Nepal’s efforts to save lives and rebuild communities after a deadly natural disaster.
Published On 7 Nov 2026
